Providing backhaul connectivity for macro and pico base stations (BSs)
constitutes a significant share of infrastructure costs in future heterogeneous
networks (HetNets). To address this issue, the emerging idea of flexible
backhaul is proposed. Under this architecture, not all the pico BSs are
connected to the backhaul, resulting in a significant reduction in the
infrastructure costs. In this regard, pico BSs without backhaul connectivity
need to communicate with their nearby BSs in order to have indirect
accessibility to the backhaul. This makes the radio resource management (RRM)
in such networks more complex and challenging. In this paper, we address the
problem of cross-layer RRM in HetNets with flexible backhaul. We formulate this
problem as a two-timescale non-convex stochastic optimization which jointly
optimizes flow control, routing, interference mitigation and link scheduling in
order to maximize a generic network utility. By exploiting a hidden convexity
of this non-convex problem, we propose an iterative algorithm which converges
to the global optimal solution. The proposed algorithm benefits from low
complexity and low signalling, which makes it scalable. Moreover, due to the
proposed two-timescale design, it is robust to the backhaul signalling latency
as well. Simulation results demonstrate the significant performance gain of the
proposed solution over various baselines.

Understanding the exosphere of exoplanets is crucial for comprehending their atmospheric dynamics. This study investigates the constraints on the exosphere of CoRoT-7b, one of the smallest exoplanets known. By analyzing observational data from the CoRoT space telescope and conducting theoretical simulations, we aimed to characterize the composition and structure of CoRoT-7b's exosphere. Our methodology involved numerical modeling of the exosphere using sophisticated algorithms to interpret the data obtained from the observations. The key findings reveal the presence of key molecules such as hydrogen, helium, and heavier elements in the exosphere of CoRoT-7b, shedding light on its atmospheric properties. Additionally, the study provides insights into the temperature distribution and escape mechanisms in the exosphere. These findings contribute to the broader understanding of exoplanetary atmospheres and their evolution. In conclusion, the research enhances the current knowledge of CoRoT-7b's exosphere and paves the way for future studies focusing on similar exoplanetary systems.

We present a study on colloidal analogues mimicking the behavior of charged and uncharged polymer chains with adjustable stiffness. The primary aim of our work is to investigate the impact of stiffness tunability on the self-assembly and structural properties of these colloidal chains. Through experimental observations and simulations, we have identified that the stiffness of the colloidal chains plays a crucial role in determining their conformational and aggregation behavior in solution. Our results reveal that increasing stiffness leads to a more extended conformation for charged colloidal chains, promoting long-range repulsive interactions, while uncharged chains tend to adopt more compact structures due to reduced entropic effects. Furthermore, by manipulating the stiffness, we demonstrate the ability to control the transition of these colloidal analogues between different assembly states, including linear chains, loops, and branched structures. Our study utilizes a combination of microscopy techniques, rheological measurements, and theoretical modeling to elucidate the relationship between stiffness, charge, and self-assembly behavior in colloidal chains. Overall, our work provides valuable insights into the design principles of colloidal systems resembling polymer chains, with implications for the development of advanced materials with tailored properties.

We investigate the potential of asteroseismic methods to constrain the envelope helium abundance in red giant stars, a crucial parameter in understanding the internal structure and evolution of these objects. Through a comprehensive analysis of a large dataset of red giant stars, we demonstrate that asteroseismic frequencies can be used to infer the envelope helium abundance with reasonable accuracy. Our approach involves the application of advanced seismic analysis techniques, including the use of frequency ratios and mode overlap, to extract information on the stellar interior structure.  Our results show that the envelope helium abundance can be reliably determined using asteroseismic frequencies, with an average uncertainty of ±0.02 dex. We also find that the method is robust against various sources of uncertainty, including observational errors and model uncertainties. Our findings suggest that asteroseismic inference of envelope helium abundance in red giant stars can provide a powerful tool for constraining stellar evolution models and testing theoretical predictions.  By combining asteroseismic observations with theoretical models of stellar structure and evolution, we can gain a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics and chemical composition of red giant stars. This, in turn, can inform our understanding of the mass-loss processes that occur during the red giant phase and the subsequent evolution of these stars into white dwarfs. Our work highlights the potential of asteroseismic methods to provide new insights into the internal structure and evolution of red giant stars.

We investigate the magnetorotational instability (MRI) within the framework of debris-disc gas, aiming to elucidate its influence on angular momentum transport and subsequent accretion processes. Our study addresses the unresolved issue of how MRI can trigger turbulence in debris discs, which are characterized by low-density environments, thereby potentially enhancing the efficiency of planetary formation. We employed both linear stability analysis and numerical simulations to explore the conditions under which MRI operates in such low-mass, transient gas environments.   Our results indicate that the presence of weak magnetic fields significantly modulates the stability of the disc, facilitating the onset of turbulence even in regimes previously thought to be non-magnetically dominated. We demonstrate that the growth rates of the instability are sensitive to the gas density and temperature profiles, suggesting that variations in these parameters can significantly alter the disc's dynamical behavior. Additionally, we contribute a novel criterion for identifying MRI viability in debris-disc scenarios, extending current theoretical frameworks.   By integrating magnetohydrodynamic simulations with observational data from young star systems, we highlight the implications of our findings for the efficiency of planetesimal formation and the evolutionary pathways of protoplanetary discs. This work bridges theoretical predictions with astrophysical observations, enriching our understanding of the role of magnetorotational dynamics in debris-disc gas and its broader implications for planetary system development.

The characterisation of ever smaller and fainter extrasolar planets requires
an intricate understanding of one's data and the analysis techniques used.
Correcting the raw data at the 10^-4 level of accuracy in flux is one of the
central challenges. This can be difficult for instruments that do not feature a
calibration plan for such high precision measurements. Here, it is not always
obvious how to de-correlate the data using auxiliary information of the
instrument and it becomes paramount to know how well one can disentangle
instrument systematics from one's data, given nothing but the data itself. We
propose a non-parametric machine learning algorithm, based on the concept of
independent component analysis, to de-convolve the systematic noise and all
non-Gaussian signals from the desired astrophysical signal. Such a `blind'
signal de-mixing is commonly known as the `Cocktail Party problem' in
signal-processing. Given multiple simultaneous observations of the same
exoplanetary eclipse, as in the case of spectrophotometry, we show that we can
often disentangle systematic noise from the original light curve signal without
the use of any complementary information of the instrument. In this paper, we
explore these signal extraction techniques using simulated data and two data
sets observed with the Hubble-NICMOS instrument. Another important application
is the de-correlation of the exoplanetary signal from time-correlated stellar
variability. Using data obtained by the Kepler mission we show that the desired
signal can be de-convolved from the stellar noise using a single time series
spanning several eclipse events. Such non-parametric techniques can provide
important confirmations of the existent parametric corrections reported in the
literature, and their associated results. Additionally they can substantially
improve the precision exoplanetary light curve analysis in the future.

In this research paper, the stability of Cosmic String Y-junctions is investigated. The objective of the study is to analyze the factors influencing the stability of Y-junction configurations in cosmic string networks. The methodology involves numerical simulations using field theory models to study the dynamics of Y-junctions and their evolution over time.   Key findings reveal that the stability of Y-junctions is dependent on various parameters, such as tensions along different segments, angles between strings, and intrinsic properties of the cosmic strings. The study also explores the effects of gravitational interactions on the stability of these Y-junctions.  The results indicate that under certain conditions, Y-junctions in cosmic string networks can exhibit stable configurations over extended periods. However, perturbations in tensions or angles can lead to instability and subsequent reconnection events.   In conclusion, this research provides valuable insights into the stability mechanisms of Cosmic String Y-junctions, shedding light on the complex dynamics of cosmic string networks and their evolution in the cosmic structure. These findings have implications for understanding the role of cosmic strings in the early universe and their potential observational signatures in cosmological phenomena.

Our work investigates variations in the Galactic star formation rate and the density thresholds required for star formation. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis utilizing observational data from various telescopes and theoretical models to understand the complexities of these phenomena. By exploring the correlation between local gas densities and star formation rates across different regions of the Galaxy, we aim to elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving star formation and the conditions necessary for it to occur. Our results reveal significant variations in the star formation rate within the Galaxy, indicating a non-uniform distribution of star-forming regions. Moreover, we have identified varying density thresholds for initiating star formation in different Galactic environments, suggesting the influence of local conditions on the star formation process. Our study also highlights the role of feedback mechanisms and the interplay between gas dynamics and star formation efficiency in shaping the observed trends. The methodology employed in this research combines statistical analysis of observational data with theoretical modeling, providing a comprehensive understanding of the factors governing star formation in the Milky Way. Overall, our findings contribute to the broader field of Galactic astrophysics by shedding light on the intricate relationship between gas properties, density thresholds, and the rate of star formation in our Galaxy.

One of the key challenges in sensor networks is the extraction of information
by fusing data from a multitude of distinct, but possibly unreliable sensors.
Recovering information from the maximum number of dependable sensors while
specifying the unreliable ones is critical for robust sensing. This sensing
task is formulated here as that of finding the maximum number of feasible
subsystems of linear equations, and proved to be NP-hard. Useful links are
established with compressive sampling, which aims at recovering vectors that
are sparse. In contrast, the signals here are not sparse, but give rise to
sparse residuals. Capitalizing on this form of sparsity, four sensing schemes
with complementary strengths are developed. The first scheme is a convex
relaxation of the original problem expressed as a second-order cone program
(SOCP). It is shown that when the involved sensing matrices are Gaussian and
the reliable measurements are sufficiently many, the SOCP can recover the
optimal solution with overwhelming probability. The second scheme is obtained
by replacing the initial objective function with a concave one. The third and
fourth schemes are tailored for noisy sensor data. The noisy case is cast as a
combinatorial problem that is subsequently surrogated by a (weighted) SOCP.
Interestingly, the derived cost functions fall into the framework of robust
multivariate linear regression, while an efficient block-coordinate descent
algorithm is developed for their minimization. The robust sensing capabilities
of all schemes are verified by simulated tests.

Capella is a spectroscopic binary consisting of two G-type giants, where the
primary (G8III) is a normal red-clump giant while the secondary (G0III) is a
chromospherically-active fast rotator showing considerable overabundance of Li
as Li-enhanced giants. Recently, Takeda & Tajitsu (2017) reported that
abundance ratios of specific light elements (e.g., [C/Fe] or [O/Fe]) in Li-rich
giants of high activity tend to be anomalously high, which they suspected to be
nothing but superficial caused by unusual atmospheric structure due to high
activity. Towards verifying this hypothesis, we determined the elemental
abundances of the primary and the secondary of Capella based on the
disentangled spectrum of each component, in order to see whether any apparent
disagreement exists between the two, which should have been formed with the
same chemical composition. We found that the primary is slightly supersolar (by
~+0.1dex) while the secondary is subsolar (by several tenths dex) for heavier
elements such as Fe, resulting in a marked discrepancy between the primary and
secondary, though such a trend is not seen for light elements (e.g., C or O).
These observational facts suggest that anomalously large [X/Fe] ratios found in
Li-rich giants were mainly due to an apparent decrease of Fe abundance, which
we speculate is caused by the overionization effect due to chromospheric UV
radiation. We thus conclude that conventional model atmosphere analysis would
fail to correctly determine the abundances of fast-rotating giants of high
activity, for which proper treatment of chromospheric effect is required for
deriving true photospheric abundances.

Temporal action detection is a very important yet challenging problem, since
videos in real applications are usually long, untrimmed and contain multiple
action instances. This problem requires not only recognizing action categories
but also detecting start time and end time of each action instance. Many
state-of-the-art methods adopt the "detection by classification" framework:
first do proposal, and then classify proposals. The main drawback of this
framework is that the boundaries of action instance proposals have been fixed
during the classification step. To address this issue, we propose a novel
Single Shot Action Detector (SSAD) network based on 1D temporal convolutional
layers to skip the proposal generation step via directly detecting action
instances in untrimmed video. On pursuit of designing a particular SSAD network
that can work effectively for temporal action detection, we empirically search
for the best network architecture of SSAD due to lacking existing models that
can be directly adopted. Moreover, we investigate into input feature types and
fusion strategies to further improve detection accuracy. We conduct extensive
experiments on two challenging datasets: THUMOS 2014 and MEXaction2. When
setting Intersection-over-Union threshold to 0.5 during evaluation, SSAD
significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art systems by increasing mAP from
19.0% to 24.6% on THUMOS 2014 and from 7.4% to 11.0% on MEXaction2.

Our study focuses on the strategic deployment of multiple aerial base stations to facilitate traffic offloading and network recovery in dynamic environments. The primary concern addressed is the efficient allocation of aerial resources to manage varying traffic demands and to enhance network resilience in the event of outages. We present a novel on-demand deployment approach that leverages the mobility and adaptability of aerial base stations to mitigate congestion and improve service continuity.  Through simulation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed strategy in distributing aerial base stations dynamically based on real-time traffic patterns and network conditions. Results show a significant reduction in network congestion levels and improved service availability during network failures compared to static deployment schemes. Our methodology integrates algorithms for optimal base station placement, trajectory planning, and resource allocation to achieve seamless coverage and efficient data offloading.  This research contributes to the emerging field of aerial networking by offering a scalable solution for enhancing network performance in scenarios with fluctuating demand and network disruptions. By leveraging the agility of aerial base stations, our approach enables on-the-fly adjustments to cope with changing traffic dynamics and maintain service quality.

Medicines exist for combating illnesses and drug stores provide an outlet for
consumers to gain access to these drugs. However, due to various factors such
as cost of production, accessibility and legal issues as well as distribution
factors, availability of these drugs at any location cannot be guaranteed at
all times. There is need for individuals and organizations such as hospitals to
be able to locate required drugs within given geographical vicinity. This is of
immense importance especially during emergencies, travel, and in cases where
the drugs are uncommon. This research work is aimed at solving this problem by
designing a system that integrates all drugstores. The integration of the drug
stores will be based on SOA concepts with web services via a central service
bus. The database systems of the drug stores will be integrated via a service
bus such that drugs can easily be searched for and the results will be
displayed based on its availability. Drugs can easily be searched for within
geographically distributed pharmaceutical databases as well as consumption of
drugs with relation to geographical locations can easily be monitored and
tracked. This will make it easy for health institutions to research on drug
consumption patterns across geographical areas and also control their usage.

In this study, we explore the observational signatures of past mass-exchange episodes in massive binaries, with a focus on the specific case of LSS 3074. Our research aims to unravel the complexities of mass transfer between massive stars in binary systems and understand how these interactions manifest in observational data. By analyzing the properties of LSS 3074, we aim to decipher the history of mass exchange events that have occurred within this system.   Our results reveal distinctive features in the spectra and light curves of LSS 3074 that can be attributed to past mass-transfer processes. Through a detailed examination of the available observational data, including radial velocities, temperature variations, and luminosity changes, we identify key indicators of past mass exchange events in this binary system.   To achieve these findings, we employ a combination of theoretical modeling and observational analysis, utilizing state-of-the-art techniques to interpret the data. Our work sheds light on the evolution of massive binaries and provides insights into the consequences of past mass-transfer episodes on the current properties of these systems. By investigating the case of LSS 3074, we contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of massive binary stars and the observational consequences of their evolutionary histories.

This study examines the universal characteristics of fractal fluctuations in global mean monthly temperature anomalies. The primary objective was to identify and quantify these characteristics through empirical analysis, providing insights into the temporal dynamics of temperature variability. Utilizing long-term temperature datasets from multiple global sources, including NASA GISS and NOAA GHCN, the methodology involved time series analysis and multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MF-DFA) to detect scaling properties indicative of fractal behavior.  Key findings revealed that the global mean monthly temperature anomalies exhibit multifractal scaling, with distinct scaling exponents across different scales, indicating complex and non-stationary fluctuations. These results suggest that temperature variations are not solely random but follow a specific hierarchical structure, which can be attributed to underlying physical processes and climate dynamics. The study also identified that the multifractal nature of temperature anomalies persists over varying temporal scales, supporting the notion that global warming is reflected in both short-term and long-term fluctuations.  In conclusion, this research underscores the utility of multifractal analysis in understanding the complex and evolving nature of temperature fluctuations. The findings contribute to our comprehension of climate variability and provide robust evidence for the existence of universal fractal characteristics in global temperature anomalies, offering valuable implications for climate modeling and predictive studies.

Clustering transformed compositional data is a crucial step in various fields like gene expression analysis and bicycle sharing systems. Compositional data, representing proportions of different parts of a whole, pose challenges due to their constrained nature and constant sum constraint.   This research aims to apply K-means clustering to transformed compositional data to uncover underlying patterns in gene expression and bicycle sharing system datasets, facilitating meaningful insights and decision-making.   The study proposes a novel approach using log-ratio transformations to handle compositional data in K-means clustering. By transforming the data, we aim to mitigate issues like spurious clusters and interpret the results effectively. The methodology is applied to both gene expression data and bicycle sharing system data to demonstrate its effectiveness and versatility.   Our results show that applying K-means clustering to transformed compositional data yields meaningful clusters that reflect biologically relevant gene expression patterns and distinct user behavior in bicycle sharing systems. The log-ratio transformation proves to be a valuable technique in enhancing clustering performance and interpretability.   This research contributes to the field by providing a robust methodology for clustering transformed compositional data using K-means, offering valuable insights in gene expression analysis and improving decision-making processes in managing bicycle sharing systems. The findings underscore the importance of appropriate data transformation in handling compositional data for clustering analysis.

This study explores the integration of Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) into heterogeneous networks (HetNets) to enhance resource utilization, reduce latency, and improve network efficiency. MEC introduces computational resources closer to users, enabling real-time processing of data closer to the source rather than relying solely on cloud servers. The objective of this research is to evaluate the performance improvements achieved by deploying MEC in HetNets compared to traditional centralized architectures. To achieve this, we employed a combination of simulation models and experimental setups that mimic real-world HetNet environments with varying densities of base stations and user distributions. Key findings indicate that MEC significantly reduces end-to-end latency and enhances service quality, particularly in scenarios where high data rates and low-latency requirements are critical. Additionally, the study reveals that optimal placement of MEC nodes can further optimize network performance by balancing resource utilization across different tiers of the network. The conclusion suggests that integrating MEC into HetNets represents a promising approach for addressing the challenges posed by the increasing demand for bandwidth-intensive services and stringent latency requirements in modern communication systems.

In protoplanetary disks, the inner radial boundary between the MRI turbulent
(`active') and MRI quiescent (`dead') zones plays an important role in models
of the disk evolution and in some planet formation scenarios. In reality, this
boundary is not well-defined: thermal heating from the star in a passive disk
yields a transition radius close to the star (<0.1 au), whereas if the disk is
already MRI active, it can self-consistently maintain the requisite
temperatures out to a transition radius of roughly 1 au. Moreover, the
interface may not be static; it may be highly fluctuating or else unstable. In
this paper, we study a reduced model of the dynamics of the active/dead zone
interface that mimics several important aspects of a real disk system. We find
that MRI-transition fronts propagate inward (a `dead front' suppressing the
MRI) if they are initially at the larger transition radius, or propagate
outward (an `active front' igniting the MRI) if starting from the smaller
transition radius. In both cases, the front stalls at a well-defined
intermediate radius, where it remains in a quasi-static equilibrium. We propose
that it is this new, intermediate stalling radius that functions as the true
boundary between the active and dead zones in protoplanetary disks. These
dynamics are likely implicated in observations of variable accretion, such as
FU Ori outbursts, as well as in those planet formation theories that require
the accumulation of solid material at the dead/active interface.

We investigated the role of centrality in identifying influential spreaders in complex networks, with a focus on the dynamic spread of information and opinions. Through a comprehensive analysis of various network structures and datasets, we observed that traditional centrality measures, such as degree centrality and closeness centrality, are not sufficient to capture the influence of spreaders in complex networks. Instead, we proposed a novel centrality measure, called "influence centrality," which incorporates the spread of information and opinions into the calculation of node influence.  Our results show that influence centrality outperforms traditional centrality measures in identifying influential spreaders, particularly in networks with complex structures and dynamic interactions. We also found that influence centrality is sensitive to the spread of information and opinions, and that it can capture the emergence of influential spreaders in the early stages of the spread process. Furthermore, we demonstrated that influence centrality can be used to identify clusters of influential spreaders, which can have significant implications for understanding the dynamics of information diffusion and opinion formation.  By developing and validating a novel centrality measure, we provide a new framework for identifying influential spreaders in complex networks. Our findings have implications for a wide range of fields, including social network analysis, information diffusion, and opinion formation, and suggest that influence centrality may be a powerful tool for understanding the dynamics of complex systems.

Three algorithms are developed for uncertainty quantification in modeling
coupled Stokes and Darcy flows. The porous media may consist of multiple
regions with different properties. The permeability is modeled as a
non-stationary stochastic variable, with its log represented as a sum of local
Karhunen-Lo\`eve (KL) expansions. The problem is approximated by stochastic
collocation on either tensor-product or sparse grids, coupled with a multiscale
mortar mixed finite element method for the spatial discretization. A
non-overlapping domain decomposition algorithm reduces the global problem to a
coarse scale mortar interface problem, which is solved by an iterative solver,
for each stochastic realization. In the traditional implementation, each
subdomain solves a local Dirichlet or Neumann problem in every interface
iteration. To reduce this cost, two additional algorithms based on
deterministic or stochastic multiscale flux basis are introduced. The basis
consists of the local flux (or velocity trace) responses from each mortar
degree of freedom. It is computed by each subdomain independently before the
interface iteration begins. The use of the multiscale flux basis avoids the
need for subdomain solves on each iteration. The deterministic basis is
computed at each stochastic collocation and used only at this realization. The
stochastic basis is formed by further looping over all local realizations of a
subdomain's KL region before the stochastic collocation begins. It is reused
over multiple realizations. Numerical tests are presented to illustrate the
performance of the three algorithms, with the stochastic multiscale flux basis
showing significant savings in computational cost.

Codon bias, a phenomenon where certain synonymous codons are preferred over others in gene sequences, has been extensively analyzed in various organisms, including $Escherichia coli$. The objective of this study is to investigate the codon bias patterns of $E. coli$ proteins that engage in physical interactions, positing that these patterns may illuminate underlying evolutionary pressures and functional constraints. Using a curated dataset of protein-protein interactions within $E. coli$, codon usage was quantitatively assessed for associated genes. The methodology involved computational analysis to calculate the relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) values and identify patterns correlating with protein interaction networks. Statistical analyses, including principal component analysis (PCA), were applied to distinguish codon bias trends among interacting partners versus non-interacting proteins. Our findings reveal a significant correlation between codon bias and protein interaction, with interacting proteins exhibiting a higher degree of codon optimization. Additionally, certain synonymous codons were consistently favored in genes encoding for central hub proteins in interaction networks, suggesting a selection pressure towards translational efficiency and accuracy due to their critical functional roles. The study concludes that codon bias in $E. coli$ is not merely a neutral feature but is intricately linked to protein interaction networks. These insights advance our understanding of molecular evolution in prokaryotic systems, establishing a foundation for further studies on the impact of codon usage on protein synthesis and cellular functionality. Such knowledge could have implications for synthetic biology applications where codon optimization is leveraged for enhanced expression of recombinant proteins.

Magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their potential applications in spintronics, including spin-based data storage devices and spin-transfer torque magnetic recording. The behavior of ballistic spin currents and torques in MTJs is crucial to understanding the underlying mechanisms of these devices. In this study, we present an analytical description of ballistic spin currents and torques in MTJs, focusing on the role of spin polarization and the impact of scattering mechanisms on spin transport.  Our analysis reveals that the spin polarization of the ferromagnetic free layer is a critical factor in determining the magnitude and direction of the ballistic spin currents. We demonstrate that the spin polarization can be influenced by the scattering mechanisms, such as spin scattering and phonon scattering, which can lead to the formation of spin-polarized currents. Furthermore, we show that the spin torque, which is essential for spin-transfer torque magnetic recording, is influenced by the spin polarization and the scattering mechanisms.  Our results indicate that the ballistic spin currents and torques in MTJs are highly dependent on the spin polarization and scattering mechanisms. We also demonstrate that the analytical description of these phenomena can be used to design and optimize MTJs for specific applications. The findings of this study provide a fundamental understanding of the behavior of ballistic spin currents and torques in MTJs, which is essential for the development of spintronics devices.

In this galaxy-wide study of NGC 300, we investigate the emission of dust from various cloud complexes. The primary objective was to understand the distribution, temperature, and kinematics of these dust clouds, which are crucial for understanding star formation processes. We employed a combination of near-infrared spectroscopy and imaging data to map the dust emission across different regions of the galaxy. Our methodology involved cross-correlation between spectral lines and continuum emission maps to derive temperature and velocity information for each dust cloud complex. The results revealed distinct patterns of dust heating and cooling, indicating the presence of both cold and warm dust components. Key findings include a correlation between high-density molecular gas and warmer dust temperatures, suggesting a direct link between dense regions and enhanced star formation activity. This study not only enhances our understanding of galactic structure but also provides insights into the interplay between dust and gas in forming stars within NGC 300.

We present Lya and UV-nebular emission line properties of bright Lya emitters
(LAEs) at z=6-7 with a luminosity of log L_Lya/[erg s-1] = 43-44 identified in
the 21-deg2 area of the SILVERRUSH early sample developed with the Subaru Hyper
Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey data. Our optical spectroscopy newly confirm 21 bright
LAEs with clear Lya emission, and contribute to make a spectroscopic sample of
96 LAEs at z=6-7 in SILVERRUSH. From the spectroscopic sample, we select 7
remarkable LAEs as bright as Himiko and CR7 objects, and perform deep
Keck/MOSFIRE and Subaru/nuMOIRCS near-infrared spectroscopy reaching the
3sigma-flux limit of ~ 2x10^{-18} erg s-1 for the UV-nebular emission lines of
He II1640, C IV1548,1550, and O III]1661,1666. Except for one tentative
detection of C IV, we find no strong UV-nebular lines down to the flux limit,
placing the upper limits of the rest-frame equivalent widths (EW_0) of ~2-4 A
for He II, C IV, and O III] lines. Here we also investigate the VLT/X-SHOOTER
spectrum of CR7 whose 6 sigma detection of He II is claimed by Sobral et al.
Although two individuals and the ESO-archive service carefully re-analyze the
X-SHOOTER data that are used in the study of Sobral et al., no He II signal of
CR7 is detected, supportive of weak UV-nebular lines of the bright LAEs even
for CR7. Spectral properties of these bright LAEs are thus clearly different
from those of faint dropouts at z~7 that have strong UV-nebular lines shown in
the various studies. Comparing these bright LAEs and the faint dropouts, we
find anti-correlations between the UV-nebular line EW_0 and UV-continuum
luminosity, which are similar to those found at z~2-3.

In this study, we present new observations of the ionized gas component in the Scutum spiral arm, utilizing the [N II] 658.3 nm and [C II] 657.3 nm emission lines. By mapping the distribution of these emission lines across a 3° sector of the Scutum arm, we provide a comprehensive view of the ionized gas content and its relation to star-forming regions. We identify several H II regions, which exhibit strong [N II] emission and are suggested to be in the process of being formed. Additionally, we find evidence for a large-scale, extended [C II] emission feature, which appears to be associated with the Gum 27 molecular cloud complex. Our findings support the model of ionized gas being generated through a combination of photoionization from nearby massive stars and shock ionization from supernova remnants. The [N II]/[C II] ratio, which is sensitive to the ionization parameter, varies significantly across the mapped region. We explore the potential causes for this variability, including variations in the underlying interstellar medium and differences in the ionization conditions within the H II regions and shocked gas. Our results contribute to the understanding of the interstellar medium in the Scutum spiral arm, providing insight into the ionized gas content and its relation to star formation. Future work will focus on mapping additional emission lines and expanding the spatial coverage to further elucidate the complex interplay between ionized gas and star formation in the Milky Way.

Let $(-A,B,C)$ be a linear system in continuous time $t>0$ with input and
output space ${\bf C}$ and state space $H$. The function
$\phi_{(x)}(t)=Ce^{-(t+2x)A}B$ determines a Hankel integral operator
$\Gamma_{\phi_{(x)}}$ on $L^2((0, \infty ); {\bf C})$; if $\Gamma_{\phi_{(x)}}$
is trace class, then the Fredholm determinant $\tau (x)=\det (I+
\Gamma_{\phi_{(x)}})$ defines the tau function of $(-A,B,C)$. Such tau
functions arise in Tracy and Widom's theory of matrix models, where they
describe the fundamental probability distributions of random matrix theory.
Dyson considered such tau functions in the inverse spectral problem for
Schr\"odinger's equation $-f''+uf=\lambda f$, and derived the formula for the
potential $u(x)=-2{{d^2}\over{dx^2}}\log \tau (x)$ in the self-adjoint
scattering case {\sl Commun. Math. Phys.} {\bf 47} (1976), 171--183. This paper
introduces a operator function $R_x$ that satisfies Lyapunov's equation
${{dR_x}\over{dx}}=-AR_x-R_xA$ and $\tau (x)=\det (I+R_x)$, without assumptions
of self-adjointness. When $-A$ is sectorial, and $B,C$ are Hilbert--Schmidt,
there exists a non-commutative differential ring ${\cal A}$ of operators in $H$
and a differential ring homomorphism $\lfloor\,\,\rfloor :{\cal A}\rightarrow
{\bf C}[u,u', \dots ]$ such that $u=-4\lfloor A\rfloor$, which provides a
substitute for the multiplication rules for Hankel operators considered by
P\"oppe, and McKean {\sl Cent. Eur. J. Math.} {\bf 9} (2011), 205--243. The
paper obtains conditions on $(-A,B,C)$ for Schr\"odinger's equation with
meromorphic $u$ to be integrable by quadratures. Special results apply to the
linear systems associated with scattering $u$, periodic $u$ and elliptic $u$.
The paper constructs a family of solutions to the Kadomtsev--Petviashivili
differential equations, and proves that certain families of tau functions
satisfy Fay's identities.\par

Visualization of thermal counterflow in He II using PIV (particle image
velocimetry) and PTV (particle tracking velocimetry) is difficult because
tracer particle motion can be influenced by both the normal fluid and
superfluid components of He II as well as the quantized vortex tangle. For
instance, an early PTV experiment observed particles moving at the normal fluid
velocity $v_n$, while a PIV experiment observed particles moving at $v_n/2$,
though the range of heat flux applied in these experiments differed by an order
of magnitude. To resolve this apparent discrepancy and explore statistics of
particle motion in thermal counterflow, we have applied PTV to a wide range of
heat flux at several fluid temperatures. We introduce a scheme for analyzing
the velocity of particles presumably moving with the normal fluid separately
from those presumably influenced by the vortex tangle. Our results show two
distinct peaks in the streamwise particle velocity PDF (probability density
function) for lower heat flux, one centered at the normal fluid velocity $v_n$
("G2") and one near $v_n/2$ ("G1"). For higher heat flux there is a single peak
centered near $v_n/2$ ("G3"). Using our separation scheme we show there is no
size difference between particles contributing to G1 and G2. We also show that
non-classical features of the transverse velocity PDF arise entirely from G1,
while the corresponding PDF for G2 exhibits classical Gaussian form. G2
transverse velocity fluctuation, backed up by second sound attenuation in
decaying counterflow, suggests large scale turbulence in the normal fluid is
absent from the two peak region. We offer a brief discussion of physical
mechanisms that may be responsible for our observations, revealing that G1
velocity fluctuations may be linked to fluctuations of vortex line velocity,
and suggest numerical simulations that may reveal underlying physics in detail.

Context. The companions of the exploding carbon-oxygen white dwarfs (CO WDs)
for producing type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are still not conclusively confirmed.
A red-giant (RG) star has been suggested to be the mass donor of the exploding
WD, named as the symbiotic channel. However, previous studies on the this
channel gave a relatively low rate of SNe Ia. Aims. We aim to systematically
investigate the parameter space, Galactic rates and delay time distributions of
SNe Ia from the symbiotic channel by employing a revised mass-transfer
prescription. Methods. We adopted an integrated mass-transfer prescription to
calculate the mass-transfer process from a RG star onto the WD. In this
prescription, the mass-transfer rate varies with the local material states.
Results. We evolved a large number of WD+RG systems, and found that the
parameter space of WD+RG systems for producing SNe Ia is significantly
enlarged. This channel could produce SNe Ia with intermediate and old ages,
contributing to at most 5% of all SNe Ia in the Galaxy. Our model increases the
SN Ia rate from this channel by a factor of 5. We suggest that the symbiotic
systems RS Oph and T CrB are strong candidates for the progenitors of SNe Ia.

We investigate the instantaneous mean-variance hedging strategy and instantaneous Sharpe ratio pricing within a regime-switching financial model, with a specific focus on equity-linked claims. Our study addresses the problem of optimizing hedging and pricing decisions under a model where the market environment fluctuates between different regimes. By incorporating regime-switching dynamics, we aim to enhance the effectiveness of risk management strategies for equity-linked claims.  Our results demonstrate that the instantaneous mean-variance hedging approach provides improved risk management compared to traditional methods, especially in volatile market conditions. Additionally, by considering the instantaneous Sharpe ratio, we enhance pricing accuracy and profitability for equity-linked claims.  Key ideas explored include the utilization of regime-switching models to capture market dynamics, the integration of mean-variance optimization for hedging, and the incorporation of the Sharpe ratio for pricing.  Methodologically, we utilize advanced mathematical tools, stochastic calculus, and optimization techniques to derive analytical results and numerical simulations that illustrate the efficacy of the proposed strategies. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of risk management and pricing techniques in finance, particularly in the context of regime-switching models and equity-linked claims.

This paper explores the implementation of a new computational tool, specifically designed for generating permutation groups and topological groups. The background of the study is rooted in the significance of these groups in mathematics, particularly in areas of algebra, geometry, and topology. The objective of this research is to present the features, functionality, and performance evaluation of the proposed tool.   The tool, named 'PermTop,' was developed using a combination of programming languages (Python and C++) and existing open-source libraries. It utilizes various algorithms for generating permutation groups and topological groups, such as the Reideme-Schreier algorithm, the Johnson-Tilley algorithm, and the Nerve Theorem.   PermTop was found to outperform existing tools in generating permutation groups and topological groups, especially for large datasets. The implementation of the algorithms in C++ allowed for faster computation times, and the use of Python for user interface and data visualization provided an intuitive and interactive user experience.   In conclusion, this paper showcases the development and implementation of PermTop, a new computational tool designed for generating permutation groups and topological groups. PermTop's superior performance and user-friendly interface make it a valuable addition to the mathematical toolkit of researchers in algebra, geometry, and topology. The tool and its source code are made publicly available for use and further development.

Popularity of content in social media is unequally distributed, with some
items receiving a disproportionate share of attention from users. Predicting
which newly-submitted items will become popular is critically important for
both hosts of social media content and its consumers. Accurate and timely
prediction would enable hosts to maximize revenue through differential pricing
for access to content or ad placement. Prediction would also give consumers an
important tool for filtering the ever-growing amount of content. Predicting
popularity of content in social media, however, is challenging due to the
complex interactions between content quality and how the social media site
chooses to highlight content. Moreover, most social media sites also
selectively present content that has been highly rated by similar users, whose
similarity is indicated implicitly by their behavior or explicitly by links in
a social network. While these factors make it difficult to predict popularity
\emph{a priori}, we show that stochastic models of user behavior on these sites
allows predicting popularity based on early user reactions to new content. By
incorporating the various mechanisms through which web sites display content,
such models improve on predictions based on simply extrapolating from the early
votes. Using data from one such site, the news aggregator Digg, we show how a
stochastic model of user behavior distinguishes the effect of the increased
visibility due to the network from how interested users are in the content. We
find a wide range of interest, identifying stories primarily of interest to
users in the network (``niche interests'') from those of more general interest
to the user community. This distinction is useful for predicting a story's
eventual popularity from users' early reactions to the story.

This study resolves a discrepancy in the abundance of Zr in the 47 Tucanae
asymptotic giant branch star Lee 2525. This star was observed using the echelle
spectrograph on the 2.3 m telescope at Siding Spring Observatory. The analysis
was undertaken by calibrating Lee 2525 with respect to the standard giant star
Arcturus. This work emphasises the importance of using a standard star with
stellar parameters comparable to the star under analysis rather than a
calibration with respect to the Sun (Koch & McWilliam 2008). Systematic errors
in the analysis process are then minimised due to the similarity in atmospheric
structure between the standard and programme stars. The abundances derived for
Lee 2525 were found to be in general agreement with the Brown & Wallerstein
(1992) values except for Zr. In this study Zr has a similar enhancement
([Zr/Fe] = +0.51 dex) to another light s-process element, Y ([Y/Fe] = +0.53
dex), which reflects current theory regarding the enrichment of s-process
elements by nuclear processes within AGB stars (Busso et al. 2001). This is
contrary to the results of Brown & Wallerstein (1992) where Zr was
under-abundant ([Zr/Fe] = +0.51 dex) and Y was over-abundant ([Y/Fe] = +0.50
dex) with respect to Fe.

We discuss two ways in which one can study two-charge supertubes as
components of generic three-charge, three-dipole charge supergravity solutions.
The first is using the Born-Infeld action of the supertubes, and the second is
via the complete supergravity solution. Even though the Born-Infeld description
is only a probe approximation, we find that it gives exactly the same essential
physics as the complete supergravity solution. Since supertubes can depend on
arbitrary functions, our analysis strengthens the evidence for the existence of
three-charge black-hole microstate geometries that depend on an infinite set of
parameters, and sets the stage for the computation of the entropy of these
backgrounds. We examine numerous other aspects of supertubes in three-charge,
three-dipole charge supergravity backgrounds, including chronology protection
during mergers, the contribution of supertubes to the charges and angular
momenta, and the enhancement of their entropy. In particular, we find that
entropy enhancement affects supertube fluctuations both along the internal and
the spacetime directions, and we prove that the charges that give the enhanced
entropy can be much larger than the asymptotic charges of the solution. We also
re-examine the embedding of five-dimensional black rings in Taub-NUT, and show
that in different coordinate patches a ring can correspond to different
four-dimensional black holes. Last, but not least, we show that all the
three-charge black hole microstate geometries constructed so far can be
embedded in AdS_3 x S^3, and hence can be related to states of the D1-D5 CFT.

In this work, we present a novel approach to the deterministic truncation of linear matroids, addressing the challenge of efficiently reducing matroid rank while preserving essential combinatorial properties. Our principal objective is to formulate an algorithmic framework that systematically truncates a given linear matroid, achieving a predetermined rank threshold without compromising its structural integrity. We develop an innovative method leveraging properties of matrix representations of matroids, allowing for a deterministic pathway to truncate without reliance on probabilistic techniques often employed in previous approaches.   Our methodology involves the strategic selection and removal of elements based on their contribution to circuit rank increments, guided by comprehensive algebraic criteria derived from matroid theory. The results demonstrate that our deterministic truncation process maintains core properties such as independence and circuit dependencies, asserting the efficacy of our approach on both theoretical and practical fronts. We validate our model through extensive computational experiments, illustrating robustness in maintaining span and bases structure across various matroid sizes and configurations.  Moreover, our findings contribute to an advanced understanding of linear matroid manipulation, providing insights with implications for related optimization problems and computational efficiency in discrete mathematics. The deterministic methodology we propose not only enhances current truncation techniques but also opens new avenues for future research in matroid theory and its applications, particularly in areas requiring exacting control over rank modification processes.

We investigate the geometric and analytical properties of CMC (constant mean curvature) hypersurfaces of semi-Riemannian groups, a class of Riemannian manifolds that generalizes the concept of Lie groups. Our approach involves the use of the Bonnet-Myers theorem, which establishes a connection between the mean curvature and the sectional curvature of a hypersurface. We derive a new characterization of CMC hypersurfaces of semi-Riemannian groups, based on the relationship between the mean curvature and the sectional curvature of the ambient manifold.  Through a series of calculations and manipulations, we show that a hypersurface of a semi-Riemannian group is CMC if and only if its mean curvature is constant and the sectional curvature of the ambient manifold is non-negative. We also establish a relationship between the mean curvature of the hypersurface and the Killing vector fields of the ambient manifold, which provides a new tool for the study of CMC hypersurfaces.  Our work provides a significant contribution to the theory of semi-Riemannian groups and CMC hypersurfaces, and has implications for the study of geometric structures on manifolds. The results obtained in this paper can be used to classify CMC hypersurfaces of semi-Riemannian groups and to study their geometric and analytical properties.

In this study, we explore the ordering and criticality in an underscreened Kondo chain by employing a combination of analytical and numerical methods to investigate its quantum and thermodynamic properties. The underscreened Kondo model serves as an intriguing paradigm for understanding anomalous magnetic behavior in correlated electron systems. We attempt to address unresolved questions regarding the competition between ferromagnetic RKKY interactions and Kondo screening in this system. Our results reveal a distinctive phase characterized by partial Kondo screening, wherein the effective magnetic moments remain at non-zero values down to zero temperature. This indicates a novel form of quantum criticality, distinct from both the conventional Kondo and RKKY regimes. Employing density matrix renormalization group techniques, we find evidence of ferromagnetic ground state order, coexisting with critical fluctuations suggestive of a quantum critical point. The observed emergent behavior diverges from expectations based on fully screened or unscreened models. Further insight is gained by developing an effective field theory that captures the complex interplay between the local Kondo screening clouds and the collective magnetic excitations along the chain. Our work underscores the importance of the underscreened Kondo model in elucidating the interplay of magnetism and strong correlations in low-dimensional systems and suggests potential for experimental validation. These findings contribute to the broader understanding of non-Fermi liquid behavior and quantum magnetism, emphasizing the pivotal role of partial screening in shaping the low-energy physics of Kondo systems.

Existing methods for interactive image retrieval have demonstrated the merit
of integrating user feedback, improving retrieval results. However, most
current systems rely on restricted forms of user feedback, such as binary
relevance responses, or feedback based on a fixed set of relative attributes,
which limits their impact. In this paper, we introduce a new approach to
interactive image search that enables users to provide feedback via natural
language, allowing for more natural and effective interaction. We formulate the
task of dialog-based interactive image retrieval as a reinforcement learning
problem, and reward the dialog system for improving the rank of the target
image during each dialog turn. To mitigate the cumbersome and costly process of
collecting human-machine conversations as the dialog system learns, we train
our system with a user simulator, which is itself trained to describe the
differences between target and candidate images. The efficacy of our approach
is demonstrated in a footwear retrieval application. Experiments on both
simulated and real-world data show that 1) our proposed learning framework
achieves better accuracy than other supervised and reinforcement learning
baselines and 2) user feedback based on natural language rather than
pre-specified attributes leads to more effective retrieval results, and a more
natural and expressive communication interface.

This study examines the variable stars located within the globular cluster M28 (NGC 6626) to enhance our understanding of stellar evolution and dynamics in dense stellar environments. The primary objective was to identify and classify variable star types present in M28, and to investigate their potential relationship with the cluster’s overall properties such as age, metallicity, and stellar interaction. Utilizing data from time-series photometry obtained through high-precision light curves, alongside archival data from space telescopes, we systematically analyzed over 2000 stars in the cluster.   Our findings included the discovery of 15 new variable stars, contributing to a total of 35 confirmed variable star candidates within M28, which include RR Lyrae and Cepheid types. The detected variability was correlated with stellar population characteristics, revealing a predominance of pulsating variables typical of older stellar populations. Additionally, we noted an interesting trend suggesting that the cluster's central concentration and dynamic interactions may influence the parameters of these variable stars.   In conclusion, our results underscore the significance of M28 as an astrophysical laboratory for studying the impact of stellar density on the evolutionary pathways of variable stars. We encourage further investigations to explore implications for the understanding of globular cluster formation, structure, and evolution, expanding the current knowledge of variable stars in globular clusters across the galaxy.

We present a theoretical framework for formal study of systematic effects in
Supernovae Type Ia (SN Ia) that utilizes 2-d simulations to implement a form of
the deflagration-detonation transition (DDT) explosion scenario. The framework
is developed from a randomized initial condition that leads to a sample of
simulated SN Ia whose Ni56 masses have a similar average and range to those
observed, and have many other modestly realistic features such as the velocity
extent of intermediate mass elements. The intended purpose is to enable
statistically well-defined studies of both physical and theoretical parameters
of the SN Ia explosion simulation. We present here a thorough description of
the outcome of the SN Ia explosions produced by our current simulations. A
first application of this framework is utilized to study the dependence of the
SN Ia on the Ne22 content, which is known to be directly influenced by the
progenitor stellar population's metallicity. Our study is very specifically
tailored to measure how the Ne22 content influences the competition between the
rise of plumes of burned material and the expansion of the star before these
plumes reach DDT conditions. This competition controls the amount of material
in nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) and therefore Ni56 produced by setting
the density at which nucleosynthesis takes place during the detonation phase of
the explosion. Although the outcome following from any particular ignition
condition can change dramatically with Ne22 content, with a sample of 20
ignition conditions we find that the systematic change in the expansion of the
star prior to detonation is not large enough to compete with the dependence on
initial neutron excess discussed by Timmes, Brown & Truran (2003). (Abridged)

Relativistic jets are ubiquitous in astrophysical systems that contain
compact objects. They transport large amounts of energy to large distances from
the source, and their interaction with the ambient medium has a crucial effect
on the evolution of the system. The propagation of the jet is characterized by
the formation of a shocked "head" at the front of the jet which dissipates the
jet's energy and a cocoon that surrounds the jet and potentially collimates it.
We present here a self consistent, analytic model that follows the evolution of
the jet and its cocoon, and describes their interaction. We show that the
critical parameter that determines the properties of the jet-cocoon system is
the dimensionless ratio between the jet's energy density and the rest-mass
energy density of the ambient medium. This parameter, together with the jet's
injection angle, also determines whether the jet is collimated by the cocoon or
not. The model is applicable to relativistic, unmagnetized, jets on all scales
and may be used to determine the conditions in AGNs jets as well as in GRBs or
microquasars. It shows that AGN and microquasar jets are hydrodynamically
collimated due to the interaction with the ambient medium, while GRB jets can
be collimated only inside a star and become uncollimated once they breakout.

Lead user driven innovation and open innovation paradigms seek to involve
consumers and common people to innovative product development projects. In
order to help developers choose ideas that meet the end users' needs, we
undertook a massive collaborative research effort and collected 40000 ideas
from 2150 common people about future mobile services that they would like to
use. We inspired each people to produce tens of mobile service ideas. In this
paper we carry out an analysis for 4000 ideas from the idea database. We had a
particular interest in whether peoples' ideas can be used in foreseeing the
technology development needs. The results show that end users produce ideas
that are conservative more than novel. Therefore, we claim that consumers'
technology foresight horizon is limited by the existing technological base. The
second finding, linked to the previous one, is that the great majority of the
ideas that consumers expressed could be realised utilizing existing
technologies. The implication of this finding is that the idea database should
be an interesting source of ideas for service developers. The third finding of
the study, related to the methodology, is that a vast number of ideas can be
collected fairly easily but analyzing them cost effectively is a challenge.

We investigate the Hubbard interactions in iron-based pnictides and chalcogenides utilizing the Slater parametrization to elucidate the complex interplay of electronic correlations in these systems. Our study addresses the inadequacies of simplistic interaction models by incorporating comprehensive screening channels and examining the frequency dependence of these interactions. We apply a combination of first-principles calculations and many-body theoretical approaches to evaluate the screened Coulomb interactions, allowing us to derive the effective Hubbard parameters with improved accuracy. By systematically analyzing the frequency-dependent behavior, we unveil the prominent screening mechanisms that play pivotal roles in these materials. Our results reveal that the dynamic screening significantly affects the strength and anisotropy of the interaction parameters across different atomic orbitals. These findings have profound implications for the theoretical understanding of superconductivity and magnetism in iron-based compounds, demonstrating that the interplay of frequency-dependent screening channels critically influences their emergent properties. We further compare our findings to experimental data, achieving a consistent description of the electronic structure and response functions. Our rigorous methodology paves the way for future studies on the electronic correlations in multifaceted systems, highlighting the necessity for incorporating detailed interaction models that transcend traditional static approximations. Ultimately, our work advances the field by offering a robust framework to better understand and predict the behavior of complex superconducting and magnetic materials, potentially guiding the design of novel compounds with optimal properties.

We consider a problem of supplying electricity to a set of $\mathcal{N}$
customers in a smart-grid framework. Each customer requires a certain amount of
electrical energy which has to be supplied during the time interval $[0,1]$. We
assume that each demand has to be supplied without interruption, with possible
duration between $\ell$ and $r$, which are given system parameters ($\ell\le
r$). At each moment of time, the power of the grid is the sum of all the
consumption rates for the demands being supplied at that moment. Our goal is to
find an assignment that minimizes the {\it power peak} - maximal power over
$[0,1]$ - while satisfying all the demands. To do this first we find the lower
bound of optimal power peak. We show that the problem depends on whether or not
the pair $\ell, r$ belongs to a "good" region $\mathcal{G}$. If it does - then
an optimal assignment almost perfectly "fills" the rectangle $time \times power
= [0,1] \times [0, A]$ with $A$ being the sum of all the energy demands - thus
achieving an optimal power peak $A$. Conversely, if $\ell, r$ do not belong to
$\mathcal{G}$, we identify the lower bound $\bar{A} >A$ on the optimal value of
power peak and introduce a simple linear time algorithm that almost perfectly
arranges all the demands in a rectangle $[0, A /\bar{A}] \times [0, \bar{A}]$
and show that it is asymptotically optimal.

Distributed hash tables suffer from several security and privacy
vulnerabilities, including the problem of Sybil attacks. Existing social
network-based solutions to mitigate the Sybil attacks in DHT routing have a
high state requirement and do not provide an adequate level of privacy. For
instance, such techniques require a user to reveal their social network
contacts. We design X-Vine, a protection mechanism for distributed hash tables
that operates entirely by communicating over social network links. As with
traditional peer-to-peer systems, X-Vine provides robustness, scalability, and
a platform for innovation. The use of social network links for communication
helps protect participant privacy and adds a new dimension of trust absent from
previous designs. X-Vine is resilient to denial of service via Sybil attacks,
and in fact is the first Sybil defense that requires only a logarithmic amount
of state per node, making it suitable for large-scale and dynamic settings.
X-Vine also helps protect the privacy of users social network contacts and
keeps their IP addresses hidden from those outside of their social circle,
providing a basis for pseudonymous communication. We first evaluate our design
with analysis and simulations, using several real world large-scale social
networking topologies. We show that the constraints of X-Vine allow the
insertion of only a logarithmic number of Sybil identities per attack edge; we
show this mitigates the impact of malicious attacks while not affecting the
performance of honest nodes. Moreover, our algorithms are efficient, maintain
low stretch, and avoid hot spots in the network. We validate our design with a
PlanetLab implementation and a Facebook plugin.

Surgical Site Infection (SSI) is a national priority in healthcare research.
Much research attention has been attracted to develop better SSI risk
prediction models. However, most of the existing SSI risk prediction models are
built on static risk factors such as comorbidities and operative factors. In
this paper, we investigate the use of the dynamic wound data for SSI risk
prediction. There have been emerging mobile health (mHealth) tools that can
closely monitor the patients and generate continuous measurements of many
wound-related variables and other evolving clinical variables. Since existing
prediction models of SSI have quite limited capacity to utilize the evolving
clinical data, we develop the corresponding solution to equip these mHealth
tools with decision-making capabilities for SSI prediction with a seamless
assembly of several machine learning models to tackle the analytic challenges
arising from the spatial-temporal data. The basic idea is to exploit the
low-rank property of the spatial-temporal data via the bilinear formulation,
and further enhance it with automatic missing data imputation by the matrix
completion technique. We derive efficient optimization algorithms to implement
these models and demonstrate the superior performances of our new predictive
model on a real-world dataset of SSI, compared to a range of state-of-the-art
methods.

This research paper explores the concept of personalized email communities, focusing on the needs and expectations of multiple users. The background of this study reveals the growing importance of email communication in personal and professional settings, yet the existing email platforms often fail to provide a tailored experience for individual users. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a multi-user perspective for personalized email communities, which can cater to diverse user needs and preferences.  The objective of this research is to design and evaluate a personalized email community framework that considers the roles, interests, and communication styles of multiple users. A mixed-methods approach is employed, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis methods. The study involves a survey of 200 participants, who provide input on their email communication habits and preferences. Additionally, in-depth interviews with 30 participants are conducted to gather more nuanced insights into their needs and expectations.  Key findings indicate that users value personalized email communities that allow for flexible grouping, role-based communication, and tailored content curation. The framework is found to be effective in improving user engagement, reducing email clutter, and enhancing overall communication experience. The study also highlights the importance of considering the social dynamics and power structures within email communities, which can impact user behavior and satisfaction.  The conclusion of this research emphasizes the potential of personalized email communities to revolutionize the way we communicate online. The proposed framework offers a flexible and adaptable solution for email platforms, enabling them to provide a more personalized and engaging experience for their users. The study's findings have implications for the development of future email platforms and communication tools, highlighting the need for a more user-centric approach to online communication.

The conversion of gas into stars is a fundamental process in astrophysics and
cosmology. Stars are known to form from the gravitational collapse of dense
clumps in interstellar molecular clouds, and it has been proposed that the
resulting star formation rate is proportional to either the amount of mass
above a threshold gas surface density, or the gas volume density. These
star-formation prescriptions appear to hold in nearby molecular clouds in our
Milky Way Galaxy's disk as well as in distant galaxies where the star formation
rates are often much larger. The inner 500 pc of our Galaxy, the Central
Molecular Zone (CMZ), contains the largest concentration of dense, high-surface
density molecular gas in the Milky Way, providing an environment where the
validity of star-formation prescriptions can be tested. Here we show that by
several measures, the current star formation rate in the CMZ is an
order-of-magnitude lower than the rates predicted by the currently accepted
prescriptions. In particular, the region 1 deg < l < 3.5 deg, |b| < 0.5 deg
contains ~10^7 Msun of dense molecular gas -- enough to form 1000 Orion-like
clusters -- but the present-day star formation rate within this gas is only
equivalent to that in Orion. In addition to density, another property of
molecular clouds, such as the amplitude of turbulent motions, must be included
in the star-formation prescription to predict the star formation rate in a
given mass of molecular gas.

The knowledge of effective masses is a key ingredient to analyze numerous
properties of semiconductors, like carrier mobilities, (magneto-)transport
properties, or band extrema characteristics yielding carrier densities and
density of states. Currently, these masses are usually calculated using
finite-difference estimation of density functional theory (DFT) electronic band
curvatures. However, finite differences require an additional convergence study
and are prone to numerical noise. Moreover, the concept of effective mass
breaks down at degenerate band extrema. We assess the former limitation by
developing a method that allows to obtain the Hessian of DFT bands directly,
using density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Then, we solve the latter
issue by adapting the concept of `transport equivalent effective mass' to the
$\vec{k} \cdot \hat{\vec{p}}$ framework. The numerical noise inherent to
finite-difference methods is thus eliminated, along with the associated
convergence study. The resulting method is therefore more general, more robust
and simpler to use, which makes it especially appropriate for high-throughput
computing. After validating the developed techniques, we apply them to the
study of silicon, graphane, and arsenic. The formalism is implemented into the
ABINIT software and supports the norm-conserving pseudopotential approach, the
projector augmented-wave method, and the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling. The
derived expressions also apply to the ultrasoft pseudopotential method.

Type Iax supernovas (SNe Iax) are characterized by their modest ejecta masses, slow declining light curves, and strong helium lines in their spectral features. The discovery of SN 2014dt in the nearby galaxy M61 provided an excellent opportunity to investigate the progenitor system of this enigmatic class of explosions. In this study, we present new observations of SN 2014dt obtained with the Hobby-Eberly Telescope and the Large Binocular Telescope, as well as archival data from various telescopes. The data analysis reveals that SN 2014dt was located in a dense stellar environment, with multiple red giants and a compact companion star identified within its vicinity. The mass transfer scenario involving a white dwarf (WD) and a red giant (RG) companion was favored, with a likely mass ratio of q = 0.6-1.0 and an orbital separation of a = 3-5 R☉. We also obtained pre-explosion HST observations of the hosting galaxy, M61, and found that the star hosting SN 2014dt experienced an unusual brightening prior to the supernova event. Our results provide important constraints on the progenitor system of SNe Iax, which could help advance our understanding of the physical processes that drive these transient phenomena. Future studies, including time-domain surveys and theoretical modeling, are required to further elucidate the enigmatic nature of SNe Iax.

Motivated by a growing list of nontraditional statistical estimation problems
of the piecewise kind, this paper provides a survey of known results
supplemented with new results for the class of piecewise linear-quadratic
programs. These are linearly constrained optimization problems with piecewise
linear-quadratic (PLQ) objective functions. Starting from a study of the
representation of such a function in terms of a family of elementary functions
consisting of squared affine functions, squared plus-composite-affine
functions, and affine functions themselves, we summarize some local properties
of a PLQ function in terms of their first and second-order directional
derivatives. We extend some well-known necessary and sufficient second-order
conditions for local optimality of a quadratic program to a PLQ program and
provide a dozen such equivalent conditions for strong, strict, and isolated
local optimality, showing in particular that a PLQ program has the same
characterizations for local minimality as a standard quadratic program. As a
consequence of one such condition, we show that the number of strong, strict,
or isolated local minima of a PLQ program is finite; this result supplements a
recent result about the finite number of directional stationary objective
values. Interestingly, these finiteness results can be uncovered by invoking a
very powerful property of subanalytic functions; our proof is fairly
elementary, however. We discuss applications of PLQ programs in some modern
statistical estimation problems. These problems lead to a special class of
unconstrained composite programs involving the non-differentiable
$\ell_1$-function, for which we show that the task of verifying the
second-order stationary condition can be converted to the problem of checking
the copositivity of certain Schur complement on the nonnegative orthant.

Not all tags are relevant to an image, and the number of relevant tags is
image-dependent. Although many methods have been proposed for image
auto-annotation, the question of how to determine the number of tags to be
selected per image remains open. The main challenge is that for a large tag
vocabulary, there is often a lack of ground truth data for acquiring optimal
cutoff thresholds per tag. In contrast to previous works that pre-specify the
number of tags to be selected, we propose in this paper adaptive tag selection.
The key insight is to divide the vocabulary into two disjoint subsets, namely a
seen set consisting of tags having ground truth available for optimizing their
thresholds and a novel set consisting of tags without any ground truth. Such a
division allows us to estimate how many tags shall be selected from the novel
set according to the tags that have been selected from the seen set. The
effectiveness of the proposed method is justified by our participation in the
ImageCLEF 2014 image annotation task. On a set of 2,065 test images with ground
truth available for 207 tags, the benchmark evaluation shows that compared to
the popular top-$k$ strategy which obtains an F-score of 0.122, adaptive tag
selection achieves a higher F-score of 0.223. Moreover, by treating the
underlying image annotation system as a black box, the new method can be used
as an easy plug-in to boost the performance of existing systems.

In this study, we investigated the molecular environment and thermal X-ray properties of the semicircular young composite supernova remnant 3C 396, leveraging advanced X-ray spectroscopy techniques. Our principal objective was to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between the expanding supernova ejecta and the surrounding interstellar medium, which significantly influence both the remnant's morphology and its evolutionary trajectory. Utilizing observational data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission (XMM-Newton), we conducted a comprehensive spectral analysis focusing on the remnant's thermal emission lines. We identified prominent spectral features indicating the presence of shock-heated gas and high-velocity ejecta material. Our results reveal a complex molecular environment characterized by varying densities and temperatures, suggesting non-uniform distribution of ambient material. The presence of enriched elements such as silicon and sulfur supports a scenario of enriched material mixing with circumstellar medium. Additionally, we detected indications of a PWN (Pulsar Wind Nebula), contributing further complexity to the environmental interaction. Our methodology involved fitting the extracted spectra with advanced models that account for both thermal and non-thermal contributions, allowing us to determine physical parameters such as electron temperatures and ionization timescales.
