which has to be solved in presence of an unknown wave disturbance. Standard
approaches to this problem (loop-shaping, LQG, $H_{\infty}$-control etc.)
require to know the spectral density of the disturbance, considered to be a
\colored noise". In this paper, we propose a novel approach to optimal roll
stabilization, approximating the disturbance by a polyharmonic signal with
known frequencies yet uncertain amplitudes and phase shifts. Linear quadratic
optimization problems in presence of polyharmonic disturbances can be solved by
means of the theory of universal controllers developed by V.A. Yakubovich. An
optimal universal controller delivers the optimal solution for any uncertain
amplitudes and phases. Using Marine Systems Simulator (MSS) Toolbox that
provides a realistic vessel's model, we compare our design method with
classical approaches to optimal roll stabilization. Among three controllers
providing the same quality of yaw steering, OUC stabilizes the roll motion most
efficiently.

We present a comprehensive study on the abundance of molecular hydrogen (H₂) and its correlation with midplane pressure in galactic environments employing non-equilibrium, turbulent, chemical models. Our investigation aims to address the gap in understanding the molecular gas phase dynamics under varied galactic conditions. Utilizing state-of-the-art simulations that integrate hydrodynamic turbulence, chemical kinetics, and thermal processes, we simulate diverse galactic environments to predict molecular hydrogen distribution. We observe a significant correlation between the midplane pressure and H₂ abundance across a spectrum of galactic conditions, providing insights into the influence of turbulent pressure on molecular cloud formation. Our results highlight the role of turbulence in non-equilibrium chemical states and their impact on molecular hydrogen dynamics, which is often disregarded in equilibrium-based models. Key ideas include the integration of multi-phase interstellar medium components and the inclusion of temporally and spatially resolved turbulence models to reproduce realistic galactic conditions. Methodologically, we utilize advanced computational techniques to solve the chemical networks and employ high-resolution simulations that capture the intricate interplay of chemical reactions and physical processes under turbulent conditions. The findings suggest a paradigm where turbulence and pressure gradients are pivotal in shaping molecular gas distribution, challenging traditional models that rely heavily on thermal equilibrium assumptions. This study provides pivotal insights into the molecular composition of the interstellar medium, offering a refined framework for interpreting observational data of molecular gas in galaxies and advancing our understanding of star formation processes.

This work investigates the limitations of $T_1$- and $T_2$-spin relaxation times of phosphorous donor electrons near interface defects between crystalline silicon and silicon dioxide. By utilizing electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, we identify that the presence of these defects significantly impacts the relaxation times of the donor electrons. Our results reveal that these interface defects act as a source of spin relaxation for the donor electrons, imposing constraints on their coherence times and relaxation mechanisms. The study aims to address the challenge of understanding and mitigating the impact of interface defects on the spin properties of phosphorous donor electrons in silicon-based systems.  The key idea behind this research is to provide insight into the fundamental dynamics of electron spins near interface defects, which is crucial for the development of spin-based quantum technologies and silicon-based quantum computing architectures. The methodology involves experimental measurements of spin relaxation times coupled with theoretical modeling to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the interaction between phosphorous donor electrons and interface defects. By shedding light on these limitations, our work contributes to the advancement of spintronics and quantum information processing technologies.

We present a comprehensive study of the high-mass young stellar object G353.273+0.641 I, focusing on its intermittent maser flare activity. Utilizing a combination of radio and millimeter-wave observations, we collected a dataset spanning over two years to investigate the dynamics of this object. Our analysis reveals a complex and dynamic environment, characterized by periodic maser flares, which we attribute to the interaction between the stellar wind and the circumstellar disk.  Through the analysis of maser variability, we demonstrate that the flares are not merely random events, but rather occur in a coordinated manner, suggesting a underlying physical mechanism. Spectral studies reveal that the masers are associated with specific molecular lines, indicating the presence of dense, cold gas in the vicinity of the object. Our results also suggest that the maser activity is linked to the stellar wind, with the flares occurring during periods of increased stellar activity.  Our study provides new insights into the maser flare activity around high-mass young stellar objects, highlighting the importance of considering the complex interplay between the stellar wind, circumstellar disk, and surrounding gas. The observed variability in maser activity is attributed to the dynamic interaction between these components, and our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of these objects.

Low Surface Brighness Galaxies (LSBs), inspite of being gas rich, have low
star formation rates and are, therefore, low surface brightness in nature. We
calculate Q$_{\rm{RW}}$, the 2-component disc stability parameter as proposed
by Romeo \& Wiegert (2011), as a function of galactocentric radius $R$ for a
sample of five LSBs, for which mass models, as obtained from HI 21cm
radio-sythesis observations and R-band photometry, were available in the
literature. We find that the median value of Q$_{\rm{RW}}^{\rm{min}}$, the
minimum of Q$_{\rm{RW}}$ over $R$, lies between 2.6 and 3.1 for our sample
LSBs, which is higher than the median value of 1.8 $\pm$ 0.3 for
Q$_{\rm{RW}}^{\rm{min}}$ for a sampleof high surface brightness galaxies (HSBs)
as obtained in earlier studies. This clearly shows that LSBs have more stable
discs than HSBs, which could explain their low star formation rates and,
possibly, their low surface brightness nature. Interestingly, the calculated
values of Q$_{\rm{RW}}$ decrease only slightly (median Q$_{\rm{RW}}^{\rm{min}}$
$\sim$ 2.3 - 3) if the discs were taken to respond to the gravitational
potential of the dark matter halo only, but reduce by $\sim$ a factor of 2-3
(median Q$_{\rm{RW}}^{\rm{min}}$ $\sim$ 0.7 - 1.5) if they respond to their
self-gravity alone. This implies that the dark matter halo is crucial in
regulating disc stability in LSBs, which may have important implications for
models of galaxy formation and evolution.

The study of fermionic dark matter models, with their simplicity and potential for integration with the Standard Model, provides critical insights into the nature of dark matter as well as the Higgs boson. This research aims to explore the interactions between simple fermionic dark matter candidates and the Higgs boson, refining our understanding of both entities' roles in the cosmic framework. We utilize effective field theory approaches and perturbative methods to examine the coupling strengths and potential interactions leading to observable phenomena at particle colliders. Through simulations involving both current experimental limits and hypothetical scenarios beyond the Standard Model, we identify characteristic signatures that could indicate the presence of fermionic dark matter. Our findings suggest that specific coupling scenarios with the Higgs boson may lead to enhanced cross-sections for dark matter detection and provide identifiable signals in collider experiments, such as missing energy events or rare Higgs decay modes. Analyses further indicate constraints on the mass range and coupling constants of fermionic dark matter particles imposed by existing collider data. These results bridge the gap between theoretical models and experimental observability, advancing the landscape of particle physics by providing viable search strategies for dark matter. Conclusively, our research not only supports the existence of fermionic dark matter within the existing theoretical framework but also outlines pathways for empirical verification, fostering a deeper understanding of the universe's dark sector and its linkage to the Higgs boson.

We investigated the interplay between supersymmetric custodial Higgs triplets and the breaking of universality in the Standard Model, with a focus on the interplay between the electroweak symmetry breaking and the supersymmetric breaking. Our analysis revealed that supersymmetric custodial Higgs triplets provide a novel framework for addressing the long-standing issue of the breaking of universality in the Standard Model. By incorporating supersymmetric Higgs triplets into the Standard Model, we found that the electroweak symmetry breaking is decoupled from the supersymmetric breaking, thereby resolving the issue of universality.  Our work employed a combination of theoretical and computational methods, including the use of effective field theories and numerical simulations. We demonstrated that supersymmetric custodial Higgs triplets can be used to generate a rich set of phenomenological parameters, including the Higgs mass spectrum and the electroweak symmetry breaking patterns. Our results also revealed that the supersymmetric breaking can be used to generate a non-universal Higgs mass spectrum, thereby resolving the issue of universality in the Standard Model.  The key findings of our study are that supersymmetric custodial Higgs triplets provide a novel framework for addressing the breaking of universality in the Standard Model, and that the supersymmetric breaking can be used to generate a non-universal Higgs mass spectrum. Our results have significant implications for the development of new physics beyond the Standard Model, and highlight the potential of supersymmetric custodial Higgs triplets as a tool for addressing long-standing issues in particle physics.

We present the results of the study of the red nova PSN J14021678+5426205
based on the observations carried out with the Russian 6-m telescope (BTA)
along with other telescopes of SAO RAS and SAI MSU. To investigate the nova
progenitor, we used the data from the Digital Sky Survey and amateur photos
available on the internet. In the period between April 1993 and July 2014, the
brightness of the progenitor gradually increased by 2.2 mag in the V band. At
the peak of the first outburst in mid-November of 2014, the star reached an
absolute visual magnitude of -12.75 mag but was discovered later, in February
2015, in a repeated outburst at the absolute magnitude of -11.65 mag. The
amplitude of the outburst was minimum among the red novae, only 5.6 mag in the
V band. The H alpha emission line and the continuum of a cool supergiant with a
gradually decreasing surface temperature were observed in the spectra. Such
process is typical for red novae, although the object under study showed
extreme parameters: maximum luminosity, maximum outburst duration, minimum
outburst amplitude, unusual shape of the light curve. This event is interpreted
as a massive OB star system components merging accompanied by the formation of
a common envelope and then the expansion of this envelope with minimal energy
losses.

In this study, we investigate the performance disparity between randomized and orthogonal spectrum allocation mechanisms in decentralized networks, specifically focusing on their impact on outage occurrences. We seek to address the critical challenge of efficiently managing spectrum resources in scenarios where multiple users compete for limited bandwidth. Through rigorous mathematical modeling and simulation approaches, we evaluate the outage probability under both allocation schemes. Our methodology encompasses the formulation of probabilistic models that characterize user behavior and network conditions, allowing for the derivation of closed-form expressions for outage probabilities.   We simulate decentralized network environments with varying user densities and mobility patterns to comprehensively assess the effectiveness of each allocation strategy. Our results indicate a clear distinction in performance metrics while randomized allocation exhibits greater flexibility and user adaptability, it paradoxically incurs higher outage rates compared to the more structured orthogonal allocations under certain traffic conditions. Notably, we observe that increased user density exacerbates outage risks in randomized allocation, while orthogonal allocation sustains lower outage probabilities through systematic resource distribution.  This analysis elucidates key trade-offs in spectrum allocation strategies, underscoring the importance of context-specific decisions in network design. Our findings contribute essential insights into the optimization of spectrum management practices, providing a foundation for future research into adaptive allocation techniques that can further enhance network reliability in decentralized settings.

In our quest to explore the universe beyond our solar system, we conducted a comprehensive search for interstellar adenine, a key nucleobase in the structure of DNA and RNA. The search was carried out using data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Green Bank Telescope (GBT). Our methodology involved analyzing molecular spectra to identify the presence of adenine, which can be distinguished by its characteristic rotational transitions. The problem we aimed to solve was the scarcity of direct evidence for interstellar adenine, despite its importance as a building block of life on Earth.  Our analysis revealed multiple promising candidates within the spectra, indicating the potential for adenine in the interstellar medium. However, further spectroscopic studies and laboratory experiments are required to confirm these findings definitively. The key ideas include the innovative use of ALMA and GBT for extraterrestrial organic molecule detection and the significance of adenine in astrobiology. This research not only expands our knowledge of the chemical complexity of space but also deepens our understanding of the origins of life in the universe.

Multiplicative noise (also known as speckle noise) models are central to the
study of coherent imaging systems, such as synthetic aperture radar and sonar,
and ultrasound and laser imaging. These models introduce two additional layers
of difficulties with respect to the standard Gaussian additive noise scenario:
(1) the noise is multiplied by (rather than added to) the original image; (2)
the noise is not Gaussian, with Rayleigh and Gamma being commonly used
densities. These two features of multiplicative noise models preclude the
direct application of most state-of-the-art algorithms, which are designed for
solving unconstrained optimization problems where the objective has two terms:
a quadratic data term (log-likelihood), reflecting the additive and Gaussian
nature of the noise, plus a convex (possibly nonsmooth) regularizer (e.g., a
total variation or wavelet-based regularizer/prior). In this paper, we address
these difficulties by: (1) converting the multiplicative model into an additive
one by taking logarithms, as proposed by some other authors; (2) using variable
splitting to obtain an equivalent constrained problem; and (3) dealing with
this optimization problem using the augmented Lagrangian framework. A set of
experiments shows that the proposed method, which we name MIDAL (multiplicative
image denoising by augmented Lagrangian), yields state-of-the-art results both
in terms of speed and denoising performance.

We have used archival RXTE PCA data to investigate timing and spectral
characteristics of the transient XTE J1817-330. The data pertains to 160 PCA
pointed observations made during the outburst period 2006, January 27 to August
2. A detailed analysis of Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) in this black hole
X-ray binary is carried out. Power density spectra were obtained using the
light curves of the source. QPOs have been detected in the 2-8 keV band in 10
of the observations. In 8 of these observations, QPOs are present in the 8-14
keV and in 5 observations in the 15-25 keV band. XTE J1817-330 is the third
black hole source from which the low frequency QPOs are clearly detected in
hard X-rays. The QPO frequency lies in ~ 4-9 Hz and the rms amplitude in
1.7-13.3% range, the amplitude being higher at higher energies. We have fitted
the PDS of the observations with Lorentzian and power law models. Energy
spectra are derived for those observations in which the QPOs are detected to
investigate any dependence of the QPO characteristic on the spectral
parameters. These spectra are well fitted with a two component model that
includes the disk black body component and a power law component. The QPO
characteristics and their variations are discussed and its implication on the
origin of the QPOs are examined

Echocardiography is essential to modern cardiology. However, human
interpretation limits high throughput analysis, limiting echocardiography from
reaching its full clinical and research potential for precision medicine. Deep
learning is a cutting-edge machine-learning technique that has been useful in
analyzing medical images but has not yet been widely applied to
echocardiography, partly due to the complexity of echocardiograms' multi view,
multi modality format. The essential first step toward comprehensive computer
assisted echocardiographic interpretation is determining whether computers can
learn to recognize standard views. To this end, we anonymized 834,267
transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) images from 267 patients (20 to 96 years, 51
percent female, 26 percent obese) seen between 2000 and 2017 and labeled them
according to standard views. Images covered a range of real world clinical
variation. We built a multilayer convolutional neural network and used
supervised learning to simultaneously classify 15 standard views. Eighty
percent of data used was randomly chosen for training and 20 percent reserved
for validation and testing on never seen echocardiograms. Using multiple images
from each clip, the model classified among 12 video views with 97.8 percent
overall test accuracy without overfitting. Even on single low resolution
images, test accuracy among 15 views was 91.7 percent versus 70.2 to 83.5
percent for board-certified echocardiographers. Confusional matrices, occlusion
experiments, and saliency mapping showed that the model finds recognizable
similarities among related views and classifies using clinically relevant image
features. In conclusion, deep neural networks can classify essential
echocardiographic views simultaneously and with high accuracy. Our results
provide a foundation for more complex deep learning assisted echocardiographic
interpretation.

A quantum mechanical model on histone modification is proposed. Along with
the methyl / acetate or other groups bound to the modified residues the torsion
angles of the nearby histone chain are supposed to participate in the quantum
transition cooperatively. The transition rate W is calculated based on the
non-radiative quantum transition theory in adiabatic approximation. By using
W's the reaction equations can be written for histone modification and the
histone modification level can be calculable from the equations, which is
decided by not only the atomic group bound to the modified residue, but also
the nearby histone chain. The theory can explain the mechanism for the
correlation between a pair of chromatin markers observed in histone
modification. The temperature dependence and the coherence-length dependence of
histone modification are deduced. Several points for checking the proposed
theory and the quantum nature of histone modification are suggested as follows:
1, The relationship between lnW and 1/T is same as usual protein folding. The
non-Arhenius temperature dependence of the histone modification level is
predicted. 2, The variation of histone modification level through point
mutation of some residues on the chain is predicted since the mutation may
change the coherence-length of the system. 3, Multi-site modification obeys the
quantum superposition law and the comparison between multi-site transition and
single modification transition gives an additional clue to the testing of the
quantum nature of histone modification.

The study of stellar spectroscopy has been instrumental in understanding the chemical composition of the Galactic metal-poor disc and the halo. However, traditional spectroscopic methods have limitations in accurately determining the chemical properties of these regions. This limitation arises due to the presence of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, which can significantly impact the accuracy of spectroscopic measurements.   This research aims to address this limitation by applying non-local thermodynamic equilibrium stellar spectroscopy to 1D and 3D models of the Galactic metal-poor disc and the halo. The 1D models simulate the effects of NLTE on the spectroscopic measurements, while the 3D models incorporate the complex spatial structures of the Galactic halo.   The results of this study indicate that the 3D models provide a more accurate representation of the chemical properties of the Galactic metal-poor disc and the halo, with a median offset of 0.3 dex in the case of alpha-elements and 0.2 dex in the case of iron-peak elements. The 1D models, on the other hand, result in a median offset of 0.5 dex for alpha-elements and 0.3 dex for iron-peak elements.   These findings suggest that the 3D models are more effective in capturing the complex spatial structures of the Galactic halo and the metal-poor disc, resulting in a more accurate representation of the chemical properties of these regions. The results of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the chemical evolution of the Galaxy, and provide a more precise framework for the interpretation of spectroscopic data.

The abstract for the research paper focusing on "Entropy entrainment and dissipation in superfluid Helium" begins with an introduction to the context of superfluid helium, followed by the objectives of the study, methodology employed, key findings, and concludes with the implications and future directions.  In superfluid helium, the unique quantum mechanical properties lead to phenomena that challenge classical thermodynamics. This research investigates the mechanisms of entropy entrainment and dissipation within superfluid helium, focusing on the interplay between macroscopic and microscopic scales. The primary objective is to elucidate how energy transport and dissipation affect the overall entropy dynamics in superfluid environments.  Experimental techniques such as heat flow measurements and neutron scattering were used to probe the behavior of superfluid helium under various conditions. The methodology involved detailed analysis of temperature gradients and phase transitions to observe the redistribution of entropy across different regions of the superfluid. Key findings revealed that entropy entrainment occurs predominantly at the boundaries between regions of different temperatures, where heat flows from warmer to cooler areas. Dissipation was observed to be more localized, with significant energy losses occurring near vortices, which are known to act as barriers to heat conduction.  The results highlight the complex interplay between thermal transport and phase coherence in superfluid helium. They suggest that understanding these processes could provide insights into fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics and could potentially inform the development of new materials and technologies exploiting superfluidity.  In conclusion, this study advances our comprehension of entropy dynamics in superfluid helium, providing foundational knowledge that could pave the way for future advancements in quantum physics and technology. Future work will focus on extending these studies to broader systems and exploring potential applications of these findings.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the merging galaxy cluster Abell 2255, focusing on the northeast radio relic. The background of this phenomenon is rooted in the complex dynamics of galaxy clusters, where the merger of two clusters can lead to the formation of a powerful radio relic. The northeast radio relic in Abell 2255 is a significant example of this process, with its unique morphology and spectral properties providing valuable insights into the cluster's evolution.  The objective of this research is to investigate the nature and evolution of the northeast radio relic in Abell 2255, with a particular emphasis on the role of the merging clusters in shaping its morphology and spectral characteristics. To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis of Suzaku observations was conducted, utilizing the X-ray and gamma-ray imaging capabilities of the onboard instruments.  The key findings of this study reveal that the northeast radio relic is a complex, multi-scale structure, with a unique morphology and spectral profile. The Suzaku observations indicate that the relic is composed of a combination of diffuse and compact components, with distinct spectral characteristics. The analysis also reveals that the relic is dynamically evolving, with changes in its morphology and spectral properties over time. These findings provide significant insights into the complex dynamics of galaxy clusters and the role of the merging clusters in shaping the evolution of radio relics.  The conclusion of this study highlights the importance of Suzaku observations in understanding the evolution of complex astrophysical phenomena, such as the merging galaxy cluster Abell 2255 and its northeast radio relic. The findings of this research contribute to our understanding of the complex interactions between galaxy clusters and the role of radio relics in the evolution of these systems.

We investigated the interplay between geometric random graphs and Rado sets within sequence spaces, addressing the challenge of characterizing the structural properties of these systems. Our primary objective was to analyze the emergence of Rado sets in the context of random geometric graphs, where vertices represent points in a metric space, and edges are formed based on proximity. We employed a combination of probabilistic methods and combinatorial topology to assemble a theoretical framework that encapsulates the behavior of these geometric constructs.   Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we established conditions under which Rado sets manifest within specific configurations of geometric random graphs. Utilizing quantitative measures, such as graph density and expected edge formation, we demonstrated a correlation between the randomness of point distribution and the likelihood of Rado sets arising. Our results reveal that under particular settings, even sparse geometric random graphs can yield extensive Rado structures, thereby contributing to the understanding of combinatorial properties in continuous domains.  Moreover, we validated our theoretical findings through simulations, which corroborated our predictions and provided empirical insights into the probabilistic nature of connectivity within sequence spaces. This research not only advances the theoretical discourse on geometric random graphs and their applications but also lays the foundation for future explorations into the complexities of combinatorial structures in stochastic environments. Our findings underscore the significance of integrating geometric perspectives into the study of Rado sets, paving the way for new methodologies in tackling related mathematical problems.

This study investigates the computation of Universal Groebner Bases (UGB) for the ideal generated by maximal minors of a generic matrix. Our work aims to address the computational complexity associated with finding UGBs for these ideals, which is crucial for applications in algebraic statistics and computational geometry. We employ Buchberger's algorithm adapted for computing UGBs over polynomial rings, focusing on efficient strategies to handle the combinatorial explosion inherent in maximal minors. Our methodology involves the implementation of specialized algorithms that exploit the structure of the matrices to reduce the computational burden. Results demonstrate significant improvements in both time and space efficiency compared to existing methods. Key findings include the successful computation of UGBs for matrices of size up to 6x6, showcasing the practical applicability and scalability of our approach. The work contributes novel insights into the theoretical and practical aspects of UGBs for maximal minors, providing a robust framework for further research in this area.

Binary stars undergo significant mass loss throughout their evolution, with adiabatic mass loss playing a crucial role in shaping their final states. This study examines the adiabatic mass loss in binary stars from the zero-age main sequence (ZAMS) to the base of the giant branch (GBB), a critical phase in their evolution.    Adiabatic mass loss in binary stars is driven by the interaction between the stellar winds of the two components, which can lead to a significant reduction in their masses. This process affects the final mass ratio of the binary system, influencing the long-term evolution of the stars. The GBB marks a transition point in the evolution of binary stars, where the stars begin to expand and cool, leading to a significant increase in their luminosity.   To investigate the adiabatic mass loss in binary stars from the ZAMS to the GBB, we aim to determine the rates and mechanisms of mass loss during this phase, and their impact on the final mass ratio and the evolution of the stars.   We employed a suite of stellar evolution models, including the MESA code, to simulate the evolution of binary stars from the ZAMS to the GBB. We also employed a 1D hydrodynamic code to calculate the stellar wind rates and mass loss rates during this phase.  Key findings Our results indicate that adiabatic mass loss in binary stars during the GBB phase is significant, with mass loss rates varying from 10^-10 to 10^-6 M⊙ yr^-1. We also find that the mass loss rates are dependent on the mass ratio of the binary system, with more massive stars experiencing higher mass loss rates. Our simulations suggest that the final mass ratio of the binary system is primarily determined by the adiabatic mass loss during the GBB phase.   This study provides new insights into the adiabatic mass loss in binary stars from the ZAMS to the GBB, highlighting its significant impact on the final mass ratio and the evolution of the stars. Our results have important implications for our understanding of binary star evolution and the formation of compact binary systems, and will inform future studies of stellar evolution and the properties of binary stars.

This work deals with gravity localization on codimension-1 brane worlds
engendered by compacton-like kinks, the so-called hybrid branes. In such
scenarios, the thin brane behaviour is manifested when the extra dimension is
outside the compact domain, where the energy density is non-trivial, instead of
asymptotically as in the usual thick brane models. The zero mode is trapped in
the brane, as required. The massive modes, although are not localized in the
brane, have important phenomenological implications such as corrections to the
Newton's law. We study such corrections in the usual thick domain wall and in
the hybrid brane scenarios. By means of suitable numerical methods, we attain
the mass spectrum for the graviton and the corresponding wavefunctions. The
spectra possess the usual linearly increasing behaviour from the Kaluza-Klein
theories. Further, we show that the 4D gravitational force is slightly
increased at short distances. The first eigenstate contributes highly for the
correction to the Newton's law. The subsequent normalized solutions have
diminishing contributions. Moreover, we find out that the phenomenology of the
hybrid brane is not different from the usual thick domain wall. The use of
numerical techniques for solving the equations of the massive modes is useful
for matching possible phenomenological measurements in the gravitational law as
a probe to warped extra dimensions.

In the study of high-mass star formation, understanding the fragmentation of molecular filaments is crucial, as these structures are the primary sites for star-forming cores. The objective of this research is to investigate the processes that govern filament fragmentation and its role in the formation of high-mass stars. By employing high-resolution simulations and observational data from instruments such as ALMA and the Herschel Space Observatory, this study examines the physical conditions and dynamics within filaments that lead to fragmentation. The methodology involves a multi-scale approach, integrating magnetohydrodynamic simulations with observations to assess the interplay of gravity, turbulence, and magnetic fields in filament evolution. Key findings reveal that filaments with higher line masses are more prone to fragment due to gravitational instability, while magnetic fields and turbulence contribute to regulating the fragmentation scale. The results indicate that the presence of magnetic fields can delay or suppress fragmentation, allowing the filaments to accumulate mass before collapsing into high-mass stars. Additionally, environmental factors such as external pressure from surrounding gas clouds influence the fragmentation pattern and intensity. This study concludes that filament fragmentation is a multi-faceted process significantly affected by initial conditions and external forces, with implications for understanding the initial mass function and star formation efficiency in high-mass regions. These insights enhance our comprehension of the initial stages of high-mass star formation and provide a foundation for future studies aiming to unravel the complexities of star-forming environments.

In spite of its importance for the study of star formation at all mass
domains, the nearby young sigma Orionis cluster still lacks a comprehensive
survey for multiplicity. We try to fill that observational gap by looking for
wide resolved binaries with angular separations between 0.4 and 4.0 arcsec. We
search for companions to 331 catalogued cluster stellar members and candidates
in public K-band UKIDSS images outside the innermost 1 arcmin, which is
affected by the glare of the bright, eponymous sigma Ori multiple system, and
investigate their cluster membership with colour-magnitude diagrams and
previous knowledge of youth features. Of the 18 identified pairs, ten have very
low individual probabilities of chance alignment (< 1 %) and are considered
here as physical pairs. Four of them are new, while the other six had been
discovered previously, but never investigated homogeneously and in detail.
Projected physical separations and magnitude differences of the ten probably
bound pairs range from 180 to 1220 au, and from 0.0 to 3.4 mag in K,
respectively. Besides, we identify two cluster stars with elongated point
spread functions. We determine the minimum frequency of wide multiplicity in
the interval of projected physical separations s = 160-1600 au in sigma Orionis
at 3.0^{+1.2}_{-1.1} %. We discover a new Lindroos system, find that massive
and X-ray stars tend to be in pairs or trios, conclude that multiplicity
truncates circumstellar discs and enhances X-ray emission, and ascribe a
reported lithium depletion in a young star to unresolved binarity in spectra of
moderate resolution. When accounting for all know multiples, including
spectroscopic binaries, the minimum frequency of multiplicity increases to
about 10 %, which implies that of the order of 80-100 unknown multiple systems
still await discovery in sigma Orionis.

The energy budget in common-envelope events (CEEs) is not well understood,
with substantial uncertainty even over to what extent the recombination energy
stored in ionised hydrogen and helium might be used to help envelope ejection.
We investigate the reaction of a red-giant envelope to heating which mimics
limiting cases of energy input provided by the orbital decay of a binary during
a CEE, specifically during the post-plunge-in phase during which the spiral-in
has been argued to occur on a time-scale longer than dynamical. We show that
the outcome of such a CEE depends less on the total amount of energy by which
the envelope is heated than on how rapidly the energy was transferred to the
envelope and on where the envelope was heated. The envelope always becomes
dynamically unstable before receiving net heat energy equal to the envelope's
initial binding energy. We find two types of outcome, both of which likely lead
to at least partial envelope ejection: "runaway" solutions in which the
expansion of the radius becomes undeniably dynamical, and superficially
"self-regulated" solutions, in which the expansion of the stellar radius stops
but a significant fraction of the envelope becomes formally dynamically
unstable. Almost the entire reservoir of initial helium recombination energy is
used for envelope expansion. Hydrogen recombination is less energetically
useful, but is nonetheless important for the development of the dynamical
instabilities. However, this result requires the companion to have already
plunged deep into the envelope; therefore this release of recombination energy
does not help to explain wide post-common-envelope orbits.

Recent advancement of rainbow tensor models based on their superintegrability
(manifesting itself as the existence of an explicit expression for a generic
Gaussian correlator) has allowed us to bypass the long-standing problem seen as
the lack of eigenvalue/determinant representation needed to establish the
KP/Toda integrability. As the mandatory next step, we discuss in this paper how
to provide an adequate designation to each of the connected gauge-invariant
operators that form a double coset, which is required to cleverly formulate a
tree-algebra generalization of the Virasoro constraints. This problem goes
beyond the enumeration problem per se tied to the permutation group, forcing us
to introduce a few gauge fixing procedures to the coset. We point out that the
permutation-based labeling, which has proven to be relevant for the Gaussian
averages is, via interesting complexity, related to the one based on the
keystone trees, whose algebra will provide the tensor counterpart of the
Virasoro algebra for matrix models. Moreover, our simple analysis reveals the
existence of nontrivial kernels and co-kernels for the cut operation and for
the join operation respectively that prevent a straightforward construction of
the non-perturbative RG-complete partition function and the identification of
truly independent time variables. We demonstrate these problems by the simplest
non-trivial Aristotelian RGB model with one complex rank-3 tensor, studying its
ring of gauge-invariant operators, generated by the keystone triple with the
help of four operations: addition, multiplication, cut and join.

The study of peculiar stars within open clusters provides pivotal insights into stellar evolution and chemical diversity. This research investigates the presence and characteristics of peculiar stars in the open cluster Hogg 16, a relatively understudied cluster situated in the Milky Way. The objective is to identify stars with unusual chemical compositions or spectral properties that deviate from standard stellar models. We employed high-resolution spectroscopy and photometric data captured through a series of observations using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Our analysis incorporated advanced spectral classification techniques and synthetic photometry to isolate candidates exhibiting peculiarities.   Key findings reveal the presence of several stars with anomalous elemental abundances, notably in helium and silicon, indicative of CP (Chemically Peculiar) star characteristics. Additionally, variability in the light curves of some targets suggests the presence of peculiar variable stars such as Delta Scuti or SX Arietis types. The statistical distribution of these peculiar stars within the cluster provides evidence supporting theories of cluster age and stellar formation mechanisms influencing chemical peculiarities.  Conclusions drawn from this research enhance the understanding of the frequency and distribution of peculiar stars in Hogg 16 and similar clusters. These findings contribute to refining models of stellar evolution, particularly concerning the impacts of magnetic fields and rotational velocities on star formation. Future research should focus on longitudinal studies to monitor these stars' changes over time and delve deeper into the theoretical modeling of their peculiarities.

We present a novel approach, the Deep Convolutional Decision Jungle (DCDJ), for image classification tasks. Our work aims to address the limitations of traditional deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in handling complex decision boundaries within images. Through the integration of decision trees within the CNN architecture, the DCDJ model can capture intricate image representations and refine classification boundaries effectively.   Our experimental results on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate superior classification performance compared to standard CNNs. The DCDJ model exhibits enhanced interpretability due to its decision tree components, allowing for a more transparent understanding of the classification process.   Key to our approach is the iterative training of decision trees within the CNN framework, enabling the model to adaptively learn complex hierarchical features through a joint optimization process. Leveraging the strengths of both decision trees and CNNs, the DCDJ model is capable of achieving state-of-the-art results on image classification tasks while maintaining interpretability and generalization capabilities.   The proposed DCDJ architecture introduces a promising direction for advancing image classification methods by combining the expressiveness of CNNs with the interpretability of decision trees. Our findings showcase the potential of integrating diverse machine learning techniques to create more robust and effective models for image analysis tasks.

The VLT LBG Redshift Survey (VLGR-S) is an ongoing project aimed at mapping the circumgalactic medium (CGM) around Lyman-break galaxy (LBG) populations at redshifts $z \sim 3$. This sixth installment focuses specifically on probing the atomic hydrogen content within the CGM of these distant galaxies using the X-Shooter spectrograph. The study employs high-resolution spectra obtained from X-Shooter to detect and measure neutral hydrogen column densities ($N_{HI}$) towards selected LBG targets. By leveraging the capabilities of X-Shooter, which offers a broad wavelength coverage and high spectral resolution, the survey aims to provide detailed insights into the physical conditions and properties of the CGM in the vicinity of high-redshift LBGs. Key findings include the characterization of the $N_{HI}$ distribution, its dependence on the LBG properties, and the identification of regions where the CGM may be more enriched in neutral hydrogen compared to the surrounding intergalactic medium. The results contribute to our understanding of the processes governing the enrichment and evolution of the CGM in the early universe, providing crucial data for cosmological models and feedback mechanisms affecting galaxy formation and evolution.

The formation of clouds affects brown dwarf and planetary atmospheres of
nearly all effective temperatures. Iron and silicate condense in L dwarf
atmospheres and dissipate at the L/T transition. Minor species such as sulfides
and salts condense in mid-late T dwarfs. For brown dwarfs below Teff=450 K,
water condenses in the upper atmosphere to form ice clouds. Currently over a
dozen objects in this temperature range have been discovered, and few previous
theoretical studies have addressed the effect of water clouds on brown dwarf or
exoplanetary spectra. Here we present a new grid of models that include the
effect of water cloud opacity. We find that they become optically thick in
objects below Teff=350-375 K. Unlike refractory cloud materials, water ice
particles are significantly non-gray absorbers; they predominantly scatter at
optical wavelengths through J band and absorb in the infrared with prominent
features, the strongest of which is at 2.8 microns. H2O, NH3, CH4, and H2 CIA
are dominant opacity sources; less abundant species such as may also be
detectable, including the alkalis, H2S, and PH3. PH3, which has been detected
in Jupiter, is expected to have a strong signature in the mid-infrared at 4.3
microns in Y dwarfs around Teff=450 K; if disequilibrium chemistry increases
the abundance of PH3, it may be detectable over a wider effective temperature
range than models predict. We show results incorporating disequilibrium
nitrogen and carbon chemistry and predict signatures of low gravity in
planetary- mass objects. Lastly, we make predictions for the observability of Y
dwarfs and planets with existing and future instruments including the James
Webb Space Telescope and Gemini Planet Imager.

This research explores the application of hyperbolic stratified nanostructures for enhancing Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS). The study aims to investigate the theoretical framework behind the design and utilization of these nanostructures to amplify Raman signals. The methodology involves computational simulations and optimization techniques to analyze the electromagnetic field enhancements within the nanostructures. The key findings reveal that hyperbolic stratified nanostructures can significantly boost SERS signals through the excitation of hyperbolic modes, enabling highly sensitive detection capabilities. The research contributes to the understanding of the underlying principles governing SERS enhancement mechanisms using hyperbolic materials. In conclusion, the findings highlight the immense potential of hyperbolic stratified nanostructures in advancing SERS-based sensing applications, paving the way for innovative technologies with enhanced performance and sensitivity.

We investigated the detection of hydrocarbon emission from S-type AGB stars, a class of asymptotic giant branch stars known for their intense mass loss. Through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric observations, we aimed to identify and characterize the hydrocarbon species responsible for the emission. Utilizing the ESPaDOnS spectrograph at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, we analyzed the spectra of 15 S-type AGB stars, covering a range of luminosities and metallicities. Our results indicate that hydrocarbon emission is a common feature among these stars, with a significant fraction displaying emission lines of acetylene (C2H2) and ethylene (C2H4). Notably, we found a strong correlation between the luminosity and the intensity of the hydrocarbon emission, suggesting a link between the star's mass loss rate and the presence of hydrocarbons. Our analysis also revealed that the hydrocarbon emission is often accompanied by a distinct spectral feature, which we attribute to the presence of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). These findings contribute to our understanding of the complex chemistry and mass loss processes occurring in S-type AGB stars, and highlight the importance of hydrocarbon emission in the context of stellar evolution and the interstellar medium.

We classify the complete set of dimension-5 operators relevant for the
resonant production of a singlet of spin 0 or 2 linearly coupled to the
Standard Model (SM). We compute the decay width of such states as a function of
the effective couplings, and provide the matching to various well-motivated New
Physics scenarios. We then investigate the possibility that one of these
neutral resonances be at the origin of the excess in diboson production
recently reported by the ATLAS collaboration. We perform a shape analysis of
the excess under full consideration of the systematic uncertainties to extract
the width $\Gamma_{\rm tot}$ of the hypothetical resonance, finding it to be in
the range 26 GeV $<\Gamma_{\rm tot}<$ 144 GeV at 95\% C.L. We then point out
that the three overlapping selections $WW$, $WZ$, $ZZ$ reported by ATLAS follow
a joint trivariate Poisson distribution, which opens the possibility of a
thorough likelihood analysis of the event rates. The background systematic
uncertainties are also included in our analysis. We show that the data do not
require $W\!Z$ production and could thus in principle be explained by neutral
resonances. We then use both the information on the width and the cross
section, which prove to be highly complementary, to test the effective
Lagrangians of singlet resonances. Regarding specific models, we find that
neither scalars coupled via the Higgs-portal nor the Randall-Sundrum (RS)
radion can explain the ATLAS anomaly. The RS graviton with all matter on the
infrared (IR) brane can in principle fit the observed excess, while the RS
model with matter propagating in the bulk requires the presence of IR brane
kinetic terms for the gauge fields.

Our work presents the findings of a comprehensive survey aiming to identify Earth-like planets and potential habitats for tardigrades among exoplanets. We analyzed data from the Kepler Space Telescope to identify exoplanets within the habitable zone of their host stars and conducted a thorough assessment of their key characteristics, such as size, surface temperature, and potential for liquid water. Our results indicate the presence of several exoplanets that exhibit Earth-like conditions, making them potential candidates for hosting life forms resembling tardigrades. By focusing on tardigrades, known for their resilience to extreme conditions, we aim to broaden the scope of habitability assessments beyond conventional measures. Furthermore, our study introduces a novel methodology for evaluating the potential habitability of exoplanets by considering the tolerance of extremophiles like tardigrades. This approach offers valuable insights into the diversity of possible habitable environments in the universe and expands the criteria for identifying potential biosignatures on distant worlds. In conclusion, our survey contributes to the ongoing search for habitable exoplanets and underscores the importance of incorporating extremophile resilience into future astrobiological studies.

The influence of Deep Learning on image identification and natural language
processing has attracted enormous attention globally. The convolution neural
network that can learn without prior extraction of features fits well in
response to the rapid iteration of Android malware. The traditional solution
for detecting Android malware requires continuous learning through
pre-extracted features to maintain high performance of identifying the malware.
In order to reduce the manpower of feature engineering prior to the condition
of not to extract pre-selected features, we have developed a coloR-inspired
convolutional neuRal networks (CNN)-based AndroiD malware Detection (R2-D2)
system. The system can convert the bytecode of classes.dex from Android archive
file to rgb color code and store it as a color image with fixed size. The color
image is input to the convolutional neural network for automatic feature
extraction and training. The data was collected from Jan. 2017 to Aug 2017.
During the period of time, we have collected approximately 2 million of benign
and malicious Android apps for our experiments with the help from our research
partner Leopard Mobile Inc. Our experiment results demonstrate that the
proposed system has accurate security analysis on contracts. Furthermore, we
keep our research results and experiment materials on http://R2D2.TWMAN.ORG.

We evaluate the Community ocean Vertical Mixing (CVMix) project version of
the K-profile parameterization (KPP). For this purpose, one-dimensional KPP
simulations are compared across a suite of oceanographically relevant regimes
against large eddy simulations (LES). The LES is forced with horizontally
uniform boundary fluxes and has horizontally uniform initial conditions,
allowing its horizontal average to be compared to one-dimensional KPP tests. We
find the standard configuration of KPP consistent with LES across many forcing
regimes, supporting the physical basis of KPP. Our evaluation motivates
recommendations for "best practices" for using KPP within ocean circulation
models, and identifies areas where further research is warranted. Further, our
test suite can be used as a baseline for evaluation of a broad suite of
boundary layer models. The original treatment of KPP recommends the matching of
interior diffusivities and their gradients to the KPP predicted values computed
in the ocean surface boundary layer (OSBL). However, we find that difficulties
in representing derivatives of rapidly changing diffusivities near the base of
the OSBL can lead to loss of simulation fidelity. We propose two alternative
approaches. We find the KPP entrainment buoyancy flux to be sensitive to
vertical grid resolution and details of how to diagnose the KPP boundary layer
depth. We modify the KPP turbulent shear velocity parameterization to reduce
resolution dependence. Additionally, our results show that the KPP
parameterized non-local tracer flux is incomplete due to the assumption that it
solely redistributes the surface tracer flux. However, examination of the LES
vertical turbulent scalar flux budgets show that non-local fluxes can exist in
the absence of surface tracer fluxes. This result motivates further studies of
the non-local flux parameterization.

In this work, we propose a novel scheme aimed at mitigating malicious behavior exhibited by mobile nodes within mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). Our approach focuses on identifying and isolating malicious nodes through a combination of proactive and reactive strategies. Proactively, we implement a distributed trust model that evaluates each node's behavior based on predefined rules and feedback mechanisms. Reactively, upon detection of suspicious activities, the system initiates a containment protocol involving isolation and communication disruption to prevent further propagation of malicious actions.  The problem work attempts to solve is the escalating threat posed by malicious nodes that can disrupt network connectivity, degrade performance, and compromise overall security. Traditional solutions often rely on centralized management, which can be impractical in dynamic MANET environments where nodes frequently change roles and locations. Our method ensures scalability and adaptability by leveraging decentralized decision-making processes.  Key ideas include the integration of a trust metric algorithm, anomaly detection techniques, and a robust containment strategy. Methodologically, we employed simulations using the ns-3 toolkit to validate our scheme's effectiveness across various network conditions and sizes. The results demonstrate a significant reduction in malicious activities, maintaining network integrity and enhancing security in MANETs. This approach not only addresses current challenges but also paves the way for future developments in secure and resilient MANET architectures.

The study of complex social and political phenomena with the perspective and
methods of network science has proven fruitful in a variety of areas, including
applications in political science and more narrowly the field of international
relations. We propose a new line of research in the study of international
conflict by showing that the multiplex fractionalization of the international
system (which we label Kantian fractionalization) is a powerful predictor of
the propensity for violent interstate conflict, a key indicator of the system's
stability. In so doing, we also demonstrate the first use of multislice
modularity for community detection in a multiplex network application. Even
after controlling for established system-level conflict indicators, we find
that Kantian fractionalization contributes more to model fit for violent
interstate conflict than previously established measures. Moreover, evaluating
the influence of each of the constituent networks shows that joint democracy
plays little, if any, role in predicting system stability, thus challenging a
major empirical finding of the international relations literature. Lastly, a
series of Granger causal tests shows that the temporal variability of Kantian
fractionalization is consistent with a causal relationship with the prevalence
of conflict in the international system. This causal relationship has
real-world policy implications as changes in Kantian fractionalization could
serve as an early warning sign of international instability.

We present the Misrepair Accumulation Theory (MAT), a novel framework for understanding the complex interplay between aging, cancer development, longevity, and adaptation. According to MAT, the accumulation of cellular misrepair, including DNA damage, epigenetic alterations, and protein misfolding, drives the progression of aging and cancer. We propose that the rate of cellular misrepair is influenced by a delicate balance between the rates of DNA repair, epigenetic reprogramming, and protein quality control. As the rate of misrepair exceeds the capacity of cellular repair mechanisms, the accumulation of misrepair leads to the emergence of senescence, cancer, and premature aging. Conversely, efficient cellular repair mechanisms can mitigate the effects of misrepair, promoting longevity and adaptation. Our theory integrates insights from aging biology, cancer research, and systems biology to provide a unified explanation for the complex relationships between aging, cancer, and longevity. We identify key regulatory nodes, including telomere length, epigenetic marks, and protein homeostasis, that modulate the rate of cellular misrepair. Our results have implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting the misrepair accumulation pathway to promote healthy aging and prevent cancer.

We investigate the dynamical structure of advective accretion flow around
stationary as well as rotating black holes. For a suitable choice of input
parameters, such as, accretion rate ($\dot {\cal M}$) and angular momentum
($\lambda$), global accretion solution may include a shock wave. The post shock
flow is located at few tens of Schwarzchild radius and it is generally very hot
and dense. This successfully mimics the so called Compton cloud which is
believed to be responsible for emitting hard radiations. Due to the radiative
loss, a significant energy from the accreting matter is removed and the shock
moves forward towards the black hole in order to maintain the pressure balance
across it. We identify the effective area of the parameter space ($\dot {\cal
M} - \lambda$) which allows accretion flows to have some energy dissipation at
the shock $(\Delta {\cal E})$. As the dissipation is increased, the parameter
space is reduced and finally disappears when the dissipation is reached its
critical value. The dissipation has a profound effect on the dynamics of
post-shock flow. By moving forward, an unstable shock whose oscillation causes
Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) in the emitted radiation, will produce
oscillations of high frequency. Such an evolution of QPOs has been observed in
several black hole candidates during their outbursts.

The Void Galaxy Survey aims to investigate star formation properties within the void regions of the universe, where conditions differ significantly from those in galaxy clusters and filaments. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of a sample of galaxies located in these voids, focusing on their stellar mass, star formation rate (SFR), and metallicity. Our methodology involves detailed spectroscopic observations using multi-object spectrographs and photometric data from wide-field surveys. Results indicate that galaxies in voids exhibit lower SFRs compared to those in dense environments, which can be attributed to lower gas densities and higher metallicities affecting star formation efficiency. Additionally, we observe a correlation between metallicity and SFR, suggesting that metal-poor environments may hinder star formation processes. These findings contribute to our understanding of how star formation is influenced by the local cosmic environment, providing insights into galaxy evolution across different scales.

In this study, we examine the correlation between the cold gas content and the stellar population attributes, specifically colours and ages, of early-type galaxies as part of the Atlas3D survey project. Through a comprehensive analysis utilizing integral field spectroscopy, we sought to resolve the longstanding question of how gas availability influences stellar evolution in elliptical and lenticular galaxies. We employed a sample of 260 nearby early-type galaxies, integrating multi-wavelength photometric measurements with cold gas data obtained from atomic and molecular line emissions, the latter detected through CO(1-0) and HI 21cm observations. Our results reveal a substantial variation in cold gas mass, with approximately 22% of our sample exhibiting detectable quantities. Notably, we find that galaxies with significant cold gas reserves demonstrate bluer colours and younger stellar ages compared to their gas-poor counterparts. These findings suggest that cold gas plays a critical role in rejuvenating stellar populations, potentially through episodic star formation events. We further analyze the distribution of cold gas across galaxy morphologies and environments, highlighting a tendency for gas-rich galaxies to reside in less dense environments. Our methodology capitalizes on robust statistical models that account for environmental density, orbital features, and morphological classifications. The insights obtained from this study thus underscore the complex interplay between cold gas presence and the evolutionary pathways of early-type galaxies. This work enhances our understanding of galactic evolution and provides a crucial reference for the theoretical modeling of stellar population dynamics in galaxy formation and transformation scenarios.

This study investigates the optimal placement of virtual inertia within power grids to enhance their stability and resilience against disturbances. Through a series of simulations employing advanced optimization algorithms, we aimed to identify the most effective locations for integrating virtual inertia units across different grid segments. Our methodology involved modeling the grid under various operational conditions and assessing the impact of different virtual inertia placements on damping oscillations and improving transient stability. Results indicate that strategic placement of virtual inertia can significantly mitigate the effects of generator outages and load imbalances, thereby enhancing overall grid performance. Key insights suggest that proximity to heavily loaded or weakly connected areas yields the greatest benefits in terms of system stability. The findings contribute to the development of guidelines for utilities aiming to integrate virtual inertia into their existing infrastructure for improved dynamic behavior and reliability.

We describe the structure of the vacuum states of quiver gauge theories
obtained via dimensional reduction over homogeneous spaces, in the explicit
example of SU(3)-equivariant dimensional reduction of Yang-Mills-Dirac theory
on manifolds of the form M x CP(2). We pay particular attention to the role of
topology of background gauge fields on the internal coset spaces, in this case
U(1) magnetic monopoles and SU(2) instantons on CP(2). The reduction of
Yang-Mills theory induces a quiver gauge theory involving coupled
Yang-Mills-Higgs systems on M with a Higgs potential leading to dynamical
symmetry breaking. The criterion for a ground state of the Higgs potential can
be written as the vanishing of a non-abelian Yang-Mills flux on the quiver
diagram, regarded as a lattice with group elements attached to the links. The
reduction of SU(3)-symmetric fermions yields Dirac fermions on M transforming
under the low-energy gauge group with Yukawa couplings. The fermionic zero
modes on CP(2) yield exactly massless chiral fermions on M, though there is a
unique choice of spin(c) structure on CP(2) for which some of the zero modes
can acquire masses through Yukawa interactions. We work out the spontaneous
symmetry breaking patterns and determine the complete physical particle
spectrum in a number of explicit examples, some of which possess quantum number
assignments qualitatively analogous to the manner in which vector bosons,
quarks and leptons acquire masses in the standard model.

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are the most effective approach to causal
discovery, but in many circumstances it is impossible to conduct RCTs.
Therefore observational studies based on passively observed data are widely
accepted as an alternative to RCTs. However, in observational studies, prior
knowledge is required to generate the hypotheses about the cause-effect
relationships to be tested, hence they can only be applied to problems with
available domain knowledge and a handful of variables. In practice, many data
sets are of high dimensionality, which leaves observational studies out of the
opportunities for causal discovery from such a wealth of data sources. In
another direction, many efficient data mining methods have been developed to
identify associations among variables in large data sets. The problem is,
causal relationships imply associations, but the reverse is not always true.
However we can see the synergy between the two paradigms here. Specifically,
association rule mining can be used to deal with the high-dimensionality
problem while observational studies can be utilised to eliminate non-causal
associations. In this paper we propose the concept of causal rules (CRs) and
develop an algorithm for mining CRs in large data sets. We use the idea of
retrospective cohort studies to detect CRs based on the results of association
rule mining. Experiments with both synthetic and real world data sets have
demonstrated the effectiveness and efficiency of CR mining. In comparison with
the commonly used causal discovery methods, the proposed approach in general is
faster and has better or competitive performance in finding correct or sensible
causes. It is also capable of finding a cause consisting of multiple variables,
a feature that other causal discovery methods do not possess.

This study investigates novel high transverse momentum phenomena observed in hadronic and nuclear collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The primary aim is to elucidate the underlying physics of these events, which are crucial for understanding the behavior of quarks and gluons in extreme conditions. Our approach involves detailed analysis of data collected from proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions at various energies. Problematically, these collisions produce complex event topologies that challenge traditional theoretical models. To address this, we employ advanced computational tools and statistical methods to isolate and characterize the rare events of interest.  Key methodologies include employing machine learning algorithms to identify patterns indicative of novel transverse momentum distributions not captured by current theoretical frameworks. We also conduct a comparative study using Monte Carlo simulations to validate our experimental findings. Results indicate the presence of previously unobserved transverse momentum correlations, particularly in heavy-ion collisions at higher energies, suggesting new degrees of freedom in the quark-gluon plasma phase. These findings underscore the need for further theoretical development to accurately describe these phenomena and pave the way for more precise predictions in high-energy physics.

Our research presents a novel, non-phenomenological model to elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving population growth behaviors. Unlike traditional models rooted in human perceptions and experiences, our approach leverages mathematical modeling to generate testable hypotheses. We integrate demographic, economic, and environmental factors to build a comprehensive framework explaining population dynamics.  We employ a system of interconnected differential equations to model the dynamics of population size, food production, and resource depletion. We derive analytical expressions for the system's steady states, providing insights into conditions leading to population growth, stability, or decline. Furthermore, we explore the influence of various demographic, economic, and environmental parameters on these results.  Our findings reveal intriguing correlations between resource scarcity, food production, and population growth. For instance, we show that when resource availability decreases, food production falls, leading to a decrease in population growth. Conversely, an increase in resource availability can result in increased food production and population growth. Moreover, we identify the optimal level of resource availability required to maintain population stability.  Our model contributes to the ongoing discourse in population dynamics research by offering a non-phenomenological perspective. It provides a solid foundation for further investigation into the interplay of demographic, economic, and environmental factors influencing population growth. Our approach highlights the value of integrating mathematical modeling and data analysis to better understand complex societal issues.

In recent years, the proliferation of optical fiber communication systems has been hindered by the nonlinear effects arising from fiber dispersion and self-phase modulation. These phenomena lead to signal distortion and data transmission errors, ultimately limiting the achievable data rates and reach. To mitigate these issues, several nonlinearity compensation algorithms have been proposed, such as the linear equalization-based methods, the adaptive finite impulse response (FIR) filters, and the artificial neural networks (ANNs). Among these approaches, the utilization of dedicated hardware, specifically fixed point (FP) processors, has shown remarkable benefits.  Our study explores the impact of implementing fixed point hardware for various nonlinearity compensation algorithms in optical fiber communication systems. We examine the performance improvements, hardware resource utilization, and energy efficiency of FP-based implementations of linear equalization, adaptive FIR filters, and ANNs. The simulations are conducted using MATLAB, followed by hardware implementation on a Xilinx Virtex-7 FPGA.  Results show that the FP-based implementations exhibit significant improvements in performance compared to software-implemented versions. For instance, linear equalization achieves up to 3dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio, while the adaptive FIR filter attains a 20% reduction in root-mean-square error. Furthermore, ANNs demonstrate a substantial improvement in signal restoration when implemented on FPGA hardware, with reduced latency and increased throughput.  Moreover, our analysis indicates that the use of fixed point hardware considerably reduces the hardware resource requirements and power consumption, making it an ideal choice for large-scale optical communication networks. However, it is worth noting that the design of efficient algorithms and architectures for FPGA implementation is crucial to fully reap these benefits.  In conclusion, our study emphasizes the importance of utilizing fixed point hardware for optical fiber nonlinearity compensation algorithms to achieve higher performance, lower resource utilization, and improved energy efficiency in optical communication systems.

Let $\mathcal H$ be the Drury-Arveson or Dirichlet space of the unit ball of
$\mathbb C^d$. The weak product $\mathcal H\odot\mathcal H$ of $\mathcal H$ is
the collection of all functions $h$ that can be written as $h=\sum_{n=1}^\infty
f_n g_n$, where $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|\|g_n\|<\infty$. We show that
$\mathcal H\odot\mathcal H$ is contained in the Smirnov class of $\mathcal H$,
i.e. every function in $\mathcal H\odot\mathcal H$ is a quotient of two
multipliers of $\mathcal H$, where the function in the denominator can be
chosen to be cyclic in $\mathcal H$. As a consequence we show that the map
$\mathcal N \to clos_{\mathcal H\odot\mathcal H} \mathcal N$ establishes a 1-1
and onto correspondence between the multiplier invariant subspaces of $\mathcal
H$ and of $\mathcal H\odot\mathcal H$.
  The results hold for many weighted Besov spaces $\mathcal H$ in the unit ball
of $\mathbb C^d$ provided the reproducing kernel has the complete Pick
property. One of our main technical lemmas states that for weighted Besov
spaces $\mathcal H$ that satisfy what we call the multiplier inclusion
condition any bounded column multiplication operator $\mathcal H \to
\oplus_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal H$ induces a bounded row multiplication operator
$\oplus_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal H \to \mathcal H$. For the Drury-Arveson space
$H^2_d$ this leads to an alternate proof of the characterization of
interpolating sequences in terms of weak separation and Carleson measure
conditions.

The High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) is a next-generation particle accelerator that requires highly efficient and reliable detectors to achieve its unprecedented luminosity. Anode-resistive Micromegas (ARMs) are a type of gas-based detector technology that has shown great promise in recent years due to their high radiation tolerance, low power consumption, and excellent spatial resolution. This study aims to investigate the performance of ARMs in the context of the HL-LHC.   The HL-LHC will operate at a luminosity 10 times higher than its predecessor, requiring detectors that can withstand the intense radiation and high-energy particle flux. Traditional detector technologies, such as silicon-based trackers, are already nearing their limits in terms of radiation tolerance and power consumption. In contrast, ARMs offer a promising solution, with their resistive anode design allowing for a more efficient and radiation-hardened detection mechanism.   This study aimed to investigate the performance of ARMs in the context of the HL-LHC, focusing on their radiation tolerance, spatial resolution, and power consumption. We also explored the potential benefits and challenges of integrating ARMs into a large-scale detector system.   We used a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and experimental measurements to evaluate the performance of ARMs in a simulated HL-LHC environment. We designed a custom ARM detector module and tested its performance in a radiation chamber, using a 50 GeV electron beam to simulate the high-energy particle flux expected at the HL-LHC.  Key findings Our results show that ARMs demonstrate excellent radiation tolerance, with a radiation-induced signal degradation of less than 10% at 10^15 ions/cm^2. The spatial resolution of the ARMs was found to be comparable to that of traditional silicon-based trackers, with a resolution of 100 μm at 1 GeV. Additionally, our measurements indicate that ARMs can operate efficiently at low power consumption, with a power consumption of less than 1 W per detector module.   The results of this study demonstrate the promising performance of ARMs in the context of the HL-LHC. While there are still challenges to be addressed, such as the development of larger-scale detector modules and improved radiation hardening techniques, ARMs offer a viable solution for the next generation of particle detectors.

We study the role of the coronal magnetic field configuration of an active
region in determining the propagation direction of a coronal mass ejection
(CME). The CME occurred in the active region 11944 (S09W01) near the disk
center on 2014 January 7 and was associated with an X1.2 flare. A new CME
reconstruction procedure based on a polarimetric technique is adopted, which
shows that the CME changed its propagation direction by around 28$^\circ$ in
latitude within 2.5 R$_\odot$ and 43$^\circ$ in longitude within 6.5 R$_\odot$
with respect to the CME source region. This significant non-radial motion is
consistent with the finding of M$\ddot{o}$stl et al. (2015). We use nonlinear
force-free field (NLFFF) and potential field source surface (PFSS)
extrapolation methods to determine the configurations of the coronal magnetic
field. We also calculate the magnetic energy density distributions at different
heights based on the extrapolations. Our results show that the active region
coronal magnetic field has a strong influence on the CME propagation direction.
This is consistent with the "channelling" by the active region coronal magnetic
field itself, rather than deflection by nearby structures. These results
indicate that the active region coronal magnetic field configuration has to be
taken into account in order to determine CME propagation direction correctly.

Soft goals, defined as objectives with imprecise, vague, or subjective criteria, are common in real-world systems. While some approaches exist to reason about or plan with soft goals, these methods often suffer from complexity and computational overhead. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that compiles soft goals away into their more precise counterparts. Our methodology leverages logical reasoning, constraint propagation, and fuzzy logic to automatically transform soft goals into a set of crisp sub-goals. We evaluated our method on several benchmark problems, demonstrating significant performance improvements compared to existing methods for soft goal reasoning. Our findings suggest that the ability to automatically compile soft goals can lead to more effective and efficient decision making in complex systems. The implications of this research extend beyond goal-driven reasoning systems, as the proposed techniques can be applied to various domains requiring imprecise or subjective information processing. Future work includes investigating how to handle more complex soft goals, such as those involving time or uncertainty, and integrating the proposed methods into larger planning and reasoning frameworks.

Using random-phase approximation spin-fluctuation theory, we study the
influence of the hybridization between iron $d$-orbitals and pnictide
$p$-orbitals on the superconducting pairing state in iron-based
superconductors. The calculations are performed for a 16-orbital Hubbard-Hund
tight-binding model of BaFe$_2$As$_2$ that includes the As-$p$ orbital degrees
