the Coulomb interaction between the protons and the resulting isospin-symmetry
breaking. The smallness of its value is related to the form of the transition
density, due to translational invariance. The calculated values of E1 and ISD
strength carried by the IS-LED depend on the effective interaction used.
Attention is drawn to the possibility that in N-not-equal-Z nuclei this
distinct mode of IS surface vibration can develop as such or mix strongly with
skin modes and thus influence the pygmy dipole strength as well as the ISD
strength function. In general, theoretical models currently in use may be unfit
to predict its precise position and strength, if at all its existence.

In this work, we propose a new approach to polynomial Lyapunov function synthesis through the application of linear relaxations to polynomial positivity conditions. Polynomial Lyapunov functions (PLFs) have been extensively used to ensure the stability of nonlinear systems, but their synthesis remains a challenging problem. We address this challenge by employing the Sum-of-Squares (SOS) method to relax the polynomial positivity conditions that arise in the Lyapunov equation. By formulating the problem as a semi-definite programming (SDP) problem, we are able to convert polynomial equations into tractable linear matrix inequalities (LMIs), thus enabling the use of efficient solvers.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to a set of benchmark nonlinear systems, including the well-known Chang system. Our results show a significant reduction in the conservatism often associated with classical Lyapunov function methods, as well as improved scalability. Furthermore, we show that our method is able to handle more complex nonlinear systems than previously possible with polynomial Lyapunov functions.  The key ideas of our approach include the use of SOS programming to relax polynomial positivity conditions, the conversion of polynomial equations into LMIs, and the application of efficient solvers to the resulting SDPs. The methodology is also shown to be effective in addressing some of the limitations of classical polynomial Lyapunov functions, such as conservatism and scalability. Overall, our results represent an important step forward in the design and analysis of polynomial Lyapunov functions for nonlinear systems.  Our approach provides a novel way to synthesize polynomial Lyapunov functions by relaxing polynomial positivity conditions, enabling the use of efficient solvers, and reducing conservatism and scalability issues. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through the synthesis of Lyapunov functions for several benchmark nonlinear systems. The proposed methodology is a significant contribution towards the design and analysis of polynomial Lyapunov functions for nonlinear systems.

This research investigates the broadband radio polarimetry of the Fornax A galaxy, focusing on the presence of depolarized patches believed to be caused by advected thermal material from NGC 1316. The objective of this study is to analyze the nature and characteristics of these depolarized patches to better understand the underlying mechanisms responsible for such phenomena. The methodology involves conducting radio polarimetric observations using broadband techniques to study the polarization properties of Fornax A in detail. The key findings reveal the existence of significant depolarized patches in the galaxy that are likely linked to the thermal material from NGC 1316, indicating a complex interplay between the two sources. Through this research, valuable insights into the interaction between Fornax A and NGC 1316 are gained, shedding light on the dynamics of thermal material advection and its impact on the polarimetric properties of galaxies. In conclusion, this study contributes to enhancing our knowledge of galaxy evolution processes and the role of thermal material advection in shaping the observed polarimetric features in radio galaxies like Fornax A.

We investigate the finite temperature expectation values of the charge and
current densities for a massive fermionic field with nonzero chemical
potential, $\mu$, in the geometry of a straight cosmic string with a magnetic
flux running along its axis. These densities are decomposed into the vacuum
expectation values and contributions coming from the particles and
antiparticles. The charge density is an even periodic function of the magnetic
flux with the period equal to the quantum flux and an odd function of the
chemical potential. The only nonzero component of the current density
corresponds to the azimuthal current. The latter is an odd periodic function of
the magnetic flux and an even function of the chemical potential. At high
temperatures, the parts in the charge density and azimuthal current induced by
the planar angle deficit and magnetic flux are exponentially small. The
asymptotic behavior at low temperatures crucially depends whether the value
$|\mu|$ is larger or smaller than the mass of the field quanta, $m$. For
$|\mu|<m$ the charge density and the contributions into the azimuthal current
coming from the particles and antiparticles are exponentially suppressed at low
temperatures. In the case $|\mu|>m$, the charge and current densities receive
two contributions coming from the vacuum expectation values and from particles
or antiparticles (depending on the sign of chemical potential). At large
distances from the string the latter exhibits a damping oscillatory behavior
with the amplitude inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

In cloud storage systems, hot data is usually replicated over multiple nodes
in order to accommodate simultaneous access by multiple users as well as
increase the fault tolerance of the system. Recent cloud storage research has
proposed using availability codes, which is a special class of erasure codes,
as a more storage efficient way to store hot data. These codes enable data
recovery from multiple, small disjoint groups of servers. The number of the
recovery groups is referred to as the availability and the size of each group
as the locality of the code. Until now, we have very limited knowledge on how
code locality and availability affect data access time. Data download from
these systems involves multiple fork-join queues operating in-parallel, making
the analysis of access time a very challenging problem. In this paper, we
present an approximate analysis of data access time in storage systems that
employ simplex codes, which are an important and in certain sense optimal class
of availability codes. We consider and compare three strategies in assigning
download requests to servers; first one aggressively exploits the storage
availability for faster download, second one implements only load balancing,
and the last one employs storage availability only for hot data download
without incurring any negative impact on the cold data download.

In this work, we investigate the application of random aerial beamforming for underlay cognitive radio systems, specifically addressing scenarios with exposed secondary users. Our study aims to enhance spectrum efficiency while minimizing interference to primary users, thus facilitating improved communication for secondary users. We propose a novel methodology that employs aerial platforms capable of dynamic beamforming to effectively manage the spatial distribution of signal power. Through extensive simulation analyses, we quantify the performance gains in terms of throughput and reliability for secondary users under various environmental conditions and user distributions.   Our results demonstrate that the random aerial beamforming technique significantly increases the probability of successful transmission for secondary users while ensuring compliance with the interference constraints imposed by primary users. We identify optimal parameters that maximize coverage and optimize energy efficiency across diverse operational scenarios. Additionally, we delve into the trade-offs between system complexity and performance enhancement, offering insights into practical implementations of our framework in real-world cognitive radio networks.   The findings underscore the crucial role of aerial beamforming in leveraging underutilized spectrum, particularly in environments where secondary users face challenges due to primary user presence. We contribute to the ongoing discourse within cognitive radio research by presenting a comprehensive analysis of random aerial beamforming, paving the way for future developments in smart and adaptive communication systems that prioritize coexistence among users in crowded frequency bands.

This research focuses on the development and optimization of distillation techniques for separating hydrogen isotopes, specifically deuterium (D) and tritium (T), with the aim of producing a polarized deuterium target suitable for high-energy physics experiments. The study employs advanced distillation methods such as pressure swing adsorption and vapor compression distillation to achieve high purity and efficient separation rates. Key findings indicate that optimized conditions significantly enhance the purity of separated isotopes, with D/T ratios exceeding 99.9%. The results demonstrate that these distillation processes can produce deuterium targets with isotopic purity and concentration necessary for polarized deuteron beam production. This work provides a robust foundation for future experiments requiring highly purified hydrogen isotopes for applications such as nuclear physics studies and radioactive ion beam facilities.

Matter/antimatter (MAM) pair production from the vacuum through intense
electric fields has been investigated theoretically for nearly a century. This
history is reviewed and proposals of MAM for intra-solar system and
interstellar propulsion systems are examined. The quantum mechanical foundation
of MAM production was developed by MAM production occurs when the electric
field strength is above the critical value at which the fields become
non-linear with self-interactions (known as the Schwinger limit).MAM production
occurs when the electric field strength is above the critical value at which
the fields become non-linear with self-interactions (known as the Schwinger
limit). As the energy density of lasers approach the critical strength of 10^16
V/cm, the feasibility and functionality of electron-positron pair production
has received growing interest. Current laser intensities are approaching within
1 order of magnitude of the Schwinger limit. Processes for lowering the
critical energy density below the Schwinger limit through additional quantum
mechanical effects have been explored. One under study at the U. of Connecticut
and the U. of Duisburg-Essen is pulsation of inhomogeneous electric fields
within a carrier wave. Another is via enhancement of quantum effects by
addition of a magnetic field parallel to the electric field. Magnetic field
enhancement to quark/anti-quark production through chiral symmetry breaking
effects in QCD was considered by J. Preskill in the 1980's. S. Pyo and D. Page
showed in 2007 that parallel magnetic fields enhance electron/positron
production via an analogous QED effect. MAM production as a highly efficient
fuel source for intra solar system and interstellar propulsion was proposed by
D. Crow in 1983. The viability of this method of propulsion will be studied,
especially from the parallel electric and magnetic field approach.

We consider a non-standard generalized model of gravity coupled to a neutral
scalar "inflaton" as well as to the fields of the electroweak bosonic sector.
The essential new ingredient is employing two alternative non-Riemannian
space-time volume-forms (non-Riemannian volume elements, or covariant
integration measure densitities) independent of the space-time metric. The
latter are defined in terms of auxiliary antisymmentric tensor gauge fields,
which although not introducing any additional propagating degrees of freedom,
trigger a series of important features such as: (i) appearance of two
infinitely large flat regions of the effective "inflaton" potential in the
corresponding Einstein frame with vastly different scales corresponding to the
"early" and "late" epochs of Universe's evolution; (ii) dynamical generation of
Higgs-like spontaneous symmetry breaking effective potential for the
SU(2)\times U(1) iso-doublet electroweak scalar in the late universe, whereas
it remains massless in the "early" universe. Next, to stabilize the
quintessential dynamics, we introduce in addition a coupling of the "inflaton"
to Gauss-Bonnet gravitational term. The latter leads to the following radical
change of the form of the total effective "inflaton" potential: its flat
regions are now converted into a local maximum corresponding to a "hill-top"
inflation in the "early" universe with no spontaneous breakdown of electroweak
gauge symmetry and, correspondigly, into a local minimum corresponding to the
"late" universe evolution with a very small value of the dark energy and with
operating Higgs mechanism.

The Space-Time SINR (Signal-to-Interference plus Noise Ratio) Random Graph is a mathematical model used to describe the propagation of radio signals in urban environments. In this context, the optimal paths for wireless networks to achieve reliable communication are crucial for efficient data transmission. However, the complex interactions between signal strength, interference, and noise in urban settings make it challenging to determine the optimal paths.   This study aims to investigate the optimal paths on the Space-Time SINR Random Graph, focusing on the impact of urban environment characteristics on network performance. The researchers employed a combination of simulation-based modeling and graph theory to analyze the network's structure and identify the optimal paths.   The simulation results show that the optimal paths are highly dependent on the urban environment, with buildings, trees, and other obstacles significantly affecting signal strength and interference levels. The researchers also found that the optimal paths tend to follow the edges of the graph with the highest SINR values, indicating that the network should prioritize the edges with the best signal-to-interference ratio.   The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of wireless networks in urban environments. By understanding the impact of urban environment characteristics on network performance, network planners can optimize the placement of base stations and the routing of data transmission to achieve reliable and efficient communication. The results of this study can be applied to various urban environments, including cities with different densities of buildings, trees, and other obstacles.

We present a novel approach for fault detection and classification in a plasma etch reactor using virtual sensors, aiming to enhance process reliability and minimize downtime in semiconductor manufacturing. Our methodology integrates data-driven modeling and machine learning techniques to create virtual sensors that provide real-time estimates of key process variables, which are otherwise difficult to measure directly. We employed a combination of historical data analysis and simulation-based techniques to establish a robust baseline of normal operating conditions.   We then developed a fault classification framework utilizing support vector machines and decision trees, trained on data collected during both normal and fault scenarios. We systematically examined various fault types, including hardware malfunctions and process anomalies, evaluating the system's response to different disturbances. Our results demonstrate a detection accuracy of over 90% for the most common fault types, significantly reducing false positives compared to traditional methods. In addition, we identified specific fault signatures that enable quicker diagnosis and targeted intervention strategies.  By implementing our virtual sensor-based system, we successfully improved the fault tolerance of plasma etch processes, thus contributing to higher yield rates and reduced operational costs. Our findings underscore the potential of leveraging virtual sensors and machine learning in the semiconductor sector, offering a scalable and efficient solution to one of the industry's critical challenges. Future work will focus on fine-tuning the classification algorithms and expanding the framework to accommodate more complex fault scenarios and multidimensional data inputs.

We evaluate the Hadamard function and the vacuum expectation value of the
current density for a massive complex scalar field in the generalized geometry
of a straight cosmic string with a finite core enclosing an arbitrary
distributed magnetic flux along the string axis. For the interior geometry, a
general cylindrically symmetric static metric tensor is used with finite
support. In the region outside the core, both the Hadamard function and the
current density are decomposed into the idealized zero-thickness cosmic string
and core-induced contributions. The only nonzero component corresponds to the
azimuthal current. The zero-thickness part of the latter is a periodic function
of the magnetic flux inside the core, with the period equal to the quantum
flux. As a consequence of the direct interaction of the quantum field with the
magnetic field inside the penetrable core, the core-induced contribution, in
general, is not a periodic function of the flux. In addition, the vacuum
current, in general, is not a monotonic function of the distance from the
string and may change the sign. For a general model of the core interior, we
also evaluate the magnetic fields generated by the vacuum current. As
applications of the general results, we have considered an impenetrable core
modeled by Robin boundary condition, a core with the Minkowski-like interior
and a core with a constant positive curvature space. Various exactly solvable
distributions of the magnetic flux are discussed.

This research investigates the limitations of refining multi-valued partial context-free language (CFL) functions with single-valued functions, focusing on the intricacies within the computational theory domain. The study aims to explore whether every multi-valued partial CFL function can be refined into a single-valued function, thereby preserving the computational properties while potentially simplifying their implementation.  To achieve this, the methodology involves analyzing various multi-valued partial CFL functions through theoretical proofs and computational simulations. Key findings reveal that not all multi-valued partial CFL functions can be fully refined into single-valued functions. Specifically, certain multi-valued functions exhibit characteristics that cannot be accurately captured by single-valued representations, highlighting inherent complexities in their computational behavior.  The research concludes that there exist multi-valued partial CFL functions that remain fundamentally different from any equivalent single-valued function, underscoring the importance of maintaining the multi-valued nature of these functions in certain contexts. This finding has implications for the design and application of computational models in areas requiring precise and nuanced handling of data.

We present the result of a study of the X-ray emission from the Galactic
Centre (GC) Molecular Clouds (MC) within 15 arcmin from Sgr A*. We use
XMM-Newton data (about 1.2 Ms of observation time) spanning about 8 years. The
MC spectra show all the features characteristic of reflection: i) intense Fe
Kalpha, with EW of about 0.7-1 keV, and the associated Kbeta line; ii) flat
power law continuum and iii) a significant Fe K edge (tau~0.1-0.3). The diffuse
low ionisation Fe K emission follows the MC distribution, nevertheless not all
MC are Fe K emitters. The long baseline monitoring allows the characterisation
of the temporal evolution of the MC emission. A complex pattern of variations
is shown by the different MC, with some having constant Fe K emission, some
increasing and some decreasing. In particular, we observe an apparent
super-luminal motion of a light front illuminating a Molecular nebula. This
might be due to a source outside the MC (such as Sgr A* or a bright and long
outburst of a X-ray binary), while it cannot be due to low energy cosmic rays
or a source located inside the cloud. We also observe a decrease of the X-ray
emission from G0.11-0.11, behaviour similar to the one of Sgr B2. The line
intensities, clouds dimensions, columns densities and positions with respect to
Sgr A*, are consistent with being produced by the same Sgr A* flare. The
required high luminosity (about 1.5~10^39 erg/s) can hardly be produced by a
binary system, while it is in agreement with a flare of Sgr A* fading about 100
years ago. The low intensity of the Fe K emission coming from the 50 and the 20
km/s MC places an upper limit of 10^36 erg/s to the mean luminosity of Sgr A*
in the last 60-90 years. The Fe K emission and variations from these MC might
have been produced by a single flare of Sgr A*.

Understanding the interaction between astrophysical ices and cosmic rays is essential for comprehending various cosmic phenomena. The infrared complex refractive index of these ices plays a crucial role in this interaction.   This research aims to investigate the effects of simulated cosmic rays on the infrared complex refractive index of astrophysical ices in laboratory conditions.   Laboratory simulations were conducted to expose astrophysical ices to cosmic ray analogs while monitoring changes in their infrared complex refractive index using spectroscopic techniques. Different types of ices commonly found in interstellar environments were utilized in the experiments.  Key findings The results indicate that the exposure of astrophysical ices to simulated cosmic rays led to significant modifications in their infrared complex refractive index. The changes observed in the refractive index provide valuable insights into the chemical processes induced by cosmic ray interactions with interstellar ices.   This study demonstrates the importance of studying the infrared properties of astrophysical ices under simulated cosmic ray exposure to better understand the complex dynamics of interstellar environments. The findings contribute to the broader field of astrochemistry and aid in advancing our knowledge of the physical and chemical processes occurring in space.

Context. The Cygnus OB2 association, the central engine of the Cygnus X
star-forming region, is the subject of an extensive INTEGRAL Key Project that
will accumulate 6Ms of observations. Analysis of 2Ms of observations by De
Becker and co-workers provides the most sensitive limit yet obtained on hard
X-ray emission from the cluster. Aims. We investigate the X-ray emission in the
20-40 keV band expected from the flaring low-mass stellar population in Cygnus
OB2. We discuss whether such emission needs to be considered in the
interpretation of existing and future X-ray observations of the region, and
whether such observations might provide insight into the high-energy processes
on low-mass pre-main sequence stars. Methods. The total hard X-ray flux from
low-mass stars is estimated by assuming the observed soft X-ray emission stems
from a superposition of flares. We further assume the ratio of hard X-ray to
soft X-ray emission is described by a scaling found for solar flares by Isola
and co-workers. Results. We estimate the low-mass stellar hard X-ray flux in
the 20-40 keV band to lie in the range ~2x10^31-6x10^32 erg/s and discuss some
potential biases that might affect this result. Conclusions. Hard X-ray
emission could lie at a level not much below the current observed flux upper
limits for Cygnus OB2. If this emission could be detected, it would provide
insight into the hard X-ray production of large flares on pre-main sequence
stars. We highlight the penetrating power of hard X-rays from low-mass stellar
populations as a possible pointer to our Galaxy's hidden star-forming clusters
and super-clusters using more sensitive observations from future missions.

We conducted a comprehensive review of cosmic-ray electrons, focusing on the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) data and observations. Our analysis aimed to shed light on the detection and characterization of these elusive particles, which are believed to originate from various astrophysical sources. Through a thorough examination of the Fermi-LAT data, we identified several key sources of cosmic-ray electrons, including the Galactic Center, the Crab Nebula, and active galactic nuclei. Our results indicate that these sources are capable of producing a significant number of electrons, which can be detected by Fermi-LAT. We also explored the implications of these findings, including the potential for these sources to produce gamma-ray bursts and the role of cosmic-ray electrons in the formation of the intergalactic medium. Utilizing a combination of Bayesian inference and Monte Carlo simulations, we developed a novel framework for the detection of cosmic-ray electrons in Fermi-LAT data. Our approach enabled us to accurately model the expected electron flux and to distinguish between different astrophysical sources. The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between cosmic-ray electrons and the surrounding environment, and have significant implications for future studies of high-energy astrophysics.

Convective driving, the mechanism originally proposed by Brickhill (1991,
1983) for pulsating white dwarf stars, has gained general acceptance as the
generic linear instability mechanism in DAV and DBV white dwarfs. This physical
mechanism naturally leads to a nonlinear formulation, reproducing the observed
light curves of many pulsating white dwarfs. This numerical model can also
provide information on the average depth of a star's convection zone and the
inclination angle of its pulsation axis. In this paper, we give two sets of
results of nonlinear light curve fits to data on the DBV GD 358. Our first fit
is based on data gathered in 2006 by the Whole Earth Telescope (WET); this data
set was multiperiodic, containing at least 12 individual modes. Our second fit
utilizes data obtained in 1996, when GD 358 underwent a dramatic change in
excited frequencies accompanied by a rapid increase in fractional amplitude;
during this event it was essentially monoperiodic. We argue that GD 358's
convection zone was much thinner in 1996 than in 2006, and we interpret this as
a result of a short-lived increase in its surface temperature. In addition, we
find strong evidence of oblique pulsation using two sets of evenly split
triplets in the 2006 data. This marks the first time that oblique pulsation has
been identified in a variable white dwarf star.

An increasingly wide range of artificial intelligence applications rely on
syntactic information to process and extract meaning from natural language text
or speech, with constituent trees being one of the most widely used syntactic
formalisms. To produce these phrase-structure representations from sentences in
natural language, shift-reduce constituent parsers have become one of the most
efficient approaches. Increasing their accuracy and speed is still one of the
main objectives pursued by the research community so that artificial
intelligence applications that make use of parsing outputs, such as machine
translation or voice assistant services, can improve their performance. With
this goal in mind, we propose in this article a novel non-binary shift-reduce
algorithm for constituent parsing. Our parser follows a classical bottom-up
strategy but, unlike others, it straightforwardly creates non-binary branchings
with just one Reduce transition, instead of requiring prior binarization or a
sequence of binary transitions, allowing its direct application to any language
without the need of further resources such as percolation tables. As a result,
it uses fewer transitions per sentence than existing transition-based
constituent parsers, becoming the fastest such system and, as a consequence,
speeding up downstream applications. Using static oracle training and greedy
search, the accuracy of this novel approach is on par with state-of-the-art
transition-based constituent parsers and outperforms all top-down and bottom-up
greedy shift-reduce systems on the Wall Street Journal section from the English
Penn Treebank and the Penn Chinese Treebank. Additionally, we develop a dynamic
oracle for training the proposed transition-based algorithm, achieving further
improvements in both benchmarks and obtaining the best accuracy to date on the
Penn Chinese Treebank among greedy shift-reduce parsers.

The main objective of this work is to determine the character of orbits of
stars moving in the meridional $(R,z)$ plane of an axially symmetric
time-independent disk galaxy model with a central massive nucleus and an
additional spherical dark matter halo component. In particular, we try to
reveal the influence of the scale length of the dark matter halo on the
different families of orbits of stars, by monitoring how the percentage of
chaotic orbits, as well as the percentages of orbits of the main regular
resonant families evolve when this parameter varies. The smaller alignment
index (SALI) was computed by numerically integrating the equations of motion as
well as the variational equations to extensive samples of orbits in order to
distinguish safely between ordered and chaotic motion. In addition, a method
based on the concept of spectral dynamics that utilizes the Fourier transform
of the time series of each coordinate is used to identify the various families
of regular orbits and also to recognize the secondary resonances that bifurcate
from them. Our numerical computations reveal that when the dark matter halo is
highly concentrated, that is when the scale length has low values the vast
majority of star orbits move in regular orbits, while on the other hand in less
concentrated dark matter halos the percentage of chaos increases significantly.
We also compared our results with early related work.

Supersymmetry is a theoretical framework that extends the Standard Model of particle physics by introducing new particles called supersymmetric partners. These partners are predicted to have the same quantum numbers as their Standard Model counterparts but differ in spin by a half unit. Measuring supersymmetry is an ongoing effort in the physics community due to its potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of particle physics and solve the hierarchy problem.  The objective of this study is to review recent experimental results in measuring supersymmetric particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The LHC is a proton-proton collider that operates at energies up to 13 TeV, providing ample opportunity to search for and discover supersymmetric particles. We begin by discussing the current status of supersymmetry searches at the LHC, focusing on the most stringent limits set by experiments such as the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Subsequently, we explore the latest experimental results from these collaborations, including searches for supersymmetric partners of the top quark, the Higgs boson, and the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP).  Our analysis indicates that, although no definitive evidence for supersymmetry has been found, the searches conducted at the LHC have set stringent upper limits on the masses of supersymmetric particles. The latest results from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations suggest that supersymmetric partners of the top quark and Higgs boson have masses below 1.5 TeV, while the LSP has a mass below 1.4 TeV. These results place significant pressure on the theoretical framework, pushing theorists to seek new solutions to address the hierarchy problem.  In conclusion, the ongoing search for supersymmetry at the LHC represents a critical area of research in particle physics. While no supersymmetric particles have been discovered yet, the experiments have set stringent mass limits, which provide crucial constraints for further theoretical investigations. As the LHC continues its operations and upcoming experiments like the FCC-hh come online, the search for supersymmetry is expected to reach a new level of sensitivity, increasing the likelihood of discovering these elusive particles.

The thermalization of hot carriers and phonons gives direct insight into the
scattering processes that mediate electrical and thermal transport. Obtaining
the scattering rates for both hot carriers and phonons currently requires
multiple measurements with incommensurate timescales. Here, transient
extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) spectroscopy on the silicon 2p core level at 100 eV
is used to measure hot carrier and phonon thermalization in Si(100) from tens
of femtoseconds to 200 ps following photoexcitation of the indirect transition
to the {\Delta} valley at 800 nm. The ground state XUV spectrum is first
theoretically predicted using a combination of a single plasmon pole model and
the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) with density functional theory (DFT). The
excited state spectrum is predicted by incorporating the electronic effects of
photo-induced state-filling, broadening, and band-gap renormalization into the
ground state XUV spectrum. A time-dependent lattice deformation and expansion
is also required to describe the excited state spectrum. The kinetics of these
structural components match the kinetics of phonons excited from the
electron-phonon and phonon-phonon scattering processes following
photoexcitation. Separating the contributions of electronic and structural
effects on the transient XUV spectra allows the carrier population, the
population of phonons involved in inter- and intra-valley electron-phonon
scattering, and the population of phonons involved in phonon-phonon scattering
to be quantified as a function of delay time.

We explore various aspects of the motion of heavy quarks in strongly-coupled
gauge theories, employing the AdS/CFT correspondence. Building on earlier work
by Mikhailov, we study the dispersion relation and energy loss of an
accelerating finite-mass quark in N=4 super-Yang-Mills, both in vacuum and in
the presence of a thermal plasma. In the former case, we notice that the
application of an external force modifies the dispersion relation. In the
latter case, we find in particular that when a static heavy quark is
accelerated by an external force, its rate of energy loss is initially
insensitive to the plasma, and there is a delay before this rate approaches the
value derived previously from the analysis of stationary or late-time
configurations.
  Following up on work by Herzog et al., we also consider the evolution of a
quark and antiquark as they separate from one another after formation, learning
how the AdS/CFT setup distinguishes between the singlet and adjoint
configurations, and locating the transition to the stage where the deceleration
of each particle is properly accounted for by a constant friction coefficient.
Additionally, we examine the way in which the energy of a quark-antiquark pair
moving jointly through the plasma scales with the quark mass. We find that the
velocity-dependence of the screening length is drastically modified in the
ultra-relativistic region, and is comparable with that of the transition
distance mentioned above.

Extensive-form games (EFGs) are a class of strategic games in which players make decisions in a sequential manner and have incomplete information. One crucial aspect of EFGs is their timeability, that is, the capability of being played under uncertainty regarding the time elapsed between actions. This abstract outlines the background of EFGs and their timeability concept, the objective of investigating the timeability of EFGs, the methodology employed, key findings, and the conclusion drawn from the research.   EFGs have attracted significant interest in various fields such as economics, game theory, computer science, and artificial intelligence. Unlike simple extensive games, EFGs include information about the entire history of the game, which makes them more complex and challenging. One practical issue when dealing with EFGs is their timeability.   The objective of this research is to study the timeability of EFGs and the factors affecting their playability under uncertainty in time. The analysis focuses on both theoretical and empirical aspects.   The study begins by reviewing existing literature on EFGs and their timeability. Subsequently, it examines several theoretical models, including static and dynamic timeability concepts. The empirical investigation utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to analyze the timeability of a well-known EFG, the Rabbit Hunt game, and its relationship with the game's complexity and randomness.  Key findings Results show that the static timeability of EFGs can be estimated based on the number of possible information sets, while dynamic timeability is influenced by the game's complexity and randomness. The simulation results demonstrate that increasing complexity and randomness significantly affect the game's timeability, making it increasingly difficult for players to decide within a given time constraint.   Understanding the timeability of EFGs is essential for practical applications and theoretical analyses. This research contributes to the literature by exploring the theoretical and empirical aspects of EFG timeability, providing insights into the factors that influence their playability under uncertainty in time. The findings can be valuable for game designers, economists, and researchers in the field of game theory and artificial intelligence.

We present our research on the enumeration of alternating sign triangles using a novel constant term approach. Alternating sign triangles stand as intricate arrangements of integers forming triangular shapes with strict constraints on their entries. The problem we address is the efficient counting of such structures while considering the symmetries inherent in their formation. Our study aims to provide a systematic method to enumerate these triangles, taking into account their alternating sign properties and the various possible configurations they can exhibit.  Through our investigations, we have successfully developed a methodology that leverages the concept of constant terms to derive formulas for enumerating alternating sign triangles. By focusing on the symmetries and constraints of these structures, we have achieved significant results in simplifying the enumeration process. Our approach involves systematically analyzing the possible arrangements of integers in alternating sign triangles, incorporating combinatorial methods to account for various symmetries and constraints present in these configurations. The outcomes of our work contribute to a deeper understanding of the enumeration of alternating sign triangles and provide a rigorous framework for future studies in this area.

Motivated by the nickel valence controversy in the perovskite nickelate
RNiO_3, we consider a one-dimensional underscreened Kondo chain consisting of
alternating spin-1 ("nickel") and electron ("oxygen") sites, which in addition
to the usual electron hopping and spin-spin interaction between the S=1 spin
and the electron also contains a spin mediated electron hopping term. Using the
density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG), we obtained the zero temperature
phase diagram of the model, as well as various correlation functions in each
phase. Importantly, for a certain range of parameters the model exhibits a
quasi-long-range spiral (QS) order. To understand the DMRG results, we
construct a mean-field theory based on a Schwinger fermion decomposition of the
S=1 spins, from which we argue that the QS phase corresponds to a phase in
proximity to the spin Bose metal state proposed by D. N. Sheng, O. I.
Motrunich, and M. P. A. Fisher [Phys. Rev. B 79, 205112 (2009)]. Notably, we
find no evidence for a phase with the symmetry of "nickel"-centered charge
order, which has been argued to arise due to site-selective Kondo screening of
half the S=1 spins, and suggest that order of this type occurs only due to an
additional energy gain from spontaneous lattice distortions, not present in
this model.

This study investigates the binary systems RX J0513.1+0851 and RX J0539.9+0956, focusing on their rapid rotation and spectroscopic characteristics. Through comprehensive spectral analysis, we identified these stars as rapidly rotating spectroscopic binaries, indicating significant angular momentum transfer within their systems. The analysis revealed that both systems exhibit high orbital velocities, which are consistent with predictions from tidal interactions. We employed advanced modeling techniques to estimate the mass and rotation rates of the stars, finding RX J0513.1+0851 to be more rapidly rotating than RX J0539.9+0956. Key insights include the detection of Rossby waves in the stellar surface, indicative of turbulent convection zones. These findings contribute to our understanding of the dynamical processes driving the evolution of young, rapidly rotating stars in binary configurations.

We present the results of a study investigating the sizes and morphologies of
redshift 4 < z < 8 galaxies in the CANDELS GOODS-S, HUDF and HUDF parallel
fields. Based on non-parametric measurements and incorporating a careful
treatment of measurement biases, we quantify the typical size of galaxies at
each redshift as the peak of the log-normal size distribution, rather than the
arithmetic mean size. Parameterizing the evolution of galaxy half-light radius
as $r_{50} \propto (1+z)^n$, we find $n = -0.20 \pm 0.26$ at bright
UV-luminosities ($0.3L_{*(z=3)} < L < L_*$) and $n = -0.47 \pm 0.62$ at faint
luminosities ($0.12L_* < L < 0.3L_*$). Furthermore, simulations based on
artificially redshifting our z~4 galaxy sample show that we cannot reject the
null hypothesis of no size evolution. We show that this result is caused by a
combination of the size-dependent completeness of high-redshift galaxy samples
and the underestimation of the sizes of the largest galaxies at a given epoch.
To explore the evolution of galaxy morphology we first compare asymmetry
measurements to those from a large sample of simulated single S\'ersic
profiles, in order to robustly categorise galaxies as either `smooth' or
`disturbed'. Comparing the disturbed fraction amongst bright ($M_{UV} \leq
-20$) galaxies at each redshift to that obtained by artificially redshifting
our z~4 galaxy sample, while carefully matching the size and UV-luminosity
distributions, we find no clear evidence for evolution in galaxy morphology
over the redshift interval 4 < z < 8. Therefore, based on our results, a bright
($M_{UV} \leq -20$) galaxy at z~6 is no more likely to be measured as
`disturbed' than a comparable galaxy at z~4, given the current observational
constraints.

Our study delves into the benefits of implementing a PeV scale left-right symmetry within theoretical physics frameworks. Through an in-depth analysis, we have identified that such a symmetrical structure not only offers elegant solutions to long-standing challenges within the Standard Model but also provides a compelling explanation for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. Our investigation demonstrates that by embracing this symmetry at the PeV scale, we can potentially offer a unifying explanation for phenomena such as neutrino masses, dark matter, and the hierarchy problem. Furthermore, our results indicate that a PeV scale left-right symmetry could pave the way for a more comprehensive understanding of fundamental interactions, pushing the boundaries of our current knowledge in particle physics. Employing a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, we showcase the viability and implications of this framework, shedding light on its potential to revolutionize our understanding of the universe at its most fundamental levels. Overall, our work highlights the significance of PeV scale left-right symmetry as a promising avenue to address key theoretical and experimental challenges in contemporary physics, inviting further exploration and scrutiny within the scientific community.

Stars with hot Jupiters have obliquities ranging from 0-180 degrees, but
relatively little is known about the obliquities of stars with smaller planets.
Using data from the California-Kepler Survey, we investigate the obliquities of
stars with planets spanning a wide range of sizes, most of which are smaller
than Neptune. First, we identify 156 planet hosts for which measurements of the
projected rotation velocity (vsini) and rotation period are both available. By
combining estimates of v and vsini, we find nearly all the stars to be
compatible with high inclination, and hence, low obliquity (less than about 20
degrees). Second, we focus on a sample of 159 hot stars (> 6000K) for which
vsini is available but not necessarily the rotation period. We find 6 stars for
which vsini is anomalously low, an indicator of high obliquity. Half of these
have hot Jupiters, even though only 3% of the stars that were searched have hot
Jupiters. We also compare the vsini distribution of the hot stars with planets
to that of 83 control stars selected without prior knowledge of planets. The
mean vsini of the control stars is lower than that of the planet hosts by a
factor of approximately pi/4, as one would expect if the planet hosts have low
obliquities. All these findings suggest that the Kepler planet-hosting stars
generally have low obliquities, with the exception of hot stars with hot
Jupiters.

The transition from quantum to classical, in the case of a quantum harmonic
oscillator, is typically identified with the transition from a quantum
superposition of macroscopically distinguishable states, such as the
Schr\"odinger cat state, into the corresponding statistical mixture. This
transition is commonly characterized by the asymptotic loss of the interference
term in the Wigner representation of the cat state. In this paper we show that
the quantum to classical transition has different dynamical features depending
on the measure for nonclassicality used. Measures based on an operatorial
definition have well defined physical meaning and allow a deeper understanding
of the quantum to classical transition. Our analysis shows that, for most
nonclassicality measures, the Schr\"odinger cat dies after a finite time.
Moreover, our results challenge the prevailing idea that more macroscopic
states are more susceptible to decoherence in the sense that the transition
from quantum to classical occurs faster. Since nonclassicality is prerequisite
for entanglement generation our results also bridge the gap between
decoherence, which appears to be only asymptotic, and entanglement, which may
show a sudden death. In fact, whereas the loss of coherences still remains
asymptotic, we have shown that the transition from quantum to classical can
indeed occur at a finite time.

We present the first high-resolution observations of 19.9-GHz methanol masers, aimed at elucidating their physical characteristics and the environments in which they are found. Methanol masers serve as critical tracers of star formation processes, yet prior studies have primarily focused on lower frequency transitions. Our observations utilized the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), allowing us to achieve unprecedented spatial resolution and sensitivity. By targeting known star-forming regions, we identified multiple distinct maser spots and analyzed their velocity structure and spatial distribution.   Our results reveal a complex interplay between the 19.9-GHz methanol masers and their surrounding environments, demonstrating that these masers are often found in proximity to other important evolutionary markers in star formation, including outflows and thermal radio sources. We observed significant differences in the maser spot structures between regions, indicating a potential correlation with varying physical conditions. Notably, we developed a new imaging technique that enhances the clarity of maser maps and improves the accuracy of our measurements.  These findings advance our understanding of the mechanisms behind methanol maser excitation and their relationship to star formation. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive framework for future studies aiming to explore the role of high-frequency masers in astrophysical phenomena. Our work underscores the importance of high-resolution observational techniques in unveiling the complexities of extraterrestrial environments, positioning 19.9-GHz methanol masers as vital tools in the study of cosmic evolution.

We present ALMA CO(1-0) and CO(3-2) observations of the brightest cluster
galaxy (BCG) in the 2A 0335+096 galaxy cluster (z = 0.0346). The total
molecular gas mass of (1.13+/-0.15) x 10^9 M_sun is divided into two
components: a nuclear region and a 7 kpc long dusty filament. The central
molecular gas component accounts for (3.2+/-0.4) x 10^8 M_sun of the total
supply of cold gas. Instead of forming a rotationally-supported ring or disk,
it is composed of two distinct, blueshifted clumps south of the nucleus and a
series of low-significance redshifted clumps extending toward a nearby
companion galaxy. The velocity of the redshifted clouds increases with radius
to a value consistent with the companion galaxy, suggesting that an interaction
between these galaxies <20 Myr ago disrupted a pre-existing molecular gas
reservoir within the BCG. Most of the molecular gas, (7.8+/-0.9) x 10^8 M_sun,
is located in the filament. The CO emission is co-spatial with a 10^4 K
emission-line nebula and soft X-rays from 0.5 keV gas, indicating that the
molecular gas has cooled out of the intracluster medium over a period of 25-100
Myr. The filament trails an X-ray cavity, suggesting that the gas has cooled
from low entropy gas that has been lifted out of the cluster core and become
thermally unstable. We are unable to distinguish between inflow and outflow
along the filament with the present data. Cloud velocities along the filament
are consistent with gravitational free-fall near the plane of the sky, although
their increasing blueshifts with radius are consistent with outflow.

Gravitational waves, predicted by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, are ripples in spacetime caused by accelerating masses. In the context of cosmology, these waves propagate through curved backgrounds like de Sitter spacetime. This study focuses on the consistency analysis of gravitational waves in de Sitter spacetime. We begin by reviewing the fundamentals of gravitational waves and de Sitter spacetime. The objective is to understand the behavior of gravitational waves in such a background and determine whether they preserve their original features or undergo modification.  To examine this issue, we employ the linearized theory of gravity and apply it to de Sitter spacetime, deriving the wave equation for gravitational waves. We then calculate the dispersion relation and the polarization tensor, both of which are critical in describing gravitational wave propagation. Our analysis reveals that gravitational waves preserve their tensor nature but exhibit modifications in their dispersion relation and polarization modes in de Sitter spacetime.  Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings in the context of observational data. While current experiments like LIGO and Virgo have only detected gravitational waves from binary mergers, our results suggest that gravitational waves from expanding universes could display different signatures. This work contributes to the ongoing exploration of gravitational waves and their interactions with curved backgrounds, paving the way for future investigations and potential improvements in observational techniques.

A recent number of analysis of cosmological data have shown indications for
the presence of extra radiation beyond the standard model at equality and
nucleosynthesis epoch, which has been usually interpreted as an effective
number of neutrinos, Neff > 3.046. In this work we establish the theoretical
basis for a particle physics-motivated model (Bound Dark Matter, BDM) which
explain the need of extra radiation. The BDM model describes dark matter
particles which are relativistic at a scale below a < ac, these particles
acquire mass with an initial velocity, vc, at scales a > ac due to
non-perturbative methods, as protons and neutrons do, this process is described
by a time dependent equation of state, w_bdm(a). Owing to this behavior the
amount of extra radiation change as a function of the scale factor, this entail
that the extra relativistic degrees of freedom Nex may also vary as a function
of the scale factor. This is favored by data at CMB and BBN epochs. We compute
the range of values of the BDM model parameters, xc = ac*vc, that explain the
values obtained for the 4He at BBN and Neff at equality. Combining different
analysis we compute the value xc = 4.13x10^{-5} and vc = 0.37. We conclude that
we can account for the apparent extra neutrino degrees of freedom Nex using a
phase transition in the dark matter with a time dependent equation of state
with no need for introducing extra relativistic particles.

In this study, we present a high-precision near-infrared (NIR) survey targeting red giant branch (RGB) stars, focusing on low-mass variable stars. Our primary objective is to identify and characterize these stars with precise radial velocities (RVs), which are crucial for understanding their stellar evolution and atmospheric properties. We employed state-of-the-art NIR spectroscopy techniques to achieve sub-kilometer precision in RV measurements, ensuring that our data surpasses existing studies in accuracy.  The survey covered a wide range of spectral types, including K and M dwarfs, which are known to be common hosts of low-mass variable stars. Through meticulous data analysis, we identified several new candidates exhibiting significant variability, some of which showed evidence of rotational modulation. Additionally, we observed clear periodicities in the RVs of these stars, providing robust evidence for their variability.  Our methodology involved extensive data reduction processes, including wavelength calibration and instrumental corrections, followed by detailed analysis using advanced statistical tools. The key insights from our work include a more accurate determination of the orbital periods and amplitudes for previously known variable stars, as well as the identification of previously unknown variability in many RGB stars.  Overall, this study not only enhances our understanding of low-mass variable stars but also provides a valuable dataset for future research into stellar dynamics and atmospheric modeling.

Rare variants have garnered significant attention in genetic association studies due to their potential role in complex traits and diseases. However, conventional association tests often struggle to detect associations due to limited sample sizes and low allele frequencies. This study introduces the Zoom-Focus Algorithm (ZFA), designed to enhance the power of rare variant association tests by optimizing the selection of genetic regions for testing. Our objective was to evaluate the efficacy of ZFA in identifying optimal testing regions that increase the likelihood of detecting true associations with rare variants. We implemented a simulated dataset based on real genomic data, utilizing ZFA to refine the target regions by considering both genetic and phenotypic variances. Through a comprehensive comparison with existing methodologies, we tested the hypothesis that ZFA improves statistical power in rare variant association tests. The results demonstrated that ZFA significantly outperformed traditional methods, yielding an average increase of 30% in power to detect associations within predefined loci. Furthermore, the algorithm effectively localized regions of interest, facilitating more precise identification of pathogenic variants. Our findings underscore the efficacy of ZFA in enhancing rare variant association testing, providing a robust framework for future genomic studies aimed at unraveling the complexities of genetic contributions to diseases. Consequently, we advocate the integration of the Zoom-Focus Algorithm into standard testing protocols to optimize genetic research outcomes.

In the current model of early Solar System evolution, the stable members of
the Jovian and Neptunian Trojan populations were captured into resonance from
the leftover reservoir of planetesimals during the outward migration of the
giant planets. As a result, both Jovian and Neptunian Trojans share a common
origin with the primordial disk population, whose other surviving members
constitute today's trans-Neptunian object (TNO) populations. The cold classical
TNOs are ultra-red, while the dynamically excited "hot" population of TNOs
contains a mixture of ultra-red and blue objects. In contrast, Jovian and
Neptunian Trojans are observed to be blue. While the absence of ultra-red
Jovian Trojans can be readily explained by the sublimation of volatile material
from their surfaces due to the high flux of solar radiation at 5AU, the lack of
ultra-red Neptunian Trojans presents both a puzzle and a challenge to formation
models. In this work we report the discovery by the Dark Energy Survey (DES) of
two new dynamically stable L4 Neptunian Trojans,2013 VX30 and 2014 UU240, both
with inclinations i >30 degrees, making them the highest-inclination known
stable Neptunian Trojans. We have measured the colors of these and three other
dynamically stable Neptunian Trojans previously observed by DES, and find that
2013 VX30 is ultra-red, the first such Neptunian Trojan in its class. As such,
2013 VX30 may be a "missing link" between the Trojan and TNO populations. Using
a simulation of the DES TNO detection efficiency, we find that there are 162
+/- 73 Trojans with Hr < 10 at the L4 Lagrange point of Neptune. Moreover, the
blue-to-red Neptunian Trojan population ratio should be higher than 17:1. Based
on this result, we discuss the possible origin of the ultra-red Neptunian
Trojan population and its implications for the formation history of Neptunian
Trojans.

The central regions of galaxies are crucial for understanding their formation and evolution. The Milky Way's nuclear cluster, hosting a supermassive black hole, is a key area for investigating the presence of a stellar cusp. This study aims to probe the spatial distribution of stars in the Galactic nuclear cluster using high angular resolution integral-field spectroscopy.   The methodology involves conducting observations with a state-of-the-art spectrograph to obtain detailed kinematic and chemical information of individual stars in the central parsec of the Galaxy. By analyzing the spectroscopic data, the study aims to identify any signatures of a missing stellar cusp, which could provide valuable insights into the dynamical processes shaping the Galactic center.  Key findings from this research include high-resolution maps of stellar properties, such as velocity dispersion and metallicity, revealing the complex nature of the nuclear cluster. The analysis of the data will shed light on the presence or absence of a stellar cusp within the central regions of the Milky Way.  In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of high angular resolution integral-field spectroscopy in unraveling the intricate stellar dynamics of the Galactic nuclear cluster. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the central regions of our Galaxy and shed light on the formation mechanisms operating in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole.

The behavior of electrons in nanostructured materials, such as metals and semiconductors, plays a crucial role in determining their electronic, optical, and transport properties. In recent years, the increasing interest in nanostructured materials has led to a growing need to understand their collective electron dynamics. This knowledge is essential for designing and developing new nanoscale devices and systems with improved performance and efficiency.  The objective of this research is to investigate the collective electron dynamics in metallic and semiconductor nanostructures, with a focus on the effects of size, shape, and surface chemistry on their electronic properties. A combination of theoretical and experimental approaches was employed to study the electron dynamics in nanostructured materials. Density functional theory (DFT) was used to simulate the electronic structure and electron dynamics of nanostructured materials, while time-resolved spectroscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) were used to study the electronic properties of individual nanostructures.  The results of this research show that the collective electron dynamics in metallic and semiconductor nanostructures are significantly affected by their size, shape, and surface chemistry. The simulations using DFT indicate that the electron dynamics in nanostructured materials are characterized by a strong dependence on the surface state and the presence of defects. The experimental results using time-resolved spectroscopy and STM confirm the theoretical predictions and provide insights into the electronic properties of individual nanostructures. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the collective electron dynamics in metallic and semiconductor nanostructures, which is essential for the design and development of new nanoscale devices and systems.

This study investigates the properties of Umbral Dots observed using high-resolution data from the New Solar Telescope (NST) and through magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. The primary objective is to understand the physical characteristics and dynamics of these structures, which are crucial for elucidating the solar chromosphere's behavior and magnetic field configurations. We employed advanced image analysis techniques to extract detailed information about the size, shape, and spatial distribution of Umbral Dots within solar umbrae. Additionally, we utilized MHD simulations to model the underlying plasma dynamics and magnetic fields that give rise to these features. Our results indicate that Umbral Dots exhibit a wide range of sizes, with some reaching up to several thousand kilometers across. They are predominantly circular in shape but can display more complex morphologies under certain conditions. Notably, our simulations reveal that the observed Umbral Dot distributions align well with theoretical predictions regarding the solar magnetic field topology. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of solar magnetism and the mechanisms governing solar activity.

In recent years, the transition from observational studies to causal rule mining has emerged as a critical focus in data analysis, addressing the limitations inherent in conventional correlational methods. This paper aims to elucidate the frameworks and methodologies that facilitate the extraction of causal relationships from observational data, highlighting the significance of these advancements in various fields such as epidemiology, social sciences, and artificial intelligence. Utilizing a systematic review approach, we assess multiple causal inference techniques, including propensity score matching, instrumental variable analysis, and the application of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Additionally, we explore the integration of machine learning algorithms with causal inference to strengthen the identification of causal rules. Our key findings indicate that while traditional observational methods may suggest associations, only through rigorous causal rule mining can we discern the underlying mechanisms and causal pathways. The results from our comparative analysis demonstrate that integrating causal reasoning within machine learning frameworks greatly enhances the discovery of actionable insights, as well as the robustness of model predictions. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings for practitioners aiming to implement evidence-based interventions. In conclusion, this study emphasizes the necessity of transitioning to causal rule mining in observational studies, as it not only enriches our understanding of complex relationships but also significantly contributes to informed decision-making in policy and practice.

The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) has unveiled an anomalous signal in the form of the so-called WMAP Haze, which presents a puzzling feature in the Galactic center's microwave emissions. This study investigates the hypothesis that the WMAP Haze is indicative of annihilating neutralino dark matter, a leading candidate in the search for a viable dark matter particle. The objective of this research is to analyze the characteristics of the WMAP Haze and evaluate its potential connection to dark matter annihilation processes. Utilizing a combination of astrophysical modeling, observational data from WMAP, and dark matter simulations, we assess the spectral properties of the Haze and compare them against expected patterns from various dark matter annihilation channels, particularly focusing on the electron-positron and gamma-ray emissions. Our key findings suggest that the intensity and spatial distribution of the WMAP Haze are consistent with the predicted signatures resulting from neutralino annihilation, particularly in regions with high matter density. Moreover, we identify a robust correlation between the Haze and gamma-ray observations from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, lending credence to the dark matter hypothesis. In conclusion, while the WMAP Haze presents a plausible signature of annihilating neutralino dark matter, further investigation and integration of multi-wavelength data are essential for a conclusive determination of its origin, particularly to discern between astrophysical background sources and potential new physics.

We prove that, when genus two curves $C/\mathbb{Q}$ with a marked Weierstass
point are ordered by height, the average number of rational points
$\#|C(\mathbb{Q})|$ is bounded. The argument follows the same ideas as the
sphere-packing proof of boundedness of the average number of integral points on
(quasiminimal Weierstrass models of) elliptic curves. That is, we bound the
number of small-height points by hand, the number of medium-height points by
establishing an explicit Mumford gap principle and using the theorem of
Kabatiansky-Levenshtein on spherical codes (this technique goes back to work of
Silverman, Helfgott, and Helfgott-Venkatesh), and the number of large-height
points by using Bombieri-Vojta's proof of Faltings' theorem.
  Explicitly, in dealing with non-small-height points we prove that the number
of rational points $(x,y)$ on $C_f: y^2 = f(x)$ satisfying $h(x) > 8 h(f)$ is
$\ll 1.872^{\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{Jac}(C)(\mathbb{Q}))}$, which has finite
average by the theorem of Bhargava-Gross on the average size of $2$-Selmer
groups of Jacobians over this family. We note that our arguments in the
small-height and large-height cases extend to general genera $g\geq 2$, though
for medium points we need to use Stoll's bounds on the non-Archimedean local
height differences in genus $2$. For example, we prove that the number of
rational points $P\in C(\mathbb{Q})$ with $h(P)\gg_g h(C)$ on $C/\mathbb{Q}$
smooth projective and of genus $g\geq 2$ is $\ll
1.872^{\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{Jac}(C)(\mathbb{Q}))}$, and that in fact the base
of the exponent can be reduced to $1.311$ once $g\gg 1$, though this is surely
known to experts (the difference is the use of the Kabatiansky-Levenshtein
bound in lieu of more elementary techniques).

The vast majority of extrasolar planets are detected by indirect detection
methods such as transit monitoring and radial velocity measurements. While
these methods are very successful in detecting short-periodic planets, they are
mostly blind to wide sub-stellar or even stellar companions on long orbits. In
our study we present high resolution imaging observations of 63 exoplanet hosts
carried out with the lucky imaging instrument AstraLux at the Calar Alto 2.2m
telescope as well as with the new SPHERE high resolution adaptive optics imager
at the ESO/VLT in the case of a known companion of specific interest. Our goal
is to study the influence of stellar multiplicity on the planet formation
process. We detected and confirmed 4 previously unknown stellar companions to
the exoplanet hosts HD197037, HD217786, Kepler-21 and Kepler-68. In addition,
we detected 11 new low-mass stellar companion candidates which must still be
confirmed as bound companions. We also provide new astrometric and photometric
data points for the recently discovered very close binary systems WASP-76 and
HD2638. Furthermore, we show for the first time that the previously detected
stellar companion to the HD185269 system is a very low mass binary. Finally we
provide precise constraints on additional companions for all observed stars in
our sample.

This study focuses on enhancing the security of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) through improved key generation techniques leveraging frequency-selective channels. Initially, we explored various frequency-selective channel models to identify their impact on signal propagation and interference patterns. Following this, we designed algorithms that exploit these characteristics to generate secure keys. The implementation involved integrating our algorithms into existing WSN frameworks, ensuring compatibility with standard protocols. Subsequently, we conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach under different network conditions, including varying node densities, communication distances, and environmental factors. Our analysis revealed significant improvements in key security and resilience against eavesdropping and impersonation attacks. Key insights include the necessity of adapting key generation methods to the unique properties of frequency-selective channels, which can lead to more robust and efficient secure communication within WSNs.

In this study, we investigate the complex dynamics of star-disk interaction in classical T Tauri stars through the application of wavelet analysis. Our primary objective is to elucidate the time-varying behavior of accretion processes and variability patterns in these young stellar objects. We analyze optical and infrared light curves obtained from a selection of classical T Tauri stars, employing wavelet transform techniques to dissect the intricate oscillatory features and identify periodicities associated with accretion bursts and disk instabilities. Our results reveal significant variability on multiple timescales, with notable periodic patterns correlating with the star's magnetic field strength and disk properties. We observe that accretion events manifest as transient wavelet peaks, indicative of localized enhancements in brightness and suggestive of magnetic interactions between the star and the surrounding accretion disk. Furthermore, we identify that these wavelet patterns can be associated with specific disk geometries and inner-disk dynamics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between stellar activity and disk behavior, highlighting the critical role of magnetic fields in regulating accretion processes. By utilizing wavelet analysis, we provide a robust framework for investigating non-stationary signals in astrophysical contexts, paving the way for future studies on stellar formation and evolution. This research enhances the comprehension of the physical processes at play in T Tauri stars and establishes a methodological approach that can be applied to similar astrophysical phenomena across various time scales.

Safety critical systems involve the tight coupling between potentially
conflicting control objectives and safety constraints. As a means of creating a
formal framework for controlling systems of this form, and with a view toward
automotive applications, this paper develops a methodology that allows safety
conditions -- expressed as control barrier functions -- to be unified with
performance objectives -- expressed as control Lyapunov functions -- in the
context of real-time optimization-based controllers. Safety conditions are
specified in terms of forward invariance of a set, and are verified via two
novel generalizations of barrier functions; in each case, the existence of a
barrier function satisfying Lyapunov-like conditions implies forward invariance
of the set, and the relationship between these two classes of barrier functions
is characterized. In addition, each of these formulations yields a notion of
control barrier function (CBF), providing inequality constraints in the control
input that, when satisfied, again imply forward invariance of the set. Through
these constructions, CBFs can naturally be unified with control Lyapunov
functions (CLFs) in the context of a quadratic program (QP); this allows for
the achievement of control objectives (represented by CLFs) subject to
conditions on the admissible states of the system (represented by CBFs). The
mediation of safety and performance through a QP is demonstrated on adaptive
cruise control and lane keeping, two automotive control problems that present
both safety and performance considerations coupled with actuator bounds.

This study investigates the relationship between the climate and thermal phase curve of 55 Cancri e, a super-Earth exoplanet known for its extreme conditions. The analysis leverages high-resolution spectroscopy data collected from the Hubble Space Telescope to probe the atmospheric dynamics and surface properties of this planet. Initially, we faced challenges in accurately interpreting the thermal signal due to the complex rotational behavior of 55 Cancri e, which causes variations in observed brightness across its orbit. To address these issues, we employed advanced statistical methods to disentangle the rotational effects from the thermal signals. Our key findings indicate that the thermal phase curve exhibits distinct patterns influenced by temperature gradients and circulation patterns within the atmosphere. These patterns correlate with modeled atmospheric circulation models, suggesting that the thermal phase curve can be used as a diagnostic tool to infer atmospheric dynamics on exoplanets. This work not only provides deeper insights into the climate system of 55 Cancri e but also offers methodologies that can be applied to other exoplanets to better understand their atmospheres and surface environments.

In this study, we investigate effective limiting absorption principles and their applications within the framework of spectral theory and partial differential equations. We aim to address the challenge of analyzing the behavior of Schrödinger operators with singular potentials, which often elude standard analytical techniques due to their complex spectral properties. By employing a rigorous mathematical approach, we derive effective limiting absorption results that extend existing theorems, enabling us to establish a deeper understanding of resonances and spectral singularities associated with these operators.  Our methodology combines harmonic analysis and perturbation theory, allowing us to derive asymptotic expansions of the resolvent in the vicinity of the essential spectrum. We utilize sophisticated techniques such as the resolvent identity and complex analysis to demonstrate that for a broader class of perturbations, the limiting absorption principle holds with optimal bounds on the resolvent estimates.   The results obtained not only unify previous findings in the literature but also open new avenues for application across various fields, including quantum mechanics and wave propagation phenomena. We illustrate this by providing concrete examples of how our theoretical advancements can be applied to solve inverse scattering problems and analyze the stability of wave solutions in nonlinear media. Our findings significantly enhance the toolkit available for researchers dealing with complex spectral problems, thereby enriching the field of mathematical physics.

In this study, we introduce X-Vine, an innovative routing protocol leveraging the inherent structure of social networks to enhance security and anonymity in communication systems. Our work addresses the critical problem of ensuring pseudonymous communication in digital networks, safeguarding user privacy against adversarial attacks while maintaining efficient routing capabilities. Through X-Vine, we employ a network of trust, modeled after social ties, to create a robust system resistant to counterfeit identity exploits and interception by malicious entities. The methodology integrates social network analysis to establish trust-based routing paths, minimizing the likelihood of exposure to potential adversaries. We utilize these paths to achieve pseudonymous routing by designing our system to encapsulate user identities within a social overlay, reducing traceability and risk of information leakage. We implemented our protocol and conducted extensive simulations to evaluate its efficacy. Our results indicate significant improvements in routing security and user anonymity compared to traditional peer-to-peer systems. X-Vine demonstrates resilience to various attack vectors, including Sybil and eavesdropping attacks, due to its dynamic and decentralized approach. Furthermore, the protocol efficiently scales with network size, showcasing its potential for widespread applicability in maintaining secure communication within diverse digital ecosystems. Our findings suggest that social network-driven routing paradigms present a viable pathway to enhancing the security and anonymity of contemporary digital communications, potentially influencing the design of future privacy-oriented networking frameworks.

Core-collapse supernovae (CC SNe), especially Type II-Plateau ones, are
thought to be important contributors to cosmic dust production. SN 2004dj, one
of the closest and brightest SN since 1987A, offered a good opportunity to
examine dust formation processes. To find signs of newly formed dust, we
analyze all available mid-infrared (MIR) archival data from the Spitzer Space
Telescope. We re-reduce and analyze data from IRAC, MIPS and IRS instruments
obtained between +98 and +1381 days after explosion, generating light curves
and spectra for each epoch. Observed spectral energy distributions are fitted
with both analytic and numerical models, using the radiative-transfer code
MOCASSIN for the latter ones. We also use imaging polarimetric data obtained at
+425 days by the Hubble Space Telescope. We present convincing evidence of dust
formation in the ejecta of SN 2004dj from MIR light curves and spectra.
Significant MIR excess flux is detected in all bands between 3.6 and 24 um. In
the optical, a ~0.8% polarization is also detected at a 2-sigma level, which
exceeds the interstellar polarization in that direction. Our analysis shows
that the freshly-formed dust around SN 2004dj can be modeled assuming a nearly
spherical shell containing amorphous carbon grains, cooling from ~700 K to ~400
K between +267 and +1246 days. Persistent excess flux has been found above 10
