um, which is explained by a cold (~115 K) dust component. If this cold dust is
of circumstellar origin, it is likely to be condensed in a cool, dense shell
between the forward and reverse shocks. Pre-existing circumstellar dust is less
likely, but cannot be ruled out. An upper limit of ~8x10^{-4} M_sun was derived
for the dust mass, which is similar to previously published values for other
dust-producing SNe.

We present a thermodynamic theory of the Kovacs effect based on the idea that
the configurational degrees of freedom of a glass-forming material are driven
out of equilibrium with the heat bath by irreversible thermal contraction and
expansion. We assume that the slowly varying configurational subsystem, i.e.
the part of the system that is described by inherent structures, is
characterized by an effective temperature, and contains a volume-related
internal variable. We examine mechanisms by which irreversible dynamics of the
fast, kinetic-vibrational degrees of freedom can cause the entropy and the
effective temperature of the configurational subsystem to increase during
sufficiently rapid changes in the bath temperature. We then use this theory to
interpret the numerical simulations by Mossa and Sciortino (MS), who observe
the Kovacs effect in more detail than is feasible in laboratory experiments.
Our analysis highlights two mechanisms for the equilibration of internal
variables. In one of these, an internal variable first relaxes toward a state
of quasi-equilibrium determined by the effective temperature, and then
approaches true thermodynamic equilibrium as the effective temperature slowly
relaxes toward the bath temperature. In the other mechanism, an internal
variable directly equilibrates with the bath temperature on intermediate
timescales, without equilibrating with the effective temperature at any stage.
Both mechanisms appear to be essential for understanding the MS results.

The Clique function is a fundamental problem in computer science involving finding the largest complete subgraph within a given graph. Its complexity has been extensively studied, with existing proofs relying on intricate mathematical arguments.    This research presents an alternative proof of the exponential monotone complexity of the Clique function. The aim is to offer a new perspective on the problem that is both intuitive and insightful, potentially leading to a better understanding of the underlying principles.   The proof combines techniques from graph theory, combinatorics, and probability theory to establish the exponential growth rate of the Clique function. By carefully analyzing the structural properties of cliques within graphs, the proof unveils a novel approach to demonstrating the inherent complexity of this classic computational challenge.   Through the proposed proof, it is revealed that the Clique function exhibits an exponential monotone complexity, shedding light on the intricate nature of finding complete subgraphs within graphs. The findings contribute to the theoretical understanding of computational complexity and provide a fresh viewpoint on this well-studied problem.   In conclusion, this research offers a new perspective on the exponential monotone complexity of the Clique function, presenting an alternative proof that enriches the existing body of knowledge. By elucidating the fundamental properties underlying the problem, the study contributes to the broader field of theoretical computer science and sets the stage for future investigations into related computational challenges.

We present a semi-empirical, largely model-independent approach for
estimating Galactic birth radii, r_birth, for Milky Way disk stars. The
technique relies on the justifiable assumption that a negative radial
metallicity gradient in the interstellar medium (ISM) existed for most of the
disk lifetime. Stars are projected back to their birth positions according to
the observationally derived age and [Fe/H] with no kinematical information
required. Applying our approach to the AMBRE:HARPS and HARPS-GTO local samples,
we show that we can constrain the ISM metallicity evolution with Galactic
radius and cosmic time, [Fe/H]_ISM(r, t), by requiring a physically meaningful
r_birth distribution. We find that the data are consistent with an ISM radial
metallicity gradient that flattens with time from ~-0.15 dex/kpc at the
beginning of disk formation, to its measured present-day value (-0.07 dex/kpc).
We present several chemo-kinematical relations in terms of mono-r_birth
populations. One remarkable result is that the kinematically hottest stars
would have been born locally or in the outer disk, consistent with thick disk
formation from the nested flares of mono-age populations and predictions from
cosmological simulations. This phenomenon can be also seen in the observed
age-velocity dispersion relation, in that its upper boundary is dominated by
stars born at larger radii. We also find that the flatness of the local
age-metallicity relation (AMR) is the result of the superposition of the AMRs
of mono-r_birth populations, each with a well-defined negative slope. The solar
birth radius is estimated to be 7.3+-0.6 kpc, for a current Galactocentric
radius of 8 kpc.

Metastability phenomena in stochastic processes, such as Glauber dynamics on random graphs, have attracted considerable attention due to their implications in diverse fields ranging from physics to computer science. This research paper aims to investigate metastability in Glauber dynamics on random graphs. The objective is to analyze the conditions under which metastable states emerge in these dynamics and characterize their properties.   The methodology involves a theoretical analysis based on tools from probability theory and statistical mechanics to study the dynamics of interacting spin systems on random graphs. Monte Carlo simulations are also employed to validate the theoretical results and provide further insights into the metastable behavior of the system.  Key findings reveal the presence of multiple metastable states in Glauber dynamics on random graphs, with transitions between these states exhibiting distinct timescales. The critical parameters governing the emergence and stability of these metastable states are identified, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving the dynamics.  In conclusion, this study enhances our understanding of metastability in Glauber dynamics on random graphs, offering valuable insights into the complex behavior of stochastic processes on large-scale networks. The findings have implications for the study of dynamical processes in various disciplines and pave the way for future research in the field of metastability on random graphs.

A while ago, I developed what I called an encryption method. The most
favorable of reviews did not see a method but a collection of techniques. Be
that as it may, the process used, is described in the paper, Windtalking
Computers. This paper is about the steganographic method described, the
cryptanalysis efforts of that method and; a real world application of that
method as an answer to the increasing problem of password file hacking. The
premise is that the technique is a variant of one time pad, using a novel way
to produce one time pad output for digital input. There is no record in the
literature of such a method being used for encryption at all. Digital
encryption generally treats the letters of the plaintext as a binary number and
does some mathematical computation to produce ciphertext. The idea of inserting
bits with a random generated key is new. Therefore (because a uniquely random
generated key is used), the encryption is cryptanalytically unbreakable and/or
computationally secure and/or information theoretic. An academic version was
made. Challenges for decryption have not produced to-date a decryption.
Advantages and disadvantages of the method are discussed.
  Hackers are constantly penetrating networks and stealing password files.
Which, once in possession of a password file, hackers individually or
collectively with distributed processing over the Internet, decrypt the values
of the hash passwords. Thereby gaining access to systems. This problem has
become sufficiently significant for CAESAR (Competition for Authenticated
Encryption: Security, Applicability, and Robustness) to make calls for papers
for solutions. Herein is one proposed solution. While one time pad presents a
problem being computationally intensive, for the relatively short length of
passwords, the cost of computation may be cost effective for the security
provided.

The Christodoulou memory is a nonlinear contribution to the
gravitational-wave field that is sourced by the gravitational-wave
stress-energy tensor. For quasicircular, inspiralling binaries, the
Christodoulou memory produces a growing, nonoscillatory change in the
gravitational-wave "plus" polarization, resulting in the permanent displacement
of a pair of freely-falling test masses after the wave has passed. In addition
to its nonoscillatory behavior, the Christodoulou memory is interesting because
even though it originates from 2.5 post-Newtonian (PN) order multipole
interactions, it affects the waveform at leading (Newtonian/quadrupole) order.
The memory is also potentially detectable in binary black-hole mergers. While
the oscillatory pieces of the gravitational-wave polarizations for
quasicircular, inspiralling compact binaries have been computed to 3PN order,
the memory contribution to the polarizations has only been calculated to
leading order (the next-to-leading order 0.5PN term has previously been shown
to vanish). Here the calculation of the memory for quasicircular, inspiralling
binaries is extended to 3PN order. While the angular dependence of the memory
remains qualitatively unchanged, the PN correction terms tend to reduce the
memory's magnitude. Explicit expressions are given for the memory contributions
to the plus polarization and the spin-weighted spherical-harmonic modes of the
metric and curvature perturbations. Combined with the recent results of
Blanchet et al.(2008), this completes the waveform to 3PN order. This paper
also discusses: (i) the difficulties in extracting the memory from numerical
simulations, (ii) other nonoscillatory effects that enter the waveform at high
PN orders, and (iii) issues concerning the observability of the memory.

The Vernam cipher (or one-time pad) has played an important rule in
cryptography because it is a perfect secrecy system. For example, if an English
text (presented in binary system) $X_1 X_2 ... $ is enciphered according to the
formula $Z_i = (X_i + Y_i) \mod 2 $, where $Y_1 Y_2 ...$ is a key sequence
generated by the Bernoulli source with equal probabilities of 0 and 1, anyone
who knows $Z_1 Z_2 ... $ has no information about $X_1 X_2 ... $ without the
knowledge of the key $Y_1 Y_2 ...$. (The best strategy is to guess $X_1 X_2 ...
$ not paying attention to $Z_1 Z_2 ... $.)
  But what should one say about secrecy of an analogous method where the key
sequence $Y_1 Y_2 ...$ is generated by the Bernoulli source with a small bias,
say, $P(0) = 0.49, $ $ P(1) = 0.51$? To the best of our knowledge, there are no
theoretical estimates for the secrecy of such a system, as well as for the
general case where $X_1 X_2 ... $ (the plaintext) and key sequence are
described by stationary ergodic processes. We consider the running-key ciphers
where the plaintext and the key are generated by stationary ergodic sources and
show how to estimate the secrecy of such systems. In particular, it is shown
that, in a certain sense, the Vernam cipher is robust to small deviations from
randomness.

Interaction of graphene with a defect layer of a 1D defective photonic
structure correspondingly could open a Dirac gap in its nonlinear energy
dispersion. Also, an excitonic gap could be created upon applied strong
magnetic fields at low temperatures. Now, the exact solution for the
transmission of the allowed defective states under the influence of a
homogeneous magnetic field requires providing a new scheme for the transfer
matrix method to cover the circularly polarized propagation of the light in THz
regime. In this paper, through an easy-to-follow framework for obtaining the
distinct expression of the related transfer matrix method, it is observed that
the hybrid defective states in the suggested optical structure undergo an
unconventional transmission map as function of Dirac gap. Moreover, it is shown
that mapping the transmission spectrum in the frequency space reveals peculiar
results for narrow-band transport of the defective states. Finally, it is
demonstrated that the transmission spectrum shows plateaus as a function of the
applied magnetic field analogues to the situations observed for the conductance
of a 2D electron gas system in the quantum Hall effect regime. This almost
simple suggested design which can be fully controlled marks the first optical
counterpart of quantum Hall effect in optics.

We conducted a comprehensive wide-field survey of emission-line stars in the IC 1396 star-forming region, utilizing a combination of optical and ultraviolet observations. Our primary objective was to identify and characterize a large sample of emission-line stars, including H II regions, Planck density filaments, and young stellar objects.   Utilizing the 2.3-meter telescope and the 2.1-meter telescope at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, we employed the ESPRESSO spectrograph to obtain high-resolution spectra of over 10,000 emission-line stars. We applied a multi-wavelength approach, incorporating data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), and the Hubble Space Telescope (HST).   Our results reveal a complex network of emission-line stars, including numerous H II regions, several Planck density filaments, and a large number of young stellar objects. We identified 345 new emission-line stars, 23 of which are associated with previously unknown H II regions. Furthermore, we discovered 12 new young stellar objects, including a few candidates for protostellar binaries.   Our survey provides a detailed map of the IC 1396 star-forming region, shedding light on the complex interplay between gas, dust, and stars in this active star-forming environment. The large sample of emission-line stars obtained in this study will facilitate future investigations into the physical properties of H II regions, Planck density filaments, and young stellar objects.

Our study introduces a novel 2-D model to analyze uncertainty sources in estimating sparse sea surface CO2 partial pressure. The model accounts for various uncertainties, including measurement errors, model errors, and temporal and spatial variations in environmental factors. We used an ensemble of five different empirical models to generate a range of CO2 partial pressure values and quantified their uncertainties using propagation of error techniques.  The primary sources of uncertainty were identified as measurement errors and model errors. Measurement errors arose from uncertainties in the sensors used to measure sea surface CO2 and were found to be the largest contributor to overall uncertainty. Model errors arose from the differences between the empirical models and the real ocean system. The temporal and spatial variations in environmental factors, such as temperature and salinity, also contributed significantly to the overall uncertainty.  We found that the total uncertainty in estimating sparse sea surface CO2 partial pressure was substantial, often exceeding 15%. The spatial distribution of uncertainty was complex and varied greatly depending on the location and environmental conditions. The largest uncertainties were found in areas with high spatial and temporal variations in environmental conditions, such as the equator and the ocean boundaries.  Our results highlight the importance of considering multiple sources of uncertainty when estimating sparse sea surface CO2 partial pressure. The proposed 2-D model can be used to evaluate the uncertainty associated with different measurements and empirical models, providing valuable insights for future research and ocean monitoring efforts. The model can also be extended to include additional sources of uncertainty, such as biologic processes and gas exchange. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing efforts to improve the accuracy and reliability of ocean CO2 measurements and enhance our understanding of the carbon cycle in the ocean.

This study investigates pulse propagation dynamics within a dispersive intracavity medium, focusing on the interplay between pulse dispersion and nonlinear effects. We employed both theoretical modeling and experimental measurements to analyze the behavior of pulses as they traverse the medium. Our primary objective was to understand how pulse shape and temporal evolution are influenced by the material's dispersion properties and nonlinearity. Theoretical analysis revealed that the pulse broadening is primarily governed by group velocity dispersion (GVD), while self-phase modulation (SPM) contributes to additional temporal distortion. Experimental validation confirmed these predictions, showing that under certain conditions, SPM can significantly alter the pulse duration, particularly at high powers. Key methodologies included the use of Fourier transform spectroscopy for precise measurement of pulse characteristics and numerical simulations to model pulse propagation accurately. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of optical pulse processing in nonlinear systems, offering insights into optimizing pulse shaping and amplification processes in various applications such as telecommunications and laser technology.

We present the discovery by the WASP-South survey, in close collaboration
with the Euler and TRAPPIST telescopes, of WASP-121 b, a new remarkable
short-period transiting hot Jupiter, whose planetary nature has been
statistically validated by the PASTIS software. The planet has a mass of
$1.183_{-0.062}^{+0.064}$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$, a radius of 1.865 $\pm$ 0.044
$R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$, and transits every $1.2749255_{-0.0000025}^{+0.0000020}$
days an active F6-type main-sequence star ($V$=10.4, $1.353_{-0.079}^{+0.080}$
$M_{\odot}$, 1.458 $\pm$ 0.030 $R_{\odot}$, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ = 6460 $\pm$ 140
K). A notable property of WASP-121 b is that its orbital semi-major axis is
only $\sim$1.15 times larger than its Roche limit, which suggests that the
planet might be close to tidal disruption. Furthermore, its large size and
extreme irradiation ($\sim$$7.1\:10^{9}$ erg $\mathrm{s}^{-1}
\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$) make it an excellent target for atmospheric studies via
secondary eclipse observations. Using the TRAPPIST telescope, we indeed detect
its emission in the $z'$-band at better than $\sim$4$\sigma$, the measured
occultation depth being 603 $\pm$ 130 ppm. Finally, from a measurement of the
Rossiter-McLaughlin effect with the CORALIE spectrograph, we infer a
sky-projected spin-orbit angle of $257.8_{-5.5}^{+5.3}$ deg. This result
indicates a significant misalignment between the spin axis of the host star and
the orbital plane of the planet, the planet being in a nearly polar orbit. Such
a high misalignment suggests a migration of the planet involving strong
dynamical events with a third body.

The Segmented Pupil Experiment for Exoplanet Detection (SPEED) aims to revolutionize the field of exoplanet detection by employing a novel segmented pupil design, which improves the precision and stability of coronagraphic imaging systems. SPEED utilizes an array of micromirrors to segment the pupil into several smaller segments, enabling precise control over the shape and position of the optical wavefronts passing through the system.  Our team has successfully demonstrated the capabilities of SPEED by simulating the segmented pupil's effect on coronagraphic imaging using a numerical model. The simulations revealed a significant improvement in the suppression of starlight, which is the primary challenge in directly imaging exoplanets. This advancement will ultimately lead to a higher contrast ratio, enabling the detection of smaller and fainter planets around nearby stars.  Furthermore, we have conducted laboratory experiments using a prototype SPEED system to validate the theoretical results. These experiments confirmed the segmented pupil's ability to improve the system's stability and reduce starlight. Our findings underscore the potential of SPEED as a promising alternative to current exoplanet detection techniques, such as the Angular Differential Imaging (ADI) and Coronagraphic Adaptive Optics (CASPIR) methods.  The key ideas in this work revolve around the segmented pupil's ability to enhance the performance of coronagraphic imaging systems for exoplanet detection. By harnessing the power of micromirror arrays, we can achieve precise control over the optical wavefronts, leading to better contrast ratios and the detection of smaller and fainter planets. The innovative SPEED design represents a crucial step forward in unlocking the secrets of exoplanetary systems and expanding our understanding of the universe.

Our research delves into the final stages of growth of massive black holes, aiming to address the perplexing question of how these celestial entities evolve in their later phases. By conducting a comprehensive analysis of observational data and theoretical models, we successfully elucidate the mechanisms governing the growth of massive black holes as they near their mature stage. Our study reveals a correlation between the cosmic environment and the accretion processes, shedding light on the factors influencing the accretion rate of black holes during the late stages of their development.  The key findings of our investigation highlight the significant role of mergers and interactions between galaxies in fueling the growth of massive black holes at their advanced stage. Furthermore, we demonstrate the impact of environmental factors such as gas supply and interactions on the feeding behavior of these black holes. Our methodology involves sophisticated simulations and statistical analyses to interpret the observed trends and make predictions about the evolution of massive black holes in the later epochs of the universe.  Overall, our work contributes to the understanding of the growth mechanisms of massive black holes at their late stage and provides valuable insights into the dynamic processes shaping these enigmatic cosmic structures.

The presented work investigates a sparse Bayesian incremental automatic
relevance determination (IARD) algorithm in the context of multipath parameter
estimation in a super-resolution regime. The corresponding estimation problem
is highly nonlinear and, in general, requires an estimation of the number of
multipath components. In the IARD approach individual multipath components are
processed sequentially, which permits a tractable convergence analysis of the
corresponding inference expressions. This leads to a simple condition, termed
here a pruning condition, that determines if a multipath component is
"sparsified" or retained in the model, thus permitting a fast and adaptive
realization of the estimation algorithm. Yet previous experiments demonstrated
that IARD fails to select the correct number of components when the parameters
entering nonlinearly the multipath model are also estimated. To understand this
effect, an analysis of the statistical structure of the pruning condition is
proposed. It is shown that the corresponding test statistic in the pruning
condition follows an extreme value distribution. As a result, the standard IARD
algorithm implements a statistical test with a very high probability of false
alarm. This leads to insertion of estimation artifacts and underestimation of
signal sparsity. Moreover, the probability of false alarm worsens as the number
of measured signal samples grows. Based on the developed statistical
interpretation of the IARD, an optimal adjustment of the pruning condition is
proposed. This permits a reliable and efficient removal of estimation artifacts
and joint estimation of signal parameters, as well as optimal model order
selection within a sparse Bayesian learning framework.

Spatial networks, in which nodes and edges are embedded in space, play a
vital role in the study of complex systems. For example, many social networks
attach geo-location information to each user, allowing the study of not only
topological interactions between users, but spatial interactions as well. The
defining property of spatial networks is that edge distances are associated
with a cost, which may subtly influence the topology of the network. However,
the cost function over distance is rarely known, thus developing a model of
connections in spatial networks is a difficult task.
  In this paper, we introduce a novel model for capturing the interaction
between spatial effects and network structure. Our approach represents a unique
combination of ideas from latent variable statistical models and spatial
network modeling. In contrast to previous work, we view the ability to form
long/short-distance connections to be dependent on the individual nodes
involved. For example, a node's specific surroundings (e.g. network structure
and node density) may make it more likely to form a long distance link than
other nodes with the same degree. To capture this information, we attach a
latent variable to each node which represents a node's spatial reach. These
variables are inferred from the network structure using a Markov Chain Monte
Carlo algorithm.
  We experimentally evaluate our proposed model on 4 different types of
real-world spatial networks (e.g. transportation, biological, infrastructure,
and social). We apply our model to the task of link prediction and achieve up
to a 35% improvement over previous approaches in terms of the area under the
ROC curve. Additionally, we show that our model is particularly helpful for
predicting links between nodes with low degrees. In these cases, we see much
larger improvements over previous models.

The propagation of GeV neutrinos through Earth is a subject of significant interest in the field of particle physics due to its potential to unlock fundamental insights into the structure and composition of our planet. This study aims to explore the interaction mechanisms and trajectory alterations of GeV neutrinos as they traverse Earth's interior. Utilizing a combination of analytic models and computational simulations, we rigorously analyze how neutrinos are affected by various terrestrial layers, including the crust, mantle, and core. Our methodology involves simulating neutrino interactions based on cross-sectional data obtained from existing neutrino detectors and geological models. The key findings indicate that the path length, density, and elemental composition of Earth's layers significantly influence the likelihood of neutrino interaction, with higher densities correlating with increased interaction probabilities. Moreover, results show measurable deviations in neutrino trajectories due to gravitational refraction, particularly when passing through the core-mantle boundary. These observations highlight variations in the neutrino absorption rates, suggesting a method to infer the composition and density distributions within Earth. The study concludes that GeV neutrinos provide a viable, non-invasive probe for geophysical investigation, complementing traditional seismological methods. Future research should focus on refining the models with real-time data from next-generation neutrino observatories to enhance our understanding of Earth's inner structure and improve the precision of our geographical and compositional insights.

Gedik et al have very recently demonstrated using a pump/probe femto-second
laser technique that the c-axis lattice parameter of LaCuO4+d temporarily
becomes expanded by as much as 2.5% following pulsed laser optical excitation
at 1.55 eV. Access to an out-of-equilibrium metastable excited state is
observed to develop on a time scale of 30 ps. Subsequently the latter state
decays displaying a still longer half-life of just over 300 ps. Observation of
the temperature independence of this laser induced interstate transfer and of
the linear dependence of the production of the metastable population upon the
energy delivered per unit area by the initiating light pulse (beyond a key
threshold fluence) have been interpreted by Gedik et al within the framework of
standard p-to-d, O-to-Cu, charge transfer excitations. By contrast these same
data are reinterpreted here in terms of pumped local pairs, within a negative-U
scenario of cuprate HTSC behaviour long advocated by the current author. The
d8-to-d10 laser-induced augmentation in the negative-U state population
(10CuIII2-) brings marked c-axis expansion by virtue of (i) the local
electrostatic charge imbalance, (ii) the increased antibonding nature of the
electron double-loading d10(p6) configuration created at pair-receptive CuIII
coordination units, and (iii) the layered nature of the cuprate crystal
structure. The new observations are related through to Rohlers striking,
standard crystallographic observations, to the stripe domain formation, and to
previous pump/probe experiments.

In this paper, we will make an attempt to clarify the relation between
three-dimensional euclidean loop quantum gravity with vanishing cosmological
constant and quantum field theory in the continuum. We will argue, in
particular, that in three spacetime dimensions the discrete spectra for the
geometric boundary observables that we find in loop quantum gravity can be
understood from the quantisation of a conformal boundary field theory in the
continuum without ever introducing spin networks or triangulations of space. At
a technical level, the starting point is the Hamiltonian formalism for general
relativity in regions with boundaries at finite distance. At these finite
boundaries, we choose specific conformal boundary conditions (the boundary is a
minimal surface) that are derived from a boundary field theory for an SU(2)
boundary spinor, which is minimally coupled to the spin connection in the bulk.
The resulting boundary equations of motion define a conformal field theory with
vanishing central charge. We will quantise this boundary field theory and show
that the length of a one-dimensional cross section of the boundary has a
discrete spectrum. In addition, we will introduce a new class of coherent
states, study the quasi-local observables that generate the quasi-local
Virasoro algebra and discuss some strategies to evaluate the partition function
of the theory.

In recent years, the exploration of supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth has primarily focused on the interplay between host galaxy characteristics and black hole accretion processes. This study investigates two distinct channels of SMBH growth within the paradigm of the galaxy mass-size plane, which delineates galaxies according to their stellar mass and effective radius. Our objective is to ascertain how these dual growth pathways correlate with and influence the evolutionary trajectories of their host galaxies. We employ a comprehensive analysis using data from large-scale surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) to map the correlation between SMBH characteristics and galaxy features. Utilizing a combination of photometric and spectroscopic data, we analyze the mass accretion rates of black holes and their host galaxies' stellar populations, employing advanced statistical models to discern growth patterns. The key findings reveal a bifurcation in growth channels one dominated by gas-rich, rapid accretion in compact, massive hosts, and another characterized by slower accretion rates in extended, less dense galaxies. This dichotomy suggests distinct evolutionary scenarios tied to environmental conditions and galaxy interaction histories. Our conclusion emphasizes the importance of these growth channels in understanding galaxy evolution and developing more accurate models of SMBH formation. By integrating these findings with contemporary cosmological simulations, the research highlights the intricate relationship between black hole growth patterns and the large-scale structure of the universe.

We have used the Australia Telescope Compact Array to undertake the first
high-resolution observations of the 19.9-GHz methanol maser transition. The
emission is coincident with the location of the targeted 6.7-GHz methanol
masers to within 0.2 arcseconds in absolute position. We find that the relative
distribution of the 19.9-GHz maser emission in our sample differs from that
observed in the 6.7-GHz transition, in contrast to the similar distribution
often seen in the 6.7- and 12.2-GHz methanol masers in many sources. We also
find that the peak velocity for the 19.9-GHz methanol masers is frequently
different from that observed in other class II transitions in the same regions.
These two results suggest that while 19.9-GHz methanol masers arise from the
same general location as other class II transitions, they are likely not
coincident on milliarcsecond scales; which has implications for
multi-transitional modelling of class II methanol maser sources. We have
investigated the properties of the OH and other classII methanol transitions
for those 107-GHz methanol masers with and without an associated 19.9-GHz
methanol maser. On the basis of these comparisons we suggest that the 19.9-GHz
transition traces an evolutionary phase around the peak of the class II maser
luminosity into its decline.

The existence of eta-mesic nuclei, a hypothesized bound state of an eta meson and a nucleus, remains a compelling topic in hadronic physics. To investigate the formation of eta-mesic nuclei, specifically eta-mesic helium (η⁴He), experimental studies were conducted using the heavy-ion collisions dd→³He n π⁰ and dd→³He p π⁻ at the WASA-at-COSY facility. The objective was to identify potential η⁴He states via missing mass spectroscopy to discern anomalies indicating bound states in the reaction channels. Utilizing the high-resolution capabilities of the WASA detector, along with the high precision beam characteristics at the COSY accelerator, data was acquired at several beam energies near the eta production threshold. The analysis focused on detecting signatures of eta-mesic formation through resonance-like structures in the invariant mass spectra of the final states. Despite the comprehensive dataset, no unambiguous evidence for eta-mesic helium was observed. The results were supplemented by a theoretical framework that included the considerations of final state interactions and background processes contributing to the spectra. Upper limits for the production cross section were established, enhancing theoretical models on eta-nucleon interactions. These findings suggest that if η⁴He exists, its binding energies and widths are likely smaller than the current detection sensitivity. The study reinforces the challenges of identifying eta-mesic states and calls for refined experimental setups and theoretical models to further explore these elusive nuclear states.

The gamma-ray population of millisecond pulsars (MSPs) detected by the Fermi
Large Area Telescope (LAT) has been steadily increasing. A number of the more
recent detections, including PSR J0034-0534, PSR J1939+2134 (B1937+21; the
first MSP ever discovered), PSR J1959+2048 (B1957+20; the first black widow
system), and PSR J2214+3000 exhibit an unusual phenomenon: nearly phase-aligned
radio and gamma-ray light curves (LCs). To account for the phase alignment, we
explore geometric models where both the radio and gamma-ray emission originate
either in the outer magnetosphere near the light cylinder (R_LC) or near the
polar caps (PCs). We obtain reasonable fits for the first three of these MSPs
in the context of "altitude-limited" outer gap (alOG) and two-pole caustic
(alTPC) geometries. The outer magnetosphere phase-aligned models differ from
the standard outer gap (OG) / two-pole caustic (TPC) models in two respects:
first, the radio emission originates in caustics at relatively high altitudes
compared to the usual low-altitude conal radio beams; second, we allow the
maximum altitude of the gamma-ray emission region as well as both the minimum
and maximum altitudes of the radio emission region to vary within a limited
range. Alternatively, there also exist phase-aligned LC solutions for emission
originating near the stellar surface in a slot gap (SG) scenario ("low-altitude
slot gap" (laSG) models). We find best-fit LCs using a Markov chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) maximum likelihood approach. Our fits imply that the phase-aligned LCs
are likely of caustic origin, produced in the outer magnetosphere, and that the
radio emission may come from close to R_LC. We lastly constrain the emission
altitudes with typical uncertainties of ~0.3R_LC. Our results describe a third
gamma-ray MSP subclass, in addition to the two (with non-aligned LCs)
previously found.

This research addresses the challenge of sound and complete bidirectional typechecking for programming languages that incorporate higher-rank polymorphism, existentials, and indexed types. Existing type systems often struggle with maintaining type safety and completeness when dealing with complex type constraints. This study proposes novel techniques to enhance the type checking process, ensuring it remains both sound (correctness) and complete (ability to check all correct programs). Utilizing bidirectional type inference, the method aims to efficiently derive type annotations for expressions while verifying their correctness. The methodology involves formalizing the language semantics, defining type reconstruction rules, and implementing algorithms for bidirectional type inference. Key findings demonstrate improved performance and robustness compared to previous approaches, particularly in handling higher-rank polymorphism and indexed types. The results highlight the potential of the proposed approach to support more expressive and scalable programming languages. This work contributes to the development of safer and more powerful type systems for advanced programming paradigms.

Let $K$ be a field, let $G$ be a finite group, and let $\bar X\rightarrow
\bar Y$ be a $G$-Galois branched cover of varieties over $K^{sep}$. Given a
mere cover model $X\rightarrow Y$ of this cover over $K$, in Part I of this
paper I observe that there is a unique minimal field $E$ over which
$X\rightarrow Y$ becomes Galois, and I prove that $E/K$ is Galois with group a
subgroup of $Aut(G)$. In Part II of this paper, by making the additional
assumption that $K$ is a field of definition (i.e., that there exists \it some
\rm Galois model over $K$), I am able to give an explicit description of the
unique minimal field of Galois action for $X\rightarrow Y$. Namely, if there
exists a $K$-rational point of $X$ above an unramified point $P\in Y(K)$ then
$E$ is contained in the intersection of the specializations at $P$ in the
various different $G$-Galois models of $\bar X\rightarrow \bar Y$ over $K$.
Using the same proof mechanism, I observe a reverse version of "The Twisting
Lemma", which asserts that the behavior of the $K$-rational points on the
various mere cover models over $K$, and the behavior of the specializations on
the various $G$-Galois models over $K$, are all governed by a single
equivalence relation (independent of the model) on the $K$-rational points of
the base variety.

Quiver gauge theories serve as important frameworks in modern theoretical physics, particularly in the study of gauge symmetries and string theory. This research investigates the dimensional reduction process and vacuum structure of quiver gauge theories, aiming to elucidate the underlying mechanisms that govern their physical behavior. The primary objective is to analyze how the dimensional reduction of these theories impacts the vacuum configurations and the associated energy dynamics.   Utilizing a combination of theoretical analysis and computational techniques, we examine the conditions under which dimensional reduction occurs and its implications on the field configurations within the quiver diagram representations. Our methodology incorporates tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory to identify the moduli spaces of vacua that emerge from the reduced dimensions.   Key findings reveal that specific choices of quiver configurations lead to distinct vacuum structures, which can be categorized based on their stability and symmetry properties. Notably, we identify a set of critical points within the parameter space where phase transitions occur, significantly altering the vacuum profiles.   In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between dimensional reduction and vacuum dynamics in quiver gauge theories. The results highlight the richness of the vacuum structure and the potential for new phenomena arising from dimensional transitions. This work lays the groundwork for further explorations into the implications of quiver gauge theories in high-energy physics and string theory.

In this work, we investigate the dust formation processes within the ejecta of the Type II-P supernova 2004dj, aiming to elucidate the mechanisms and timescales of dust creation in such environments. By employing a combined approach of spectroscopic analysis and radiative transfer modeling, we analyze observational data spanning from optical to infrared wavelengths. Our study identifies signatures indicative of dust formation beginning approximately 300 days post-explosion, coinciding with the emergence of infrared excesses and attenuation of optical emissions. Utilizing these data, we model the spectral energy distribution, which reveals the presence of newly formed silicate and carbonaceous grains. Our results demonstrate that the dust grain size distribution and total dust mass align with theoretical predictions, supporting a scenario where significant amounts of dust can form in the dense cool core of the supernova ejecta. Further, we establish that the dust formation efficiency in SN2004dj closely correlates with the progenitor's mass loss history and circumstellar medium density prior to explosion. This study provides substantial evidence that large-scale dust production is feasible in Type II-P supernovae, thereby contributing measurably to the dust content of young galaxies. Our analysis presents key insights into the physical conditions that favor dust condensation, offering a framework for future research on dust formation in other supernovae. As such, this work stands as an inaugural quantitative assessment, laying a foundation for comparative studies of dust evolution in various stellar end-of-life scenarios.

This study focuses on the development and analysis of bounded monochromatic components in random graphs, a fundamental concept in graph theory and combinatorics. Random graphs have been extensively used to model various real-world systems, including social networks, biological networks, and communication networks, where the presence of monochromatic components can have significant implications for understanding the structure and behavior of these systems.  The objective of this research is to investigate the existence, size, and distribution of bounded monochromatic components in random graphs, with a focus on understanding the interplay between the graph's structure and the emergence of these components. To achieve this, we employ a combination of analytical and computational methods, including the use of probabilistic models, Monte Carlo simulations, and graph algorithms.  Our results show that bounded monochromatic components are a ubiquitous feature of random graphs, with a significant proportion of graphs exhibiting large, connected monochromatic components. We demonstrate that the size and distribution of these components are influenced by the graph's degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and other structural properties. Furthermore, we identify a set of conditions under which bounded monochromatic components are guaranteed to exist, and provide bounds on their size in terms of the graph's parameters.  Our findings have significant implications for understanding the behavior of complex systems, including social networks, epidemiological models, and network security systems. By providing a better understanding of the emergence and properties of bounded monochromatic components in random graphs, this research contributes to the development of more accurate models and simulations of these systems, and has the potential to inform the design of more effective algorithms and interventions.

We present a new cosmological galaxy formation model, $\nu^2$GC, as an
updated version of our previous model $\nu$GC. We adopt the so-called
"semi-analytic" approach, in which the formation history of dark matter halos
is computed by ${\it N}$-body simulations, while the baryon physics such as gas
cooling, star formation and supernova feedback are simply modeled by
phenomenological equations. Major updates of the model are as follows: (1) the
merger trees of dark matter halos are constructed in state-of-the-art ${\it
N}$-body simulations, (2) we introduce the formation and evolution process of
supermassive black holes and the suppression of gas cooling due to active
galactic nucleus (AGN) activity, (3) we include heating of the intergalactic
gas by the cosmic UV background, and (4) we tune some free parameters related
to the astrophysical processes using a Markov chain Monte Carlo method. Our
${\it N}$-body simulations of dark matter halos have unprecedented box size and
mass resolution (the largest simulation contains 550 billion particles in a
1.12 Gpc/h box), enabling the study of much smaller and rarer objects. The
model was tuned to fit the luminosity functions of local galaxies and mass
function of neutral hydrogen. Local observations, such as the Tully-Fisher
relation, size-magnitude relation of spiral galaxies and scaling relation
between the bulge mass and black hole mass were well reproduced by the model.
Moreover, the model also well reproduced the cosmic star formation history and
the redshift evolution of rest-frame ${\it K}$-band luminosity functions. The
numerical catalog of the simulated galaxies and AGNs is publicly available on
the web.

The rapid proliferation of mobile ad-hoc networks (MANETs) necessitates an in-depth understanding of the performance of Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) variants in such dynamic environments. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of TCP Reno, New Reno, and Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) in the context of MANETs, focusing on their efficiency in data transmission and network reliability. A comprehensive simulation methodology was employed, utilizing advanced network simulation tools to mimic real-world MANET conditions characterized by variable node mobility, fluctuating link quality, and varying traffic loads. Key performance metrics, including throughput, latency, and packet loss rate, were analyzed across different scenarios. The findings demonstrate that while TCP Reno exhibits a basic performance level, it struggles with high packet loss rates often encountered in MANETs. In contrast, New Reno shows improved performance in scenarios with multiple packet losses, particularly during bursty traffic conditions. However, SACK outperformed both variants in terms of throughput and latency, especially when network conditions were unstable, as it effectively minimizes unnecessary retransmissions and enhances data delivery accuracy. Overall, this research underscores the necessity for adaptive TCP mechanisms tailored for the unique challenges posed by MANETs, emphasizing SACK as a superior choice for optimizing network performance. The insights gained from this survey can guide future developments in TCP optimization specific to mobile ad-hoc environments, potentially leading to more robust communication protocols suited for mobile applications.

We investigate the dynamical properties of families of holomorphic mappings, focusing on their behavior under iteration and the resulting structure of their Julia sets. Our primary goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics arising from these mappings and their implications for the broader field of complex analysis. We systematically analyze various families of holomorphic functions, employing techniques from both classical and modern dynamical systems theory. Specifically, we utilize tools such as bifurcation theory, parameter spaces, and potential theory to characterize the stability and instability of orbits within these families.   Our results reveal that certain parameter values lead to notably distinct dynamical behavior, including the emergence of chaotic regions and the existence of stable periodic points. Furthermore, we demonstrate the presence of bifurcation phenomena where small changes in parameters significantly alter the dynamical landscape. We also explore the role of invariant measures and ergodicity in understanding the long-term behavior of iterates.  Through rigorous analysis, we establish connections between the geometry of the mapping families and the intricacies of their dynamical properties. The findings contribute to the existing literature by providing fresh insights into the classification of holomorphic mappings based on their dynamical characteristics. Our work highlights the rich interplay between complex analysis and dynamical systems, paving the way for future research directions in understanding holomorphic dynamics.

Recent years have seen tremendous progress in creating complex atomic
many-body quantum systems. One approach is to use macroscopic, effectively
thermodynamic ensembles of ultracold atoms to create quantum gases and strongly
correlated states of matter, and to analyze the bulk properties of the
ensemble. The opposite approach is to build up microscopic quantum systems atom
by atom - with complete control over all degrees of freedom. Until now, the
macroscopic and microscopic strategies have been fairly disconnected. Here, we
present a "quantum gas microscope" that bridges the two approaches, realizing a
system where atoms of a macroscopic ensemble are detected individually and a
complete set of degrees of freedom of each of them is determined through
preparation and measurement. By implementing a high-resolution optical imaging
system, single atoms are detected with near-unity fidelity on individual sites
of a Hubbard regime optical lattice. The lattice itself is generated by
projecting a holographic mask through the imaging system. It has an arbitrary
geometry, chosen to support both strong tunnel coupling between lattice sites
and strong on-site confinement. On one hand, this new approach can be used to
directly detect strongly correlated states of matter. On the other hand, the
quantum gas microscope opens the door for the addressing and read-out of
large-scale quantum information systems with ultracold atoms.

This research paper investigates the OH masers associated with the star-forming region IRAS 19092+0841. The objective is to explore the properties and distribution of the OH maser emission in this region. Observations were conducted using the Very Large Array (VLA) to analyze the spectral profiles and spatial distribution of the maser features. The study found multiple OH maser components showing distinct velocities, indicating different regions of maser activity within the molecular cloud associated with IRAS 19092+0841. By analyzing the polarization properties of the maser emission, a magnetic field structure was inferred for the region. Additionally, the variation in maser flux densities over time provided insights into the physical conditions and dynamics of the maser sources. The findings suggest that the OH masers in IRAS 19092+0841 are associated with complex structures and processes related to high-mass star formation. Overall, this study enhances our understanding of the role of masers in probing the environment around massive young stars and contributes to the broader knowledge of star formation regions.

In this study, we present our research on patient flow prediction through the application of discriminative learning of mutually-correcting processes. The primary aim of our work is to enhance hospital resource allocation and optimize patient care by accurately forecasting the flow of patients within healthcare systems. Our research utilizes a novel approach by considering patient flow as a series of interconnected processes that mutually influence each other. We address the inherent complexity and dynamic nature of patient flow patterns by leveraging discriminative learning techniques to model and predict these interdependent processes.   The results obtained from our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methodology in accurately predicting patient flow within hospital settings. By capturing the interplay between different stages of patient care, our approach outperforms traditional forecasting methods and offers a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics driving patient flow. Our findings highlight the potential of discriminative learning techniques in improving operational efficiency and decision-making in healthcare facilities.   Overall, our work contributes to the field of healthcare management by offering a data-driven approach to patient flow prediction that considers the intricate relationships between various stages of patient care. This research opens up new avenues for leveraging machine learning techniques to optimize resource allocation and enhance patient outcomes in healthcare systems.

In our study, we investigate the formation of divalent Rydberg atoms in optical lattices, focusing on the intensity landscape and the concept of magic trapping. We explore the creation of these atoms through selective excitation techniques, which allow us to control their spatial distribution within the lattice. Our results reveal distinct patterns in the intensity landscape, influenced by the symmetry and periodicity of the lattice. We find that certain lattice configurations, known as magic settings, facilitate the stable trapping of these atoms, enhancing their coherence and stability. The methodology involves precise control over laser parameters and the use of density matrix tomography to analyze the atomic states. Our findings contribute to the understanding of Rydberg atom interactions in structured environments, offering potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum simulation.

We are looking for a holographic explanation of nuclear forces, especially
the attractive forces. Recently, the repulsive hard core of a nucleon-nucleon
potential was obtained in the Sakai-Sugimoto model, and we show that a
generalized version of that model -- with an asymmetric configuration of the
flavor D8 branes -- also has an attractive potential. While the repulsive
potential stems from the Chern-Simons interactions of the U(2) flavor gauge
fields in 5D, the attractive potential is due to a coupling of the gauge fields
to a scalar field describing fluctuations of the flavor branes' geometry. At
intermediate distances r between baryons -- smaller than R_KK=O(1)/M_{omega
meson} but larger than the radius rho=R_KK/sqrt('t Hooft coupling) of the
instanton at the core of a baryon -- both the attractive and the repulsive
potentials behave as 1/r^2, but the attractive potential is weaker: Depending
on the geometry of the flavor D8 branes, the ratio C=-V_attr/V_rep ranges from
0 to 1/9. The 5D scalar fields also affect the isovector tensor and spin-spin
forces, and the overall effect is similar to the isoscalar central forces:
V(r)->(1-C)*V(r).
  At longer ranges $r\gtrsim R_{\rm KK}$, we find that the attractive potential
decays faster than the repulsive potential, so the net potential is always
repulsive. This unrealistic behavior may be peculiar to the Sakai-Sugimoto-like
models, or it could be a general problem of the large N_c limit inherent in
holography.

The abstract focuses on the performance analysis of channel estimation techniques utilizing 1-bit analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) in communication systems, particularly addressing the challenge of estimating the channel parameters when the quantization threshold is unknown. Given the limitations imposed by the use of 1-bit ADCs, such as reduced resolution and increased noise, the primary objective is to investigate how these factors impact the accuracy of channel estimation.  The study employs simulations and theoretical analysis to explore different channel models, including flat and frequency-selective channels, and various signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. The methodology involves comparing traditional channel estimation methods with those optimized specifically for 1-bit ADCs, incorporating techniques like iterative algorithms and machine learning-based approaches to mitigate the effects of the unknown quantization threshold.  Key findings indicate that the accuracy of channel estimation significantly degrades when the quantization threshold is not known, leading to higher estimation errors. However, leveraging advanced optimization algorithms and adaptive techniques can improve the performance. Specifically, the research demonstrates that machine learning-based methods, which learn from the data generated by the 1-bit ADC, offer promising improvements in terms of estimation accuracy compared to conventional approaches.  In conclusion, the research underscores the critical role of accurate quantization threshold estimation in enhancing the performance of channel estimation using 1-bit ADCs. Future work should focus on developing more robust methodologies to estimate the quantization threshold and integrating these techniques into practical communication systems.

This study investigates the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) in the context of Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) with flavor, with a focus on the interplay between the CME and the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. The CME is a phenomenon in which the magnetic field generated by a chiral imbalance in the plasma affects the hadronic spectrum, leading to a shift in the mass of hadrons. The AdS/CFT framework provides a powerful tool for studying the CME, as it allows for a systematic exploration of the interplay between the magnetic field and the chiral properties of the plasma.  The objective of this research is to explore the CME in AdS/CFT with flavor, with a focus on the impact of the magnetic field on the hadronic spectrum. We employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to investigate the CME in this context. Our approach involves solving the Dirac equation in the presence of a magnetic field, and then using the resulting solutions to compute the hadronic spectrum.  The key findings of this study reveal that the CME in AdS/CFT with flavor is a complex phenomenon, influenced by the interplay between the magnetic field and the chiral properties of the plasma. We find that the magnetic field affects the hadronic spectrum in a non-trivial way, leading to a shift in the mass of hadrons that is dependent on the strength of the magnetic field. Furthermore, we observe that the CME is accompanied by a significant change in the hadronic spectrum, which is related to the chiral properties of the plasma. These results provide new insights into the CME in AdS/CFT with flavor, and have important implications for our understanding of the behavior of quark-gluon plasas in extreme conditions.  In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive exploration of the CME in AdS/CFT with flavor, highlighting the complex interplay between the magnetic field and the chiral properties of the plasma. Our results demonstrate the importance of considering the flavor properties of the plasma in the study of the CME, and have significant implications for our understanding of the behavior of quark-gluon plasas in extreme conditions.

We investigate the application of the entropy method to the study of special fast diffusion with slow asymptotics on a Riemannian manifold. Our approach involves the use of a novel combination of the entropy method and the theory of flow on Riemannian manifolds, enabling us to derive a new class of heat kernel estimates that capture the slow asymptotic behavior of the diffusion process.  Through a series of rigorous mathematical derivations, we establish the validity of the entropy method for special fast diffusion on a Riemannian manifold, demonstrating that it provides a precise and efficient framework for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the diffusion process. Our key results include the derivation of a new heat kernel estimate that exhibits a slow asymptotic behavior, as well as the establishment of a new bound on the error term of the heat kernel estimate.  Our analysis is based on a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including the use of the entropy method, the theory of flow on Riemannian manifolds, and advanced mathematical tools such as curvature estimates and Sobolev inequalities. By leveraging these techniques, we are able to demonstrate the efficacy of the entropy method for special fast diffusion on a Riemannian manifold, and to establish a new foundation for the study of this class of diffusion processes.

This research explores the implications of the Goldstone theorem within the context of spontaneously broken global symmetries, specifically focusing on the SO(2) group. The study aims to demonstrate how the Goldstone theorem ensures the naturalness of physical systems, particularly by eliminating the need for fine-tuning in the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism. By examining the mathematical underpinnings of spontaneous symmetry breaking, the research elucidates that the theorem mandates the existence of massless particles, which correspond to the Goldstone bosons. This leads to a natural explanation for the masses of other particles, thereby avoiding the requirement for fine-tuning parameters in the Higgs potential. Key findings include the derivation of the Higgs boson mass formula from the spontaneous symmetry breaking condition, highlighting the theorem's role in maintaining the consistency between gauge symmetry and observed particle masses. The conclusion underscores the significance of the Goldstone theorem in providing a robust framework for understanding particle physics, ensuring naturalness and minimizing the need for ad hoc fine-tuning assumptions.

This research abstract focuses on the investigation of galactic gamma-ray sources detected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope with energies exceeding 100 GeV. Historically, high-energy gamma-ray astronomy has been dominated by extragalactic sources, such as blazars and pulsar wind nebulae. However, recent observations from Fermi have revealed a significant population of galactic gamma-ray sources at these energies, challenging the traditional understanding of gamma-ray emission.  The primary objective of this study is to identify and characterize galactic gamma-ray sources, particularly those associated with nearby star-forming regions and supernova remnants, that can be observed with the capabilities of the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). The methodology employed involves detailed analysis of Fermi LAT data, including both short-term variability studies and long-term flux measurements, to distinguish between astrophysical phenomena and instrumental effects.  Key findings include the identification of several galactic gamma-ray sources that exhibit characteristic spectral features indicative of cosmic ray interactions within dense environments. These sources often show significant temporal variability, which provides valuable insights into the physical processes occurring near these energetic particles. Additionally, the study highlights the need for more precise models to explain the emission mechanisms, taking into account the complex interplay between cosmic rays and magnetic fields.  Conclusively, this research underscores the importance of continued monitoring of galactic gamma-ray sources using advanced instruments like the Fermi LAT. It suggests that there is a substantial population of galactic gamma-ray emitters at energies above 100 GeV, necessitating further investigations to elucidate their nature and origin.

This research investigates a prompt radio transient linked to a gamma-ray superflare originating from the young M dwarf binary DG CVn. The objective of this study is to analyze the characteristics and implications of this radio transient event. Methodology involves the collection and analysis of multi-wavelength observational data, including radio and gamma-ray observations, to understand the nature of the event. Key findings reveal the association of the radio transient with the gamma-ray superflare, highlighting the energetic phenomena occurring within the DG CVn system. The study provides insights into the connection between radio emission and gamma-ray flares in M dwarf binaries, shedding light on the physical processes at play in these environments. In conclusion, this research contributes to a better comprehension of the complex interactions and high-energy events occurring in young M dwarf binaries like DG CVn.

We investigate the possibility that Dark Energy, a mysterious component driving the accelerating expansion of the universe, is a manifestation of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) effects. Our work attempts to reconcile the apparent incompatibility between the QCD framework, which describes the strong nuclear force, and the cosmological scale phenomena of Dark Energy.   Utilizing a novel approach that integrates QCD-inspired models with the standard model of cosmology, we derive a modified Friedmann equation that incorporates QCD effects. Our analysis reveals a potential connection between the QCD vacuum energy density and the observed Dark Energy density. We further explore the implications of this connection by investigating the impact of QCD effects on the evolution of the universe's large-scale structure.  Our results suggest that the QCD nature of Dark Energy could be a viable explanation for the accelerating expansion of the universe. We also identify a key role for the QCD vacuum energy density in modulating the cosmological perturbations, providing a possible link to the observed properties of the universe. By integrating QCD-inspired models with the standard model of cosmology, we have shed new light on the interplay between the strong nuclear force and the cosmological scale phenomena, offering a promising avenue for future research.

We discuss a generalized self-consistent mean field (MF) treatment, based on
the selection of an arbitrary subset of operators for representing the system
density matrix, and its application to the problem of entanglement evaluation
in composite quantum systems. As a specific example, we examine in detail a
pair MF approach to the ground state (GS) of dimerized spin 1/2 systems with
anisotropic ferromagnetic-type XY and XYZ couplings in a transverse field,
including chains and arrays with first neighbor and also longer range
couplings. The approach is fully analytic and able to capture the main features
of the GS of these systems, in contrast with the conventional single spin MF.
Its phase diagram differs significantly from that of the latter, exhibiting
(Sz) parity breaking just in a finite field window if the coupling between
pairs is sufficiently weak, together with a fully dimerized phase below this
window and a partially aligned phase above it. It is then shown that through
symmetry restoration, the approach is able to correctly predict not only the
concurrence of a pair, but also its entanglement with the rest of the chain,
which shows a pronounced peak in the parity breaking window. Perturbative
corrections allow to reproduce more subtle observables like the entanglement
between weakly coupled spins and the low lying energy spectrum. All predictions
are tested against exact results for finite systems.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of entanglement spreading in quantum systems through the lens of holography, specifically focusing on the AdS/CFT correspondence. Our objective is to elucidate the mechanisms underpinning the rapid dissemination of quantum information in strongly coupled systems. We utilize a holographic model to simulate the entanglement evolution post-quantum quench. By applying the Ryu-Takayanagi prescription, we calculate the entanglement entropy and track its temporal progression. Our findings indicate a remarkable agreement between holographic predictions and results derived from numerical simulations in lower-dimensional quantum field theories, suggesting that entanglement propagates at a rate consistent with the anticipated speed of light in the dual gravitational theory. Moreover, we observe distinct patterns of entanglement growth reflecting the system's thermalization process, marked by an initial linear surge followed by a plateau, aligning with the quasi-particle picture predictions for integrable models. Additionally, the entanglement velocity—a critical parameter dividing linear and nonlinear growth regimes—presents universal characteristics indicative of the underlying physics. Our research provides substantive evidence that holography serves as a powerful framework for characterizing entanglement spreading, offering insights into non-equilibrium dynamics that extend beyond traditional perturbative techniques. This approach has significant implications for understanding quantum chaos, black hole information paradox, and the interconnectedness of gravity and quantum field theories. Through this work, we contribute to the broader effort to comprehend the fundamental principles governing information theory in quantum gravity contexts.

We investigated the design and optimal configuration of full-duplex Multiple Access Control (MAC) protocols for cognitive radio networks, taking into account the detrimental effects of self-interference. Our analysis revealed that traditional full-duplex MAC protocols, which operate under the assumption of ideal conditions, are highly susceptible to self-interference-induced errors and packet losses.   To address this issue, we developed a novel MAC protocol framework that incorporates self-interference modeling and mitigation techniques. Our framework, dubbed "Self-Interference-Aware Full-Duplex MAC" (SIFA-MAC), employs advanced signal processing and machine learning algorithms to detect and adapt to changing self-interference patterns in real-time.   We conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of SIFA-MAC in various cognitive radio networks, considering different self-interference scenarios and channel conditions. The results show that SIFA-MAC outperforms traditional full-duplex MAC protocols by achieving significantly lower packet loss rates and improved throughput.   Moreover, we demonstrated the effectiveness of SIFA-MAC in real-world environments by deploying it on a cognitive radio testbed and evaluating its performance in the presence of self-interference. Our findings indicate that SIFA-MAC can effectively mitigate self-interference and maintain reliable communication in cognitive radio networks.   The key contributions of our work lie in the development of a self-interference-aware MAC protocol framework and its experimental validation. Our research provides a foundation for the design and optimization of full-duplex MAC protocols for cognitive radio networks, enabling reliable and efficient communication in the presence of self-interference.

A large set of techniques needed to compute decay rates at the two-loop level
are derived and systematized. The main emphasis of the paper is on the two
Standard Model decays H -> gamma gamma and H -> g g. The techniques, however,
have a much wider range of application: they give practical examples of general
rules for two-loop renormalization; they introduce simple recipes for handling
internal unstable particles in two-loop processes; they illustrate simple
procedures for the extraction of collinear logarithms from the amplitude. The
latter is particularly relevant to show cancellations, e.g. cancellation of
collinear divergencies. Furthermore, the paper deals with the proper treatment
of non-enhanced two-loop QCD and electroweak contributions to different
physical (pseudo-)observables, showing how they can be transformed in a way
that allows for a stable numerical integration. Numerical results for the
two-loop percentage corrections to H -> gamma gamma, g g are presented and
discussed. When applied to the process pp -> gg + X -> H + X, the results show
that the electroweak scaling factor for the cross section is between -4 % and +
6 % in the range 100 GeV < Mh < 500 GeV, without incongruent large effects
around the physical electroweak thresholds, thereby showing that only a
complete implementation of the computational scheme keeps two-loop corrections
under control.

In the era of big data, automatic semantic annotation of textual data has emerged as a crucial task for effective information retrieval and analysis. This study proposes a novel machine learning based analytical framework for semantic annotation, focusing on identifying and assigning semantically relevant concepts to textual data.   The traditional approaches for semantic annotation are rule-based and rely on handcrafted features, which are inadequate to handle the complexity and volatility of big data. Machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning models, offer a promising alternative for semantic annotation due to their ability to learn patterns from large amounts of data and generalize to new contexts.   The objective of this research is to develop and evaluate a machine learning based analytical framework for semantic annotation that can effectively handle the complexity and volatility of big data, while providing high accuracy and scalability.   The proposed framework utilizes a deep learning model, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), as a text representation layer to capture semantic context and extract features for semantic annotation. An iterative annotation process based on the EM (Expectation-Maximization) algorithm is employed to refine the annotations and improve the overall accuracy.  Key findings Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets, such as SemCor and CoNLL, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in identifying and assigning semantically relevant concepts to textual data, while maintaining high accuracy and scalability. The results also show that the proposed framework outperforms traditional rule-based and machine learning models in terms of precision, recall, and F1 score.   In conclusion, this study presents a machine learning based analytical framework for semantic annotation, which utilizes a deep learning model and an iterative annotation process to effectively handle the complexity and volatility of big data. The proposed framework offers significant improvements in accuracy, scalability, and applicability compared to traditional rule-based and machine learning models, making it a valuable tool for automatic semantic annotation of textual data.

In this study, we investigate the onset of secondary stellar generations within giant star-forming regions and massive star clusters. Our research aims to elucidate the conditions under which new generations of stars are initiated, focusing on the interplay between metallicity, star formation rates, and gravitational collapse. We employ detailed stellar evolution models coupled with observations from various wavelengths to analyze the chemical abundances in these environments. The problem we address is the transition from primordial to secondary stellar populations, highlighting the role of massive stars as catalysts for nucleosynthesis. Key methodologies include spectral analysis, high-resolution imaging, and numerical simulations. Results indicate that the presence of massive stars significantly enhances the production of heavy elements, leading to the enrichment of the interstellar medium and subsequent formation of secondary generations. This work underscores the importance of studying these environments to understand the full spectrum of star formation and the chemical evolution of galaxies.

In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of anti-correlated time lags in the Z source GX 5-1, with a focus on their potential implications for the structure of its accretion disk. Employing a robust dataset obtained from high temporal resolution observations, we analyzed the time lags between soft and hard X-ray photon fluxes, uncovering a significant anti-correlation. Our results suggest the existence of a truncated accretion disk, whereby variations in the inner disk radius modulate the observed X-ray emissions. We applied Fourier-resolved spectroscopic techniques to delineate the energy-dependent time lag profiles, enabling us to infer the dynamic processes within the accretion flow. Consistent with theoretical models, our findings indicate that the anti-correlated lags originate from Compton upscattering of soft photons by a hot electron corona located above the inner disk edge. This supports the hypothesis that the disk truncation, possibly caused by magnetospheric interactions, leads to the observed variability phenomena. Through comparative analysis with other Z sources, we bolster the case for a universal mechanism governing the disk-corona interactions in such systems. Our methodical approach, integrating observational data with spectral modeling, proves critical in advancing our comprehension of accretion physics, offering a coherent explanation for the anti-correlated time lag behavior. These insights contribute valuable constraints for theoretical models of accretion disk truncation and highlight the intricate relationship between disk geometry and X-ray variability in neutron star binaries. Further observational verification and advanced simulations are warranted to refine our understanding of these complex astrophysical processes.

We report the discovery of a parsec-scale radio jet in the active galactic nucleus (AGN) of IC 883 using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations. IC 883, a nearby Seyfert 1.9 galaxy, has long been known to exhibit variable nonthermal emission in its radio, optical, and X-ray bands, suggesting the presence of an AGN. However, no definitive evidence of a radio jet had been obtained until now.  Our VLBI observations at 8.4 GHz revealed a radio source with an asymmetric structure, consisting of a bright core and two distinct components. We interpret these components as the AGN jet and a counter-jet, respectively. The proper motion measurements of these components revealed a projected jet speed of approximately 0.6c and a jet angle of 20 degrees to the line of sight.  Our analysis suggests that the AGN in IC 883 is powered by a supermassive black hole with a mass of 2.3 x 10^7 M☉, based on the jet power and the radio luminosity. The discovery of a parsec-scale radio jet in IC 883 provides important insights into the AGN unification scheme and the role of jets in AGN feedback.
