liquid's affinity for a surface. A scalable metric for quantifying wettability
is needed, especially given the emergence of technologies exploiting
liquid-solid interactions at the nanoscale. Here we combine nanoscale
experiments with molecular-level simulation to study the breakdown of spherical
droplet shapes at small length scales. We demonstrate how measured droplet
topographies increasingly reveal non-spherical features as volumes shrink, in
agreement with theoretical predictions. Ultimately, the nanoscale liquid
flattens out to form layer-like molecular assemblies, instead of droplets, at
the solid surface. For the lack of a consistent contact angle at small scales,
we introduce a droplet's adsorption energy density as a new metric for a
liquid's affinity for a surface. We discover that extrapolating the macroscopic
idealization of a drop to the nanoscale, though it does not geometrically
resemble a realistic droplet, can nonetheless recover its adsorption energy if
line tension is properly included.

IEEE 802.15.4 takes a center stage in IoT as Low- Rate Wireless Personal Area
Networks(LR-WPANs). The standard specifies Offset Quadrature Phase Shift Keying
Physical Layer (O-QPSK PHY) with half-sine pulse shaping which can be either
analyzed under the class of M-ary PSK signals (QPSK signal with offset) or as
Minimum Shift Keying (MSK) signal. M-ary PSK demodulation is requires perfect
carrier and has minimal error. MSK signals which falls under Continuous Phase
Frequency Shift Keying can be demodulated non-coherently but error performance
is not as good. In our paper, this dual nature of IEEE 802.15.4 PHY is
exploited to propose a dual mode receiver comprising of QPSK demodulator chain
and MSK demodulator chain as a single system on chip. The mode can be
configured manually depending on the type of application or based on the
feedback from a Signal to Noise (SNR) indicator employed in the proposed
receiver. M-ary PSK chain is selected for lower SNRs and MSK for higher SNRs.
Each of these properties are analyzed in detail for both demodulator chains and
we go on to prove that MSK detection can be used for low power, low complex and
low latency while QPSK detection is employed for minimal error.

For quantum mechanics of a charged particle in a classical external
electromagnetic field, there is an apparent puzzle that the matrix element of
the canonical momentum and Hamiltonian operators is gauge dependent. A
resolution to this puzzle is recently provided by us in [2]. Based on the
separation of the electromagnetic potential into pure gauge and gauge invariant
parts, we have proposed a new set of momentum and Hamiltonian operators which
satisfy both the requirement of gauge invariance and the relevant commutation
relations. In this paper we report a check for the case of the hydrogen atom
problem: Starting from the Hamiltonian of the coupled electron, proton and
electromagnetic field, under the infinite proton mass approximation, we derive
the gauge invariant hydrogen atom Hamiltonian and verify explicitly that this
Hamiltonian is different from the Dirac Hamiltonian, which is the time
translation generator of the system. The gauge invariant Hamiltonian is the
energy operator, whose eigenvalue is the energy of the hydrogen atom. It is
generally time-dependent. In this case, one can solve the energy eigenvalue
equation at any specific instant of time. It is shown that the energy
eigenvalues are gauge independent, and by suitably choosing the phase factor of
the time-dependent eigenfunction, one can ensure that the time-dependent
eigenfunction satisfies the Dirac equation.

The Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is a signal analysis method that
separates multi-component signals into single oscillatory modes called
intrinsic mode functions (IMFs), each of which can generally be associated to a
physical meaning of the process from which the signal is obtained. When the
phenomena of mode mixing occur, as a result of the EMD sifting process, the
IMFs can lose their physical meaning hindering the interpretation of the
results of the analysis. In the paper, "One or Two frequencies? The Empirical
Mode Decomposition Answers", Gabriel Rilling and Patrick Flandrin [3] presented
a rigorous mathematical analysis that explains how EMD behaves in the case of a
composite two-tones signal and the amplitude and frequency ratios by which EMD
will perform a good separation of tones. However, the authors did not propose a
solution for separating the neighboring tones that will naturally remain mixed
after an EMD. In this paper, based on the findings by Rilling and Flandrin, a
method that can separate neighbouring spectral components, that will naturally
remain within a single IMF, is presented. This method is based on reversing the
conditions by which mode mixing occurs and that were presented in the map by
Rilling and Flandrin in the above mentioned paper. Numerical experiments with
signals containing closely spaced spectral components shows the effective
separation of modes that EMD can perform after this principle is applied. The
results verify also the regimes presented in the theoretical analysis by
Rilling and Flandrin.

We investigate the prevalence and characteristics of luminous X-ray active galactic nuclei (AGN) within galaxy clusters, aiming to elucidate their role in cluster dynamics and evolution. Our analysis encompasses a comprehensive survey of X-ray data sourced from both observational campaigns and archival databases, targeting a diverse sample of galaxy clusters. We employ advanced statistical techniques to quantify the correlation between AGN luminosity and cluster properties such as mass, temperature, and core dynamics. Our results reveal a significant association between the presence of luminous X-ray AGN and the thermal properties of the intra-cluster medium, suggesting that AGN feedback mechanisms significantly influence cluster formation and evolution processes. We also identify a notable trend in AGN activity that peaks at a specific cluster mass, indicating a critical threshold for AGN emergence. Additionally, we explore the spectral properties of these AGN, documenting distinct emission features that correlate with their environmental conditions. Our study concludes that luminous X-ray AGN serve as pivotal players within galaxy clusters, mediating the interplay between galaxy evolution and the surrounding intracluster environment. This research not only contributes to the understanding of AGN behavior in dense environments but also provides insights into the broader implications of AGN feedback in cosmological models of structure formation. By advancing methodologies that integrate multi-wavelength observations and simulations, we lay the groundwork for future inquiries into the complex relationship between AGN activity and large-scale structure in the universe.

China has experienced a spectacular economic growth in recent decades. Its
economy grew more than 48 times from 1980 to 2013. How are the other countries
reacting to China's rise? Do they see it as an economic opportunity or a
security threat? In this paper, we answer this question by analyzing online
news reports about China published in Australia, France, Germany, Japan,
Russia, South Korea, the UK and the US. More specifically, we first analyze the
frequency with which China has appeared in news headlines, which is a measure
of China's influence in the world. Second, we build a Naive Bayes classifier to
study the evolving nature of the news reports, i.e., whether they are economic
or political. We then evaluate the friendliness of the news coverage based on
sentiment analysis. Empirical results indicate that there has been increasing
news coverage of China in all the countries under study. We also find that the
emphasis of the reports is generally shifting towards China's economy. Here
Japan and South Korea are exceptions: they are reporting more on Chinese
politics. In terms of global sentiment, the picture is quite gloomy. With the
exception of Australia and, to some extent, France, all the other countries
under examination are becoming less positive towards China.

Motivated by the Pati-Salam Grand Unified Theory, we study $(4+1)d$
topological insulators with $SU(4) \times SU(2)_1 \times SU(2)_2$ symmetry,
whose $(3+1)d$ boundary has 16 flavors of left-chiral fermions, which form
representations $(\mathbf{4}, \mathbf{2}, \mathbf{1})$ and $(\bar{\mathbf{4}},
\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2})$. The key result we obtain is that, without any
interaction, this topological insulator has a $\mathbb{Z}$ classification,
namely any quadratic fermion mass operator at the $(3+1)d $ boundary is
prohibited by the symmetries listed above; while under interaction this system
becomes trivial, namely its $(3+1)d$ boundary can be gapped out by a properly
designed short range interaction without generating nonzero vacuum expectation
value of any fermion bilinear mass, or in other words, its $(3+1)d$ boundary
can be driven into a "strongly coupled symmetric gapped (SCSG) phase". Based on
this observation, we propose that after coupling the system to a dynamical
$SU(4) \times SU(2)_1 \times SU(2)_2$ lattice gauge field, the Pati-Salam GUT
can be fully regularized as the boundary states of a $(4+1)d$ topological
insulator with a {\it thin} fourth spatial dimension, the thin fourth dimension
makes the entire system generically a $(3+1)d$ system. The mirror sector on the
opposite boundary will {\it not} interfere with the desired GUT, because the
mirror sector is driven to the SCSG phase by a carefully designed interaction
and is hence decoupled from the GUT.

The Standard Model of particle physics, while highly successful in describing the behavior of fundamental particles, falls short in explaining the origin of the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. The Littlest Higgs Model, a variant of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, aims to address this issue by introducing a new Higgs boson and a T-parity breaking mechanism. In this context, the B_s - anti-B_s mixing phenomenon, a process where the two B-mesons mix and change their properties, is a crucial tool to probe the CP-violating effects. CP-violation, a fundamental aspect of the Standard Model, refers to the difference in behavior between matter and antimatter in particle physics processes.  This study investigates the implications of T-parity breaking in the Littlest Higgs Model on the B_s - anti-B_s mixing process, focusing on the potential CP-violation effects. The framework employed in this research is based on the renormalization group evolution of the Yukawa couplings, which enables the calculation of the B_s - anti-B_s mixing matrix elements. By analyzing the results of numerical simulations, we find that the T-parity breaking mechanism can indeed generate significant CP-violating effects in the B_s - anti-B_s mixing process. These findings have important implications for the understanding of the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe and for the development of new experimental strategies to probe CP-violation in B-meson processes. The results of this study provide new insights into the interplay between T-parity breaking and CP-violation in the Littlest Higgs Model, highlighting the potential of this framework to explain the origin of the matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Context. The properties of the X-ray emission lines are a fundamental tool
for studying the nature of the matter surrounding the neutron star and the
phenomena that produce these lines. Aims. The aim of this work is to analyze
the X-ray spectrum of 4U 1538-52 obtained by the XMM-Newton observatory and to
look for the presence of diagnostic lines in the energy range 0.3-11.5 keV.
Methods. We used a 54 ks PN & MOS/XMM-Newton observation of the high mass X-ray
binary 4U 1538-52 covering the orbital phase between 0.75 to 1.00 (the
eclipse-ingress). We have modelled the 0.3-11.5 keV continuum emission with
three absorbed power laws and looked for the emission lines. Results. We found
previously unreported recombination lines, in this system, at 2.4 keV, 1.9 keV
and 1.3 keV, consistent with the presence of highly ionized states of S XV He?,
Si XIII He? and Mg K? or Mg XI He?. On the other hand, both out of eclipse and
in eclipse we detect a fluorescence iron emission line at 6.4 keV which is
resolved into two components: a narrow ($\sigma \leq$ 10 eV) fluorescence Fe K?
line plus one hot line from highly photoionized Fe XXV. Conclusions. The
detection of new recombination lines during eclipse-ingress in 4U 1538-52
indicates that there is an extended ionized region surrounding the neutron
star.

It is quite relevant the extension of decoration transformation for quantum
spin models since most of the real materials could be well described by
Heisenberg type models. Here we propose an exact quantum decoration
transformation and also showing interesting properties such as the persistence
of symmetry and the symmetry breaking during this transformation. Although the
proposed transformation, in principle, cannot be used to map exactly a quantum
spin lattice model into another quantum spin lattice model, since the operators
are non-commutative. However, it is possible the mapping in the "classical"
limit, establishing an equivalence between both quantum spin lattice models. To
study the validity of this approach for quantum spin lattice model, we use the
Zassenhaus formula, and we verify how the correction could influence the
decoration transformation. But this correction could be useless to improve the
quantum decoration transformation because it involves the
second-nearest-neighbor and further nearest neighbor couplings, which leads
into a cumbersome task to establish the equivalence between both lattice
models. This correction also gives us valuable information about its
contribution, for most of the Heisenberg type models, this correction could be
irrelevant at least up to the third order term of Zassenhaus formula. This
transformation is applied to a finite size Heisenberg chain, comparing with the
exact numerical results, our result is consistent for weak xy-anisotropy
coupling. We also apply to bond-alternating Ising-Heisenberg chain model,
obtaining an accurate result in the limit of the quasi-Ising chain.

In this study, we directly characterized the relative strength and momentum dependence of electron-phonon coupling (EPC) through resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS). Our approach involved probing EPC effects across a range of phonon momenta and strengths by analyzing the spectral response of materials with known EPC mechanisms. We employed RIXS measurements on two prototypical systems one featuring strong EPC due to charge transfer states and another with weaker EPC driven by localized excitations. The results revealed distinct spectral features indicative of varying EPC strengths and their momentum dependencies. Specifically, we observed that the intensity of the RIXS signal decreases as the momentum of the phonon increases, indicating a reduction in the coupling strength with higher phonon momenta. This investigation not only confirms previous theoretical predictions but also provides empirical evidence for the momentum-dependent nature of EPC, enhancing our understanding of its role in correlated electronic systems.

Recent works have shown that it is possible to automatically predict
intrinsic image properties like memorability. In this paper, we take a step
forward addressing the question: "Can we make an image more memorable?".
Methods for automatically increasing image memorability would have an impact in
many application fields like education, gaming or advertising. Our work is
inspired by the popular editing-by-applying-filters paradigm adopted in photo
editing applications, like Instagram and Prisma. In this context, the problem
of increasing image memorability maps to that of retrieving "memorabilizing"
filters or style "seeds". Still, users generally have to go through most of the
available filters before finding the desired solution, thus turning the editing
process into a resource and time consuming task. In this work, we show that it
is possible to automatically retrieve the best style seeds for a given image,
thus remarkably reducing the number of human attempts needed to find a good
match. Our approach leverages from recent advances in the field of image
synthesis and adopts a deep architecture for generating a memorable picture
from a given input image and a style seed. Importantly, to automatically select
the best style a novel learning-based solution, also relying on deep models, is
proposed. Our experimental evaluation, conducted on publicly available
benchmarks, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach for
generating memorable images through automatic style seed selection

The interstellar medium (ISM) has a multiphase structure characterized by
gas, dust and molecules. The gas can be found in different charge states:
neutral, low-ionized (warm) and high-ionized (hot). It is possible to probe the
multiphase ISM through the observation of its absorption lines and edges in the
X-ray spectra of background sources. We present a high-quality RGS spectrum of
the low-mass X-ray binary GS 1826-238 with an unprecedent detailed treatment of
the absorption features due to the dust and both the neutral and ionized gas of
the ISM. We constrain the column density ratios within the different phases of
the ISM and measure the abundances of elements such as O, Ne, Fe and Mg. We
found significant deviations from the proto-Solar abundances: oxygen is
over-abundant by a factor 1.23 +/- 0.05, neon 1.75 +/- 0.11, iron 1.37 +/- 0.17
and magnesium 2.45 +/- 0.35. The abundances are consistent with the measured
metallicity gradient in our Galaxy: the ISM appears to be metal-rich in the
inner regions. The spectrum also shows the presence of warm/hot ionized gas.
The gas column has a total ionization degree less than 10%. We also show that
dust plays an important role as expected from the position of GS 1826-238: most
iron appears to be bound in dust grains, while 10-40% of oxygen consists of a
mixture of dust and molecules.

Precise measurement of Higgs boson couplings is an important task for
International Linear Collider (ILC) experiments and will facilitate the
understanding of the particle mass generation mechanism.
  In this study, the measurement accuracies of the Higgs boson branching
fractions to the $b$ and $c$ quarks and gluons, $\Delta Br(H\to b\bar{b},\sim
c\bar{c},\sim gg)/Br$, were evaluated with the full International Large
Detector model (\texttt{ILD\_00}) for the Higgs mass of 120 GeV at the
center-of-mass (CM) energies of 250 and 350 GeV using neutrino, hadronic and
leptonic channels and assuming an integrated luminosity of $250 {\rm fb^{-1}}$,
and an electron (positron) beam polarization of -80% (+30%).
  We obtained the following measurement accuracies of the Higgs cross section
times branching fraction ($\Delta (\sigma \cdot Br)/\sigma \cdot Br$) for decay
of the Higgs into $b\bar{b}$, $c\bar{c}$, and $gg$; as 1.0%, 6.9%, and 8.5% at
a CM energy of 250 GeV and 1.0%, 6.2%, and 7.3% at 350 GeV, respectively.
  After the measurement accuracy of the cross section ($\Delta\sigma/\sigma$)
was corrected using the results of studies at 250 GeV and their extrapolation
to 350 GeV, the derived measurement accuracies of the branching fractions
($\Delta Br/Br$) to $b\bar{b}$, $c\bar{c}$, and gg were 2.7%, 7.3%, and 8.9% at
a CM energy of 250 GeV and 3.6%, 7.2%, and 8.1% at 350 GeV, respectively.

We investigate the dust energy balance problem in edge-on spiral galaxies, a long-standing challenge in understanding the evolution of dust in these systems. Through a comprehensive analysis of Herschel Space Observatory data, we examine the dust temperature, size distribution, and optical depth of 15 edge-on spiral galaxies. Our results indicate a significant correlation between dust temperature and galaxy rotation velocity, suggesting that dust is heated by the gravitational energy released during galaxy mergers. We also find that the size distribution of dust grains is consistent with a power-law distribution, indicative of a dynamic equilibrium between dust formation and destruction. Notably, our analysis reveals a significant dust optical depth, which implies that dust is an important contributor to the infrared emission of these galaxies. By integrating Herschel observations with simulations of galaxy evolution, we demonstrate that the dust energy balance problem can be resolved through the incorporation of dust formation and destruction processes. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of dust in shaping the evolution of edge-on spiral galaxies, and highlight the importance of considering dust dynamics in galaxy evolution models.

The search for lead-free multiferroic materials has gained significant attention due to environmental concerns, with Bi₂FeTiO₆ emerging as a promising candidate. This study aims to investigate the magnetoelectric properties of Bi₂FeTiO₆ through a theoretical framework. Using density functional theory (DFT), we explore the structural, electronic, and ferroelectric characteristics of this compound, focusing on its potential as a lead-free alternative in various applications. The computational simulations revealed a stable orthorhombic phase with minimal lattice distortions, contributing to robust ferroelectric polarization. The electronic structure analysis demonstrated a bandgap suitable for practical device applications while preserving intrinsic magnetic ordering. Magnetization studies highlighted the presence of a canted antiferromagnetic ordering, which, when coupled with ferroelectricity, indicates potential for significant magnetoelectric coupling. Such coupling is crucial for the development of multifunctional devices that exploit both electric and magnetic field controls. Our findings indicate that the intrinsic properties of Bi₂FeTiO₆, including its adequate bandgap and scalable polarization, make it an excellent candidate for further experimental validation and practical application. By providing a comprehensive theoretical understanding, this work lays the groundwork for subsequent experimental pursuits aimed at harnessing the multiferroic characteristics of Bi₂FeTiO₆, offering an environmentally benign and viable path forward in the realm of advanced functional materials.

This study presents an ab-initio investigation into the behavior of gap opening and screening effects in gated bilayer graphene. The computational approach employs density functional theory (DFT) to analyze the electronic structure and mechanical properties of bilayer graphene with different gate dielectric materials and gating voltages. Two scenarios are considered the absence and presence of screening effects in the gating process. The results demonstrate that, in the absence of screening effects, the gate voltage causes a reduction in the bandgap, while the gated bilayer graphene exhibits an increasing strain with the increase in gate voltage. The presence of screening effects results in a smaller gap reduction and a less pronounced strain behavior. Furthermore, the screening effects enhance the sensitivity of the gating process to the gate dielectric material's choice. The findings contribute to the understanding of the fundamental physics behind the gating effects in bilayer graphene and provide crucial insights for the design and optimization of graphene-based devices.

The study of photonic Dirac monopoles and skyrmions represents a significant advancement in the understanding of topological phenomena in photonic systems. This research aims to explore the spin-1 quantization associated with these entities, focusing on their potential applications in advanced optical technologies. A systematic theoretical framework was constructed based on Maxwell's equations adapted to account for the topological properties of light. Employing numerical simulations, we analyzed various configurations of photonic crystals and discovered the emergence of spin-1 modes linked to Dirac monopoles and skyrmions. Key findings demonstrate that these monopoles exhibit unique light-matter interactions, leading to tunable optical responses dependent on the quantization of spin states. The results show that by manipulating the geometrical properties of the photonic system, one can induce robust skyrmionic states that support stable data encoding at the quantum level. This innovation opens pathways for developing multifunctional photonic devices that integrate data processing, storage, and transmission. The conclusion emphasizes the significance of harnessing photonic Dirac monopoles and skyrmions for future quantum technology applications, underscoring their role in advancing our understanding of topological states in photonics. This work not only enriches the theoretical landscape but also paves the way for practical implementations that could revolutionize information technology.

Probabilistic Count Matrix Factorization (PCMF) is a powerful tool for understanding complex biological systems, such as single cell expression data. In recent years, the availability of high-throughput sequencing technologies has led to an exponential increase in single cell expression data. However, the analysis of this data poses unique challenges due to its high-dimensionality, sparsity, and technical variability.  The primary objective of this study is to apply PCMF to single cell expression data and evaluate its performance in terms of identifying biological themes and discovering novel genes. To achieve this, we first preprocess the raw data by aligning reads to a reference transcriptome, quantifying gene expression levels, and removing batch effects. We then apply PCMF to the count matrix obtained from the processed data. Our results show that PCMF identifies biologically meaningful topics, such as immune response, metabolism, and signaling pathways, with high accuracy. Moreover, we discover novel genes not previously known to be involved in these processes. Additionally, we evaluate the robustness of our results to technical variability by simulating sequencing errors and comparing the results with those obtained from error-free data.  In conclusion, this study demonstrates the utility of PCMF for analyzing single cell expression data. Our findings suggest that PCMF can be an effective tool for identifying biological themes and discovering novel genes, even in the presence of technical variability. Future work includes applying PCMF to larger single cell expression datasets to further explore its potential and investigate its applications in other areas of biology.  PCMF, a probabilistic approach for matrix factorization, effectively uncovers biological themes and discoveries of novel genes in single cell expression data. We preprocess raw data, removing batch effects, aligning reads to reference transcriptomes, and quantifying gene expression. PCMF identifies topics like immune response, metabolism, and signaling pathways with high accuracy. Novel genes that are not previously known are also discovered. We assessed its robustness to technical variability through simulated sequencing errors. PCMF's potential is promising for large single cell expression datasets and other biological applications.

A causal structure is a relationship between observed variables that in
general restricts the possible correlations between them. This relationship can
be mediated by unobserved systems, modelled by random variables in the
classical case or joint quantum systems in the quantum case. One way to
differentiate between the correlations realisable by two different causal
structures is to use entropy vectors, i.e., vectors whose components correspond
to the entropies of each subset of the observed variables. To date, the
starting point for deriving entropic constraints within causal structures are
the so-called Shannon inequalities (positivity of entropy, conditional entropy
and conditional mutual information). In the present work we investigate what
happens when non-Shannon entropic inequalities are included as well. We show
that in general these lead to tighter outer approximations of the set of
realisable entropy vectors and hence enable a sharper distinction of different
causal structures. Since non-Shannon inequalities can only be applied amongst
classical variables, it might be expected that their use enables an entropic
distinction between classical and quantum causal structures. However, this
remains an open question. We also introduce techniques for deriving inner
approximations to the allowed sets of entropy vectors for a given causal
structure. These are useful for proving tightness of outer approximations or
for finding interesting regions of entropy space. We illustrate these
techniques in several scenarios, including the triangle causal structure.

The Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) monitoring program TANAMI
provides bi-monthly, dualfrequency (8GHz and 22GHz) observations of
extragalactic jets with milliarcsecond resolution south of -30 deg declination
using the Australian Long Baseline Array (LBA) and additional radio telescopes
in Antarctica, Chile, New Zealand and South Africa. Supporting programs provide
multiwavelength coverage of the Fermi/LAT sources of the TANAMI sample, in
order to construct simultaneous broadband spectral energy distributions (SEDs),
as well as rapid follow-ups of high energy flares. The main purpose of this
project is to study the radio-gamma-ray connection seen in the jets of active
galactic nuclei (AGN) via simultaneous monitoring of their VLBI structure and
broadband emission in order to distinguish between different proposed emission
models. Here we give a brief description of the TANAMI program and will then
focus on its current status: (1) We present some results on the first
simultaneous dual-frequency images of the whole sample resulting in spectral
index maps of the parsec-scale core-jet structure. (2) The TANAMI array allows
us to observe the closest radio galaxy Centaurus A with unprecedented high
angular resolution resulting in the best-ever image of an AGN jet. We
constructed the best resolved spectral index map of its jet-counterjet system
revealing multiple possible production sites of gamma-rays recently detected by
Fermi/LAT. With the first epochs of the TANAMI monitoring, we can study the
proper jet motion of individual jet components of Cen A on sub-parsec scales.
(3) Since the launch of Fermi/LAT we added newly detected gamma-ray bright AGN
to the TANAMI observing list which is built as a combined radio and gamma-ray
selected sample. For most of these sources the TANAMI observations obtain the
first VLBI images ever made.

We investigate the influence of spacecraft trajectory on the detection of magnetic clouds in the interplanetary medium. Our research addresses the critical problem of accurately identifying and characterizing these solar phenomena, as their interaction with the Earth's magnetosphere can significantly impact space weather conditions. Through a series of simulation frameworks, we analyze various trajectory scenarios of spacecraft in relation to known magnetic cloud events recorded over the past decade. We employ advanced data analysis techniques, including wavelet transforms and magnetic field modeling, to assess the sensitivity of detection metrics based on trajectory parameters such as angle of approach, speed, and distance from the solar wind source. Our findings reveal a pronounced dependency of detection probability on spacecraft orientation, with optimal configurations yielding a 30% increase in successful identifications of magnetic clouds compared to suboptimal trajectories. Additionally, we propose a set of guidelines for mission planning and instrumentation design aimed at enhancing detection capabilities. The investigation underscores the necessity of considering trajectory factors in future solar observation missions, particularly those aimed at improving forecasts of space weather effects on terrestrial technology and infrastructure. We conclude that trajectory optimization plays a vital role in the successful detection and study of magnetic clouds, advocating for its integration into the operational planning of space exploration and solar research initiatives.

This study investigates the possibility of a stable bucky-diamond structure within silicon carbide (SiC) clusters. Previous research has explored various nanostructures in carbon allotropes like graphene and nanotubes, leading to an interest in analogous structures in other group IV elements such as SiC. Through density functional theory calculations, we aimed to identify and characterize the bucky-diamond arrangement within SiC clusters. Key findings indicate that while bucky-diamond-like structures can exist stably in SiC, they are not as prevalent as their carbon counterparts due to the different electronic and geometric properties of Si and C atoms. Additionally, the stability of these structures varies with cluster size and composition. This research contributes to the understanding of unique structural features in SiC and highlights the differences in behavior compared to carbon-based systems.

In this study, we reexamined the primordial lithium abundance problem, a long-standing challenge to the Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) theory. By analyzing updated cosmological data, we found a possible solution to the discrepancy between the predicted and observed primordial lithium abundance. Our analysis indicates that the solution lies in the baryonic density of the universe. We utilized a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to sample the posterior probability distribution functions of the cosmological parameters, including the baryon density, using an updated version of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) power spectrum. Our results show that a higher baryonic density value, consistent with the Planck data, can significantly improve the agreement between the observed and predicted lithium abundance. However, the tensions between the high baryonic density solution and the other observational data, such as the Hubble constant measurement and the galaxy cluster abundance, suggest that additional physics beyond the standard Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model may be required to explain the discrepancies. Further investigations are necessary to determine the exact nature of this physics and its implications for the fundamental constants and initial conditions of the universe. Our findings highlight the importance of ongoing efforts to improve the precision of observational data and theoretical models to better understand the primordial abundances of light elements and the evolution of the universe as a whole. The reevaluation of the primordial lithium abundance problem and its potential link to the baryonic density of the universe provides new insights into the early universe and the need for further exploration of new physics beyond the standard ΛCDM model. This work underscores the significance of continued data collection and theoretical advancements in the fields of cosmology and astrophysics.

We study hedging and pricing of unattainable contingent claims in a
non-Markovian regime-switching financial model. Our financial market consists
of a bank account and a risky asset whose dynamics are driven by a Brownian
motion and a multivariate counting process with stochastic intensities. The
interest rate, drift, volatility and intensities fluctuate over time and, in
particular, they depend on the state (regime) of the economy which is modelled
by the multivariate counting process. Hence, we can allow for stressed market
conditions. We assume that the trajectory of the risky asset is continuous
between the transition times for the states of the economy and that the value
of the risky asset jumps at the time of the transition. We find the hedging
strategy which minimizes the instantaneous mean-variance risk of the hedger's
surplus and we set the price so that the instantaneous Sharpe ratio of the
hedger's surplus equals a predefined target. We use Backward Stochastic
Differential Equations. Interestingly, the instantaneous mean-variance hedging
and instantaneous Sharpe ratio pricing can be related to no-good-deal pricing
and robust pricing and hedging under model ambiguity. We discuss key properties
of the optimal price and the optimal hedging strategy. We also use our results
to price and hedge mortality-contingent claims with financial components
(equity-linked insurance claims) in a combined insurance and regime-switching
financial model.

In this study, we address the challenge of dense semantic labeling of sub-decimeter resolution images, which is pivotal for various applications including urban planning, environmental monitoring, and autonomous navigation. We employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of semantic segmentation tasks at this high resolution. Our methodology involves designing a multi-scale CNN architecture that effectively captures contextual information while preserving fine-grained details essential for distinguishing between closely related classes, such as different types of vegetation and urban materials.   We systematically evaluate our approach using a comprehensive dataset consisting of high-resolution aerial imagery and ground truth annotations. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) score that exceeds previous benchmarks in the domain. Furthermore, we implement data augmentation techniques and transfer learning to mitigate overfitting and enhance model generalizability across varying terrains.   Our findings indicate that the integration of hierarchical feature extraction and attention mechanisms within the CNN framework significantly improves labeling performance, particularly in complex urban environments. We highlight the potential of our approach to provide detailed and accurate semantic maps that can be leveraged for real-time applications. This research contributes to the advancement of machine learning techniques in remote sensing, underscoring the importance of high-resolution image analysis for future technological developments.

Energetic gamma rays (GeV to TeV photon energy) have been detected toward
several supernova remnants (SNR) associated with molecular clouds. If the gamma
rays are produced mainly by hadronic processes rather than leptonic processes
like bremsstrahlung, then the flux of energetic cosmic ray (CR) nuclei (>1 GeV)
required to produce the gamma rays can be inferred at the site where the
particles are accelerated in SNR shocks. It is of great interest to understand
the acceleration of the CR of lower energy (<1 GeV) accompanying the energetic
component. These particles of lower energy are most effective in ionizing
interstellar gas, leaving an observable imprint on the interstellar ion
chemistry. A correlation of energetic gamma radiation with enhanced
interstellar ionization can thus support the hadronic origin of the gamma rays
and constrain the acceleration of ionizing CR in SNR. We propose a method to
test the hadronic origin of GeV gamma rays from SNR associated with a molecular
cloud. We use observational gamma ray data for each of these SNR known,
modeling the observations to obtain the underlying proton spectrum assuming
that the gamma rays are produced by pion decay. Assuming that the acceleration
mechanism does not only produce high energy protons, but also low energy
protons, this proton spectrum at the source is then used to calculate the
ionization rate of the molecular cloud. Ionized molecular hydrogen triggers a
chemical network forming molecular ions. The relaxation of these ions results
in characteristic line emission, which can be predicted. We show that the
ionization rate for at least two objects is more than an order of magnitude
above Galactic average for molecular clouds, hinting at an enhanced formation
rate of molecular ions. There will be interesting opportunities to measure
crucial molecular ions in the infrared and submillimeter-wave parts of the
spectrum.

Recently, we proposed a simultaneous quantum and classical communication
(SQCC) protocol, where random numbers for quantum key distribution (QKD) and
bits for classical communication are encoded on the \emph{same} weak coherent
pulse, and decoded by the \emph{same} coherent receiver. Such a scheme could be
appealing in practice since a single coherent communication system can be used
for multiple purposes. However, previous studies show that the SQCC protocol
can only tolerate very small phase noise. This makes it incompatible with the
coherent communication scheme using a true local oscillator (LO), which
presents a relatively high phase noise due to the fact that the signal and the
LO are generated from two independent lasers. In this paper, we improve the
phase noise tolerance of the SQCC scheme using a true LO by adopting a refined
noise model where phase noises originated from different sources are treated
differently: on one hand, phase noise associated with the coherent receiver may
be regarded as \emph{trusted} noise, since the detector can be calibrated
locally and the photon statistics of the detected signals can be determined
from the measurement results; on the other hand, phase noise due to the
instability of fiber interferometers may be regarded as \emph{untrusted} noise,
since its randomness (from the adversary's point to view) is hard to justify.
Simulation results show the tolerable phase noise in this refined noise model
is significantly higher than that in the previous study where all the phase
noises are assumed to be untrusted. We conduct an experiment to show the
required phase stability can be achieved in a coherent communication system
using a true LO.

The study of vacuum currents induced by a magnetic flux in the vicinity of a cosmic string is a subject of considerable interest in theoretical physics, particularly in understanding quantum field behaviors in topologically non-trivial spacetimes. This research investigates the nature of these currents when the cosmic string is modeled with a finite core, as opposed to an idealized infinitely thin line. The primary objective is to analyze how the finite core's structure affects the characteristics of the induced vacuum currents. Utilizing methods from quantum field theory, particularly within the framework of cylindrical geometries, this study employs gauge field configurations that include a homogeneous magnetic flux distribution within the core. The methodology involves solving the Dirac equation in these geometries and calculating the vacuum expectation value of the current density. Key findings indicate that the core's finite size significantly modifies the radial and angular distribution of the currents. Notably, the induced currents exhibit a dependency not only on the strength of the magnetic flux but also on the geometric and material properties of the core. These effects become prominent at distances comparable to the core's size, diverging from behaviors observed in the idealized thin string case. The results suggest that cosmological models involving such finite-core strings could exhibit distinct electromagnetic properties, impacting theoretical predictions in cosmic string theory. Conclusively, considering a finite-core model provides a more realistic and comprehensive understanding of vacuum phenomena around cosmic strings, which could have implications for both cosmology and related quantum field theories.

We present the results of a study of the time-averaged spectral energy
distributions (SEDs) of eight flat spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) present in
the second catalog of high energy sources detected beyond 50 GeV by the {\it
Fermi}-Large Area Telescope (2FHL). Both leptonic and hadronic scenarios are
adopted to explain the multi-wavelength SEDs and we find them to be marginally
consistent with the 2FHL spectra above 50 GeV. We derive the expected degree of
X-ray and $\gamma$-ray polarizations both for the average and elevated activity
states and note that: (i) a hadronic radiative model consistently predicts a
higher degree of high energy polarization compared to leptonic ones, and (ii)
the X-ray polarization degree is higher than the $\gamma$-ray polarization in
the leptonic scenario, but similar to the $\gamma$-ray polarization if the
observed radiation is powered by hadronic processes. From the leptonic
modeling, the location of the $\gamma$-ray emitting region is found to be at
the outer edge of the broad line region (BLR) and is consistent with the
$\gamma\gamma$ opacity estimates for the $\gamma$-ray absorption by the BLR. We
conclude that a majority of the FSRQs could be detected by the upcoming
Cherenkov Telescope Array, though future high energy polarimeters will be able
to detect them only during elevated activity states, which could provide
supportive evidence for the hadronic origin of the X-ray and $\gamma$-ray
emission.

Volatile species beneath mid-ocean ridges play a critical role in geochemical processes during the formation and evolution of oceanic crust. This study aims to investigate the mechanisms of deep melting, channelized transport, focusing, and metasomatism of volatiles in these geological environments. We employed a multi-disciplinary approach, utilizing geochemical analyses, petrological studies, and numerical modeling to elucidate the interactions between volatiles and mantle-derived materials. Our findings indicate that deep melting is significantly influenced by the presence of volatiles, which lower the solidus temperatures of mantle rocks, thereby facilitating the generation of melts. Furthermore, we observed that channelized transport mechanisms, particularly through porous flow, enhance the efficiency of volatile migration towards the mid-ocean ridge system. This leads to localized focusing of volatiles, which significantly influences the chemical composition of erupted magmas. Additionally, metasomatic processes were identified as pivotal in altering the mineralogy and geochemistry of the mantle, resulting in the enrichment of certain trace elements. The implications of these processes extend beyond magma generation, influencing tectonic activity and hydrothermal systems associated with mid-ocean ridges. Our research underscores the complexity of volatile interactions beneath mid-ocean ridges and their profound impact on the geological and geochemical evolution of oceanic crust. These findings contribute to the broader understanding of Earth's volatile cycle and aid in predicting the behavior of volcanic systems in response to changes in mantle conditions.

Given a hypergraph $H = (V,E)$, what is the smallest subset $X \subseteq V$
such that $e \cap X \neq \emptyset$ holds for all $e \in E$? This problem,
known as the hitting set problem, is a basic problem in parameterized
complexity theory. There are well-known kernelization algorithms for it, which
get a hypergraph $H$ and a number $k$ as input and output a hypergraph $H'$
such that (1) $H$ has a hitting set of size $k$ if, and only if, $H'$ has such
a hitting set and (2) the size of $H'$ depends only on $k$ and on the maximum
cardinality $d$ of edges in $H$. The algorithms run in polynomial time, but are
highly sequential. Recently, it has been shown that one of them can be
parallelized to a certain degree: one can compute hitting set kernels in
parallel time $O(d)$ -- but it was conjectured that this is the best parallel
algorithm possible. We refute this conjecture and show how hitting set kernels
can be computed in constant parallel time. For our proof, we introduce a new,
generalized notion of hypergraph sunflowers and show how iterated applications
of the color coding technique can sometimes be collapsed into a single
application.

We present here one of the first high resolution spectroscopic observations
of coronal rain, performed with the CRISP instrument at the Swedish Solar
Telescope. This work constitutes the first attempt to assess the importance of
coronal rain in the understanding of the coronal magnetic field in active
regions. A large statistical set is obtained in which dynamics (total
velocities and accelerations), shapes (lengths and widths), trajectories
(angles of fall) and thermodynamic properties (temperatures) of the
condensations are derived. Specifically, we find that coronal rain is composed
of small and dense chromospheric cores with average widths and lengths of 310
km and 710 km respectively, average temperatures below 7000 K, displaying a
broad distribution of falling speeds with an average of 70 km/s and
accelerations largely below the effective gravity along loops. Through
estimates of the ion-neutral coupling in the blobs we show that coronal rain
acts as a tracer of the coronal magnetic field, thus supporting the
multi-strand loop scenario, and acts as a probe of the local thermodynamic
conditions in loops. We further find that the cooling in neighboring strands
occurs simultaneously in general suggesting a similar thermodynamic evolution
among strands, which can be explained by a common footpoint heating process.
Constraints for coronal heating models of loops are thus provided. Estimates of
the fraction of coronal volume with coronal rain give values between 7% and
30%. Estimates of the occurrence time of the phenomenon in loops set times
between 5 and 20 hours, implying that coronal rain may be a common phenomenon,
in agreement with the frequent observations of cool downflows in EUV lines. The
coronal mass drain rate in the form of coronal rain is estimated to be on the
order of 5x10^9 g/s, a significant quantity compared to the estimate of mass
flux into the corona from spicules.

This research endeavors to investigate the stabilization of $s$-wave superconductivity in electron-doped BaFe$_2$As$_2$ through arsenic $p$-orbital hybridization. Our study sheds light on the fundamental understanding of the interplay between electronic structure and superconductivity in iron-based superconductors. Through a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental measurements, we have demonstrated that the hybridization of arsenic $p$ orbitals with the iron $d$ orbitals plays a crucial role in enhancing the superconducting transition temperature in electron-doped BaFe$_2$As$_2$. Our results reveal that the formation of electron pockets near the Fermi level due to arsenic $p$-orbital hybridization leads to an increase in the density of states at the Fermi level, promoting the onset of superconductivity. Additionally, we have identified a strong coupling between the electron and hole bands, further supporting the stabilization of $s$-wave superconductivity in the material. This study not only provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying superconductivity in iron-based compounds but also offers a pathway for enhancing and controlling superconducting properties through orbital hybridization.

In this work, we present a comprehensive study on the development and analysis of electro-neutral models for the dynamic Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) system in a two-dimensional context. Our primary objective is to address the challenge of simulating ionic transport in electro-neutral regions, which is often encountered in both natural and engineered systems. Traditional PNP models do not adequately capture the dynamics in electro-neutral scenarios due to inherent assumptions about charge distribution and potential gradients. We introduce a novel electro-neutral framework that modifies the classical PNP equations to better represent the ion transport dynamics under conditions of negligible net charge. Our methodology involves the derivation of a set of electro-neutral equations by implementing continuity conditions and asymptotic analysis to approximate the spatial variations of the electric field. The resulting model is both computationally efficient and consistent with the physical characteristics of electro-neutral environments. We perform analytical verifications and numerical simulations to validate the efficacy and accuracy of our proposed model. The results indicate significant improvements in stability and convergence, along with enhanced prediction capabilities in capturing ionic distributions. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate that the electro-neutral models accurately represent scenarios where traditional models fail due to their underlying assumptions. This work contributes a robust theoretical framework and computational tool for modeling ionic transport in electro-neutral systems and offers valuable insights for applications in fields such as electrochemical systems, physiological ion channels, and environmental science. Our findings lay the groundwork for future extensions into three-dimensional analyses and more complex biological and chemical systems.

We present a comprehensive study of the three-dimensional modeling of the molecular ion HCO$^+$ and its isotopologues in the low-mass proto-star IRAS16293$-$2422. Our primary objective is to elucidate the chemical processes and physical conditions that govern the formation and distribution of HCO$^+$ in this protostellar environment. We employed a hybrid approach that combines radiative transfer modeling, hydrodynamic simulations, and a detailed chemical network to simulate the complex interplay between gas dynamics and chemical evolution.   Our results indicate that HCO$^+$ and its isotopologues exhibit distinct spatial distributions, influenced significantly by the density and temperature gradients within the proto-stellar core. We observe a marked enhancement of HCO$^+$ in computational regions associated with shock fronts, which we attribute to differential ionization and the dissociative recombination processes occurring in the dense gas. Notably, we identified where the isotopic ratios vary, reflecting the influence of localized physical conditions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the important role of turbulence in modulating the abundance of HCO$^+$ isotopologues, thereby providing insights into the evolutionary stages of the proto-star.  This research contributes to our understanding of the molecular chemistry in low-mass star formation regions and the dynamical processes that affect the chemical composition of proto-stellar envelops. The findings enhance our ability to interpret observational data from astrophysical sources and refine models of star formation and chemical evolution in the universe.

This work introduces ImVerde, a novel approach for learning network representation from imbalanced data by leveraging a vertex-diminished random walk strategy. The key problem we address is the challenge posed by imbalanced network data, where certain nodes are underrepresented, leading to biased representations. Our method aims to mitigate this issue by adjusting the random walk probabilities based on the vertex degree distribution, giving less weight to high-degree nodes and enhancing the sampling of low-degree nodes.   We conducted experiments on various real-world imbalanced networks and compared the performance of ImVerde against state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that ImVerde consistently outperforms existing approaches in terms of representation quality, particularly for nodes with low degree. Additionally, our method shows robustness in preserving the structural properties of the network while improving the representation of underrepresented nodes.   The methodology involves integrating the vertex-diminished random walk into a representation learning framework that effectively captures the network topology while addressing imbalanced data distribution. By enhancing the sampling of low-degree nodes, ImVerde achieves more balanced and informative representations, crucial for downstream network analysis tasks. Overall, our work contributes a promising solution to learning network representation from imbalanced data, improving the overall performance and fairness of representation learning algorithms.

Orion KL is one of the most frequently observed sources in the Galaxy, and
the site where many molecular species have been discovered for the first time.
With the availability of powerful wideband backends, it is nowadays possible to
complete spectral surveys in the entire mm-range to obtain a spectroscopically
unbiased chemical picture of the region. In this paper we present a sensitive
spectral survey of Orion KL, made with one of the 34m antennas of the Madrid
Deep Space Communications Complex in Robledo de Chavela, Spain. The spectral
range surveyed is from 41.5 to 50 GHz, with a frequency spacing of 180 kHz
(equivalent to about 1.2 km/s, depending on the exact frequency). The rms
achieved ranges from 8 to 12 mK. The spectrum is dominated by the J=1-0 SiO
maser lines and by radio recombination lines (RRLs), which were detected up to
Delta_n=11. Above a 3-sigma level, we identified 66 RRLs and 161 molecular
lines corresponding to 39 isotopologues from 20 molecules; a total of 18 lines
remain unidentified, two of them above a 5-sigma level. Results of radiative
modelling of the detected molecular lines (excluding masers) are presented. At
this frequency range, this is the most sensitive survey and also the one with
the widest band. Although some complex molecules like CH_3CH_2CN and CH_2CHCN
arise from the hot core, most of the detected molecules originate from the low
temperature components in Orion KL.

We perform a detailed hadron-level study on the sensitivity of Higgs boson
pair production via the $WW^{*}WW^{*}$ channel with the final state $3 \ell 2
j$ + missing $E_T$ at the LHC with the collision energy $\sqrt{S} = 14$ TeV and
a future 100 TeV collider. To avoid the huge background from $pp \to Z W +
\textrm{jets}$ processes, we confine to consider the four lepton patterns:
$e^\pm e^\pm \mu^\mp $ and $\mu^\pm \mu^\pm e^\mp$. We propose a partial
reconstruction method to determine the most reliable combination. After that,
we examine a few crucial observables which can discriminate efficiently signal
and background events, especially we notice that the observable $m_{\rm T2}$ is
very efficient. For the LHC 14 TeV collisions, with an accumulated 3000
fb$^{-1}$ dataset, we find that the sensitivity of this mode can reach up to
1.5 $\sigma$ for the Standard Model and the triple coupling of Higgs boson
$\lambda_3$ in the simplest effective theory can be constrained into the range
[-1, 8] at $95\%$ confidence level; at a 100 TeV collider with the integrated
luminosity 3000 fb$^{-1}$, the sensitivity can reach up to 13 $\sigma$ for the
Standard Model and we find that all values of $\lambda_3$ in the effective
theory can be covered up to 3$\sigma$ even without optimising signals. To
precisely measure the triple coupling of Higgs boson $\lambda_3=1$ of the
Standard Model at a 100 TeV collider, by using the invariant mass of three
leptons which is robust to against the contamination of underlying events and
pileup effects and by performing a $\chi^2$ analysis, we find that it can be
determined into a range [0.8, 1.5] at $95\%$ confidence level.

This is the second of two papers where we study the asymptotics of the
generalized Nariai solutions and its relation to the cosmic no-hair conjecture.
In the first paper, the author suggested that according to the cosmic no-hair
conjecture, the Nariai solutions are non-generic among general solutions of
Einstein's field equations in vacuum with a positive cosmological constant. We
checked that this is true within the class of spatially homogeneous solutions.
In this paper now, we continue these investigations within the spatially
inhomogeneous Gowdy case. On the one hand, we are motivated to understand the
fundamental question of cosmic no-hair and its dynamical realization in more
general classes than the spatially homogeneous case. On the other hand, the
results of the first paper suggest that the instability of the Nariai solutions
can be exploited to construct and analyze physically interesting cosmological
black hole solutions in the Gowdy class, consistent with certain claims by
Bousso in the spherically symmetric case. However, in contrast to that, we find
that it is not possible to construct cosmological black hole solutions by means
of small Gowdy symmetric perturbations of the Nariai solutions and that the
dynamics shows a certain new critical behavior. For our investigations, we use
the numerical techniques based on spectral methods which we introduced in a
previous publication.

This study focuses on an initial and boundary value problem for a large class of quasilinear hyperbolic systems, which are derived from an atmospheric model. The atmospheric model is governed by a set of nonlinear partial differential equations that describe the behavior of atmospheric variables such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed. These equations are quasilinear hyperbolic, meaning that they can be written in a form that separates the variables and has a clear direction of propagation.  The objective of this research is to develop a numerical method for solving these systems, which are often difficult to solve analytically due to their complexity and nonlinearity. The method is based on a finite difference scheme, which discretizes the spatial and temporal derivatives of the system. The scheme is then solved using a combination of iterative techniques and linear algebra methods.  The key findings of this study are that the proposed numerical method is able to accurately capture the behavior of the atmospheric model, including the propagation of waves and the formation of fronts. The method is also shown to be stable and efficient, with a high degree of accuracy and a low computational cost. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the method can be applied to a wide range of atmospheric models, including those with different types of nonlinearity and dispersion.  The results of this study have significant implications for the prediction of atmospheric phenomena, such as weather patterns and climate change. By providing a robust and efficient numerical method for solving these systems, this research can contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable models of the atmosphere.

As small solid grains grow into larger ones in protoplanetary nebulae, or in
the cloudy atmospheres of exoplanets, they generally form porous aggregates
rather than solid spheres. A number of previous studies have used highly
sophisticated schemes to calculate opacity models for irregular, porous
particles with size much smaller than a wavelength. However, mere growth itself
can affect the opacity of the medium in far more significant ways than the
detailed compositional and/or structural differences between grain constituents
once aggregate particle sizes exceed the relevant wavelengths. This physics is
not new; our goal here is to provide a model that provides physical insight and
is simple to use in the increasing number of protoplanetary nebula evolution,
and exoplanet atmosphere, models appearing in recent years, yet quantitatively
captures the main radiative properties of mixtures of particles of arbitrary
size, porosity, and composition. The model is a simple combination of effective
medium theory with small-particle closed-form expressions, combined with
suitably chosen transitions to geometric optics behavior. Calculations of
wavelength-dependent emission and Rosseland mean opacity are shown and compared
with Mie theory. The model's fidelity is very good in all comparisons we have
made, except in cases involving pure metal particles or monochromatic opacities
for solid particles with size comparable to the wavelength.

The velocity, position, and action variable evolution of a tidal stream drawn
out of a star cluster in a triaxial isochrone potential containing a sub-halo
population reproduces many of the orbital effects of more general cosmological
halos but allows easy calculation of orbital actions. We employ a spherical
shell code which we show accurately reproduces the results of a tree gravity
code for a collisionless star cluster. Streams from clusters on high
eccentricity orbits, $e\gtrsim 0.6$, can spread out so much that the amount of
material at high enough surface density to stand out on the sky may be only a
few percent of the stream's total mass. Low eccentricity streams remain more
spatially coherent, but sub-halos both broaden the stream and displace the
centerline with details depending on the orbits allowed within the potential.
Overall, the majority of stream particles have changes in their total actions
of only 1-2\%, leaving the mean stream relatively undisturbed. A halo with 1\%
of the mass in sub-halos typically spreads the velocity distribution about a
factor of two wider than would be expected for a smooth halo. Strong density
variations, "gaps", along with mean velocity offsets, are clearly detected in
low eccentricity streams for even a 0.2\% sub-halo mass fraction. Around one
hundred velocity measurements per kiloparsec of stream will enable tests for
the presence of a local sub-halo density as small as 0.2-0.5\% of the local
mass density, with about 1\% predicted for 30 kiloparsec orbital radii streams.

The present study explores the behavior of hard ellipses in the context of their equation of state, structural properties, and self-diffusion coefficients. Hard ellipses, as a non-spherical model for hard particles, have garnered significant attention due to their applicability to various systems such as colloidal suspensions and liquid crystals. To investigate the equation of state, we employed the perturbation theory approach based on the diamond lattice structure, which accurately models the behavior of hard ellipses in the high-density limit. We derived analytical expressions for the virial coefficients and equation of state, showing excellent agreement with simulation results. Furthermore, we explored the structure of hard ellipses through a semi-empirical potential function that preserves the rotational symmetry and accounts for the anisotropic shape of the ellipses. The structural properties, such as the radial distribution functions and orientation correlation functions, were analyzed, revealing distinct differences compared to hard spheres. Lastly, we examined the self-diffusion coefficients of hard ellipses using the Green-Kubo formalism, revealing significant anisotropic behavior. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of non-spherical hard particles and highlight the importance of considering shape anisotropy in investigations of transport properties and phase behavior.

This work was conducted to design, implement, and evaluate a new model of
measuring Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) performance of real time network.
The proposed model Biological Kurd Messenger (BIOKM) has two main goals: First
is to run the model efficiently, second is to obtain high TCP performance via
real time network using bio-computing technique, especially molecular
calculation because it provides wisdom results and it can exploit all
facilities of phylogentic analysis. To measure TCP performance two protocols
were selected Internet Relay Chat Daemon (IRCD) and File Transfer Protocol
(FTP), the BIOKM model consists of two applications Kurd Messenger Server Side
(KMSS) and Kurd Messenger Client Side (KMCS) written in Java programming
language by implementing algorithms of BIOKM Server and Client application. The
paper also includes the implementation of hybridized model algorithm based on
Neighbor-Joining (NJ) method to measure TCP performance, then implementing
algorithm of Little law (steady state) for single server queue as a comparison
with bio-computing algorithm. The results obtained by using bio-computing and
little law techniques show very good performance and the two techniques result
are very close to each other this is because of local implementation. The main
tools which have been used in this work can be divided into software and
hardware tools.
  Keywords: Biological Kurd Messenger (BIOKM), Kurd Messenger Phylogenetic
tree, Hybridized Model, Little Law, TCP Performance.

In this study, we explored the potential of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the classification of subvisible protein aggregates (SVPAs) from micro-flow images, while bypassing the need for explicit morphological feature specification. Traditional methods for SVPA detection and characterization rely heavily on manual feature extraction based on visual inspection, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Moreover, these methods can be prone to subjective interpretation, leading to inconsistent and unreliable results. To address these challenges, we proposed the application of deep CNNs as a powerful alternative for the automatic detection and characterization of SVPAs. Our model was trained on a large dataset of micro-flow images, with SVPAs annotated by domain experts. We implemented transfer learning using a pre-trained CNN, VGG16, to extract features and reduce the amount of labeled training data required. Our model was then fine-tuned using a small set of labeled SVPA images and validated using an independent dataset. The results demonstrated an outstanding performance of our CNN model in the classification of SVPAs from micro-flow images, with an accuracy of 94.5%. These results surpass the performance of traditional manual feature extraction methods and show promise for the automation of SVPA detection and characterization. The proposed methodology illustrates the potential of deep learning techniques to circumvent the need for explicit feature specification and revolutionize the analysis of complex micro-flow imaging data. Future work includes expanding the dataset and evaluating the applicability of the method to other complex micro-flow imaging applications.

This study investigates the timing analysis of periodic radio and optical brightness variations observed in the ultracool dwarf star TVLM 513-46546. Previous studies have noted its unique variability, with both radio and optical light curves exhibiting quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). Our objective was to refine the timing of these QPOs by employing advanced statistical methods and high-resolution data analysis techniques.  The methodology involved cross-correlation functions (CCFs) to identify and synchronize the timings of radio and optical signals. High-resolution spectroscopy from multiple epochs provided detailed spectral information necessary for precise timing measurements. Additionally, machine learning algorithms were applied to detect subtle variations that might not be evident through traditional methods.  Key findings indicate that the radio and optical QPOs exhibit nearly identical periods, supporting the hypothesis of common physical mechanisms driving their variability. However, there are slight discrepancies in their amplitudes and phases, suggesting different underlying processes or environmental influences. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a correlation between the timing of the radio QPOs and the star's rotation period, hinting at a possible connection to magnetic activity.  In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive examination of the timing characteristics of the radio and optical variability in TVLM 513-46546, enhancing our understanding of its astrophysical properties. The findings contribute to the broader field of ultracool dwarf stars and their variability studies.

We compute the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG) disorder- correlator
function R(v) for d-dimensional elastic manifolds pinned by a random potential
in the limit of infinite embedding space dimension N. It measures the
equilibrium response of the manifold in a quadratic potential well as the
center of the well is varied from 0 to v. We find two distinct scaling regimes:
(i) a "single shock" regime, v^2 ~ 1/L^d where L^d is the system volume and
(ii) a "thermodynamic" regime, v^2 ~ N. In regime (i) all the equivalent
replica symmetry breaking (RSB) saddle points within the Gaussian variational
approximation contribute, while in regime (ii) the effect of RSB enters only
through a single anomaly. When the RSB is continuous (e.g., for short-range
disorder, in dimension 2 <= d <= 4), we prove that regime (ii) yields the
large-N FRG function obtained previously. In that case, the disorder correlator
exhibits a cusp in both regimes, though with different amplitudes and of
different physical origin. When the RSB solution is 1-step and non- marginal
(e.g., d < 2 for SR disorder), the correlator R(v) in regime (ii) is
considerably reduced, and exhibits no cusp. Solutions of the FRG flow
corresponding to non-equilibrium states are discussed as well. In all cases the
regime (i) exhibits a cusp non-analyticity at T=0, whose form and thermal
rounding at finite T is obtained exactly and interpreted in terms of shocks.
The results are compared with previous work, and consequences for manifolds at
finite N, as well as extensions to spin glasses and related models are
discussed.

The study explores the diphoton Higgs signal strength within the framework of universal extra dimensions (UED), a theoretical model proposing additional spatial dimensions beyond the conventional three. This model predicts significant modifications to the properties of particles in the Standard Model, potentially altering Higgs boson decay channels. The objective is to assess how the presence of these extra dimensions influences the Higgs boson decay into diphotons, a critical channel for Higgs detection at high-energy colliders. The methodology involves developing a theoretical framework incorporating UED into the Standard Model Lagrangian and performing numerical calculations to evaluate the modified Higgs production and decay rates. Key components include quantifying the effects of Kaluza-Klein (KK) modes, which are excitations resultant from compactified extra dimensions, on the loop processes affecting the Higgs-to-diphoton transition. The analysis highlights an enhancement in the diphoton signal strength attributed to KK contributions, suggesting potential deviations from the Standard Model predictions observable at future collider experiments. Key findings emphasize the sensitivity of the diphoton channel to the presence of compactified extra dimensions, providing a novel probe for extra-dimensional theories. The conclusion underscores the significance of diphoton measurements as a tool for exploring new physics, with the potential to refine the parameters of UED models or even rule them out, thereby advancing our understanding of fundamental forces and particle interactions. The study offers a framework for interpreting future experimental data, aiding in the search for evidence of extra dimensions.

We investigate the nucleosynthesis of heavy elements in the winds ejected by
accretion disks formed in neutron star mergers. We compute the element
formation in disk outflows from hypermassive neutron star (HMNS) remnants of
variable lifetime, including the effect of angular momentum transport in the
disk evolution. We employ long-term axisymmetric hydrodynamic disk simulations
to model the ejecta, and compute r-process nucleosynthesis with tracer
particles using a nuclear reaction network containing $\sim 8000$ species. We
find that the previously known strong correlation between HMNS lifetime,
ejected mass, and average electron fraction in the outflow is directly related
to the amount of neutrino irradiation on the disk, which dominates mass
ejection at early times in the form of a neutrino-driven wind. Production of
lanthanides and actinides saturates at short HMNS lifetimes ($\lesssim 10$ ms),
with additional ejecta contributing to a blue optical kilonova component for
longer-lived HMNSs. We find good agreement between the abundances from the disk
outflow alone and the solar r-process distribution only for short HMNS
lifetimes ($\lesssim 10$ ms). For longer lifetimes, the rare-earth and third
r-process peaks are significantly under-produced compared to the solar pattern,
requiring additional contributions from the dynamical ejecta. The
nucleosynthesis signature from a spinning black hole (BH) can only overlap with
that from a HMNS of moderate lifetime ($\lesssim 60$ ms). Finally, we show that
angular momentum transport not only contributes with a late-time outflow
component, but that it also enhances the neutrino-driven component by moving
material to shallower regions of the gravitational potential, in addition to
providing additional heating.

We employed soft- and hard-X-ray standing-wave angle-resolved photoemission to investigate the depth-resolved composition and electronic structure of buried layers and interfaces in a LaNiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ superlattice. Our approach enabled us to probe the electronic properties of layers at depths ranging from 0.5 to 10 nm, revealing a complex interplay between the LaNiO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$ components. By analyzing the angle-resolved photoemission spectra, we identified distinct electronic states at the LaNiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface and in the buried LaNiO$_3$ layer, which were found to be influenced by the oxygen 2p states from the SrTiO$_3$ substrate. The observed electronic structure was found to be consistent with a layered, perovskite-like arrangement of the constituent materials, with the LaNiO$_3$ layer exhibiting a mixed valence state and the SrTiO$_3$ layer displaying a purely Ti$^{4+}$ configuration. These findings provide new insights into the electronic properties of buried layers and interfaces in perovskite superlattices, highlighting the potential for tailoring the electronic structure of these systems to achieve specific functional properties.

The input of the Test Cover problem consists of a set $V$ of vertices, and a
collection ${\cal E}=\{E_1,..., E_m\}$ of distinct subsets of $V$, called
tests. A test $E_q$ separates a pair $v_i,v_j$ of vertices if $|\{v_i,v_j\}\cap
E_q|=1.$ A subcollection ${\cal T}\subseteq {\cal E}$ is a test cover if each
pair $v_i,v_j$ of distinct vertices is separated by a test in ${\cal T}$. The
objective is to find a test cover of minimum cardinality, if one exists. This
problem is NP-hard.
  We consider two parameterizations the Test Cover problem with parameter $k$:
(a) decide whether there is a test cover with at most $k$ tests, (b) decide
whether there is a test cover with at most $|V|-k$ tests. Both
parameterizations are known to be fixed-parameter tractable. We prove that none
have a polynomial size kernel unless $NP\subseteq coNP/poly$. Our proofs use
the cross-composition method recently introduced by Bodlaender et al. (2011)
and parametric duality introduced by Chen et al. (2005). The result for the
parameterization (a) was an open problem (private communications with Henning
Fernau and Jiong Guo, Jan.-Feb. 2012). We also show that the parameterization
(a) admits a polynomial size kernel if the size of each test is upper-bounded
by a constant.

Noncausal, or anticipative, heavy-tailed processes generate trajectories
featuring locally explosive episodes akin to speculative bubbles in financial
time series data. For $(X_t)$ a two-sided infinite $\alpha$-stable moving
average (MA), conditional moments up to integer order four are shown to exist
