V}_{\gamma}^\beta$ of all sequences isomorphic to $\mathcal E$.
  Thus, the space ${}_2{\mathbb V}_{\gamma}^\beta$ carries a stratification
given by the subsets of type ${\mathbb V}_\Delta$. We compute the dimension of
each stratum and show that the boundary of a stratum ${\mathbb V}_\Delta$
consists exactly of those ${\mathbb V}_{\Delta'}$ where $\Delta'$ is obtained
from $\Delta$ by a non-empty sequence of arc moves of five possible types {\bf
(A) -- (E)}.
  The case where all three partitions are fixed has been studied in [3] and
[4]. There, arc moves of types {\bf (A) -- (D)} suffice to describe the
boundary of a ${\mathbb V}_\Delta$ in ${\mathbb V}_{\alpha,\gamma}^\beta$. Our
fifth move {\bf (E)}, "explosion", is needed to break up an arc into two poles
to allow for changes in the partition $\alpha$.

We study the quantum effects of a test Klein-Gordon field in a Vaidya
spacetime consisting of a collapsing null shell that forms a Schwazschild black
hole, by explicitly obtaining, in a $(1+1)$-dimensional model, the Wightman
function, the renormalised stress-energy tensor, and by analysing particle
detector rates along stationary orbits in the exterior black hole region, and
make a comparison with the folklore that the Unruh state is the state that
emerges from black hole formation. In the causal future of the shell, we find a
negative ingoing flux at the horizon that agrees precisely with the Unruh state
calculation, and is the source of black hole radiation, while in the future
null infinity we find that the radiation flux output in the Unruh state is an
upper bound for the positive outgoing flux in the collapsing null shell
spacetime. This indicates that back-reaction estimates based on Unruh state
calculations over-estimate the energy output carried by so-called pre-Hawking
radiation. The value of the output predicted by the Unruh state is however
approached exponentially fast. Finally, we find that at late times, stationary
observers in the exterior black hole region in the collapsing shell spacetime
detect the local Hawking temperature, which is also well characterised by the
Unruh state, coming from right-movers. Early-time discrepancies between the
detector rates for the Unruh state and for the state in the collapsing shell
spacetime are explored numerically.

We present a novel approach to model emissive correlated systems using a quantum statistical ensemble. Emissive correlated systems, such as quantum dots in a host matrix or organic molecules with strongly coupled excitons, exhibit unique optical properties due to the interplay between the emission of individual emitters and their interactions. Traditional modeling approaches based on single emitters or independent emitter ensembles fail to capture these effects. Our methodology utilizes a reduced density matrix approach to describe the system, with the density matrix evolved under the master equation. We implement this approach for a system of four strongly interacting emitters and validate the results using Fano factor measurements. The quantum statistical ensemble captures the effects of emission correlations and can be extended to larger systems. Our results demonstrate the utility of this approach for studying the optical properties of emissive correlated systems and provide a valuable tool for the design of new materials and devices. The quantum statistical ensemble approach offers a versatile and powerful framework to describe the dynamics of correlated quantum systems and opens new avenues for the understanding and control of their optical properties. The methodology can be applied to various systems, including quantum dots, organic molecules, and other correlated emitters, providing insights into their unique optical behavior and potential applications.

We study the evaporation and condensation of CO and CO_2 during the embedded
stages of low-mass star formation by using numerical simulations. We focus on
the effect of luminosity bursts, similar in magnitude to FUors and EXors, on
the gas-phase abundance of CO and CO_2 in the protostellar disk and infalling
envelope. The evolution of a young protostar and its environment is followed
based on hydrodynamical models using the thin-disk approximation, coupled with
a stellar evolution code and phase transformations of CO and CO_2. The
accretion and associated luminosity bursts in our model are caused by disk
gravitational fragmentation followed by quick migration of the fragments onto
the forming protostar. We found that bursts with luminosity on the order of
100-200 L_sun can evaporate CO ices in part of the envelope. The typical
freeze-out time of the gas-phase CO onto dust grains in the envelope (a few
kyr) is much longer than the burst duration (100-200 yr). This results in an
increased abundance of the gas-phase CO in the envelope long after the system
has returned into a quiescent stage. In contrast, luminosity bursts can
evaporate CO_2 ices only in the disk, where the freeze-out time of the
gas-phase CO_2 is comparable to the burst duration. We thus confirm that
luminosity bursts can leave long-lasting traces in the abundance of gas-phase
CO in the infalling envelope, enabling the detection of recent bursts as
suggested by previous semi-analytical studies.

It is well established that multiple reference sets may occur for a decision
making unit (DMU) in the non-radial DEA (data envelopment analysis) setting. As
our first contribution, we differentiate between three types of reference set.
First, we introduce the notion of unary reference set (URS) corresponding to a
given projection of an evaluated DMU. The URS includes efficient DMUs that are
active in a specific convex combination producing the projection. Because of
the occurrence of multiple URSs, we introduce the notion of maximal reference
set (MRS) and define it as the union of all the URSs associated with the given
projection. Since multiple projections may occur in non-radial DEA models, we
further define the union of the MRSs associated with all the projections as
unique global reference set (GRS) of the evaluated DMU. As the second
contribution, we propose and substantiate a general linear programming (LP)
based approach to identify the GRS. Since our approach makes the identification
through the execution of a single primal-based LP model, it is computationally
more efficient than the existing methods for its easy implementation in
practical applications. Our last contribution is to measure returns to scale
using a non-radial DEA model. This method effectively deals with the occurrence
of multiple supporting hyperplanes arising either from multiplicity of
projections or from non-full dimensionality of minimum face. Finally, an
empirical analysis is conducted based on a real-life data set to demonstrate
the ready applicability of our approach.

In this study, we investigate the pressure-temperature phase diagram of SrTiO3 (strontium titanate) up to 53 GPa, elucidating the complex interplay between applied pressure and temperature. Our research aims to resolve ambiguities surrounding phase transitions in SrTiO3 under extreme conditions. Utilizing advanced synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, complemented by first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we identify and characterize multiple structural phases as a function of varying pressures and temperatures. Our results reveal the presence of a high-pressure cubic to tetragonal phase transition commencing at approximately 31 GPa. This transition is evidenced by the emergence of distinctive soft modes in the phonon spectrum. At higher pressures, around 48 GPa, we observe an additional orthorhombic phase, distinct from lower-pressure phases, characterized by dramatic shifts in Raman-active modes. Key insights gleaned from DFT calculations suggest that these phase transitions are driven by the destabilization of Ti-O bonds and the consequent modifications in lattice dynamics. Our pressure-temperature phase diagram provides a comprehensive map showing phase boundaries, transition pressures, and critical temperatures, contributing significantly to understanding stress-induced modifications in perovskite oxides. We conclude that our findings not only enhance the fundamental understanding of phase transition mechanisms in SrTiO3 but also extend potential applications in pressure-dependent tuning of functional properties in similar perovskite materials. Thus, our work provides a vital framework for future explorations in the field of material science concerning high-pressure phenomena in metal oxides.

In this study, we investigate the relationship between cluster properties and the quenching rate of star formation in galaxies. We systematically analyze a sample of galaxy clusters, focusing on their mass, morphology, and environmental density, to ascertain whether these characteristics significantly influence the rate at which star formation is quenched. Our methodology combines observational data from large astronomical surveys with theoretical models of galaxy evolution, employing statistical techniques to identify correlations between cluster properties and quenching rates.  Our results demonstrate a clear correlation between high cluster mass and increased quenching rates, suggesting that more massive clusters exert stronger gravitational forces that inhibit star formation. Additionally, we observe that clusters with a greater concentration of galaxies tend to have enhanced quenching rates, further indicating the role of environmental factors in this process. We also consider the impact of morphological features, revealing that clusters with elliptical shapes possess higher quenching rates compared to their irregular counterparts.  By synthesizing these findings, we contribute to the understanding of how large-scale structures in the universe influence galaxy evolution. We propose that the quenching mechanisms are predominantly driven by environmental pressure and cluster dynamics, which can be further explored in future studies. Our work not only elucidates the intricate interplay between cluster properties and star formation rates but also sets the stage for future research on the implications of these relationships for cosmic structure formation and evolution.

We present a detailed study of the rest-optical (3600-7000 Angstrom) nebular
spectra of ~380 star-forming galaxies at z~2-3 obtained with Keck/MOSFIRE as
part of the Keck Baryonic Structure Survey (KBSS). The KBSS-MOSFIRE sample is
representative of star-forming galaxies at these redshifts, with stellar masses
M*=10^9-10^11.5 M_sun and star formation rates SFR=3-1000 M_sun/yr. We focus on
robust measurements of many strong diagnostic emission lines for individual
galaxies: [O II]3727,3729, [Ne III]3869, H-beta, [O III]4960,5008, [N
II]6549,6585, H-alpha, and [S II]6718,6732. Comparisons with observations of
typical local galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and between
subsamples of KBSS-MOSFIRE show that high-redshift galaxies exhibit a number of
significant differences in addition to the well-known offset in log([O
III]/H-beta) and log([N II]/H-alpha). We argue that the primary difference
between H II regions in z~2.3 galaxies and those at z~0 is an enhancement in
the degree of nebular excitation, as measured by [O III]/H-beta and R23=log[([O
III]+[O II])/H-beta]. At the same time, KBSS-MOSFIRE galaxies are ~10 times
more massive than z~0 galaxies with similar ionizing spectra and have higher
N/O (likely accompanied by higher O/H) at fixed excitation. These results
indicate the presence of harder ionizing radiation fields at fixed N/O and O/H
relative to typical z~0 galaxies, consistent with Fe-poor stellar population
models that include massive binaries, and highlight a population of massive,
high-specific star formation rate galaxies at high-redshift with systematically
different star formation histories than galaxies of similar stellar mass today.

The quenching rate is known to depend on galaxy stellar mass and environment,
however, possible dependences on the hosting halo properties, such as mass,
richness, and dynamical status, are still debated. The determination of these
dependences is hampered by systematics, induced by noisy estimates of cluster
mass or by the lack of control on galaxy stellar mass, which may mask existing
trends or introduce fake trends. We studied a sample of local clusters (20 with
0.02<z<0.1 and log(M200/Msun)>14), selected independent of the galaxy
properties under study, having homogeneous optical photometry and X-ray
estimated properties. Using those top quality measurements of cluster mass,
hence of cluster scale, richness, iron abundance, and cooling time/presence of
a cool-core, we study the simultaneous dependence of quenching on these cluster
properties on galaxy stellar mass M and normalised cluster-centric distance
r/r200. We found that the quenching rate can be completely described by two
variables only, galaxy stellar mass and normalised cluster-centric distance,
and is independent of halo properties (mass, richness, iron abundance, presence
of a cool-core, and central cooling time). These halo properties change, in
most cases, by less than 3% the probability that a galaxy is quenched, once the
mass-size (M200-r200) scaling relation is accounted for through cluster-centric
distance normalisation.

Micromegas technology is a promising candidate to replace Atlas forward muon
chambers -tracking and trigger- for future HL-LHC upgrade of the experiment.
The increase on background and pile-up event probability requires detector
performances which are currently under studies in intensive RD activities.
  We studied performances of four different resistive Micromegas detectors with
different read-out strip pitches. These chambers were tested using \sim120 GeV
momentum pions, at H6 CERN-SPS beam line in autumn 2010. For a strip pitch 500
micrometers we measure a resolution of \sim90 micrometers and a efficiency of
~98%. The track angle effect on the efficiency was also studied. Our results
show that resistive techniques induce no degradation on the efficiency or
resolution, with respect to the standard Micromegas. In some configuration the
resistive coating is able to reduce the discharge currents at least by a factor

In recent years, the exponential growth of spatiotemporal data has posed significant challenges in efficiently evaluating reachability queries within large contact datasets. This paper aims to address the need for an efficient method to traverse and query such vast datasets, which are critical in applications like urban planning, transportation, and emergency management. We propose a novel algorithm that combines advanced indexing techniques with optimized traversal strategies to enhance the speed and accuracy of reachability query evaluations.   The methodology involves the development of a hierarchical data structure that organizes contact information based on temporal and spatial constraints, allowing for rapid querying through reduced search space. We conducted extensive experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithm compared to existing traditional methods. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly reduces query response times while maintaining high accuracy, with improvements of up to 75% in efficiency over baseline techniques.  In conclusion, the research presents a scalable solution for efficient reachability query evaluations in large spatiotemporal contact datasets, with the potential to enhance decision-making processes across various fields that rely on spatiotemporal data. The results emphasize the importance of innovative data structuring and algorithm design in managing large-scale datasets, paving the way for future advancements in spatiotemporal data analytics.

Pluripotency in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells is a pivotal aspect of developmental biology and regenerative medicine. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms governing pluripotency remain poorly understood. This study aims to explore pluripotency from a stochastic and dynamical perspective, integrating mathematical modeling with experimental data to elucidate the complex regulatory networks involved. We employed a combination of single-cell RNA sequencing and time-lapse imaging to investigate the temporal dynamics of gene expression in mouse ES cells under varying conditions. By applying stochastic modeling techniques, we identified critical factors that influence cell fate decisions between pluripotent states and differentiation. Our key findings reveal that fluctuations in transcriptional activity, coupled with protein interactions, play a significant role in maintaining pluripotency and facilitating transitions between various cellular states. Additionally, we demonstrated that certain external stimuli can alter the stochastic landscape of pluripotency, leading to diverse differentiation outcomes. These results suggest that pluripotency should be viewed not merely as a stable identity but as a dynamic and probabilistic process. The insights gained from this research provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms that regulate cell fate decisions in ES cells, which could inform future studies in stem cell biology and therapeutic applications. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of integrating stochastic and dynamical approaches in the study of pluripotent stem cells to better comprehend their behavior and potential in regenerative medicine.

The next generation of cosmological surveys will operate over unprecedented
scales, and will therefore provide exciting new opportunities for testing
general relativity. The standard method for modelling the structures that these
surveys will observe is to use cosmological perturbation theory for linear
structures on horizon-sized scales, and Newtonian gravity for non-linear
structures on much smaller scales. We propose a two-parameter formalism that
generalizes this approach, thereby allowing interactions between large and
small scales to be studied in a self-consistent and well-defined way. This uses
both post-Newtonian gravity and cosmological perturbation theory, and can be
used to model realistic cosmological scenarios including matter, radiation and
a cosmological constant. We find that the resulting field equations can be
written as a hierarchical set of perturbation equations. At leading-order,
these equations allow us to recover a standard set of Friedmann equations, as
well as a Newton-Poisson equation for the inhomogeneous part of the Newtonian
energy density in an expanding background. For the perturbations in the
large-scale cosmology, however, we find that the field equations are sourced by
both non-linear and mode-mixing terms, due to the existence of small-scale
structures. These extra terms should be expected to give rise to new
gravitational effects, through the mixing of gravitational modes on small and
large scales - effects that are beyond the scope of standard linear
cosmological perturbation theory. We expect our formalism to be useful for
accurately modelling gravitational physics in universes that contain non-linear
structures, and for investigating the effects of non-linear gravity in the era
of ultra-large-scale surveys.

This research explores the distributions and Euler systems associated with the general linear group GL(n), focusing on their theoretical foundations and applications. The study aims to establish a framework for understanding these systems, which are essential in number theory for studying arithmetic properties of automorphic forms and Galois representations. The methodology involves constructing distributions using local and global techniques, and then linking them to Euler systems through the use of Iwasawa theory. Key findings include the explicit construction of certain Euler systems for GL(n) that satisfy the compatibility conditions expected from conjectures like the Bloch-Kato conjecture. The research concludes by demonstrating how these systems can be used to prove non-vanishing results for L-functions attached to automorphic representations of GL(n).

This research paper investigates the physics of three-dimensional bosonic topological insulators, with a focus on surface deconfined criticality and the quantized magnetoelectric effect. Topological insulators are a class of materials that exhibit insulating behavior in their interior while conducting electricity on their surface. Bosonic topological insulators, in particular, are characterized by the presence of bosonic excitations, which lead to distinct properties that differ from their fermionic counterparts.  The objective of this study is to explore the interplay between surface deconfined criticality and the quantized magnetoelectric effect in three-dimensional bosonic topological insulators. Surface deconfined criticality refers to the phenomenon where the surface of a topological insulator exhibits a critical behavior, characterized by the emergence of a non-trivial topological phase. The quantized magnetoelectric effect, on the other hand, is a phenomenon where the magnetization and electric polarization of a material are quantized, leading to a finite energy gap between the two.  To investigate these phenomena, we employ a combination of theoretical and numerical methods, including density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations. Our results show that the surface of a three-dimensional bosonic topological insulator exhibits a critical behavior, characterized by the emergence of a non-trivial topological phase. Furthermore, we find that the quantized magnetoelectric effect is a direct consequence of the surface deconfined criticality, leading to a finite energy gap between the magnetization and electric polarization.  Our study provides a deeper understanding of the physics of three-dimensional bosonic topological insulators, with implications for the design of novel topological insulator materials and devices. The results of this research have the potential to open up new avenues for the exploration of topological phases and the discovery of new materials with unique properties.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the radial distribution of satellite galaxies around massive red galaxies, shedding light on the interplay between dark and luminous matter in the universe. Utilizing a large sample of galaxy clusters and groups, we have observed the radial distribution of satellite galaxies to be characterized by a distinct bimodal profile, with a prominent peak at intermediate radial distances. Our results indicate that the distribution of satellite galaxies is influenced by the presence of dark matter, which plays a crucial role in shaping the radial distribution of these galaxies.  Through a combination of observational and theoretical approaches, we have investigated the role of dark matter in governing the radial distribution of satellite galaxies. Our analysis reveals that the presence of dark matter is essential in explaining the observed bimodal profile, with dark matter halos acting as a bridge between the inner regions of massive red galaxies and the outer reaches of the satellite galaxies. Furthermore, we have found that the radial distribution of satellite galaxies is also influenced by the presence of luminous matter, with the distribution of stars and gas in satellite galaxies playing a significant role in shaping their radial distribution.  Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of dark and luminous matter in the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters and groups. The observed bimodal profile of the radial distribution of satellite galaxies suggests that the distribution of dark matter is a key factor in determining the radial distribution of these galaxies, and our results highlight the importance of considering the interplay between dark and luminous matter in the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters and groups.

Type-II Weyl points, characterized by their unique band structure and topological properties, have garnered significant interest in condensed matter physics. This research investigates the generation of controllable type-II Weyl points through periodic driving of a two-dimensional system. The primary objective of this study is to explore how external periodic modulation can induce transitions between trivial and non-trivial topological phases, subsequently leading to the formation of type-II Weyl points.   We employ a theoretical framework grounded in k-space analysis and band structure calculations to simulate the dynamics of the system under periodic driving conditions. Using a tight-binding model, we systematically vary driving parameters to identify optimal conditions for the emergence of type-II Weyl points. Our findings reveal a clear dependence of the Weyl point positions on the frequency and amplitude of the periodic driving, allowing for precise control over their formation and stability.  The results indicate that periodic driving not only facilitates the generation of type-II Weyl points but also enables manipulation of their annihilation and creation, thus providing a pathway for the engineering of topological materials in practical applications. This study contributes to the understanding of non-equilibrium topological phenomena and suggests potential avenues for the development of advanced electronic and photonic devices based on controllable topological states. Ultimately, our findings highlight the role of periodic driving as a versatile technique for harnessing the exotic properties of Weyl semimetals in future technological advancements.

Nuclear mixing is a critical process during the outburst phase of classical novae, significantly impacting their light curves and nuclear burning rates. Accurately measuring the extent and timing of this mixing process is essential for understanding the underlying physical mechanisms and predicting the observable phenomena of novae explosions. In this study, we present the development and implementation of a novel nuclear mixing meter for classical novae based on hydrodynamic modeling.  Our approach employs a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model to simulate the nova ejecta, taking into account the effects of various nuclear burning species and their respective diffusion coefficients. The model incorporates a mixing efficiency parameter, allowing for the exploration of different mixing regimes. The modeled light curve is then compared to observed nova data to constrain the mixing efficiency parameter.  We test our nuclear mixing meter on three well-observed classical novae V1183 Scorpii (1994), V339 Delphini (1997), and V2491 Cygni (2013). Our results show that the mixing efficiency parameter ranges from 0.1 to 0.4, with an average value of 0.25. This finding indicates a moderate degree of nuclear mixing occurring in these novae. The predicted light curve shapes agree well with the observed data, validating our methodology and highlighting its potential for application to future nova events.  Our research contributes significantly to the field of classical nova studies by providing a robust and observable metric for nuclear mixing, shedding light on the complex interplay between hydrodynamic processes and nuclear burning during the outburst phase of novae. The insights gained from this study will inform theoretical models, enrich our understanding of nova explosions, and potentially contribute to the discovery and interpretation of novel phenomena in nova observations.

This work investigates the impact of higher-order nonlinearities on amplification and squeezing in Josephson parametric amplifiers. Our study reveals that these higher-order nonlinearities significantly affect the performance of the amplifiers, leading to deviations from the previously established theoretical predictions. By exploring the interplay between these nonlinearities and the amplifier's operation, we aim to address the discrepancies between theoretical models and experimental results observed in these systems.  To tackle this problem, we employ a comprehensive theoretical framework that incorporates higher-order nonlinearities into the analysis of the Josephson parametric amplifiers. Through numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we demonstrate the distinct influence of these nonlinear terms on the amplification and squeezing processes within the amplifiers. Our results highlight the importance of considering higher-order effects in the design and optimization of Josephson parametric amplifiers for practical applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication systems.  Overall, this research enhances our understanding of the intricate dynamics of Josephson parametric amplifiers in the presence of higher-order nonlinearities, shedding light on potential challenges and opportunities for further improving the performance of these devices.

This study presents Herschel-HIFI observations of H2O, NH3, and N2H+ towards high-mass starless and proto-stellar clumps identified by the Hi-GAL survey. The background of these regions is characterized by the presence of dense molecular clouds, which are thought to be the precursors to the formation of high-mass stars. However, the exact mechanisms that govern the collapse and star formation processes within these clouds are still not well understood.  The objective of this research is to investigate the chemical composition of these high-mass starless and proto-stellar clumps using H2O, NH3, and N2H+ as tracers. By analyzing the line intensities and ratios of these molecules, we aim to shed light on the physical conditions and chemical processes that occur within these regions.  The Herschel-HIFI observations were conducted using the HIFI instrument on the Herschel Space Observatory, which provided high-resolution spectra of the target lines. The data were then analyzed using a combination of Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to account for the uncertainties associated with the observations.  The key findings of this study reveal that the chemical composition of the high-mass starless and proto-stellar clumps is characterized by a high abundance of H2O and NH3, with N2H+ being present in smaller quantities. The line ratios and intensities indicate that the clumps are in a state of collapse, with the molecules being formed through grain surface chemistry and subsequent desorption. The results suggest that the collapse process is driven by the presence of a dense core, which is surrounded by a shell of gas and dust. The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of the star formation process and the role of chemical processes in regulating the collapse of high-mass star-forming regions.  The study concludes that the Herschel-HIFI observations provide valuable insights into the chemical composition and physical conditions of high-mass starless and proto-stellar clumps, and highlight the importance of considering the chemical processes that occur within these regions in order to understand the star formation process.

Chiral symmetry is a fundamental symmetry of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) which is broken in the hadron sector at low temperatures and densities. However, theoretical calculations suggest that this symmetry could be restored in the excited baryon states at high energies and densities. Experimental evidence for chiral restoration in excited baryons has been a subject of intense research in recent years. In this study, we present alternative experimental methods to investigate chiral restoration in excited $\Lambda$(1405) baryon states using pion-nucleon (πN) interactions. We use two approaches the reaction $\pi N \rightarrow \Lambda (1405) K Y$ and the reaction $\Lambda (1405) \rightarrow p K \pi$ to study the chiral restoration phenomenon. Our results indicate that the excited $\Lambda$(1405) states exhibit a significant change in their spectral properties, suggesting possible chiral symmetry restoration. Furthermore, we provide a comparative analysis with other experimental studies on the topic and discuss the implications of our findings for the understanding of chiral restoration in the hadron sector. These results add to the growing body of evidence supporting the theoretical predictions of chiral symmetry restoration in excited baryon states, providing valuable insights into the behavior of QCD matter under extreme conditions.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of hadronic b->s transitions in a non-universal Z' model, providing a detailed examination of the underlying mechanisms governing these processes. The non-universal Z' model, which deviates from the conventional Standard Model of particle physics, is a promising framework for understanding the complex interplay between the third generation of quarks and the electroweak gauge bosons.  The objective of this research is to investigate the hadronic b->s transitions within the non-universal Z' model, with a focus on the interplay between the Z' boson and the b quark. The study employs a combination of theoretical calculations and numerical simulations to explore the effects of varying Z' boson parameters on the b->s transition rates.  The results of this analysis reveal significant deviations from the Standard Model predictions, indicating that the non-universal Z' model can provide a more accurate description of the b->s transitions. Notably, the study finds that the introduction of a non-universal Z' boson can account for the observed anomalies in the b->s decay rates, thereby providing a potential explanation for the observed discrepancies.  This research contributes to our understanding of the non-universal Z' model and its implications for the Standard Model of particle physics. The findings of this study have important implications for the development of a more comprehensive theory of particle physics, and highlight the need for further investigation into the properties of the Z' boson.

Statistical mechanics provides a framework to understand the behavior of complex systems comprising a large number of particles. The large deviation theory offers a powerful tool to study rare events and fluctuations in these systems, which are often crucial in determining their properties.   This research paper aims to explore the application of the large deviation approach in statistical mechanics. The objective is to analyze how this method can offer insights into the dynamics and behavior of systems that deviate significantly from the average.   The methodology involves theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to investigate the role of large fluctuations in various statistical mechanical systems. By utilizing the tools of large deviation theory, the research delves into understanding the probability distributions of extreme events and their impact on system dynamics.  Key findings reveal that the large deviation approach provides a quantitative framework to characterize rare events and fluctuations in statistical mechanics accurately. It sheds light on the significance of extreme fluctuations in system behavior and how they shape macroscopic properties.  In conclusion, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of the large deviation approach in elucidating the behavior of complex systems in statistical mechanics, emphasizing the importance of rare events and fluctuations in determining system properties.

Index coding achieves bandwidth savings by jointly encoding the messages
demanded by all the clients in a broadcast channel. The encoding is performed
in such a way that each client can retrieve its demanded message from its side
information and the broadcast codeword. In general, in order to decode its
demanded message symbol, a receiver may have to observe the entire transmitted
codeword. Querying or downloading the codeword symbols might involve costs to a
client -- such as network utilization costs and storage requirements for the
queried symbols to perform decoding. In traditional index coding solutions,
this 'client aware' perspective is not considered during code design. As a
result, for these codes, the number of codeword symbols queried by a client per
decoded message symbol, which we refer to as 'locality', could be large. In
this paper, considering locality as a cost parameter, we view index coding as a
trade-off between the achievable broadcast rate (codeword length normalized by
the message length) and locality, where the objective is to minimize the
broadcast rate for a given value of locality and vice versa. We show that the
smallest possible locality for any index coding problem is 1, and that the
optimal index coding solution with locality 1 is the coding scheme based on
fractional coloring of the interference graph. We propose index coding schemes
with small locality by covering the side information graph using acyclic
subgraphs and subgraphs with small minrank. We also show how locality can be
accounted for in conventional partition multicast and cycle covering solutions
to index coding. Finally, applying these new techniques, we characterize the
locality-broadcast rate trade-off of the index coding problem whose side
information graph is the directed 3-cycle.

Religious beliefs could facilitate human cooperation [1-6], promote civic
engagement [7-10], improve life satisfaction [11-13] and even boom economic
development [14-16]. On the other side, some aspects of religion may lead to
regional violence, intergroup conflict and moral prejudice against atheists
[17-23]. Analogous to the separation of races [24], the religious segregation
is a major ingredient resulting in increasing alienation, misunderstanding,
cultural conflict and even violence among believers of different faiths
[18,19,25]. Thus far, quantitative understanding of religious segregation is
rare. Here we analyze a directed social network extracted from weibo.com (the
largest directed social network in China, similar to twitter.com), which is
consisted of 6875 believers in Christianism, Buddhism, Islam and Taoism. This
religion network is highly segregative, with only 1.6% of links connecting
individuals in different religions. Comparative analysis shows that the extent
of segregation for different religions is much higher than that for different
races and slightly higher than that for different political parties. The few
cross-religion links play a critical role in maintaining network connectivity,
being remarkably more important than links with highest betweennesses [26] or
bridgenesses [27]. Further content analysis shows that 46.7% of these
cross-religion links are probably related to charitable issues. Our findings
provide quantitative insights into religious segregation and valuable clues to
encourage cross-religion communications.

The production of pairs of Higgs bosons at hadron colliders provides unique
information on the Higgs sector and on the mechanism underlying electroweak
symmetry breaking (EWSB). Most studies have concentrated on the gluon fusion
production mode which has the largest cross section. However, despite its small
production rate, the vector-boson fusion channel can also be relevant since
even small modifications of the Higgs couplings to vector bosons induce a
striking increase of the cross section as a function of the invariant mass of
the Higgs boson pair. In this work, we exploit this unique signature to propose
a strategy to extract the $hhVV$ quartic coupling and provide model-independent
constraints on theories where EWSB is driven by new strong interactions. We
take advantage of the higher signal yield of the $b\bar b b\bar b$ final state
and make extensive use of jet substructure techniques to reconstruct signal
events with a boosted topology, characteristic of large partonic energies,
where each Higgs boson decays to a single collimated jet . Our results
demonstrate that the $hhVV$ coupling can be measured with 45% (20%) precision
at the LHC for $\mathcal{L}=$ 300 (3000) fb$^{-1}$, while a 1% precision can be
achieved at a 100 TeV collider.

It has recently been demonstrated that black hole dynamics at large D is dual
to the motion of a probe membrane propagating in the background of a spacetime
that solves Einstein's equations. The equation of motion of this membrane is
determined by the membrane stress tensor. In this paper we `improve' the
membrane stress tensor derived in earlier work to ensure that it defines
consistent probe membrane dynamics even at finite $D$ while reducing to
previous results at large D. Our improved stress tensor is the sum of a Brown
York term and a fluid energy momentum tensor. The fluid has an unusual equation
of state; its pressure is nontrivial but its energy density vanishes. We
demonstrate that all stationary solutions of our membrane equations are
produced by the extremisation of an action functional of the membrane shape.
Our action is an offshell generalization of the membrane's thermodynamical
partition function. We demonstrate that the thermodynamics of static spherical
membranes in flat space and global AdS space exactly reproduces the
thermodynamics of the dual Schwarzschild black holes even at finite D. We study
the long wavelength dynamics of membranes in AdS space, and demonstrate that
the boundary `shadow' of this membrane dynamics is boundary hydrodynamics with
with a definite constitutive relation. We determine the explicit form of shadow
dual boundary stress tensor upto second order in derivatives of the boundary
temperature and velocity, and verify that this stress tensor agrees exactly
with the fluid gravity stress tensor to first order in derivatives, but
deviates from the later at second order and finite D.

Cosmic strings can be created in the early universe during symmetry-breaking
phase transitions, such as might arise if the gauge structure of the standard
model is extended by additional U(1) factors at high energies. Cosmic strings
present in the early universe form a network of long horizon-length segments,
as well as a population of closed string loops. The closed loops are unstable
against decay, and can be a source of non-thermal particle production. In this
work we compute the density of WIMP dark matter formed by the decay of gauge
theory cosmic string loops derived from a network of long strings in the
scaling regime or under the influence of frictional forces. We find that for
symmetry breaking scales larger than 10^10 GeV, this mechanism has the
potential to account for the observed relic density of dark matter. For
symmetry breaking scales lower than this, the density of dark matter created by
loop decays from a scaling string network lies below the observed value. In
particular, the cosmic strings originating from a U(1) gauge symmetry broken
near the electroweak scale, that could lead to a massive Z' gauge boson
observable at the LHC, produce a negligibly small dark matter relic density by
this mechanism.

Vertical counter-current laminar gas-liquid flows are prevalent in various industrial and natural processes, yet their stability characteristics remain inadequately understood. This study aims to investigate both linear and nonlinear instability mechanisms within these flows to enhance the predictability of operational conditions in relevant applications. Employing a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we derive the stability criteria and analyze the bifurcation behaviors of the flow regime under different operating conditions, such as phase velocities and liquid properties. Our findings reveal distinct stability thresholds for linear and nonlinear regimes, highlighting the transition points where laminar flows become susceptible to perturbations. Furthermore, we identify the emergence of chaotic oscillations in the nonlinear regime, which have significant implications for flow efficiency and mass transfer rates. The results indicate that increasing gas velocity tends to extend the stability region, while variations in liquid viscosity and density exhibit complex interactions that can either stabilize or destabilize the flow. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics governing gas-liquid interactions in counter-current flows and provide valuable guidance for optimizing process design in related applications. The study concludes that a comprehensive approach combining both linear and nonlinear analyses is essential for accurately predicting flow behavior and enhancing process efficiency in engineering applications involving gas-liquid systems.

Classical models for the propagation of ultrasound waves are the Westervelt
equation, the Kuznetsov and the Khokhlov-Zabolotskaya-Kuznetsov equations. The
Jordan-Moore-Gibson-Thompson equation is a prominent example of a Partial
Differential Equation (PDE) model which describes the acoustic velocity
potential in ultrasound wave propagation, where the paradox of infinite speed
of propagation of thermal signals is eliminated; the use of the constitutive
Cattaneo law for the heat flux, in place of the Fourier law, accounts for its
being of third order in time. Aiming at the understanding of the fully
quasilinear PDE, a great deal of attention has been recently devoted to its
linearization -- referred to in the literature as the Moore-Gibson-Thompson
equation -- whose mathematical analysis is also of independent interest, posing
already several questions and challenges. In this work we consider and solve a
quadratic control problem associated with the linear equation, formulated
consistently with the goal of keeping the acoustic pressure close to a
reference pressure during ultrasound excitation, as required in medical and
industrial applications. While optimal control problems with smooth controls
have been considered in the recent literature, we aim at relying on controls
which are just $L^2$ in time; this leads to a singular control problem and to
non-standard Riccati equations. In spite of the unfavourable combination of the
semigroup describing the free dynamics that is not analytic, with the
challenging pattern displayed by the dynamics subject to boundary control, a
feedback synthesis of the optimal control as well as well-posedness of operator
Riccati equations are established.

In this paper, we study theoretically the behavior of a pulse as it
propagates through an intracavity fast-light medium. The method of using a
transfer function to determine a pulse after it passes through a cavity is well
known. However, this approach cannot be used to determine the behavior of the
pulse inside the cavity. To circumvent this constraint, we use an approach that
starts by finding a self-consistent solution for a monochromatic field of
infinite spatial and temporal extents, and determine its amplitudes before,
inside, and after the cavity. We then construct a Gaussian input pulse by
adding a set of these waves, properly phased and weighted, to represent a
moving pulse before the cavity. Adding these waves at various time intervals
then yields the complete spatial profile everywhere, including before, inside
and after the cavity. We first confirm the prediction of this model by
analyzing the behavior of a pulse passing through an empty cavity, and
comparing the prediction of the output with the one produced by the transfer
function method. We then apply the technique to a cavity containing a
fast-light medium. The resulting model allows us to visualize the behavior of
the pulse as it propagates superluminally inside the cavity, and interferes
with itself through multiple bounces. For a vanishing group index, an
interference pattern is formed immediately after the pulse enters the cavity,
with an output pulse emerging with no time delay or distortion. The results
obtained here illustrates the physical mechanism behind pulse propagation
through a white light cavity, a process we have proposed earlier for realizing
a high bandwidth, long delay data buffering system

This study investigates the color distributions of elliptical galaxies as observed through both the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) and Spitzer Space Telescope, aiming to enhance understanding of their stellar populations and formation histories. The primary objective is to analyze the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of a representative sample of elliptical galaxies across different wavelengths, tracking how these colors correlate with physical properties such as age, metallicity, and star formation rates. Utilizing high-resolution imaging and photometric data from GALEX in the ultraviolet and Spitzer in the mid-infrared, we conducted a comparative analysis of color indices, focusing on the UV-optical and optical-infrared regimes. Our findings reveal a distinct correlation between the UV colors and the recent star formation activity within these galaxies, while mid-infrared colors are more indicative of the underlying stellar population age and metallicity. Moreover, we observe a systematic trend where redder elliptical galaxies tend to exhibit lower specific star formation rates, emphasizing the impact of environmental factors on galaxy evolution. The results suggest a nuanced understanding of elliptical galaxies, proposing that color differences arise from a combination of evolutionary processes, including dry merging and environmental quenching. In conclusion, this research provides vital insights into the evolutionary pathways of elliptical galaxies, highlighting the roles played by both recent and ancient stellar components in shaping their observed colors across different wavelengths.

This study explores the nonsequential double ionization (NDI) mechanism in helium atoms under the influence of two-color infrared (IR) and XUV laser fields. The research delves into the collision-excitation ionization process as a significant pathway for NDI, distinguishing it from previous studies that predominantly focused on direct excitation pathways. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy and numerical simulations, the work investigates how the relative phase and intensity of the IR and XUV fields influence the probability of collision-excitation ionization events. Key findings indicate that the presence of XUV radiation significantly enhances the likelihood of collision-excitation ionization compared to IR alone. Additionally, the phase relationship between the IR and XUV fields plays a crucial role in modulating the ionization dynamics. The results suggest that collision-excitation processes can contribute substantially to the total NDI yield, providing insights into the complex interplay between different ionization mechanisms under these extreme field conditions. This study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of nonsequential ionization processes and their dependence on laser field parameters.

Millimeter wave (mmWave) communication systems have gained significant attention for their potential in achieving high data rates. Hybrid precoding techniques have been proposed to overcome the hardware limitations in realizing the fully digital precoding structures in these systems. This paper presents a hardware-efficient analog network structure for hybrid precoding in mmWave systems.   The objective of this research is to design an analog network that optimally distributes the precoding task between the digital and analog domains to reduce hardware complexity while maintaining performance. The methodology involves formulating an optimization problem to determine the analog beamforming weights that maximize the system capacity under hardware constraints.  Key findings of the study show that the proposed analog network structure achieves performance close to fully digital precoding with significantly reduced hardware requirements. The system demonstrates improved energy efficiency and lower complexity compared to traditional analog-only or fully digital precoding approaches.  In conclusion, the hardware-efficient analog network structure presented in this research offers a promising solution for implementing hybrid precoding in mmWave systems, paving the way for cost-effective and energy-efficient communication systems capable of supporting high data rates.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a popular framework for modeling heterogeneity in
data for regression, classification, and clustering. For regression and cluster
analyses of continuous data, MoE usually use normal experts following the
Gaussian distribution. However, for a set of data containing a group or groups
of observations with heavy tails or atypical observations, the use of normal
experts is unsuitable and can unduly affect the fit of the MoE model. We
introduce a robust MoE modeling using the $t$ distribution. The proposed $t$
MoE (TMoE) deals with these issues regarding heavy-tailed and noisy data. We
develop a dedicated expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate the
parameters of the proposed model by monotonically maximizing the observed data
log-likelihood. We describe how the presented model can be used in prediction
and in model-based clustering of regression data. The proposed model is
validated on numerical experiments carried out on simulated data, which show
the effectiveness and the robustness of the proposed model in terms of modeling
non-linear regression functions as well as in model-based clustering. Then, it
is applied to the real-world data of tone perception for musical data analysis,
and the one of temperature anomalies for the analysis of climate change data.
The obtained results show the usefulness of the TMoE model for practical
applications.

The formation and evolution of stellar bowshock nebulae are critical to understanding stellar dynamics and interstellar interactions. This research investigates the infrared photometric properties of 709 candidate stellar bowshock nebulae identified through a systematic survey across various regions of the Milky Way. Our objective was to analyze the infrared emissions and assess their correlation with environmental variables, such as stellar velocity and ambient medium density. The methodology involved utilizing data from infrared surveys, specifically the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) and the Spitzer Space Telescope, supplemented by ground-based observations. We employed photometric analysis techniques to extract and compare the emission profiles of these nebulae, focusing on key wavelengths associated with dust and gas interactions. Key findings reveal distinct patterns in the infrared signatures of bowshock nebulae, including variations in brightness and color indices that correlate with the characteristics of their associated stars. Notably, we observed a trend indicating that higher-velocity stars produce more pronounced infrared emissions, suggesting enhanced dust heating and subsequent emission processes. Our study concludes that the infrared photometric properties of stellar bowshock nebulae provide invaluable insights into the mechanisms of stellar wind interaction with the interstellar medium. These results enhance our understanding of the life cycle of stars and the impact of their movements on the galactic environment, paving the way for future research in stellar astrophysics and nebular dynamics.

A model of fast radio bursts, which enlists young, short period extragalactic
magnetars satisfying $B/P > 2 \times 10^{16}$~G~s$^{-1}$ (1~G =
1~statvolt~cm$^{-1}$) as the source, is proposed. When the parallel component
$\bE_\parallel$ of the surface electric field (under the scenario of a vacuum
magnetosphere) of such pulsars approaches 5 \% of the critical field $E_c =
m_e^2 c^3/(e\hbar)$, in strength, the field can readily decay via the Schwinger
mechanism into electron-positron pairs, the back reaction of which causes
$\bE_\parallel$ to oscillate on a characteristic timescale smaller than the
development of a spark gap. Thus, under this scenario, the open field line
region of the pulsar magnetosphere is controlled by Schwinger pairs, and their
large creation and acceleration rates enable the escaping pairs to coherently
emit radio waves directly from the polar cap. The majority of the energy is
emitted at frequencies $\lesssim 1$~GHz where the coherent radiation has the
highest yield, at a rate large enough to cause the magnetar to lose spin
significantly over timescale $\ap$ a few $\times 10^{-3}$~s, the duration of a
fast radio burst. Owing to circumstellar environment of a young magnetar,
however, the $\lesssim 1$~GHz radiation is likely to be absorbed or reflected
by the overlying matter. It is shown that the brightness of the remaining
(observable) frequencies of $\ap 1$~GHz and above are on par with a typical
fast radio burst. Unless some spin-up mechanism is available to recover the
original high rotation rate that triggered the Schwinger mechanism, the fast
radio burst will not be repeated again in the same magnetar.

This research paper investigates the optimization of virtual function placement for service chaining in cloud networks considering partial orders and anti-affinity rules. The objective is to minimize latency and resource allocation while adhering to the specified constraints. The methodology involves developing a mathematical model based on integer linear programming to address the placement problem considering both partial ordering of services and anti-affinity requirements. Key findings include the proposal of an efficient algorithm that optimally places virtual functions, considering the complex interactions between services in the chain and respect to anti-affinity constraints. The algorithm demonstrates improved performance in terms of reducing latency and resource utilization compared to existing methods. In conclusion, the study showcases the significance of considering partial orders and anti-affinity rules in virtual function placement for service chaining in cloud networks to enhance the overall network efficiency and performance.

We investigate the energy gap evolution across the superconductivity dome in single crystals of (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ by employing a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical models. Our study aims to address the fundamental question of how the superconducting state emerges and evolves as a function of doping in iron-based superconductors. Through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements, we observe the evolution of the superconducting gap in the electronic band structure as the doping level is varied. Our results reveal a non-monotonic behavior of the superconducting gap, showing an initial increase at low dopings, followed by a decrease towards optimal doping. This unexpected trend challenges existing theoretical frameworks and provides new insights into the complex interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in these materials.  Furthermore, by analyzing the temperature dependence of the superconducting gap through specific heat measurements, we extract important information about the pairing mechanism and the nature of the superconducting state in (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. Our findings shed light on the connection between the electronic structure and superconducting properties in iron-based superconductors, offering valuable contributions to the understanding of high-temperature superconductivity in these materials. Our study underscores the importance of a comprehensive approach combining experimental observations with theoretical modeling to elucidate the intricate physics of high-temperature superconductors.

This book is a collection of papers dedicated to the memory of Yehuda Vardi.
Yehuda was the chair of the Department of Statistics of Rutgers University when
he passed away unexpectedly on January 13, 2005. On October 21--22, 2005, some
150 leading scholars from many different fields, including statistics,
telecommunications, biomedical engineering, bioinformatics, biostatistics and
epidemiology, gathered at Rutgers in a conference in his honor. This conference
was on ``Complex Datasets and Inverse Problems: Tomography, Networks, and
Beyond,'' and was organized by the editors. The present collection includes
research work presented at the conference, as well as contributions from
Yehuda's colleagues. The theme of the conference was networks and other
important and emerging areas of research involving incomplete data and
statistical inverse problems. Networks are abundant around us: communication,
computer, traffic, social and energy are just a few examples. As enormous
amounts of network data are collected in this information age, the field has
attracted a great amount of attention from researchers in statistics and
computer engineering as well as telecommunication providers and various
government agencies. However, few statistical tools have been developed for
analyzing network data as they are typically governed by time-varying and
mutually dependent communication protocols sitting on complicated
graph-structured network topologies. Many prototypical applications in these
and other important technologies can be viewed as statistical inverse problems
with complex, massive, high-dimensional and possibly biased/incomplete data.
This unifying theme of inverse problems is particularly appropriate for a
conference and volume dedicated to the memory of Yehuda. Indeed he made
influential contributions to these fields, especially in medical tomography,
biased data, statistical inverse problems, and network tomography.

In our study, we explored the reliability of ammonia (NH3) as a temperature probe for cold cloud cores using observational data from various observatories. Employing a large sample of molecular lines from the NH3 (J, K) = (1, 1) transition, we analyzed the temperature structure of cold cloud cores in Taurus, Ophiuchus, and Perseus using Herschel Space Observatory and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations.  Our findings reveal a strong linear correlation between NH3 temperatures and those derived from dust continuum measurements, confirming the reliability of NH3 as a temperature proxy. We attribute this correlation to the excellent thermal coupling between NH3 molecules and their surroundings. However, the accuracy of NH3 as a temperature probe varies with the cloud conditions, such as cloud radius and column density. The higher the column density and cloud radius, the more accurate the NH3 temperature measurements.  Moreover, we investigated the sources of temperature discrepancies and determined that those discrepancies can be attributed to the presence of grain surface temperatures and the contribution of neighboring warm cloud components to the observed NH3 emission. To minimize temperature discrepancies, we propose observing NH3 emission with high spectral and spatial resolution.  In conclusion, our study highlights the reliability of NH3 as a temperature probe for cold cloud cores, confirming its potential for accurate temperature measurements. However, it is essential to consider cloud conditions and potential temperature discrepancies to ensure the highest possible accuracy. Future work includes the exploration of other molecular lines and the examination of temperature measurements in the context of cloud evolution.

This study explores the interaction between switch operators and push-the-button (PTB) games within a sequential compound over rulesets. The primary objective was to investigate how these elements influence gameplay dynamics and player strategies. Methodologically, we employed a combination of qualitative and quantitative analysis, including game mechanics evaluation, user testing, and statistical modeling to understand the interplay between switch operators and PTB games. Key findings indicate that the presence of switch operators significantly enhances strategic depth by introducing conditional outcomes, which can either simplify or complicate the game's progression based on player choices. Additionally, the integration of PTB games into the ruleset created new opportunities for emergent gameplay, leading to increased player engagement and replay value. However, the complexity introduced by these elements also posed challenges in terms of accessibility, particularly for novice players. The study concludes with recommendations for designers aiming to incorporate such features in their rule sets, emphasizing the need for balanced design to accommodate diverse player skill levels while maintaining strategic complexity.

This research paper investigates the Lasso-type recovery of sparse representations for high-dimensional data, a fundamental problem in machine learning and signal processing. High-dimensional data, often encountered in various fields such as image and speech processing, can be represented by a large number of parameters, making it challenging to identify the underlying low-dimensional structure. Traditional methods, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and singular value decomposition (SVD), are not effective in recovering the sparse representation of high-dimensional data due to the curse of dimensionality.  The objective of this research is to develop an efficient and robust method for Lasso-type recovery of sparse representations in high-dimensional data. We propose a novel algorithm, called Lasso-Boost, which combines the strengths of Lasso regression and boosting techniques to recover the sparse representation. The proposed algorithm leverages the sparsity-inducing property of Lasso regression and the adaptive learning mechanism of boosting to iteratively update the sparse representation and improve its accuracy.  Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Lasso-Boost in recovering sparse representations of high-dimensional data. We compare Lasso-Boost with state-of-the-art methods and show that it outperforms them in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The key findings of this research include the ability of Lasso-Boost to accurately recover sparse representations in high-dimensional data, its robustness to noise and outliers, and its computational efficiency. The conclusions of this research highlight the potential of Lasso-Boost as a powerful tool for recovering sparse representations in high-dimensional data, and its applications in various fields such as image and speech processing.

In this study, we investigate the detection and characterization of emission lines in the X-ray spectrum of the high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) 4U 1538-52 using data obtained from the XMM-Newton observatory. Our work aims to enhance the understanding of the physical processes occurring in the vicinity of neutron stars in HMXBs, particularly focusing on the line-forming regions and their contributions to the overall spectral properties. We employ a comprehensive approach that utilizes both the EPIC and RGS instruments aboard XMM-Newton to perform high-resolution spectroscopy. We apply advanced data reduction techniques and model fitting procedures to analyze the collected spectra, targeting specific emission lines that are indicative of the ionization states and elemental abundances in the system. Our findings reveal the presence of several significant emission lines, including Fe K-alpha, which exhibit characteristics that suggest complex ionization structures and dynamics. The detection of these lines provides critical insights into the accretion processes and the stellar wind interaction with the neutron star's magnetosphere. Furthermore, we observe variations in the line profiles suggesting the influence of orbital dynamics and potential anisotropic emission due to geometrical effects. Our methodology effectively combines both observational data and theoretical modeling, allowing us to map out the conditions in the emission region. This study not only advances the understanding of 4U 1538-52 but also contributes to the broader comprehension of emission line mechanisms in X-ray binaries, providing a template for future investigations of similar astrophysical systems.

Quenching, the cessation of star formation, is one of the most significant
events in the life cycle of galaxies. We show here the first evidence that the
Milky Way experienced a generalised quenching of its star formation at the end
of its thick disk formation $\sim$9 Gyr ago. Elemental abundances of stars
studied as part of the APOGEE survey reveal indeed that in less than $\sim$2
Gyr the star formation rate in our Galaxy dropped by an order-of-magnitude.
Because of the tight correlation between age and alpha abundance, this event
reflects in the dearth of stars along the inner disk sequence in the
[Fe/H]-[$\alpha$/Fe] plane. Before this phase, which lasted about 1.5 Gyr, the
Milky Way was actively forming stars. Afterwards, the star formation resumed at
a much lower level to form the thin disk. These events are very well matched by
the latest observation of MW-type progenitors at high redshifts. In late type
galaxies, quenching is believed to be related to a long and secular exhaustion
of gas. In our Galaxy, it occurred on a much shorter time scale, while the
chemical continuity before and after the quenching indicates that it was not
due to the exhaustion of the gas. While quenching is generally associated with
spheroids, our results show that it also occurs in galaxies like the Milky Way,
possibly when they are undergoing a morphological transition from thick to thin
disks. Given the demographics of late type galaxies in the local universe, in
which classical bulges are rare, we suggest further that this may hold true
generally in galaxies with mass lower than or approximately $M^*$, where
quenching could be directly a consequence of thick disk formation. We emphasize
that the quenching phase in the Milky Way could be contemporaneous with, and
related to, the formation of the bar. We sketch a scenario on how a strong bar
may inhibit star formation.

The theory of compact operators plays a crucial role in functional analysis, particularly in the context of infinite-dimensional spaces. This paper presents a comprehensive classification of the spaces of compact operators on C([1, α], l_p) spaces, where 1 < p < ∞. The objective is to delineate the structural properties of these operators in connection with the topology of the underlying function spaces. Utilizing a combination of descriptive set theory and operator algebra, we first establish a framework for characterizing compact operators through their effects on continuity and convergence of sequences in C([1, α], l_p). The methodology includes the examination of the behavior of these operators under various topological conditions, supported by a series of theorems that relate compactness to the properties of the space l_p. Key findings reveal that the compact operators on C([1, α], l_p) can be effectively categorized into distinct classes based on their spectra and norm structures, revealing intrinsic linkages to classical results concerning bounded linear operators. Furthermore, the results indicate that the compact operators on these spaces exhibit unique behaviors that are critically determined by the interplay between α and p, with ramifications for their applications in quantum mechanics and numerical analysis. In conclusion, this classification not only enhances the understanding of compact operators in the context of C([1, α], l_p) spaces but also lays the groundwork for further explorations into the topological aspects of operator theory in infinite-dimensional settings.

We present the first comprehensive evolutionary analysis of the rest-frame UV
spectroscopic properties of star-forming galaxies at z ~ 2-4. We match samples
at different redshifts in UV luminosity and stellar mass, and perform
systematic measurements of spectral features and stellar population modeling.
By creating composite spectra grouped according to Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width
(EW), and various galaxy properties, we study the evolutionary trends among
Ly$\alpha$, low- and high-ionization interstellar (LIS and HIS) absorption
features, and integrated galaxy properties. We also examine the redshift
evolution of Ly$\alpha$ and LIS absorption kinematics, and fine-structure
emission EWs. The connections among the strengths of Ly$\alpha$, LIS lines, and
dust extinction are redshift-independent, as is the decoupling of Ly$\alpha$
and HIS line strengths, and the bulk outflow kinematics as traced by LIS lines.
Stronger Ly$\alpha$ emission is observed at higher redshift at fixed UV
luminosity, stellar mass, SFR, and age. Much of this variation in average
Ly$\alpha$ strength with redshift, and the variation in Ly$\alpha$ strength at
fixed redshift, can be explained in terms of variations in neutral gas covering
fraction and/or dust content in the ISM and CGM. However, based on the
connection between Ly$\alpha$ and CIII] emission strengths, we additionally
find evidence for variations in the intrinsic production rate of Ly$\alpha$
photons at the highest Ly$\alpha$ EWs. The challenge now is to understand the
observed evolution in neutral gas covering fraction and dust extinction within
a coherent model for galaxy formation, and make robust predictions for the
escape of ionizing radiation at z > 6.

This research paper investigates the approximations used to calculate many-body Green's functions, which are crucial for understanding the cohesive properties of quantum systems. The objective of the study is to provide insights into the fundamental equations that govern these functions and to assess the effectiveness of various approximation methods in capturing the essential physics of many-body interactions. We employed a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques to analyze the behavior of Green's functions in different physical contexts, such as fermionic systems and spin-lattice models. Our findings reveal that traditional mean-field approaches often fail to accurately describe the correlations present in strongly interacting systems, while advanced techniques, such as diagrammatic and functional renormalization group methods, offer significant improvements. Additionally, we explored the implications of self-consistent approximations and their influence on the convergence of many-body solutions. The results demonstrate that a careful balance between computational efficiency and accuracy is pivotal when modeling complex quantum interactions. In conclusion, our study emphasizes the necessity of developing new approximation strategies that incorporate non-perturbative effects to enhance the reliability of many-body Green's functions in theoretical predictions. This work not only contributes to the existing body of knowledge but also sets the stage for future developments in the field of condensed matter physics.

Sinking and resuspension are the most important processes determining the
distribution of bentho--pelagic diatoms in the water column and influencing
their variability. From the bentho--pelagic time series 1991-2008 we analyzed
weekly concentrations of the diatom Paralia sulcata in the German Bight. The
analysis was carried out for lower wind ranges (<10 m/s) at two different
seasons characterized by distinct sea surface conditions. Our results showed
that the relationship between wind and diatom concentrations was much
influenced by seasonal conditions: the decrease of abundances at higher winds
was more pronounced in summer. Additional sampling procedure of species at two
different water depths (bottom and surface layers) in the years 2007-2009
showed that in summer the surface abundance of species decreased substantially
with increasing wind. In contrast, in winter the decrease of the surface
concentration of species was less pronounced. To explain observed seasonal
variations numerical simulations of plankton--like particles were performed
using a two--dimensional turbulence model. Numerical simulations were carried
using parameters corresponding to averaged winter and summer temperature and
salinity at the study site. We showed that the reduction of cell counts was
possibly linked to the changes in sinking of diatoms due to the altered
buoyancy of algal cells. Our numerical results identified reduction of sinking
speed of particles for the parameters corresponding to winter conditions.

Context. The wind mass transfer from a giant to its white dwarf companion in
symbiotic binaries is not well understood. For example, the efficiency of wind
mass transfer of the canonical Bondi-Hoyle accretion mechanism is too low to
power the typical luminosities of the accretors. However, recent observations
and modelling indicate a considerably more efficient mass transfer in symbiotic
binaries.
  Aims. We determine the velocity profile of the wind from the giant at the
near-orbital-plane region of eclipsing S-type symbiotic binaries EG And and SY
Mus, and derive the corresponding spherical equivalent of the mass-loss rate.
With this approach, we indicate the high mass transfer ratio.
  Methods. We achieved this aim by modelling the observed column densities
taking into account ionization of the wind of the giant, whose velocity profile
is derived using the inversion of Abel's integral operator for the hydrogen
column density function.
  Results. Our analysis revealed the spherical equivalent of the mass-loss rate
from the giant to be a few times 10^{-6}M_{Sun}/yr, which is a factor of >=10
higher than rates determined by methods that do not depend on the line of
sight. This discrepancy rules out the usual assumption that the wind is
spherically symmetric. As our values were derived from near-orbital-plane
column densities, these values can be a result of focusing the wind from the
giant towards the orbital plane.
  Conclusions. Our findings suggests that the wind from giants in S-type
symbiotic stars is not spherically symmetric, since it is enhanced at the
orbital plane and, thus, is accreted more effectively onto the hot component.

This study investigates the phenomenon of an isotropic to an anisotropic transition in a fractional quantum Hall (FQH) state. The initial problem addressed was the understanding of how topological properties change as external parameters are varied, leading to distinct states with different degrees of anisotropy. To address this, we employed a combination of theoretical calculations and numerical simulations based on the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method. Our results demonstrate that under specific conditions, a FQH state initially characterized by isotropic order can evolve into one exhibiting anisotropic features, indicating a phase transition. Key insights include the identification of critical values of magnetic field and density that trigger this transition, which were corroborated through DMRG simulations. The findings highlight the importance of studying the interplay between topological order and external parameters in quantum systems, offering potential implications for future research on quantum materials and condensed matter physics.

Enstatite chondrites are a rare and primitive class of meteorites, providing valuable insights into the early solar system's formation conditions. These meteorites are characterized by their low iron content, high magnesium, and distinctive mineralogy. The formation conditions of enstatite chondrites remain poorly understood, and further research is needed to elucidate their origin.
