This study focuses on the Sahara 97096 meteorite, classified as an EH3 chondrite, which contains a significant proportion of olivine-bearing chondrules. The objective of this research is to investigate the formation conditions of enstatite chondrites through the analysis of trace element geochemistry of olivine-bearing chondrules in Sahara 97096.   A combination of electron microprobe, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS), and secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) was employed to analyze the major and minor elements in olivine-bearing chondrules. The results indicate that the chondrules exhibit a range of olivine compositions, suggesting a complex formation history. The geochemical signatures of the chondrules are characterized by high magnesium and low iron, which are consistent with the EH3 classification of the Sahara 97096 meteorite.   The key findings of this study reveal that the olivine-bearing chondrules in Sahara 97096 exhibit a distinct geochemical signature, which is indicative of a unique formation environment. The results suggest that the formation conditions of enstatite chondrites were influenced by a combination of solar nebular processes and terrestrial differentiation.   In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the formation conditions of enstatite chondrites, highlighting the importance of olivine-bearing chondrules in understanding the early solar system's evolution. The geochemical signatures of these chondrules offer a window into the complex formation history of enstatite chondrites, providing a framework for further research into the origins of these enigmatic meteorites.

This research paper explores the concept of Wireless Physical-Layer Identification (WPLI), focusing on its modeling and validation. The study aims to establish a comprehensive understanding of how WPLI can be used to identify and classify wireless communication systems at the physical layer, which is crucial for enhancing security, privacy, and efficient resource allocation in wireless networks. The research methodology involves theoretical analysis of various signal characteristics and mathematical models that enable the identification process. Additionally, experimental validations using real-world data from different wireless communication scenarios are conducted to validate the effectiveness and accuracy of these models. Key findings indicate that the proposed models achieve high identification rates across diverse environments, thereby demonstrating the practical utility of WPLI techniques. The conclusion emphasizes the importance of further development and integration of WPLI into existing and future wireless communication technologies to address emerging challenges such as advanced cyber threats and spectrum management.

In this study, we develop an effective action framework dedicated to analyzing higher-order relativistic tidal interactions within binary systems, subsequently aligning these insights with their effective one body (EOB) description. Our approach provides a systematic methodology to incorporate tidal effects at higher-order post-Newtonian (PN) expansions, addressing a crucial gap in precise waveform modeling necessary for gravitational wave astronomy. We calculate tidal corrections up to the fifth PN order, ensuring that these effects are consistently integrated within the EOB formalism. We employ an effective field theory (EFT) strategy to derive the relativistic corrections in a manner that is both computationally efficient and fundamentally coherent. By implementing our methodology, we substantially enhance the fidelity of the EOB model, allowing for more accurate predictions of gravitational waveforms from compact binary coalescences involving neutron stars or black hole-neutron star systems. The results demonstrate improved waveform matching with numerical relativity simulations, providing a robust tool for precision testing of gravitational theories. Our solutions address the complex problem of incorporating relativistic tidal effects in a way that maintains analytical tractability and computational efficacy. Through rigorous analysis, we also identify subtle deviations between waveforms generated with and without higher-order tidal effects, underscoring the necessity of their inclusion in future observational efforts. Our contribution lays critical groundwork for leveraging tidal interactions as probes of neutron star structure, thereby enhancing the scientific yield of current and upcoming gravitational wave detections. The methodologies presented have significant implications for both theoretical development and practical application in the realm of astrological observation and interpretation.

Based on masers with measured trigonometric parallaxes, we have redetermined
the spatial orientation parameters of the Local (Orion) arm. Using 23 sources
(the Gould Belt objects were excluded), we have found that their spatial
distribution can be approximated by a very narrow ellipsoid elongated in the
direction L_1=77.1+/-2.9^o whose symmetry plane is inclined to the Galactic
plane at an angle of 5.6+/-0.2^o. The longitude of the ascending node of the
symmetry plane is l_\Omega=70+/-3^o. A new estimate for the pitch angle of the
Local spiral arm has been obtained by an independent method: i=12.9+/-2.9^o.
Previously, a belt of young B stars, the de Vaucouleurs.Dolidze belt, was
pointed out on the celestial sphere with parameters close to such an
orientation. We have refined the spatial orientation parameters of this belt
based on a homogeneous sample of protostars. The de Vaucouleurs.Dolidze belt
can be identified with the Local arm, with the belt proper as a continuous band
on the celestial sphere like the Gould Belt being absent due to the
peculiarities of the spatial orientation of the Local arm. Using the entire
sample of 119 Galactic masers, we have shown that the third axis of their
position ellipsoid has no deviation from the direction to the Galactic pole:
B_3=89.7+/-0.1^o.

Shape from shading is a challenging problem in computer vision and image processing, aiming to recover the 3D shape of an object from its 2D shading image. In this research, we propose a machine learning approach for Shape from Shading to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of existing methods.   The objective of this study is to train a deep neural network to learn the complex mapping between shading patterns and corresponding surface orientations. We employ a dataset of synthetic images with ground truth surface normals to facilitate the training process. The neural network architecture is designed to effectively capture the intricate relationships between pixel intensities and surface gradients.  Our methodology involves training the network using a combination of loss functions tailored to the specific characteristics of Shape from Shading problem. Additionally, we incorporate a data augmentation strategy to improve the model generalization to diverse real-world scenarios.  Key findings of our research demonstrate that the proposed machine learning approach outperforms traditional Shape from Shading algorithms in terms of accuracy and robustness. The trained neural network exhibits superior performance in recovering surface orientations from shading images under various lighting conditions.  In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of machine learning techniques in advancing Shape from Shading research, paving the way for more accurate and efficient 3D shape recovery from 2D images.

The abstract focuses on developing a straightforward and objective approach for the identification of reproducible resting-state networks (RSNs) using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). This study aims to establish a reliable framework for detecting RSNs that can be consistently replicated across different sessions or even different datasets. Utilizing machine learning algorithms, specifically support vector machines (SVM), we aimed to identify stable brain connectivity patterns associated with predefined RSNs such as default mode network (DMN), salience network, and sensorimotor network. The methodology involved preprocessing fMRI data to extract time-series from brain regions, followed by feature selection and training SVM classifiers. Key findings indicate that our approach achieved high accuracy in distinguishing between RSNs and non-RSNs, demonstrating robustness and reproducibility. The proposed method not only simplifies the process but also enhances the interpretability of RSNs, facilitating further studies in neuroscientific research. In conclusion, this study offers a valuable tool for researchers aiming to investigate the stability and consistency of RSNs in various neurological conditions and states.

The Gaia mission promises to deliver precision astrometry at an unprecedented
level, heralding a new era for discerning the kinematic and spatial coordinates
of stars in our Galaxy. Here, we present a new technique for estimating the age
of tidally disrupted globular cluster streams using the proper motions and
parallaxes of tracer stars. We evolve the collisional dynamics of globular
clusters within the evolving potential of a Milky Way-like halo extracted from
a cosmological $\Lambda$CDM simulation and analyze the resultant streams as
they would be observed by Gaia. The simulations sample a variety of globular
cluster orbits, and account for stellar evolution and the gravitational
influence of the disk of the Milky Way. We show that a characteristic
timescale, obtained from the dispersion of the proper motions and parallaxes of
stars within the stream, is a good indicator for the time elapsed since the
stream has been freely expanding away due to the tidal disruption of the
globular cluster. This timescale, in turn, places a lower limit on the age of
the cluster. The age can be deduced from astrometry using a modest number of
stars, with the error on this estimate depending on the proximity of the stream
and the number of tracer stars used.

Provided a complete set of putative $k$-body reductions of a multipartite
quantum state, can one determine if a joint state exists? We derive necessary
conditions for this to be true. In contrast to what is known as the quantum
marginal problem, we consider a setting where the labeling of the subsystems is
unknown. The problem can be seen in analogy to Ulam's reconstruction conjecture
in graph theory. The conjecture - still unsolved - claims that every graph on
at least three vertices can uniquely be reconstructed from the set of its
vertex-deleted subgraphs. When considering quantum states, we demonstrate that
the non-existence of joint states can, in some cases, already be inferred from
a set of marginals having the size of just more than half of the parties. We
apply these methods to graph states, where many constraints can be evaluated by
knowing the number of stabilizer elements of certain weights that appear in the
reductions. This perspective links with constraints that were derived in the
context of quantum error-correcting codes and polynomial invariants. Some of
these constraints can be interpreted as monogamy-like relations that limit the
correlations arising from quantum states. Lastly, we provide an answer to
Ulam's reconstruction problem for generic quantum states.

We present a novel multi-scale computational model to investigate the correlation patterns in B cell VDJ gene segment usage within the zebrafish immune repertoire. Our study addresses the challenge of understanding the complex selection processes underlying V(D)J recombination and its variability across different scales, from molecular mechanisms to organism-level immune responses. Utilizing high-throughput sequencing data, we develop a hybrid framework integrating stochastic modeling with machine learning techniques to capture and predict VDJ segment utilization patterns. Key innovations of our methodology include a probabilistic model that simulates VDJ rearrangements and a novel algorithm for identifying significant correlations between gene segment usage and functional diversity in the zebrafish B cell receptor repertoire.  We validate our model against empirical data, achieving high concordance in predicting lineage-specific segment usage frequencies and correlations across temporal and anatomical scales. Results reveal non-random associations in VDJ segment selection, suggestive of evolutionary constraints and functional adaptive mechanisms in zebrafish. Our findings also highlight potential analogs in vertebrate adaptive immune systems, providing insights into the evolutionary dynamics of immune diversification. The model offers a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of immunogenetic variation and can be applied to other species to explore general principles of immune repertoire formation. This work lays the foundation for future explorations into the adaptive strategies of immune systems, contributing to the broader field of systems immunology and immunogenetics.

This study presents a method to identify the accretion phase of active galactic nuclei (AGN) within field galaxies, focusing on distinguishing between quiescent and active states. Utilizing multi-wavelength data including optical spectra, near-infrared imaging, and radio observations, we employed machine learning techniques to classify galaxies based on their nuclear emission-line ratios and spectral features indicative of AGN activity. Key findings indicate that galaxies with high specific star formation rates but low nuclear emission-line ratios are more likely to be in the quiescent phase, while those showing strong nuclear emission lines and signatures of nuclear heating are classified as being in the accretion phase. The methodology successfully categorized 86% of the sample galaxies into their respective phases, providing a robust framework for identifying AGN activity in field galaxies. The results contribute to our understanding of AGN evolution and the feedback mechanisms between AGN and host galaxies.

We present new calculations of pion and kaon decay constants using a chiral perturbation theory framework that incorporates resonance contributions. The key idea behind our approach is to model the intermediate resonances as quasielastic degrees of freedom in a meson propagator, allowing for a consistent treatment of both the resonance and non-resonance regions. We adopt a resonance model based on a relativistic Breit-Wigner parameterization and apply it to the O(p^4) leading order contribution to the decay constants. Our approach improves the convergence of chiral perturbation theory by reducing the size of high energy logarithms in the loop integrals.  The numerical results for the pion decay constant are in good agreement with the experimental value, while for the kaon decay constant, we find a significant deviation from the experimental data, suggesting that beyond leading order corrections or contributions from higher mass resonances are important. We discuss the implications of our findings for the determination of the quark condensate and the possible extension of our method to other observables.  Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the interpretation of hadronic resonance effects in low energy hadronic physics, addressing the long-standing problem of accurately modeling the behavior of decay constants in the presence of resonances. The methodology employed in this study can be applied to other decay constants, form factors, and other hadronic observables, providing valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of the strong interaction.

In this study, we delved into the intricate relationship between molecular structure and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) strength in the magnetism of metal-benzene-metal (MBM) sandwiches. Our investigations spanned single molecules to infinite wires, elucidating the evolution of magnetic properties as the system size increased.  To probe the underlying electronic structure of the MBM systems, we employed a combined approach, integrating theoretical calculations using density functional theory and experimental techniques such as X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurements. Our calculations revealed that the interplay of SOC and molecular structure significantly influenced the magnetic properties.  We discovered that in single MBM molecules, the SOC strength and molecular alignment played crucial roles in determining the magnetic anisotropy and the magnetic moments' orientations. In larger MBM systems, the interaction between neighboring molecules gave rise to spin-spin interactions, leading to long-range magnetic order and collective phenomena such as spin waves.  To explore the behavior of MBM wires, we used a series of self-assembling methods to synthesize the structures and performed magnetometry measurements. Our results demonstrated that the magnetic properties of the MBM wires depended on the MBM unit cell's orientation relative to the wire direction, providing insights into designing and manipulating magnetic properties in one-dimensional systems.  In summary, this study shed light on the complex interplay of molecular structure and SOC strength in the magnetism of MBM sandwiches and emphasized the importance of this relationship for understanding magnetism in nanostructures and potential applications in spintronics and data storage technologies.

Neutron star mergers (NSM) are significant sources of heavy r-process elements, which are crucial for understanding the evolution of galaxies. The hypermassive neutron star (HMNS) phase, lasting up to several tens of milliseconds, plays a pivotal role in r-process nucleosynthesis. This study explores the relationship between HMNS lifetimes and the production of r-process elements during NSM. We performed calculations using a one-dimensional nucleon transport code and a nuclear reaction network, considering the effects of HMNS mass and rotation on the cooling process. The results indicate that shorter HMNS lifetimes lead to more neutron-rich conditions and enhance the synthesis of r-process elements. Conversely, longer HMNS lifetimes allow for more efficient cooling, resulting in less neutron-rich conditions and a decrease in r-process production. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of HMNS magnetic fields on the r-process element distribution. Our findings suggest that stronger magnetic fields lead to the formation of smaller and denser droplets, thereby influencing the final abundance pattern of r-process elements. Overall, this work provides crucial insights into the interplay between HMNS lifetimes and r-process nucleosynthesis, shedding light on the astrophysical origins of heavy elements.

The mixed morphology class of supernova remnants has centrally peaked X-ray
emission along with a shell-like morphology in radio emission. White & Long
proposed that these remnants are evolving in a cloudy medium wherein the clouds
are evaporated via thermal conduction once being overrun by the expanding
shock. Their analytical model made detailed predictions regarding temperature,
density and emission profiles as well as shock evolution. We present numerical
hydrodynamical models in 2D and 3D including thermal conduction, testing the
White & Long model and presenting results for the evolution and emission from
remnants evolving in a cloudy medium. We find that, while certain general
results of the White & Long model hold, such as the way the remnants expand and
the flattening of the X-ray surface brightness distribution, in detail there
are substantial differences. In particular we find that the X-ray luminosity is
dominated by emission from shocked cloud gas early on, leading to a bright peak
which then declines and flattens as evaporation becomes more important. In
addition, the effects of thermal conduction on the intercloud gas, which is not
included in the White & Long model, are important and lead to further
flattening of the X-ray brightness profile as well as lower X-ray emission
temperatures.

This study presents a novel numerical scheme designed to approximate invariant distributions of constrained diffusions. The primary challenge addressed is the computational complexity and theoretical difficulties associated with obtaining these distributions, especially in high-dimensional spaces where analytical solutions are often unavailable. Our approach integrates advanced techniques from numerical analysis and stochastic processes to develop an efficient algorithm that can handle the constraints inherent in the system being studied.  The methodology involves discretizing the state space and employing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to generate samples that converge to the invariant distribution. To ensure accuracy and efficiency, we incorporate adaptive sampling strategies and variance reduction techniques. The effectiveness of our scheme is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world constrained diffusion models. Results show significant improvements in convergence rates and accuracy compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios with complex constraints.  Key insights include the importance of carefully designing the proposal distribution within the MCMC framework to effectively navigate the constrained state space. Additionally, the role of preconditioning in accelerating the convergence of the numerical scheme is highlighted. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of how to numerically approximate invariant distributions of constrained diffusions, paving the way for more accurate and computationally efficient simulations in various applications such as finance, physics, and biology.

We introduce two hierarchies of clause-sets, SLUR_k and UC_k, based on the
classes SLUR (Single Lookahead Unit Refutation), introduced in 1995, and UC
(Unit refutation Complete), introduced in 1994.
  The class SLUR, introduced in [Annexstein et al, 1995], is the class of
clause-sets for which unit-clause-propagation (denoted by r_1) detects
unsatisfiability, or where otherwise iterative assignment, avoiding obviously
false assignments by look-ahead, always yields a satisfying assignment. It is
natural to consider how to form a hierarchy based on SLUR. Such investigations
were started in [Cepek et al, 2012] and [Balyo et al, 2012]. We present what we
consider the "limit hierarchy" SLUR_k, based on generalising r_1 by r_k, that
is, using generalised unit-clause-propagation introduced in [Kullmann, 1999,
2004].
  The class UC, studied in [Del Val, 1994], is the class of Unit refutation
Complete clause-sets, that is, those clause-sets for which unsatisfiability is
decidable by r_1 under any falsifying assignment. For unsatisfiable clause-sets
F, the minimum k such that r_k determines unsatisfiability of F is exactly the
"hardness" of F, as introduced in [Ku 99, 04]. For satisfiable F we use now an
extension mentioned in [Ansotegui et al, 2008]: The hardness is the minimum k
such that after application of any falsifying partial assignments, r_k
determines unsatisfiability. The class UC_k is given by the clause-sets which
have hardness <= k. We observe that UC_1 is exactly UC.
  UC_k has a proof-theoretic character, due to the relations between hardness
and tree-resolution, while SLUR_k has an algorithmic character. The
correspondence between r_k and k-times nested input resolution (or tree
resolution using clause-space k+1) means that r_k has a dual nature: both
algorithmic and proof theoretic. This corresponds to a basic result of this
paper, namely SLUR_k = UC_k.

This paper explores the concept of "Cocktail Parties" in the context of exoplanets. The term refers to the presence of multiple signals in exoplanetary data that make it challenging to distinguish individual planetary signatures. We present a novel approach using advanced signal processing techniques to disentangle these complex signals and uncover hidden exoplanets within the data. Our methodology involves the application of machine learning algorithms to identify patterns and extract relevant information from the noisy signals.  Through our experimentation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting exoplanets in data previously deemed inconclusive due to the presence of overlapping signals. Our results show a significant improvement in the accuracy of exoplanet detection, especially in cases where traditional methods fall short. By overcoming the challenges posed by "Cocktail Party" scenarios, we contribute to enhancing the efficiency and reliability of exoplanet discovery processes.  Overall, this work addresses a critical issue in exoplanet research by providing a robust framework for analyzing complex data sets with overlapping signals. The application of advanced signal processing techniques and machine learning algorithms offers a promising solution to the problem of disentangling signals in exoplanetary data, ultimately advancing our understanding of planetary systems beyond our solar system.

As our understanding of the past in a bouncing universe is limited, it
becomes difficult to propose a cosmological model which can give some
understanding of the causal structure of the bouncing universe. In this article
we address the issue related to the particle horizon problem in the bouncing
universe models. It is shown that in many models the particle horizon does not
exist, and consequently the horizon problem is trivially solved. In some cases
a bouncing universe can have a particle horizon and we specify the conditions
for its existence. In the absence of a particle horizon the Hubble surface
specifies the causal structure of a bouncing universe. We specify the complex
relationship between the Hubble surface and the particle horizon when the
particle horizon exists. The article also address the issue related to the
event horizon in a bouncing universe. A toy example of a bouncing universe is
first presented where we specify the conditions which dictate the presence of a
particle horizon. Next we specify the causal structures of three widely used
bouncing models. The first case is related to quintom matter bounce model, the
second one is loop quantum cosmology based bounce model and lastly $f(R)$
gravity induced bounce model. We present a brief discussion on the horizon
problem in bouncing cosmologies. We point out that the causal structure of the
various bounce models fit our general theoretical predictions.

In this paper, we consider the problem of partitioning active users in a
manner that facilitates multi-access without collision. The setting is of a
noisy, synchronous, Boolean, multi-access channel where $K$ active users (out
of a total of $N$ users) seek to access. A solution to the partition problem
places each of the $N$ users in one of $K$ groups (or blocks) such that no two
active nodes are in the same block. We consider a simple, but non-trivial and
illustrative case of $K=2$ active users and study the number of steps $T$ used
to solve the partition problem. By random coding and a suboptimal decoding
scheme, we show that for any $T\geq (C_1 +\xi_1)\log N$, where $C_1$ and
$\xi_1$ are positive constants (independent of $N$), and $\xi_1$ can be
arbitrary small, the partition problem can be solved with error probability
$P_e^{(N)} \to 0$, for large $N$. Under the same scheme, we also bound $T$ from
the other direction, establishing that, for any $T \leq (C_2 - \xi_2) \log N$,
the error probability $P_e^{(N)} \to 1$ for large $N$; again $C_2$ and $\xi_2$
are constants and $\xi_2$ can be arbitrarily small. These bounds on the number
of steps are lower than the tight achievable lower-bound in terms of $T \geq
(C_g +\xi)\log N $ for group testing (in which all active users are identified,
rather than just partitioned). Thus, partitioning may prove to be a more
efficient approach for multi-access than group testing.

We discover an explicit expansion formula for the powers $s$ of the Euler
Product (or Dedekind $\eta$-function) in terms of hook lengths of partitions,
where the exponent $s$ is any complex number. Several classical formulas have
been derived for certain integers $s$ by Euler, Jacobi, Klein, Fricke, Atkin,
Winquist, Dyson and Macdonald. In particular, Macdonald obtained expansion
formulas for the integer exponents $s$ for which there exists a semi-simple Lie
algebra of dimension $s$. For the type $A_l^{(a)}$ he has expressed the
$(t^2-1)$-st power of the Euler Product as a sum of weighted integer vectors of
length $t$ for any integer $t$. Kostant has considered the general case for any
positive integer $s$ and obtained further properties.
  -----
  The present paper proposes a new approach. We convert the weighted vectors of
length $t$ used by Macdonald in his identity for type $A_l^{(a)}$ to weighted
partitions with free parameter $t$, so that a new identity on the latter
combinatorial structures can be derived without any restrictions on $t$. The
surprise is that the weighted partitions have a very simple form in terms of
hook lengths of partitions. As applications of our formula, we find some new
identities about hook lengths, including the "marked hook formula". We also
improve a result due to Kostant. The proof of the Main Theorem is based on
Macdonald's identity for $A_l^{(a)}$ and on the properties of a bijection
between $t$-cores and integer vectors constructed by Garvan, Kim and Stanton.

The dense interiors of massive galaxies are among the most intriguing
environments in the Universe. In this paper we ask when these dense cores were
formed and determine how galaxies gradually assembled around them. We select
galaxies that have a stellar mass >3x10^10 Msun inside r=1 kpc out to z=2.5,
using the 3D-HST survey and data at low redshift. Remarkably, the number
density of galaxies with dense cores appears to have decreased from z=2.5 to
the present. This decrease is probably mostly due to stellar mass loss and the
resulting adiabatic expansion, with some contribution from merging. We infer
that dense cores were mostly formed at z>2.5, consistent with their largely
quiescent stellar populations. While the cores appear to form early, the
galaxies in which they reside show strong evolution: their total masses
increase by a factor of 2-3 from z=2.5 to z=0 and their effective radii
increase by a factor of 5-6. As a result, the contribution of dense cores to
the total mass of the galaxies in which they reside decreases from ~50% at
z=2.5 to ~15% at z=0. Because of their early formation, the contribution of
dense cores to the total stellar mass budget of the Universe is a strong
function of redshift. The stars in cores with M_1kpc>3x10^10 Msun make up ~0.1%
of the stellar mass density of the Universe today but 10%-20% at z~2, depending
on their IMF. The formation of these cores required the conversion of ~10^11
Msun of gas into stars within ~1 kpc, while preventing significant star
formation at larger radii.

In this work, we investigate the generation of long-range distance-independent entanglement in spin chains through Kondo impurities. Spin chains are a promising platform for quantum information transfer; however, achieving robust entanglement over long distances remains challenging. We propose a novel approach by introducing Kondo impurities strategically placed in the chain, which facilitates the establishment of entanglement between distant spins. Employing a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we demonstrate that the Kondo effect induces a uniform coupling interaction, effectively binding distant spin sites. This interaction leads to emergent entangled states that are remarkably stable against variations in distance between impurities.  Our methodological framework involves mapping the problem onto an effective low-energy model, followed by perturbative renormalization group analysis to capture the impurity-induced correlations. We also employ exact diagonalization to validate the analytical predictions and assess the impact of disorder on the system's entanglement properties. Results reveal that the inclusion of Kondo impurities not only enhances the entanglement length scale but also renders it largely independent of chain length, opening pathways for scalable quantum networks. Additionally, we identify parameter regimes where the entanglement is maximized, offering insights into the practical realization of such systems in experimental settings.  As a solution to the prevailing issue of distance dependency in spin-based quantum systems, our approach provides a robust method for achieving long-range entanglement through localized impurities, highlighting a significant advancement in quantum information science. This study offers a foundational step towards the practical implementation of entanglement-enabled technologies in challenging quantum computing architectures.

We present our investigation into potential technosignatures from 14 planetary systems identified in the Kepler field, utilizing the Green Bank Telescope to observe frequencies ranging from 1.15 to 1.73 GHz. Our primary objective was to identify artificial electromagnetic signals that could indicate the presence of advanced extraterrestrial civilizations. We developed a comprehensive methodology that involved targeted observations of selected systems based on their known exoplanetary compositions and the likelihood of hosting intelligent life. Using advanced signal processing techniques, we filtered and analyzed the collected data to distinguish between terrestrial interference and potential signals of extraterrestrial origin.   We detected several candidate signals during our observations, but after thorough analysis, we attributed these to terrestrial sources and astronomical phenomena. Notably, we established stringent upper limits on the detectability of technosignatures within the specified frequency range, informing future observational strategies in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Our results reaffirm the importance of choosing optimal targets and frequencies in the ongoing quest for technosignatures, highlighting the necessity of robust methodologies for data interpretation. Furthermore, we emphasize the significance of cross-collaborative efforts in the field of astrobiology and radio astronomy to refine our understanding and expand our search parameters for signs of intelligent life beyond Earth. Ultimately, our work contributes to the broader initiative of advancing technosignature detection techniques while setting an important precedent for future observational campaigns targeting diverse planetary systems.

We consider an efficient computational framework for speeding up several
machine learning algorithms with almost no loss of accuracy. The proposed
framework relies on projections via structured matrices that we call Structured
Spinners, which are formed as products of three structured matrix-blocks that
incorporate rotations. The approach is highly generic, i.e. i) structured
matrices under consideration can either be fully-randomized or learned, ii) our
structured family contains as special cases all previously considered
structured schemes, iii) the setting extends to the non-linear case where the
projections are followed by non-linear functions, and iv) the method finds
numerous applications including kernel approximations via random feature maps,
dimensionality reduction algorithms, new fast cross-polytope LSH techniques,
deep learning, convex optimization algorithms via Newton sketches, quantization
with random projection trees, and more. The proposed framework comes with
theoretical guarantees characterizing the capacity of the structured model in
reference to its unstructured counterpart and is based on a general theoretical
principle that we describe in the paper. As a consequence of our theoretical
analysis, we provide the first theoretical guarantees for one of the most
efficient existing LSH algorithms based on the HD3HD2HD1 structured matrix
[Andoni et al., 2015]. The exhaustive experimental evaluation confirms the
accuracy and efficiency of structured spinners for a variety of different
applications.

This study explores non-stationary resource allocation policies tailored for delay-constrained video streaming in Internet-of-Things (IoT)-enabled networks. Focusing on the dynamic nature of IoT environments where device connectivity and traffic patterns fluctuate significantly, the objective is to enhance video quality and reduce latency while optimizing resource utilization. Aiming to address the challenges posed by unpredictable network conditions, the research proposes adaptive resource allocation strategies that adjust according to real-time network demands and video traffic characteristics. Methodologically, a simulation framework was developed using a combination of queuing theory and machine learning techniques to evaluate the performance of these policies. Key findings indicate that non-stationary resource allocation significantly improves video delivery quality under varying network conditions compared to static allocation methods. The study concludes with recommendations for practical implementation, emphasizing the importance of continuous monitoring and adaptation to ensure efficient and reliable video streaming in IoT environments.

This research paper explores the application of prime and natural numbers in data hiding techniques, with a focus on developing a novel method for secure data transmission. The increasing demand for secure data transmission in various fields, such as finance and healthcare, has led to the development of numerous data hiding techniques. However, these techniques often rely on complex algorithms and cryptographic methods, which can be computationally expensive and vulnerable to attacks.  The objective of this research is to propose a novel data hiding technique using prime and natural numbers, which can provide a high level of security and efficiency. The proposed technique utilizes the properties of prime numbers, such as their uniqueness and distribution, to create a hidden message. Natural numbers are used to generate a key that is used to encrypt and decrypt the message.  The methodology employed in this research involves the use of prime number theory and number theory techniques to develop a novel data hiding algorithm. The algorithm uses a combination of prime number generation and natural number manipulation to create a hidden message. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated using various metrics, including security, efficiency, and robustness.  The key findings of this research indicate that the proposed data hiding technique using prime and natural numbers provides a high level of security and efficiency. The algorithm is able to hide messages with a high level of accuracy and is resistant to attacks. The results also show that the proposed technique is more efficient than existing data hiding techniques, making it suitable for real-world applications.  The conclusion of this research highlights the potential of prime and natural numbers in data hiding techniques. The proposed algorithm provides a novel and efficient method for secure data transmission, and its potential applications in various fields are significant. Further research is needed to explore the limitations and potential improvements of the proposed technique.

During the "WISE at 5: Legacy and Prospects" conference in Pasadena, CA --
which ran from February 10 - 12, 2015 -- attendees were invited to engage in an
interactive session exploring the future uses of the Wide-field Infrared Survey
Explorer (WISE) data. The 65 participants -- many of whom are extensive users
of the data -- brainstormed the top questions still to be answered by the
mission, as well as the complementary current and future datasets and
additional processing of WISE/NEOWISE data that would aid in addressing these
most important scientific questions. The results were mainly bifurcated between
topics related to extragalactic studies (e.g. AGN, QSOs) and substellar mass
objects. In summary, participants found that complementing WISE/NEOWISE data
with cross-correlated multiwavelength surveys (e.g. SDSS, Pan-STARRS, LSST,
Gaia, Euclid, etc.) would be highly beneficial for all future mission goals.
Moreover, developing or implementing machine-learning tools to comb through and
understand cross-correlated data was often mentioned for future uses. Finally,
attendees agreed that additional processing of the data such as co-adding WISE
and NEOWISE and extracting a multi-epoch photometric database and parallax and
proper motion catalog would greatly improve the scientific results of the most
important projects identified. In that respect, a project such as MaxWISE which
would execute the most important additional processing and extraction as well
as make the data and catalogs easily accessible via a public portal was deemed
extremely important.

The Voyager 1 and 2 Ultraviolet Spectrometer (UVS) solar and stellar
occultation dataset represents one of the primary, pre-Cassini sources of
information that we have on the neutral upper atmosphere of Saturn. Despite its
importance, however, the full set of occultations has never received a
consistent, nor complete, analysis, and the results derived from the initial
analyses over thirty years ago left questions about the temperature and density
profiles unanswered. We have reanalyzed all six of the UVS occultations (three
solar and three stellar) to provide an up-to-date, pre-Cassini view of Saturn's
upper atmosphere. From the Voyager UVS data, we have determined vertical
profiles for H2, H, CH4, C2H2 , C2H4, and C2H6, as well as temperature. Our
analysis also provides explanations for the two different thermospheric
temperatures derived in earlier analyses (400-450 K versus 800 K) and for the
unusual shape of the total density profile noted by Hubbard et al. (1997).
Aside from inverting the occultation data to retrieve densities and
temperatures, we have investigated the atmospheric structure through a series
of photochemical models to infer the strength of atmospheric mixing and other
physical and chemical properties of Saturn's mesopause region during the
Voyager flybys. We find that the data exhibit considerable variability in the
vertical profiles for methane, suggesting variations in vertical winds or the
eddy diffusion coefficient as a function of latitude and/or time in Saturn's
upper atmosphere. The results of our reanalysis will provide a useful baseline
for interpreting new data from Cassini, particularly in the context of change
over the past three decades.

X-rays from very young stars are powerful probes to investigate the
mechanisms at work in the very first stages of the star formation and the
origin of X-ray emission in very young stars. We present results from a 500 ks
long observation of the Rho Ophiuchi cloud with a XMM-Newton large program
named DROXO, aiming at studying the X-ray emission of deeply embedded Young
Stellar Objects (YSOs). The data acquired during the DROXO program were reduced
with SAS software, and filtered in time and energy to improve the signal to
noise of detected sources; light curves and spectra were obtained. We detected
111 sources, 61 of them associated with rho Ophiuchi YSOs as identified from
infrared observations with ISOCAM. Specifically, we detected 9 out of 11 Class
I, 31 out of 48 Class II and 15 out 16 Class III objects. Six objects out of 21
classified Class III candidates are also detected. At the same time we suggest
that 15 Class III candidates that remain undetected at log Lx < 28.3 are not
related to the cloud population. The global detection rate is ~64%. We have
achieved a flux sensitivity of ~5 x 10^{-15} erg s^{-1} cm^{-2}. The Lx to
L_bol ratio shows saturation at a value of ~ -3.5 for stars with T_eff <= 5000
K or 0.7 M_sun as observed in the Orion Nebula. The plasma temperatures and the
spectrum absorption show a decline with YSO class, with Class I YSOs being
hotter and more absorbed than Class II and III YSOs. In one star (GY 266) with
infrared counterpart in 2MASS and Spitzer catalogs we have detected a soft
excess in the X-ray spectrum which is best fitted by a cold thermal component
less absorbed than the main thermal component of the plasma. Such a soft
component hints to the presence of plasma heated by shocks due to jets outside
the dense circumstellar material.

Protoplanetary disks play a crucial role in planet formation, with the growth of dust particles being a significant aspect of this process. This study aims to develop a sub-grid model for dust particle growth that can be integrated into hydrodynamical simulations of protoplanetary disks. We employ a combination of analytical approaches and numerical methods to refine the existing models of dust dynamics, addressing limitations related to resolution and computational efficiency. The methodology involves incorporating a detailed treatment of particle collision and fragmentation processes into the hydrodynamical framework, allowing for more accurate representation of dust growth across various sizes and environments within the disk. Key findings indicate that the inclusion of our sub-grid model leads to enhanced dust growth rates, particularly in regions of high density and turbulence. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that our model effectively captures the transition from a regime dominated by random collisions to one governed by gravitational interactions, significantly influencing the size distribution of dust particles over time. The results imply that incorporating such a sub-grid approach in simulations can markedly improve understanding of planetesimal formation processes and the evolution of protoplanetary disks. In conclusion, this research provides a robust framework for future studies, highlighting the importance of accurately modeling dust dynamics to elucidate the complexities of planet formation in protoplanetary environments.

In this work, we investigate the implications of loop quadratic contributions on the mechanism of Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) in the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics. Our approach is based on a one-loop effective potential formalism, which allows us to systematically study the effects of heavy particle masses on the EWSB dynamics.  The results of our calculations reveal that the loop quadratic contributions significantly modify the shape of the effective potential in the vicinity of the EWSB vacuum solution. This effect is crucial for understanding the renormalizability of the SM Higgs boson mass, which is a long-standing challenge in the context of naturalness. Specifically, we find that the Higgs boson mass receives significant corrections from the top quark loop, leading to a more modest fine-tuning requirement compared to the tree-level result.  Our analysis also sheds light on the issue of the vacuum stability in the SM, which has been a matter of debate for several decades. We show that the presence of the loop quadratic terms can help in stabilizing the EWSB vacuum, making it a more robust solution for the physical vacuum of the universe.  Moreover, we extend our calculations to include the electroweak corrections to the loop quadratic contributions, which can further refine the precision of our results. Our methodology and findings represent an important step towards a better understanding of the EWSB mechanism and its implications for the SM of particle physics.  In conclusion, we have presented a detailed study of the impact of loop quadratic contributions on the Electroweak Symmetry Breaking mechanism in the Standard Model of particle physics. Our results provide new insights into the renormalizability of the SM Higgs boson mass, the vacuum stability of the EWSB vacuum, and the overall consistency of the SM framework. The methodology employed in our analysis can be applied to other beyond the Standard Model scenarios to investigate the effects of loop quadratic terms on various symmetry breaking mechanisms.

We investigate the production of bottomonium states associated with a photon in high-energy \(e^+e^-\) collisions, focusing on conditions achievable at next-generation high luminosity colliders. Our primary objective is to understand the dynamics and cross-section of this process, which has implications for testing quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and exploring the properties of heavy quarkonium states. We apply next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD corrections to our calculations, thereby enhancing the theoretical predictions of bottomonium production rates.   Utilizing rigorous perturbative techniques, we systematically include both virtual and real photon emissions in our analysis. We parameterize the cross-section in terms of the polarization of the bottomonium state and employ advanced numerical methods to integrate the results over the relevant phase space. Our findings indicate a significant enhancement in the cross-section when NLO corrections are incorporated, which underscores the importance of these higher-order terms in accurately describing the physical process.   Additionally, we examine the sensitivity of the production rates to various experimental parameters, such as collider energy and luminosity. The results suggest that the detection of bottomonium plus a photon can provide critical information about the binding dynamics of heavy quarkonium and offer a sensitive probe of the strong interaction at short distances. Overall, our work establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework for exploring bottomonium production at future high-luminosity \(e^+e^-\) colliders and sets the stage for potential experimental investigations.

This research investigates the competition between supersolid phases and magnetization plateaux in a frustrated easy-axis antiferromagnet arranged on a triangular lattice. Utilizing theoretical models and computational simulations, the study aims to elucidate the complex interplay between magnetic order and superfluid behavior in such systems. Key objectives include identifying distinct phases where supersolidity emerges and characterizing the magnetization states that coexist with these phases. The methodologies employed involve Monte Carlo simulations and density functional theory calculations to explore the phase diagram and determine the stability of various configurations. Notably, the analysis reveals multiple magnetization plateaux alongside the appearance of supersolid phases, indicating intricate interactions between magnetic ordering and superfluidity. The findings contribute to our understanding of quantum critical phenomena in frustrated magnets and offer insights into the emergence of unconventional phases in strongly correlated electron systems.

Plankton-like particles play a crucial role in biogeochemical cycles by sinking through the ocean's water column. This study aims to compare observations of sinking plankton-like particles with a numerical model to understand the changes in their sinking behavior. The methodology involves collecting observational data on sinking rates of plankton-like particles in various oceanic regions and comparing this with simulations from a numerical model that accounts for different environmental conditions. Key findings reveal discrepancies between observed sinking rates and model predictions, highlighting the need for further refinement of the numerical model to better represent the complexities of particle sinking dynamics. The study concludes that while the numerical model provides valuable insights, incorporating additional factors such as biological activity and particle composition is essential for accurately capturing variations in plankton-like particle sinking behavior. Understanding these changes is crucial for enhancing our knowledge of carbon fluxes in the ocean and their implications for marine ecosystems.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic events in the universe, and understanding their emission mechanisms is crucial for astrophysical research. This paper investigates the constraints on the synchrotron emission mechanism that is often proposed to explain the observed characteristics of GRB afterglows. The primary objective is to analyze the underlying physical conditions and the relevant parameters that influence the synchrotron process within the context of GRBs. We employ a combination of theoretical modeling and observational data analysis, focusing on the spectral energy distribution and light curves of a sample of well-studied GRBs. By examining the relationship between the synchrotron radiation and the environment surrounding the explosion, we identify key constraints such as magnetic field strength, electron energy distribution, and the effective angle of emission. Our findings reveal that while synchrotron emission can adequately describe certain GRB features, limitations arise under extreme conditions, such as in the presence of dense circumburst media or varying magnetic turbulence. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these constraints for the broader understanding of GRB physics, including the potential role of alternative emission mechanisms. In conclusion, our analysis highlights that while synchrotron radiation remains a significant contributor to GRB emission, a comprehensive model must incorporate additional effects to fully account for the diverse observational phenomena associated with these extraordinary cosmic events.

We investigate the mid-infrared (mid-IR) variability of Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) in the star-forming region Lynds 1688, utilizing data from the YSOVAR project. Our study aims to understand the variability characteristics of YSOs and ascertain the physical mechanisms driving these changes. By analyzing time-series photometry obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we have identified and classified mid-IR variability patterns in a sample of YSOs within this region. Our methodology involved the application of robust statistical techniques to determine periodicity and amplitude of variability, alongside spectral energy distribution fitting to refine YSO classification. We observe a significant variability in a majority of the studied YSOs, with flux changes ranging from 0.1 to 1.2 magnitudes. A notable outcome is the identification of both stochastic and periodic sources, with periods spanning from days to weeks. Additionally, we correlate mid-IR variability with accretion and disk processes, utilizing complementary data from near-IR and optical surveys. Our results suggest that mid-IR variability is primarily driven by a combination of accretion dynamics and disk instabilities, potentially influenced by stellar magnetic fields. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the circumstellar environments of YSOs and provide crucial insights into the early stages of stellar evolution. This study underscores the significance of continuous monitoring and multi-wavelength observations in revealing the complex nature of young stellar systems. Future work will expand this analysis to additional star-forming regions, enhancing our knowledge of YSO variability across different environments.

This paper delves into the nonequilibrium thermodynamics governing the Kovacs effect, a phenomenon observed in the mechanical response of polymers when subjected to non-monotonic loading processes. The objective of this research is to investigate the underlying principles of the Kovacs effect through a theoretical framework based on nonequilibrium thermodynamics. To achieve this, a combination of experimental studies and mathematical modeling is employed to analyze the behavior of polymers under various loading conditions. Key findings reveal that the Kovacs effect is intricately linked to the nonequilibrium nature of polymer systems, with the memory and rejuvenation effects being manifestations of the system's dynamic response to external stimuli. Through this study, a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between nonequilibrium thermodynamics and the mechanical behavior of polymers during the Kovacs effect is obtained. In conclusion, this research contributes to elucidating the fundamental principles governing the nonequilibrium thermodynamics of the Kovacs effect, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of polymer materials under non-monotonic loading conditions.

In this research, we present our findings on the application of the Edgeworth streaming model for analyzing redshift space distortions in galaxy surveys. Redshift space distortions occur due to the peculiar velocities of galaxies, causing an apparent elongation of structures along the line of sight. The Edgeworth streaming model offers a novel approach to quantifying these distortions by expanding the probability distribution function of galaxy pairwise velocities beyond the Gaussian assumption, thus capturing higher-order statistical moments.  Our work aims to address the limitations of the standard linear theory in accurately modeling the observed clustering patterns in redshift space. By incorporating the Edgeworth streaming model, we seek to improve the precision of cosmological parameter estimation and enhance our understanding of the dynamics of large-scale structure formation. Our key contribution lies in demonstrating the efficacy of this model in enhancing the accuracy of galaxy power spectrum measurements, particularly at small scales where non-linear effects dominate.  To achieve this, we utilize mock galaxy catalogs and employ sophisticated statistical techniques to fit the Edgeworth streaming model to the observed redshift distortions. Our methodology involves analyzing the performance of the model against existing data sets from cosmological simulations and galaxy surveys. The results showcase the ability of the Edgeworth streaming model to provide refined insights into the underlying physics of redshift space distortions, thus paving the way for more robust cosmological constraints in future observational analyses.

Density-functional theory calculations are performed to investigate hydrogen
transport in the proton conductor BaSnO$_3$. Structural optimizations in the
stable and saddle point configurations for transfer and reorientation allow
description of the high-temperature classical and semi-classical regimes, in
which diffusion occurs by over-barrier motion. At lower temperature (typically
below 300 K), we describe a thermally-assisted quantum regime. In this regime,
transfer and reorientation occur when the surrounding matrix adopts particular
"coincidence" configurations in which quantum tunneling is favored. Both the
non-adiabatic and the adiabatic cases are examined. In the adiabatic case, the
energy landscape of hydrogen in the coincidence configuration is very flat,
with very low coincidence energy barriers. Path-integral molecular dynamics
simulations of the H atom in the coincidence potential reveal, in the transfer
case, highly quantum behavior up to T=300 K (the density of probability of H in
the coincidence configuration, has its maximum at the saddle point, due to the
fact that the zero-point energy exceeds the coincidence energy barrier).
Arguments are given that support the adiabatic picture for the transfer
mechanism. This suggests existence of this state of hydrogen during the very
short lifetime of the coincidence configurations ($\sim$ 10$^{-13}$ s), as a
transition state for the transfer mechanism. Remarkably, such state is
identical to that of ice X, a highly quantum phase of ice observed at high
pressures $\approx$ 100 GPa. In the case of reorientation, typical times for
existence of the coincidence configuration and for protonic motion are roughly
equal, suggesting that the adiabatic picture is not valid. Protonic transfer
and reorientation in oxides are therefore governed by radically different
mechanisms below room temperature.

In this study, we address the challenge of inference in incomplete graphical models by proposing an innovative approach based on latent tree aggregation. Graphical models are powerful tools for capturing complex dependencies among variables in high-dimensional data; however, incomplete data poses significant hurdles in making reliable inferences. Our work specifically targets scenarios where data is missing not at random, which further complicates conventional methods. We introduce a novel framework that constructs latent trees to capture the underlying structure of the graphical model, thereby accommodating incomplete information and providing reliable inference.  Using a combination of maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference techniques, we aggregate local tree structures to form cohesive latent representations. These latent trees serve as an intermediary inferential tool, mitigating the effects of data sparsity and enhancing the interpretability of the graphical model. Our methodology exhibits robustness in approximating the global structure, as demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.  The results confirm that our latent tree aggregation approach significantly improves inference accuracy compared to traditional methods such as expectation-maximization (EM) and variational inference, particularly under conditions of extreme data incompleteness. The proposed methodology not only achieves higher precision in estimating model parameters but also offers computational efficiency, making it suitable for large-scale applications.  Our findings suggest that aggregating latent tree structures provides a viable and effective strategy for incomplete graphical model inference, paving the way for further advancements in modeling complex datasets with missing information. Future work will explore the application of this framework to dynamic and adaptive graphical models.

We present a study on the numerical simulations of supernova remnant (SNR) evolution within a cloudy interstellar medium (ISM) environment. The aim of this work is to investigate the impact of the presence of clouds on the evolution of SNRs and their interaction with the surrounding ISM. Our results show that the presence of clouds significantly affects the dynamics and morphology of SNRs, leading to complex shock interactions and fragmentation of the remnant. By varying the cloud properties such as density, size, and distribution, we have observed a range of behaviors in SNR evolution, including cloud destruction, ablation, and cloud-SNR merger scenarios. Our simulations also reveal the importance of radiative cooling and thermal conduction in shaping the evolution of SNRs in a cloudy ISM. The key findings of this study provide insights into the role of clouds in the evolution of SNRs and have implications for understanding the observed diversity in SNR environments in the galaxy. The methodology employed in this research involves solving the hydrodynamics equations coupled with radiative cooling and thermal conduction in a 3D numerical simulation framework. Overall, our study contributes to the advancement of our understanding of SNR evolution in complex ISM environments.

This research investigates the explicit expansion of powers of the Euler Product in relation to partition hook lengths, a significant area of interest in the intersection of number theory and combinatorics. The objective is to derive a comprehensive formula that expresses these powers as explicit sums over partitions, incorporating the combinatorial elements of hook lengths. Building upon existing frameworks of partition theory and Euler products, we employ advanced techniques in generating functions and asymptotic analysis. By systematically analyzing the contributions of hooks at various lengths, we develop a formula that elucidates the relationship between the multiplicative structures of Euler products and additive partition functions. The key findings reveal that the expansion captures intricate dependencies on partition structures, offering new insights into the multiplicative nature of number theoretic functions and partitions. Specifically, it identifies precise coefficients that accentuate the contributions of structures governed by hook lengths, thereby advancing understanding of their combinatorial significance. These results provide a robust foundation for further exploration into the modular forms and symmetric function theory, potentially unlocking new avenues for research in partitions and their applications. In conclusion, this study not only presents a novel expansion formula with practical applications in mathematical analysis but also enhances the theoretical framework for exploring connections between seemingly disparate mathematical areas, fostering deeper interdisciplinary comprehension and potential future breakthroughs in both theoretical and applied mathematics.

RCW 38 is a deeply embedded young (~1 Myr), massive star cluster located at a
distance of 1.7 kpc. Twice as dense as the Orion Nebula Cluster, orders of
magnitude denser than other nearby star forming regions, and rich in massive
stars, RCW 38 is an ideal place to look for potential differences in brown
dwarf formation efficiency as a function of environment. We present deep, high
resolution adaptive optics data of the central ~0.5x0.5 pc^2 obtained with NACO
at the Very Large Telescope. Through comparison with evolutionary models we
determine masses and extinction for ~480 candidate members, and derive the
first Initial Mass Function (IMF) of the cluster extending into the substellar
regime. Representing the IMF as a set of power laws in the form
dN/dM~M^(-alpha), we derive the slope alpha = 1.60+-0.13 for the mass range 0.5
- 20 MSun which is shallower than the Salpeter slope, but in agreement with
results in several other young massive clusters. At the low-mass side, we find
alpha = 0.71+-0.11 for masses between 0.02 and 0.5 MSun, or alpha = 0.81+-0.08
for masses between 0.02 and 1 MSun. Our result is in agreement with the values
found in other young star-forming regions, revealing no evidence that a
combination of high stellar densities and the presence of numerous massive
stars affect the formation efficiency of brown dwarfs and very-low mass stars.
We estimate that the Milky Way galaxy contains between 25 and 100 billion brown
dwarfs (with masses > 0.03 MSun).

We present the THESEUS space mission concept, a next-generation survey telescope designed to study the formation and evolution of galaxies. Our science case is centered on the investigation of galaxy evolution, dark matter, and dark energy through the observation of galaxy clusters and large-scale structure. We have developed a novel design that incorporates a 2.5-meter primary mirror, a high-efficiency camera system, and a sophisticated data processing pipeline.  Through a series of detailed simulations and modeling, we have assessed the performance of the THESEUS mission, demonstrating its ability to achieve high precision and accuracy in the measurement of galaxy properties. Our results indicate that THESEUS will be capable of detecting subtle variations in galaxy distributions, providing valuable insights into the role of dark matter and dark energy in shaping the large-scale structure of the universe.  We have also explored the feasibility of incorporating advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, into the data processing pipeline to enhance the mission's scientific return. Our analysis suggests that THESEUS will be well-suited to take advantage of these emerging technologies, enabling the discovery of new astrophysical phenomena and the refinement of our understanding of the universe.

Three dimensional (3D) magnetic field information on molecular clouds and
cores is important for revealing their kinematical stability (magnetic support)
against gravity which is fundamental for studying the initial conditions of
star formation. In the present study, the 3D magnetic field structure of the
dense starless core FeSt 1-457 is determined based on the near-infrared
polarimetric observations of the dichroic polarization of background stars and
simple 3D modeling. With an obtained angle of line-of-sight magnetic
inclination axis $\theta_{\rm inc}$ of $45^{\circ}\pm10^{\circ}$ and previously
determined plane-of-sky magnetic field strength $B_{\rm pol}$ of $23.8\pm12.1$
$\mu{\rm G}$, the total magnetic field strength for FeSt 1-457 is derived to be
$33.7\pm18.0$ $\mu{\rm G}$. The critical mass of FeSt 1-457, evaluated using
both magnetic and thermal/turbulent support is ${M}_{\rm cr} = 3.70\pm0.92$
${\rm M}_{\odot}$, which is identical to the observed core mass, $M_{\rm
core}=3.55\pm0.75$ ${\rm M}_{\odot}$. We thus conclude that the stability of
FeSt 1-457 is in a condition close to the critical state. Without infalling gas
motion and no associated young stars, the core is regarded to be in the
earliest stage of star formation, i.e., the stage just before the onset of
dynamical collapse following the attainment of a supercritical condition. These
properties would make FeSt 1-457 one of the best starless cores for future
studies of the initial conditions of star formation.

This research paper investigates the population of low mass stars and brown dwarfs in the Praesepe star cluster, aiming to enhance our understanding of stellar formation and evolution processes. Utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based telescopes, the study examines the mass distribution, luminosity, and temperatures of these celestial objects within Praesepe.   Our methodology involves analyzing photometric and spectroscopic data to classify stars and brown dwarfs based on their physical properties. By comparing observational data with theoretical models, we aim to identify any discrepancies and improve existing stellar evolutionary models.  Key findings reveal a high abundance of low mass stars and a significant population of brown dwarfs within Praesepe. The mass distribution shows a peak at around 0.3 solar masses with a steep decline towards lower masses, indicating ongoing star formation processes in the cluster. Moreover, the derived temperatures and luminosities provide insights into the age and composition of these objects.  In conclusion, this study contributes to the growing body of research on low mass stars and brown dwarfs, shedding light on the formation and evolution of stellar populations in the Praesepe cluster. The findings underscore the importance of continued observational studies in understanding the complexities of star formation and the diversity of objects in stellar clusters.

Flavor physics has long been an intriguing subject in particle physics, with the Standard Model (SM) failing to explain various experimental observations. In this context, we investigate the effects of a light Z' boson emerging from a Simple Extended Grand Unified Theory (SO(10) GUT) on flavor physics. We consider a particular extension of the SM, namely the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), and study the impact of the Z' boson on quark and lepton mixing matrices and CP violation.  Our calculations are based on the minimal SO(10) model, assuming the Z' to be a gauge boson with a mass below the electroweak scale. The Z' exchange contributions to quark mixing are studied using the standard approach, while lepton mixing is investigated via the Type-I and Type-II see-saw mechanisms. We also consider the implications of the Z' boson for electric dipole moments (EDMs) and lepton flavor violation (LFV).  Our results show that the presence of the Z' boson significantly influences quark and lepton mixing, leading to noticeable modifications in the values of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix elements and the Pontecorvo-Maki-Nakagawa-Sakata (PMNS) matrix elements. These modifications can be tested in ongoing and future flavor physics experiments. Additionally, our study indicates that the Z' boson may contribute to the observed EDMs and LFV phenomena, suggesting that future searches for these effects could provide strong constraints on the mass and couplings of the Z' boson.  In conclusion, our work presents a comprehensive analysis of the impact of a light Z' boson from SO(10) GUT on flavor physics. We demonstrate that the Z' boson can provide explanations for various flavor anomalies and provide testable predictions for ongoing and future experiments.

The proliferation of online social networks has given rise to the emergence of deviant communities, where individuals with non-conformist values and behaviors congregate and interact. These communities often exist outside the mainstream social structures, fostering a sense of belonging and identity among their members. Despite their growing presence, the behavior of deviant communities in online social networks remains poorly understood. This study aims to explore the dynamics of deviant communities in online social networks, with a focus on their formation, maintenance, and impact on individual and societal levels.  Using a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data, this study conducted in-depth interviews with members of online deviant communities and analyzed online forum posts, social media profiles, and other digital data. The findings reveal that deviant communities in online social networks are characterized by a sense of exclusivity, with members often engaging in shared activities and rituals that reinforce their sense of belonging. The study also highlights the role of online platforms in facilitating the formation and maintenance of deviant communities, as well as the impact of these communities on individual mental health and well-being.  The study's findings have significant implications for our understanding of deviant behavior in online social networks, and highlight the need for further research into the complex dynamics of these communities. The study's results also underscore the importance of considering the online context in which deviant communities form and operate, and the need for policymakers and practitioners to develop strategies for mitigating the potential negative consequences of these communities.

We have observed NGC5194 (M51a) as part of the CHemical Abundances of Spirals
(CHAOS) project. Using the Multi Object Double Spectrographs (MODS) on the
Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) we are able to measure one or more of the
temperature-sensitive auroral lines ([O III] 4363, [N II] 5755, [S III] 6312)
and thus measure "direct" gas-phase abundances in 29 individual HII regions. [O
III] 4363 is only detected in two HII regions both of which show indications of
excitation by shocks. We compare our data to previous direct abundances
measured in NGC5194 and find excellent agreement for all but one region
(Delta[log(O/H)] ~ 0.04). We find no evidence of trends in Ar/O, Ne/O, or S/O
within NGC5194 or compared to other galaxies. We find modest negative gradients
in both O/H and N/O with very little scatter (sigma < 0.08 dex), most of which
can be attributed to random error and not to intrinsic dispersion. The
gas-phase abundance gradient is consistent with the gradients observed in other
interacting galaxies, which tend to be shallower than gradients measured in
isolated galaxies. The N/O ratio (<log(N/O)> = -0.62) suggests secondary
nitrogen production is responsible for a significantly larger fraction of
nitrogen (e.g., factor of 8-10) relative to primary production mechanisms than
predicted by theoretical models.

Nuclear spin imaging at the atomic level is essential for the understanding
of fundamental biological phenomena and for applications such as drug
discovery. The advent of novel nano-scale sensors has given hope of achieving
the long-standing goal of single-protein, high spatial-resolution structure
determination in their natural environment and ambient conditions. In
particular, quantum sensors based on the spin-dependent photoluminescence of
Nitrogen Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have recently been used to detect
nanoscale ensembles of external nuclear spins. While NV sensitivity is
approaching single-spin levels, extracting relevant information from a very
complex structure is a further challenge, since it requires not only the
ability to sense the magnetic field of an isolated nuclear spin, but also to
achieve atomic-scale spatial resolution. Here we propose a method that, by
exploiting the coupling of the NV center to an intrinsic quantum memory
associated with the Nitrogen nuclear spin, can reach a tenfold improvement in
spatial resolution, down to atomic scales. The spatial resolution enhancement
is achieved through coherent control of the sensor spin, which creates a
dynamic frequency filter selecting only a few nuclear spins at a time. We
propose and analyze a protocol that would allow not only sensing individual
spins in a complex biomolecule, but also unraveling couplings among them, thus
elucidating local characteristics of the molecule structure.

In this study, we address the challenge of forming geometric shapes, specifically planes, using synchronous mobile robots without relying on chirality. Our approach involves a distributed algorithm that enables each robot to make decisions based on local information and simple rules. The robots are programmed to move in unison, adjusting their velocities and directions to ensure they collectively construct a plane. We simulate various scenarios to test the robustness and efficiency of our method. The results demonstrate that our synchronous control strategy allows robots to accurately form a plane, overcoming challenges such as initial orientation discrepancies and varying speeds among the robots. Key methodologies include the use of communication protocols, velocity adjustments, and synchronization techniques. Through rigorous testing, we have validated that our approach is effective and scalable, offering a novel solution to the problem of plane formation in a decentralized manner.

This study investigates the properties of heavy tetraquarks in lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at a pion mass approaching physical values. Heavy tetraquarks are exotic four-quark states that are predicted by certain models of strong interaction and are of great interest for testing the validity of these models. However, the calculation of their properties is a challenging task due to the presence of strong interactions and the confinement of quarks.  The objective of this research is to provide a detailed understanding of the mass spectrum, decay constants, and other properties of heavy tetraquarks in lattice QCD at a pion mass of approximately 140 MeV, which is close to the physical value. To achieve this, we employ a combination of lattice gauge theory simulations and analytical techniques to extract the properties of heavy tetraquarks.  Our results show that the mass spectrum of heavy tetraquarks is consistent with the expectations of certain models, with some tetraquarks exhibiting a clear pattern of mass splitting. We also observe a significant dependence of the decay constants on the mass of the tetraquark. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a non-trivial correlation between the mass of the tetraquark and the pion mass. These findings provide valuable insights into the properties of heavy tetraquarks and shed light on the underlying strong interactions.  The implications of our results are significant for our understanding of the strong interaction and the properties of heavy exotic states.
