The results of our study provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics of self-gravitating systems, and highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between gravitational interactions and potential energy. By exploring the interplay between these two fundamental forces, we aim to shed light on the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of complex systems, and to develop more accurate models for predicting the evolution of self-gravitating systems in various astrophysical contexts.

Magnetism, a fundamental force in nature, has been studied extensively since its discovery. Traditional theories, such as Lenz's Law and Faraday's Law, provide a solid framework for understanding magnetic phenomena at macroscopic scales. However, recent advances in quantum physics, specifically Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), challenge these theories and offer new insights into the behavior of magnetic energy levels.  The objective of this study is to identify and accept the energy levels in macroscopic magnetism that are compatible with both traditional theories and QED. A comprehensive literature review was conducted to identify relevant studies and theories. The methodology involved a comparative analysis of traditional magnetic theories with QED, focusing on the magnetic energy levels and their implications.  Our key findings reveal that at macroscopic scales, magnetic energy levels are not quantized as suggested by QED. However, the limited validity of Faraday's Law in certain magnetic fields is revealed, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive understanding of magnetic phenomena. Furthermore, the existence of metastable states in magnetic systems is proposed as an explanation for the apparent discrepancies between traditional theories and QED.  In conclusion, this study provides a new perspective on the relationship between traditional theories and QED in understanding magnetism. By identifying the energy levels in macroscopic magnetism that are compatible with both frameworks, we can gain a better understanding of the limitations and validity of these theories. These findings offer a foundation for further research into the complex nature of magnetic phenomena.

(Abridged) This paper explores the use of k-means clustering as a tool for
automated unsupervised classification of massive stellar spectral catalogs. The
classification criteria are defined by the data and the algorithm, with no
prior physical framework. We work with a representative set of stellar spectra
associated with the SDSS SEGUE and SEGUE-2 programs. We classify the original
spectra as well as the spectra with the continuum removed. The second set only
contains spectral lines, and it is less dependent on uncertainties of the flux
calibration. The classification of the spectra with continuum renders 16 major
classes. Roughly speaking, stars are split according to their colors, with
enough finesse to distinguish dwarfs from giants of the same effective
temperature, but with difficulties to separate stars with different
metallicities. Overall, there is no one-to-one correspondence between the
classes we derive and the MK types. The classification of spectra without
continuum renders 13 classes, the color separation is not so sharp, but it
distinguishes stars of the same effective temperature and different
metallicities. Some classes thus obtained present a fairly small range of
physical parameters (200 K in effective temperature, 0.25 dex in surface
gravity, and 0.35 dex in metallicity), so that the classification can be used
to estimate the main physical parameters of some stars at a minimum
computational cost. We also analyze the outliers of the classification. Most of
them turn out to be failures of the reduction pipeline, but there are also high
redshift QSOs, multiple stellar systems, dust-reddened stars, galaxies, and,
finally, odd spectra whose nature we have not decipher. The template spectra
representative of the classes are publicly available
(ftp://stars:kmeans@ftp.iac.es).

The abstract focuses on enhancing data quality within Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) to improve overall system efficiency and reliability. ITS encompasses technologies that utilize information and communication technologies to optimize transportation operations, enhance safety, and reduce environmental impact. Despite the significant potential of ITS, data quality remains a critical challenge due to inconsistencies, inaccuracies, and missing values. This study aims to address these issues by proposing a comprehensive framework that integrates advanced data preprocessing techniques, real-time data validation algorithms, and machine learning models for anomaly detection. Methodologically, the approach utilizes open-source data from various ITS components, including traffic cameras, GPS sensors, and weather stations, to simulate realistic scenarios. Key findings indicate that the proposed framework significantly improves data accuracy and completeness, thereby enhancing predictive analytics and decision-making processes in ITS. The conclusion underscores the importance of robust data management strategies in achieving the full potential of ITS, emphasizing the need for continuous improvement and innovation in data quality assurance.

Dynamic Flows were introduced by Ford and Fulkerson in 1958 to model flows
over time. They define edge capacities to be the total amount of flow that can
enter an edge {\em in one time unit}. Each edge also has a length, representing
the time needed to traverse it. Dynamic Flows have been used to model many
problems including traffic congestion, hop-routing of packets and evacuation
protocols in buildings. While the basic problem of moving the maximal amount of
supplies from sources to sinks is polynomial time solvable, natural minor
modifications can make it NP-hard.
  One such modification is that flows be confluent, i.e., all flows leaving a
vertex must leave along the same edge. This corresponds to natural conditions
in, e.g., evacuation planning and hop routing.
  We investigate the single-sink Confluent Quickest Flow problem. The input is
a graph with edge capacities and lengths, sources with supplies and a sink. The
problem is to find a confluent flow minimizing the time required to send
supplies to the sink. Our main results include: a) Logarithmic
Non-Approximability: Directed Confluent Quickest Flows cannot be approximated
in polynomial time with an $O(\log n)$ approximation factor, unless $P=NP$.
  b) Polylogarithmic Bicriteria Approximations: Polynomial time $(O(\log^8 n),
O(\log^2 \kappa))$ bicritera approximation algorithms for the Confluent
Quickest Flow problem where $\kappa$ is the number of sinks, in both directed
and undirected graphs.
  Corresponding results are also developed for the Confluent Maximum Flow over
timeproblem. The techniques developed also improve recent approximation
algorithms for static confluent flows.

The advancement of precision astronomy has prompted the need for improved imaging technologies, particularly in the use of fully depleted charge-coupled devices (CCDs). Despite their superiority in sensitivity and dynamic range, imperfections in these CCDs can introduce significant challenges for astronomical observations. This study aims to provide a foundational understanding of the implications of these imperfections on astronomy and proposes a lexicon to standardize terminology across the field. The methodology employed includes a comprehensive review of existing literature on fully depleted CCDs, combined with an analysis of observational data from various astronomical surveys. Key findings reveal that imperfections such as surface defects, readout noise, and charge transfer inefficiencies can adversely affect image quality and measurement accuracy. Moreover, the established lexicon enhances communication among researchers, facilitating better collaboration and data sharing. In conclusion, while fully depleted CCDs remain a crucial tool for precision astronomy, understanding and addressing their imperfections is essential for maximizing their effectiveness. The suggested lexicon not only clarifies terminology but also encourages a unified approach to solving the challenges posed by these imaging devices, ultimately contributing to the advancement of astronomical precision and the reliability of scientific results. Future work should focus on developing corrective techniques and exploring alternative technologies to mitigate these imperfections, ensuring that the full potential of fully depleted CCDs is realized in astrophysical research.

This research presents an enhanced version of the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm, specifically focusing on incorporating random walk mechanisms to improve its performance. The traditional PSO algorithm simulates the social behavior of birds searching for food, where particles represent potential solutions that navigate through a search space guided by their personal best and the global best position. In this study, the objective was to refine the exploration and exploitation capabilities of PSO by introducing random walks into the particle movement dynamics. The modifications were aimed at enhancing the algorithm's ability to escape local optima and find global optima more efficiently.  The methodology involved implementing a modified PSO algorithm with random walks, where each particle’s velocity update equation was augmented to include a term representing a random walk component. This modification was tested on several benchmark optimization problems to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results indicated that the modified PSO algorithm exhibited improved convergence speed and robustness compared to the standard PSO, particularly in complex and multimodal landscapes.  The key findings demonstrated that the addition of random walk components significantly enhanced the algorithm’s exploration abilities, leading to better solutions in terms of both quality and diversity. These enhancements were supported by statistical analysis showing lower average computational time and higher success rates in finding optimal solutions across various test cases.  In conclusion, the integration of random walks into the PSO framework resulted in a more effective optimization algorithm capable of handling complex optimization problems more efficiently. Future work will explore further refinements and applications of this modified PSO algorithm.

We compare the network of aggregated journal-journal citation relations
provided by the Journal Citation Reports (JCR) 2012 of the Science and Social
Science Citation Indexes (SCI and SSCI) with similar data based on Scopus 2012.
First, global maps were developed for the two sets separately; sets of
documents can then be compared using overlays to both maps. Using fuzzy-string
matching and ISSN numbers, we were able to match 10,524 journal names between
the two sets; that is, 96.4% of the 10,936 journals contained in JCR or 51.2%
of the 20,554 journals covered by Scopus. Network analysis was then pursued on
the set of journals shared between the two databases and the two sets of unique
journals. Citations among the shared journals are more comprehensively covered
in JCR than Scopus, so the network in JCR is denser and more connected than in
Scopus. The ranking of shared journals in terms of indegree (that is, numbers
of citing journals) or total citations is similar in both databases overall
(Spearman's \r{ho} > 0.97), but some individual journals rank very differently.
Journals that are unique to Scopus seem to be less important--they are citing
shared journals rather than being cited by them--but the humanities are covered
better in Scopus than in JCR.

The study of solar-like oscillations, a fundamental aspect of stellar evolution, has garnered significant attention in recent years. Red giants in open clusters offer a unique opportunity to constrain the amplitudes of these oscillations, providing valuable insights into the internal dynamics of these stars. The Kepler space telescope has revolutionized the field by enabling the detection of oscillations in a large sample of red giants in open clusters.  This research aims to investigate the amplitudes of solar-like oscillations in red giants in open clusters, utilizing data from the Kepler space telescope. By analyzing the frequency and amplitude of oscillations in these stars, we seek to constrain the internal structure and composition of red giants, shedding light on the complex processes governing their evolution. The study focuses on the open clusters M67, M44, and M35, which contain a diverse range of red giants with varying levels of internal mixing and convective zone properties.  Our analysis reveals that the amplitudes of solar-like oscillations in red giants are consistent with theoretical predictions, indicating that these stars are indeed oscillating. Furthermore, we find that the amplitude of oscillations is correlated with the internal mixing and convective zone properties of the stars, suggesting that these processes play a crucial role in shaping the oscillation amplitudes. The results of this study provide new constraints on the internal dynamics of red giants, informing our understanding of the complex processes governing their evolution and the formation of their internal structures.

In this study, we present the design and experimental demonstration of a nanostring resonator network for frequency control and coherent excitation transfer. The proposed network consists of multiple nanostrings interconnected with electromechanical gaps, which serve as tunable capacitors and enable frequency selective excitations. By precisely controlling the electromechanical gap sizes and voltages, we achieve selective excitation of individual nanostrings and demonstrate coherent excitation transfer between neighboring resonators with high efficiency.  We first perform numerical simulations to understand the frequency response of the network and optimize the gap sizes for desired resonant frequencies. We then fabricate and characterize the network using an external electric field to tune the gap sizes and achieve selective excitation and coherent transfer. Measured results show a high degree of coherence between the resonators with transfer efficiencies up to 75%.  Furthermore, we explore the potential applications of the proposed resonator network in sensitive biosensors and frequency multipliers. The ability to selectively excite individual resonators and transfer coherence between them opens new opportunities for developing complex sensing and signal processing systems. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of designing and fabricating nanostring resonator networks for precise frequency control and coherent energy transfer, advancing the field of nanophonics and its applications.  In summary, this work presents the design and experimental demonstration of a nanostring resonator network for frequency control and coherent excitation transfer. By interconnecting multiple nanostrings with electromechanical gaps, we achieve selective excitation and coherent transfer between neighboring resonators with high efficiency. The proposed network exhibits potential applications in biosensors and frequency multipliers, and our results provide a foundation for future studies in complex sensing and signal processing systems.

We investigated the de Broglie wavelength and frequency of scattered electrons in the Compton effect, a phenomenon where the interaction between electromagnetic radiation and free electrons results in a transfer of energy and momentum. Our experimental approach involved the scattering of monochromatic X-rays on a thin metal target, allowing us to measure the scattered electron energy and momentum. We utilized the Compton scattering formula to calculate the de Broglie wavelength and frequency of the scattered electrons, and compared the results with theoretical predictions. Our findings indicate a good agreement between experimental and theoretical values, validating the application of de Broglie principles in the Compton effect. We observed that the de Broglie wavelength and frequency of scattered electrons are directly related to the energy and momentum transfer, and that the Compton shift is a direct consequence of the interaction between the photon and the electron. The results also suggest that the Compton effect can be used to study the properties of electrons at the atomic scale. By analyzing the de Broglie wavelength and frequency of scattered electrons, we gained insight into the underlying physics of the Compton effect and its potential applications in fields such as quantum mechanics and materials science.

Outbursts are known to begin with a sudden appearance and steep brightening
of a "stellar nucleus" --- an unresolved image of a plume of material on its
way from the comet's surface and an initial stage of an expanding halo of
ejecta. Since the brightness of this feature is routinely reported, together
with astrometry, by most comet observers as the "nuclear magnitude," it is
straightforward to determine the onset time, a fundamental parameter of any
outburst, by inspecting the chronological lists of such observations for a
major jump in the nuclear brightness. Although it is inadmissible to mix
nuclear magnitudes by different observers without first carefully examining
their compatibility, the time constraints obtained from data sets reported by
different observers can readily be combined. The intersection of these sets
provides the tightest possible constraint on the outburst's onset time. Applied
to comet 168P/Hergenrother during its 2012 return to perihelion, three
outbursts were detected and their timing determined with good to excellent
accuracy. Six fragmentation events experienced by the comet are shown to have
occurred in the same period of time as the outbursts. Three companions are
likely to have broken off from the primary in the first outburst, two
companions in the second outburst, and one companion in the last outburst. All
companions were short-lived, belonging to the class of excessively brittle
fragments. Yet, the results suggest that most of the mass lost in the first
outburst remained relatively intact during the liftoff, while the opposite was
the case in the last outburst.

In this paper, we study the problem of processing continuous range queries in
a hierarchical wireless sensor network. Contrasted with the traditional
approach of building networks in a "flat" structure using sensor devices of the
same capability, the hierarchical approach deploys devices of higher capability
in a higher tier, i.e., a tier closer to the server. While query processing in
flat sensor networks has been widely studied, the study on query processing in
hierarchical sensor networks has been inadequate. In wireless sensor networks,
the main costs that should be considered are the energy for sending data and
the storage for storing queries. There is a trade-off between these two costs.
Based on this, we first propose a progressive processing method that
effectively processes a large number of continuous range queries in
hierarchical sensor networks. The proposed method uses the query merging
technique proposed by Xiang et al. as the basis and additionally considers the
trade-off between the two costs. More specifically, it works toward reducing
the storage cost at lower-tier nodes by merging more queries, and toward
reducing the energy cost at higher-tier nodes by merging fewer queries (thereby
reducing "false alarms"). We then present how to build a hierarchical sensor
network that is optimal with respect to the weighted sum of the two costs. It
allows for a cost-based systematic control of the trade-off based on the
relative importance between the storage and energy in a given network
environment and application. Experimental results show that the proposed method
achieves a near-optimal control between the storage and energy and reduces the
cost by 0.989~84.995 times compared with the cost achieved using the flat
(i.e., non-hierarchical) setup as in the work by Xiang et al.

We present the fifth installment of the NIHAO suite of simulations, which address the apparent disagreement between the large-scale structure predictions of the ΛCDM model and the observed circular velocities of nearby field galaxies. Our methodology involves employing state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulations and utilizing halo-modeling techniques to model the galaxy response to cosmic structure.  The results of our simulations reveal a significant impact of baryonic physics on the galaxy circular velocity profile, reconciling the apparent discrepancy. We find that the stellar mass component of galaxies plays a crucial role in this agreement, as it efficiently redistributes mass from the outer regions to the central parts through dynamical friction and tidal stripping. Furthermore, the inclusion of baryonic feedback mechanisms, such as supernova-driven winds and active galactic nuclei feedback, results in a suppression of star formation in the outer regions, effectively reducing the amount of matter contributing to the observed circular velocity profile.  Our findings are supported by various observational studies and provide a new perspective on the longstanding tension between the ΛCDM model and the nearby field galaxies' circular velocity data. We argue that the inclusion of baryonic processes is a viable solution to this conflict, paving the way for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between cosmic structure and the formation and evolution of galaxies.  In summary, NIHAO V uncovers the critical role of baryonic physics in explaining the observed circular velocity profile of nearby field galaxies, reconciling the apparent disagreement between the ΛCDM model's predictions and observational data. Our approach provides a promising avenue for resolving this longstanding issue in the context of cosmological simulations.

We propose that, within the standard model, the correlation between the
$t\bar{t}$ forward--backward asymmetry $A_{t\bar t}$ and the corresponding
lepton-based asymmetry $A_l$ -- at the differential level -- is strong and
rather clean both theoretically and experimentally. Hence a combined
measurement of the two distributions as a function of the lepton $p_T$, a
direct and experimentally clean observable, would lead to a potentially
unbiased and normalization-free test of the standard model prediction. To check
the robustness of our proposal we study how the correlation is affected by
mis-measurement of the $t\bar t$ system transverse momenta, acceptance cuts,
scale dependence and compare the results of MCFM, POWHEG (with & without PYTHIA
showering), and SHERPA's CSSHOWER in first-emission mode. We find that the
shape of the relative differential distribution $A_{l} (p^{l}_{T})
[A_{t\bar{t}} (p^l_T)]$ is only moderately distorted hence supporting the
usefulness of our proposal. Beyond the first emission, we find that the
correlation is not accurately captured by lowest-order treatment. We also
briefly consider other differential variables such as the system transverse
mass and the canonical $t\bar t$ invariant mass. Finally, we study new physics
scenarios where the correlation is significantly distorted and therefore can be
more readily constrained or discovered using our method.

If dark matter particles pair annihilate into stable Standard Model
particles, a population of energetic, non-thermal electrons and positrons is
necessarily produced. The secondary radiation resulting from the energy losses
of this non-standard population (including synchrotron and inverse Compton
up-scattering of background radiation photons) in turn produces a peculiar
multi-wavelength spectrum, extending from radio to gamma-ray frequencies. We
give here an overview of multi-wavelength searches for dark matter, including
the expected injection spectrum and production rate of electrons and positrons
from dark matter annihilation, the computation of the effects of propagation
and energy losses and the actual multi-wavelength emission. We then outline the
application of this general framework to the case of galaxy clusters
(specifically Coma, 1E 0657-56 - the so-called Bullet cluster - and Ophiuchus)
and of dwarf spheroidal galaxies (including Draco, Fornax, Ursa Minor and
Carina). We also review the application of multi-wavelength search strategies
to our own Milky Way, and more specifically to the Galactic center environment,
to dark galactic mini-halos and to the so-called WMAP haze and other radio
data. We argue that multi-wavelength observations will complement gamma-ray
observations as probes of particle dark matter, since the expected luminosities
at different frequencies are generically comparable. The indirect search for
dark matter with astronomical observations at various frequencies is therefore
a crucial and indispensable element in the quest for the fundamental nature of
dark matter.

We study the proximity effect in superconductor-ferromagnet (SF) structure
with a narrow domain wall (DW) at the SF interface. The width of the domain
wall is assumed to be larger than the Fermi wave length, but smaller than other
characteristic lengths (for example, the ''magnetic'' length). The transmission
coefficient is supposed to be small so that we deal with a weak proximity
effect. Solving the linearized Eilenberger equation, we find analytical
expressions for quasiclassical Green's functions. These functions describe the
short-range (SR) condensate components, singlet and triplet with zero
projection of the total spin on the quantization z-axis, induced in F due to
the proximity effect as well as long-range odd triplet component (LRTC) with a
nonzero projection of the total spin of Cooper pairs on the $z$% -axis. The
amplitude of the LRTC essentially depends on the product $h\tau $ and increases
with increasing the exchange energy $h$ ($\tau $ is the elastic scattering
time). We calculate the Josephson current in SFS junction with a thickness of
the F layer much greater than the penetration length of the SR components. The
Josephson critical current caused by the LRTC may be both positive and negative
depending on chirality of the magnetic structure in F.
  The density of states (DOS) in a diffusive SF bilayer is also analyzed. It is
shown that the contributions of the SR and LR components to the DOS in F have a
different dependence on the thickness $d$ of the F layer (nonmonotonous and
monotonous).

The Ising model is a fundamental statistical mechanics model used to describe the behavior of magnetic materials. However, the model's simplicity is compromised by the presence of disorder, which leads to the phenomenon of replica symmetry breaking. This breaking of symmetry is a hallmark of spin glasses, a class of disordered magnetic materials. Recent studies have suggested that the metastate interpretation of replica symmetry breaking may provide insight into the behavior of these systems. This research explores the application of the metastate interpretation to short-range Ising spin glasses, a specific class of disordered systems. The objective of this study is to investigate the role of the metastate in the breakdown of replica symmetry in short-range Ising spin glasses.   To achieve this objective, a numerical simulation approach was employed, utilizing the Monte Carlo method to generate configurations of the Ising model. The results of these simulations were analyzed using the replica exchange method, which allows for the estimation of the free energy landscape of the system. The findings of this study indicate that the metastate interpretation provides a more comprehensive understanding of the replica symmetry breaking in short-range Ising spin glasses. Specifically, the results suggest that the metastate plays a crucial role in the breakdown of replica symmetry, and that the system's behavior can be accurately described using this interpretation. Overall, this research provides new insights into the behavior of short-range Ising spin glasses, and highlights the importance of the metastate interpretation in understanding the phenomenon of replica symmetry breaking.

This study focuses on the implementation and performance of a novel approach to calculate the total cross section for Higgs boson production in association with a W or Z boson at Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) using the POWHEG BOX interfaced to GoSam. The POWHEG BOX is a widely used event generator for particle physics processes, while GoSam is a parton-level matrix element generator that enables the accurate calculation of cross sections at NLO. The merging of the POWHEG BOX and GoSam is performed within the MiNLO framework, which is a set of tools designed to facilitate the combination of matrix element generators with parton-level event generators. By leveraging the strengths of both the POWHEG BOX and GoSam, this approach aims to improve the accuracy and reliability of Higgs boson production cross sections at NLO. The study explores the impact of this merged approach on the total cross section, focusing on the Higgs boson + W boson and Higgs boson + Z boson channels. The results show that the merged approach yields significant improvements in accuracy and stability, particularly in the high-mass regions of the Higgs boson. The findings of this study have important implications for the theoretical understanding of Higgs boson production at NLO, and pave the way for future applications in precision physics and collider phenomenology.

We report the detection of the largest glitch observed in the Crab pulsar, a millisecond pulsar with a period of approximately 33 milliseconds. Our analysis of 30 years of radio and X-ray observations reveals a significant departure from the pulsar's typical spin-down behavior, characterized by a 6.3 millisecond glitch that occurred in 1998. This event, which is the largest ever recorded in the Crab pulsar, is believed to have resulted from the sudden loss of rotational energy, potentially caused by the collapse of a neutron star wind funnel or the excitation of a superconducting vortex in the neutron star's crust.  Our results are obtained through the analysis of archival data from the Parkes Radio Telescope and the X-ray telescope Chandra, as well as simulations of the pulsar's spin evolution. We employed a Bayesian inference framework to constrain the parameters of the pulsar's magnetic field and crustal properties, and our findings suggest that the glitch was likely caused by a combination of factors, including the interaction between the pulsar's magnetic field and its crust.  The discovery of this large glitch has significant implications for our understanding of the Crab pulsar's internal dynamics and the mechanisms that govern its spin evolution. Our results also highlight the importance of long-term monitoring of millisecond pulsars, which can provide insights into the complex interactions between the pulsar's magnetic field, crust, and surrounding environment.

This study investigates the assembly history of the Milky Way's central bulge by analyzing its globular cluster population, specifically focusing on the double red clump (dRC) phenomenon. The background is established by the known role of globular clusters as potential building blocks of galactic bulges, with their stellar populations providing crucial insights into the formation processes. The primary objective is to identify and quantify the contribution of these clusters to the dRC population within the Milky Way bulge, which can reveal information about the merging events and star formation histories that shaped the galaxy's structure.  Methodologically, the analysis utilizes spectroscopic data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to characterize the dRCs within the Milky Way bulge. By comparing the observed properties of these clusters with theoretical models, we aim to reconstruct the evolutionary pathways of the globular clusters and assess their role in assembling the bulge. The key findings include evidence for multiple episodes of cluster mergers, suggesting a complex merger history involving various progenitor galaxies. This supports the hypothesis that the Milky Way's bulge was formed through the accretion of smaller systems over cosmic time.  The conclusion highlights the significance of the dRC phenomenon in understanding the assembly of the Milky Way's central region. The results indicate that the majority of the dRC stars likely originated from the mergers of numerous globular clusters, corroborating the idea that the Milky Way's bulge is a composite of several past mergers. This study underscores the importance of globular clusters as valuable tracers for reconstructing the assembly history of the Milky Way.

The study of astrophysical neutrinos holds significant promise for unveiling the fundamental properties of neutrinos and their sources. This research investigates the flavor ratios of astrophysical neutrinos in the presence of sterile neutrinos, hypothesized extensions to the Standard Model of particle physics. The objective is to determine the impact of sterile neutrinos on the flavor composition of astrophysical neutrinos detected on Earth, which may deviate from the expected electron, muon, and tau neutrino ratios of 111. We employed both analytical and numerical methods, considering different mixing angles and mass-squared differences that characterize sterile neutrinos. The simulation of neutrino propagation from cosmic distances to Earth incorporated both matter effects and vacuum oscillations, offering a comprehensive analysis of flavor transformation. Key findings reveal that the inclusion of one or more sterile neutrinos significantly alters the expected flavor ratios due to additional mixing and possible resonance effects in the dense environments of astrophysical sources. A notable increase in the sterile neutrino component and corresponding depletion in the detectable flavor states were observed under specific parameter regimes, challenging current predictions and potentially affecting the interpretation of neutrino data from astrophysical sources. The study concludes that the presence of sterile neutrinos offers a plausible explanation for deviations from anticipated neutrino flavor ratios and underscores the necessity for precise measurements by neutrino observatories. This could have profound implications on neutrino physics, suggesting new physics beyond the three-active neutrino paradigm. Further experimental validation is essential to ascertain the role of sterile neutrinos in altering observed flavor ratios.

We present new analytic solutions for one-zone (fully mixed) chemical
evolution models and explore their implications. In contrast to existing
analytic models, we incorporate a realistic delay time distribution for Type Ia
supernovae (SNIa) and can therefore track the separate evolution of
$\alpha$-elements produced by core collapse supernovae (CCSNe) and iron peak
elements synthesized in both CCSNe and SNIa. In generic cases, $\alpha$ and
iron abundances evolve to an equilibrium at which element production is
balanced by metal consumption and gas dilution, instead of continuing to
increase over time. The equilibrium absolute abundances depend principally on
supernova yields and the outflow mass loading parameter $\eta$, while the
equilibrium abundance ratio [$\alpha$/Fe] depends mainly on yields and
secondarily on star formation history. A stellar population can be metal-poor
either because it has not yet evolved to equilibrium or because high outflow
efficiency makes the equilibrium abundance itself low. Systems with ongoing gas
accretion develop metallicity distribution functions (MDFs) that are sharply
peaked, while "gas starved" systems with rapidly declining star formation have
broadly peaked MDFs. A burst of star formation that consumes a significant
fraction of a system's available gas can temporarily boost [$\alpha$/Fe] by
0.1-0.3 dex, a possible origin for rare, $\alpha$-enhanced stars with
intermediate age or high metallicity. Other sudden transitions in system
properties can produce surprising behavior, including backward evolution of a
stellar population from high metallicity to low metallicity. An Appendix
provides a user's guide for calculating enrichment histories, [$\alpha$/Fe]
tracks, and MDFs for a wide variety of scenarios, including flexible forms of
star formation history.

We present a series of numerical simulations that explore how the `X-factor',
$X_{CO}$ -- the conversion factor between the observed integrated CO emission
and the column density of molecular hydrogen -- varies with the environmental
conditions in which a molecular cloud is placed. Our investigation is centred
around two environmental conditions in particular: the cosmic ray ionisation
rate (CRIR) and the strength of the interstellar radiation field (ISRF). Since
both these properties of the interstellar medium have their origins in massive
stars, we make the assumption in this paper that both the strength of the ISRF
and the CRIR scale linearly with the local star formation rate (SFR). The cloud
modelling in this study first involves running numerical simulations that
capture the cloud dynamics, as well as the time-dependent chemistry, and ISM
heating and cooling. These simulations are then post-processed with a line
radiative transfer code to create synthetic 12CO (1-0) emission maps from which
$X_{CO}$ can be calculated. We find that for 1e4 solar mass virialised clouds
with mean density 100 cm$^{-3}$, $X_{CO}$ is only weakly dependent on the local
SFR, varying by a factor of a few over two orders of magnitude in SFR. In
contrast, we find that for similar clouds but with masses of 1e5 solar masses,
the X-factor will vary by an order of magnitude over the same range in SFR,
implying that extra-galactic star formation laws should be viewed with caution.
However, for denser ($10^4$ cm$^{-3}$), super-virial clouds such as those found
at the centre of the Milky Way, the X-factor is once again independent of the
local SFR.

As astronomers, we have long been fascinated by the exoplanet KIC 12557548 b, a Jupiter-sized world orbiting a Sun-like star. Our team conducted a comprehensive analysis of the Kepler spacecraft's light curves data to investigate potential signs of disintegration. Our findings reveal a significant decrease in the planet's brightness, with a mean semi-annual dip of approximately 0.013 magnitudes. We attribute this phenomenon to the disintegration of the planet's outer layers, possibly due to collisional or tidal heating. To support our hypothesis, we analyzed the spectral energy distribution of the system and identified the presence of emission lines not previously detected, suggestive of condensates and gas in the planet's atmosphere. Additionally, we studied the star's UV emission and detected an unusual increase, consistent with the disintegration of a planetary body. The implications of these findings are profound, as they provide the first observational evidence of a planet's disintegration. Our results also contribute to the understanding of the complex processes that shape planetary systems and the role that tidal and collisional forces play in determining planetary evolution. Our research is also important for the development of future observational programs aimed at studying disintegrating planets and characterizing their atmospheres. The study of such planets can provide valuable insights into the physical processes that drive the formation and evolution of planets in our universe. In summary, we report on the evidence for the disintegration of exoplanet KIC 12557548 b, detected through changes in its light curve, spectral energy distribution, and star's UV emission. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of planetary evolution and the identification of disintegrating planets as a distinct class of astronomical objects.

We consider the genesis and dynamics of interfacial instability in gas-liquid
flows, using as a model the two-dimensional channel flow of a thin falling film
sheared by counter-current gas. The methodology is linear stability theory
(Orr-Sommerfeld analysis) together with direct numerical simulation of the
two-phase flow in the case of nonlinear disturbances. We investigate the
influence of three main flow parameters (density contrast between liquid and
gas, film thickness, pressure drop applied to drive the gas stream) on the
interfacial dynamics. Energy budget analyses based on the Orr-Sommerfeld theory
reveal various coexisting unstable modes (interfacial, shear, internal) in the
case of high density contrasts, which results in mode coalescence and mode
competition, but only one dynamically relevant unstable internal mode for low
density contrast. The same linear stability approach provides a quantitative
prediction for the onset of (partial) liquid flow reversal in terms of the gas
and liquid flow rates. A study of absolute and convective instability for low
density contrast shows that the system is absolutely unstable for all but two
narrow regions of the investigated parameter space. Direct numerical
simulations of the same system (low density contrast) show that linear theory
holds up remarkably well upon the onset of large-amplitude waves as well as the
existence of weakly nonlinear waves. In comparison, for high density contrasts
corresponding more closely to an air-water-type system, although the linear
stability theory is successful at determining the most-dominant features in the
interfacial wave dynamics at early-to-intermediate times, the short waves
selected by the linear theory undergo secondary instability and the wave train
is no longer regular but rather exhibits chaotic dynamics and eventually, wave
overturning.

The study aims to develop a 3D regression neural network model for the accurate quantification of enlarged perivascular spaces (EPS) in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Given the importance of EPS in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, identifying their presence and extent is crucial. Traditional methods often involve manual segmentation which can be time-consuming and subjective. This research proposes an automated approach using a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture trained with MRI datasets. The objective is to improve the precision and efficiency of EPS quantification by leveraging deep learning techniques. The methodology involved training the network on a diverse dataset of MRI scans annotated for EPS. Key findings indicate that the proposed 3D regression CNN achieves superior performance compared to existing manual segmentation techniques, with a significant reduction in both inter- and intra-rater variability. The model demonstrates high accuracy in delineating EPS, enabling more reliable quantification and aiding in the early diagnosis and monitoring of neurodegenerative conditions. The results suggest that this automated method has potential for clinical applications in neuroimaging.

This research investigates the structural and algorithmic properties of stable matching lattices derived from "nearby" instances of the stable marriage problem, aiming to understand how slight variations in input affect the structure and solution space of these lattices. The study employs a rigorous mathematical framework to analyze the lattice structures, focusing on identifying patterns and changes that arise when comparing stable matchings across different input configurations. Methodologically, it utilizes combinatorial optimization techniques and graph theory to model and analyze the relationships between various instances. Key findings include the identification of invariant structures within the lattices and the discovery of algorithms that can efficiently navigate these structures. The research concludes by proposing new algorithms for solving stable matching problems based on insights gained from analyzing the lattices, demonstrating improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy.

The Pleiades star cluster is a well-known site for studying the formation and evolution of low-mass stars. Recent surveys have identified several L- and T-type brown dwarf candidates in the Pleiades cluster based on their proper motions, which offer valuable insights into the substellar population in this region.   This research aims to conduct spectroscopic follow-up observations of L- and T-type proper-motion member candidates in the Pleiades to confirm their membership, determine their physical properties, and investigate their atmospheric characteristics.   Utilizing medium-resolution spectroscopy, we observed a sample of identified proper-motion candidates in the Pleiades cluster. We analyzed their spectral features, compared them to known standards, and calculated their effective temperatures, surface gravities, and metallicity to verify cluster membership and classify their spectral types accurately.  Key findings Our spectroscopic follow-up revealed a significant number of L- and T-type brown dwarf members in the Pleiades cluster, indicating a diverse substellar population within the cluster. We identified distinctive spectral signatures and peculiarities in some objects, providing insights into their formation and evolutionary histories.   The spectroscopic analysis of L- and T-type proper-motion member candidates in the Pleiades cluster confirms the presence of substellar members and enriches our understanding of the formation and evolution of brown dwarfs in this environment. Further studies focusing on individual objects will enhance our knowledge of the substellar population within young star clusters like the Pleiades.

We have studied the Earth matter effect on the oscillation of upward going
GeV neutrinos by taking into account the three active neutrino flavors. For
neutrino energy in the range 3 to 12 GeV we observed three distinct resonant
peaks for the oscillation process $\nu_e\leftrightarrow \nu_{\mu,\tau}$ in
three \textit{distinct} densities. However, according to the most realistic
density profile of the Earth, the second peak at neutrino energy 6.18 GeV
corresponding to the density $6.6\,g/cm^3$ does not exist. So the resonance at
this energy can not be of MSW-type. For the calculation of observed flux of
these GeV neutrinos on Earth, we considered two different flux ratios at the
source, the standard scenario with the flux ratio $1:2:0$ and the muon damped
scenario with $0:1:0$. It is observed that at the detector while the standard
scenario gives the observed flux ratio $1:1:1$, the muon damped scenario has a
different ratio. For muon damped case with $E_{\nu} < 20$ GeV, we always get
observed neutrino fluxes as $\Phi_{\nu_e} < \Phi_{\nu_\mu}\simeq
\Phi_{\nu_\tau}$ and for $E_{\nu} > 20$ GeV, we get the average
$\Phi_{\nu_e}\sim 0$ and $\Phi_{\nu_\mu}\simeq \Phi_{\nu_\tau}\simeq 0.45$. The
upcoming PINGU will be able to shed more light on the nature of the resonance
in these GeV neutrinos and hopefully will also be able to discriminate among
different processes of neutrino production at the source in GeV energy range.

The recent study in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ correspondence shows that the tree level
contribution and 1-loop correction of holographic R\'enyi entanglement entropy
(HRE) exactly match the direct CFT computation in the large central charge
limit. This allows the R\'enyi entanglement entropy to be a new window to study
the AdS/CFT correspondence. In this paper we generalize the study of R\'enyi
entanglement entropy in pure AdS$_3$ gravity to the massive gravity theories at
the critical points. For the cosmological topological massive gravity (CTMG),
the dual conformal field theory (CFT) could be a chiral conformal field theory
or a logarithmic conformal field theory (LCFT), depending on the asymptotic
boundary conditions imposed. In both cases, by studying the short interval
expansion of the R\'enyi entanglement entropy of two disjoint intervals with
small cross ratio $x$, we find that the classical and 1-loop HRE are in exact
match with the CFT results, up to order $x^6$. To this order, the difference
between the massless graviton and logarithmic mode can be seen clearly.
Moreover, for the cosmological new massive gravity (CNMG) at critical point,
which could be dual to a logarithmic CFT as well, we find the similar agreement
in the CNMG/LCFT correspondence. Furthermore we read the 2-loop correction of
graviton and logarithmic mode to HRE from CFT computation. It has distinct
feature from the one in pure AdS$_3$ gravity.

We present new and accurate near-infrared (NIR) J, K-band time series data
for the Galactic globular cluster (GC) M5 = NGC5904. Data were collected with
SOFI at the NTT (71 J + 120 K images) and with NICS at the TNG (25 J + 22 K
images) and cover two orthogonal strips across the center of the cluster of
\approx 5 \times 10 arcmin^{2} each. These data allowed us to derive accurate
mean K-band magnitudes for 52 fundamental (RR_{ab}) and 24 first overtone
(RR_{c}) RR Lyrae stars. Using this sample of RR Lyrae stars, we find that the
slope of the K-band Period Luminosity (PLK) relation (-2.33 \pm 0.08) agrees
quite well with similar estimates available in the literature. We also find,
using both theoretical and empirical calibrations of the PLK relation, a true
distance to M5 of (14.44 \pm 0.02) mag. This distance modulus agrees very well
(1\sigma) with distances based on main sequence fitting method and on kinematic
method (14.44 \pm 0.41 mag, \citealt{rees_1996}), while is systematically
smaller than the distance based on the white dwarf cooling sequence (14.67 \pm
0.18 mag, \citealt{layden2005}), even if with a difference slightly larger than
1\sigma. The true distance modulus to M5 based on the PLJ relation (14.50 \pm
0.08 mag) is in quite good agreement with the distance based on the PLK
relation further supporting the use of NIR PL relations for RR Lyrae stars to
improve the precision of the GC distance scale.

The canonical problem of solving a system of linear equations arises in
numerous contexts in information theory, communication theory, and related
fields. In this contribution, we develop a solution based upon Gaussian belief
propagation (GaBP) that does not involve direct matrix inversion. The iterative
nature of our approach allows for a distributed message-passing implementation
of the solution algorithm. In the first part of this thesis, we address the
properties of the GaBP solver. We characterize the rate of convergence, enhance
its message-passing efficiency by introducing a broadcast version, discuss its
relation to classical solution methods including numerical examples. We present
a new method for forcing the GaBP algorithm to converge to the correct solution
for arbitrary column dependent matrices.
  In the second part we give five applications to illustrate the applicability
of the GaBP algorithm to very large computer networks: Peer-to-Peer rating,
linear detection, distributed computation of support vector regression,
efficient computation of Kalman filter and distributed linear programming.
Using extensive simulations on up to 1,024 CPUs in parallel using IBM Bluegene
supercomputer we demonstrate the attractiveness and applicability of the GaBP
algorithm, using real network topologies with up to millions of nodes and
hundreds of millions of communication links. We further relate to several other
algorithms and explore their connection to the GaBP algorithm.

We complete the classification, up to isomorphism, of the spaces of compact
operators on C([1, gamma], l_p) spaces, 1<p< infinity. In order to do this, we
classify, up to isomorphism, the spaces of compact operators {\mathcal K}(E,
F), where E= C([1, lambda], l_p) and F=C([1,xi], l_q) for arbitrary ordinals
lambda and xi and 1< p \leq q< infinity.
  More precisely, we prove that it is relatively consistent with ZFC that for
any infinite ordinals lambda, mu, xi and eta the following statements are
equivalent:
  (a) {\mathcal K}(C([1, lambda], l_p), C([1, xi], l_q)) is isomorphic to
{\mathcal K}(C([1, mu], l_p), C([1, eta], l_q)) .
  (b) lambda and mu have the same cardinality and C([1,xi]) is isomorphic to
C([1, eta]) or there exists an uncountable regular ordinal alpha and 1 \leq m,
n < omega such that C([1, xi]) is isomorphic to C([1, alpha m]) and C([1,eta])
is isomorphic to C([1, alpha n]).
  Moreover, in ZFC, if lambda and mu are finite ordinals and xi and eta are
infinite ordinals then the statements (a) and (b') are equivalent.
  (b') C([1,xi]) is isomorphic to C([1, eta]) or there exists an uncountable
regular ordinal alpha and 1 \leq m, n \leq omega such that C([1, xi]) is
isomorphic to C([1, alpha m]) and C([1,eta]) is isomorphic to C([1, alpha n]).

This study presents a novel metric for estimating transmission from genetic and epidemiological data, providing a framework for comparing transmission trees. The current understanding of transmission dynamics is often hindered by the scarcity of high-quality data, particularly in regions with limited genetic sequencing capabilities. Existing methods for estimating transmission rely heavily on assumptions and often produce conflicting results.   To address this limitation, we developed a new metric, termed the "Transmission Efficiency Index" (TEI), which integrates genetic and epidemiological data to estimate transmission rates. The TEI is based on the ratio of the number of cases directly linked to an individual to the total number of cases in the outbreak. We evaluated the TEI using a combination of simulated data and real-world outbreak scenarios, comparing its performance to existing methods.   Our results show that the TEI outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and consistency, particularly in scenarios with limited data. The TEI also demonstrates a strong correlation with the true transmission rates, suggesting its potential for informing public health policy and outbreak response. The development of the TEI provides a valuable tool for researchers and public health practitioners seeking to estimate transmission rates and compare transmission trees.

A close examination of the Maxwell-Lorentz theory of electrodynamics reveals
that polarization and magnetization of material media need not be treated as
local averages over small volumes - volumes that nevertheless contain a large
number of electric and/or magnetic dipoles. Indeed, Maxwell's macroscopic
equations are exact and self-consistent mathematical relations between
electromagnetic fields and their sources, which consist of free charge, free
current, polarization, and magnetization. When necessary, the discrete nature
of the constituents of matter and the granularity of material media can be
handled with the aid of special functions, such as Dirac's delta-function. The
energy of the electromagnetic field and the exchange of this energy with
material media are treated with a single postulate that establishes the
Poynting vector S = ExH as the rate of flow of electromagnetic energy under all
circumstances. Similarly, the linear and angular momentum densities of the
fields are simple functions of the Poynting vector that can be unambiguously
evaluated at all points in space and time, irrespective of the type of material
media, if any, that might reside at various locations. Finally, we examine the
Einstein-Laub force- and torque-density equations, and point out the
consistency of these equations with the preceding postulates, with the
conservation laws, and with the special theory of relativity. The set of
postulates thus obtained constitutes a foundation for the classical theory of
electrodynamics.

The fundamental role played by black holes in many areas of physics makes it
highly important to explore the nature of their stability. The stability of
charged Reissner-Nordstr\"om black holes to {\it neutral} (gravitational and
electromagnetic) perturbations was established almost four decades ago.
However, the stability of these charged black holes under {\it charged}
perturbations has remained an open question due to the complexity introduced by
the well-known phenomena of superradiant scattering: A charged scalar field
impinging on a charged Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole can be {\it amplified}
as it scatters off the hole. If the incident field has a non-zero rest mass,
then the mass term effectively works as a mirror, preventing the energy
extracted from the hole from escaping to infinity. One may suspect that the
superradiant amplification of charged fields by the charged black hole may lead
to an instability of the Reissner-Nordstr\"om spacetime (in as much the same
way that rotating Kerr black holes are unstable under rotating scalar
perturbations). However, in this Letter we show that, for charged
Reissner-Nordstr\"om black holes in the regime ${(Q/M)}^2\leq 8/9$, the two
conditions which are required in order to trigger a possible superradiant
instability [namely: (1) the existence of a trapping potential well outside the
black hole, and (2) superradiant amplification of the trapped modes] cannot be
satisfied simultaneously. Our results thus support the stability of charged
Reissner-Nordstr\"om black holes under charged scalar perturbations in the
regime ${(Q/M)}^2\leq 8/9$.

In the field of software testing, the testing of constrained multi-objective systems is a challenging task due to the complex nature of the objectives and the constraints involved. To address this challenge, several problem-solving tools, such as the Difficulty Adjustable and Scalable Constrained Multi-objective Test (DAS-CMT) problem toolkit, have been proposed.  The primary objective of this study is to present the DAS-CMT problem toolkit, a novel approach for testing constrained multi-objective systems with difficulty adjustability and scalability features. The toolkit is designed to tackle the complexity and size of real-world systems by employing an efficient algorithm for generating test cases that consider multiple objectives and constraints simultaneously.  To develop the DAS-CMT problem toolkit, we first review the related work in the area of multi-objective testing and constraint-based testing. Then, we describe the design and implementation of the toolkit, focusing on the difficulty adjustability and scalability features. The difficulty adjustability is achieved by introducing a penalty function that adapts the test generation process based on the system's difficulty level, while the scalability is ensured through the use of a parallelized algorithm and a pruning mechanism that reduces the search space.  The key findings of our experimental evaluation show that the DAS-CMT problem toolkit significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both the number of identified defects and the computational time, particularly in large and complex systems. Moreover, we demonstrate that the toolkit is effective in handling various types of constraints and multiple objectives.  In conclusion, this study proposes the DAS-CMT problem toolkit, an efficient and scalable approach for testing constrained multi-objective systems. The proposed toolkit offers the benefits of difficulty adjustability, ensuring that the testing process is tailored to the specific system, and scalability, making it suitable for large and complex systems. The results of our evaluation suggest that the DAS-CMT problem toolkit can significantly improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the testing process for constrained multi-objective systems.

In our work, we advance the precision of next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) computations by focusing on the specific processes of Higgs boson decay to two photons (H → γγ) and to two gluons (H → g g). These processes are crucial for accurate predictions in the context of Higgs physics and have significant implications for experimental verification at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We thoroughly address the inherent challenges of NNLO computation, particularly the management of infrared singularities and intricate loop integrals. Our methodology synthesizes cutting-edge techniques such as sector decomposition and subtraction methods, allowing for the efficient treatment of divergences and enabling more stable numerical evaluations. We incorporate the latest developments in the computation of scattering amplitudes and employ effective field theory frameworks to simplify complex multiscale problems. The results demonstrate enhanced accuracy in predicted cross-sections and branching ratios, providing refined theoretical benchmarks for experimental data comparison. By meticulously handling both virtual and real corrections, we achieve a considerable improvement in computational performance and precision. This work not only contributes to the depth of theoretical understanding but also serves as a robust resource for ongoing and future measurements in particle physics. Our study underscores the necessity of continuous development in computational techniques to meet the demanding precision requirements posed by contemporary high-energy experiments. We conclude with potential avenues for future work, targeting further refinements in NNLO calculations applicable to additional processes within the Standard Model and beyond.

We investigated the development of efficient online learning algorithms for large-scale peptide identification, a crucial task in proteomics research. Our primary objective was to design and evaluate machine learning models that can process vast amounts of peptide sequence data in real-time, thereby enabling the identification of novel peptides and proteins.  To address the challenges associated with large-scale peptide identification, we developed a novel online learning framework that incorporates advanced techniques from deep learning and ensemble methods. Our approach leverages a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and gradient boosting, which enables the efficient processing of peptide sequence data and the identification of patterns and relationships between peptides.  Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our online learning framework in identifying novel peptides and proteins from large-scale datasets. We achieved significant improvements in accuracy and speed compared to traditional machine learning methods, with an average processing time of 10 minutes per million peptides. Additionally, our framework was able to identify novel peptides and proteins with a high degree of precision, demonstrating its potential for large-scale peptide identification applications.  We also explored the use of transfer learning and data augmentation techniques to further improve the performance of our online learning framework. These techniques enabled us to adapt our models to different datasets and applications, thereby increasing their generalizability and versatility. Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of online learning algorithms for large-scale peptide identification and highlight the importance of developing efficient and scalable machine learning methods for proteomics research.

The thermal phase curve of 55 Cancri e is the first measurement of the
temperature distribution of a tidally locked Super-Earth, but raises a number
of puzzling questions about the planet's climate. The phase curve has a high
amplitude and peak offset, suggesting that it has a significant eastward
hot-spot shift as well as a large day-night temperature contrast. We use a
general circulation model to model potential climates, and investigate the
relation between bulk atmospheric composition and the magnitude of these
seemingly contradictory features. We confirm theoretical models of tidally
locked circulation are consistent with our numerical model of 55 Cnc e, and
rule out certain atmospheric compositions based on their thermodynamic
properties. Our best-fitting atmosphere has a significant hot-spot shift and
day-night contrast, although these are not as large as the observed phase
curve. We discuss possible physical processes which could explain the
observations, and show that night-side cloud formation from species such as SiO
from a day-side magma ocean could potentially increase the phase curve
amplitude and explain the observations. We conclude that the observations could
be explained by an optically thick atmosphere with a low mean molecular weight,
a surface pressure of several bar and a strong eastward circulation, with
night-side cloud formation a possible explanation for the difference between
our model and the observations.

This research paper addresses the problem of asymptotic error-free partitioning over noisy Boolean multi-access channels. The objective of this study is to develop a partitioning technique that can achieve error-free communication despite the presence of noise in the multi-access channels. The methodology involves the design and analysis of an advanced partitioning algorithm that can effectively mitigate the impact of noise on the transmitted signals. Key findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing partitioning methods in terms of error correction and signal reliability. Through simulations and theoretical analysis, the research highlights the effectiveness of the proposed technique in improving the communication quality over noisy Boolean multi-access channels. In conclusion, the study contributes a novel approach to error-free partitioning in the context of noisy communication channels, offering significant potential for enhancing the reliability of data transmission systems in practical applications.

This study explores the integration of case-based reasoning (CBR) in the development of personalized sketching methodologies for human facial portraits. Recognizing the uniqueness of individual artistic styles, the objective is to facilitate the creation of custom sketching processes that align with distinct personal preferences and techniques. The research employs a structured CBR approach, wherein previous instances of artists' work are systematically analyzed. By employing a comprehensive database of annotated portrait sketches, the methodology leverages historical data to inform current artistic decisions, allowing artists to reflect their unique styles more accurately. The key findings of this study suggest that CBR significantly enhances the learning curve for artists, enabling them to produce sketches that are both skillful and reflective of their inherent styles. By drawing parallels between historical and contemporary sketching strategies, artists can adapt and evolve their techniques over time. Furthermore, the CBR framework provides adaptive feedback, which is instrumental in correcting stylistic inconsistencies, while also offering new possibilities for creative exploration. In conclusion, the implementation of case-based reasoning in learning to sketch human facial portraits emphasizes the value of historical artistic patterns in nurturing personal style development. This approach not only supports artists in honing their craft but also promotes the evolution of unique artistic expressions, contributing to diverse perspectives in the field of visual arts. Through this study, CBR emerges as a valuable tool in personalized art education, underscoring its potential to redefine traditional approaches to learning art.

The abstract for the research paper on "The Mass Accretion Rate of Galaxy Clusters A Measurable Quantity" begins with an overview of the current understanding of mass accretion rates in galaxy clusters, highlighting the challenges in measuring these rates. It then outlines the objectives of the study, which aim to develop new techniques for accurately quantifying mass accretion rates in galaxy clusters. The methodology section describes the observational data sets used, including X-ray observations, gravitational lensing, and spectroscopic surveys, along with theoretical models employed to interpret the data. Key findings include the derivation of mass accretion rates for several galaxy clusters, demonstrating significant variability across different clusters and environments. Finally, the conclusion synthesizes the results, emphasizing the importance of these measurements for understanding the growth and evolution of galaxy clusters, their role in cosmic structure formation, and the feedback mechanisms between galaxies and the intergalactic medium.

Context. Maser emission is a strong tool for studying high mass star forming
regions and their evolutionary stages. OH masers in particular can trace the
circumstellar material around protostars and determine their magnetic field
strengths at milliarcsecond resolution.
  Aims. Imaging OH maser mission towards high mass protostellar objects to
determine their evolutionary stages and to locate the detected maser emission
in the process of high mass star formation.
  Methods. In 2007, we surveyed OH maser towards 217 high mass protostellar
objects to study its presence. In this paper, we present a follow up MERLIN
observations of a ground state OH maser emission towards one of these objects,
IRAS 19092+0841.
  Results. Emission from the two OH main spectral lines, 1665 and 1667 MHz,
were detected close to the central object. The positions and velocities of the
OH maser features have been determined. The masers are distributed over a
region of ~ 500 corresponding to 22400 AU (or ~ 0.1 pc) at a distance of 4.48
kpc. The polarization properties of the OH maser features were determined as
well. We identify three Zeeman pairs from which we inferred a magnetic field
strength of ~ 4:4mG pointing towards the observer.
  Conclusions. The relatively small velocity spread and the relatively wide
spacial distribution of the OH maser features support the suggestion that this
object could be in an early evolutionary state before the presence of disk
and/or jet/outfows.

We investigate the matter creation processes during the reheating period at
the end of inflation in the early Universe, by using the irreversible
thermodynamic of open systems. The matter content of the Universe is assumed to
consist of the inflationary scalar field, which, through its decay, generates
relativistic matter, and pressureless dark matter, respectively. At the early
stages of reheating the inflationary scalar field transfers its energy to the
newly created matter particles, with the field energy decreasing to near zero.
The general equations governing the irreversible matter creation during
reheating are obtained by combining the thermodynamics description of the
matter creation and the gravitational field equations. A dimensionless form of
the general system of the reheating equations is also introduced. The role of
the different inflationary scalar field potentials is analyzed by using
analytical and numerical methods, and the evolution of the matter and scalar
field densities, as well as of the cosmological parameters during reheating,
are obtained. Typically, the values of the energy densities of relativistic
matter and dark matter reach their maximum when the Universe is reheated up to
the reheating temperature, which is determined for each case, as a function of
the scalar field decay width, the scalar field particle mass, and of the
cosmological parameters. An interesting result is that particle production
leads to the acceleration of the Universe during the reheating phase, with the
deceleration parameter showing a complex dynamics. Once the energy density of
the scalar field becomes negligible with respect to the matter densities, the
expansion of the Universe decelerates, and inflation has a graceful exit after
reheating.

Due to its high carrier mobility, broadband absorption, and fast response
time, graphene is attractive for optoelectronics and photodetection
applications. However, the extraction of photoelectrons in conventional
metal-graphene junction devices is limited by their small junction area, where
the typical photoresponsivity is lower than 0.01 AW-1. On the other hand, the
atomically thin layer of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) is a two-dimensional (2d)
nanomaterial with a direct and finite band gap, offering the possibility of
acting as a 2d light absorber. The optoelectronic properties of the
heterostructure of these two films is therefore of great interest. The growth
of large-area graphene using chemical vapour deposition (CVD) has become mature
nowadays. However, the growth of large-area MoS2 monolayer is still
challenging. In this work, we show that a large-area and continuous MoS2
monolayer is achievable using a CVD method. Both graphene and MoS2 layers are
transferable onto desired substrates, making possible immediate and large-scale
optoelectronic applications. We demonstrate that a phototransistor based on the
graphene/MoS2 heterostructure is able to provide a high photoresponsivity
greater than 107 A/W while maintaining its ultrathin and planar structure. Our
experiments show that the electron-hole pairs are produced in the MoS2 layer
after light absorption and subsequently separated across the layers.
Contradictory to the expectation based on the conventional built-in electric
field model for metal-semiconductor contacts, photoelectrons are injected into
the graphene layer rather than trapped in MoS2 due to the alignment of the
graphene Fermi level with the conduction band of MoS2. The band alignment is
sensitive to the presence of a perpendicular electric field arising from, for
example, Coulomb impurities or an applied gate voltage, resulting in a tuneable
photoresponsivity.

In this study, we propose a novel subspace clustering method based on the multivariate-t distribution. Unlike traditional subspace clustering algorithms that require the number of subspaces and dimensions to be known, our proposed method identifies the optimal number of subspaces and their dimensions based on data. We achieve this by modeling the subspace distribution with the multivariate-t distribution, a generalization of the multivariate normal distribution, and leveraging its flexibility and robustness to handle noise and outliers.     Our method involves two main steps subspace estimation and subspace identification. In the subspace estimation step, we use an iterative algorithm, including the expectation-maximization algorithm, to estimate the density parameters and subspace means of the multivariate-t distribution based on the data. In the subspace identification step, we apply a modified version of the X-means algorithm to detect the optimal number of clusters and their corresponding subspaces.     We conducted extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art subspace clustering algorithms, including the Local Subspace Model, Maximum Mean Discrepancy, and Subspace K-means. Furthermore, our method is robust to noise and outliers, making it suitable for various data analysis tasks.     In conclusion, we present a novel and effective subspace clustering method based on the multivariate-t distribution, which identifies the optimal number of subspaces and their dimensions from data. Our method is robust to noise and outliers and outperforms several state-of-the-art subspace clustering algorithms. Future work includes applying our method to more complex and large-scale datasets and exploring its potential applications in different domains.

The second eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix and its associated eigenvector
are fundamental features of an undirected graph, and as such they have found
widespread use in scientific computing, machine learning, and data analysis. In
many applications, however, graphs that arise have several \emph{local} regions
of interest, and the second eigenvector will typically fail to provide
information fine-tuned to each local region. In this paper, we introduce a
locally-biased analogue of the second eigenvector, and we demonstrate its
usefulness at highlighting local properties of data graphs in a semi-supervised
manner. To do so, we first view the second eigenvector as the solution to a
constrained optimization problem, and we incorporate the local information as
an additional constraint; we then characterize the optimal solution to this new
problem and show that it can be interpreted as a generalization of a
Personalized PageRank vector; and finally, as a consequence, we show that the
solution can be computed in nearly-linear time. In addition, we show that this
locally-biased vector can be used to compute an approximation to the best
partition \emph{near} an input seed set in a manner analogous to the way in
which the second eigenvector of the Laplacian can be used to obtain an
approximation to the best partition in the entire input graph. Such a primitive
is useful for identifying and refining clusters locally, as it allows us to
focus on a local region of interest in a semi-supervised manner. Finally, we
provide a detailed empirical evaluation of our method by showing how it can
applied to finding locally-biased sparse cuts around an input vertex seed set
in social and information networks.

One of the most promising frameworks for understanding the anomalies of cold
and supercooled water postulates the existence of two competing,
interconvertible local structures. If the non-ideality in the Gibbs energy of
mixing overcomes the ideal entropy of mixing of these two structures, a
liquid-liquid phase transition, terminated at a liquid-liquid critical point,
is predicted. Various versions of the "two-structure equation of state" (TSEOS)
based on this concept have shown remarkable agreement with both experimental
data for metastable, deeply supercooled water and simulations of molecular
water models. However, existing TSEOSs were not designed to describe the
negative pressure region and do not account for the stability limit of the
liquid state with respect to the vapor. While experimental data on supercooled
water at negative pressures may shed additional light on the source of the
anomalies of water, such data are very limited. To fill this gap, we have
analyzed simulation results for TIP4P/2005, one of the most accurate classical
water models available. We have used recently published simulation data, and
performed additional simulations, over a broad range of positive and negative
pressures, from ambient temperature to deeply supercooled conditions. We show
that, by explicitly incorporating the liquid-vapor spinodal into a TSEOS, we
are able to match the simulation data for TIP4P/2005 with remarkable accuracy.
In particular, this equation of state quantitatively reproduces the lines of
extrema in density, isothermal compressibility, and isobaric heat capacity.
Contrary to an explanation of the thermodynamic anomalies of water based on a
"retracing spinodal", the liquid-vapor spinodal in the present TSEOS continues
monotonically to lower pressures upon cooling, influencing but not giving rise
to density extrema and other thermodynamic anomalies.

We investigate the expansion of bosons and fermions in a homogeneous lattice
after a sudden removal of the trapping potential using exact numerical methods.
As a main result, we show that in one dimension, both bosonic and fermionic
Mott insulators expand with the same velocity, irrespective of the interaction
strength, provided the expansion starts from the ground state of the trapped
