gas. Furthermore, their density profiles become identical during the expansion:
The asymptotic density dynamics is identical to that of initially localized,
non-interacting particles, and the asymptotic velocity distribution is flat.
The expansion velocity for initial correlated Mott insulating states is
therefore independent of the interaction strength and particle statistics.
Interestingly, this non-equilibrium dynamics is sensitive to the interaction
driven quantum phase transition in the Bose-Hubbard model: While being constant
in the Mott phase, the expansion velocity decreases in the superfluid phase and
vanishes for large systems in the non-interacting limit. These results are
compared to the set-up of a recent experiment [PRL 110, 205301 (2013)], where
the trap opening was combined with an interaction quench from infinitely strong
interactions to finite values. We carry out an analogous analysis for a
two-component Fermi gas, with similar observations. In addition, we study the
effect of breaking the integrability of hard-core bosons in different ways:
While the fast ballistic expansion from the ground state of Mott insulators in
one dimension remains unchanged for finite interactions, we observe strong
deviations from this behavior on a two-leg ladder even in the hard-core case.
This change in dynamics bares similarities with the dynamics in the dimensional
crossover from one to two dimensions observed in the aformentioned experimental
study.

Several widely used methods for the calculation of band structures and photo
emission spectra, such as the GW approximation, rely on Many-Body Perturbation
Theory. They can be obtained by iterating a set of functional differential
equations relating the one-particle Green's function to its functional
derivative with respect to an external perturbing potential. In the present
work we apply a linear response expansion in order to obtain insights in
various approximations for Green's functions calculations. The expansion leads
to an effective screening, while keeping the effects of the interaction to all
orders. In order to study various aspects of the resulting equations we
discretize them, and retain only one point in space, spin, and time for all
variables. Within this one-point model we obtain an explicit solution for the
Green's function, which allows us to explore the structure of the general
family of solutions, and to determine the specific solution that corresponds to
the physical one. Moreover we analyze the performances of established
approaches like $GW$ over the whole range of interaction strength, and we
explore alternative approximations. Finally we link certain approximations for
the exact solution to the corresponding manipulations for the differential
equation which produce them. This link is crucial in view of a generalization
of our findings to the real (multidimensional functional) case where only the
differential equation is known.

A global quench is an interesting setting where we can study thermalization
of subsystems in a pure state. We investigate entanglement entropy (EE) growth
in global quenches in holographic field theories and relate some of its aspects
to quantities characterizing chaos. More specifically we obtain four key
results:
  1. We prove holographic bounds on the entanglement velocity $v_E$ and the
butterfly effect speed $v_B$ that arises in the study of chaos.
  2. We obtain the EE as a function of time for large spherical entangling
surfaces analytically. We show that the EE is insensitive to the details of the
initial state or quench protocol.
  3. In a thermofield double state we determine analytically the two-sided
mutual information between two large concentric spheres separated in time.
  4. We derive a bound on the rate of growth of EE for arbitrary shapes, and
develop an expansion for EE at early times.
  In a companion paper arXiv:1608.05101, we put these results in the broader
context of EE growth in chaotic systems: we relate EE growth to the chaotic
spreading of operators, derive bounds on EE at a given time, and compare the
holographic results to spin chain numerics and toy models. In this paper, we
perform holographic calculations that provide the basis of arguments presented
in that paper.

The abstract focuses on the application of the anisotropic bond model to analyze second-harmonic generation (SHG) from amorphous media. The study aims to understand the microscopic origins of SHG signals in disordered materials by employing the anisotropic bond model, which accounts for the directional dependence of interatomic interactions. Utilizing computational methods and simulations, the research investigates how the disorder-induced anisotropy affects the SHG efficiency and polarization properties. Key findings reveal that the SHG intensity and polarization orientation are significantly influenced by the anisotropy of bonds within the amorphous structure. These results provide insights into the mechanisms governing SHG in amorphous systems and pave the way for more accurate modeling and prediction of SHG signals in complex materials.

This study investigates the effectiveness of utilizing Blippar Augmented Reality (AR) Browser in the practical training of mechanical engineers. Background research reveals that traditional teaching methods often fall short in conveying complex mechanical concepts, leading to difficulties in student comprehension and retention. In contrast, AR technology has shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes by providing immersive and interactive experiences. The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of Blippar AR Browser on the practical training of mechanical engineers, with a focus on improving their understanding of mechanical systems and developing problem-solving skills. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods. A sample of 50 mechanical engineering students participated in a 12-week training program, which consisted of two groups one using Blippar AR Browser and the other using traditional teaching methods. The results show a significant improvement in students' understanding of mechanical concepts and problem-solving skills in the Blippar AR Browser group compared to the control group. Furthermore, student feedback revealed a high level of engagement and satisfaction with the AR-based training. The findings suggest that incorporating Blippar AR Browser into practical training can be an effective strategy for enhancing mechanical engineers' learning outcomes. The study's results have implications for educators and training institutions seeking to improve the effectiveness of their teaching methods.

This research paper explores the empirical capacity achievable through feedback in memoryless additive models. The objective is to analyze the impact of feedback on enhancing the empirical capacity of such models. The methodology involves studying memoryless additive models with feedback to understand how feedback mechanisms can improve the capacity of these models. The key findings indicate that incorporating feedback in memoryless additive models can significantly increase their empirical capacity, allowing for more efficient and accurate data processing. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that utilizing feedback mechanisms in memoryless additive models is a promising approach to boost empirical capacity and enhance the overall performance of these models.

In this review, recent progress in theoretical models for blazar emission
will be summarized. The salient features of both leptonic and lepto-hadronic
approaches to modeling blazar spectral energy distributions will be reviewed. I
will present sample modeling results of spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of
different types of blazars along the blazar sequence, including Fermi
high-energy gamma-ray data, using both types of models. Special emphasis will
be placed on the implications of the recent very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray
detections of non-traditional VHE gamma-ray blazars, including intermediate and
low-frequency-peaked BL Lac objects and even flat-spectrum radio quasars. Due
to the featureless optical spectra of BL Lac objects, the redshifts of several
BL Lacs remain unknown. I will briefly discuss possible constraints on their
redshift using spectral modeling of their SED including Fermi + ground-based
VHE gamma-ray data. It will be shown that in some cases, spectral modeling with
time-independent single-zone models alone is not sufficient to constrain
models, as both leptonic and lepto-hadronic models are able to provide
acceptable fits to the overall SED. Subsequently, recent developments of
time-dependent and inhomogeneous blazar models will be discussed, including
detailed numerical simulations as well as a semi-analytical approach to the
time-dependent radiation signatures of shock-in-jet models.

The next generation of exoplanet space photometry missions proposed by both
NASA and ESA promise to discover small transiting planets around the nearest
and brightest main-sequence stars. The physical and rotational properties of
these stars, in conjunction with Gaia-precision distances, can be used to
determine the inclination of the stellar rotation axis. Given edge-on orbital
paths for transiting planets, stellar inclinations can be interpreted as
obliquities projected into the line of sight, which can be used to more clearly
reveal the system architectures of small planets and the factors that drive
their orbital evolution. To demonstrate the method, we use a sample of
simulated target stars for the NASA Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite
(TESS) mission. Based on predicted characteristics of these stars and likely
measurement uncertainties, we show that the expected TESS discoveries will
allow us to finely differentiate the true underlying obliquity distribution.
Under conservative assumptions in our illustrative example--in which the true
distribution is assumed to contain systems drawn from both well-aligned and
isotropic distributions (e.g., due to multiple migration channels)--the correct
fractions can be determined to within $0.15$, thus enabling constraints on the
evolutionary processes that shape system architectures. Moreover, because of
the excellent astrometric precision expected from Gaia, this technique will
also be applicable to the large number of planets already discovered by
${\textit Kepler}$ orbiting much more distant stars.

Semantic labeling (or pixel-level land-cover classification) in ultra-high
resolution imagery (< 10cm) requires statistical models able to learn high
level concepts from spatial data, with large appearance variations.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) achieve this goal by learning
discriminatively a hierarchy of representations of increasing abstraction.
  In this paper we present a CNN-based system relying on an
downsample-then-upsample architecture. Specifically, it first learns a rough
spatial map of high-level representations by means of convolutions and then
learns to upsample them back to the original resolution by deconvolutions. By
doing so, the CNN learns to densely label every pixel at the original
resolution of the image. This results in many advantages, including i)
state-of-the-art numerical accuracy, ii) improved geometric accuracy of
predictions and iii) high efficiency at inference time.
  We test the proposed system on the Vaihingen and Potsdam sub-decimeter
resolution datasets, involving semantic labeling of aerial images of 9cm and
5cm resolution, respectively. These datasets are composed by many large and
fully annotated tiles allowing an unbiased evaluation of models making use of
spatial information. We do so by comparing two standard CNN architectures to
the proposed one: standard patch classification, prediction of local label
patches by employing only convolutions and full patch labeling by employing
deconvolutions. All the systems compare favorably or outperform a
state-of-the-art baseline relying on superpixels and powerful appearance
descriptors. The proposed full patch labeling CNN outperforms these models by a
large margin, also showing a very appealing inference time.

Using first-principles density functional calculations, electronic and
optical properties of ferromagnetic semiconductor EuO are investigated. In
particular, we have developed a way to obtain the spin-dependent optical
response of the magnetic materials, which is helpful to verify the
spin-dependent band structure of EuO. Significantly different optical responses
from spin-up and spin-down channels are obtained in both linear and nonlinear
cases, making it possible to distinguish contributions from different
spin-channels in the optical absorption spectra if spin-flip process can be
neglected. In addition, the red-shift of the absorption edge from paramagnetic
to ferromagnetic ordering is explained by exchange interactions. Using such
method, we have also compared the optical properties of multiferroic EuO which
is induced by strong epitaxial strain. Our results show that from tensile to
compressive strain, the blue-shift of the leading absorption peaks in the
optical spectra, the red-shift of the optical band gap in spin-up state can be
observed, consistent to the energy difference between spin-splitting orbits.
The spin-dependent nonlinear optical properties reveal that in the infrared and
visible light region, the contributions to second-harmonic generation (SHG)
susceptibilities are mainly from spin-majority channels. In addition, the
strain effect is also discussed. With the increase of epitaxial strain, the
larger energy shift of the leading absorption peaks, and the more remarkable
nonlinear optical response can be obtained.

This study investigates the assembly of supermassive black hole seeds through the examination of their growth rates, accretion processes, and initial mass distributions across various cosmic epochs. Our research employs numerical simulations that model the hierarchical merging of gas-rich structures within dark matter halos, focusing on the conditions under which these seeds can evolve into the massive black holes observed at the centers of galaxies today. Key findings indicate that efficient accretion rates and the presence of high-density environments play crucial roles in seed growth. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the initial mass of black hole seeds is tightly correlated with the mass of their host dark matter halos, suggesting a connection between the formation of massive black holes and the assembly of large-scale structure in the universe. The methodologies employed include state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulations and semi-analytical models, which are used to constrain and test theoretical predictions regarding the formation and evolution of supermassive black hole seeds.

Dark matter halos are essential components of galaxies, influencing their dynamics and evolution. This study investigates how the structure of spherical dark matter halos impacts the types of orbits observed in disk galaxies. The objective is to understand the relationship between dark matter halo properties and the behavior of stars within galaxies. Through computational simulations based on numerical integration of the equations of motion, various halo structures are considered, ranging from concentrated to more extended distributions. Analysis of the types of orbits resulting from these different halo configurations reveals distinct patterns of stellar motion within disk galaxies. Key findings demonstrate that the concentration and mass distribution of dark matter halos significantly affect the orbits of stars, with implications for the overall stability and kinematics of disk galaxies. In conclusion, the structure of spherical dark matter halos plays a crucial role in shaping the dynamics of disk galaxies, highlighting the intricate connection between the invisible dark matter component and the observable stellar populations in galactic systems.

The study of cosmic anisotropy offers critical insights into the early stages of the universe and its subsequent evolution. This research paper aims to investigate the behavior of anisotropy within the framework of big-bounce cosmology, a model positing that our universe undergoes cyclic phases of expansion and contraction rather than a singular Big Bang event. Employing analytical and numerical approaches, we analyze the evolution of anisotropic perturbations in a series of cosmological models characterized by varying equations of state and initial conditions. Our findings reveal that anisotropic stress can significantly influence the dynamics of the universe during the bounce phase, leading to distinctive patterns in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies. Notably, we observe that the amplitude and scale of anisotropic features can serve as potential indicators for distinguishing between big-bounce scenarios and traditional Big Bang models. Furthermore, the interaction between anisotropies and the cosmic expansion rate during contracting phases suggests modifications to current gravitational theories at play in extreme curvature regimes. In conclusion, this study enhances our understanding of how anisotropic behavior manifests in big-bounce cosmologies, providing a foundation for further exploration into the implications of cyclic models in the broader context of cosmological theory and observational astronomy. The results of this research may ultimately bridge the gap between theoretical predictions and astrophysical observations, thus enriching the ongoing discourse on the universe's origins and fate.

We investigated the feasibility of utilizing Physarum Wires, a biological network of mycelium, to design and implement practical circuits. Our initial attempts to integrate Physarum Wires with electronic components resulted in limited success, as the mycelium's tendency to grow in unpredictable patterns and the lack of control over its behavior hindered the development of functional circuits.   However, after refining our approach, we successfully integrated Physarum Wires with microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and developed a novel circuit design that leveraged the mycelium's ability to navigate and adapt to its environment. Our results demonstrate that Physarum Wires can be used to create complex networks and patterns, allowing for the implementation of basic logic gates and digital circuits.  The key to our success lay in the use of a custom-designed substrate that enabled the mycelium to grow in a controlled manner, and the incorporation of sensors and actuators to interact with the mycelium and influence its behavior. By combining the unique properties of Physarum Wires with traditional electronic components, we were able to create a hybrid system that demonstrated the potential for biological-inspired circuit design.  Our findings have significant implications for the development of novel, biologically-inspired electronic systems, and highlight the need for further research into the application of biological networks in circuit design.

(Abridged) In the recent controversy about the role of TP-AGB stars in
evolutionary population synthesis (EPS) models of galaxies, one particular
aspect is puzzling: TP-AGB models aimed at reproducing the lifetimes and
integrated fluxes of the TP-AGB phase in Magellanic Cloud (MC) clusters, when
incorporated into EPS models, are found to overestimate the TP-AGB contribution
in resolved star counts and integrated spectra of galaxies. In this paper, we
call attention to a particular evolutionary aspect that in all probability is
the main cause of this conundrum. As soon as stellar populations intercept the
ages at which RGB stars first appear, a sudden change in the lifetime of the
core He-burning phase causes a temporary boost in the production rate of
subsequent evolutionary phases, including the TP-AGB. For a timespan of about
0.1 Gyr, triple TP-AGB branches develop at slightly different initial masses,
causing their frequency and contribution to the integrated luminosity of the
stellar population to increase by a factor of 2. The boost occurs just in the
proximity of the expected peak in the TP-AGB lifetimes, and for ages of 1.6
Gyr. Coincidently, this relatively narrow age interval happens to contain the
few very massive MC clusters that host most of the TP-AGB stars used to
constrain stellar evolution and EPS models. This concomitance makes the
AGB-boosting particularly insidious in the context of present EPS models. The
effect brings about three main consequences. (1) Present estimates of the
TP-AGB contribution to the integrated light of galaxies derived from MC
clusters, are biased towards too large values. (2) The relative TP-AGB
contribution of single-burst populations falling in this critical age range
cannot be accurately derived by the fuel consumption theorem. (3) A careful
revision of AGB star populations in intermediate-age MC clusters is urgently
demanded.

This research focuses on enhancing the accuracy of cancer prognosis prediction through the application of balanced stratified sampling techniques. Traditional methods often face challenges in ensuring representative samples, leading to biased predictions. By employing balanced stratified sampling, the study aims to mitigate these issues by dividing the patient data into strata based on relevant characteristics such as tumor type, stage, and treatment history, and then selecting proportional samples from each stratum. The methodology involves preprocessing the dataset, applying stratification criteria, and utilizing machine learning algorithms like Random Forest and Support Vector Machines (SVM) for prognosis prediction. Key findings indicate that balanced stratified sampling significantly improves the predictive models' performance, reducing error rates and enhancing the reliability of prognosis predictions. The study concludes with recommendations for incorporating stratified sampling into clinical practice to better inform treatment decisions and improve patient outcomes.

This study investigates the relationship between betweenness and diversity in journal citation networks as measures of interdisciplinarity. The interdisciplinarity of research is a crucial aspect of modern academic landscapes, as it fosters the exchange of ideas and knowledge across disciplines. However, traditional measures of interdisciplinarity, such as co-authorship and co-citation analysis, have limitations in capturing the complexity of interdisciplinary research.  Betweenness centrality, a measure of a node's connectivity within a network, is often used to assess the centrality of journals in citation networks. By analyzing the citation patterns of journals in various fields, this study aims to identify the journals that exhibit high betweenness centrality and are also diverse in their citation patterns. The objective of this research is to explore the potential of betweenness and diversity as measures of interdisciplinarity, and to contribute to the development of a more nuanced understanding of interdisciplinary research.  The study employed a large-scale analysis of citation networks from various disciplines, using a combination of network analysis and machine learning techniques. The results show that journals with high betweenness centrality and diversity in citation patterns are more likely to be interdisciplinarily oriented, and that these journals play a crucial role in facilitating the exchange of ideas across disciplines. The findings of this study have implications for the evaluation of research quality, the identification of knowledge gaps, and the development of strategies to promote interdisciplinary research.

In this work, we address the problem of scheduling with outliers by developing an enhanced model that accounts for unusual data points in optimizing task allocations. Traditional scheduling algorithms assume homogeneous data distributions, often leading to suboptimal performance when outliers are present. We propose a novel approach that integrates robust statistical techniques to identify and manage outliers effectively, thereby minimizing their impact on overall scheduling efficiency. Our methodology involves an initial outlier detection phase using a modified clustering algorithm, followed by a dynamic scheduling strategy that reallocates tasks based on both standard and outlier data distribution characteristics. We conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach against established scheduling algorithms. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in the makespan and overall resource utilization, highlighting the robustness of our model in diverse scenarios with varying outlier prevalence. Furthermore, our model shows substantial adaptability, maintaining high efficiency under different workload conditions and demonstrating resilience against systemic scheduling disruptions. We underscore the importance of accounting for data anomalies in developing efficient scheduling protocols, which are increasingly pertinent in complex systems such as cloud computing and project management. Our findings contribute to the advancement of scheduling theory by presenting empirical evidence that integrating outlier management leads to more resilient and adaptable scheduling frameworks. Future work will focus on refining the outlier detection phase and exploring real-time applications to further enhance practical utility.

This study explores the evolution of electron magnetic (EM) distribution within the core of an active region over time. Utilizing high-resolution observations from solar observatories, the research aims to understand the dynamic changes in EM distribution as they correlate with the development and evolution of sunspots and other solar phenomena. The methodology involves detailed analysis of spectroscopic data collected during multiple solar rotations, focusing on the core regions where EM distributions are most pronounced. Key findings indicate significant variations in EM density and polarization vectors, which reflect underlying magnetic field configurations. These variations suggest that the EM distribution evolves dynamically in response to magnetic reconnection events and plasma flows within the active region. The study concludes by proposing models that can better predict the temporal behavior of EM distributions in the solar corona, contributing to our understanding of solar dynamics and space weather forecasting.

We use high spectral resolution (R > 8000) data covering 3800-13000\r{A} to
study the physical conditions of the broad line region (BLR) of nine nearby
Seyfert 1 galaxies. Up to six broad HI lines are present in each spectrum. A
comparison - for the first time using simultaneous optical to near-infrared
observations - to photoionisation calculations with our devised simple scheme
yields the extinction to the BLR at the same time as determining the density
and photon flux, and hence distance from the nucleus, of the emitting gas. This
points to a typical density for the HI emitting gas of 10$^{11}$cm$^{-3}$ and
shows that a significant amount of this gas lies at regions near the dust
sublimation radius, consistent with theoretical predictions. We also confirm
that in many objects the line ratios are far from case B, the best-fit
intrinsic broad-line H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratios being in the range 2.5-6.6 as
derived with our photoionization modeling scheme. The extinction to the BLR,
based on independent estimates from HI and HeII lines, is A$_V$ $\le$ 3 for
Seyfert 1-1.5s, while Seyfert 1.8-1.9s have A$_V$ in the range 4-8. A
comparison of the extinction towards the BLR and narrow line region (NLR)
indicates that the structure obscuring the BLR exists on scales smaller than
the NLR. This could be the dusty torus, but dusty nuclear spirals or filaments
could also be responsible. The ratios between the X-ray absorbing column N$_H$
and the extinction to the BLR are consistent with the Galactic gas-to-dust
ratio if N$_H$ variations are considered.

We study pseudogap phenomena and Fermi-arc formation experimentally observed
in typical two dimensional doped Mott insulators, namely, underdoped cuprate
superconductors. To develop a physically unequivocal theory, we start from the
slave-boson mean-field theory for the Hubbard model on a square lattice. Our
crucial step is to further take into account the charge dynamics and
fluctuations. The extra charge fluctuations seriously modify low-energy
single-particle spectra of doped Mott insulators near the Fermi level: An
electron added around an empty site (or a hole added around a doubly occupied
site) constitutes composite fermion (cofermion), called holo-electron (or
doublo-hole) at low energy in distinction from the normal quasiparticles. These
unexplored composite fermions substantiate the extra charge fluctuation. We
show that the quasiparticles hybridize with the holo-electrons and
doublo-holes. The resultant hybridization gap is identified as the pseudogap
observed in the underdoped region of the high-T_c cuprates. Because the Fermi
level crosses the top (bottom) of the low-energy band formed just below (above)
the hybridization gap in the hole-doped (electron-doped) case, it causes a
Fermi-surface reconstruction, namely, a topological change in the Fermi surface
forced by the penetration of zeros of the quasiparticle Green function. This
reconstruction signals the emergence of a non-Fermi-liquid phase. The
pseudogap, and the resultant formation of pocket or arc of the Fermi surface
reproduce the experimental results for the cuprate superconductors in the
underdoped region. The pairing channel opens not only between two
quasiparticles but also between a quasiparticle and a cofermion. This pairing
solves the puzzle of the dichotomy between the d-wave superconductivity and the
precursors of the the insulating gap in the antinodal region.

We report the emergence of electronic edge states in time-periodically driven
strained armchair terminated graphene nanoribbons. This is done by considering
a short-pulse spatial-periodic strain field. Then, the tight-binding
Hamiltonian of the system is mapped into a one dimensional ladder. The time
periodicity is considered within the Floquet formalism. Thus the quasienergy
spectrum is found numerically by diagonalizing the evolution operator. For some
particular cases, the quasienergy spectrum is found analytically. We find that
the system is able to support gapless and gapped phases. Very different edge
states emerge for both the gapless and the gapful phases. In the case of the
gapped phase, edge states emerge at the gap centered at zero quasienergy,
although the Chern number is zero due to the chiral symmetry of the system. For
the gapless phase, besides edge states at zero quasienergy, cosine like edge
states which merge and coexist with the bulk band are observed. To confirm the
topological nature of these edge states, we analytically obtained the effective
Hamiltonian and its spectrum for a particular case, finding that the edge
states are topologically weak. Finally, we found analytically the evolution of
band edges and its crossings as a function of the driven period. Topological
modes arise at such crossings.

We present CARMA CO (J=1-0) observations and Herschel PACS spectroscopy,
characterizing the outflow properties toward extremely young and deeply
embedded protostars in the Orion molecular clouds. The sample comprises a
subset of the Orion protostars known as the PACS Bright Red Sources (PBRS)
(Stutz et al. 2013). We observed 14 PBRS with CARMA and 8 of these 14 with
Herschel, acquiring full spectral scans from 55 micron to 200 micron. Outflows
are detected in CO (J=1-0) from 8 of 14 PBRS, with two additional tentative
detections; outflows are also detected from the outbursting protostar HOPS 223
(V2775 Ori) and the Class I protostar HOPS 68. The outflows have a range of
morphologies, some are spatially compact, <10000 AU in extent, while others
extend beyond the primary beam. The outflow velocities and morphologies are
consistent with being dominated by intermediate inclination angles (80 deg > i
> 20 deg). This confirms the interpretation of the very red 24 micron to 70
micron colors of the PBRS as a signpost of high envelope densities, with only
one (possibly two) cases of the red colors resulting from edge-on inclinations.
We detect high-J (J_up > 13) CO lines and/or H_2O lines from 5 of 8 PBRS and
only for those with detected CO outflows. The far-infrared CO rotation
temperatures of the detected PBRS are marginally colder (~230 K) than those
observed for most protostars (~300 K), and only one of these 5 PBRS has
detected [OI] 63 micron emission. The high envelope densities could be
obscuring some [OI] emission and cause a ~20 K reduction to the CO rotation
temperatures.

The study investigates the spatial and dynamical relationships between the Gould Belt, the de Vaucouleurs-Dolidze Belt, and the Orion Arm—three significant structures within the Milky Way impacting our understanding of local galactic architecture. The objective is to enhance comprehension of their interconnections, origins, and influence on star formation processes. Using a combination of star count data, spectroscopic surveys, and astrometric databases, including GAIA DR3, we mapped the spatial distribution and kinematic properties of these structures. We employed statistical analyses to evaluate correlation patterns and theoretical modeling to simulate their past and predict future trajectories. Key findings indicate that the Gould Belt and the de Vaucouleurs-Dolidze Belt exhibit overlapping features with distinct dynamical characteristics, suggesting differing origins but shared evolutionary pathways within the heliocentric vicinity. The research highlights that these belts are dynamically linked to broader galactic structures like the Orion Arm, demonstrating a complex interplay that governs the local stellar population distribution and activity. Analyzing stellar ages and metallicities reveals temporal patterns that imply synchronized star formation bursts potentially triggered by large-scale galactic events. The results offer new insights into the evolutionary narrative of these structures and underscore their role in shaping the solar neighborhood. The study concludes that collaborative forces of galactic differentials and external stimuli are crucial to accurately model the evolution of the Milky Way's structural components, thus fostering a more integrative understanding of our galaxy's dynamic composition and history.

Discrete optimization is a central problem in mathematical optimization with
a broad range of applications, among which binary optimization and sparse
optimization are two common ones. However, these problems are NP-hard and thus
difficult to solve in general. Combinatorial search methods such as
branch-and-bound and exhaustive search find the global optimal solution but are
confined to small-sized problems, while coordinate descent methods such as
coordinate gradient descent are efficient but often suffer from poor local
minima. In this paper, we consider a hybrid method that combines the
effectiveness of combinatorial search and the efficiency of coordinate descent.
Specifically, we consider random strategy or/and greedy strategy to select a
subset of coordinates as the working set, and then perform global combinatorial
search over the working set based on the original objective function. In
addition, we provide some optimality analysis and convergence analysis for the
proposed method. Our method finds stronger stationary points than existing
methods. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on some sparse
optimization and binary optimization applications. As a result, our method
achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy. For example, our
method generally outperforms the well-known orthogonal matching pursuit method
in sparse optimization.
  Keywords: Sparsity Optimization, Binary Optimization, Coordinate Descent,
Combinatorial Search, Discrete Optimization, Convergence Analysis.

Despite the progress achieved by kinetic theory, the search of possible exact
kinetic equations remains elusive to date. This concerns, specifically, the
issue of the validity of the conjecture proposed by Grad (Grad, 1972) and
developed in a seminal work by Lanford (Lanford, 1974) that kinetic equations -
such as the Boltzmann equation for a gas of classical hard spheres - might
result exact in an appropriate asymptotic limit, usually denoted as
Boltzmann-Grad limit. The Lanford conjecture has actually had a profound
influence on the scientific community, giving rise to a whole line of original
research in kinetic theory and mathematical physics. Nevertheless, certain
aspects of the theory remain to be addressed and clarified. The purpose of this
paper is to investigate the possible existence of the strong Boltzmann-Grad
limit for the BBGKY hierarchy. Contrary to previous approaches in which the
w*-convergence was considered for the definition of the Boltzmann-Grad limit
functions, based on their construction in terms of time-series expansions
obtained from the BBGKY hierarchy, here we look for the possible existence of
strong limit functions in the sense of local convergence in phase space. The
result is based on the adoption of the Klimontovich approach to statistical
mechanics, permitting the explicit representation of the $s$-body reduced
distribution functions in terms of the Klimontovich probability density.

In this comment, we address the temperature dependence of ultracold neutron (UCN) loss rates reported in the article by Korobkina et al. Our analysis reveals a significant discrepancy between their experimental findings and theoretical predictions. We propose a possible explanation for this disagreement through a reevaluation of the neutron-nucleus interaction potential used in the experimental calculations. Specifically, we suggest incorporating an additional term in the potential to more accurately model the behavior of UCN in the presence of a material.      The authors of the original article measured UCN loss rates at temperatures ranging from 283 K to 315 K using a β-decay spectrometer. They observed a notable increase in loss rates as the temperature rose. Our comment challenges the validity of this temperature dependence, as we argue that it may be artificially introduced due to inadequate modeling of the neutron-nucleus interaction potential. We demonstrate this through a comparative analysis of the experimental results with corresponding theoretical calculations based on different potential models. Our calculations indicate that the inclusion of the proposed additional term leads to a significantly improved agreement between the experimental and theoretical loss rates.      Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the complex physical processes involved in UCN loss. This is of particular importance for applications in various research areas, including neutron-based measurements, nuclear physics, and material science. We suggest that future experiments should consider the implications of our results by incorporating more accurate potential models to ensure the validity and reliability of their findings.      Overall, our comment sheds light on the importance of rigorous modeling in experimental research, and highlights the need for continuous improvement in theoretical approaches to accurately describe and predict physical phenomena.

Observations of radio halos and relics in galaxy clusters indicate efficient
electron acceleration. Protons should likewise be accelerated, suggesting that
clusters may also be sources of very high-energy (VHE; E>100 GeV) gamma-ray
emission. We report here on VHE gamma-ray observations of the Coma galaxy
cluster with the VERITAS array of imaging Cherenkov telescopes, with
complementing Fermi-LAT observations at GeV energies. No significant gamma-ray
emission from the Coma cluster was detected. Integral flux upper limits at the
99% confidence level were measured to be on the order of (2-5)*10^-8\ ph. m^-2
s^-1 (VERITAS, >220 GeV} and ~2*10^-6 ph. m^-2 s^-1 (Fermi, 1-3 GeV),
respectively. We use the gamma-ray upper limits to constrain CRs and magnetic
fields in Coma. Using an analytical approach, the CR-to-thermal pressure ratio
is constrained to be < 16% from VERITAS data and < 1.7% from Fermi data
(averaged within the virial radius). These upper limits are starting to
constrain the CR physics in self-consistent cosmological cluster simulations
and cap the maximum CR acceleration efficiency at structure formation shocks to
be <50%. Assuming that the radio-emitting electrons of the Coma halo result
from hadronic CR interactions, the observations imply a lower limit on the
central magnetic field in Coma of (2 - 5.5) muG, depending on the radial
magnetic-field profile and on the gamma-ray spectral index. Since these values
are below those inferred by Faraday rotation measurements in Coma (for most of
the parameter space), this {renders} the hadronic model a very plausible
explanation of the Coma radio halo. Finally, since galaxy clusters are
dark-matter (DM) dominated, the VERITAS upper limits have been used to place
constraints on the thermally-averaged product of the total self-annihilation
cross section and the relative velocity of the DM particles, <\sigma v>. (abr.)

We present the theory of how to achieve phase measurements with the minimum
possible variance in ways that are readily implementable with current
experimental techniques. Measurements whose statistics have high-frequency
fringes, such as those obtained from NOON states, have commensurately high
information yield. However this information is also highly ambiguous because it
does not distinguish between phases at the same point on different fringes. We
provide schemes to eliminate this phase ambiguity in a highly efficient way,
providing phase estimates with uncertainty that is within a small constant
factor of the Heisenberg limit, the minimum allowed by the laws of quantum
mechanics. These techniques apply to NOON state and multi-pass interferometry,
as well as phase measurements in quantum computing. We have reported the
experimental implementation of some of these schemes with multi-pass
interferometry elsewhere. Here we present the theoretical foundation, and also
present some new experimental results. There are three key innovations to the
theory in this paper. First, we examine the intrinsic phase properties of the
sequence of states (in multiple time modes) via the equivalent two-mode state.
Second, we identify the key feature of the equivalent state that enables the
optimal scaling of the intrinsic phase uncertainty to be obtained. This enables
us to identify appropriate combinations of states to use. The remaining
difficulty is that the ideal phase measurements to achieve this intrinic phase
uncertainty are often not physically realizable. The third innovation is to
solve this problem by using realizable measurements that closely approximate
the optimal measurements, enabling the optimal scaling to be preserved.

This study explores the process of learning to bid in competitive scenarios without prior knowledge of one's own value or worth. It delves into how individuals adapt their bidding strategies based on observed outcomes and feedback from others. Utilizing a combination of experimental design and observational studies, the research investigates the cognitive and behavioral patterns that emerge as participants gain experience. Key findings indicate that individuals initially rely heavily on external cues such as past bids and market trends before developing more personalized bidding strategies. The study also highlights the role of social influence and group dynamics in shaping initial and subsequent bids. Ultimately, the research concludes that through iterative learning and adaptation, individuals can effectively learn to bid without knowing their exact value, leading to improved strategic decision-making in competitive environments.

The rapid advancements in mobile and wireless networking technologies have significantly influenced the evolution of deep learning applications. This survey aims to systematically review the integration of deep learning techniques within mobile and wireless networks, focusing on their potential to enhance network performance and user experience. The methodology involves a comprehensive literature review, synthesizing findings from recent research articles, conference papers, and technical reports that discuss the deployment of deep learning algorithms in key areas such as resource allocation, network optimization, security, and interference management. Key findings reveal that deep learning approaches have shown promising results in predicting network traffic patterns, improving data transmission efficiency, and enhancing the robustness of network security measures. Moreover, several case studies highlight the successful implementation of deep learning models in real-world scenarios, demonstrating improvements in latency and throughput. Despite the progress, this survey identifies critical challenges such as the need for efficient model training on resource-constrained devices and the implications of privacy and data security. The conclusion emphasizes that while deep learning presents transformative opportunities for mobile and wireless networking, addressing these challenges is essential for its sustainable integration. Future research directions are proposed, including the necessity for hybrid models that combine traditional networking techniques with advanced deep learning methods, to further optimize performance and adaptability in rapidly evolving networking environments.

I discuss a number of novel phenomenological features of QCD in high
transverse momentum reactions. The presence of direct higher-twist processes,
where a proton is produced directly in the hard subprocess, can explain the
"baryon anomaly" -- the large proton-to-pion ratio seen at RHIC in high
centrality heavy ion collisions. Direct hadronic processes can also account for
the deviation from leading-twist PQCD scaling at fixed x_T = 2p_T/\sqrt s. I
suggest that the "ridge" -- the same-side long-range rapidity correlation
observed at RHIC in high centrality heavy ion collisions is due to the imprint
of semihard DGLAP gluon radiation from initial-state partons which have
transverse momenta biased toward the trigger. Rescattering interactions from
gluon-exchange, normally neglected in the parton model, have a profound effect
in QCD hard-scattering reactions, leading to leading-twist single-spin
asymmetries, diffractive deep inelastic scattering, diffractive hard hadronic
reactions, the breakdown of the Lam-Tung relation in Drell-Yan reactions,
nuclear shadowing --all leading-twist dynamics not incorporated in the
light-front wavefunctions of the target computed in isolation. Antishadowing is
shown to be quark flavor specific and thus different in charged and neutral
deep inelastic lepton-nucleus scattering. I also discuss the consequences of
color-octet intrinsic heavy quark distributions in the proton for heavy
particle and Higgs production at high x_F. The AdS/CFT correspondence between
Anti-de Sitter space and conformal gauge theories allows one to compute the
analytic form of frame-independent light-front wavefunctions of mesons and
baryons and to compute quark and gluon hadronization at the amplitude level.

The verification of multithreaded software is still a challenge. This comes
mainly from the fact that the number of thread interleavings grows
exponentially in the number of threads. The idea that thread interleavings can
be studied with a matrix calculus is a novel approach in this research area.
Our sparse matrix representations of the program are manipulated using a lazy
implementation of Kronecker algebra. One goal is the generation of a data
structure called Concurrent Program Graph (CPG) which describes all possible
interleavings and incorporates synchronization while preserving completeness.
We prove that CPGs in general can be represented by sparse adjacency matrices.
Thus the number of entries in the matrices is linear in their number of lines.
Hence efficient algorithms can be applied to CPGs. In addition, due to
synchronization only very small parts of the resulting matrix are actually
needed, whereas the rest is unreachable in terms of automata. Thanks to the
lazy implementation of the matrix operations the unreachable parts are never
calculated. This speeds up processing significantly and shows that this
approach is very promising. Various applications including data flow analysis
can be performed on CPGs. Furthermore, the structure of the matrices can be
used to prove properties of the underlying program for an arbitrary number of
threads. For example, deadlock freedom is proved for a large class of programs.

We investigate hypergraphic LP relaxations for the Steiner tree problem,
primarily the partition LP relaxation introduced by Koenemann et al. [Math.
Programming, 2009]. Specifically, we are interested in proving upper bounds on
the integrality gap of this LP, and studying its relation to other linear
relaxations. Our results are the following. Structural results: We extend the
technique of uncrossing, usually applied to families of sets, to families of
partitions. As a consequence we show that any basic feasible solution to the
partition LP formulation has sparse support. Although the number of variables
could be exponential, the number of positive variables is at most the number of
terminals. Relations with other relaxations: We show the equivalence of the
partition LP relaxation with other known hypergraphic relaxations. We also show
that these hypergraphic relaxations are equivalent to the well studied
bidirected cut relaxation, if the instance is quasibipartite. Integrality gap
upper bounds: We show an upper bound of sqrt(3) ~ 1.729 on the integrality gap
of these hypergraph relaxations in general graphs. In the special case of
uniformly quasibipartite instances, we show an improved upper bound of 73/60 ~
1.216. By our equivalence theorem, the latter result implies an improved upper
bound for the bidirected cut relaxation as well.

This study investigates single top-quark production via both strong and electroweak supersymmetric (SUSY) flavor-changing neutral currents at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our analysis employs advanced Monte Carlo simulations to model the complex interactions within the SUSY framework, focusing on processes that lead to single top-quark events. We aim to identify distinctive signatures such as displaced vertices and missing transverse momentum, which are characteristic of SUSY contributions. By comparing these results against data from CMS and ATLAS experiments, we explore the feasibility of distinguishing between SUSY-induced single top-quark production and other backgrounds. Key methodologies include detailed event reconstruction algorithms and stringent cuts to enhance signal purity. The results reveal significant discrepancies in the measured event rates compared to predictions from Standard Model expectations, suggesting the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model. This research underscores the potential of future high-energy collider experiments to probe SUSY models through their impact on single top-quark production mechanisms.

We investigate the entanglement dynamics of quantum systems in a Kerr spacetime to elucidate the interplay between quantum information processes and general relativistic effects. Our study focuses on assessing how entanglement is influenced when quantum fields evolve in the vicinity of a rotating black hole, characterized by the Kerr metric. Using the framework of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, we develop a robust method to quantify entanglement by employing the concept of the entanglement entropy. To address the complex geometry of Kerr spacetime, we implement a mode decomposition approach that accommodates the axial symmetry and rotational characteristics of the black hole. Our findings reveal that the black hole's rotational parameter uniquely modulates entanglement dynamics, inducing both decoherence and entanglement generation depending on the initial state configuration and field parameters. We observe that the dragging effect inherent in Kerr geometry causes significant alterations in the entanglement distribution between spatial regions, which we model through Bogoliubov transformations. Furthermore, the ergosphere's interaction with quantum fields presents a novel non-local entanglement channel not present in static spacetimes. This study provides insights into potential mechanisms by which rotating black holes can be harnessed for quantum information storage and transmission. Our results pave the way for future explorations into quantum protocols in strong gravitational fields, offering a foundational understanding that bridges quantum mechanics with general relativity. Through this work, we contribute crucial advancements to the theoretical underpinnings necessary for developing gravitationally robust quantum technologies.

The quenching of star formation in the Milky Way remains a pivotal topic in understanding the lifecycle of galaxies. Our study utilizes high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) to investigate periods of reduced star formation in our Galaxy. Focusing on comprehensive elemental abundance analyses, we aim to identify signatures of quenching episodes and elucidate the mechanisms driving these processes. We examined data from over 100,000 stars across diverse Galactic components, enabling precise age dating and chemical profiling. Our methodology combines observational data with advanced chemical evolution models to trace the temporal evolution of the Milky Way’s star formation rates. Key findings reveal that a significant quenching event occurred approximately 7 billion years ago, characterized by a marked decline in the formation of young stars and specific elemental abundance patterns indicative of suppressed star formation environments. This period coincides with a series of external perturbers, including potential accretion events and interactions with satellite galaxies, suggesting a complex interplay between intrinsic and extrinsic factors contributing to quenching. Our results provide compelling evidence that the Galaxy experienced phases of dynamic evolution punctuated by significant shifts in star-forming activity. In conclusion, the integration of spectroscopic data with theoretical models offers profound insights into the quiescent phases of the Milky Way, advancing our understanding of galactic evolution and the overarching processes leading to periods of diminished star formation. This study underscores the critical role of detailed chemical investigations in unraveling the nuanced history of our Galaxy.

This study investigates the application of Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) sparse image reconstruction techniques to improve the efficiency and accuracy of radio astronomy imaging. LOFAR, a next-generation radio telescope, operates at low frequencies and suffers from significant challenges in reconstructing high-resolution images from its sparse and distributed array of antennas. Traditional image reconstruction methods, such as the standard Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) approach, are computationally intensive and often fail to achieve optimal performance due to the limited number of available data points.  The objective of this research is to develop and evaluate novel sparse image reconstruction algorithms specifically designed for LOFAR data, leveraging the unique characteristics of the telescope's array configuration. Our approach combines the strengths of compressed sensing and sparse Bayesian learning techniques to efficiently recover the underlying image from the LOFAR data. We evaluate the performance of our proposed method using a combination of simulated and real LOFAR data, comparing it to the standard MLE approach and other state-of-the-art methods.  Our results show that the proposed sparse image reconstruction algorithm achieves significant improvements in image quality and reconstruction time, outperforming the standard MLE approach and other methods. The algorithm is particularly effective in recovering faint and compact sources, which are challenging to detect in LOFAR data. The findings of this research have important implications for the future of LOFAR and other next-generation radio telescopes, enabling more efficient and accurate imaging of the sky.

The Planck satellite data have revealed intriguing anomalies, suggesting the existence of extra relativistic degrees of freedom (XRDF) beyond the standard model (SM) of particle physics. This study explores the possibility of accommodating XRDF without introducing new particles, by modifying the SM Lagrangian through an extension to the metric tensor. The extension preserves the Lorentz invariance and introduces a new vector degree of freedom, leading to an effective extra scalar degree of freedom. We employ a background field approach to study the effects of this modification on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies, and use Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis to determine the best-fit parameters. The results suggest that the XRDF contribution to the CMB anisotropies is consistent with the Planck data, and the introduction of the new vector degree of freedom improves the fit significantly. The implications of these findings are discussed, including potential tests of the proposed model through future experiments. Our work provides a novel and intriguing framework for accommodating XRDF without introducing new particles, which could shed new light on the nature of dark energy and the fundamental laws of physics.

This research explores the incorporation of molecular hydrogen (H₂) and carbon monoxide (CO) into galaxy simulations, considering the effects of dust evolution. The study aims to improve our understanding of interstellar medium dynamics within galaxies by accurately representing gas molecules and their interactions with dust grains. Utilizing a suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, we incorporated realistic dust properties and evolution models to simulate the formation and destruction of dust grains. By tracking the chemical abundances of H₂ and CO, we examined how these molecules vary across different galactic environments. Key findings indicate that the presence of dust significantly influences the formation and distribution of H₂ and CO, affecting star formation rates and feedback processes. The analysis reveals that regions with higher dust content exhibit more efficient molecular gas cooling and enhanced star formation activity. This work contributes to refining galaxy formation models by integrating detailed physical processes, thereby providing a more comprehensive framework for studying the interplay between stellar evolution, galactic structure, and molecular gas chemistry.

Survivable network design is crucial for ensuring reliable communication systems in the face of failures. This paper proposes an implicit optimization approach to address the survivability of network designs. The objective is to minimize the impact of failures on network performance while considering costs and constraints. The methodology involves formulating the survivable network design problem as an optimization model that accounts for both primary and backup paths. By leveraging implicit optimization techniques, such as implicit enumeration and implicit filtering, the approach efficiently explores a large solution space. The key findings suggest that the implicit optimization approach leads to significant improvements in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency compared to traditional methods. In conclusion, the proposed method offers a promising solution for designing survivable networks that can effectively withstand failures while optimizing network resources. This research contributes to the advancement of network design strategies that prioritize survivability in the face of unforeseen events.

We investigated the elasticity of DNA and the impact of dendrimer binding on its mechanical properties. Our experiments utilized atomic force microscopy (AFM) to measure the extension and relaxation of DNA molecules under various stretching conditions. We found that the elasticity of DNA varies significantly with the degree of stretching, with the most elastic regions exhibiting a linear relationship between force and extension. Notably, our results indicate that dendrimer binding significantly enhances the elasticity of DNA, particularly at higher stretching forces. This enhancement is attributed to the interaction between dendrimer surface groups and the phosphate backbone of DNA, which facilitates the transfer of mechanical energy and reduces the energy required for DNA extension. Furthermore, we observed that the binding of dendrimers to DNA leads to a reduction in the number of free ends, resulting in a more uniform and stable molecule. Our findings have significant implications for the design of novel DNA-based nanoscale devices and systems, where the controlled manipulation of DNA elasticity is crucial for achieving precise mechanical behavior. By elucidating the relationship between dendrimer binding and DNA elasticity, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between DNA and its environment, and paves the way for the development of innovative applications in fields such as biomedicine and materials science.

Computational analysis of time-course data with an underlying causal
structure is needed in a variety of domains, including neural spike trains,
stock price movements, and gene expression levels. However, it can be
challenging to determine from just the numerical time course data alone what is
coordinating the visible processes, to separate the underlying prima facie
causes into genuine and spurious causes and to do so with a feasible
computational complexity. For this purpose, we have been developing a novel
algorithm based on a framework that combines notions of causality in philosophy
with algorithmic approaches built on model checking and statistical techniques
for multiple hypotheses testing. The causal relationships are described in
terms of temporal logic formulae, reframing the inference problem in terms of
model checking. The logic used, PCTL, allows description of both the time
between cause and effect and the probability of this relationship being
observed. We show that equipped with these causal formulae with their
associated probabilities we may compute the average impact a cause makes to its
effect and then discover statistically significant causes through the concepts
of multiple hypothesis testing (treating each causal relationship as a
hypothesis), and false discovery control. By exploring a well-chosen family of
potentially all significant hypotheses with reasonably minimal description
length, it is possible to tame the algorithm's computational complexity while
exploring the nearly complete search-space of all prima facie causes. We have
tested these ideas in a number of domains and illustrate them here with two
examples.

This research investigates the redshift evolution of rest-UV spectroscopic properties in Lyman Break Galaxies at redshifts approximately ranging from 2 to 4. The primary objective is to understand how the rest-UV spectroscopic features of these galaxies evolve over this redshift range. The methodology employed in this study involves collecting and analyzing rest-UV spectroscopic data from a sample of Lyman Break Galaxies at different redshift bins within the specified range. Key findings reveal systematic changes in the rest-UV spectroscopic properties of Lyman Break Galaxies as redshift increases from 2 to 4. Specifically, we observe variations in the strengths of key spectral features and in the overall shape of the rest-UV spectra. These variations provide insights into the physical properties and evolutionary processes at play in Lyman Break Galaxies during this critical redshift period. In conclusion, our research contributes to a better understanding of the evolution of galaxies in the early universe, shedding light on the mechanisms driving the observed changes in rest-UV spectroscopic properties in Lyman Break Galaxies at redshifts between 2 and 4.

Galaxy pre-processing in substructures around z$\sim$0.4 galaxy clusters has been investigated through a combination of observational and theoretical methodologies. Utilizing data from the XYZ telescope, the study aims to understand the mechanisms driving galaxy evolution within these environments. By examining the properties and distributions of galaxies in substructures, including their star formation rates and morphologies, key insights into the pre-processing effects before galaxies enter the clusters are obtained. The methodology involves analyzing the spatial relationships between galaxies and their parent clusters, as well as conducting simulations to model the interactions occurring in these regions. The key findings reveal that galaxies in substructures exhibit distinct characteristics compared to those closer to the cluster core, indicating significant environmental influences even at early cosmic epochs. Overall, the results suggest that galaxy pre-processing in substructures plays a crucial role in shaping the galaxy population in clusters, impacting their star formation histories and overall evolution. This research sheds light on the complex processes governing galaxy evolution and highlights the importance of considering the broader cluster environment in understanding the formation of galaxies at intermediate redshifts.

We investigate the presence and characteristics of water clouds in Y dwarfs and exoplanets, aiming to enhance our understanding of atmospheric composition and cloud formation processes in substellar and planetary bodies. Using sophisticated atmospheric models combined with observational data from both ground-based and space-based telescopes, we analyze the spectral signatures indicative of water vapor and cloud formation within these celestial atmospheres. Our results reveal detectable water cloud formation in a significant fraction of Y dwarfs, suggesting that these objects, previously considered dry and cloud-free, may harbor complex meteorological phenomena. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to exoplanets located in diverse environments, identifying variations in cloud composition and structure influenced by factors such as temperature, pressure, and atmospheric chemistry. We employ a comparative methodology, juxtaposing our findings with existing models of cloud behavior in gas giant planets, thereby bridging the gap between exoplanetary science and brown dwarf characterization. We present the implications of our findings, highlighting how the presence of water clouds can modify the energy balance and potentially affect habitability in certain exoplanets. Our study underscores the importance of water clouds in understanding the climate dynamics of both Y dwarfs and exoplanets, ultimately paving the way for future observational campaigns and theoretical explorations aimed at elucidating the atmospheric properties of these intriguing celestial objects. This work serves as a pivotal step towards integrating knowledge from astrochemistry, atmospheric physics, and planetary science, contributing to a more comprehensive framework for studying distant worlds.

Using a sample of 69,919 red giants from the SDSS-III/APOGEE Data Release 12,
we measure the distribution of stars in the [$\alpha$/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] plane and
the metallicity distribution functions (MDF) across an unprecedented volume of
the Milky Way disk, with radius $3<R<15$ kpc and height $|z|<2$ kpc. Stars in
the inner disk ($R<5$ kpc) lie along a single track in [$\alpha$/Fe] vs.
[Fe/H], starting with $\alpha$-enhanced, metal-poor stars and ending at
[$\alpha$/Fe]$\sim0$ and [Fe/H]$\sim+0.4$. At larger radii we find two distinct
sequences in [$\alpha$/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] space, with a roughly solar-$\alpha$
sequence that spans a decade in metallicity and a high-$\alpha$ sequence that
merges with the low-$\alpha$ sequence at super-solar [Fe/H]. The location of
the high-$\alpha$ sequence is nearly constant across the disk, however there
are very few high-$\alpha$ stars at $R>11$ kpc. The peak of the midplane MDF
shifts to lower metallicity at larger $R$, reflecting the Galactic metallicity
gradient. Most strikingly, the shape of the midplane MDF changes systematically
with radius, with a negatively skewed distribution at $3<R<7$ kpc, to a roughly
Gaussian distribution at the solar annulus, to a positively skewed shape in the
outer Galaxy. For stars with $|z|>1$ kpc or [$\alpha$/Fe]$>0.18$, the MDF shows
little dependence on $R$. The positive skewness of the outer disk MDF may be a
signature of radial migration; we show that blurring of stellar populations by
orbital eccentricities is not enough to explain the reversal of MDF shape but a
simple model of radial migration can do so.

This study investigates the moments of exit times from wedges for non-homogeneous random walks with asymptotically zero drifts. The concept of exit times from wedges is a fundamental problem in probability theory, and understanding its properties is crucial for various applications in finance, physics, and engineering. The non-homogeneous random walk model is particularly interesting because it can be used to describe real-world phenomena where the underlying dynamics change over time.  The objective of this research is to derive and analyze the moments of exit times from wedges for non-homogeneous random walks with asymptotically zero drifts. To achieve this, we employ a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. We first derive an expression for the moments of exit times using the Feynman-Kac formula, which is a powerful tool for solving partial differential equations. We then validate our results using numerical simulations, which provide a more realistic representation of the underlying dynamics.  Our key findings indicate that the moments of exit times from wedges for non-homogeneous random walks with asymptotically zero drifts exhibit non-trivial behavior. Specifically, we find that the moments of exit times grow polynomially with time, and the rate of growth depends on the specific parameters of the random walk. These results have important implications for the analysis and modeling of real-world phenomena, such as option pricing and risk management.  In conclusion, this research provides a comprehensive analysis of the moments of exit times from wedges for non-homogeneous random walks with asymptotically zero drifts. Our results have significant implications for the development of more accurate models and methods for analyzing complex systems, and they contribute to the ongoing understanding of the properties of non-homogeneous random walks.

This study explores the intricate relationships between orbispaces, orthogonal spaces, and the universal compact Lie group from a topological and algebraic perspective. The motivation behind this research stems from the need to better understand the role orbispaces play in the framework of modern geometry and their connections with representation theory. Our primary objective was to delineate how the structures of orthogonal spaces can be effectively modeled through orbispaces and how these relationships yield insights into the properties of the universal compact Lie group.   To achieve this, we employed a combination of homotopical techniques and categorical frameworks, alongside traditional topological methods, enabling a comprehensive analysis of the underlying structures. Key findings reveal that orbispaces not only serve as a generalization of classical spaces but also offer a robust categorical model for studying the actions of compact Lie groups. Moreover, we demonstrated that the interaction between orbispaces and orthogonal representations leads to new avenues for realizing complex algebraic structures within the context of group actions.  In conclusion, our results illuminate the profound connections among these mathematical domains, suggesting that orbispaces can act as a unifying framework for understanding representations of the universal compact Lie group. This research contributes to the field by providing new theoretical insights and opens up further investigations into the application of orbispaces in various areas of mathematics and theoretical physics.

As the proportion of total power supplied by renewable sources increases, it
gets more costly to use reserve generation to compensate for the variability of
renewables like solar and wind. Hence attention has been drawn to exploiting
flexibility in demand as a substitute for reserve generation. Flexibility has
different attributes. In this paper we consider loads requiring a constant
power for a specified duration (within say one day), whose flexibility resides
in the fact that power may be delivered at any time so long as the total
duration of service equals the load's specified duration. We give conditions
under which a variable power supply is adequate to meet these flexible loads,
and describe how to allocate the power to the loads. We also characterize the
additional power needed when the supply is inadequate. We study the problem of
allocating the available power to loads to maximize welfare, and show that the
welfare optimum can be sustained as a competitive equilibrium in a forward
market in which electricity is sold as service contracts differentiated by the
duration of service and power level. We compare this forward market with a spot
market in their ability to capture the flexiblity inherent in
duration-differentiated loads.

We investigated the spintronics properties of a graphene nanodisk-lead system, aiming to develop a novel quasi-ferromagnet for spin-based electronic applications. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements, we successfully fabricated and characterized the graphene nanodisk-lead system, demonstrating the emergence of quasi-ferromagnetic behavior. Our results show that the graphene nanodisk exhibits a high spin polarization of approximately 95%, resulting from the interplay between the spin-orbit coupling and the lead-induced spin polarization. By carefully tuning the graphene nanodisk's size and lead doping levels, we achieved a high spin polarization and a large anomalous Hall effect, indicating the potential for efficient spin-based electronics.   Our theoretical analysis revealed that the quasi-ferromagnetism arises from the interplay between the graphene's intrinsic spin-orbit coupling and the lead-induced spin polarization, resulting in a large spin polarization and anomalous Hall effect. Experimental measurements confirmed this theoretical prediction, demonstrating the feasibility of using graphene nanodisks as quasi-ferromagnets in spintronics applications. Our findings open up new avenues for the development of spin-based electronic devices, including spin-based transistors, logic gates, and memory devices.

Online platforms are an increasingly popular tool for people to produce,
promote or sell their work. However recent studies indicate that social
disparities and biases present in the real world might transfer to online
platforms and could be exacerbated by seemingly harmless design choices on the
site (e.g., recommendation systems or publicly visible success measures). In
this paper we analyze an exclusive online community of teams of design
professionals called Dribbble and investigate apparent differences in outcomes
by gender. Overall, we find that men produce more work, and are able to show it
to a larger audience thus receiving more likes. Some of this effect can be
explained by the fact that women have different skills and design different
images. Most importantly however, women and men position themselves differently
in the Dribbble community. Our investigation of users' position in the social
network shows that women have more clustered and gender homophilous following
relations, which leads them to have smaller and more closely knit social
networks. Overall, our study demonstrates that looking behind the apparent
patterns of gender inequalities in online markets with the help of social
networks and product differentiation helps us to better understand gender
differences in success and failure.

This study presents a dual approach to circuit quantization utilizing loop charges as a fundamental tool. The first part of our methodology involves applying the loop charge theorem to derive quantized circuit solutions, which are then validated through numerical simulations. In the second part, we explore a variational approach where the energy functional is minimized subject to the constraints imposed by the loop charge theorem. Both approaches yield consistent results, confirming the validity of our dual strategy. Problematically, previous methods often encountered difficulties in accurately quantizing circuits with non-trivial topologies. Our dual approach overcomes these challenges by providing a more comprehensive framework that accounts for both the global topology and local node voltages simultaneously. Key ideas include the integration of loop charges into circuit analysis and the development of a unified theoretical basis for quantization across different circuit configurations. Methodologically, we employed analytical derivations supported by computational validations to substantiate the effectiveness of our dual approach to circuit quantization.

Dynamic epidemic models have proven valuable for public health decision
makers as they provide useful insights into the understanding and prevention of
infectious diseases. However, inference for these types of models can be
difficult because the disease spread is typically only partially observed e.g.
in form of reported incidences in given time periods. This chapter discusses
how to perform likelihood-based inference for partially observed Markov
epidemic models when it is relatively easy to generate samples from the Markov
transmission model while the likelihood function is intractable. The first part
of the chapter reviews the theoretical background of inference for partially
observed Markov processes (POMP) via iterated filtering. In the second part of
the chapter the performance of the method and associated practical difficulties
are illustrated on two examples. In the first example a simulated outbreak data
set consisting of the number of newly reported cases aggregated by week is
fitted to a POMP where the underlying disease transmission model is assumed to
be a simple Markovian SIR model. The second example illustrates possible model
extensions such as seasonal forcing and over-dispersion in both, the
transmission and observation model, which can be used, e.g., when analysing
routinely collected rotavirus surveillance data. Both examples are implemented
using the R-package pomp (King et al., 2016) and the code is made available
online.
