The research aims to address the challenge of efficiently encoding and transmitting correlated data streams between multiple parties without direct communication between them. We propose a novel method that leverages the inherent redundancy in data using Kolmogorov complexity as a measure of information content. Our approach involves identifying patterns and dependencies within the data streams through statistical analysis and then compressing these patterns into a minimal Kolmogorov complexity representation. This allows for the transmission of compressed data along with an encoding of the necessary dependencies, enabling the receivers to reconstruct the original data streams independently. Through experimental evaluations conducted on various datasets, we demonstrate significant improvements in compression rates compared to traditional Slepian-Wolf coding methods. Key methodologies include rigorous statistical analysis to identify dependencies and efficient algorithms for encoding and decoding based on Kolmogorov complexity estimates. These findings contribute to advancements in distributed data compression techniques, particularly in scenarios where direct communication is limited or costly.

Non-classical states of light, such as entangled photon pairs and number
states, are essential for fundamental tests of quantum mechanics and optical
quantum technologies. The most widespread technique for creating these quantum
resources is the spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) of laser light
into photon pairs. Conservation of energy and momentum in this process, known
as phase-matching, gives rise to strong correlations which are used to produce
two-photon entanglement in various degrees of freedom. It has been a
longstanding goal of the quantum optics community to realise a source that can
produce analogous correlations in photon triplets, but of the many approaches
considered, none have been technically feasible. In this paper we report the
observation of photon triplets generated by cascaded down-conversion. Here each
triplet originates from a single pump photon, and therefore quantum
correlations will extend over all three photons in a way not achievable with
independently created photon pairs. We expect our photon-triplet source to open
up new avenues of quantum optics and become an important tool in quantum
technologies. Our source will allow experimental interrogation of novel quantum
correlations, the post-selection free generation of tripartite entanglement
without post- selection and the generation of heralded entangled-photon pairs
suitable for linear optical quantum computing. Two of the triplet photons have
a wavelength matched for optimal transmission in optical fibres, ideally suited
for three-party quantum communication. Furthermore, our results open
interesting regimes of non-linear optics, as we observe spontaneous
down-conversion pumped by single photons, an interaction also highly relevant
to optical quantum computing.

In the Galaxy there are 64 Be X-ray binaries known to-date. Out of those, 42
host a neutron star, and for the reminder the nature of a companion is not
known. None, so far, is known to host a black hole. There seems to be no
apparent mechanism that would prevent formation or detection of Be stars with
black holes. This disparity is referred to as a missing Be -- black hole X-ray
binary problem. We point out that current evolutionary scenarios that lead to
the formation of Be X-ray binaries predict that the ratio of these binaries
with neutron stars to the ones with black holes is rather high F_NStoBH=10-50,
with the more likely formation models providing the values at the high end. The
ratio is a natural outcome of (i) the stellar initial mass function that
produces more neutron stars than black holes and (ii) common envelope evolution
(i.e. a major mechanism involved in the formation of interacting binaries) that
naturally selects progenitors of Be X-ray binaries with neutron stars (binaries
with comparable mass components have more likely survival probabilities) over
ones with black holes (which are much more likely to be common envelope
mergers). A comparison of this ratio (i.e. F_NStoBH=30) with the number of
confirmed Be -- neutron star X-ray binaries (42) indicates that the expected
number of Be -- black hole X-ray binaries is of the order of only 0-2. This is
entirely consistent with the observed Galactic sample.

Neutrinos, a class of elementary particles, have long been considered to be massless. However, recent observations of the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure suggest that neutrinos may possess a non-zero mass. This mass leads to higher-order perturbations in the distribution of neutrinos, which in turn affect the large-scale structure of the universe.   The objective of this paper is to study the impact of higher-order massive neutrino perturbations on the large-scale structure of the universe.   We employ the publicly available BoltzTraP code to calculate the power spectrum of higher-order neutral density fluctuations. We use the Cosmic Microwave Background Five-Year data to estimate the neutrino mass and cold dark matter density parameters. We assume a flat ΛCDM universe with adiabatic initial conditions and analyze the effects of varying neutrino mass on large-scale structure.   Our results show that higher-order massive neutrino perturbations result in a significant reduction of power in the linear regime of large-scale structure, particularly on small scales. This reduction is due to the free-streaming of neutrinos, which causes the transfer of power from small to large scales. We also find that the amplitude of the matter power spectrum on large scales is insensitive to neutrino mass.   Our study provides new insights into the role of neutrinos in the large-scale structure of the universe. The higher-order neutrino perturbations, which have been neglected in previous studies, play a crucial role in shaping the distribution of matter on large scales. Our findings suggest that future observations of the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure can be used to constrain the neutrino mass and probe the nature of neutrino interactions.

The abstract focuses on a review of Apriori-based algorithms optimized for execution on the MapReduce framework, highlighting their efficiency and scalability in handling large datasets. Initially, the background discusses the fundamental principles of Apriori algorithm, emphasizing its role in association rule mining. It then delves into the limitations of traditional Apriori when applied to big data, particularly in terms of time and resource consumption. Following this, the objective outlines the aim of optimizing the Apriori algorithm for distributed computing environments using MapReduce.   The methodology section elaborates on how the Apriori algorithm was adapted for execution on the MapReduce framework, detailing modifications made to the original algorithm to leverage parallel processing capabilities. This includes the use of map functions to generate candidate itemsets and reduce functions to filter out non-supportable itemsets, all while maintaining the core logic of the algorithm.  Key findings reveal significant improvements in processing speed and scalability compared to traditional Apriori implementations. The experiments conducted demonstrate that the optimized Apriori algorithm can handle larger datasets with greater efficiency, thereby reducing execution times substantially. Additionally, these optimizations enable the algorithm to scale effectively as the size of the dataset increases.  In conclusion, the review underscores the effectiveness of applying Apriori-based algorithms within the MapReduce framework, presenting a viable solution for efficient big data analysis tasks. This approach not only enhances computational performance but also ensures robust scalability, making it an attractive option for real-world applications involving massive datasets.

Evidence from the BICEP2 experiment for a significant gravitational-wave
background has focussed attention on inflaton potentials $V(\phi) \propto
\phi^\alpha$ with $\alpha=2$ ("chaotic" or "$m^2\phi^2$" inflation) or with
smaller values of $\alpha$, as may arise in axion-monodromy models. Here we
show that reheating considerations may provide additional constraints to these
models. The reheating phase preceding the radiation era is modeled by an
effective equation-of-state parameter $w_{\rm re}$. The canonical reheating
scenario is then described by $w_{\rm re}=0$. The simplest $\alpha=2$ models
are consistent with $w_{\rm re} = 0$ for values of $n_s$ well within the
current $1\sigma$ range. Models with $\alpha=1$ or $\alpha=2/3$ require a more
exotic reheating phase, with $-1/3<w_{\rm re}<0$, unless $n_s$ falls above the
current $1\sigma$ range. Likewise, models with $\alpha=4$ require a physically
implausible $w_{\rm re}>1/3$, unless $n_s$ is close to the lower limit of the
$2\sigma$ range. For $m^2\phi^2$ inflation and canonical reheating as a
benchmark, we derive a relation $\log_{10}\left(T_{\rm re}/10^6\,{\rm GeV}
\right) \simeq 2000\,(n_s-0.96)$ between the reheat temperature $T_{\rm re}$
and the scalar spectral index $n_s$. Thus, if $n_s$ is close to its central
value, then $T_{\rm re}\lesssim 10^6$~GeV, just above the electroweak scale. If
the reheat temperature is higher, as many theorists may prefer, then the scalar
spectral index should be closer to $n_s\simeq0.965$ (at the pivot scale
$k=0.05\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$), near the upper limit of the $1\sigma$ error range.
Improved precision in the measurement of $n_s$ should allow $m^2\phi^2$,
axion-monodromy, and $\phi^4$ models to be distinguished, even without precise
measurement of $r$, and to test the $m^2\phi^2$ expectation of
$n_s\simeq0.965$.

Piecewise linear-quadratic programs (PLQP) represent a class of mathematical optimization problems characterized by objective functions that are piecewise composed of linear and quadratic segments. Despite their utility in various fields such as finance, engineering, and operations research, efficient computational strategies for solving PLQPs remain underexplored. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating the structural properties and solution techniques pertaining to PLQPs. The methodology involves an in-depth theoretical analysis of PLQP properties followed by the development and implementation of novel solution algorithms. Specifically, we integrate convex analysis and nonlinear programming techniques to formulate a comprehensive solution framework.   Key findings from the research indicate that PLQPs exhibit inherent convexity under specific conditions, enabling the application of efficient convex optimization methods. The proposed algorithm demonstrates significant improvements in computational efficiency when compared to conventional linear programming approaches, particularly in handling large-scale problems. Additionally, the adaptability of the algorithm allows for its application across a variety of problem settings, offering a robust tool for practitioners.   In conclusion, this study not only enhances the understanding of the mathematical underpinnings of PLQPs but also provides a practical algorithmic solution for their resolution. Future research could explore the integration of this framework with machine learning techniques to address dynamic applications, further broadening the scope and applicability of piecewise linear-quadratic programming in real-world optimization scenarios.

We present a novel approach for the joint detection and super-resolution estimation of multipath signal parameters, leveraging Incremental Automatic Relevance Determination (IARD). Our work addresses the challenge of accurately estimating signal parameters in environments characterized by multipath propagation, which often leads to degraded performance in traditional estimation techniques. By employing IARD, we enable the adaptive selection of relevant features while dynamically discarding irrelevant ones, thus enhancing the estimation accuracy and computational efficiency.   Through extensive simulations, we validate our method against standard benchmarks, demonstrating a significant improvement in parameter estimation accuracy and resolution capabilities under different noise conditions and multipath scenarios. Our results indicate that the proposed framework not only outperforms conventional methods in terms of parameter detection rates but also reduces the computational burden associated with high-dimensional data.   Moreover, the integration of joint detection and super-resolution techniques within the IARD framework reveals a synergistic effect, leading to improved estimation results compared to separate processing approaches. The key methodological innovations include the iterative refinement of signal parameter estimates based on a likelihood criterion and the incorporation of prior information about the multipath structure to further enhance performance.   In conclusion, our findings underline the effectiveness of IARD for the joint detection and super-resolution estimation of multipath signals, offering a robust solution to challenges posed by complex signal environments, which paves the way for advancements in various applications, such as wireless communications and radar systems.

The B[e] stars are a class of luminous, hot, and highly variable objects found in various galaxies, characterized by strong emission lines and unusual spectral profiles. Among these objects, HD 50138 III is a unique case, exhibiting a complex and dynamic spectrum with significant variability in its photospheric lines. This study aims to investigate the short-term line profile variability of the photospheric lines of HD 50138 III, a galactic unclassified B[e] star.  The objective of this research is to analyze the line profile variability of HD 50138 III, focusing on the H-alpha, H-beta, and He I lines, which are commonly used to study the properties of B[e] stars. A comprehensive analysis of high-resolution spectroscopic data was performed, covering a period of 12 months, to identify the frequency, amplitude, and duration of the line profile variability.  The results show that the photospheric lines of HD 50138 III exhibit significant variability, with a frequency of line profile changes of 3.5 cycles per day. The amplitude of the variability ranges from 10% to 30% of the mean line intensity, and the duration of the changes is typically on the order of 1-3 days. The line profile variability is correlated with the star's luminosity and spectral type, suggesting a relationship between the variability and the star's internal dynamics.  The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of B[e] stars, highlighting the importance of monitoring their variability to study their internal properties and behavior. The results also provide new insights into the relationship between line profile variability and the star's physical properties, which can be used to improve our understanding of these enigmatic objects.

Luminous quasars, characterized by exceptionally bright emissions from their accretion disks, are valuable probes of cosmic evolution and feedback processes in the early universe. This study investigates the outflow characteristics of luminous quasars at redshift $\sim0.4-0.8$, a transitional period in galaxy evolution. The primary objective is to examine the relationship between quasar outflows and their host galaxy properties, utilizing data from high-resolution spectroscopy of broad and narrow emission lines. We analyzed a sample of 50 luminous quasars, measuring outflow velocities and assessing their correlation with various parameters, including black hole mass and luminosity. Our methodology employed state-of-the-art spectral fitting techniques, combined with hydrodynamic simulations to model the impact of quasar feedback on surrounding interstellar media. Key findings reveal significant outflow velocities, with a mean value of approximately 1700 km/s, suggesting strong kinetic feedback effects that can influence star formation in host galaxies. Additionally, a correlation was identified between outflow strength and quasar luminosity, indicating that more luminous quasars tend to drive more powerful outflows. The results imply that the energetic outflows from these quasars play a critical role in regulating star formation and gas dynamics in their host galaxies, thus contributing to the understanding of the interplay between supermassive black holes and their environments in the early universe. In conclusion, this study enhances the understanding of quasar-related feedback mechanisms and their implications for galactic evolution during the specified redshift range.

Here we measure the absolute magnitude distributions (H-distribution) of the
dynamically excited and quiescent (hot and cold) Kuiper Belt objects (KBOs),
and test if they share the same H-distribution as the Jupiter Trojans. From a
compilation of all useable ecliptic surveys, we find that the KBO
H-distributions are well described by broken power-laws. The cold population
has a bright-end slope, $\alpha_{\textrm{1}}=1.5_{-0.2}^{+0.4}$, and break
magnitude, $H_{\textrm{B}}=6.9_{-0.2}^{+0.1}$ (r'-band). The hot population has
a shallower bright-end slope of, $\alpha_{\textrm{1}}=0.87_{-0.2}^{+0.07}$, and
break magnitude $H_{\textrm{B}}=7.7_{-0.5}^{+1.0}$. Both populations share
similar faint end slopes of $\alpha_2\sim0.2$. We estimate the masses of the
hot and cold populations are $\sim0.01$ and $\sim3\times10^{-4} \mbox{
M$_{\bigoplus}$}$. The broken power-law fit to the Trojan H-distribution has
$\alpha_\textrm{1}=1.0\pm0.2$, $\alpha_\textrm{2}=0.36\pm0.01$, and
$H_{\textrm{B}}=8.3$. The KS test reveals that the probability that the Trojans
and cold KBOs share the same parent H-distribution is less than 1 in 1000. When
the bimodal albedo distribution of the hot objects is accounted for, there is
no evidence that the H-distributions of the Trojans and hot KBOs differ. Our
findings are in agreement with the predictions of the Nice model in terms of
both mass and H-distribution of the hot and Trojan populations. Wide field
survey data suggest that the brightest few hot objects, with
$H_{\textrm{r'}}\lesssim3$, do not fall on the steep power-law slope of fainter
hot objects. Under the standard hierarchical model of planetesimal formation,
it is difficult to account for the similar break diameters of the hot and cold
populations given the low mass of the cold belt.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic events in the universe, often resulting in detectable optical afterglows. This study aims to investigate the characteristics and underlying mechanisms of optical afterglows, focusing on their peaks, plateaus, and decay profiles. By analyzing observational data from a sample of GRBs collected via space and ground-based telescopes, we study the temporal and spectral evolution of afterglows. Employing a combination of light curve modeling and spectral analysis, we assess the influence of the burst environment and progenitor characteristics on these features. Our findings indicate that the peak luminosity of optical afterglows is closely correlated with the inferred energy release and geometry of the GRB event. Plateaus, observed in a subset of afterglows, suggest prolonged central engine activity or interaction with the circumstellar medium, challenging the simplistic fireball model. Decay rates vary significantly, hinting at differences in local environments and energy dissipation mechanisms. Additionally, we identify several correlations between optical and multi-wavelength afterglow properties, suggesting that a comprehensive model should integrate broadband data. This work contributes to a nuanced understanding of the complex dynamics influencing GRB afterglows and highlights the need for coordinated observational efforts to capture the full range of GRB behavior. Future research should focus on integrating theoretical models with diverse observational datasets to unravel the intricate processes governing these astrophysical phenomena.

A spring-dashpot system based on the Voigt model was developed to model the
correlation between abdominal respiratory motion and tumor motion during lung
radiotherapy. The model was applied to clinical data comprising 52 treatment
beams from 10 patients, treated on the Mitsubishi Real-Time Radiation Therapy
system, Sapporo, Japan. In Stage 1, model parameters were optimized for
individual patients and beams to determine reference values and to investigate
how well the model can describe the data. In Stage 2, for each patient the
optimal parameters determined for a single beam were applied to data from other
beams to investigate whether a beam-specific set of model parameters is
sufficient to model tumor motion over a course of treatment.
  In Stage 1 the baseline root mean square (RMS) residual error for all
individually-optimized beam data was 0.90 plus or minus 0.40 mm. In Stage 2,
patient-specific model parameters based on a single beam were found to model
the tumor position closely, even for irregular beam data, with a mean increase
with respect to Stage 1 values in RMS error of 0.37 mm. On average the obtained
model output for the tumor position was 95% of the time within an absolute
bound of 2.0 mm and 2.6 mm in Stage 1 and 2, respectively.
  The model was capable of dealing with baseline, amplitude and frequency
variations of the input data, as well as phase shifts between the input tumor
and output abdominal signals. These results indicate that it may be feasible to
collect patient-specific model parameters during or prior to the first
treatment, and then retain these for the rest of the treatment period. The
model has potential for clinical application during radiotherapy treatment of
lung tumors.

The study investigates the anomalous low-temperature magnetoelastic properties of nanogranular (CoFeB)$_{x}$-(SiO$_{2}$)$_{1-x}$ composites, a class of materials known for their unique and tunable magnetic and elastic characteristics. The primary objective is to understand how varying the concentration 'x' of the ferromagnetic alloy affects the magnetoelastic behavior at cryogenic temperatures. A series of (CoFeB)$_{x}$-(SiO$_{2}$)$_{1-x}$ samples were synthesized using a co-sputtering technique, followed by structural and compositional characterizations to ensure consistency across the varying compositions. Magnetoelastic properties were probed using low-temperature magnetization and stress-strain measurements in the range of 2-30 K. Our findings reveal significant deviations from predicted magnetoelastic responses, particularly below 20 K, indicating that interfacial effects and quantum mechanical interactions in the nanogranular system play a crucial role. The dependence of magnetoelastic coefficients on 'x' was found to be non-linear, highlighting complex interactions between the magnetic grains and the non-magnetic matrix. Moreover, specific compositions exhibited an unexpected enhancement in mechanical stiffness which correlated with magnetic ordering transitions. These results suggest a coupling mechanism between the electronic states and the elastic properties, profoundly influenced by the nanoscale architecture. In conclusion, the unique low-temperature magnetoelastic properties observed in this composite system offer insights into designing advanced materials with tailored properties for applications such as magnetic sensors and actuators at cryogenic conditions. Further exploration into electronic structure and stress contributions is warranted to fully elucidate the underpinning mechanisms.

The advent of advanced observational facilities has significantly enhanced our understanding of the early universe, particularly in the study of cosmic inflation. This research paper presents a joint analysis of data from the BICEP2/Keck Array and the Planck satellite, focusing on the implications of polarized cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation. The primary objective of this study is to reconsolidate measurements of B-mode polarization and temperature anisotropies to provide a coherent picture of the inflationary epoch. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset, we employed sophisticated statistical techniques, including Bayesian analysis, to interpret the combined datasets and quantify the significance of primordial gravitational waves. Key findings indicate that while the BICEP2/Keck Array data suggest evidence of B-mode polarization consistent with inflationary gravitational waves, the Planck results provide constraints that challenge the robustness of these detections when foreground contamination is taken into account. Notably, our joint analysis reveals a revised upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio, which is crucial for interpreting the energy scale of inflation. This research underscores the importance of multi-facility approaches in cosmological studies and the need for careful foreground modeling. In conclusion, our findings advocate for further investigations to reconcile existing discrepancies, suggesting that a deeper understanding of cosmic inflation requires collaborations across multiple observational platforms to enhance the fidelity of cosmological models.

Motivated by models of human decision making proposed to explain commonly
observed deviations from conventional expected value preferences, we formulate
two stochastic multi-armed bandit problems with distorted probabilities on the
reward distributions: the classic $K$-armed bandit and the linearly
parameterized bandit settings. We consider the aforementioned problems in the
regret minimization as well as best arm identification framework for
multi-armed bandits. For the regret minimization setting in $K$-armed as well
as linear bandit problems, we propose algorithms that are inspired by Upper
Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithms, incorporate reward distortions, and exhibit
sublinear regret. For the $K$-armed bandit setting, we derive an upper bound on
the expected regret for our proposed algorithm, and then we prove a matching
lower bound to establish the order-optimality of our algorithm. For the
linearly parameterized setting, our algorithm achieves a regret upper bound
that is of the same order as that of regular linear bandit algorithm called
Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty Linear (OFUL) bandit algorithm, and unlike
OFUL, our algorithm handles distortions and an arm-dependent noise model. For
the best arm identification problem in the $K$-armed bandit setting, we propose
algorithms, derive guarantees on their performance, and also show that these
algorithms are order optimal by proving matching fundamental limits on
performance. For best arm identification in linear bandits, we propose an
algorithm and establish sample complexity guarantees. Finally, we present
simulation experiments which demonstrate the advantages resulting from using
distortion-aware learning algorithms in a vehicular traffic routing
application.

Deep-Earth volatile cycles couple the mantle with near-surface reservoirs.
Volatiles are emitted by volcanism and, in particular, from mid-ocean ridges,
which are the most prolific source of basaltic volcanism. Estimates of volatile
extraction from the asthenosphere beneath ridges typically rely on measurements
of undegassed lavas combined with simple petrogenetic models of the mean degree
of melting. Estimated volatile fluxes have large uncertainties; this is partly
due to a poor understanding of how volatiles are transported by magma in the
asthenosphere. Here, we assess the fate of mantle volatiles through numerical
simulations of melting and melt transport at mid-ocean ridges. Our simulations
are based on two-phase, magma/mantle dynamics theory coupled to idealised
thermodynamic model of mantle melting in the presence of water and carbon
dioxide. We combine simulation results with catalogued observations of all
ridge segments to estimate a range of likely volatile output from the global
mid-ocean ridge system. We thus predict global MOR crust production of 66-73
Gt/yr (22-24 km3/yr) and global volatile output of 52-110 Mt/yr, corresponding
to mantle volatile contents of 100--200~ppm. We find that volatile extraction
is limited: up to half of deep, volatile-rich melt is not focused to the axis
but is rather deposited along the LAB. As these distal melts crystallise and
fractionate, they metasomatise the base of the lithosphere, creating
rheological heterogeneity that could contribute to the seismic signature of the
LAB.

In this study, we present a unified theoretical framework for the description of nonlinear higher-order hydrodynamics, combining both kinetic and hydrodynamic approaches within a nonequilibrium statistical ensemble. Using the Boltzmann equation as the foundation, we extend the traditional hydrodynamic closure methods by introducing higher-order moments and nonlocal correlation functions. These extensions enable us to account for nonlinear hydrodynamic effects, which are crucial for accurately modeling complex fluid systems.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by investigating the well-known Burgers' equation and the more intricate MHD shock tube problem. For Burgers' equation, we show that our nonequilibrium statistical ensemble approach yields exact results when compared to the analytical solution, while existing hydrodynamic closure methods fail. For the MHD shock tube problem, our method captures the complex shock structure and enables us to investigate the effects of magnetic fields on fluid dynamics.  Additionally, our approach allows for the exploration of the underlying kinetic structures, providing insights into the microscopic processes that give rise to the observed macroscopic behavior. This includes the identification of precursor waves and their impact on shock formation.  Our work advances the understanding of nonlinear hydrodynamic phenomena and provides a versatile theoretical framework that can be applied to various fields, such as plasma physics, combustion engineering, and fluid mechanics. This new approach also paves the way for further developments in the area of nonequilibrium statistical ensemble theories and their applications to hydrodynamics and related fields.  In summary, we present a unified theoretical framework for nonlinear higher-order hydrodynamics, which combines kinetic and hydrodynamic approaches within a nonequilibrium statistical ensemble. Our method is shown to yield accurate results for complex fluid systems and provides valuable insights into the underlying microscopic processes.

In this work, we present low-complexity scheduling policies aimed at achieving both throughput and asymptotic delay optimality in multi-channel wireless networks. The problem of balancing network performance metrics under channel constraints is addressed through the development of novel algorithms that minimize computational overhead while ensuring optimal resource allocation. Our approach integrates aspects of Markov Decision Processes (MDP) and reinforcement learning techniques to dynamically adjust channel access probabilities based on current network conditions. Results demonstrate significant improvements in throughput and delay performance compared to existing static scheduling methods, with complexity reduced by over 80%. Key methodologies include policy iteration and Q-learning, which enable the system to adapt to varying traffic loads without manual intervention. The effectiveness of these policies is validated through simulations across a range of network scenarios, showcasing their applicability in both homogeneous and heterogeneous multi-channel environments.

We investigated the existence of Erdos-Hajnal-type theorems in the context of hypergraphs, a generalization of graphs that can represent complex relationships between multiple entities. Our primary objective was to establish a theoretical framework for understanding the structure and properties of hypergraphs, with a focus on their asymptotic behavior.   We began by revisiting the seminal Erdos-Hajnal-type theorems in graph theory, which have been instrumental in shaping our understanding of graph structure. However, these theorems have yet to be adapted to the realm of hypergraphs, where the relationships between entities are more intricate and nuanced.   To address this gap, we developed a novel approach that leverages advanced techniques from hypergraph theory and combinatorial design. Our method involved constructing a framework that enables the identification of hypergraph analogues of the classic graph-theoretic results. We then applied this framework to a range of hypergraph-specific problems, including the study of hypergraph Ramsey numbers and the existence of hypergraph-free subgraphs.   Our results demonstrate that the fundamental principles underlying Erdos-Hajnal-type theorems in graph theory can be extended to the hypergraph setting. We showed that certain hypergraph Ramsey numbers can be bounded in terms of graph Ramsey numbers, and that the existence of hypergraph-free subgraphs can be characterized in terms of graph-free subgraphs. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of hypergraph structure and the development of algorithms for hypergraph optimization.

Building discriminative representations for 3D data has been an important
task in computer graphics and computer vision research. Convolutional Neural
Networks (CNNs) have shown to operate on 2D images with great success for a
variety of tasks. Lifting convolution operators to 3D (3DCNNs) seems like a
plausible and promising next step. Unfortunately, the computational complexity
of 3D CNNs grows cubically with respect to voxel resolution. Moreover, since
most 3D geometry representations are boundary based, occupied regions do not
increase proportionately with the size of the discretization, resulting in
wasted computation. In this work, we represent 3D spaces as volumetric fields,
and propose a novel design that employs field probing filters to efficiently
extract features from them. Each field probing filter is a set of probing
points --- sensors that perceive the space. Our learning algorithm optimizes
not only the weights associated with the probing points, but also their
locations, which deforms the shape of the probing filters and adaptively
distributes them in 3D space. The optimized probing points sense the 3D space
"intelligently", rather than operating blindly over the entire domain. We show
that field probing is significantly more efficient than 3DCNNs, while providing
state-of-the-art performance, on classification tasks for 3D object recognition
benchmark datasets.

We examine He I 10830 profile morphologies for a sample of 56 Herbig Ae/Be
stars (HAEBES). We find significant differences between HAEBES and CTTSs in the
statistics of both blue-shifted absorption (i.e. mass outflows) and red-shifted
absorption features (i.e. mass infall or accretion). Our results suggest that,
in general, Herbig Be (HBe) stars do not accrete material from their inner
disks in the same manner as CTTSs, which are believed to accrete material via
magnetospheric accretion, while Herbig Ae (HAe) stars generally show evidence
for magnetospheric accretion. We find no evidence in our sample of narrow
blue--shifted absorption features which are typical indicators of inner disk
winds and are common in He I 10830 profiles of CTTSs. The lack of inner disk
wind signatures in HAEBES, combined with the paucity of detected magnetic
fields on these objects, suggests that accretion through large magnetospheres
which truncate the disk several stellar radii above the surface is not as
common for HAe and late-type HBe stars as it is for CTTSs. Instead, evidence is
found for smaller magnetospheres in the maximum red-shifted absorption
velocities in our HAEBE sample. These velocities are, on average, a smaller
fraction of the system escape velocity than is found for CTTSs, suggesting
accretion is taking place closer to the star. Smaller magnetospheres, and
evidence for boundary layer accretion in HBe stars, may explain the less common
occurrence of red--shifted absorption in HAEBES. Evidence is found that smaller
magnetospheres may be less efficient at driving outflows compared to CTTS
magnetospheres.

We present a novel approach to designing safety-critical systems by leveraging control barrier functions (CBFs) in quadratic programs. Our method enables the formal analysis and optimization of system safety, ensuring the robustness of control policies against unforeseen disturbances. By formulating safety constraints as quadratic inequalities, we can effectively capture the dynamics of complex systems and derive rigorous guarantees on the system's behavior. Our approach combines the strengths of CBFs, which provide a robust and computationally efficient means of ensuring safety, with the flexibility of quadratic programs, which allow for the incorporation of multiple objectives and constraints. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in guaranteeing system safety for a range of case studies. Our results show that the proposed approach can achieve optimal control policies that satisfy stringent safety requirements, while also accommodating multiple performance objectives. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient, enabling the analysis and optimization of large-scale systems. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the development of safety-critical systems, highlighting the potential benefits and limitations of the proposed approach.

Graph partitioning and local data exploration are fundamental challenges in graph theory and data analysis, impacting various applications from social network analysis to community detection. This paper presents a novel local spectral method for graphs aimed at enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of graph partitions while enabling localized exploration of data structures. The primary objective is to devise a method that leverages the spectral properties of graphs to optimize partitioning schemes and facilitate insightful local analysis.   The proposed methodology employs a combination of spectral clustering and localized spectral embeddings to identify optimal partitions within large-scale graphs while maintaining computational efficiency. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, the efficacy of this local spectral method is evaluated against established partitioning techniques. Key findings indicate that our method significantly reduces computational costs and improves the quality of partitions, yielding enhanced modularity and cohesive communities without sacrificing the granularity of local exploration.   Furthermore, the application of this method to real-world data graphs illustrates its capacity to reveal interesting local structures and relationships, thereby facilitating richer data interpretations. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that a local spectral approach can effectively address both graph partitioning and local exploration challenges, offering a robust tool for researchers and practitioners to analyze complex networks with greater precision and insight. The implications of this research extend to various domains, including social sciences, biology, and machine learning, highlighting the versatility of spectral methods in graph analysis.

We use a discrete-time proportional hazards model of time to involuntary
employment termination. This model enables us to examine both the continuous
effect of the age of an employee and whether that effect has varied over time,
generalizing earlier work [Kadane and Woodworth J. Bus. Econom. Statist. 22
(2004) 182--193]. We model the log hazard surface (over age and time) as a
thin-plate spline, a Bayesian smoothness-prior implementation of penalized
likelihood methods of surface-fitting [Wahba (1990) Spline Models for
Observational Data. SIAM]. The nonlinear component of the surface has only two
parameters, smoothness and anisotropy. The first, a scale parameter, governs
the overall smoothness of the surface, and the second, anisotropy, controls the
relative smoothness over time and over age. For any fixed value of the
anisotropy parameter, the prior is equivalent to a Gaussian process with linear
drift over the time--age plane with easily computed eigenvectors and
eigenvalues that depend only on the configuration of data in the time--age
plane and the anisotropy parameter. This model has application to legal cases
in which a company is charged with disproportionately disadvantaging older
workers when deciding whom to terminate. We illustrate the application of the
modeling approach using data from an actual discrimination case.

The abstract focuses on the epoch of disk assembly in galaxies, specifically using z~2 as a reference point. This period, occurring approximately 10 billion years ago, marks a critical phase where the formation of galactic disks begins to accelerate significantly. The research aims to investigate the properties and dynamics of star formation within these newly forming disks. Utilizing a combination of observational data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and simulations, the study seeks to understand how gas accretion, feedback mechanisms, and gravitational instabilities contribute to the development of galactic disks during this epoch.  Methodologically, the analysis involves detailed spectroscopic measurements of distant galaxies at redshifts corresponding to z~2, combined with numerical models that simulate galaxy evolution. Key findings include the identification of high-mass star-forming regions within these galaxies, which exhibit distinct signatures indicative of ongoing disk assembly. Additionally, the study highlights the role of supermassive black holes and their activity in regulating the rate and morphology of disk formation.  Concluding, the research underscores the importance of understanding the conditions under which galaxies acquire their characteristic spiral or elliptical structures. Insights gained from this study provide valuable context for contemporary galaxy formation theories and offer a deeper understanding of the early stages of cosmic structure formation.

In this work, we address the challenges associated with sparse time-frequency representations in the context of dynamical systems. Traditional time-frequency analysis methods often struggle with achieving a balance between time and frequency resolution, which can lead to difficulties in accurately capturing the dynamics of complex systems. We propose a novel framework that leverages the advantage of sparse representations to improve the resolution and interpretability of time-frequency analysis. By employing sparsity-promoting techniques such as lasso regression and basis pursuit, we enhance the extraction of meaningful features from time-series data that are governed by underlying dynamical systems.  Our methodology involves constructing a sparse representation of the time-frequency plane using an adaptive basis that modulates according to the dynamical behavior of the system. We implement a series of computational experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the performance of the proposed framework. The results demonstrate significant improvements in terms of representation compactness and accuracy in capturing key dynamic characteristics when compared to conventional time-frequency methods.  Furthermore, we develop a theoretical foundation to support the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating its robustness in maintaining the structural integrity of the underlying dynamical model while ensuring computational efficiency. Consequently, our work contributes to a deeper understanding and enhancement of sparse representations, providing a compelling solution to the limitations faced by existing time-frequency analytical methods within dynamical systems analysis. The framework holds significant implications for applications in fields such as signal processing, control systems, and systems biology.

Dark energy, the dominant energy component of the universe, remains one of the greatest mysteries in modern cosmology. Its nature and origin are still unknown. In recent years, standard sirens have emerged as a promising tool for probing dark energy properties. These sirens include type Ia supernovae and gravitational waves from merging neutron stars and black holes. By comparing the luminosity distances and redshift data of these standard sirens with the predictions of cosmological models, we can infer the properties of dark energy.  In this study, we reconstructed the equation of state (EoS) of dark energy using data from the latest observational surveys, such as the Pantheon sample of supernovae and the LIGO/Virgo catalog of gravitational wave events. We employed the Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to sample the posterior probability distributions of the EoS parameters. Our results are consistent with a cosmological constant model (LambdaCDM), but we also found evidence for an evolving EoS. We further examined the implications of our findings for the Hubble constant tension and the nature of dark energy.  Our results demonstrate that standard sirens can be used to constrain the properties of dark energy, offering new insights into the enigma of the universe's dominant energy component. By combining data from various observational probes, we can improve the precision and accuracy of our dark energy measurements and help pave the way for a better understanding of this elusive phenomenon.

The abstract focuses on vacuum instability phenomena observed in the context of slowly varying electric fields. Historically, vacuum fluctuations have been studied under conditions of high-frequency electric fields, but recent advancements have highlighted the importance of examining these instabilities in the regime of slowly varying fields. This research aims to explore how slowly varying electric fields can induce vacuum instability, which has implications for various physical systems such as plasma physics, astrophysics, and particle accelerators.  The methodology involves theoretical modeling and numerical simulations of charged particle motion within the influence of slowly varying electric fields. The study employs perturbation theory and quantum field theory to analyze the stability of vacuum states under different parameters of the electric field, including its frequency and amplitude.  Key findings indicate that while high-frequency fields typically lead to vacuum decay due to the Casimir effect, slowly varying fields can exhibit distinct behaviors, including the emergence of new types of instabilities and thresholds for vacuum instability. These findings suggest that the dynamics of vacuum states in slowly varying fields require careful consideration, especially in applications where such fields are prevalent.  In conclusion, this research contributes to our understanding of vacuum instability in slowly varying electric fields, providing insights into the behavior of quantum fields under less extreme conditions. The results could have significant implications for technological applications and fundamental physics research.

We study the evolution of non-periodic cosmic string loops containing
Y-junctions, such as may form during the evolution of a network of (p,q) cosmic
superstrings. We set up and solve the Nambu-Goto equations of motion for a loop
with junctions, focusing attention on a specific static and planar initial loop
configuration. After a given time, the junctions collide and the Nambu-Goto
description breaks down. We also study the same loop configuration in a
U(1)xU(1) field theory model that allows composite vortices with corresponding
Y-junctions. We show that the field theory and Nambu-Goto evolution are
remarkably similar until the collision time. However, in the field theory
evolution a new phenomenon occurs: the composite vortices can unzip, producing
in the process new Y-junctions, whose separation may grow significantly,
destabilizing the configuration. In particular, an initial loop with two
Y-junctions may evolve to a configuration with six Y-junctions (all distant
from each other). Setting up this new configuration as an initial condition for
Nambu Goto strings, we solve for its evolution and establish conditions under
which it is stable to the decay mode seen in the field theory case. Remarkably,
the condition closely matches that seen in the field theory simulations, and is
expressed in terms of simple parameters of the Nambu-Goto system. This implies
that there is an easy way to understand the instability in terms of which
region of parameter space leads to stable or unstable unzippings.

This study focuses on developing a personalized model for predicting pancreatic tumor growth through group learning techniques. The work attempts to address the significant challenge of individual variability in pancreatic cancer progression, which has traditionally been overlooked by existing predictive models. Our approach involves clustering patients based on their clinical characteristics and genetic profiles, then training a predictive model for each cluster separately. These models are subsequently aggregated using group learning algorithms to create a unified prediction system that accounts for both intra-cluster and inter-cluster variations. Results indicate that our personalized approach outperforms traditional models in terms of accuracy and reliability, particularly when applied to subsets of patients with similar characteristics but distinct biological profiles. Key methodologies employed include unsupervised clustering, supervised learning, and ensemble aggregation techniques, all aimed at enhancing the predictive capabilities of the system while minimizing overfitting.

Herein, we describe new methods to produce colloidal particle chains of three
stiffness regimes that can be observed on a single-particle level, that is, on
the level of the monomers that make up the chain; the chains can even be
observed in concentrated systems without using molecular tracers. These methods
rely on the following: dipolar interactions induced by external electric fields
in combination with long-range charge repulsion to assemble the particles into
chains only, and a bonding step to ensure that the particles remain assembled
as chains even after the external field is switched off. We can control the
length and the flexibility of the chains. Additionally, we demonstrate that our
method is generally applicable by using it to prepare several other colloidal
polymers, such as block-copolymer chains, which are formed by combining rigid
and flexible chains, spherocylinders, which are formed by heating rigid chains,
and both atactic and isotactic chains, which are formed from
heterodimericparticle monomer units. We demonstrate that the flexibility of the
charged chains can be tuned from very rigid (rod-like) to semiflexible (as in
the simplified polymer model of beads on a string) by changing the ionic
strength. This method can, in principle, be used with any type of colloidal
particle. Moreover, our systems can be matched in terms of refractive index and
density, so that bulk measurements in real space are possible.

of a symmetric $G-$homogeneous space (where $G$ is a simply-connected

$\mathfrak g$ of $G$ operates naturally on the cohomology group with support :
$H^c_C(L)$. One gives here a necessary condition on the cell $C$ for that
$\mathfrak g-$module have a finite dimensional simple subquotient. As
applications one calculates the Euler-Poincar\'e characteristic of $L$ over $X$
and one estimates the higher cohomology group $H^d(X,L)$, $d \ge 0$, with exact
formulae in some cases among which the case of the complete conic variety. --

A catalogue of the morphological features for the complete Spitzer Survey of
Stellar Structure in Galaxies (S$^4$G), including 2352 nearby galaxies, is
presented. The measurements are made using 3.6 $\mu$m images, largely tracing
the old stellar population; at this wavelength the effects of dust are also
minimal. The measured features are the sizes, ellipticities, and orientations
of bars, rings, ringlenses, and lenses. Measured in a similar manner are also
barlenses (lens-like structures embedded in the bars), which are not lenses in
the usual sense, being rather the more face-on counterparts of the boxy/peanut
structures in the edge-on view. In addition, pitch angles of spiral arm
segments are measured for those galaxies where they can be reliably traced.
More than one pitch angle may appear for a single galaxy. All measurements are
made in a human-supervised manner so that attention is paid to each galaxy. We
used isophotal analysis, unsharp masking, and fitting ellipses to measured
structures. We find that the sizes of the inner rings and lenses normalized to
barlength correlate with the galaxy mass: the normalized sizes increase toward
the less massive galaxies; it has been suggested that this is related to the
larger dark matter content in the bar region in these systems. Bars in the low
mass galaxies are also less concentrated, likely to be connected to the mass
cut-off in the appearance of the nuclear rings and lenses. We also show
observational evidence that barlenses indeed form part of the bar, and that a
large fraction of the inner lenses in the non-barred galaxies could be former
barlenses in which the thin outer bar component has dissolved.

The burgeoning volume of healthcare data presents significant challenges, particularly concerning missing information, which can impede the reliability of outcomes in trauma studies. This research aims to address the issue of missing data within large healthcare datasets by employing advanced imputation techniques in a case study focusing on unknown trauma outcomes. We conducted a retrospective analysis of a comprehensive trauma registry, encompassing over 30,000 records with substantial missing data. Various imputation methods, including multiple imputation and predictive mean matching, were applied to evaluate their effectiveness in recovering lost information. Our findings reveal that multiple imputation notably improved the accuracy of outcome predictions while maintaining the integrity of the dataset. Specifically, the application of this technique reduced bias in estimates related to mortality and morbidity rates, enhancing the validity of findings drawn from the data. Furthermore, we identified critical variables influencing the likelihood of trauma outcomes, underscoring the importance of complete data in making informed clinical decisions. This study concludes that systematic approaches to handling missing data, especially in the context of trauma outcomes, can significantly enhance research quality and healthcare delivery. The implications of our findings highlight the necessity for healthcare organizations to adopt robust data governance practices that mitigate the occurrence of missing data and facilitate comprehensive analysis of patient outcomes.

We compare threshold resummation in QCD, as performed using soft-collinear
effective theory (SCET), to the standard perturbative QCD formalism based on
factorization and resummation of Mellin moments of partonic cross-sections. We
consider various forms of the SCET result, which correspond to different
choices of the soft scale mu_s that characterizes this approach. We derive a
master formula that relates the SCET resummation to the QCD result for any
choice of mu_s. We then use it first, to show that if SCET resummation is
performed in N-Mellin moment space by suitable choice of mu_s it is equivalent
to the standard perturbative approach. Next, we show that if SCET resummation
is performed by choosing for mu_s a partonic momentum variable, the
perturbative result for partonic resummed cross-sections is again reproduced,
but like its standard perturbative counterpart it is beset by divergent
behaviour at the endpoint. Finally, using the master formula we show that when
mu_s is chosen as a hadronic momentum variable the SCET and standard approach
are related through a multiplicative (convolutive) factor, which contains the
dependence on the Landau pole and associated divergence. This factor depends on
the luminosity in a non-universal way; it lowers by one power of log the
accuracy of the resummed result, but it is otherwise subleading if one assumes
the luminosity not to contain logarithmically enhanced terms. Therefore, the
SCET approach can be turned into a prescription to remove the Landau pole from
the perturbative result, but the price to pay for this is the reduction by one
logarithmic power of the accuracy at each order and the need to make
assumptions on the parton luminosity.

We present an innovative application of Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) for the detection of seismic waves, addressing the critical need for real-time monitoring and early warning systems in seismology. Our methodology leverages the principles of HTM, particularly its capacity for anomaly detection and pattern recognition in temporal data, allowing us to identify significant seismic events with high precision.   We collected extensive seismic data from various geological settings to train our algorithm, utilizing both synthetic and real-world seismic signals. Our results demonstrate that the HTM model exhibits superior sensitivity and specificity compared to traditional detection methods. We achieved a detection accuracy exceeding 90%, significantly reducing false positives and negatives in seismic event identification. Furthermore, our algorithm showed remarkable robustness against noise, which is often prevalent in seismic data, ensuring reliable performance under varied environmental conditions.  By integrating HTM's unsupervised learning capabilities, we allow for continuous adaptation to evolving seismic patterns, enhancing the predictive power of our system. This research not only provides a viable solution for real-time seismic wave detection but also contributes to the broader field of machine learning applications in geoscience. We conclude that HTM-based frameworks can transform how we approach seismic event detection, potentially leading to faster and more effective responses to seismic hazards, ultimately safeguarding communities and infrastructure. Future work will focus on refining our methodology and expanding its applicability to other forms of geophysical data.

We investigate two problems for a class C of regular word languages. The
C-membership problem asks for an algorithm to decide whether an input language
belongs to C. The C-separation problem asks for an algorithm that, given as
input two regular languages, decides whether there exists a third language in C
containing the first language, while being disjoint from the second. These
problems are considered as means to obtain a deep understanding of the class C.
  It is usual for such classes to be defined by logical formalisms. Logics are
often built on top of each other, by adding new predicates. A natural
construction is to enrich a logic with the successor relation. In this paper,
we obtain simple self-contained proofs of two transfer results: we show that
for suitable logically defined classes, the membership, resp. the separation
problem for a class enriched with the successor relation reduces to the same
problem for the original class.
  Our reductions work both for languages of finite words and infinite words.
The proofs are mostly self-contained, and only require a basic background on
regular languages. This paper therefore gives new, simple proofs of results
that were considered as difficult, such as the decid- ability of the membership
problem for the levels 1, 3/2, 2 and 5/2 of the dot-depth hierarchy.

This study investigates the ballistic thermal transport phenomena in lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) at room temperature. Building on previous work that suggested the existence of ballistic thermal transport in certain materials at low temperatures, this research aims to extend these observations to room temperature conditions. To achieve this, we employed a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental techniques, including transient grating spectroscopy and time-resolved photoluminescence measurements. Our results indicate that at room temperature, LiNbO₃ exhibits significant ballistic thermal transport characteristics, which deviate from classical phonon transport models. Key findings include a reduction in thermal conductivity attributed to the dominance of acoustic phonons over optical phonons, leading to enhanced heat dissipation mechanisms. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of thermal transport behavior in ferroelectric materials and could have implications for their application in thermoelectric devices and energy conversion technologies.

This research paper investigates the 1997 event in the Crab Pulsar observed in X-rays. The objective is to analyze the peculiar characteristics of this event and its implications on our understanding of pulsar dynamics. The methodology involves analyzing X-ray data collected from various telescopes to study the temporal and spectral evolution of the event.   Key findings reveal unique X-ray flux variations and spectral changes during the 1997 event, suggesting complex processes at play in the Crab Pulsar. The data also indicate a potential link between the event and surrounding nebula activity.   In conclusion, the 1997 event in the Crab Pulsar showcases a distinctive behavior in X-rays, indicating intricate dynamics within the pulsar system. Further research is needed to fully comprehend the nature of these events and their impact on pulsar evolution.

Our research delves into the phenomenon of thermal tides in fluid extrasolar planets, aiming to unravel their intricate patterns and implications. By conducting numerical simulations, we sought to understand the complex interplay between the rotation of the planet, its atmosphere, and the thermal tides induced by the host star. Our findings reveal that thermal tides have a profound impact on the atmospheric dynamics of these planets, influencing circulation patterns and heat distribution. We discovered that the strength and phase of thermal tides are highly sensitive to factors such as orbital distance, rotation rate, and atmospheric composition.  Our work addresses the critical gap in understanding the thermal tides in fluid extrasolar planets, offering insights into the underlying mechanisms that govern their climate and atmosphere. By studying these phenomena, we contribute to the broader field of exoplanet research, shedding light on the diversity of planetary systems beyond our solar system. Our methodology involved implementing advanced computational models to simulate the behavior of thermal tides under varying conditions, providing a comprehensive analysis of their implications. Ultimately, our research advances the understanding of the complex dynamics shaping the climates of fluid extrasolar planets and paves the way for future investigations into these intriguing celestial bodies.

We have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of self-optimized superconductivity at cuprate interfaces by exploiting the interlayer phase separation. Our approach involves the strategic manipulation of oxygen vacancies and CuO2 layering at the interfaces of cuprate superconductors, leading to the emergence of superconducting properties.   Through a series of experiments, we have observed that the deliberate introduction of oxygen vacancies and the subsequent phase separation of the CuO2 layers at the interfaces significantly enhances the superconducting critical temperature, Tc. By carefully controlling the interlayer spacing and oxygen vacancy density, we have been able to optimize the superconducting properties of the cuprate interfaces, resulting in a substantial increase in Tc.   Our findings are attributed to the enhanced electronic correlations and reduced disorder at the interfaces, which facilitate the formation of Cooper pairs and the emergence of superconductivity. The interlayer phase separation also enables the creation of a more ordered and coherent superconducting state, leading to improved critical current densities and reduced critical current-temperature hysteresis.   The self-optimized superconductivity attainable through interlayer phase separation at cuprate interfaces offers a promising avenue for the development of high-temperature superconducting materials with improved performance and reduced material costs. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms and to optimize the interlayer phase separation for practical applications.

This study examines the properties of weak products of complete Pick spaces, a class of Banach spaces that have been extensively studied in the context of operator theory and functional analysis. A complete Pick space is a Banach space equipped with a Pick function, a continuous linear functional that satisfies certain properties, such as the Pick identity. The weak product of two Banach spaces X and Y is a Banach space consisting of all pairs (x, y) of elements from X and Y, equipped with a norm that is induced by the norms of X and Y.   The objective of this research is to investigate the relationship between the properties of complete Pick spaces and their weak products. Specifically, we aim to determine the conditions under which the weak product of two complete Pick spaces is also a complete Pick space. To this end, we develop a characterization of the weak products of complete Pick spaces, using a combination of functional analysis techniques and operator theory tools.  Our results show that the weak product of two complete Pick spaces is a complete Pick space if and only if one of the spaces is a Hilbert space. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the Pick functions of the individual spaces and the Pick function of the weak product. These findings have implications for the study of operator algebras and the properties of Banach spaces, and provide new insights into the structure of weak products of complete Pick spaces.

Pixel detectors are used in the innermost part of the multi purpose
experiments at LHC and are therefore exposed to the highest fluences of
ionising radiation, which in this part of the detectors consists mainly of
charged pions. The radiation hardness of all detector components has thoroughly
been tested up to the fluences expected at the LHC. In case of an LHC upgrade,
the fluence will be much higher and it is not yet clear how long the present
pixel modules will stay operative in such a harsh environment. The aim of this
study was to establish such a limit as a benchmark for other possible detector
concepts considered for the upgrade.
  As the sensors and the readout chip are the parts most sensitive to radiation
damage, samples consisting of a small pixel sensor bump-bonded to a CMS-readout
chip (PSI46V2.1) have been irradiated with positive 200 MeV pions at PSI up to
6E14 Neq and with 21 GeV protons at CERN up to 5E15 Neq.
  After irradiation the response of the system to beta particles from a Sr-90
source was measured to characterise the charge collection efficiency of the
sensor. Radiation induced changes in the readout chip were also measured. The
results show that the present pixel modules can be expected to be still
operational after a fluence of 2.8E15 Neq. Samples irradiated up to 5E15 Neq
still see the beta particles. However, further tests are needed to confirm
whether a stable operation with high particle detection efficiency is possible
after such a high fluence.

In this study, we examine the impact of memory mechanisms on opinion dynamics within social systems. We seek to address the gap in understanding how individual memory influences collective opinion formation and evolution. Specifically, we investigate the effects of different memory functions—such as persistence, decay, and renewal—on the spread and sustainability of opinions over time. Utilizing agent-based modeling, we simulate populations where agents interact and exchange opinions while accounting for memory-induced factors that govern the retention and modification of these opinions. Our key findings indicate that memory plays a critical role in stabilizing social consensus or fostering opinion polarization. Under conditions of strong memory persistence, communities are more likely to achieve consensus as past interactions weigh heavily in present opinion considerations. Conversely, in scenarios where memory rapidly decays, we observe increased susceptibility to external influences, leading to a fragmentation of opinions or alternatively, a rapid transition to new dominant views. We further demonstrate that the introduction of periodic memory renewal supports adaptability within dynamic environments, allowing populations to adjust harmoniously to external perturbations. This research underscores the importance of memory in shaping opinion trajectories and offers insights into the design of information dissemination strategies, with potential applications in public policy and social media analytics. Our approach highlights the complex interplay between cognitive processes and social interaction, paving the way for more comprehensive models of sociocognitive phenomena.

Acoustic peaks in the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background in
spherically symmetric inhomogeneous cosmological models are studied. At the
photon-baryon decoupling epoch, the universe may be assumed to be dominated by
non-relativistic matter, and thus we may treat radiation as a test field in the
universe filled with dust which is described by the Lema\^itre-Tolman-Bondi
(LTB) solution. First, we give an LTB model whose distance-redshift relation
agrees with that of the concordance $\Lambda$CDM model in the whole redshift
domain and which is well approximated by the Einstein-de Sitter universe at and
before decoupling. We determine the decoupling epoch in this LTB universe by
Gamow's criterion and then calculate the positions of acoustic peaks. Thus
obtained results are not consistent with the WMAP data. However, we find that
one can fit the peak positions by appropriately modifying the LTB model,
namely, by allowing the deviation of the distance-redshift relation from that
of the concordance $\Lambda$CDM model at $z>2$ where no observational data are
available at present. Thus there is still a possibility of explaining the
apparent accelerated expansion of the universe by inhomogeneity without
resorting to dark energy if we abandon the Copernican principle. Even if we do
not take this extreme attitude, it also suggests that local, isotropic
inhomogeneities around us may seriously affect the determination of the density
contents of the universe unless the possible existence of such inhomogeneities
is properly taken into account.

Motivated by the possibility of enhancing dark matter (DM) self-interaction
cross-section $\sigma_{\rm self}$, we have revisited the issue of DM
annihilation through a Breit-Wigner resonance. In this case thermally averaged
annihilation cross-section has strong temperature dependence, whereas elastic
scattering of DM on the thermal bath particles is suppressed. This leads to the
early kinetic decoupling of DM and an interesting interplay in the evolution of
DM density and temperature that can be described by a set of coupled Boltzmann
equations. The standard Breit-Wigner parametrization of a resonance propagator
is also corrected by including momentum dependence of the resonance width. It
has been shown that this effects may change predictions of DM relic density by
more than order of magnitude in some regions of the parameter space. Model
independent discussion is illustrated within a theory of Abelian vector dark
matter. The model assumes extra $U(1)$ symmetry group factor and an additional
complex Higgs field needed to generate a mass for the dark vector boson, which
provides an extra neutral Higgs boson $h_2$. We discuss the resonance
amplification of $\sigma_{\rm self}$. It turns out that if DM abundance is
properly reproduced, the Fermi-LAT data favor heavy DM and constraint the
enhancement of $\sigma_{\rm self}$ to the range, which cannot provide a
solution to the small-scale structure problems.}

This paper considers the capacity of a diffusion-based molecular
communication link assuming the receiver uses chemical reactions. The key
contribution is we show that enzymatic reaction cycles, which is a class of
chemical reactions commonly found in cells consisting of a forward and a
backward enzymatic reaction, can improve the capacity of the communication
link. The technical difficulty in analysing enzymatic reaction cycles is that
their reaction rates are nonlinear. We deal with this by assuming that the
amount of certain chemicals in the enzymatic reaction cycle is large. In order
to simplify the problem further, we use singular perturbation to study a
particular operating regime of the enzymatic reaction cycles. This allows us to
derive a closed-form expression of the channel gain. This expression suggests
that we can improve the channel gain by increasing the total amount of
substrate in the enzymatic reaction cycle. By using numerical calculations, we
show that the effect of the enzymatic reaction cycle is to increase the channel
gain and to reduce the noise, which results in a better signalto- noise ratio
and in turn a higher communication capacity. Furthermore, we show that we can
increase the capacity by increasing the total amount of substrate in the
enzymatic reaction cycle.

Dilute magnetic impurities in a disordered Fermi liquid are considered close
to the Anderson metal-insulator transition (AMIT). Critical Power law
correlations between electron wave functions at different energies in the
vicinity of the AMIT result in the formation of pseudogaps of the local density
of states. Magnetic impurities can remain unscreened at such sites. We
determine the density of the resulting free magnetic moments in the zero
temperature limit. While it is finite on the insulating side of the AMIT, it
vanishes at the AMIT, and decays with a power law as function of the distance
to the AMIT. Since the fluctuating spins of these free magnetic moments break
the time reversal symmetry of the conduction electrons, we find a shift of the
AMIT, and the appearance of a semimetal phase. The distribution function of the
Kondo temperature $T_{K}$ is derived at the AMIT, in the metallic phase and in
the insulator phase. This allows us to find the quantum phase diagram in an
external magnetic field $B$ and at finite temperature $T$. We calculate the
resulting magnetic susceptibility, the specific heat, and the spin relaxation
rate as function of temperature. We find a phase diagram with finite
temperature transitions between insulator, critical semimetal, and metal
phases. These new types of phase transitions are caused by the interplay
between Kondo screening and Anderson localization, with the latter being
shifted by the appearance of the temperature-dependent spin-flip scattering
rate. Accordingly, we name them Kondo-Anderson transitions (KATs).

In this study, we explore the concept of "Be Your Own Prada," focusing on how individuals can synthesize fashion elements to achieve a cohesive and personalized style. Our work addresses the challenge of creating a unique yet structurally coherent wardrobe by integrating various fashion trends and styles. We conducted a series of interviews and surveys among participants to understand their preferences and constraints in fashion choices. Utilizing these insights, we developed a methodology that encourages users to identify key structural components—such as colors, fabrics, and silhouettes—and then explore how these can be synthesized across different garments and outfits. The results demonstrate significant improvements in self-confidence and satisfaction with one's personal fashion choices. Key methodologies involved data analysis, trend synthesis, and iterative design processes. Our findings suggest that fostering a deeper understanding of one’s own aesthetic preferences, combined with strategic synthesis techniques, can lead to more satisfying and cohesive fashion choices.

The hard X-ray detector (HXD) onboard {\it Suzaku} measured soft
$\gamma$-rays from the Type Ia supernova SN2014J at $77\pm2$ days after the
explosion. Although the confidence level of the signal is about 90\% (i.e., $2
\sigma$), the $3 \sigma$ upper limit has been derived at $< 2.2 \times10^{-4}$
ph s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in the 170 -- 250 keV band as the first independent
measurement of soft $\gamma$-rays with an instrument other than {\it INTEGRAL}.
For this analysis, we have examined the reproducibility of the NXB model of
HXD/GSO using blank sky data. We find that the residual count rate in the 90 --
500 keV band is distributed around an average of 0.19\% with a standard
deviation of 0.42\% relative to the NXB rate. The averaged residual signals are
consistent with that expected from the cosmic X-ray background. The flux of
SN2014J derived from {\it Suzaku} measurements taken in one snapshot at
$t=77\pm2$ days after the explosion is consistent with the {\it INTEGRAL}
values averaged over the period between $t=$50 and 100 days and also with
explosion models of single or double degenerate scenarios. Being sensitive to
the total ejecta mass surrounding the radioactive material, the ratio between
continuum and line flux in the soft gamma-ray regime might distinguish
different progenitor models. The {\it Suzaku} data have been examined with this
relation at $t=77\pm2$ days, but could not distinguish models between single
and double degenerate-progenitors. We disfavor explosion models with larger
$^{56}$Ni masses than 1 $M_\odot$, from our $1 \sigma$ error on the 170-250 keV
X-ray flux of $(1.2\pm0.7) \times10^{-4}$ ph s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$.

Graphical network inference is used in many fields such as genomics or
ecology to infer the conditional independence structure between variables, from
measurements of gene expression or species abundances for instance. In many
practical cases, not all variables involved in the network have been observed,
and the samples are actually drawn from a distribution where some variables
have been marginalized out. This challenges the sparsity assumption commonly
made in graphical model inference, since marginalization yields locally dense
structures, even when the original network is sparse. We present a procedure
for inferring Gaussian graphical models when some variables are unobserved,
that accounts both for the influence of missing variables and the low density
of the original network. Our model is based on the aggregation of spanning
trees, and the estimation procedure on the Expectation-Maximization algorithm.
We treat the graph structure and the unobserved nodes as missing variables and
compute posterior probabilities of edge appearance. To provide a complete
methodology, we also propose several model selection criteria to estimate the
number of missing nodes. A simulation study and an illustration flow cytometry
data reveal that our method has favorable edge detection properties compared to
