existing graph inference techniques. The methods are implemented in an R
package.

Water and hydroxyl, once thought to be found only in the primitive airless
bodies that formed beyond roughly 2.5-3 AU, have recently been detected on the
Moon and Vesta, which both have surfaces dominated by evolved, non-primitive
compositions. In both these cases, the water/OH is thought to be exogenic,
either brought in via impacts with comets or hydrated asteroids or created via
solar wind interactions with silicates in the regolith or both. Such exogenic
processes should also be occurring on other airless body surfaces. To test this
hypothesis, we used the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) to measure
reflectance spectra (2.0 to 4.1 {\mu}m) of two large near-Earth asteroids
(NEAs) with compositions generally interpreted as anhydrous: 433 Eros and 1036
Ganymed. OH is detected on both of these bodies in the form of absorption
features near 3 {\mu}m. The spectra contain a component of thermal emission at
longer wavelengths, from which we estimate thermal of 167+/- 98 J m-2s-1/2K-1
for Eros (consistent with previous estimates) and 214+/- 80 J m-2s-1/2K-1 for
Ganymed, the first reported measurement of thermal inertia for this object.
These observations demonstrate that processes responsible for water/OH creation
on large airless bodies also act on much smaller bodies.

We performed long-slit optical spectroscopy (GTC-OSIRIS) of 6 radio-loud QSOs
at redshifts $2<z<3$, known to have giant ($\sim 50$-100 kpc) Lyman-$\alpha$
emitting nebulae, and detect extended Lyman-$\alpha$ emission for 4, with
surface brightness $\sim10^{-16}$ ergs $\rm cm^{-2}s^{-1}arcsec^{-2}$ and line
width FWHM 400-1100 (mean 863) km $\rm s^{-1}$. We also observed the $z\simeq
5.9$ radio-loud QSO, SDSS J2228+0110, and find evidence of a $\geq 10$ kpc
extended Lyman-$\alpha$ emission nebula, a new discovery for this high-redshift
object.
  Spatially-resolved kinematics of the 5 nebulae are examined by fitting the
Lyman-$\alpha$ wavelength at a series of positions along the slit. We found the
line-of-sight velocity $\Delta(v)$ profiles to be relatively flat. However, 3
of the nebulae appear systematically redshifted by 250-460 km $\rm s^{-1}$
relative to the Lyman-$\alpha$ line of the QSO (with no offset for the other
two), which we argue is evidence for infall. One of these (Q0805+046) had a
small ($\sim 100$ km $\rm s^{-1}$) velocity shift across its diameter and a
steep gradient at the centre. Differences in line-of-sight kinematics between
these 5 giant nebulae and similar nebulae associated with high-redshift radio
galaxies (which can show steep velocity gradients) may be due to an orientation
effect, which brings infall/outflow rather than rotation into greater
prominence for the sources observed `on-axis' as QSOs.

This research paper investigates the hydrostatic pressure effects on pure and doped La1-xRxAgSb2 (R = Ce, Nd) charge-density-wave compounds. The objective is to comprehend the influence of hydrostatic pressure on the physical properties of these compounds. The methodology involved synthesizing La1-xRxAgSb2 compounds through solid-state reactions and applying hydrostatic pressure using a diamond anvil cell while monitoring various properties using techniques like X-ray diffraction, resistivity, and specific heat measurements. The key findings reveal that the application of hydrostatic pressure induces significant changes in the structural and electronic properties of the studied compounds, such as modifications in the charge-density-wave transitions and the electrical resistivity behavior. These changes vary depending on the doping element (Ce, Nd) and its concentration. Overall, this study highlights the tunability of the physical properties of La1-xRxAgSb2 compounds under hydrostatic pressure conditions. The results suggest promising avenues for further exploration and potential technological applications of these materials.

The theory of large deviations is concerned with the exponential decay of
probabilities of large fluctuations in random systems. These probabilities are
important in many fields of study, including statistics, finance, and
engineering, as they often yield valuable information about the large
fluctuations of a random system around its most probable state or trajectory.
In the context of equilibrium statistical mechanics, the theory of large
deviations provides exponential-order estimates of probabilities that refine
and generalize Einstein's theory of fluctuations. This review explores this and
other connections between large deviation theory and statistical mechanics, in
an effort to show that the mathematical language of statistical mechanics is
the language of large deviation theory. The first part of the review presents
the basics of large deviation theory, and works out many of its classical
applications related to sums of random variables and Markov processes. The
second part goes through many problems and results of statistical mechanics,
and shows how these can be formulated and derived within the context of large
deviation theory. The problems and results treated cover a wide range of
physical systems, including equilibrium many-particle systems, noise-perturbed
dynamics, nonequilibrium systems, as well as multifractals, disordered systems,
and chaotic systems. This review also covers many fundamental aspects of
statistical mechanics, such as the derivation of variational principles
characterizing equilibrium and nonequilibrium states, the breaking of the
Legendre transform for nonconcave entropies, and the characterization of
nonequilibrium fluctuations through fluctuation relations.

The optical light-curves of GRB afterglows display either peaks or plateaus.
  We identify 16 afterglows of the former type, 17 of the latter, and 4 with
broad peaks, that could be of either type. The optical energy release of these
two classes is similar and is correlated with the GRB output, the correlation
being stronger for peaky afterglows, which suggests that the burst and
afterglow emissions of peaky afterglows are from the same relativistic ejecta
and that the optical emission of afterglows with plateaus arises more often
from ejecta that did not produce the burst emission.
  Consequently, we propose that peaky optical afterglows are from impulsive
ejecta releases and that plateau optical afterglows originate from long-lived
engines, the break in the optical light-curve (peak or plateau end) marking the
onset of the entire outflow deceleration.
  In the peak luminosity--peak time plane, the distribution of peaky afterglows
displays an edge with L_p \propto t_p^{-3}, which we attribute to variations
(among afterglows) in the ambient medium density. The fluxes and epochs of
optical plateau breaks follow a L_b \propto t_b^{-1} anticorrelation.
  Sixty percent of 25 afterglows that were well-monitored in the optical and
X-rays show light-curves with comparable power-law decays indices and
achromatic breaks. The other 40 percent display three types of decoupled
behaviours: i) chromatic optical light-curve breaks (perhaps due to the peak of
the synchrotron spectrum crossing the optical), ii) X-ray flux decays faster
than in the optical (suggesting that the X-ray emission is from local
inverse-Compton scattering), and iii) chromatic X-ray light-curve breaks
(indicating that the X-ray emission is from external up-scattering).

We investigated the construction of a comprehensive, globally interconnected data infrastructure that would foster interdisciplinary research and collaboration. Our endeavor aimed to develop a standardized framework for data sharing, integration, and analysis across diverse disciplines and geographical regions.  Through a comprehensive literature review and stakeholder engagement, we identified key challenges in building a unified data infrastructure, including data fragmentation, interoperability issues, and unequal access to data resources. We proposed a modular, open-architectural approach to address these challenges, incorporating cutting-edge technologies such as blockchain, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing.  Our results indicate that the proposed framework can effectively integrate data from various sources, facilitate data discovery, and enable real-time analytics. We also demonstrated the feasibility of deploying the framework in a real-world setting, leveraging partnerships with leading research institutions and data providers.  Our key findings highlight the importance of establishing a global data governance structure to ensure data quality, security, and accountability. We also identified the need for standardized data formats, common data standards, and data literacy training to facilitate effective data sharing and collaboration.  Our methodology involved a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data analysis techniques. We employed a mixed-methods design, integrating both exploratory and descriptive studies to examine the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed framework.

We present an effcient Monte-Carlo method for lattice glass models which are
characterized by hard constraint conditions. The basic idea of the method is
similar to that of the $N$-fold way method. By using a list of sites into which
we can insert a particle, we avoid trying a useless transition which is
forbidden by the constraint conditions. We applied the present method to a
lattice glass model proposed by Biroli and M{\'e}zard. We first evaluated the
efficiency of the method through measurements of the autocorrelation function
of particle configurations. As a result, we found that the efficiency is much
higher than that of the standard Monte-Carlo method. We also compared the
efficiency of the present method with that of the $N$-fold way method in
detail. We next examined how the efficiency of extended ensemble methods such
as the replica exchange method and the Wang-Landau method is inflnuenced by the
choice of the local update method. The results show that the efficiency is
considerably improved by the use of efficient local update methods. For
example, when the number of sites $N_{\rm site}$ is 1024, the ergodic time
$\tau_{\rm E}$ of the replica exchange method in the grand-canonical ensemble,
which is the average round-trip time of a replica in chemical-potential space,
with the present local update method is more than $10^2$ times shorter than
that with the standard local update method. This result shows that the
efficient local update method is quite important to make extended ensemble
methods more effective.

In this paper, we address the challenge of consistently estimating the missing mass in statistical models characterized by heavy-tails and sparse data distributions. Missing mass quantification, critical for applications like biodiversity estimation and data compression, has traditionally lacked reliable methods for consistent estimation, especially in large data contexts with numerous unseen categories. We propose a novel estimator that leverages a Bayesian nonparametric framework, incorporating Dirichlet process mixtures to capture the complex underlying distribution of the data effectively. By integrating Monte Carlo sampling techniques, we meticulously manage computational intractability without compromising estimator accuracy.  We systematically validate our approach through a robust set of synthetic and real-world data experiments, comparing it against existing methodologies such as Good-Turing and frequentist sampling strategies. Results demonstrate that our estimator consistently outperforms competing methods in terms of mean square error across varying scenarios with different levels of sparsity and tail behavior. Our method exhibits strong convergence properties, and its performance gains are more pronounced in cases with a high number of unobserved categories. Additionally, we present theoretical guarantees underpinning the estimator's consistency and asymptotic normality, reinforcing its applicability to diverse domains.  The advancement of our proposed solution provides a significant step toward resolving limitations in current practices, offering reliable missing mass estimates that facilitate more informed decision-making across ecological studies and information theory applications. Future work could extend these foundations to explore extensions with hierarchical Bayesian models for multi-domain tasks.

The global evolution of protoplanetary disks (PPDs) has recently been shown
to be largely controlled by the amount of poloidal magnetic flux threading the
disk, which is further controlled by the poorly understood process of magnetic
flux transport. In weakly ionized gas as in PPDs, magnetic flux is largely
frozen in the electron fluid, except when resistivity is large. When the disk
is largely laminar, we show that the relative drift between the electrons and
ions (the Hall-drift), and the ions and neutral fluids (ambipolar-drift) can
play a dominant role on the transport of magnetic flux. Using two-dimensional
simulations that incorporate the Hall effect and ambipolar diffusion (AD) with
prescribed diffusivities, we show that when large-scale poloidal field is
aligned with disk rotation, the Hall effect rapidly drags magnetic flux inward
at the midplane region, while it slowly pushes flux outward above/below the
midplane. This leads to a highly radially elongated field configuration as a
global manifestation of the Hall-shear instability. This field configuration
further promotes rapid outward flux transport by AD at the midplane, leading to
instability saturation. In quasi-steady state, magnetic flux is transported
outward at approximately the same rate at all heights, and the rate is
comparable to the Hall-free case. For anti-aligned field polarity, the Hall
effect consistently transports magnetic flux outward, leading to a largely
vertical field configuration in the midplane region. The field lines in the
upper layer first bend radially inward and then outward to launch a disk wind.
Overall, the net rate of outward flux transport is about twice faster than the
aligned case. In addition, the rate of flux transport increases with increasing
disk magnetization. The absolute rate of transport is sensitive to disk
microphysics which remains to be explored in future studies.

Classically, coding theory has been concerned with the problem of
transmitting a single message in a format which is robust to noise. Recently,
researchers have turned their attention to designing coding schemes to make
two-way conversations robust to noise. That is, given an interactive
communication protocol $\Pi$, an \emph{interactive coding scheme} converts
$\Pi$ into another communication protocol $\Pi'$ such that, even if errors are
introduced during the execution of $\Pi'$, the parties are able to determine
what the outcome of running $\Pi$ would be in a noise-free setting.
  We consider the problem of designing interactive coding schemes which allow
the parties to simulate the original protocol using little memory.
Specifically, given any communication protocol $\Pi$ we construct robust
simulating protocols which tolerate a constant noise rate and require the
parties to use only $O(\log d \log s)$ memory, where $d$ is the depth of $\Pi$
and $s$ is a measure of the size of $\Pi$. Prior to this work, all known coding
schemes required the parties to use at least $\Omega(d)$ memory, as the parties
were required to remember the transcript of the conversation thus far.
Moreover, our coding scheme achieves a communication rate of
$1-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ over oblivious channels and
$1-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon\log\log\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}})$ over adaptive
adversarial channels, matching the conjecturally optimal rates. Lastly, we
point to connections between fault-tolerant circuits and coding for interactive
communication with small memory.

In this study, we investigate the atomistic mechanisms underlying the trapped-charge driven degradation of perovskite solar cells. Our research addresses the critical challenge of improving the stability and longevity of perovskite solar cells, which is essential for their commercial viability. We employ a multiscale simulation approach, integrating density functional theory (DFT) calculations with kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations, to elucidate the behavior of charge carriers and their interactions within the perovskite lattice in the presence of trapped charges. Our findings reveal that charge trapping at defect sites in the perovskite structure significantly accelerates degradation processes by facilitating ion migration and promoting phase segregation. Specifically, we identify the role of halide vacancies and interstitials in enhancing the mobility of ions, thereby exacerbating the structural instability. The DFT calculations highlight that the deeper energy levels associated with these defects act as charge traps, which in turn alters the local electrostatic environment, leading to increased defect formation energy. Our KMC simulations further demonstrate that the presence of trapped charges can alter the kinetic pathways of degradation, showing an increased rate of compositional segregation and phase decomposition under operational conditions. By providing a detailed atomistic insight into degradation pathways, our results suggest potential avenues for enhancing the chemical stability of perovskite materials. Strategies such as defect passivation and compositional engineering emerge as promising approaches to mitigate charge trapping effects, thereby prolonging device stability. This study lays a foundational understanding that can guide the engineering of more durable perovskite solar cells.

In this study, we explore the intricate connection between the circumgalactic medium (CGM) and the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies, utilizing data from the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph on the Hubble Space Telescope - Gas-Phase Galaxy Survey (COS-GASS). We aim to unravel the complex interplay that governs baryonic cycling processes within galaxy environments. Our methodology involves a comprehensive analysis of ultraviolet absorption lines, with a focus on tracing the distribution and dynamics of gas within the CGM and how these features correlate with the properties of the ISM. Through detailed spectral fitting and modeling, we observe a pronounced chemical and kinematic continuity between the CGM and the ISM, suggesting a symbiotic exchange of materials. The results indicate that both inflows and outflows significantly influence the CGM structure, with inflows potentially enriching the ISM in metals, thereby affecting star formation processes. Distinct trends reveal that galaxies with higher star formation rates exhibit more active baryon cycling, evidenced by enhanced CGM absorption features. By elucidating these connections, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution processes. Importantly, our findings underscore the necessity of considering both the CGM and ISM in tandem to fully appreciate galaxy dynamics and the lifelong cycle of baryons within galaxies. This comprehensive framework and the resultant data set provide critical insights for future theoretical and observational efforts aimed at dissecting the multi-phase nature of galactic environments. Our study represents a significant step towards delineating the unified picture of galaxy evolutionary mechanisms.

Dust grain evolution in spatially resolved T Tauri binaries is a complex process influenced by the interaction between the binary system and its surrounding environment. T Tauri stars are pre-main-sequence objects characterized by strong stellar activity, which leads to the formation and destruction of dust grains. In spatially resolved T Tauri binaries, the interaction between the two stars and their circumstellar disks can significantly impact dust grain evolution.  This study aimed to investigate the spatially resolved evolution of dust grains in T Tauri binaries using high-contrast imaging and spectroscopic observations. We observed a sample of 10 T Tauri binaries with high spatial resolution using the VLT/SPHERE instrument and obtained spectroscopic data using the ESPRESSO spectrograph. Our observations revealed a significant difference in dust grain evolution between the two components of the binary systems.  The key findings of this study show that the dust grain evolution in T Tauri binaries is influenced by the mass ratio of the binary system, with more massive components exhibiting faster dust grain destruction. We also found that the dust grain population in the outer disk of the binary system is shaped by the interaction between the two stars and their disks. The spectroscopic data revealed the presence of different dust grain populations in the two components of the binary system, which are likely to be influenced by the different stellar activity and disk geometry.  Our study provides new insights into the complex process of dust grain evolution in T Tauri binaries and highlights the importance of considering the interaction between the binary system and its surrounding environment. The findings of this study have implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of planetary systems and the role of dust grains in shaping the architecture of circumstellar disks.

Problem Statement: The huge number of information on the web as well as the
growth of new inexperienced users creates new challenges for information
retrieval. It has become increasingly difficult for these users to find
relevant documents that satisfy their individual needs. Certainly the current
search engines (such as Google, Bing and Yahoo) offer an efficient way to
browse the web content. However, the result quality is highly based on uses
queries which need to be more precise to find relevant documents. This task
still complicated for the majority of inept users who cannot express their
needs with significant words in the query. For that reason, we believe that a
reformulation of the initial user's query can be a good alternative to improve
the information selectivity. This study proposes a novel approach and presents
a prototype system called PRESY (Profile-based REformulation SYstem) for
information retrieval on the web. Approach: It uses an incremental approach to
categorize users by constructing a contextual base. The latter is composed of
two types of context (static and dynamic) obtained using the users' profiles.
The architecture proposed was implemented using .Net environment to perform
queries reformulating tests. Results: The experiments gives at the end of this
article show that the precision of the returned content is effectively
improved. The tests were performed with the most popular searching engine (i.e.
Google, Bind and Yahoo) selected in particular for their high selectivity.
Among the given results, we found that query reformulation improve the first
three results by 10.7% and 11.7% of the next seven returned elements. So as we
can see the reformulation of users' initial queries improves the pertinence of
returned content.

This study investigates the properties of magnetars, specifically those that adhere to the Born-Infeld electrodynamics model, which predicts stronger magnetic fields compared to the classical toroidal fields. The primary objective was to explore whether these stronger fields could explain observed phenomena not fully accounted for by classical models. Using numerical simulations and theoretical calculations based on Born-Infeld theory, we aimed to determine if such magnetars could generate larger magnetic fields, leading to distinct signatures in their electromagnetic emissions and potential gravitational waves (GWs). Key findings indicate that Born-Infeld magnetars indeed exhibit significantly higher magnetic field strengths, up to several times those predicted by Maxwell's equations. These enhanced fields have implications for the emission mechanisms and stability of magnetars, suggesting that they may emit more intense and complex electromagnetic radiation. Furthermore, the enhanced fields can affect the structure of the surrounding neutron star atmosphere, potentially altering the observed spectra and polarization patterns. Regarding GWs, our simulations show that Born-Infeld magnetars could produce distinctive GW signals with higher amplitudes and unique frequency content compared to conventional models. This research highlights the importance of considering non-linear electrodynamics in understanding magnetar behavior and its potential impact on future GW observations, particularly in distinguishing between different classes of sources.

The time evolution of the electromagnetic emission from blazars, in
particular high frequency peaked sources (HBLs), displays irregular activity
not yet understood. In this work we report a methodology capable of
characterizing the time behavior of these variable objects. The Maximum
Likelihood Blocks (MLBs) is a model-independent estimator which sub-divides the
light curve into time blocks, whose length and amplitude are compatible with
states of constant emission rate of the observed source. The MLBs yields the
statistical significance in the rate variations and strongly suppresses the
noise fluctuations in the light curves. We apply the MLBs for the first time on
the long term X-ray light curves (RXTE/ASM) of Mkn~421,Mkn~501, 1ES 1959+650
and 1ES 2155-304, which consist of more than 10 years of observational data
(1996-2007). Using the MLBs interpretation of RXTE/ASM data, the integrated
time flux distribution is determined for each single source considered. We
identify in these distributions the characteristic level as well as the flaring
states of the blazars. All the distributions show a significant component at
negative flux values, most probably caused by an uncertainty in the background
subtraction and by intrinsic fluctuations of RXTE/ASM. This effect interests in
particular short time observations. In order to quantify the probability that
the intrinsic fluctuations give rise to a false identification of a flare, we
study a population of very faint sources and their integrated time flux
distribution. We determine duty cycle or fraction of time a source spent in the
flaring state of the source Mkn~421, Mkn~501, 1ES 1959+650 and 1ES 2155-304.
Moreover, we study the random coincidences between flares and generic sporadic
events such as high energy neutrinos or flares in other wavelengths.

This research paper explores Rosennean Complexity from the perspective of an applied mathematician. The background of the study elucidates the growing importance of understanding complex systems in various fields, inspiring a mathematical examination of Rosennean Complexity.  The objective of this paper is to provide insights into how mathematical concepts can be applied to analyze and comprehend Rosennean Complexity. Through a thorough review of existing literature and theoretical frameworks, the research aims to establish a mathematical foundation for studying complex systems based on Rosennean principles.  Methodology involves a systematic analysis of Rosennean Complexity, drawing parallels with mathematical theories such as chaos theory, fractals, and differential equations. By applying mathematical models and simulations, the study demonstrates how these tools can enhance our understanding of complex systems within the framework of Rosennean philosophy.  Key findings highlight the efficacy of mathematical approaches in elucidating the intricacies of Rosennean Complexity. The study reveals the potential of mathematical tools to unravel patterns, predict behaviors, and offer new perspectives on complex phenomena in diverse disciplines.  In conclusion, this research paper underscores the significance of integrating mathematics into the study of Rosennean Complexity, emphasizing the role of quantitative analysis in unveiling the underlying structures of complex systems. By bridging mathematics and complexity theory, this study advocates for a more holistic and systematic approach to understanding the intricacies of the world around us.

In this study, we present a novel approach to predicting the underground argon content (UAC) for dark matter experiments, utilizing machine learning techniques and geochemical data. We aim to mitigate the uncertainties in the estimation of argon concentrations in deep underground laboratories, which can significantly impact the sensitivity of dark matter detection.  Our methodology consists of a two-step procedure first, data collection from various sources, including published geochemical surveys and in-situ measurements of UAC. We apply a stringent data curation process to ensure data quality and consistency. In the second step, we employ machine learning algorithms, including support vector regression and artificial neural networks, to develop predictive models based on the collected data. The predictive models aim to estimate UAC values at potential dark matter experiment sites.  We evaluate the performance of our models using various metrics, such as root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R²), and cross-validation scores. The results demonstrate that our models achieve an RMSE of below 0.5% and R² above 0.8, indicating good predictive accuracy. The models also generalize well to new data, achieving high cross-validation scores.  Our findings can help improve the design and planning of future dark matter experiments by providing more accurate predictions of UAC values at potential sites, thus reducing experimental uncertainties and enhancing the sensitivity of the experiments. Future work includes expanding the dataset and incorporating additional geophysical data to further refine our models and improve their applicability to a broader range of sites.

A fundamental challenge in synthesis from examples is designing a learning
algorithm that poses the minimal number of questions to an end user while
guaranteeing that the target hypothesis is discovered. Such guarantees are
practically important because they ensure that end users will not be
overburdened with unnecessary questions.
  We present SPEX -- a learning algorithm that addresses the above challenge.
SPEX considers the hypothesis space of formulas over first-order predicates and
learns the correct hypothesis by only asking the user simple membership queries
for concrete examples. Thus, SPEX is directly applicable to any learning
problem that fits its hypothesis space and uses membership queries.
  SPEX works by iteratively eliminating candidate hypotheses from the space
until converging to the target hypothesis. The main idea is to use the
implication order between hypotheses to guarantee that in each step the
question presented to the user obtains maximal pruning of the space. This
problem is particularly challenging when predicates are potentially correlated.
  To show that SPEX is practically useful, we expressed two rather different
applications domains in its framework: learning programs for the domain of
technical analysts (stock trading) and learning data structure specifications.
The experimental results show that SPEX's optimality guarantee is effective: it
drastically reduces the number of questions posed to the user while
successfully learning the exact hypothesis.

The $^{18}$Ne($\alpha$,$p$)$^{21}$Na reaction provides a pathway for breakout
from the hot CNO cycles to the $rp$-process in type I x-ray bursts. To better
determine this astrophysical reaction rate, the resonance parameters of the
compound nucleus $^{22}$Mg have been investigated by measuring the resonant
elastic scattering of $^{21}$Na+$p$. An 89 MeV $^{21}$Na radioactive ion beam
was produced at the CNS Radioactive Ion Beam Separator and bombarded an 8.8
mg/cm$^2$ thick polyethylene target. The recoiled protons were measured at
scattering angles of $\theta_{c.m.}$$\approx 175 {^\circ}$ and 152${^\circ}$ by
three $\Delta E$-$E$ silicon telescopes. The excitation function was obtained
with a thick-target method over energies $E_x$($^{22}$Mg)=5.5--9.2 MeV. The
resonance parameters have been determined through an $R$-matrix analysis. For
the first time, the $J^{\pi}$ values for ten states above the alpha threshold
in $^{22}$Mg have been experimentally determined in a single consistent
measurement. We have made three new $J^{\pi}$ assignments and confirmed seven
of the ten tentative assignments in the previous work. The
$^{18}$Ne($\alpha$,$p$)$^{21}$Na reaction rate has been recalculated, and the
astrophysical impact of our new rate has been investigated through one-zone
postprocessing x-ray burst calculations. We find that the
$^{18}$Ne($\alpha$,$p$)$^{21}$Na rate significantly affects the peak nuclear
energy generation rate and the onset temperature of this breakout reaction in
these phenomena.

In this study, we have investigated variable stars within the open cluster NGC 7044 using photometric data collected over a period of five years. The primary objective was to identify and characterize these variable stars, which include RR Lyrae variables, Cepheid variables, and long-period variables. We employed standard photometric techniques, including the analysis of light curves and period-luminosity relations, to determine the fundamental parameters of these stars such as their periods, amplitudes, and luminosities.  Our research revealed a total of 18 RR Lyrae variables, 3 Cepheid variables, and 5 long-period variables within NGC 7044. These findings were significant as they provided insights into the age and metallicity of the cluster. We also utilized these variables to estimate the distance to NGC 7044 by applying the Period-Luminosity relationship. Our results indicate that NGC 7044 is approximately 1.6 kiloparsecs from Earth, consistent with previous studies but providing a more precise measurement based on our detailed analysis.  The methodologies involved rigorous data reduction, careful examination of light curves, and statistical analysis to ensure accurate parameter determination. This work not only contributes to the understanding of NGC 7044 but also enhances our knowledge of variable stars and their utility in cosmology and astrophysics.

We present results of a survey of CCS, HC$_{3}$N, and HC$_{5}$N toward 40
dark cloud cores to search for "Carbon-Chain--Producing Regions(CCPRs)", where
carbon-chain molecules are extremely abundant relative to NH$_{3}$, as in
L1495B, L1521B, L1521E, and the cyanopolyyne peak of TMC-1. We have mainly
observed toward cores where the NH$_{3}$ lines are weak, not detected, or not
observed in previous surveys, and the CCS, HC$_{3}$N, and HC$_{5}$N lines have
been detected toward 17, 17, and 5 sources, respectively. Among them, we have
found a CCPR, L492, and its possible candidates, L1517D, L530D, L1147, and
L1172B. They all show low abundance ratios of [NH$_{3}$]/[CCS] (hereafter
called the NH$_{3}$/CCS ratio) indicating the chemical youth. Combining our
results with those of previous surveys, we have found a significant variation
of the NH$_{3}$/CCS ratio among dark cloud cores and among molecular cloud
complexes. Such a variation is also suggested by the detection rates of
carbon-chain molecules. For instance, the NH$_{3}$/CCS ratios are higher and
the detection rates of carbon-chain molecules are lower in the Ophiuchus cores
than in the Taurus cores. An origin of these systematic abundance variation is
discussed in terms of the difference in the evolutionary stage or the
contraction timescale. We have also identified a carbon-chain-rich star-forming
core, L483, where intense HC$_{3}$N and HC$_{5}$N lines are detected. This is a
possible candidate for a core with "Warm Carbon-Chain Chemistry".

In this study, we delve into the intricacies of Shirshov's height theorem and present new subexponential estimations for its parameters. Shirshov's theorem provides an upper bound on the number of generators needed to present a given group. Previous work on estimating Shirshov's height relied primarily on exponential bounds, which can be too conservative in some cases. We employ modern algebraic techniques, specifically the Reideme-Schreier method, to derive new and improved subexponential estimations for the Shirshov height. Our results hold for virtually free groups, and we demonstrate their applicability with examples. Furthermore, we discuss connections to related topics, such as the Burnside problem and the Novikov conjecture, and suggest directions for future research.  Our research builds upon previous work by Shpilrain (2007) and Shpilrain and Sapir (2011), who initiated the study of subexponential estimations for the number of generators in various algebraic structures. We extend their work to the context of Shirshov's height theorem and provide new insights into the efficiency of generating presentations for groups.  The Reideme-Schreier method plays a crucial role in our approach. This method allows us to bound the length of elements in finite presentations and effectively estimate the Shirshov height. The key idea is to utilize the Reideme graph structure to derive subexponential estimations, which are significantly better than exponential bounds in some cases. The methodology involves constructing Reideme graphs for the given group and analyzing their properties to derive upper bounds on the Shirshov height.  Our results have important implications for practical applications of group theory, such as in cryptography, coding theory, and algorithmic game theory. The improved subexponential estimations can lead to more efficient algorithms for generating group presentations and solving related problems.

With the advent of reliable positioning technologies and prevalence of
location-based services, it is now feasible to accurately study the propagation
of items such as infectious viruses, sensitive information pieces, and malwares
through a population of moving objects, e.g., individuals, mobile devices, and
vehicles. In such application scenarios, an item passes between two objects
when the objects are sufficiently close (i.e., when they are, so-called, in
contact), and hence once an item is initiated, it can penetrate the object
population through the evolving network of contacts among objects, termed
contact network. In this paper, for the first time we define and study
reachability queries in large (i.e., disk-resident) contact datasets which
record the movement of a (potentially large) set of objects moving in a spatial
environment over an extended time period. A reachability query verifies whether
two objects are "reachable" through the evolving contact network represented by
such contact datasets. We propose two contact-dataset indexes that enable
efficient evaluation of such queries despite the potentially humongous size of
the contact datasets. With the first index, termed ReachGrid, at the query time
only a small necessary portion of the contact network which is required for
reachability evaluation is constructed and traversed. With the second approach,
termed ReachGraph, we precompute reachability at different scales and leverage
these precalculations at the query time for efficient query processing. We
optimize the placement of both indexes on disk to enable efficient index
traversal during query processing. We study the pros and cons of our proposed
approaches by performing extensive experiments with both real and synthetic
data. Based on our experimental results, our proposed approaches outperform
existing reachability query processing techniques in contact n...[truncated].

We present the Space-based multi-band astronomical Variable Object Monitor
(SVOM), a future satellite mission for Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) studies, developed
in cooperation between the Chinese National Space Agency (CNSA), the Chinese
Academy of Science (CAS), the French Space Agency (CNES) and French research
institutes. The scientific objectives of the SVOM GRB studies cover their
classification (GRB diversity and unity of the model), their physics (particle
acceleration and radiation mechanisms), their progenitors, cosmological studies
(host galaxies, star formation history, re-ionization, cosmological
parameters), and fundamental physics (origin of cosmic rays, Lorentz
invariance, gravitational wave sources). From 2015 on, SVOM will provide fast
and accurate localizations of all known types of GRB, and determine the
temporal and spectral properties of the GRB emission, thanks to a set of four
onboard instruments. The trigger system of the coded-mask telescope ECLAIRs
onboard SVOM images the sky in the 4-120 keV energy range, in order to detect
and localize GRB in its 2 sr-wide field of view. The low-energy threshold of
ECLAIRs is well suited for the detection of highly red-shifted GRB. The
high-energy coverage is extended up to 5 MeV thanks to a non-imaging gamma-ray
spectrometer. GRB alerts are sent in real-time to the ground observers
community, and a spacecraft slew is performed in order to place the GRB within
the narrow fields of view of a soft X-ray telescope and a visible-band
telescope, to refine the GRB position and study its early afterglow.
Ground-based robotic telescopes and wide-angle cameras complement the onboard
instruments. A large fraction of GRB will have redshift determinations, thanks
to an observing strategy optimized to facilitate follow-up observations by
large ground-based spectroscopic telescopes.

We investigated the relay-pair selection in buffer-aided successive opportunistic relaying using a multi-antenna source, with the aim of optimizing the performance of wireless networks. Our approach involved analyzing the impact of relay-pair selection on the buffer-aided successive opportunistic relaying protocol, with a focus on multi-antenna sources.   Through simulations, we demonstrated that relay-pair selection can significantly improve the performance of buffer-aided successive opportunistic relaying, particularly in scenarios with limited buffer resources. Our results showed that the relay-pair selection scheme can effectively reduce the average delay and packet loss rates, while also improving the throughput.   We proposed a novel relay-pair selection algorithm that takes into account the antenna gains and buffer constraints of the multi-antenna source. The algorithm uses a machine learning-based approach to optimize the relay-pair selection, allowing for real-time adaptation to changing channel conditions.   Our simulation results showed that the proposed algorithm outperformed existing relay-pair selection schemes, achieving a 25% reduction in average delay and a 15% increase in throughput. The key insights gained from this study highlight the importance of relay-pair selection in buffer-aided successive opportunistic relaying, and demonstrate the potential of multi-antenna sources to improve wireless network performance.

The frequencies and phases of emission from extra-solar sources measured by
Earth-bound observers are modulated by the motions of the observer with respect
to the source, and through relativistic effects. These modulations depend
critically on the source's sky-location. Precise knowledge of the modulations
are required to coherently track the source's phase over long observations, for
example, in pulsar timing, or searches for continuous gravitational waves. The
modulations can be modelled as sky-location and time-dependent time delays that
convert arrival times at the observer to the inertial frame of the source,
which can often be the Solar system barycentre. We study the use of reduced
order modelling for speeding up the calculation of this time delay for any
sky-location. We find that the time delay model can be decomposed into just
four basis vectors, and with these the delay for any sky-location can be
reconstructed to sub-nanosecond accuracy. When compared to standard routines
for time delay calculation in gravitational wave searches, using the reduced
basis can lead to speed-ups of 30 times. We have also studied components of
time delays for sources in binary systems. Assuming eccentricities $< 0.25$ we
can reconstruct the delays to within 100s of nanoseconds, with best case
speed-ups of a factor of 10, or factors of two when interpolating the basis for
different orbital periods or time stamps. In long-duration phase-coherent
searches for sources with sky-position uncertainties, or binary parameter
uncertainties, these speed-ups could allow enhancements in their scopes without
large additional computational burdens.

This research explores the application of node-varying graph filters in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The objective is to enhance the performance of CNNs by incorporating node-varying filters, which can adapt to the local structure of the data represented as a graph. A novel methodology is proposed to integrate node-varying filters into the convolutional layers of CNNs, allowing for more expressive and adaptive feature learning.   Key findings of this study show that CNNs equipped with node-varying graph filters outperform traditional CNN architectures on graph-structured data tasks, such as social network analysis and molecular property prediction. The experiments conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in capturing complex relationships between nodes in a graph.  In conclusion, the incorporation of node-varying graph filters in CNNs presents a promising direction for improving the performance of graph-based deep learning models. By enabling CNNs to effectively learn and exploit the intricate topology of graph data, this research contributes to advancing the field of graph neural networks and expanding the applicability of deep learning techniques to various domains.

In this study, we explore the phase diagram and pair correlations of the Gaussian core model in high Euclidean dimensions. The Gaussian core model is a system of particles with a pair potential defined by a Gaussian function with a hardcore repulsion. Our work aims to investigate the phase behavior and structural properties of this model as the dimensionality of space increases. By employing both analytical calculations and computer simulations, we have uncovered intriguing results. We have identified the existence of a rich phase diagram with various phases such as gas, liquid, and crystal appearing in high dimensions. Additionally, our analysis of pair correlations has revealed intricate patterns indicative of the underlying structural organization of the particles. Our findings shed new light on the behavior of the Gaussian core model in high Euclidean dimensions and provide valuable insights into the nature of dense systems in such regimes. This work contributes to the understanding of phase transitions and structural order in high-dimensional systems, with potential implications for diverse fields ranging from statistical physics to materials science.

We investigated the implementation of One Time Pad (OTP) for password protection, integrating T.E.C. steganography and secure password transmission protocols to enhance data security. Our primary aim was to address vulnerabilities associated with traditional password storage and transmission methods, which are susceptible to interception and unauthorized access. By employing T.E.C. steganography, we embedded OTPs within innocuous digital files, allowing for covert sharing of cryptographic keys without revealing their presence. Simultaneously, we developed a protocol for secure password transmission that utilizes asymmetric encryption coupled with ephemeral key exchanges to ensure that passwords remain confidential during transfers.   We conducted experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methodologies against standard transmissive attacks and unauthorized access attempts. Our results indicated a significant reduction in the probability of successful password interception while also achieving high levels of user transparency. Notably, the combination of T.E.C. steganography with secure transmission protocols yielded a robust system capable of protecting sensitive data in various digital environments.  In conclusion, our work presents a novel approach to password protection through the hybridization of OTP with advanced steganographic techniques and encryption protocols, contributing substantially to the field of cybersecurity. Future work will involve refining these methods for broader applications and exploring their performance against emerging threats.

This research explores the computational simulation of model cohesive powders, focusing on the influence of different assembling procedures and contact laws on powders in low consolidation states. The investigation aims to enhance the understanding of the mechanical behavior of cohesive particulate materials, which is critical for numerous industrial applications. A discrete element method (DEM) was employed to model the powders, taking into account varied contact laws, including linear and nonlinear models, as well as diverse assembling techniques such as deposition and compression methods. Detailed simulations were conducted to evaluate how these factors affect the powder's macroscopic properties, such as bulk density and shear strength. Our findings indicate significant differences in the behavior of powders based on the initial assembly procedure; particularly, the deposition method exhibited higher porosity and lower consolidation compared to compression techniques. Furthermore, non-linear contact laws were found to better capture the behavior of cohesive powders, providing more realistic predictions of material response under low consolidation. These results highlight the importance of selecting appropriate modeling strategies to accurately predict the performance of cohesive materials in industrial processes. The study adds to the growing body of knowledge in powder technology, offering a framework for optimizing the design and development of processes involving cohesive powders, ultimately aiding in the development of more efficient and reliable industrial applications.

The variance-gamma (VG) distributions form a four parameter family that
includes as special and limiting cases the normal, gamma and Laplace
distributions. Some of the numerous applications include financial modelling
and approximation on Wiener space. Recently, Stein's method has been extended
to the VG distribution. However, technical difficulties have meant that bounds
for distributional approximations have only been given for smooth test
functions (typically requiring at least two derivatives for the test function).
In this paper, which deals with symmetric variance-gamma (SVG) distributions,
and a companion paper \cite{gaunt vgii}, which deals with the whole family of
VG distributions, we address this issue. In this paper, we obtain new bounds
for the derivatives of the solution of the SVG Stein equation, which allow for
approximations to be made in the Kolmogorov and Wasserstein metrics, and also
introduce a distributional transformation that is natural in the context of SVG
approximation. We apply this theory to obtain Wasserstein or Kolmogorov error
bounds for SVG approximation in four settings: comparison of VG and SVG
distributions, SVG approximation of functionals of isonormal Gaussian
processes, SVG approximation of a statistic for binary sequence comparison, and
Laplace approximation of a random sum of independent mean zero random
variables.

We present a novel supervised clustering approach designed to enhance fMRI-based inference of brain states, addressing the limitations of existing unsupervised methods that can overlook critical variances in neural activity patterns. Our methodology involves the integration of supervised learning techniques with traditional clustering algorithms, facilitating the accurate identification and characterization of distinct brain states corresponding to specific cognitive or behavioral tasks. We utilized a comprehensive dataset comprising fMRI scans from multiple subjects engaged in various cognitive activities. Through rigorous feature extraction, we emphasized spatial and temporal patterns of brain activation, which we then leveraged to train a classifier capable of discriminating between brain states.   Our results demonstrate that the supervised clustering approach significantly outperforms conventional unsupervised algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy and interpretability. The model achieved an average accuracy rate of 87% in distinguishing between different brain states, as validated through cross-validation techniques. Furthermore, we identified key brain regions prominently involved in the distinct states, offering insights into their functional roles.   We conclude that our supervised clustering framework not only enhances the precision of brain state inference but also provides a robust tool for understanding the dynamic nature of neural processes during cognitive tasks. This work encourages further exploration into the application of supervised learning in neuroimaging and highlights its potential impact on the field of cognitive neuroscience.

In the study of complex systems, understanding the interactions between multiple time series is crucial for identifying underlying patterns and dynamical relationships. This research aims to extend coherence and phase synchronization analysis to pairs of multivariate time series, addressing the limitations of conventional approaches that often overlook zero-lag contributions. Utilizing advanced statistical techniques, we developed a framework to separate relevant phase relationships from spurious correlations, thereby enabling a more precise analysis of temporal synchronization among multiple signals. The methodology was applied to simulated and real-world datasets, including neural and financial time series, to validate its efficacy. Key findings reveal that the proposed method significantly enhances the ability to detect true synchronization signals while minimizing the influence of artifacts associated with zero-lag interactions. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates that multivariate coherence can reveal nuanced relationships that would remain undetected through traditional univariate methods. Our results indicate that this generalization offers a powerful tool for researchers in various fields, from neuroscience to finance, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics present in multivariate systems. In conclusion, the removal of zero-lag contributions provides a more accurate reflection of the genuine coherence between time series, leading to improved insights into their interdependencies and the systems they represent. This advancement paves the way for future research aimed at unraveling the complexities of dynamical systems through enhanced temporal analysis techniques.

This research paper focuses on the development of faster small-constant-periodic merging networks, which are crucial in high-speed data processing systems. Merging networks are fundamental components in these systems, responsible for aggregating and distributing data among multiple processing units. However, existing merging networks often suffer from significant latency and scalability issues, particularly for small-scale applications.  The objective of this research is to design and optimize a novel merging network architecture that minimizes latency and maximizes throughput for small-constant-periodic data streams. By analyzing the characteristics of small-constant-periodic data, we identified key challenges such as packet fragmentation, synchronization overhead, and data skewness. To address these challenges, we propose a novel merging network architecture that incorporates a hybrid packet scheduling approach, adaptive packet buffering, and a novel synchronization mechanism.  Our proposed architecture was evaluated using a combination of theoretical analysis, simulation, and experimental results. The results show that our architecture outperforms state-of-the-art merging networks in terms of latency and throughput, while maintaining a constant period of operation. Specifically, we achieved a 30% reduction in latency and a 25% increase in throughput compared to the best existing architectures. These findings demonstrate the potential of our proposed architecture for improving the performance of small-scale data processing systems. The results of this research have significant implications for the design and optimization of merging networks in high-speed data processing systems.

In this work, we address the problem of efficiently solving the Steiner Tree Problem, a fundamental combinatorial optimization challenge with significant applications in network design. Traditional linear programming (LP) relaxations for this problem often face limitations in terms of tightness and computational complexity. We propose novel hypergraphic LP relaxations that leverage the structural properties of hypergraphs to enhance the relaxation strength while maintaining computational tractability. Our approach involves extending the classic graph-based formulations to hypergraphs, which encapsulate higher-order connectivity information that standard edge-based models cannot capture.   Through rigorous analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our hypergraphic LP relaxations significantly improve upon traditional methods, yielding tighter bounds that improve solution quality for Steiner Tree instances. We also develop efficient algorithms for solving the proposed hypergraphic formulations, using cutting-edge techniques in polyhedral theory and combinatorial optimization. Our results indicate that the hypergraphic approach reduces the duality gap observed in standard LP relaxations, thereby enhancing the robustness of heuristic methods that rely on these formulations.   Additionally, we present comparative studies that highlight the improved computational efficiency of our method relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques. The key contribution lies in our ability to model complex inter-node relationships succinctly, which provides deeper insights into the underlying network structure. This advancement not only broadens the scope of applicable scenarios for LP-based methods but also sets a foundational framework for exploring hypergraphic relaxations in other combinatorial optimization problems.

The existence of an extra Z' inspired from heterotic-string theory at
accessible energy scales attracted considerable interest in the particle
physics literature. Surprisingly, however, the construction of
heterotic--string derived models that allow for an extra Z' to remain unbroken
down to low scales has proven to be very difficult. The main reason being that
the U(1) symmetries that are typically discussed in the literature are either
anomalous or have to be broken at a high scale to generate light neutrino
masses. In this paper we use for that purpose the self duality property under
the spinor vector duality, which was discovered in free fermionic
heterotic-string models. The chiral massless states in the self--dual models
fill complete 27 representations of E6. The anomaly free gauge symmetry in the
effective low energy field theory of our string model is $SU(4)_C\times
SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R\times U(1)_\zeta$, where $U(1)_\zeta$ is the family
universal $U(1)$ symmetry that descends from E6, and is typically anomalous in
other free fermionic heterotic-string models. Our model therefore allows for
the existence of a low scale Z', which is a combination of $B-L$, $T_{3_L}$ and
$T_{3_R}$. The string model is free of exotic fractionally charged states in
the massless spectrum. It contains exotic SO(10) singlet states that carry
fractional, non--E6 charge, with respect to $U(1)_\zeta$. These non-E6 states
arise in the string model due to the breaking of the E6 symmetry by discrete
Wilson lines. They represent a distinct signature of the string vacua and
cannot arise in E6 Grand Unified Theories. They may provide viable dark matter
candidates.

RE J2248-511 is one of only 14 non-blazar AGN detected in the far ultraviolet
by the ROSAT Wide Field Camera implying a large ultrasoft X-ray flux. This soft
X-ray excess is strongly variable on year timescales, a common property of
Narrow Line Seyfert 1s, yet its optical linewidths classify this source as a
broad-lined Seyfert 1. We use four nearly simultaneous optical--X-ray SEDs
spanning 7 years to study the spectral shape and long term variability of RE
J2248-511.
  Here we show that the continuum SED for the brightest epoch dataset is
consistent with the mean SED of a standard quasar, and matches well to that
from an XMM-SDSS sample of AGN with <M/M_Sun> ~ 10^8 and <L/L_Edd> ~ 0.2. All
the correlated optical and soft X-ray variability can be due entirely to a
major absorption event. The only remarkable aspect of this AGN is that there is
no measurable intrinsic X-ray absorption column in the brightest epoch dataset.
The observed FUV flux is determined by the combination of this and the fact
that the source lies within a local absorption `hole'. RE J2248-511, whose
variable, ultrasoft X-ray flux once challenged its BLS1 classification,
demonstrates that characterisation of such objects requires multi-epoch,
multi-wavelength campaigns.

Pluripotent embryonic stem cells are of paramount importance for biomedical
research thanks to their innate ability for self-renewal and differentiation
into all major cell lines. The fateful decision to exit or remain in the
pluripotent state is regulated by complex genetic regulatory network. Latest
advances in transcriptomics have made it possible to infer basic topologies of
pluripotency governing networks. The inferred network topologies, however, only
encode boolean information while remaining silent about the roles of dynamics
and molecular noise in gene expression. These features are widely considered
essential for functional decision making. Herein we developed a framework for
extending the boolean level networks into models accounting for individual
genetic switches and promoter architecture which allows mechanistic
interrogation of the roles of molecular noise, external signaling, and network
topology. We demonstrate the pluripotent state of the network to be a broad
attractor which is robust to variations of gene expression. Dynamics of exiting
the pluripotent state, on the other hand, is significantly influenced by the
molecular noise originating from genetic switching events which makes cells
more responsive to extracellular signals. Lastly we show that steady state
probability landscape can be significantly remodeled by global gene switching
rates alone which can be taken as a proxy for how global epigenetic
modifications exert control over stability of pluripotent states.

This study investigates the behavior of Floquet topological systems in the vicinity of band crossings, with a focus on reservoir-induced coherence and steady-state entropy production. Floquet systems, characterized by periodic driving, exhibit rich topological properties that can give rise to exotic quantum phenomena. However, the interplay between topological phases and the effects of external reservoirs on these systems remains poorly understood.   The objective of this research is to explore the interplay between Floquet topological systems and reservoir-induced coherence, with a particular emphasis on the impact on steady-state entropy production. By employing a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we examine the behavior of Floquet systems near band crossings, where the interplay between topological phases and the reservoir-induced coherence is expected to be most pronounced.   Our results reveal that the reservoir-induced coherence can significantly impact the steady-state entropy production of Floquet systems, leading to a complex interplay between the topological phases and the reservoir. We find that the coherence induced by the reservoir can give rise to a non-trivial steady-state entropy production, which is characterized by a non-zero value of the entropy current. Furthermore, we observe that the steady-state entropy production is sensitive to the strength and frequency of the driving, as well as the properties of the reservoir.   The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the interplay between Floquet topological systems and external reservoirs, and highlight the importance of considering the effects of reservoir-induced coherence on the behavior of these systems.

Astrophysical objects such as active-galactic nuclei (AGN) and gamma-ray
bursts (GRBs) can be sources of high energy, astrophysical neutrinos. The decay
of charged pions produces electron and muon-flavor neutrinos from the primary
decay of the pion, and from the secondary decay of the resulting charged
lepton. At low energies we expect the flavor ratio
$\Phi_{\nu_e}:\Phi_{\nu_\mu}:\Phi_{\nu_\tau}$ to be $1:2:0$ at the source. We
are interested in the flavor ratios as measured on Earth after the neutrinos
propagate over cosmic distance scales from the source. If we only consider
vacuum flavor transition probabilities between the three active flavors then we
expect a measured flavor ratio of $1:1:1$ up to small corrections from
$\theta_{13}$ and non-maximal $\theta_{23}$. When we include mixing with two
additional flavors of sterile neutrinos then we see corrections to this ratio
up to $\sim 30%$. Furthermore, if we consider energy-loss of the charged
leptons involved in the pion decay from cosmic sources then these flux ratios
depend on the neutrino energy. We examine these energy-dependent flavor ratios
using a specific model for sterile neutrino mixing, and compare to expected
ratios when only three neutrino flavors are considered. At energies $E_\nu >$ 1
TeV the flavor ratios observed in experiments such as IceCube can probe the
existence of sterile neutrinos.

The intermetallic compound LaAgSb2 displays two charge-density-wave (CDW)
transitions, which were detected with measurements of electrical resistivity
(rho), magnetic susceptibility, and X-ray scattering; the upper transition
takes place at T1 approx. 210 K, and it is accompanied by a large anomaly in
rho(T), whereas the lower transition is marked by a much more subtle anomaly at
T2 approx. 185 K. We studied the effect of hydrostatic pressure (P) on the
formation of the upper CDW state in pure and doped La1-xRxAgSb2 (R = Ce, Nd)
compounds, by means of measurements of rho(T) for P < 23 kbar. We found that
the hydrostatic pressure, as well as the chemical pressure introduced by the
partial substitution of the smaller Ce and Nd ions for La, result in the
suppression of the CDW ground state, e.g. the reduction of the ordering
temperature T1. The values of dT1/dP are approx. 2-4 times higher for the
Ce-doped samples as compared to pure LaAgSb2, or even La0.75Nd0.25AgSb2
Nd-doped with a comparable T1 (P=0). This increased sensitivity to pressure may
be due to increasing Ce- hybridization under pressure. The magnetic ordering
temperature of the cerium-doped compounds is also reduced by pressure, and the
high pressure behavior of the Ce-doped samples is dominated by Kondo impurity
scattering.

Motivated by studies on the recurrent properties of animal and human
mobility, we introduce a path-dependent random walk model with long range
memory for which not only the mean square displacement (MSD) can be obtained
exactly in the asymptotic limit, but also the propagator. The model consists of
a random walker on a lattice, which, at a constant rate, stochastically
relocates at a site occupied at some earlier time. This time in the past is
chosen randomly according to a memory kernel, whose temporal decay can be
varied via an exponent parameter. In the weakly non-Markovian regime, memory
reduces the diffusion coefficient from the bare value. When the mean backward
jump in time diverges, the diffusion coefficient vanishes and a transition to
an anomalous subdiffusive regime occurs. Paradoxically, at the transition, the
process is an anti-correlated L\'evy flight. Although in the subdiffusive
regime the model exhibits some features of the continuous time random walk with
infinite mean waiting time, it belongs to another universality class. If memory
is very long-ranged, a second transition takes place to a regime characterized
by a logarithmic growth of the MSD with time. In this case the process is
asymptotically Gaussian and effectively described as a scaled Brownian motion
with a diffusion coefficient decaying as 1/t.

In this study, we present the results of our research focused on measuring detailed chemical abundances from co-added medium-resolution spectra. Our work aims to address the challenge of accurately determining chemical compositions in astronomical objects with limited spectral resolution, such as Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies and globular clusters. By conducting tests on these stellar systems, we have developed a methodology that allows for the extraction of precise abundance information despite the spectral constraints.  Our approach involves combining multiple spectra to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and enhance the measurement accuracy of elemental abundances. We employ various spectral synthesis techniques and abundance analysis tools to extract detailed chemical information, including the abundance of key elements crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of these stellar systems.  Through our analyses, we have successfully demonstrated the feasibility and reliability of measuring detailed chemical abundances from co-added medium-resolution spectra. Our findings provide valuable insights into the chemical enrichment histories and stellar populations of Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies and globular clusters, contributing to the broader understanding of galactic evolution and stellar nucleosynthesis processes.

We present a study exploring the nature and properties of the Circum-Galactic
Medium (CGM) and its connection to the atomic gas content in the interstellar
medium (ISM) of galaxies as traced by the HI 21cm line. Our sample includes 45
low-z (0.026-0.049) galaxies from the GALEX Arecibo SDSS Survey. Their CGM was
probed via absorption in the spectra of background Quasi-Stellar Objects at
impact parameters of 63 to 231kpc. The spectra were obtained with the Cosmic
Origins Spectrograph aboard the Hubble Space Telescope. We detected neutral
hydrogen (Ly$\alpha$ absorption-lines) in the CGM of 92% of the galaxies. We
find the radial profile of the CGM as traced by the Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width
can be fit as an exponential with a scale length of roughly the virial radius
of the dark matter halo. We found no correlation between the orientation of
sightline relative to the galaxy major axis and the Ly$\alpha$ equivalent
width. The velocity spread of the circumgalactic gas is consistent with that
seen in the atomic gas in the interstellar medium. We find a strong correlation
(99.8% confidence) between the gas fraction (M(HI)/M*) and the
impact-parameter-corrected Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width. This is stronger than
the analogous correlation between corrected Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width and
SFR/M* (97.5% confidence). These results imply a physical connection between
the HI disk and the CGM, which is on scales an order-of-magnitude larger. This
is consistent with the picture in which the HI disk is nourished by accretion
of gas from the CGM.

The interstellar medium (ISM) is a complex and dynamic environment characterized by the presence of various molecular and atomic species (Ferland et al., 2001). Among these, solid hydrogen (s-H2) has been detected in several astrophysical environments, such as circumstellar disks (Carretti et al., 2014), planetary rings (Taylor et al., 2003), and dense molecular clouds (Oka et al., 2001). However, the physical conditions leading to the formation and persistence of s-H2 in the ISM remain elusive.     In this study, we present the results of a theoretical investigation into the formation and stability of s-H2 clusters in the ISM using molecular dynamics simulations. We find that s-H2 clusters can form in cold and dense regions of the ISM where the hydrogen density exceeds 10^4 cm^-3 and the temperature is below 10 K. Our simulations reveal that the formation of s-H2 clusters is driven by the self-assembly of hydrogen molecules through van der Waals forces, followed by the condensation of these clusters into larger aggregates. We further demonstrate that the interaction of s-H2 clusters with cosmic rays can lead to their fragmentation and destruction.     Our results provide insights into the physical conditions required for the formation and stability of s-H2 clusters in the ISM. They also highlight the importance of considering the role of solid hydrogen in the interstellar environment and its potential impact on the evolution of astrophysical systems. Future work will focus on exploring the properties and dynamics of s-H2 clusters in more detail and investigating their role in the chemistry of the ISM.

This study investigates the magnetic field structures within the simulated Milky Way-like disk galaxies formed as part of the Auriga project. The research employs magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the galactic dynamo process, focusing on the generation and evolution of magnetic fields over cosmic time. Results indicate that the galactic dynamo operates efficiently, producing both large-scale spiral arms and small-scale turbulence in the interstellar medium. Key findings include the predominance of toroidal magnetic field components in the disk regions, with poloidal fields being predominantly confined to the central bulge. The methodology involves detailed analysis of magnetic field strength, orientation, and distribution across various galactic scales. These studies highlight the importance of magnetic fields in shaping the structure and dynamics of galaxies, contributing to our understanding of how magnetic fields influence the evolution of disk galaxies.

The Kondo resonance is a fundamental concept in condensed matter physics that describes the temperature dependence of the magnetic susceptibility of a heavy fermion system. In this context, the Kondo resonance is a quasiparticle excitations that emerges due to the interaction between the localized spin and the conduction electrons. The Kondo resonance plays a crucial role in understanding the behavior of heavy fermion systems, which are characterized by strong correlations between the electrons and the lattice.  Recent studies have shown that the Kondo resonance can be quenched by an external perturbation, leading to a sudden change in the magnetic behavior of the system. However, the time evolution of the Kondo resonance in response to a quench is not well understood. In this study, we investigate the time evolution of the Kondo resonance in a heavy fermion system subjected to a quench, using a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations.  Our results show that the Kondo resonance exhibits a non-equilibrium dynamics, characterized by a slow relaxation towards an equilibrium state. The time evolution of the Kondo resonance is dominated by the interaction between the localized spin and the conduction electrons, which leads to a strong correlation between the quasiparticle excitations and the lattice. We also find that the quench leads to a non-trivial dynamics of the Kondo resonance, characterized by a complex interplay between the localized spin and the conduction electrons. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of heavy fermion systems under the influence of external perturbations, and have important implications for the understanding of the Kondo resonance in a wide range of systems.

In this paper, we propose a robust and parsimonious approach using Deep
Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) to recognize and interpret interior space.
DCNN has achieved incredible success in object and scene recognition. In this
study we design and train a DCNN to classify a pre-zoning indoor space, and
from a single phone photo to recognize the learned space features, with no need
of additional assistive technology. We collect more than 600,000 images inside
MIT campus buildings to train our DCNN model, and achieved 97.9% accuracy in
validation dataset and 81.7% accuracy in test dataset based on spatial-scale
fixed model. Furthermore, the recognition accuracy and spatial resolution can
be potentially improved through multiscale classification model. We identify
the discriminative image regions through Class Activating Mapping (CAM)
technique, to observe the model's behavior in how to recognize space and
interpret it in an abstract way. By evaluating the results with
misclassification matrix, we investigate the visual spatial feature of interior
space by looking into its visual similarity and visual distinctiveness, giving
insights into interior design and human indoor perception and wayfinding
research. The contribution of this paper is threefold. First, we propose a
robust and parsimonious approach for indoor navigation using DCNN. Second, we
demonstrate that DCNN also has a potential capability in space feature learning
and recognition, even under severe appearance changes. Third, we introduce a
DCNN based approach to look into the visual similarity and visual
distinctiveness of interior space.

In this study, we investigate the circumstellar medium (CSM) of massive stars as a possible origin for the broad emission lines observed in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the observational data and theoretical models to understand the characteristics of CSM and its potential influence on GRBs. Our research suggests that the dense and structured CSM of massive stars can produce broad emission lines, similar to those observed in GRBs.  We employ hydrodynamic simulations to model the CSM interactions with the GRB jet. The simulations reveal that the CSM can significantly affect the observed emission features of GRBs. Specifically, we find that the CSM can produce broad and asymmetric lines, as observed in GRB afterglows. Moreover, the observed spectral evolution of GRBs can be explained by the evolving CSM interaction with the GRB jet.  We also examine the observational data of various GRBs, comparing their spectral features with those of stellar winds and supernova remnants. Our analysis reveals notable similarities between GRB emission lines and those of massive stars' CSM. This evidence supports the hypothesis that massive stars' CSM may be a significant contributor to the broad emission lines in GRB observations.  In conclusion, our research sheds new light on the connection between the CSM of massive stars and the broad emission lines observed in GRBs. We provide compelling evidence that the CSM can produce broad lines and shape the observed spectra of GRB afterglows. Our findings demonstrate the importance of studying CSM properties to better understand the astrophysical processes associated with GRBs.  Keywords circumstellar medium, massive stars, gamma-ray bursts, emission lines, hydrodynamic simulations.

The abstract for the research paper titled "The Evolution of Low Mass, Close Binary Systems with a Neutron Star Component A Detailed Grid" outlines the study's objectives, methodologies, key findings, and conclusions.
