likelihood estimator, and we shall show, via some typical examples, that the
$\rho$-estimators perform better from various points of view.

This study investigates the deceptive nature of the boundary conditions of a specific class of nonlinear (1+2)-dimensional boundary value problems. The issues surrounding these boundary conditions arise from their seemingly inconsistent application, leading to two distinct solutions. Our approach involves identifying the underlying conditional symmetries, which allow us to construct an equivalent problem with consistent boundary conditions.     By employing the Lie point symmetries method, we discover a set of infinitesimal generators that reveal the underlying symmetry structure. Furthermore, we apply the Painlevé analysis method to investigate the integrability of the system, which leads to the classification of the boundary value problem based on Painlevé transcendents. The consistent boundary conditions found through symmetry analysis yield results that correspond to the physically more realistic solution.     The implications of our findings extend to various areas of mathematical physics and engineering, where boundary conditions play a critical role in determining system behavior. Our work demonstrates the importance of symmetry analysis in unraveling the complexities of nonlinear systems and establishing a clear understanding of the physical implications of the boundary conditions. The techniques used in this study provide a valuable framework for analyzing similar problems, allowing for a deeper comprehension of their underlying structures and behaviors.     In conclusion, this investigation reveals the deceptive nature of the boundary conditions of a specific class of nonlinear (1+2)-dimensional boundary value problems and provides a methodology for identifying and constructing consistent boundary conditions through the use of Lie point symmetries and Painlevé analysis. The results of our study have significant implications for mathematical physics and engineering, highlighting the importance of symmetry analysis in understanding complex nonlinear systems.

The W^+W^- cross section has remained one of the most consistently discrepant
channels compared to SM predictions at the LHC, measured by both ATLAS and CMS
at 7 and 8 TeV. Developing a better modeling of this channel is crucial to
understanding properties of the Higgs and potential new physics. In this paper
we investigate the effects of NNLL transverse momentum resummation in measuring
the W^+W^- cross section. In the formalism we employ, transverse momentum
resummation does not change the total inclusive cross section, but gives a more
accurate prediction for the p_T distribution of the diboson system. By
re-weighting the p_T distribution of events produced by Monte Carlo generators,
we find a systematic shift that decreases the experimental discrepancy with the
SM prediction by approximately 3-7% depending on the MC generator and parton
shower used. The primary effect comes from the jet veto cut used by both
experiments. We comment on the connections to jet veto resummation, and other
methods the experiments can use to test this effect. We also discuss the
correlation of resummation effects in this channel with other diboson channels.
Ultimately p_T resummation improves the agreement between the SM and
experimental measurements for most generators, but does not account for the
measured ~20% difference with the SM and further investigations into this
channel are needed.

Galaxy mergers are crucial for the evolution of galaxies, yet the measurement of the galaxy merger fraction (GMF) at redshift z ~ 0 - 3 remains a discrepancy due to varying methodologies and assumptions.  The objective of this study is to investigate the causes of this discrepancy and propose a standardized methodology for accurately measuring the GMF at z ~ 0 - 3.  We conduct a systematic review of the existing literature on GMF measurements, analyzing the methodologies and assumptions used. We also perform a Monte Carlo simulation to quantify the impact of uncertainties in stellar mass, star formation history, and morphology on GMF measurements.  Our analysis reveals that the main causes of the discrepancy are the choice of stellar mass estimation method and assumptions regarding the star formation history. We propose a new methodology that accounts for these factors and reduces the uncertainty in GMF measurements. Our Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed methodology results in a more consistent GMF measurement across different redshifts.  The discrepancy in GMF measurements at z ~ 0 - 3 can be resolved by adopting a standardized methodology that accounts for uncertainties in stellar mass estimation and star formation history. The proposed methodology provides a more accurate and consistent measurement of the GMF, contributing to a better understanding of galaxy evolution.  This study investigates the causes of the discrepancy in galaxy merger fraction (GMF) measurements at redshift z ~ 0 - 3. Through a systematic review of the literature and Monte Carlo simulations, we reveal that the main causes of the discrepancy are the choice of stellar mass estimation method and assumptions regarding star formation history. A new methodology is proposed to address these factors and reduce uncertainty, resulting in a more consistent GMF measurement across different redshifts. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of galaxy evolution.

This research paper investigates the constraints on cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and dark matter through gamma-ray observations of the Coma Cluster of Galaxies using data from the VERITAS and Fermi telescopes. The study aims to understand the interplay between these components within the cluster, shedding light on the underlying physics of cosmic ray acceleration, magnetic field amplification, and dark matter distribution. Methodologically, the research combines data from the VERITAS ground-based observatory and the Fermi space telescope to analyze the gamma-ray emission from the Coma Cluster. Key findings suggest the presence of cosmic rays interacting with the magnetic fields and dark matter content of the cluster, providing insights into the complex dynamics of these fundamental astrophysical components. The results offer valuable constraints on the properties of cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and dark matter in the Coma Cluster, contributing to our broader understanding of galaxy clusters and the universe's large-scale structure. In conclusion, the study demonstrates the power of combining multiwavelength observations to probe the astrophysical processes at play in galaxy clusters, offering new perspectives on the intricate relationship between cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and dark matter in cosmic environments.

In this study, we present an analysis of the soft gamma-ray emission from supernova SN2014J, utilizing data acquired from the Suzaku space observatory. Our goal is to enhance the understanding of gamma-ray emission characteristics during the post-explosion phase of Type Ia supernovae and to address the limitations in current models that predict these emissions. We employ Suzaku's Hard X-ray Detector (HXD) and X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) to capture the photon data in the 10–300 keV range, focusing on spectra that are particularly indicative of the radioactive decay of isotopes such as Nickel-56 and Cobalt-56.   The methodology involves a comprehensive data reduction process followed by high-sensitivity spectral analysis. By constructing detailed light curves and energy spectra, we effectively isolate the gamma-ray lines and continua that correlate with the expected decay paths. We identify the distinct 158 keV and 812 keV lines, confirming the presence of radioactive decay products. The results reveal discrepancies in the low-energy gamma-ray emissions when compared to standard supernova models, suggesting additional processes at play during the explosion or subsequent cooling phases.  Our findings contribute new insights into the synthesis of heavy elements and energy release mechanisms in Type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, the precision of Suzaku's measurements provides constraints for refining theoretical models of supernovae and enhances predictions for future observations, particularly in early detection and flux measurement techniques. This work underscores the importance of integrating multi-wavelength data and advances the field's comprehension of stellar explosion dynamics and nucleosynthesis.

We present a detailed analysis of the nebular spectra of the transitional Type Ia Supernovae 2007on and 2011iv, highlighting the presence of broad, multiple components that are indicative of aspherical explosion cores. Our investigation reveals that the spectra of these events exhibit a complex structure, featuring multiple emission lines and a broad, flat continuum, which is characteristic of non-spherical explosion geometries. Through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data, we demonstrate that the observed spectral features are the result of a combination of thermal and non-thermal processes, which are influenced by the asymmetry of the explosion core. Our results are consistent with the notion that these supernovae exhibit a "bump" or "bump-like" structure in their explosion profiles, which is thought to be a consequence of the interaction between the explosion core and the surrounding circumstellar medium. Our analysis suggests that the observed spectral features are a direct consequence of the complex dynamics of the explosion core, and that the multiple components of the spectra can be used to constrain models of Type Ia supernovae explosion mechanisms. By providing new insights into the explosion dynamics of these objects, our study sheds light on the underlying physics of these enigmatic events and has implications for our understanding of the most luminous explosions in the universe.

This research paper explores the application of Bordered Floer homology to manifolds with torus boundaries via immersed curves. Bordered Floer homology is a novel approach to studying the topology of manifolds with boundary, particularly those with non-trivial boundary components. In this context, the torus boundary plays a crucial role in shaping the topology of the manifold.   The objective of this research is to develop a systematic method for computing Bordered Floer homology for manifolds with torus boundaries via immersed curves. Immersed curves are used as a tool to encode information about the boundary of the manifold, allowing for a more precise analysis of the topology.   The methodology employed in this research involves the use of Heegaard splittings to construct immersed curves on the torus boundary. These curves are then used to compute the Bordered Floer homology of the manifold via a combination of Floer homology and Heegaard Floer homology.   Key findings of this research include the development of a new algorithm for computing Bordered Floer homology via immersed curves, as well as the application of this algorithm to a variety of manifolds with torus boundaries. These results demonstrate the power of Bordered Floer homology in studying the topology of manifolds with boundary, particularly those with non-trivial boundary components.   In conclusion, this research provides a new framework for studying the topology of manifolds with torus boundaries via immersed curves. The development of this framework has significant implications for our understanding of the topology of manifolds with boundary, and opens up new avenues for research in this area.

This research paper investigates the secrecy capacity of a class of broadcast channels (BCs) where one user is the legitimate receiver and another user is the eavesdropper aiming to overhear confidential information. The study aims to determine the maximum rate at which secret messages can be transmitted from the transmitter to the legitimate receiver while preventing the eavesdropper from decoding the message. Utilizing information-theoretic techniques, we derive the achievable secrecy rate region for a specific BC model characterized by correlated sources and multiple access interference. The methodology involves formulating the problem as a constrained optimization task, considering the channel state information available at the transmitter and receiver. Key findings reveal that the secrecy capacity increases with the diversity order of the channel, indicating that increasing the number of transmit antennas can significantly enhance security performance. Additionally, it is observed that inter-user correlation and interference from other users impact the achievable secrecy rate negatively. The conclusions highlight the importance of employing suitable modulation schemes and coding strategies to achieve optimal secrecy rates under practical channel conditions.

In this study, we present a coarsening model on the d-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$, which employs biased zero-energy flips to simulate the dynamic evolution of interacting particle systems. This model serves as a fundamental basis for understanding the behaviour of various physical systems, such as the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (ASEP), and facilitates the development of efficient simulation techniques.  Our primary objective is to derive a rigorous result for the large deviations of the coarsening model, specifically focusing on the rare event occurrence probabilities. We achieve this using an exponential large deviation bound, which holds under general conditions on the initial configurations and the interaction energies. The analysis entails determining the rate functional and its Legendre transformation, employing tools from probability theory and mathematical statistics.  The methodology employed in our investigation involves a Markovian approach, with the coarsening dynamics described by a sequence of finite-volume Gibbs measures, governed by local equilibrium conditions. We then employ a large-volume limit and spatial coarsening scaling to derive the macroscopic behaviour of the system.  Our key findings reveal the existence of an exponential large deviation principle, which allows for the accurate estimation of the rare event probabilities in coarsening systems. This result not only sheds light on the rare event dynamics of the coarsening model but also provides valuable insights for the analysis of other interacting particle systems, like the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process.  In conclusion, this work provides a deep understanding of the coarsening dynamics and offers a rigorous analytical framework for the analysis of rare events in the coarsening model. By employing an exponential large deviation bound, we not only gain insights into the underlying physical processes but also pave the way for the development of efficient simulation techniques for various interacting particle systems.

Asynchronous rotation and orbital eccentricity lead to time-dependent
irradiation of the close-in gas giant exoplanets -- the hot Jupiters. This
time-dependent surface heating gives rise to fluid motions which propagate
throughout the planet. We investigate the ability of this "thermal tide" to
produce a quadrupole moment which can couple to the stellar gravitational tidal
force. While previous investigations discussed planets with solid surfaces,
here we focus on entirely fluid planets in order to understand gas giants with
small cores. The Coriolis force, thermal diffusion and self-gravity of the
perturbations are ignored for simplicity. First, we examine the response to
thermal forcing through analytic solutions of the fluid equations which treat
the forcing frequency as a small parameter. In the "equilibrium tide" limit of
zero frequency, fluid motion is present but does not induce a quadrupole
moment. In the next approximation, finite frequency corrections to the
equilibrium tide do lead to a nonzero quadrupole moment, the sign of which
torques the planet {\it away} from synchronous spin. We then numerically solve
the boundary value problem for the thermally forced, linear response of a
planet with neutrally stratified interior and stably stratified envelope. The
numerical results find quadrupole moments in agreement with the analytic
non-resonant result at sufficiently long forcing period. Surprisingly, in the
range of forcing periods of 1-30 days, the induced quadrupole moments can be
far larger than the analytic result due to response of internal gravity waves
which propagate in the radiative envelope. We discuss the relevance of our
results for the spin, eccentricity and thermal evolution of hot Jupiters.

We hope to be able (in the future) to carefully analyze this structure and to
tie the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension two to certain Zeta functions, thereby
invoking a powerful arithmetic machinery to handle the two dimensional Jacobian
Conjecture. Let us denote by ${\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2)$ the semigroup of two
dimensional Keller mappings. We would like to prove something like the
following: a) That there exists an infinite index set $I$, and a family of
mappings indexed by $I$, $\{F_i\,|\,i\in I\} \subset {\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2)$
such that $$ {\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2)={\rm Aut}(\mathbb{C}^2)\cup\bigcup_{i\in I}
R_{F_i}({\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2)), $$ where if $i\ne j$ then $R_{F_i}({\rm
et}(\mathbb{C}^2))\cap R_{F_j}({\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2))=\emptyset$. b) That the
parallel representation to the representation described in (a) above holds
true, this time with respect to the left composition operators $L_{G_j}$.
  These two claims will be the basis for a fractal structure on ${\rm
et}(\mathbb{C}^2)$ because the pieces $R_{F_i}({\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2))$ are
similar to each other in the sense that they are homeomorphic, and we further
have the scaling property of self-similarity, namely $R_F({\rm
et}(\mathbb{C}^2))$ is homeomorphic to its proper subspace $R_{G\circ F}({\rm
et}(\mathbb{C}^2))$ that is homeomorphic to its proper subspace $R_{H\circ
G\circ F}({\rm et}(\mathbb{C}^2))$ etc . This is the right place to remark that
the purpose of the current paper is to start and develop the parallel theory
for entire functions in one complex variable. Results in this setting will hint
that there are hopes to accomplish the above objective.

Recently Herzog has shown that deconfinement of AdS/QCD can be realized, in
the hard-wall model where the small radius region is removed in the
asymptotically AdS space, via a first order Hawking-Page phase transition
between a low temperature phase given by a pure AdS geometry and a high
temperature phase given by the AdS black hole in Poincare coordinates. In this
paper we first extend Herzog's work to the hard wall AdS/QCD model in curved
spaces by studying the thermodynamics of AdS black holes with spherical or
negative constant curvature horizon, dual to a non-supersymmetric Yang-Mills
theory on a sphere or hyperboloid respectively. For the spherical horizon case,
we find that the temperature of the phase transition increases by introducing
an infrared cutoff, compared to the case without the cutoff; For the hyperbolic
horizon case, there is a gap for the infrared cutoff, below which the
Hawking-Page phase transition does not occur. We also discuss charged AdS black
holes in the grand canonical ensemble, corresponding to a Yang-Mills theory at
finite chemical potential, and find that there is always a gap for the infrared
cutoff due to the existence of a minimal horizon for the charged AdS black
holes with any horizon topology.

This study investigates the long-range hydrodynamic effects of a single vesicle in linear flow. The background section discusses the importance of understanding the behavior of individual vesicles in complex biological environments, where they often exhibit non-Newtonian fluid properties. The objective of this research is to elucidate the influence of a single vesicle on the surrounding fluid using computational fluid dynamics simulations. In the methodology section, we present the model used for the simulations, which includes the vesicle shape, elastic membrane properties, and the fluid properties of a Newtonian fluid or a non-Newtonian fluid. The key findings of the study reveal that the presence of a single vesicle induces a time-dependent far-field velocity profile and a significant pressure drop downstream. The velocity profile exhibits an oscillatory behavior, with a high-speed region upstream and a stagnation region downstream. The pressure drop is attributed to the vesicle deformability and the shear-thinning properties of the non-Newtonian fluid. The conclusion emphasizes the implications of these findings for the design of microfluidic devices, where the interactions between vesicles and the fluid can significantly affect their performance. This work contributes to the growing body of research on the non-equilibrium behavior of individual vesicles in fluid flows and provides insights into the long-range hydrodynamic effects in complex biological systems.

This paper summarizes the introductory presentation for a workshop that
explored the challenges of making precision astronomical measurements using
deeply depleted (thick) CCDs. While thick CCDs provide definite advantages in
terms of increased quantum efficiency at NIR wavelengths, and reduced fringing
from atmospheric emission lines, these devices also exhibit undesirable
features that pose a challenge to precision determination of the positions,
fluxes, and shapes of astronomical objects, and features in astronomical
spectra. Many of the effects seen in these devices arise from lateral
electrical fields within the detector, that produce charge transport anomalies
that have been previously misinterpreted as quantum efficiency variations.
Performing simplistic flat-fielding introduces systematic errors in the image
processing pipeline. One measurement challenge is devising a calibration method
that can distinguish genuine quantum efficiency variations from charge
transport effects. Given the scientific benefits of improving both the
precision and accuracy of astronomical measurements, we need to identify,
characterize, and overcome these various detector artifacts. In retrospect,
many of the detector features first identified in thick CCDs also afflict
measurements made with more traditional CCD detectors, albeit often at a
reduced level. I provide a qualitative overview of the physical effects we
think are responsible for the observed device properties, and provide some
perspective for the work that lies ahead. Finally, I take this opportunity to
make a plea for establishing a clear and consistent vocabulary when describing
these various detector features, and make some suggestions for a standard
lexicon based on discussions at the workshop.

Nonlinearity mitigation using digital signal processing has been shown to
increase the achievable data rates of optical fiber transmission links. One
especially effective technique is digital back propagation (DBP), an algorithm
capable of simultaneously compensating for linear and nonlinear channel
distortions. The most significant barrier to implementing this technique,
however, is its high computational complexity. In recent years, there have been
several proposed alternatives to DBP with reduced computational complexity,
although such techniques have not demonstrated performance benefits
commensurate with the complexity of implementation. In order to fully
characterize the computational requirements of DBP, there is a need to model
the algorithm behavior when constrained to the logic used in a digital coherent
receiver. Such a model allows for the analysis of any signal recovery algorithm
in terms of true hardware complexity which, crucially, includes the bit-depth
of the multiplication operation. With a limited bit depth, there is
quantization noise, introduced with each arithmetic operation, and it can no
longer be assumed that the conventional DBP algorithm will outperform its low
complexity alternatives. In this work, DBP and a single nonlinear step DBP
implementation, the \textit{Enhanced Split Step Fourier} method (ESSFM), were
compared with linear equalization using a generic software model of fixed point
hardware. The requirements of bit depth and fast Fourier transform (FFT) size
are discussed to examine the optimal operating regimes for these two schemes of
digital nonlinearity compensation. For a 1000 km transmission system, it was
found that (assuming an optimized FFT size), in terms of SNR, the ESSFM
algorithm outperformed the conventional DBP for all hardware resolutions up to
13 bits.

In recent years, the demand for efficient spectrum utilization has intensified, leading to a growing interest in opportunistic spectrum access (OSA) networks. This paper investigates the conditions under which channel bonding enhances the performance of OSA networks, focusing on scenarios where multiple channels can be used concurrently by secondary users without causing interference to primary users. The objective is to identify the threshold of channel availability that maximizes the benefits of channel bonding, ultimately improving overall network throughput and reducing latency.   A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining theoretical modeling with simulation experiments that varied channel availability, user density, and traffic patterns. Results indicate that channel bonding significantly improves network performance when a minimum of three channels is accessible, leading to enhanced data rates and reduced transmission delays. Interestingly, the advantages diminish in environments with high primary user activity, where the potential for interference affects the effectiveness of bonding.   The findings suggest that careful management of channel availability and user behavior is crucial to optimizing the benefits of channel bonding. In conclusion, channel bonding proves to be a powerful tool for enhancing the performance of OSA networks, especially in conditions where multiple unused channels are available. This research contributes valuable insights for network designers aiming to improve spectrum utilization in opportunistic environments, suggesting a strategic focus on channel availability to leverage the full potential of bonding techniques.

This research explores the enhancement of acoustic properties in foam materials through the adjustment of membrane levels. Acoustic foams are widely used for sound absorption, and optimizing their properties can significantly impact their effectiveness. The objective of this study is to examine how variations in membrane levels within these materials can modify their sound absorption and insulation capabilities. Utilizing a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental procedures, we analyzed foam samples with differing membrane levels. The models applied included empirical and computational simulations that predicted sound absorption coefficients based on changes in membrane structure. Experimental tests were conducted in controlled environments to validate these predictions, employing impedance tubes to measure sound absorption across a range of frequencies. Key findings indicate that specific adjustments to membrane levels result in significant improvements in low-frequency sound absorption, demonstrating the potential for customizing foam materials for targeted acoustic environments. Moreover, the results suggest a promising correlation between membrane tuning and enhanced multi-frequency absorption, particularly in complex acoustic settings. Concluding, this study provides evidence that tailored modifications at the membrane level can elevate the acoustic performance of foam materials significantly. These insights offer valuable implications for the design and application of acoustic materials in both industrial and consumer contexts, advocating for further exploration into membrane tuning as a versatile method for acoustic optimization.

In this study, we investigate the chemical composition of TS 01, recognized as the most oxygen-deficient planetary nebula discovered to date. The primary objective of this research is to explore the process of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) nucleosynthesis within a metal-poor binary star system, shedding light on the formation and evolution of such oxygen-deficient nebulae. Through spectroscopic analysis of TS 01, we identified unique elemental abundance patterns, particularly a stark deficiency in oxygen levels. Our results suggest that the metal-poor environment and binary star interactions have crucial implications for the nucleosynthesis pathways leading to the observed chemical composition in TS 01. By utilizing advanced spectroscopic techniques and theoretical models, we aimed to unravel the complex interplay of nuclear processes and stellar dynamics shaping the elemental abundances in this peculiar planetary nebula. Our methodology involved high-resolution spectroscopy coupled with abundance determinations to provide insights into the underlying mechanisms driving the nucleosynthesis in metal-poor environments. The findings of this work contribute to a deeper understanding of AGB nucleosynthesis in binary star systems and offer valuable perspectives on the chemical evolution of oxygen-deficient planetary nebulae.

Based on an empirical study of real field traffic data measured in 1996--2014
through road detectors installed on German freeways, we reveal physical
features of empirical nuclei for spontaneous traffic breakdown in free flow at
highway bottlenecks. It is shown that the source of a nucleus for traffic
breakdown is the solely difference between empirical spontaneous and induced
traffic breakdowns at a highway bottleneck. Microscopic traffic simulations
with a stochastic traffic flow model in the framework of three-phase theory
explain the empirical findings. It turns out that in the most cases, a nucleus
for empirical spontaneous traffic breakdown occurs through an interaction of
one of waves in free flow with an empirical permanent speed disturbance
localized at a highway bottleneck. The wave is a localized structure in free
flow, in which the total flow rate is larger and the speed averaged across the
highway is smaller than outside the wave. The waves in free flow appear due to
oscilations in the percentage of slow vehicles; these waves propagate with the
average speed of slow vehicles in free flow (about 85--88 km/h for German
highways). Any of the waves exhibits a two-dimensional asymmetric
spatiotemporal structure: Wave's characteristics are different in different
highway lanes.

The origin and evolution of cosmic accelerators remain one of the most intriguing mysteries in astrophysics. A unique potential avenue for their investigation has emerged with the advent of the next-generation high-energy neutrino telescopes, as highlighted in the Astronomy Decadal Survey (2010-2020) Science White Paper. These instruments, designed to detect ultra-high-energy (UHE) neutrinos, offer a novel method to probe the extreme environments that accelerate particles to energies far beyond those achievable on Earth.  Our study aims to leverage the capabilities of these neutrino telescopes by exploring how they can unveil new insights into cosmic accelerators. We propose that the detection of neutrinos originating from the vicinity of active galactic nuclei (AGN) or gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) could provide direct evidence for the acceleration mechanisms at work. Our methodology involves simulating neutrino events expected from AGN and GRBs, analyzing their spectral signatures, and comparing them with data collected by neutrino telescopes. Additionally, we will employ advanced statistical techniques to identify patterns indicative of particle acceleration.  Key findings from our analysis suggest that certain neutrino fluxes observed by current and future neutrino telescopes align with theoretical predictions of neutrino production from AGN and GRBs. Furthermore, the timing and spatial distribution of detected neutrinos can reveal information about the environments surrounding these sources, offering unprecedented details on the conditions necessary for particle acceleration.  In conclusion, the integration of neutrino astronomy with traditional electromagnetic observations promises to revolutionize our understanding of cosmic accelerators. By providing a complementary view of these elusive phenomena, UHE neutrino telescopes stand poised to make groundbreaking discoveries that have the potential to redefine our comprehension of the universe's most energetic processes.

We investigated the impact of galactic effects on habitability, a phenomenon long hypothesized to influence the emergence and maintenance of life on Earth. Our research sought to elucidate the relationship between galactic radiation, stellar activity, and planetary habitability, with a focus on the detection of biosignatures in exoplanetary atmospheres.  Through a comprehensive review of existing literature and the development of a novel analytical framework, we identified key galactic effects that may impact habitability, including cosmic rays, gamma-ray bursts, and high-energy particle fluxes. Our analysis revealed that these effects can alter planetary atmospheres, potentially disrupting the delicate balance of chemical and biological processes necessary for life.  We applied our framework to a sample of 100 exoplanets, assessing the potential impact of galactic effects on their habitability. Our results indicate that a significant proportion of exoplanets are vulnerable to galactic radiation, which can lead to the degradation of atmospheric gases and the disruption of planetary ecosystems.  Our findings have important implications for the search for extraterrestrial life, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between galactic effects and planetary habitability. By integrating galactic effects into habitability assessments, we can better identify promising exoplanets and refine our search for biosignatures.

We investigate the temporal correlation between outburst activities and fragmentation events of Comet 168P/Hergenrother, aiming to elucidate the dynamic processes influencing its behavior. Our study leverages observational data spanning multiple apparitions of the comet. We utilize photometric measurements to identify outburst events and high-resolution imagery to detect fragmentation incidents. By implementing statistical time-series analysis, we examine the timing and frequency of these phenomena, seeking to discern patterns suggestive of underlying physical mechanisms.  Our results indicate a significant temporal association between major outburst occurrences and subsequent fragmentation events. Specifically, we observe that fragmentation episodes predominantly follow intense outbursts, suggesting a causal linkage where increased outgassing pressure may facilitate structural destabilization of the nucleus. Moreover, we identify periodic trends in the activity cycles of Comet 168P/Hergenrother, postulating a relation between these recurring patterns and its orbital dynamics.  By employing computational models simulating thermal stresses and volatile sublimation on the comet's surface, we further corroborate our observational findings. These models predict stress accumulation during perihelion, aligning with our empirical data on the timing of observed events. Through this comprehensive approach, we propose a framework explaining the temporal correlation of outbursts and fragmentation as a consequence of thermally driven subsurface processes.  Our study contributes to the understanding of cometary evolution, providing insights into the mechanisms governing comet disintegration and activity, with implications for predicting future behavior of small Solar System bodies.

By following the Kazantsev theory and taking into account both microscopic
and turbulent diffusion of magnetic fields, we develop a unified treatment of
the kinematic and nonlinear stages of turbulent dynamo, and study the dynamo
process for a full range of magnetic Prandtl number Pm and ionization
fractions. We find a striking similarity between the dependence of dynamo
behavior on Pm in a conducting fluid and R (a function of ionization fraction)
in partially ionized gas. In a weakly ionized medium, the kinematic stage is
largely extended, including not only exponential growth but a new regime of
dynamo characterized by linear-in-time growth of magnetic field strength, and
the resulting magnetic energy is much higher than the kinetic energy carried by
viscous-scale eddies. Unlike the kinematic stage, the subsequent nonlinear
stage is unaffected by microscopic diffusion processes and has a universal
linear-in-time growth of magnetic energy with the growth rate as a constant
fraction $3/38$ of the turbulent energy transfer rate, showing good agreement
with earlier numerical results. Applying the analysis to the first stars and
galaxies, we find that the kinematic stage is able to generate a field strength
only an order of magnitude smaller than the final saturation value. But the
generation of large-scale magnetic fields can only be accounted for by the
relatively inefficient nonlinear stage and requires longer time than the
free-fall time. It suggests that magnetic fields may not have played a
dynamically important role during the formation of the first stars.

In this study, we present evidence supporting the existence of a triaxial dark matter halo in the Milky Way galaxy, derived from the analysis of the Sagittarius stellar tidal stream. By utilizing data from Gaia and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we have reconstructed the shape and orientation of the dark matter halo by fitting a dynamical model to the observed tidal stream. Our results indicate that a triaxial halo provides a significantly better fit to the observed stream morphology compared to a spheroidal model, suggesting that the Milky Way's dark matter distribution is more complex than previously thought. The presence of a triaxial halo has important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of the Milky Way, as well as for predictions of dark matter detection experiments. Our methodology combines state-of-the-art numerical simulations with sophisticated statistical techniques to constrain the parameters of the dark matter halo. By incorporating the Sagittarius stellar tidal stream as a powerful probe of the Milky Way's gravitational potential, we have demonstrated the potential of this method to provide new insights into the nature of dark matter in our galaxy.

We present a novel approach to computing hitting set kernels utilizing AC^0-circuits. The problem we address is the efficient identification of minimal hitting sets in combinatorial optimization and constraint satisfaction problems. Our work seeks to overcome the computational complexity associated with conventional algorithms by leveraging the inherent properties of AC^0-circuits. Through our methodology, we demonstrate that AC^0-circuits can efficiently determine hitting set kernels by exploiting their parallel processing capabilities and succinct representation of functions. Our results showcase a significant improvement in the computational efficiency of finding hitting sets when compared to traditional methods. By harnessing the power of AC^0-circuits, our approach offers a more scalable and time-efficient solution for identifying hitting set kernels in various applications. Our key contributions lie in demonstrating the effectiveness of employing AC^0-circuits for this task and providing a detailed analysis of their computational advantages. This research sheds light on a promising direction for accelerating hitting set kernel computations, with implications for diverse fields such as bioinformatics, machine learning, and logic synthesis.

In the context of observations of the rest-frame ultraviolet and optical
emission from distant galaxies, we explore the emission-line properties of
photoionization models of active and inactive galaxies. Our aim is to identify
new line-ratio diagnostics to discriminate between gas photoionization by
active galactic nuclei (AGN) and star formation. We use a standard
photoionization code to compute the emission from AGN narrow-line regions and
compare this with calculations of the nebular emission from star-forming
galaxies achieved using the same code. We confirm the appropriateness of widely
used optical spectral diagnostics of nuclear activity versus star formation and
explore new diagnostics at ultraviolet wavelengths. We find that combinations
of a collisionally excited metal line or line multiplet, such as CIV 1548,1551,
OIII]1661,1666, NIII]1750, [SiIII]1883+[SiIII]1892 and [CIII]1907+CIII]1909,
with the HeII 1640 recombination line are individually good discriminants of
the nature of the ionizing source. Diagrams involving at least 3 of these lines
allow an even more stringent distinction between active and inactive galaxies,
as well as valuable constraints on interstellar gas parameters and the shape of
the ionizing radiation. Several line ratios involving Ne-based emission lines,
such as [NeIV]2424, [NeIII]3343 and [NeV]3426, are also good diagnostics of
nuclear activity. Our results provide a comprehensive framework to identify the
sources of photoionization and physical conditions of the ionized gas from the
ultraviolet and optical nebular emission from galaxies. This will be
particularly useful to interpret observations of high-redshift galaxies with
future facilities, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and extremely large
ground-based telescopes.

At the final stage of terrestrial planet formation, known as the giant impact
stage, a few tens of Mars-sized protoplanets collide with one another to form
terrestrial planets. Almost all previous studies on the orbital and accretional
evolution of protoplanets in this stage have been based on the assumption of
perfect accretion, where two colliding protoplanets always merge. However,
recent impact simulations have shown that collisions among protoplanets are not
always merging events, that is, two colliding protoplanets sometimes move apart
after the collision (hit-and-run collision). As a first step towards studying
the effects of such imperfect accretion of protoplanets on terrestrial planet
formation, we investigated the merging criteria for collisions of rocky
protoplanets. Using the smoothed particle hydrodynamic (SPH) method, we
performed more than 1000 simulations of giant impacts with various parameter
sets, such as the mass ratio of protoplanets, $\gamma$, the total mass of two
protoplanets, $M_{\rm T}$, the impact angle, $\theta$, and the impact velocity,
$v_{\rm imp}$. We investigated the critical impact velocity, $v_{\rm cr}$, at
the transition between merging and hit-and-run collisions. We found that the
normalized critical impact velocity, $v_{\rm cr}/v_{\rm esc}$, depends on
$\gamma$ and $\theta$, but does not depend on $M_{\rm T}$, where $v_{\rm esc}$
is the two-body escape velocity. We derived a simple formula for $v_{\rm
cr}/v_{\rm esc}$ as a function of $\gamma$ and $\theta$, and applied it to the
giant impact events obtained by \textit{N}-body calculations in the previous
studies. We found that 40% of these events should not be merging events.

The integration of Gene Ontology (GO) terms into network alignment is an evolving challenge in bioinformatics, demanding innovative approaches for accurate and efficient performance. This study introduces SANA NetGO, a novel combinatorial method leveraging GO terms to enhance the scoring of network alignments. The main objective is to improve the biological relevance of network alignments by effectively incorporating semantic similarities derived from GO annotations. Our methodology involves a combinatorial optimization framework that applies GO term similarity scores to align gene networks. By employing a heuristic search algorithm, we maximize the GO-based alignment score, aiming for superior biological insights. Key findings demonstrate that SANA NetGO significantly improves alignment quality compared to traditional sequence-based methods. It successfully captures functional relationships by accommodating the hierarchical nature of the GO structure, thus delivering more biologically meaningful results. In evaluations across several biological datasets, our approach consistently outperformed existing methods in terms of both the quality of alignments and computational efficiency. The SANA NetGO pipeline provides a robust tool for researchers seeking more nuanced alignments, ultimately aiding the discovery of conserved functional motifs across species. In conclusion, SANA NetGO represents a promising advancement in network biology, offering a sophisticated mechanism for integrating ontological information into network analysis, and paving the way for future exploration of cross-species biological interactions.

This research paper characterizes transiting extrasolar planets using narrow-band photometry observations from the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) equipped with the OSIRIS instrument. The study aims to enhance the precision and quality of transit light curve measurements by employing narrow-band filters to isolate specific wavelengths that are sensitive to the planetary atmosphere. Utilizing data from several transiting exoplanets, including Kepler-186f and HD 209458b, the research employs advanced statistical techniques to analyze transit depths and transit timing variations. Key findings include improved estimates of exoplanet radii and atmospheric compositions, as well as the detection of subtle transit timing variations indicative of tidal effects. The results contribute to our understanding of the atmospheres and interiors of exoplanets, providing valuable insights into their formation and evolution. This work highlights the potential of narrow-band photometry for detailed characterization of transiting exoplanets, underscoring the importance of complementary observational techniques in extrasolar planet science.

The transcriptional regulation of gene expression is a fundamental process in the development of Drosophila melanogaster embryos. In this study, we developed a stochastic model to describe the dynamics of gene transcription on Drosophila melanogaster embryos. The model is based on a reaction-diffusion system, where transcription factors and RNA polymerase interact with the chromatin structure in a diffusion-driven manner. We incorporated spatial and temporal variations of transcription factor concentrations and chromatin accessibility, which are known to impact gene expression. The model incorporates a Poisson distribution to represent the stochastic nature of the gene expression process. The objective of this research was to understand the impact of transcription factor concentration and chromatin accessibility variations on gene transcription dynamics. We applied the model to a well-studied gene regulatory network, the Bicoid gene network, and compared the model outputs with experimental data. Our results demonstrated that the model can accurately capture the spatial and temporal gene expression patterns observed in embryos. Furthermore, we found that fluctuations in transcription factor concentrations and chromatin accessibility can lead to variations in gene expression. In conclusion, this study presents a stochastic model for gene transcription on Drosophila melanogaster embryos, which provides a framework for understanding the impact of transcription factor concentration and chromatin accessibility variations on gene expression dynamics. The model can be applied to other gene regulatory networks and provides insights into the stochastic nature of gene expression during embryonic development.

The monitoring of quiescent emission from neutron star transients with
accretion outbursts long enough to significantly heat the neutron star crust
has opened a new vista onto the physics of dense matter. In this paper we
construct models of the thermal relaxation of the neutron star crust following
the end of a protracted accretion outburst. We confirm the finding of Shternin
et al., that the thermal conductivity of the neutron star crust is high,
consistent with a low impurity parameter. We describe the basic physics that
sets the broken power-law form of the cooling lightcurve. The initial power law
decay gives a direct measure of the temperature profile, and hence the thermal
flux during outburst, in the outer crust. The time of the break, at hundreds of
days post-outburst, corresponds to the thermal time where the solid transitions
from a classical to quantum crystal, close to neutron drip. We calculate in
detail the constraints on the crust parameters of both KS 1731-260 and MXB
1659-29 from fitting their cooling lightcurves. Our fits to the lightcurves
require that the neutrons do not contribute significantly to the heat capacity
in the inner crust, and provide evidence in favor of the existence of a neutron
superfluid throughout the inner crust. Our fits to both sources indicate an
impurity parameter of order unity in the inner crust.

The Lasso is an attractive technique for regularization and variable
selection for high-dimensional data, where the number of predictor variables
$p_n$ is potentially much larger than the number of samples $n$. However, it
was recently discovered that the sparsity pattern of the Lasso estimator can
only be asymptotically identical to the true sparsity pattern if the design
matrix satisfies the so-called irrepresentable condition. The latter condition
can easily be violated in the presence of highly correlated variables. Here we
examine the behavior of the Lasso estimators if the irrepresentable condition
is relaxed. Even though the Lasso cannot recover the correct sparsity pattern,
we show that the estimator is still consistent in the $\ell_2$-norm sense for
fixed designs under conditions on (a) the number $s_n$ of nonzero components of
the vector $\beta_n$ and (b) the minimal singular values of design matrices
that are induced by selecting small subsets of variables. Furthermore, a rate
of convergence result is obtained on the $\ell_2$ error with an appropriate
choice of the smoothing parameter. The rate is shown to be optimal under the
condition of bounded maximal and minimal sparse eigenvalues. Our results imply
that, with high probability, all important variables are selected. The set of
selected variables is a meaningful reduction on the original set of variables.
Finally, our results are illustrated with the detection of closely adjacent
frequencies, a problem encountered in astrophysics.

The search for 4He-eta bound states was performed with the WASA-at-COSY
facility via the measurement of the excitation function for the dd->3He n pi0
and dd->3He p pi- processes. The beam momentum was varied continuously between
2.127 GeV/c and 2.422 GeV/c, corresponding to the excess energy for the dd->4He
eta reaction ranging from Q=-70 MeV to Q=30 MeV. The luminosity was determined
based on the dd->3He n reaction and quasi-free proton-proton scattering via
dd->pp n_spectator n_spectator reactions. The excitation functions determined
independently for the measured reactions do not reveal a structure which could
be interpreted as a narrow mesic nucleus. Therefore, the upper limits of the
total cross sections for the bound state production and decay in
dd->(4He-eta)_bound->3He n pi0 and dd->(4He-eta)_bound->3He p pi- processes
were determined taking into account the isospin relation between both the
channels considered. The results of the analysis depend on the assumptions of
the N* momentum distribution in the anticipated mesic-4He. Assuming as in the
previous works, that this is identical with the distribution of nucleons bound
with 20 MeV in 4He, we determined that (for the mesic bound state width in the
range from 5 MeV to 50 MeV) the upper limits at 90% confidence level are about
3 nb and about 6 nb for npi0 and ppi- channels, respectively. However, based on
the recent theoretical findings of the N*(1535) momentum distribution in the
N*-3He nucleus bound by 3.6 MeV, we find that the WASA-at-COSY detector
acceptance decreases and hence the corresponding upper limits are 5 nb and 10
nb for npi0 and ppi- channels respectively.

The Rosen-Zener model for association of atoms in a Bose-Einstein condensate
is studied. Using a nonlinear Volterra integral equation, we obtain an analytic
formula for final probability of the transition to the molecular state for weak
interaction limit. Considering the strong coupling limit of high field
intensities, we show that the system reveals two different time-evolution
pictures depending on the detuning of the frequency of the associating field.
For both limit cases we derive highly accurate formulas for the molecular state
probability valid for the whole range of variation of time. Using these
formulas, we show that at large detuning regime the molecule formation process
occurs almost non-oscillatory in time and a Rosen-Zener pulse is not able to
associate more than one third of atoms at any time point. The system returns to
its initial all-atomic state at the end of the process and the maximal
transition probability is achieved when the field intensity reaches its peak.
In contrast, at small detuning the evolution of the system displays
large-amplitude oscillations between atomic and molecular populations. We find
that the shape of the oscillations in the first approximation is defined by the
field detuning only. Finally, a hidden singularity of the Rosen-Zener model due
to the specific time-variation of the field amplitude at the beginning of the
interaction is indicated. It is this singularity that stands for many of the
qualitative and quantitative properties of the model. The singularity may be
viewed as an effective resonance-touching.

This study investigates the evolutionary paths of transition galaxies at redshift z~0, with a focus on star formation and hydrogen (HI) properties. These galaxies, situated at the intersection of the red sequence and the blue cloud, exhibit characteristics of both, making them ideal probes of galaxy evolution. By analyzing a sample of 100 transition galaxies, we have identified a range of HI properties, including gas mass, gas-to-stellar mass ratio, and gas depletion time, which vary systematically with stellar mass and star formation rate.  Our results suggest that transition galaxies at z~0 have undergone significant star-forming episodes in the past, resulting in the depletion of their HI gas reservoirs. However, we also find that these galaxies retain a significant amount of gas, which is often found in the form of low-mass stars and molecular gas. The star formation histories of these galaxies are characterized by a peak in star formation rates around 1-2 Gyr ago, followed by a decline in star formation activity. We have also found that the HI properties of transition galaxies are correlated with their stellar mass and star formation rate, suggesting that these properties are tightly linked to galaxy evolution.  Our study provides new insights into the evolutionary paths of transition galaxies at z~0, highlighting the complex interplay between star formation, gas accretion, and galaxy evolution. The findings of this research have implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, star formation, and the role of gas in shaping the properties of galaxies.

Stable Principal Component Pursuit (SPCP) has emerged as a pivotal technique in robust PCA, effectively distinguishing low-rank structures from sparse noise in high-dimensional datasets. However, conventional algorithms often face computational inefficiencies, especially in large-scale applications. This study aims to develop fast first-order methods to enhance the computational feasibility of SPCP without compromising accuracy. We propose an innovative algorithmic framework combining accelerated gradient descent and proximal operators to leverage the underlying geometry of the problem, ensuring convergence to an optimal solution efficiently. Our methodology includes a detailed theoretical analysis of convergence rates, alongside empirical evaluations across various datasets, highlighting performance metrics such as runtime and accuracy when contrasted against existing state-of-the-art techniques. Key findings reveal that our proposed methods significantly reduce computation time while maintaining robustness against noise, achieving up to a 50% improvement in processing speed. These results signify the potential of fast first-order methods in practical applications, particularly in domains requiring real-time data analysis, such as image processing and finance. In conclusion, our research not only addresses the time complexity associated with SPCP but also positions the proposed methods as viable alternatives for practitioners aiming to implement efficient and reliable high-dimensional analysis techniques in diverse fields.

In this work, we present a comprehensive study of energy-efficient neuromorphic classifiers designed to address the challenge of power consumption in machine learning applications. We aim to develop a model that not only retains high classification accuracy but also minimizes energy usage, addressing the pressing need for sustainability in artificial intelligence technologies. Through the application of spiking neural networks, we implement an architecture that emulates biological computing processes, enabling significant reductions in power consumption. We employ a hybrid learning algorithm that combines supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to optimize performance without excessive resource expenditure. Our results demonstrate that the proposed neuromorphic classifiers achieve competitive accuracy rates, surpassing 90% in benchmark datasets, while consuming up to 50% less energy compared to traditional deep learning models. We analyze the trade-offs between classification speed and energy efficiency, illustrating the potential of our approach in real-world applications. Furthermore, we explore the integration of hardware accelerators, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), that enhance computational efficiency for our neuromorphic architecture. Our findings offer insights into the future of energy-efficient machine learning paradigms, emphasizing the promise of neuromorphic systems in advancing artificial intelligence with sustainable practices. We encourage further research in this domain, advocating for broader adoption of energy-efficient classifiers across various ecological contexts in technology. Overall, our research contributions lay a foundation for developing smarter, greener AI solutions in an increasingly energy-conscious world.

We present the results of calculations of surface relaxations, energetics,
and bonding properties for CaTiO3 (001) and (011) surfaces using a hybrid B3PW
description of exchange and correlation. We consider both CaO and TiO2
terminations of the non-polar (001) surface, and Ca, TiO and O terminations of
the polar (011) surface. On the (001) surfaces, we find that all upper-layer
atoms relax inwards on the CaO-terminated surface, while outward relaxations of
all atoms in the second layer are found for both terminations. For the
TiO2-terminated (001) surface, the largest relaxations are on the second-layer
atoms. The surface rumpling is much larger for the CaO-terminated than for the
TiO2-terminated (001) surface, but their surface energies are quite similar at
0.94eV and 1.13eV respectively. In contrast, different terminations of the
(011) CaTiO3 surface lead to very different surface energies of 1.86eV, 1.91eV,
and 3.13eV for the O-terminated, Ca-terminated, and TiO-terminated (011)
surface respectively. Our results for surface energies contrast sharply with
those of Zhang et al. [Phys. Rev. B 76, 115426 (2007)], where the authors found
a rather different pattern of surface energies. We predict a considerable
increase of the Ti-O chemical bond covalency near the (011) surface as compared
both to the bulk and to the (001) surface.

Transmission over multiple frequency bands combined into one logical channel
speeds up data transfer for wireless networks. On the other hand, the
allocation of multiple channels to a single user decreases the probability of
finding a free logical channel for new connections, which may result in a
network-wide throughput loss. While this relationship has been studied
experimentally, especially in the WLAN configuration, little is known on how to
analytically model such phenomena. With the advent of Opportunistic Spectrum
Access (OSA) networks, it is even more important to understand the
circumstances in which it is beneficial to bond channels occupied by primary
users with dynamic duty cycle patterns. In this paper we propose an analytical
framework which allows the investigation of the average channel throughput at
the medium access control layer for OSA networks with channel bonding enabled.
We show that channel bonding is generally beneficial, though the extent of the
benefits depend on the features of the OSA network, including OSA network size
and the total number of channels available for bonding. In addition, we show
that performance benefits can be realized by adaptively changing the number of
bonded channels depending on network conditions. Finally, we evaluate channel
bonding considering physical layer constraints, i.e. throughput reduction
compared to the theoretical throughput of a single virtual channel due to a
transmission power limit for any bonding size.

The emission from young stellar objects (YSOs) in the mid-IR is dominated by
the inner rim of their circumstellar disks. We present an IR-monitoring survey
of about 800 objects in the direction of the Lynds 1688 (L1688) star forming
region over four visibility windows spanning 1.6 years using the \emph{Spitzer}
space telescope in its warm mission phase. Among all lightcurves, 57 sources
are cluster members identified based on their spectral-energy distribution and
X-ray emission. Almost all cluster members show significant variability. The
amplitude of the variability is larger in more embedded YSOs. Ten out of 57
cluster members have periodic variations in the lightcurves with periods
typically between three and seven days, but even for those sources, significant
variability in addition to the periodic signal can be seen. No period is stable
over 1.6 years. Non-periodic lightcurves often still show a preferred timescale
of variability which is longer for more embedded sources. About half of all
sources exhibit redder colors in a fainter state. This is compatible with
time-variable absorption towards the YSO. The other half becomes bluer when
fainter. These colors can only be explained with significant changes in the
structure of the inner disk. No relation between mid-IR variability and stellar
effective temperature or X-ray spectrum is found.

We are conducting a Jansky VLA Ka-band (8 mm and 1 cm) and C-band (4 cm and
6.4 cm) survey of all known protostars in the Perseus Molecular Cloud,
providing resolution down to $\sim$0.06'' and $\sim$0.35" in Ka-band and
C-band, respectively. Here we present first results from this survey that
enable us to examine the source NGC 1333 IRAS2A in unprecedented detail and
resolve it into a proto-binary system separated by 0.621"$\pm$0.006" ($\sim$143
AU) at 8 mm, 1 cm, and 4 cm. These 2 sources (IRAS2A VLA1 and VLA2) are likely
driving the two orthogonal outflows known to originate from IRAS2A. The
brighter source IRAS2A VLA1 is extended perpendicular to its outflow in the VLA
data, with a deconvolved size of 0.055" ($\sim$13 AU), possibly tracing a
protostellar disk. The recently reported candidate companions (IRAS2A MM2 and
MM3) are not detected in either our VLA data, CARMA 1.3 mm data, or SMA 850
$\mu$m data. SMA CO ($J=3\rightarrow2$), CARMA CO ($J=2\rightarrow1$), and
lower resolution CARMA CO ($J=1\rightarrow0$) observations are used to examine
the outflow origins and the nature of the candidate companions to IRAS2A VLA1.
The CO ($J=3\rightarrow2$) and ($J=2\rightarrow1$) data show that IRAS2A MM2 is
coincident with a bright CO emission spot in the east-west outflow, and IRAS2A
MM3 is within the north-south outflow. In contrast, IRAS2A VLA2 lies at the
east-west outflow symmetry point. We propose that IRAS2A VLA2 is the driving
source of the East-West outflow and a true companion to IRAS2A VLA1, whereas
IRAS2A MM2 and MM3 may not be protostellar.

The crystal-fields causing $|J>$ electron states splittings of the same
second moment $\sigma^{2}$ can produce different total splittings $\Delta E$
magnitudes. Based on the numerical data on crystal-field splittings for the
representative sets of crystal-field Hamiltonians ${\cal H}_{\rm
CF}=\sum_{k}\sum_{q}B_{kq}C_{q}^{(k)}$ with fixed indexes either $k$ or $q$,
the potentials leading to the extreme $\Delta E$ have been identified. For all
crystal-fields the admissible ranges $(\Delta E_{min},\Delta E_{max})$ have
been found numerically for $1\leq J\leq 8$. The extreme splittings are reached
in the crystal-fields for which ${\cal H}_{\rm CF}s$ are the definite
superpositions of the $C_{q}^{(k)}$ components with different rank $k=2,4$ and
6 and the same index $q$. Apart from few exceptions, the lower limits $\Delta
E_{min}$ occur in the axial fields of ${\cal H}_{\rm
CF}(q=0)=B_{20}C_{0}^{(2)}+B_{40}C_{0}^{(4)}+B_{60}C_{0}^{(6)}$, whereas the
upper limits $\Delta E_{max}$ in the low symmetry fields of ${\cal H}_{\rm
CF}(q=1)=B_{21}C_{1}^{(2)}+B_{41}C_{1}^{(4)}+B_{61}C_{1}^{(6)}$. Mixing the
${\cal H}_{\rm CF}$ components with different $q$ yields a secondary effect and
does not determine the extreme splittings. The admissible $\Delta E_{min}$
changes with $J$ from $2.00\sigma$ to $2.40\sigma$, whereas the $\Delta
E_{max}$ from $2.00\sigma$ to $4.10\sigma$. The maximal gap $\Delta
E_{max}-\Delta E_{min}=2.00\sigma$ has been found for the states $|J=4>$. Not
all the nominally allowed total splittings, preserving $\sigma^{2}=const$
condition, are physically available, and in consequence not all virtual
splittings diagrams can be observed in real crystal-fields.

We report the results of a joint analysis of data from BICEP2/Keck Array and
Planck. BICEP2 and Keck Array have observed the same approximately 400 deg$^2$
patch of sky centered on RA 0h, Dec. $-57.5\deg$. The combined maps reach a
depth of 57 nK deg in Stokes $Q$ and $U$ in a band centered at 150 GHz. Planck
has observed the full sky in polarization at seven frequencies from 30 to 353
GHz, but much less deeply in any given region (1.2 $\mu$K deg in $Q$ and $U$ at
143 GHz). We detect 150$\times$353 cross-correlation in $B$-modes at high
significance. We fit the single- and cross-frequency power spectra at
frequencies $\geq 150$ GHz to a lensed-$\Lambda$CDM model that includes dust
and a possible contribution from inflationary gravitational waves (as
parameterized by the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$), using a prior on the
frequency spectral behavior of polarized dust emission from previous \planck\
analysis of other regions of the sky. We find strong evidence for dust and no
statistically significant evidence for tensor modes. We probe various model
variations and extensions, including adding a synchrotron component in
combination with lower frequency data, and find that these make little
difference to the $r$ constraint. Finally we present an alternative analysis
which is similar to a map-based cleaning of the dust contribution, and show
that this gives similar constraints. The final result is expressed as a
likelihood curve for $r$, and yields an upper limit $r_{0.05}<0.12$ at 95%
confidence. Marginalizing over dust and $r$, lensing $B$-modes are detected at
$7.0\,\sigma$ significance.

To understand the spatial deployment of base stations (BSs) is the first step
to analyze the performance of cellular networks and further design efficient
networking protocols. Poisson point process (PPP), which has been widely
adopted to characterize the deployment of BSs and established the reputation to
give tractable results in the stochastic geometry analyses, usually assumes a
static BS deployment density in homogeneous PPP (HPPP) models or delicately
designed location-dependent density functions in in-homogeneous PPP (IPPP)
models. However, the simultaneous existence of attractiveness and repulsiveness
among BSs practically deployed in a large-scale area defies such an assumption,
and the $\alpha$-stable distribution, one kind of heavy-tailed distributions,
has recently demonstrated superior accuracy to statistically model the varying
BS density in different areas. In this paper, we start with these new findings
and investigate the intrinsic feature (i.e., the spatial self-similarity)
embedded in the BSs. Afterwards, we refer to a generalized PPP setup with
$\alpha$-stable distributed density and theoretically derive the related
coverage probability. In particular, we give an upper bound of the derived
coverage probability for high signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)
thresholds and show the monotonically decreasing property of this bound with
respect to the variance of BS density. Besides, we prove that our model could
reduce to the single-tier HPPP for some special cases, and demonstrate the
superior accuracy of the $\alpha$-stable model to approach the real
environment.

In this study, we examine the properties of primitive abundant numbers and weird numbers, specifically focusing on those possessing a large number of prime factors. Primitive abundant numbers, being abundant yet not divisible by any smaller abundant number, present intriguing insights into the structure of numerical abundance. Weird numbers, on the other hand, are defined as abundant numbers for which no subset of whole divisors sums to the number itself. We aim to explore how the presence of numerous prime factors influences the characteristics of these categories of numbers. Our methodology involves developing algorithms to efficiently identify and classify such numbers, leveraging advancements in computational number theory. We employ sieving techniques and factorization methods to ascertain the prime factor compositions and abundance attributes. The results unearthed several novel sequences of primitive abundant and weird numbers, distinguished by their high density of prime factors. Furthermore, we observed that the number of prime factors contributes non-linearly to the complexity of classifying numbers into these two categories. Our research offers new theoretical insights into the interplay between factor multiplicity and number theory properties, and posits potential implications for broader mathematical conjectures concerning numeric abundance and deficiency. This work advances the field by providing a framework for further exploration of the intersection between abundance, weirdness, and prime factorization, setting a foundation for ongoing and future investigations into this rich area of study.

In this work, we investigate the conditional moments of noncausal alpha-stable processes and explore their application in predicting the likelihood of bubble crashes in financial markets. Alpha-stable processes are powerful tools in modeling heavy-tailed distributions and offering substantial insights into the probabilistic nature of market fluctuations. However, their noncausal nature poses challenges in deriving predictive analytics, which is crucial for risk management and decision-making. We address these challenges by introducing a novel methodology that leverages the conditional moments of these processes, allowing us to capture the intricate dynamics of alpha-stable characteristics more accurately. Our main contributions include deriving explicit expressions for the conditional moments under noncausal settings, thus enhancing the predictive capabilities of models concerned with catastrophic financial events, such as asset bubble crashes. We utilize a Bayesian inference framework to estimate the parameters of our proposed model, ensuring robustness and adaptability to various market conditions. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive empirical analysis using historical financial data to validate our approach. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in forecasting the odds of bubble crashes, as our model more accurately identifies periods of heightened risk compared to traditional methods. This study advances the theoretical understanding of noncausal processes and provides a practical tool for practitioners to better anticipate and mitigate the adverse effects of market downturns. In doing so, we contribute to the ongoing discourse on economic stability and the need for sophisticated modeling techniques in finance. We anticipate that our findings will prompt further research into noncausal systems and their applications in financial risk prediction.

This paper discusses a continuum approach to track the evolution of
permeability in granular rocks by accounting for the combined effect of
porosity changes, grain breakage and cement bond damage. To account for such a
broad range of microscopic processes under general loading paths, the Breakage
Mechanics theory is used and the computed mechanical response is linked with
the Kozeny equation, i.e. a permeability model able to evaluate the reduction
of the hydraulic conductivity resulting from the simultaneous loss of porosity
and growth of surface area. In particular, the evolution of the internal
variables of the model has been linked to idealized geometric schemes at
particle scale, with the goal to distinguish the contribution of the fines
generated by the disaggregation of the cement matrix from that of the broken
fragments resulting from the crushing of the skeleton. Compression/flow
experiments available in the literature for different granular rocks are used
to validate the proposed methodology. The analyses illustrate that the drop of
the permeability of damaged rocks would be severely underestimated without an
accurate computation of the growth of surface area, as well as that the
distributed fragmentation of skeleton particles tends to have stronger
implications than the generation of cement fines. These findings, along with
the satisfactory agreement between model predictions and experiments, stress
the benefits of adopting microstructure-based constitutive laws for the
analysis of coupled hydro-mechanical problems.

The disk fraction, the percentage of stars with disks in a young cluster, is
widely used to investigate the lifetime of the protoplanetary disk, which can
impose an important constraint on the planet formation mechanism. The
relationship between the decay timescale of the disk fraction and the mass
dissipation timescale of an individual disk, however, remains unclear. Here we
investigate the effect of the disk mass function (DMF) on the evolution of the
disk fraction. We show that the time variation in the disk fraction depends on
the spread of the DMF and the detection threshold of the disk. In general, the
disk fraction decreases more slowly than the disk mass if a typical initial DMF
and a detection threshold are assumed. We find that, if the disk mass decreases
exponentially, {the mass dissipation timescale of the disk} can be as short as
$1\,{\rm Myr}$ even when the disk fraction decreases with the time constant of
${\sim}2.5\,{\rm Myr}$. The decay timescale of the disk fraction can be an
useful parameter to investigate the disk lifetime, but the difference between
the mass dissipation of an individual disk and the decrease in the disk
fraction should be properly appreciated to estimate the timescale of the disk
mass dissipation.

Gravitational-wave observations of compact binaries have the potential to
uncover the distribution of masses and angular momenta of black holes and
neutron stars in the universe. The binary components' physical parameters can
be inferred from their effect on the phasing of the gravitational-wave signal,
but a partial degeneracy between the components' mass ratio and their angular
momenta limits our ability to measure the individual component masses. At the
typical signal amplitudes expected by the Advanced Laser Interferometer
Gravitational-wave Observatory (signal-to-noise ratios between 10 and 20), we
show that it will in many cases be difficult to distinguish whether the
components are neutron stars or black holes. We identify when the masses of the
binary components could be unambiguously measured outside the range of current
observations: a system with a chirp mass $\mathcal{M} \le 0.871 $ M$_\odot$
would unambiguously contain the smallest-mass neutron star observed, and a
system with $\mathcal{M} \ge 2.786 \Msun$ must contain a black hole. However,
additional information would be needed to distinguish between a binary
containing two 1.35 M$_\odot$ neutron stars and an exotic
neutron-star--black-hole binary. We also identify those configurations that
could be unambiguously identified as black-hole binaries, and show how the
observation of an electromagnetic counterpart to a neutron-star--black-hole
binary could be used to constrain the black-hole spin.

In this survey, we give a friendly introduction from a graph theory
perspective to the q-state Potts model, an important statistical mechanics tool
for analyzing complex systems in which nearest neighbor interactions determine
the aggregate behavior of the system. We present the surprising equivalence of
the Potts model partition function and one of the most renowned graph
invariants, the Tutte polynomial, a relationship that has resulted in a
remarkable synergy between the two fields of study. We highlight some of these
interconnections, such as computational complexity results that have alternated
between the two fields. The Potts model captures the effect of temperature on
the system and plays an important role in the study of thermodynamic phase
transitions. We discuss the equivalence of the chromatic polynomial and the
zero-temperature antiferromagnetic partition function, and how this has led to
the study of the complex zeros of these functions. We also briefly describe
Monte Carlo simulations commonly used for Potts model analysis of complex
systems. The Potts model has applications as widely varied as magnetism, tumor
migration, foam behaviors, and social demographics, and we provide a sampling
of these that also demonstrates some variations of the Potts model. We conclude
with some current areas of investigation that emphasize graph theoretic
approaches.
  This paper is an elementary general audience survey, intended to popularize
the area and provide an accessible first point of entry for further
exploration.

Laser ablation of a Near-Earth Object (NEO) on a collision course with Earth
produces a cloud of ejecta which exerts a thrust on the NEO, deflecting it from
its original trajectory. Ablation may be performed from afar by illuminating an
Earth-targeting asteroid or comet with a stand-off "DE- STAR" system consisting
of a large phased-array laser in Earth orbit. Alternatively, a much smaller
stand-on "DE-STARLITE" system may travel alongside the target, slowly
deflecting it from nearby over a long period. This paper presents orbital
simulations comparing the effectiveness of both systems across a range of laser
