and NEO parameters. Simulated parameters include magnitude, duration and, for
the stand-on system, direction of the thrust, as well as the type, size and
orbital characteristics of the target NEO. These simulations indicate that
deflection distance is approximately proportional to the magnitude of thrust
and to the square of the duration of ablation, and is inversely proportional to
the mass. Furthermore, deflection distance shows strong dependence on thrust
direction with the optimal direction of thrust varying with the duration of
laser activity. As one example, consider a typical 325 m asteroid: beginning 15
yr in advance, just 2 N of thrust from a ~20 kW stand-on DE-STARLITE system is
sufficient to deflect the asteroid by 2 R_e. Numerous scenarios are discussed
as is a practical implementation of such a system consistent with current
launch vehicle capabilities.

Threshold resummation in Soft-Collinear Effective Theory (SCET) and perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) are two distinct approaches for handling threshold singularities in cross-section calculations. In this study, we provide an analytic comparison of these two methods.   Our objective is to investigate the differences and similarities in the treatment of threshold resummation between SCET and perturbative QCD. We aim to identify the advantages and limitations of each approach in calculating observables near partonic threshold regions.  Methodology involves a detailed comparison of the resummation techniques used in SCET and perturbative QCD. We analyze the key mathematical structures underlying both methods and compare their applicability in different kinematic regimes.  Key findings show that while both SCET and perturbative QCD offer powerful tools for resumming threshold logarithms, they approach the problem from different theoretical frameworks. SCET emphasizes factorization and effective field theory techniques, whereas perturbative QCD relies on traditional Feynman diagram calculations. The comparison highlights the complementary nature of the two approaches.  In conclusion, our analysis provides insights into the strengths and weaknesses of threshold resummation in SCET and perturbative QCD. Understanding these differences is crucial for improving the precision of predictions in collider experiments and enhancing our theoretical understanding of QCD dynamics.

The increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events have necessitated the development of effective storm detection systems. Traditional methods rely on manual observation and ground-based monitoring, which are time-consuming and often ineffective. This research paper proposes a novel approach to storm detection using visual learning techniques applied to satellite images.    Satellite images have become a crucial tool for monitoring weather patterns and detecting storms. However, the vast amounts of data generated by satellite imagery require sophisticated processing techniques to extract meaningful information. Visual learning techniques, such as deep learning and convolutional neural networks, have shown promise in image classification and object detection tasks.    This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of visual learning-based approaches for storm detection from satellite images. The proposed system will utilize a combination of image preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification techniques to identify storms with high accuracy.    A dataset of satellite images was collected from various sources, including NASA and the European Space Agency. The dataset was preprocessed to remove noise and enhance image quality. A deep learning-based approach was employed to extract features from the images, which were then fed into a classification model to predict storm presence. The performance of the system was evaluated using various metrics, including accuracy, precision, and recall.   The proposed system achieved an average accuracy of 92.5% in detecting storms from satellite images. The results showed that the visual learning-based approach outperformed traditional methods, which relied on manual observation and ground-based monitoring. The system's ability to detect storms in real-time and with high accuracy makes it a valuable tool for weather forecasting and emergency response.   The proposed visual learning-based approach for storm detection from satellite images demonstrates promising results and has the potential to revolutionize the field of storm detection. The system's ability to process large amounts of data in real-time and with high accuracy makes it an attractive solution for weather forecasting and emergency response applications.

Herschel/HIFI observations toward the compact HII region W51 has revealed the
presence of a cold dense core along its line of sight in a high-velocity stream
located just in front of W51. This detection has been made possible through
absorption measurements of low-energy transitions of HDO, NH3, and C3 against
the bright background emitted by the star-forming region. We present a
follow-up study of this core using the high sensitivity and high spectral
resolution provided by the IRAM 30-meter telescope. We report new detections of
this core in absorption for DCO+ (2-1, 3-2), H13CO+ (1-0), DNC (3-2), HN13C
(1-0), p-H2CO (202-101, 303-202), and in emission for o-NH2D. We also report
interferometric observation of this last species using the IRAM/NOEMA
telescope, revealing the fragmented nature of the source through the detection
of two cores, separated by 0.19 - 0.24 pc, with average sizes of less than 0.16
- 0.19 pc. From a non-LTE analysis, we are able to estimate the density (~2.5e4
cm-3) and temperature (~10 K) of this component, typical of what is found in
dark clouds. This component (called W51-core) has the same DCO+/HCO+ ratio
(0.02) as TMC-1 and a high DNC/HNC ratio (0.14). Detection of these deuterated
species indicates that W51-core is similar to an early-phase low-mass
star-forming region, formed from the interaction between the W51 giant
molecular cloud and the high-velocity stream in front of it. The W51 complex
being at about 5 kpc, these findings lead to what is the first detection of the
earliest phase of low-mass star-forming region at such a large distance.

The intergalactic medium (IGM) is a vast reservoir of gas that surrounds galaxies. Cold streams, filaments of cold gas in the IGM, are thought to be the primary mode of gas accretion into galaxies. This study investigates the formation and evolution of Lyman-alpha blobs (LABs), extended and luminous structures associated with HI gas in the IGM, from cold streams.  Using high-resolution simulations, we modeled the infall of cold streams onto a Milky Way-mass galaxy and followed the evolution of LABs along the cold streams. We found that the Lyman-alpha radiation emitted by the galaxy ionizes the neutral hydrogen gas in the cold streams, forming LABs. The size, shape, and luminosity of LABs depend on the streaming velocity and the cooling efficiency of the gas in the cold streams.  Our results show that Lyman-alpha blobs from cold streams can have sizes ranging from a few kpc to tens of kpc and can significantly impact galaxy formation. These structures may provide the necessary conditions for the formation of large-scale galactic structures, such as disks, bulges, and bars, as well as the assembly of central supermassive black holes.  Furthermore, we propose that Lyman-alpha blobs from cold streams could be observed as the so-called "Cosmic Fanaras," large-scale structures detected in HI observations of the IGM. This discovery could provide new insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the universe.  In conclusion, this study provides a better understanding of the formation and evolution of Lyman-alpha blobs from cold streams, their impact on galaxy formation, and their potential observational implications. The findings have implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution in the context of the cosmic web and the intergalactic medium.

Nested quantum annealing correction (NQAC) is an error correcting scheme for
quantum annealing that allows for the encoding of a logical qubit into an
arbitrarily large number of physical qubits. The encoding replaces each logical
qubit by a complete graph of degree $C$. The nesting level $C$ represents the
distance of the error-correcting code and controls the amount of protection
against thermal and control errors. Theoretical mean-field analyses and
empirical data obtained with a D-Wave Two quantum annealer (supporting up to
$512$ qubits) showed that NQAC has the potential to achieve a scalable
effective temperature reduction, $T_{\rm eff} \sim C^{-\eta}$, with $\eta \leq
2$. We confirm that this scaling is preserved when NQAC is tested on a D-Wave
2000Q device (supporting up to $2048$ qubits). In addition, we show that NQAC
can be also used in sampling problems to lower the effective temperature of a
quantum annealer. Such effective temperature reduction is relevant for
machine-learning applications. Since we demonstrate that NQAC achieves error
correction via an effective reduction of the temperature of the quantum
annealing device, our results address the problem of the "temperature scaling
law for quantum annealers", which requires the temperature of quantum annealers
to be reduced as problems of larger sizes are attempted to be solved.

Optical and NIR observations of the type Ia supernova SN 2014J in M82 are
presented. The observed light curves are found to be similar to normal SNe Ia,
with a decline rate parameter $\Delta m_{15}(B) = 1.08 \pm 0.03$. The supernova
reached $B$-band maximum on JD 2456690.14, at an apparent magnitude $m_B(max) =
11.94$. The optical spectra show a red continuum with deep interstellar Na~{\sc
i} absorption, but otherwise resemble those of normal SNe Ia. The Si~{\sc ii}
$\lambda 6355$ feature indicates a velocity of $\sim 12\,000$ km s$^{-1}$ at
$B$-band maximum, which places SN 2014J at the border of the Normal Velocity
and High Velocity group of SNe Ia. The velocity evolution of SN 2014J places it
in the Low Velocity Gradient subclass, whereas the equivalent widths of Si~{\sc
ii} features near $B$-band maximum place it at the border of the Core Normal
and Broad Line subclasses of SNe Ia. An analytic model fit to the bolometric
light curve indicates that a total of $\sim 1.3$ M$_{\odot}$ was ejected in the
explosion, and the ejected $^{56}$Ni mass $M_{Ni} \sim 0.6$ M$_{\odot}$. The
low [Fe~{\sc iii}] $\lambda4701$ to [Fe~{\sc ii}] $\lambda5200$ ratio in the
nebular spectra of SN 2014J hints towards clumpiness in the ejecta. Optical
broadband, linear polarimetric observations of SN 2014J obtained on four epochs
indicate an almost constant polarization ($P_{\rm R} \sim$2.7 per cent;
$\theta$ $\sim$37$^\circ$), which suggests that the polarization signal is of
interstellar origin.

Among the approaches to the proposed mitigation and remediation of the space
debris problem is the de-orbiting of objects in low Earth orbit through
irradiation by ground-based high-intensity pulsed lasers. Laser ablation of a
thin surface layer causes target recoil, resulting in the depletion of orbital
angular momentum and accelerated atmospheric re-entry. However, both the
magnitude and direction of the recoil are shape dependent, a feature of the
laser-based remediation concept that has received little attention. Since the
development of a predictive capability is desirable, we have investigated the
dynamical response to ablation of objects comprising a variety of shapes. We
derive and demonstrate a simple analytical technique for calculating the
ablation-driven transfer of linear momentum, emphasizing cases for which the
recoil is not exclusively parallel to the incident beam. For the purposes of
comparison and contrast, we examine one case of momentum transfer in the
low-intensity regime, where photon pressure is the dominant momentum transfer
mechanism, showing that shape and orientation effects influence the target
response in a similar, but not identical, manner. We address the related
problem of target spin and, by way of a few simple examples, show how ablation
can alter the spin state of a target, which often has a pronounced effect on
the recoil dynamics.

This study explores the three-dimensional torques and power generated by the horse forelimb joints during the trot gait. The primary objective was to quantify joint torques and powers to understand the dynamic mechanics of the forelimbs. Data collection involved high-speed video analysis and force plate measurements while horses trotted at various speeds. Joint moments were calculated from kinematic data, and joint powers were derived from these moments and angular velocities. Key findings indicated that the fetlock joint exhibited the highest torque and power generation among the analyzed joints, especially during the support phase. Additionally, the concept of joint power asymmetry was identified, with significant differences observed between the right and left limbs. The results suggest that the fetlock joint plays a crucial role in stabilizing the limb during the trot, with potential implications for injury prevention and rehabilitation strategies. The study concludes by highlighting the importance of considering three-dimensional joint dynamics in understanding equine locomotion and musculoskeletal function.

We investigate the mass function of black holes, a fundamental parameter in understanding the evolution of galaxies and the growth of supermassive black holes. Our analysis is based on a comprehensive review of the latest gravitational wave measurements from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and Virgo Collaborations, as well as theoretical models of black hole formation and evolution. We find that the observed mass function of black holes is consistent with predictions from the merger rate of stellar-mass black holes and the growth of supermassive black holes through mergers with smaller black holes. However, our results also indicate a possible discrepancy in the predicted and observed mass function for the most massive black holes, which may be indicative of alternative formation mechanisms or modifications to our current understanding of black hole physics. Our analysis highlights the importance of gravitational wave astronomy in constraining the mass function of black holes and provides new insights into the complex interplay between stellar evolution, black hole formation, and galaxy evolution. We propose a framework for further investigation, incorporating both theoretical and observational approaches to better understand the mass function of black holes and its implications for our understanding of the universe.

In recent years, the study of random walk models has gained considerable attention, particularly in the context of anomalous diffusion processes observed in various physical phenomena. This research paper explores a novel solvable random walk model with memory, positing that the inclusion of memory effects alters classical diffusion dynamics. The objective of this study is to establish a theoretical framework for understanding how memory influences both the statistical properties of random walks and their relation to Markovian models. Utilizing a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations, we derive the probability distribution functions associated with the proposed memory-driven random walk model. We then compare the resultant dynamics with traditional Markovian models of diffusion, characterized by a lack of memory. Key findings reveal that the incorporation of memory leads to non-linear dynamics and superdiffusive behavior, which deviates from the simple Gaussian profiles typical of Markovian processes. Additionally, we identify specific conditions under which the memory contributions can be systematically integrated into Markovian frameworks, thus providing a broader understanding of anomalous diffusion. The results highlight the significance of memory effects in stochastic processes and suggest potential applications in fields ranging from biological systems to financial markets. In conclusion, our findings indicate that memory plays a crucial role in the dynamics of random walks and offer profound implications for the characterization of complex systems exhibiting anomalous diffusion behaviors.

This study addresses the pressing need for effective maintenance tools in academia, where outdated and inefficient methods hinder research productivity. The current landscape of academic research is characterized by an overwhelming volume of data, increasing complexity, and the need for streamlined workflows. However, the development and implementation of maintenance tools to support these processes remain a significant challenge.   The primary objective of this research is to establish a systematic process for developing maintenance tools in academia, focusing on the needs and constraints of researchers. Through a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods, this study gathers insights from academics, researchers, and maintenance personnel.   The findings reveal that the development of effective maintenance tools requires a multidisciplinary approach, incorporating insights from various stakeholders, and a deep understanding of the specific research needs and workflows. The study also highlights the importance of collaboration, adaptability, and continuous evaluation in the development and implementation of maintenance tools.   Key findings indicate that a tailored, needs-based approach is essential for the development of maintenance tools, and that a systematic process can facilitate the integration of technology, workflow optimization, and stakeholder engagement.   The study concludes that the proposed process provides a structured framework for the development of maintenance tools in academia, addressing the complexities and challenges associated with this task. By adopting this process, researchers can enhance their productivity, streamline their workflows, and improve the overall quality of their research outputs.

We investigated the angular dependence of antiferromagnetic order induced by paramagnetism in a d-wave superconductor, shedding light on the complex interplay between magnetic and superconducting properties. Through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we explored the effects of varying the angle between the magnetic field and the superconducting order parameter on the emergence of antiferromagnetic order.  Our results indicate that a specific range of magnetic field orientations, corresponding to a particular phase of the superconducting order parameter, leads to the stabilization of antiferromagnetic order. This phenomenon is characterized by a non-trivial dependence on the angle between the magnetic field and the superconducting order parameter, with the emergence of antiferromagnetic order occurring at a critical angle that separates a paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic phase.  Our calculations reveal that the angular dependence of antiferromagnetic order can be understood through the interplay between the superconducting pairing and the magnetic exchange interactions. Specifically, we found that the exchange interactions between the magnetic moments are mediated by the superconducting order parameter, leading to a non-trivial dependence on the angle between the magnetic field and the superconducting order parameter.  Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of the interplay between magnetic and superconducting properties in d-wave superconductors, and provide a framework for the study of antiferromagnetic order in these systems.

Imaging polarimetry is an important tool for the study of cosmic magnetic
fields. In our Galaxy, polarization levels of a few up to $\sim$10\% are
measured in the submillimeter dust emission from molecular clouds and in the
synchrotron emission from supernova remnants. Only few techniques exist to
image the distribution of polarization angles, as a means of tracing the
plane-of-sky projection of the magnetic field orientation. At submillimeter
wavelengths, polarization is either measured as the differential total power of
polarization-sensitive bolometer elements, or by modulating the polarization of
the signal. Bolometer arrays such as LABOCA at the APEX telescope are used to
observe the continuum emission from fields as large as $\sim0\fdg2$ in
diameter. %Here we present the results from the commissioning of PolKa, a
polarimeter for Here we present PolKa, a polarimeter for LABOCA with a
reflection-type waveplate of at least 90\% efficiency. The modulation
efficiency depends mainly on the sampling and on the angular velocity of the
waveplate. For the data analysis the concept of generalized synchronous
demodulation is introduced. The instrumental polarization towards a point
source is at the level of $\sim0.1$\%, increasing to a few percent at the
$-10$db contour of the main beam. A method to correct for its effect in
observations of extended sources is presented. Our map of the polarized
synchrotron emission from the Crab nebula is in agreement with structures
observed at radio and optical wavelengths. The linear polarization measured in
OMC1 agrees with results from previous studies, while the high sensitivity of
LABOCA enables us to also map the polarized emission of the Orion Bar, a
prototypical photon-dominated region.

In this work, we focus on utilizing data to investigate the top quark forward-backward asymmetry by employing a lepton-based handle. The top quark, being the heaviest known elementary particle, plays a crucial role in probing the Standard Model and searching for new physics phenomena. However, the origin of the top quark forward-backward asymmetry observed at the Tevatron remains a puzzle. Our study aims to address this issue by delving into the underlying mechanisms through a lepton-focused approach. By analyzing data using advanced methodologies, we have identified key patterns that shed light on the asymmetry's behavior. Our results show a promising correlation between the lepton properties and the asymmetry, hinting at a deeper connection between these variables. Through meticulous data analysis and theoretical considerations, we propose a refined understanding of the top quark forward-backward asymmetry, contributing to the ongoing efforts in unraveling the mysteries of particle physics. Our methodology blends cutting-edge data-driven techniques with fundamental theoretical principles, offering a comprehensive framework for studying this intriguing phenomenon. This study not only advances our knowledge of the top quark asymmetry but also provides a roadmap for future explorations in high-energy physics.

The devastating consequences of World War I had a profound impact on the development of Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, particularly in the aftermath of the war. This period saw a significant shift in the scientific landscape, as the war's end marked a turning point in the global understanding of space, time, and gravity. The war's aftermath witnessed a surge in theoretical physics, with Einstein's theory of general relativity gaining widespread acceptance.  Einstein's groundbreaking work, introduced in 1915, posited that gravity is not a force, but rather the curvature of spacetime caused by massive objects. This paradigm shift challenged the long-held Newtonian understanding of space and time, and its implications were far-reaching. As the war drew to a close, Einstein's theory began to gain traction among scientists, who saw its potential to revolutionize our understanding of the universe.  This study examines the impact of World War I on the development of Einstein's theory of general relativity, with a focus on the key figures and events that contributed to its widespread acceptance. Through a critical analysis of primary sources, including Einstein's writings and correspondence, as well as historical accounts of the war and its aftermath, this research sheds light on the complex interplay between science, politics, and culture in shaping the course of modern physics. By exploring the historical context in which Einstein's theory emerged, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the role of World War I in shaping the development of modern physics and the enduring legacy of Einstein's relativity.

We study spin transport through a normal metal-spin superconductor junction.
A spin-flip reflection is demonstrated at the interface, where a spin-up
electron incident from the normal metal can be reflected as a spin-down
electron and the spin $2\times \hbar/2$ will be injected into the spin
superconductor. When the (spin) voltage is smaller than the gap of the spin
superconductor, the spin-flip reflection determines the transport properties of
the junction. We consider both graphene-based (linear-dispersion-relation) and
quadratic-dispersion-relation normal metal-spin superconductor junctions in
detail. For the two-dimensional graphene-based junction, the spin-flip
reflected electron can be along the specular direction (retro-direction) when
the incident and reflected electron locates in the same band (different bands).
A perfect spin-flip reflection can occur when the incident electron is normal
to the interface, and the reflection coefficient is slightly suppressed for the
oblique incident case. As a comparison, for the one-dimensional
quadratic-dispersion-relation junction, the spin-flip reflection coefficient
can reach 1 at certain incident energies. In addition, both the charge current
and the spin current under a charge (spin) voltage are studied. The spin
conductance is proportional to the spin-flip reflection coefficient when the
spin voltage is less than the gap of the spin superconductor. These results
will help us get a better understanding of spin transport through the normal
metal-spin superconductor junction.

We investigate the nanoscale phase separation phenomenon in hole-doped manganites, focusing on the complex interplay between charge, spin, and lattice degrees of freedom. Our study delves into the intricate mechanisms governing phase separation in these materials, shedding light on the fundamental physics driving their unique properties. Through advanced microscopy techniques, including scanning tunneling microscopy and transmission electron microscopy, we unveil the intricate nanoscale structures that emerge in hole-doped manganites. Our results reveal a highly non-uniform distribution of charge and spin within the materials, indicative of phase separation phenomena on the nanoscale.   The key objective of this work is to unravel the underlying principles behind nanoscale phase separation in hole-doped manganites and to elucidate its implications for the material's macroscopic properties. By employing a combination of experimental observations and theoretical modeling, we provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms driving phase separation and its impact on the electronic and magnetic behavior of these complex oxides. Our findings contribute to the broader field of condensed matter physics by offering insights into the role of nanoscale phase separation in tuning the functional properties of correlated electron systems.

In order to meet the requirement of high data rates for the next generation
wireless systems, the efficient implementation of receiver algorithms is
essential. On the other hand, the rapid development of technology motivates the
investigation of programmable implementations. This paper summarizes the design
of a programmable turbo decoder as an applicationspecific instruction-set
processor (ASIP) using Transport Triggered Architecture (TTA). The processor
architecture is designed in such manner that it can be programmed to support
other receiver algorithms, for example, decoding based on the Viterbi
algorithm. Different suboptimal maximum a posteriori (MAP) algorithms are used
and compared to one another for the softinput soft-output (SISO) component
decoders in a single TTA processor. The max-log-MAP algorithm outperforms the
other suboptimal algorithms in terms of latency. The design enables the
designer to change the suboptimal algorithms according to the bit error rate
(BER) performance requirement. Unlike many other programmable turbo decoder
implementations, quadratic polynomial permutation (QPP) interleaver is used in
this work for contention-free memory access and to make the processor 3GPP LTE
compliant. Several optimization techniques to enable real time processing on
programmable platforms are introduced. Using our method, with a single
iteration 31.32 Mbps throughput is achieved for the max-log-MAP algorithm for a
clock frequency of 200 MHz.

We present theories of `Natural Neutrinos' in which neutral fermionic top
partner fields are simultaneously the right-handed neutrinos (RHN), linking
seemingly disparate aspects of the Standard Model structure: a) The RHN top
partners are responsible for the observed small neutrino masses, b) They help
ameliorate the tuning in the weak scale and address the little hierarchy
problem, and c) The factor of $3$ arising from $N_c$ in the top-loop Higgs mass
corrections is countered by a factor $3$ from the number of vector-like
generations of RHN. The RHN top partners may arise in
pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone-Boson (pNGB) Higgs models such as the Twin Higgs, as
well as more general Composite, Little, and Orbifold Higgs scenarios, and three
simple example models are presented. This framework firmly predicts a TeV-scale
seesaw, as the RHN masses are bounded to be below the TeV scale by naturalness.
The generation of light neutrino masses relies on a collective breaking of
lepton number, allowing for comparatively large neutrino Yukawa couplings and a
rich associated phenomenology. The structure of the neutrino mass mechanism
realizes in certain limits the Inverse or Linear classes of seesaw. Natural
Neutrino models are testable at a variety of current and future experiments,
particularly in tests of lepton universality, searches for lepton flavor
violation, and precision electroweak and Higgs coupling measurements possible
at high energy $e^+ e^-$ and hadron colliders.

We present an analysis of far--infrared (FIR) [CII] and [OI] fine structure
line and continuum observations obtained with $Herschel$/PACS, and CO(1-0)
observations obtained with the IRAM Plateau de Bure Interferometer, of Lyman
Break Analogs (LBAs) at $z\sim 0.2$. The principal aim of this work is to
determine the typical ISM properties of $z\sim 1-2$ Main Sequence (MS)
galaxies, with stellar masses between $10^{9.5}$ and $10^{11}$ $M_{\odot}$,
which are currently not easily detectable in all these lines even with ALMA and
NOEMA. We perform PDR modeling and apply different IR diagnostics to derive the
main physical parameters of the FIR emitting gas and dust and we compare the
derived ISM properties to those of galaxies on and above the MS at different
redshifts. We find that the ISM properties of LBAs are quite extreme (low gas
temperature, high density and thermal pressure) with respect to those found in
local normal spirals and more active local galaxies. LBAs have no [CII] deficit
despite having the high specific star formation rates (sSFRs) typical of
starbursts. Although LBAs lie above the local MS, we show that their ISM
properties are more similar to those of high-redshift MS galaxies than of local
galaxies above the main sequence. This data set represents an important
reference for planning future ALMA [CII] observations of relatively low-mass MS
galaxies at the epoch of the peak of the cosmic star formation.

In response to the burgeoning interest in asteroid mining as outlined in the ASIME 2016 White Paper, our study delves into the critical aspects that need to be addressed by potential asteroid miners. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of various challenges faced by asteroid miners, including regulatory frameworks, technological readiness levels, and resource utilization strategies. We have identified key questions posed by asteroid miners regarding long-term sustainability, cost-effectiveness, and the ethical implications of space resource exploitation.  Our methodology involves a systematic review of existing literature on asteroid mining, stakeholder consultations, and simulations of mining operations. The results reveal that while significant progress has been made in developing technologies suitable for asteroid mining, there remains a need for robust international policies and agreements to ensure equitable access and sustainable practices. Additionally, the economic viability of asteroid mining depends heavily on reducing operational costs through innovation and efficiency improvements.  The key ideas explored include the necessity of collaborative research efforts between private sector companies and governmental bodies, the importance of establishing clear guidelines for space resource utilization, and the potential role of public-private partnerships in fostering technological advancements. Our findings suggest that addressing these issues will be crucial for the successful implementation of asteroid mining ventures and their integration into the broader space economy.

The coldest known brown dwarf, WISE J0855-0714, with a temperature of 270 K, poses an intriguing challenge for astronomers due to its extreme faintness. To gain insights into its atmospheric properties and investigate any potential variability, this study utilizes Spitzer Space Telescope's InfraRed Array Camera (IRAC) and Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) data. We first analyze the photometric data obtained from IRAC observations, revealing periodic dimming events with amplitudes ranging from 3% to 15%, corresponding to a brightness variation of approximately 0.03 magnitudes. The periodicity and amplitude of these events exhibit no clear trends, suggesting that they may originate from cloud activity or other atmospheric phenomena.  Subsequently, we explore the spectral variations by analyzing the high-resolution IRS spectra. We detect a clear methane absorption feature, confirming the presence of methane in the brown dwarf's atmosphere. Additionally, we observe a significant variability in the spectral shape, which cannot be fully explained by cloud coverage. This may suggest the presence of surface heterogeneity or other atmospheric processes.  Our findings provide valuable insights into the atmospheric properties and potential variability of the coldest known brown dwarf. The detected periodic dimming events may originate from cloud activity or other atmospheric phenomena, while the spectral variations cannot be fully explained by cloud coverage alone. Further investigations are required to fully understand the complex dynamics of this intriguing object.  This research employs the Spitzer Space Telescope to photometrically monitor the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE J0855-0714. The study analyzes the data obtained from InfraRed Array Camera (IRAC) and Infrared Spectrograph (IRS), revealing periodic dimming events and spectral variations. The findings provide insights into the atmospheric properties and potential variability of this intriguing object, suggesting the presence of cloud activity, atmospheric phenomena, or surface heterogeneity. Further investigations are needed to fully understand the complex dynamics of the coldest known brown dwarf.

In 2009, the first author introduced a class of zeta functions, called
`distance zeta functions', which has enabled us to extend the existing theory
of zeta functions of fractal strings and sprays (initiated by the first author
and his collaborators in the early 1990s) to arbitrary bounded (fractal) sets
in Euclidean spaces of any dimensions. A closely related tool is the class of
`tube zeta functions', defined using the tube function of a fractal set. These
zeta functions exhibit deep connections with Minkowski contents and upper box
(or Minkowski) dimensions, as well as, more generally, with the complex
dimensions of fractal sets. In particular, the abscissa of (Lebesgue, i.e.,
absolute) convergence of the distance zeta function coincides with the upper
box dimension of a set. We also introduce a class of transcendentally
quasiperiodic sets, and describe their construction based on a sequence of
carefully chosen generalized Cantor sets with two auxilliary parameters. As a
result, we obtain a family of "maximally hyperfractal" compact sets and
relative fractal drums (i.e., such that the associated fractal zeta functions
have a singularity at every point of the critical line of convergence).
Finally, we discuss the general fractal tube formulas and the Minkowski
measurability criterion obtained by the authors in the context of relative
fractal drums (and, in particular, of bounded subsets of the N-dimensional
Euclidean space).

We propose a new method for representing data sets with a set of binary
feature functions. We compute both the dyadic set structure determined by an
order on the binary features together with the canonical product coefficient
parameters for the associated dyadic measure and a variant of a nerve
simplicial complex determined by the support of the dyadic measure together
with its betti numbers. The product coefficient parameters characterize the
relative skewness of the dyadic measure at dyadic scales and localities. The
more abstract betti number statistics summarize the simplicial geometry of the
support of the measure and satisfy a differential privacy property. Both types
of statistics can be computed algorithmically from the binary feature
representation of the data. This representation provides a new method for
pre-processing data into automatically generated features which explicitly
characterize the dyadic statistics and geometry of the data. useful for
statistical fusion, decision-making, inference, multi-scale hypothesis testing
and visualization. We illustrated the methods on a data quality data set. We
exploit a representation lemma for dyadic measures on the unit interval
(Fefferman, Kenig and Pipher) reformulated for measures on dyadic sets by
Bassu, Jones, Ness and Shallcross. We prove that dyadic sets with dyadic
measures have a canonical set of binary features and determine canonical nerve
simplicial complexes. We compare our methods with other results for measures on
sets with tree structures, recent multi-resolution theory, and persistent
homology and suggest links to differential privacy, Bayesian reasoning and
algebraic statistics.

In this paper, we present a fully fiber-based one-way Quantum Key
Distribution (QKD) system implementing the Gaussian-Modulated Coherent States
(GMCS) protocol. The system employs a double Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI)
configuration in which the weak quantum signal and the strong Local Oscillator
(LO) go through the same fiber between Alice and Bob, and are separated into
two paths inside Bob's terminal. To suppress the LO leakage into the signal
path, which is an important contribution to the excess noise, we implemented a
novel scheme combining polarization and frequency multiplexing, achieving an
extinction ratio of 70dB. To further minimize the system excess noise due to
phase drift of the double MZI, we propose that, instead of employing phase
feedback control, one simply let Alice remap her data by performing a rotation
operation. We further present noise analysis both theoretically and
experimentally. Our calculation shows that the combined polarization and
frequency multiplexing scheme can achieve better stability in practice than the
time-multiplexing scheme, because it allows one to use matched fiber lengths
for the signal and the LO paths on both sides of the double MZI, greatly
reducing the phase instability caused by unmatched fiber lengths. Our
experimental noise analysis quantifies the three main contributions to the
excess noise, which will be instructive to future studies of the GMCS QKD
systems. Finally, we demonstrate, under the "realistic model" in which Eve
cannot control the system within Bob's terminal, a secure key rate of
0.3bit/pulse over a 5km fiber link. This key rate is about two orders of
magnitude higher than that of a practical BB84 QKD system.

This study presents the results of a comprehensive analysis of planetary systems orbiting low-mass stars, focusing on K2 candidate systems observed during campaigns 1-7. Low-mass stars are the most common type of star in the galaxy, yet their planetary systems remain poorly understood due to the challenges associated with detecting exoplanets around these faint and cool stars. The K2 mission, a space-based telescope, has provided unprecedented opportunities to study these systems, and this research aims to characterize the properties of planetary systems orbiting low-mass K2 candidate stars.  The objective of this study is to identify and characterize the planetary systems of K2 candidate stars, focusing on the detection of planets, determination of their orbital parameters, and analysis of the host star properties. A total of 150 K2 candidate systems were selected for analysis, and a combination of radial velocity measurements, transit photometry, and asteroseismic data were used to detect and characterize the planets. The results show that a significant fraction of K2 candidate systems harbor planets, with a median number of planets per system of 2.2.  The key findings of this study indicate that the planetary systems of K2 candidate stars are diverse, with systems exhibiting a range of planetary architectures and host star properties. The study also reveals that the detection of planets around low-mass K2 candidate stars is often facilitated by the presence of stellar activity, such as spots or magnetic fields. The findings of this research have significant implications for our understanding of planetary system formation and evolution, and highlight the importance of continued observations of K2 candidate systems in the search for life beyond Earth.

In this paper, we establish a connection between the recently developed
data-driven time-frequency analysis \cite{HS11,HS13-1} and the classical second
order differential equations. The main idea of the data-driven time-frequency
analysis is to decompose a multiscale signal into a sparsest collection of
Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) over the largest possible dictionary via
nonlinear optimization. These IMFs are of the form $a(t) \cos(\theta(t))$ where
the amplitude $a(t)$ is positive and slowly varying. The non-decreasing phase
function $\theta(t)$ is determined by the data and in general depends on the
signal in a nonlinear fashion. One of the main results of this paper is that we
show that each IMF can be associated with a solution of a second order ordinary
differential equation of the form $\ddot{x}+p(x,t)\dot{x}+q(x,t)=0$. Further,
we propose a localized variational formulation for this problem and develop an
effective $l^1$-based optimization method to recover $p(x,t)$ and $q(x,t)$ by
looking for a sparse representation of $p$ and $q$ in terms of the polynomial
basis. Depending on the form of nonlinearity in $p(x,t)$ and $q(x,t)$, we can
define the degree of nonlinearity for the associated IMF. %and the
corresponding coefficients for the associated highest order nonlinear terms.
This generalizes a concept recently introduced by Prof. N. E. Huang et al.
\cite{Huang11}. Numerical examples will be provided to illustrate the
robustness and stability of the proposed method for data with or without noise.
This manuscript should be considered as a proof of concept.

As a result of improvements in power semiconductors, moderate frequency
switching supplies can now provide the hundreds of amps typically required by
accelerators with zero-to-peak noise in the kHz region ~0.06% in current or
voltage mode. Modeling was undertaken using a finite electromagnetic program to
determine if eddy currents induced in the solid steel of CEBAF magnets and
small supplemental additions would bring the error fields down to the 5ppm
level needed for beam quality. The expected maximum field of the magnet under
consideration is 0.85T and the DC current required to produce that field is
used in the calculations. An additional 0.1% current ripple is added to the DC
current at discrete frequencies 360 Hz, 720 Hz or 7200 Hz. Over the region of
the pole within 0.5% of the central integrated BdL the resulting AC field
changes can be reduced to less than 1% of the 0.1% input ripple for all
frequencies, and a sixth of that at 7200 Hz. Doubling the current, providing
1.5T central field, yielded the same fractional reduction in ripple at the beam
for the cases checked. For light sources with aluminum vacuum vessels and full
energy linac injection, the combination of solid core dipoles and switching
power supplies may result in significant cost savings.

Software Analytics (SA) is a new branch of big data analytics that has
recently emerged (2011). What distinguishes SA from direct software analysis is
that it links data mined from many different software artifacts to obtain
valuable insights. These insights are useful for the decision-making process
throughout the different phases of the software lifecycle. Since SA is
currently a hot and promising topic, we have conducted a systematic literature
review, presented in this paper, to identify gaps in knowledge and open
research areas in SA. Because many researchers are still confused about the
true potential of SA, we had to filter out available research papers to obtain
the most SA-relevant work for our review. This filtration yielded 19 studies
out of 135. We have based our systematic review on four main factors: which
software practitioners SA targets, which domains are covered by SA, which
artifacts are extracted by SA, and whether these artifacts are linked or not.
The results of our review have shown that much of the available SA research
only serves the needs of developers. Also, much of the available research uses
only one artifact which, in turn, means fewer links between artifacts and fewer
insights. This shows that the available SA research work is still embryonic
leaving plenty of room for future research in the SA field.

In this study, we investigate the quasiparticle density of states (QDOS) and localization properties in the cuprate superconductors using a combination of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and theoretical calculations based on the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). Our ARPES measurements reveal that the QDOS of the cuprate superconductors exhibits strong correlations and localization effects, particularly in the antinodal region. Theoretical calculations using the DMFT approach provide insights into the origin of these effects, suggesting that the strong correlations and random doping fluctuations lead to the formation of a correlated Mott insulator state, which is a precursor to the superconducting state.     Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the QDOS, localization, and distributed disorder by considering the effect of the lattice disorder on the quasiparticle states. Our results show that the disorder enhances the localization effects and broadens the QDOS, leading to a reduction in coherence and an increase in inelastic scattering. These findings are important for understanding the unconventional superconducting properties of the cuprate superconductors, and they provide a platform for further investigations into the role of disorder in these materials.     In summary, we present experimental and theoretical evidence that the quasiparticle density of states in the cuprate superconductors is strongly influenced by correlations and localization effects, particularly in the antinodal region. Theoretical calculations based on the DMFT approach provide insights into the origin of these effects and suggest that the strong correlations and random doping fluctuations lead to the formation of a correlated Mott insulator state. The role of disorder in the QDOS and localization properties is also explored, revealing that disorder enhances localization effects and broadens the QDOS. These findings have important implications for understanding the unconventional superconducting properties of the cuprate superconductors and for developing new materials with improved superconducting properties.

In the context of general relativity, the near-horizon structure of escape zones around electrically charged particles in rotating black holes is a complex and poorly understood phenomenon. This study aims to investigate the effects of a weakly magnetized rotating black hole on the near-horizon structure of escape zones of electrically charged particles.   The objective of this research is to explore the interplay between the electric and magnetic fields of the charged particles and the rotating black hole, with a focus on the resulting near-horizon structure of the escape zones. A combination of numerical relativity simulations and analytical calculations is employed to model the behavior of charged particles in the vicinity of the black hole.   The key findings of this study reveal that the presence of a weakly magnetized rotating black hole significantly modifies the near-horizon structure of escape zones of electrically charged particles. The simulations demonstrate that the magnetic field of the black hole plays a crucial role in shaping the escape zones, leading to the formation of complex, non-spherical structures. Furthermore, the analytical calculations indicate that the rotation of the black hole affects the charge distribution of the particles, resulting in a non-uniform charge density within the escape zones.   This research contributes to our understanding of the interactions between charged particles and rotating black holes, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of the near-horizon environment. The findings have implications for our understanding of various astrophysical phenomena, including the behavior of charged particles in strong-field environments and the properties of black hole magnetism.

Multi-epoch observations with ACS and WFC3 on HST provide a unique and
comprehensive probe of stellar dynamics within 47 Tucanae. We confront analytic
models of the globular cluster with the observed stellar proper motions that
probe along the main sequence from just above 0.8 to 0.1M$_\odot$ as well as
white dwarfs younger than one gigayear. One field lies just beyond the
half-light radius where dynamical models (\eg lowered Maxwellian distributions)
make robust predictions for the stellar proper motions. The observed proper
motions in this outer field show evidence for anisotropy in the velocity
distribution as well as skewness; the latter is evidence of rotation. The
measured velocity dispersions and surface brightness distributions agree in
detail with a rotating, anisotropic model of the stellar distribution function
with mild dependence of the proper-motion dispersion on mass. However, the best
fitting models under-predict the rotation and skewness of the stellar
velocities. In the second field, centered on the core of the cluster, the mass
segregation in proper motion is much stronger. Nevertheless the model developed
in the outer field can be extended inward by taking this mass segregation into
account in a heuristic fashion. The proper motions of the main-sequence stars
yield a mass estimate of the cluster of $1.31 \pm 0.02 \times 10^6
\mathrm{M}_\odot$ at a distance of 4.7 kpc. By comparing the proper motions of
a sample of giant and sub-giant stars with the observed radial velocities we
estimate the distance to the cluster kinematically to be $4.29 \pm 0.47$ kpc.

We investigate the maximal energy of bipartite bicyclic graphs, a conjecture that has been open in the field of graph theory for several years. Through a combination of computational and theoretical approaches, we attempt to solve this conjecture by analyzing a large dataset of bipartite bicyclic graphs. Our computational analysis reveals that the maximal energy of these graphs is not a fixed value, but rather a function of the graph's structure. We develop a novel algorithm to compute this function, which we use to test our conjecture on a wide range of bipartite bicyclic graphs. Our results show that the maximal energy of bipartite bicyclic graphs can be significantly improved by optimizing the graph's structure, particularly by adding or removing edges. We also develop a theoretical framework to understand the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon, which we use to derive a general formula for the maximal energy of bipartite bicyclic graphs. Our key findings are that the maximal energy is closely related to the graph's spectral gap, and that it can be optimized using a simple greedy algorithm. These results provide new insights into the properties of bipartite bicyclic graphs and shed light on the solution to the conjecture, providing a general framework for the optimal design of such graphs.

The resonant caustic perturbation (RCP) is a complex and intriguing phenomenon that arises in nonlinear water wave systems. In this study, we present an investigation into the characterization of the RCP using both numerical simulations and experimental observations. The background of the problem is discussed, highlighting the importance of the RCP in various applications such as ocean waves, fluid dynamics, and hydrodynamics.  The objective of this research is to gain a better understanding of the physical mechanisms behind the RCP and to provide a comprehensive description of its key features. To achieve this goal, we employ a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. The methodology section describes the setup of our numerical model, including the equations governing the fluid motion and the boundary conditions used. We also outline the procedures for conducting experiments in a wave tank to obtain measurements of the RCP.  Our key findings reveal that the RCP is a highly periodic and dynamic phenomenon, with the periodicity depending on the wave conditions and the geometry of the system. Furthermore, we find that the RCP is characterized by the presence of a narrow, sharp crest that moves back and forth across the wave surface, accompanied by a strong vortex street in the wake. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex physics underlying the RCP, and provide a valuable basis for further research in this area.  In conclusion, this paper sheds new light on the RCP by providing a detailed characterization of its key features through both numerical simulations and experimental observations. Our results offer insights into the underlying physical mechanisms and provide a valuable basis for future research in this important and challenging field.

The accurate calculation of long-range potentials on three-dimensional lattices, especially in the presence of defects, poses significant challenges in computational physics and material sciences. This study aims to develop an efficient Tucker tensor method that facilitates fast grid-based summation of such potentials. We employed the Tucker decomposition framework to represent the multidimensional potential fields in a reduced tensor format, leveraging their low-rank structure to speed up computations. By applying this method to various configurations of 3D lattices with synthetic defects, we compared its performance against traditional summation algorithms. Our results indicate a substantial reduction in computational time, achieving up to an 85% decrease in processing time without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrated the method's scalability and adaptability for varying lattice sizes and defect densities. The Tucker tensor method not only accelerates the evaluation of long-range interactions but also enhances the feasibility of simulating complex systems with defects. This approach opens new avenues for exploring material behaviors and physical phenomena that are contingent on the intricate interplay of long-range forces in disordered lattices. Our findings provide a robust computational tool that can be integrated into larger frameworks for studying a variety of physical systems, thereby contributing to the advancement of simulation capabilities in material science and related fields.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) has raised the boundaries of cloud
computing by offering unparalleled levels of control and flexibility to system
administrators over their virtualized environments. To properly embrace this
new era of SDN-driven network architectures, the research community must not
only consider the impact of SDN over the protocol stack, but also on its
overlying networked applications. In this big ideas paper, we study the impact
of SDN on the design of future message-oriented middleware, specifically
pub/sub systems. We argue that key concepts put forth by SDN can be applied in
a meaningful fashion to the next generation of pub/sub systems. First, pub/sub
can adopt a logically centralized controller model for maintenance, monitoring,
and control of the overlay network. We establish a parallel with existing work
on centralized pub/sub routing and discuss how the logically centralized
controller model can be implemented in a distributed manner. Second, we
investigate the separation of the control and data plane, which is integral to
SDN, which can be adopted to raise the level of decoupling in pub/sub. We
introduce a new model of pub/sub which separates the traditional publisher and
subscriber roles into flow regulators and producer/consumers of data. We then
present use cases that benefit from this approach and study the impact of
decoupling for performance.

In this study, we explore the global response to China's ascendant position on the world stage, examining both the admiration and apprehension it elicits. Our aim is to discern the underlying factors and dynamics shaping international perceptions, utilizing a mixed-methods research approach that integrates quantitative survey data with qualitative case studies. We collected data from geopolitical analysts, economic forecasters, and political commentators across diverse regions to capture a comprehensive picture of global sentiments.  Our findings indicate a dichotomous reaction countries with strong economic ties to China express favorable views, emphasizing opportunities for trade and growth. Conversely, regions perceiving a strategic threat exhibit heightened trepidation, especially where China's burgeoning influence is perceived to challenge local geopolitical dominance or economic systems. This polarization is further nuanced by cultural and historical contexts, where past interactions with China color present attitudes.  Key methodologies employed include principal component analysis to distill complex data sets into discernible patterns, and thematic coding to extract nuanced narratives from qualitative interviews. Through this robust analysis, we identify major thematic drivers of these perceptions, including economic interdependency, military expansion, and soft power initiatives, which collectively influence the global diplomatic landscape.  Ultimately, our work provides critical insights into the multifaceted global discourse surrounding China's rise, offering a nuanced understanding of international relationships in this transformative era. This research underscores the importance of multi-dimensional strategies in foreign policy formulation, addressing both cooperation and contention in an increasingly interconnected world.

We present recent UV laboratory spectra of various polycyclic aromatic
hydrocarbons (PAHs) and explore the potential of these molecules as carriers of
the DIBs. From a detailed comparison of gas-phase and Ne-matrix absorption
spectra of anthracene, phenanthrene, pyrene, 2,3-benzofluorene,
benzo[ghi]perylene, and hexabenzocoronene with new interstellar spectra, we
infer upper limits in the abundance of these PAHs in the interstellar medium.
Upper limits in the column densities of anthracene of $0.8 - 2.8 \times
10^{12}$\ cm$^{-2}$ and of pyrene and 2,3-benzofluorene ranging from $2 - 8
\times 10^{12}$\ cm$^{-2}$ are inferred. Upper limits in the column densities
of benzo[ghi]perylene are $0.9 - 2.4 \times 10^{13}$ and $10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$
for phenanthrene. The measurements indicate fractional abundances of
anthracene, pyrene, and 2,3-benzofluorene of a few times $10^{-10}$. Upper
limits in the fractional abundance of benzo[ghi]perylene of a few times
$10^{-9}$ and of phenanthrene of few times $10^{-8}$ are inferred. {Toward CPD
$-32^\circ 1734$, we found near 3584 {\AA} an absorption line of OH$^+$, which
was discovered in the interstellar medium only very recently.
  The fractional abundances of PAHs inferred here are up to two orders of
magnitude lower than estimated total PAH abundances in the interstellar medium.
This indicates that either neutral PAHs are not abundant in translucent
molecular clouds, or that a PAH population with a large variety of molecules is
present.

We address the long-standing challenge of improving the performance of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which are widely adopted in various applications due to their ability to model complex relationships between inputs and outputs. Our primary objective is to develop consistent and efficient algorithms for breaking the gridlock in MoE models, which are often characterized by slow convergence rates, high computational costs, and poor generalization capabilities.  Through a comprehensive analysis of the existing literature, we identify key issues with traditional MoE algorithms, including the use of fixed weights, limited exploration of the model space, and inadequate handling of model uncertainty. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that integrates Bayesian optimization, ensemble methods, and neural architecture search. Our approach, which we term "MoE-Bayes-Ensemble," enables the efficient exploration of the model space, adaptive weight updates, and uncertainty quantification.  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art MoE models in terms of convergence speed, model capacity, and generalization performance. Specifically, we achieve a significant reduction in the number of training epochs required to achieve optimal performance, as well as improved accuracy and robustness on unseen data. Our findings have important implications for the development of efficient and effective MoE models, which can be applied to a wide range of applications, including natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning.

In the digital age, social media platforms have become prominent communication tools, shaping social interaction and public discourse. Despite their benefits, social media networks have also given rise to a significant increase in online hate speech. Detecting and characterizing hateful users on Twitter is crucial for understanding the extent of this problem and developing effective countermeasures.  This study aims to characterize and detect hateful users on Twitter by analyzing their posting behavior, linguistic features, and network structures. We employed a multi-step approach first, we collected a dataset of tweets related to controversial topics using labeled hate speech data. Next, we applied sentiment analysis and named entity recognition techniques to identify potentially hateful tweets. Subsequently, we used graph theory to examine the network structures of hateful and non-hateful users.  Our results indicate that hateful users tend to exhibit distinct posting behaviors, including a higher frequency of tweeting and a greater number of mentions and replies. Linguistically, their tweets show a higher occurrence of abusive language and dehumanizing terms. Furthermore, our network analysis reveals that hateful users often create echo chambers, engaging primarily with like-minded individuals.  Our findings contribute to the growing body of literature on online hate speech and provide insights for developing more effective strategies to detect and mitigate its negative impacts. Future work includes exploring the potential use of machine learning algorithms to improve hate speech detection and evaluating the efficacy of different interventions for addressing online hate.  In conclusion, this study characterizes and detects hateful users on Twitter by analyzing their posting behavior, linguistic features, and network structures. Hateful users exhibit distinct patterns in their posting behavior and linguistic choices, as well as create echo chambers in their networks. Understanding these patterns is crucial for developing effective countermeasures against online hate speech.

Learning low-dimensional embeddings of knowledge graphs is a powerful
approach used to predict unobserved or missing edges between entities. However,
an open challenge in this area is developing techniques that can go beyond
simple edge prediction and handle more complex logical queries, which might
involve multiple unobserved edges, entities, and variables. For instance, given
an incomplete biological knowledge graph, we might want to predict "em what
drugs are likely to target proteins involved with both diseases X and Y?" -- a
query that requires reasoning about all possible proteins that {\em might}
interact with diseases X and Y. Here we introduce a framework to efficiently
make predictions about conjunctive logical queries -- a flexible but tractable
subset of first-order logic -- on incomplete knowledge graphs. In our approach,
we embed graph nodes in a low-dimensional space and represent logical operators
as learned geometric operations (e.g., translation, rotation) in this embedding
space. By performing logical operations within a low-dimensional embedding
space, our approach achieves a time complexity that is linear in the number of
query variables, compared to the exponential complexity required by a naive
enumeration-based approach. We demonstrate the utility of this framework in two
application studies on real-world datasets with millions of relations:
predicting logical relationships in a network of drug-gene-disease interactions
and in a graph-based representation of social interactions derived from a
popular web forum.

Non-local radiative transfer in strongly inverted masers represents a crucial phenomenon in astrophysical settings, particularly in the study of interstellar molecular clouds and maser emissions. The objective of this research is to analyze the mechanisms governing non-local interactions in masers with high population inversions, focusing on the implications for radiation transport and amplification processes. Utilizing a comprehensive approach that combines theoretical modeling with numerical simulations, we investigate the impact of non-local effects on the line profiles and gain characteristics of strongly inverted masers. Our findings indicate that non-local radiative transfer significantly alters the expected behavior of maser emissions, resulting in broader and more complex line profiles than predicted by local models. Notably, we observe that these non-local interactions lead to enhanced amplification over extended distances, with implications for the detectability and strength of maser emissions in various astrophysical contexts. Furthermore, this study elucidates the role of spatial distribution and optical depth on the radiative processes in these systems. In conclusion, our research underscores the importance of considering non-local radiative effects in the analysis of strongly inverted masers, paving the way for a more accurate understanding of their behavior and significance in astrophysics. These insights could have far-reaching consequences for our knowledge of molecular astrophysics and the dynamics of maser phenomena in the universe.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a global sub-millimeter wavelength very
long baseline interferometry array, is now resolving the innermost regions
around the supermassive black holes Sgr A* and M87. Using black hole images
from both simple geometric models and relativistic magnetohydrodynamical
accretion flow simulations, we perform a variety of experiments to assess the
promise of the EHT for studying strong gravity and accretion physics during the
stages of its development. We find that (1) the addition of the LMT and ALMA
along with upgraded instrumentation in the "Complete" stage of the EHT allow
detection of the photon ring, a signature of Kerr strong gravity, for predicted
values of its total flux; (2) the inclusion of coherently averaged closure
phases in our analysis dramatically improves the precision of even the current
array, allowing (3) significantly tighter constraints on plausible accretion
models and (4) detections of structural variability at the levels predicted by
the models. While observations at 345 GHz circumvent problems due to
interstellar electron scattering in line-of-sight to the galactic center, short
baselines provided by CARMA and/or the LMT could be required in order to
constrain the overall shape of the accretion flow. Given the systematic
uncertainties in the underlying models, using the full complement of two
observing frequencies (230 and 345 GHz) and sources (Sgr A* and M87) may be
critical for achieving transformative science with the EHT experiment.

The Standard Galactic Reddening Map (SGRM) is a fundamental tool for astrophysical research, providing a relationship between Galactic extinction and interstellar reddening. However, recent studies have questioned the accuracy of this map, particularly in regions of low reddening where passive galaxies are prevalent. In this work, we investigate the impact of passive galaxies on the SGRM by re-evaluating the relationship between reddening and extinction using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS).  We find that the SGRM underestimates the extinction values for passive galaxies, leading to incorrect reddening estimates when applied to these galaxies. Our analysis suggests that the cause of this discrepancy is the failure of the SGRM to account for the different dust properties in passive galaxies compared to star-forming galaxies.  To correct the SGRM, we propose a new empirical relation based on the observed relationship between reddening and extinction for passive galaxies. This correction improves the accuracy of reddening estimates for passive galaxies, which are crucial for studying the properties of these galaxies, such as their star formation histories and metallicities. Our findings have significant implications for ongoing and future studies that rely on the SGRM for accurate reddening and extinction estimates, particularly in the context of large-scale galaxy surveys.

Context: Multiple stellar systems are unique laboratories for astrophysics.
Analysis of their orbital dynamics may reveal invaluable information about the
physical properties of the participating stars. Unfortunately, there are only a
few known and well described multiple systems, this is even more so for systems
located outside the Milky Way galaxy. A particularly interesting situation
occurs when the inner binary in a compact triple system is eclipsing. This is
because the stellar interaction, typically resulting in precession of orbital
planes, may be observable as a variation of depth of the eclipses on a long
timescale. Aims: We aim to present a novel method to determine compact triples
using publicly available photometric data from large surveys. Here we apply it
to eclipsing binaries (EBs) in Magellanic Clouds from OGLE III database.
Methods: We analyzed light curves (LCs) of 26121 LMC and 6138 SMC EBs with the
goal to identify those for which the orbital inclination varies in time.
Archival LCs of the selected systems, when complemented by our own observations
with Danish 1.54m telescope, were thoroughly analyzed using the PHOEBE program.
Time dependence of the EB's inclination was described using the theory of
orbital-plane precession. By observing the parameter-dependence of the
precession rate, we were able to constrain the third companion mass and its
orbital period around EB. Results: We identified 58 candidates of new compact
triples in Magellanic Clouds. This is the largest published sample of such
systems so far. Eight of them were analyzed thoroughly and physical parameters
of inner binary were determined together with an estimation of basic
characteristics of the third star. These data may provide important clues about
stellar formation mechanisms for objects with different metalicity than found
in our galactic neighborhood.

The time-resolved spectral analysis of GRB090227B, made possible by the
Fermi-GBM data, allows to identify in this source the missing link between the
genuine short and long GRBs. Within the Fireshell model [...] we predict
genuine short GRBs: bursts with the same inner engine of the long bursts but
endowed with a severely low value of the Baryon load, B<~5x10^{-5}. A first
energetically predominant emission occurs at the transparency of the e+e-
plasma, the Proper-GRB (P-GRB), followed by a softer emission, the extended
afterglow. The typical separation between the two emissions is expected to be
[...] 10^{-3}-10^{-2}s. We identify the P-GRB [...] in the first 96ms of
emission, where a thermal component with [...] kT=(517+/-28)keV and a flux
comparable with the non thermal part of the spectrum is observed. This non
thermal component as well as the subsequent emission, where there is no
evidence for a thermal spectrum, is identified with the extended afterglow. We
deduce a theoretical cosmological redshift z=1.61+/-0.14. We then derive the
total energy E^{tot}_{e+e-}=(2.83+/-0.15)x10^{53}erg, [...]
B=(4.13+/-0.05)x10^{-5}, the Lorentz factor at transparency
\Gamma_tr=(1.44+/-0.01)x10^4, and the intrinsic duration \Delta t'~0.35s. We
also determine the average density of the CircumBurst Medium (CBM),
<n_CBM>=(1.90+/-0.20)x10^{-5} #/cm^3. There is no evidence of beaming in the
system. In view of the energetics and of the Baryon load of the source, as well
as of the low interstellar medium and of the intrinsic time scale of the
signal, we identify the GRB progenitor as a binary neutron star. From the
recent progress in the theory of neutron stars, we obtain masses of the stars
m_1=m_2=1.34M_Sun and their corresponding radii R_1=R_2=12.24km and thickness
of their crusts ~0.47km, consistent with the above values of the Baryon load,
of the energetics and of the time duration of the event.

The Abella interactive theorem prover has proven to be an effective vehicle
for reasoning about relational specifications. However, the system has a
limitation that arises from the fact that it is based on a simply typed logic:
formalizations that are identical except in the respect that they apply to
different types have to be repeated at each type. We develop an approach that
overcomes this limitation while preserving the logical underpinnings of the
system. In this approach object constructors, formulas and other relevant
logical notions are allowed to be parameterized by types, with the
interpretation that they stand for the (infinite) collection of corresponding
constructs that are obtained by instantiating the type parameters. The proof
structures that we consider for formulas that are schematized in this fashion
are limited to ones whose type instances are valid proofs in the simply typed
logic. We develop schematic proof rules that ensure this property, a task that
is complicated by the fact that type information influences the notion of
unification that plays a key role in the logic. Our ideas, which have been
implemented in an updated version of the system, accommodate schematic
polymorphism both in the core logic of Abella and in the executable
specification logic that it embeds.

Machine learning algorithms, when applied to sensitive data, pose a distinct
threat to privacy. A growing body of prior work demonstrates that models
produced by these algorithms may leak specific private information in the
training data to an attacker, either through the models' structure or their
observable behavior. However, the underlying cause of this privacy risk is not
well understood beyond a handful of anecdotal accounts that suggest overfitting
and influence might play a role.
  This paper examines the effect that overfitting and influence have on the
ability of an attacker to learn information about the training data from
machine learning models, either through training set membership inference or
attribute inference attacks. Using both formal and empirical analyses, we
illustrate a clear relationship between these factors and the privacy risk that
arises in several popular machine learning algorithms. We find that overfitting
is sufficient to allow an attacker to perform membership inference and, when
the target attribute meets certain conditions about its influence, attribute
inference attacks. Interestingly, our formal analysis also shows that
overfitting is not necessary for these attacks and begins to shed light on what
other factors may be in play. Finally, we explore the connection between
membership inference and attribute inference, showing that there are deep
connections between the two that lead to effective new attacks.

We investigate the galaxy quenching process at intermediate redshift using a
sample of $\sim4400$ galaxies with $M_{\ast} > 10^{9}M_{\odot}$ between
redshift 0.5 and 1.0 in all five CANDELS fields. We divide this sample, using
the integrated specific star formation rate (sSFR), into four sub-groups:
star-forming galaxies (SFGs) above and below the ridge of the star-forming main
sequence (SFMS), transition galaxies and quiescent galaxies. We study their
$UVI$ ($U-V$ versus $V-I$) color gradients to infer their sSFR gradients out to
twice effective radii. We show that on average both star-forming and transition
galaxies at all masses are not fully quenched at any radii, whereas quiescent
galaxies are fully quenched at all radii. We find that at low masses ($M_{\ast}
= 10^{9}-10^{10}M_{\odot}$) SFGs both above and below the SFMS ridge generally
have flat sSFR profiles, whereas the transition galaxies at the same masses
generally have sSFRs that are more suppressed in their outskirts. In contrast,
at high masses ($M_{\ast} > 10^{10.5}M_{\odot}$), SFGs above and below the SFMS
ridge and transition galaxies generally have varying degrees of more
centrally-suppressed sSFRs relative to their outskirts. These findings indicate
that at $z\sim~0.5-1.0$ the main galaxy quenching mode depends on its already
formed stellar mass, exhibiting a transition from "the outside-in" at $M_{\ast}
\leq 10^{10}M_{\odot}$ to "the inside-out" at $M_{\ast} > 10^{10.5}M_{\odot}$.
In other words, our findings support that internal processes dominate the
quenching of massive galaxies, whereas external processes dominate the
quenching of low-mass galaxies.

We investigate the estimation of current density in space plasmas through a comparative analysis of multi-point versus single-point measurement techniques. Current density is a pivotal parameter in understanding plasma dynamics and electromagnetic interactions in various astrophysical and space environments.
