Baseline-dependent window functions (BDWFs) have been proposed as a potential solution for both data compression and field-of-interest (FoI) shaping in radio interferometry. In this study, we investigate the use of BDWFs for data compression and FoI shaping in radio interferometry. We first review the background of radio interferometry and the need for efficient data processing techniques. We then discuss the theory behind BDWFs and their potential advantages for data compression and FoI shaping. To evaluate the performance of BDWFs, we implement them in the Common Astronomy Software Application package (CASA) for data processing. We compare the compression ratio and the computational cost of BDWFs with those of other popular data compression techniques, such as the Wiener filter and the adaptive gridding algorithm. We also investigate the impact of BDWFs on the image quality and FoI shape. Our results show that BDWFs offer significant data compression ratios while maintaining high image quality. Compared to the Wiener filter and the adaptive gridding algorithm, BDWFs require less computational resources and provide more flexible control over the FoI shape. Our findings suggest that BDWFs are a promising approach for data compression and FoI shaping in radio interferometry. In conclusion, this study contributes to the development of more efficient data processing techniques for radio interferometry by investigating the use of BDWFs for data compression and FoI shaping. Our results demonstrate the potential of BDWFs as a powerful tool for reducing data volume and shaping the FoI in radio interferometry, making observations more feasible and efficient.

The study of carbon dioxide (CO2) abundance in comets provides critical insights into the composition of the early solar system and the processes that shaped planetary bodies. This research focuses on the CO2 abundance measured in three distinct comets C/2012 K1 (PanSTARRS), C/2012 K5 (LINEAR), and 290P/Jager, utilizing data acquired from the Spitzer Space Telescope. The primary objective was to ascertain the differences in CO2 content among these comets, thereby enhancing the understanding of their origin and evolutionary history. Methodologically, infrared spectroscopy was employed to analyze the spectral data obtained from observations conducted during their respective perihelion passages. A comprehensive analysis of CO2 signatures was undertaken, along with comparative assessments of other volatiles present in the cometary nuclei. Key findings reveal that C/2012 K1 exhibits a notably higher CO2 abundance than C/2012 K5, while 290P/Jager's CO2 levels are relatively moderate. These variations suggest differing formation environments and thermal histories, hinting at a complex evolutionary backdrop for these comets. In conclusion, the results underscore the diversity of carbon dioxide content in comets and imply a rich tapestry of processes influencing their development. This study not only contributes to the existing body of knowledge regarding cometary chemistry but also provides a foundation for future investigations looking to explore the relationship between cometary composition and solar system evolution.

This study examines the influence of geodetic precession on the evolution of high-energy pulsar pulse profiles, utilizing the striped-wind model. Geodetic precession is a relativistic effect that modifies the orientation of the pulsar's magnetic moment relative to its spin axis, affecting the radiation pattern observed from Earth. By employing this model, we aim to understand how this precession impacts the observed variability of pulsar pulses at high energies. Our methodology involves numerical simulations of pulsar emission processes under varying geodetic precession conditions, comparing these results with observational data. Key findings indicate that geodetic precession can induce significant changes in the pulse shape and profile variability over time, with periods ranging from days to years. These variations are particularly pronounced during specific phases of the precession cycle. The results suggest that geodetic precession plays a crucial role in the long-term evolution of pulsar high-energy pulse profiles, offering insights into the interplay between relativistic effects and pulsar emission mechanisms. The conclusions emphasize the necessity of incorporating geodetic precession in theoretical models to accurately predict pulsar high-energy radiation behavior.

The thesis is divided into two parts. In the first part the low-energy limit
of quantum gravity is analysed, whereas in the second we deal with the
high-energy domain. In the first part, by applying the effective field theory
point of view to the quantization of general relativity, detectable, though
tiny, quantum effects in the position of Newtonian Lagrangian points of the
Earth-Moon system are found. In order to make more realistic the quantum
corrected model proposed, the full three-body problem where the Earth and the
Moon interact with a generic massive body and the restricted four-body problem
involving the perturbative effects produced by the gravitational presence of
the Sun in the Earth-Moon system are also studied. After that, a new quantum
theory having general relativity as its classical counterpart is analysed. By
exploiting this framework, an innovative interesting prediction involving the
position of Lagrangian points within the context of general relativity is
described. Furthermore, the new pattern provides quantum corrections to the
relativistic coordinates of Earth-Moon libration points of the order of few
millimetres. The second part of the thesis deals with the Riemannian curvature
characterizing the boosted form assumed by the Schwarzschild-de Sitter metric.
The analysis of the Kretschmann invariant and the geodesic equation shows that
the spacetime possesses a "scalar curvature singularity" within a 3-sphere and
that it is possible to define what we here call "boosted horizon", a sort of
elastic wall where all particles are surprisingly pushed away, suggesting that
such "boosted geometries" are ruled by a sort of "antigravity effect".
Eventually, the equivalence with the coordinate shift method is invoked in
order to demonstrate that all $\delta^2$ terms appearing in the Riemann
curvature tensor give vanishing contribution in distributional sense.

In this study, we investigate the impact of reheating constraints on inflationary models, focusing on the interplay between inflationary predictions and post-inflationary dynamics. By analyzing the reheating phase characterized by the reheating temperature, \( T_{\text{reh}} \), and the equation-of-state parameter, \( w_{\text{reh}} \), we aim to bridge the gap between theoretical predictions and observational data. Our primary goal is to delineate parameter spaces for various inflation models, such as chaotic, hilltop, and plateau-like potentials, which are consistent with current cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations and reheating conditions. We employ analytical and numerical techniques to derive bounds on \( T_{\text{reh}} \) and \( w_{\text{reh}} \) arising from constraints on the scalar spectral index, \( n_s \), and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, \( r \). By adopting a model-independent approach, we explore a wide range of potential reheating scenarios. Our results reveal that feasible reheating processes lead to distinct ranges for \( n_s \) and \( r \), further constrained by the duration and nature of reheating. We find that lower reheating temperatures correlate with tighter constraints on inflation models, which suggests preferred histories of the early universe. Moreover, the incorporation of reheating constraints narrows the parameter space of viable inflationary models, emphasizing the intricate dependence of inflationary dynamics on post-inflationary evolution. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating reheating conditions in the analysis of inflationary theories, and they highlight the potential of future observations to elucidate the rich tapestry of the universe's expansion history.

It is generally thought that an ultracompact X-ray binary is composed with a
neutron star and a helium white dwarf donor star. As one of the most compact
binaries, 4U 1820-303 in globular cluster NGC 6624 was predicted an
orbital-period derivative at a rate of $\dot{P}/P\sim1.1\times10^{-7}$ ${\rm
yr^{-1}}$ if the mass transfer is fully driven by gravitational radiation.
However, the recent analysis of the 16 ${\rm yr}$ data from \textit{Rossi X-ray
Timing Explorer} and other historical records yielded a negative orbital-period
derivative in the past $35$ yr. In this work, we propose an evolutionary
circumbinary (CB) disk model to account for this anomalous orbital-period
derivative. 4U 1820-30 was known to undergo superbust events caused by runaway
thermal nuclear burning on the neutron star. We assume that for a small
fraction of the superbursts, part of the ejected material may form a CB disk
around the binary. If the recurrence time of such superbursts is $\sim10,000$
yr and $\sim10$% of the ejected mass feeds a CB disk, the abrupt
angular-momentum loss causes a temporary orbital shrink, and the donor's radius
and its Roche-lobe radius do not keep in step. Driven by mass transfer and
angular-momentum loss, the binary would adjust its orbital parameters to
recover a new stable stage. Based on the theoretical analysis and numerical
simulation, we find that the required feed mass at the CB disk is approximately
$\sim 10^{-8}$ ${\rm M_{\odot}}$.

We report the results of high-precision Zeeman polarimetric observations of three T Tauri stars, revealing the presence of large-scale magnetic fields in their circumstellar disks. By analyzing the Stokes parameters of the Hα emission line, we were able to obtain magnetic field strengths, morphologies, and orientations. Our findings suggest that the magnetic fields extend from the stellar surface into the inner disk regions, with strengths reaching up to 3 kG and a dipole geometry. These results are significant as they provide important insights into the dynamical role of magnetic fields in circumstellar disks. Magnetic fields have long been suspected to play a key role in shaping the structure and evolution of protoplanetary disks. Our observations support this hypothesis, demonstrating that magnetic forces can confine plasma and regulate the transport of angular momentum and mass within the disk. Additionally, the detected magnetic fields may also influence the process of planet formation, potentially affecting the alignment of planetary orbits and the distribution of planetesimal sizes. Previous studies have attempted to infer the presence of magnetic fields in circumstellar disks through various methods, including microwave and infrared polarimetry and magnetic flux emergence events. However, the high level of contamination and complexity of these techniques limit their applicability and accuracy. In contrast, Zeeman polarimetry offers a more direct and robust method for measuring magnetic fields, as it relies on the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of a magnetic field. Our observations represent a major step forward in the study of magnetic fields in circumstellar disks, opening new avenues for understanding the physical processes shaping these structures and the planetary systems that form within them. The key methodology in our study involved the use of high-resolution spectroscopy and advanced data reduction techniques to extract the Stokes parameters of the Hα emission line. We also employed a non-LTE radiative transfer model to account for the effects of line saturation and Doppler broadening. The analysis of the Stokes parameters allowed us to derive the magnetic field strengths, morphologies, and orientations in the disks, providing valuable insights into the dynamical role of magnetic fields in protoplanetary disks.

This research explores the application of Floquet engineering techniques to manipulate the properties of Haldane Chern insulators and investigate chiral bosonic phase transitions. Building upon previous studies that established the theoretical foundation of Haldane Chern insulators and their chiral bosonic phase transitions, this work aims to leverage Floquet engineering to control these phases dynamically. The methodology involves periodically driving a system with a time-periodic perturbation, enabling the manipulation of topological phases through the introduction of effective magnetic fields. Key findings include the observation of tunable chiral edge states and the demonstration of how external parameters can be used to induce transitions between distinct chiral bosonic phases. The study highlights the potential for utilizing these controllable systems in future quantum technologies, such as topological quantum computing and spintronics. The conclusions emphasize the importance of understanding and engineering such phases for advancing the field of quantum materials and their applications.

In this study, we investigate the attraction properties of general urn processes, with particular emphasis on their applicability to a class of interacting reinforced particle systems. Urn processes, a fundamental model in probability theory, exhibit a wide range of behaviors due to reinforcement mechanisms, where the probability of drawing a particular color increases with the frequency of its past occurrences. Our work addresses the challenge of characterizing the long-term dynamics of such processes, especially in high-dimensional and interacting configurations.  We employ a combination of analytical techniques and stochastic approximations to explore the attraction basins and stability regions of these urn processes. Our methodology integrates elements from reinforcement learning, stochastic dynamics, and interacting particle systems to provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing complex behaviors induced by particle interactions.  Key findings indicate that under specific conditions, the long-term behavior of these systems stabilizes towards a predictable set of configurations. We further demonstrate that the interaction between particles significantly alters the reinforcement dynamics, leading to modified attraction profiles compared to non-interacting models. These results substantiate the robustness of our approach in uncovering the underlying structures governing multi-agent reinforced dynamics.  The implications of our research extend to various domains, including ecological modeling, social network analysis, and computational neuroscience, where understanding the emergence of collective behavior from individual interactions is crucial. Future work will focus on extending our theoretical findings to empirical validations within these fields, offering deeper insights into the mechanisms driving complex system behaviors.

Sparse coding (Sc) has been studied very well as a powerful data
representation method. It attempts to represent the feature vector of a data
sample by reconstructing it as the sparse linear combination of some basic
elements, and a $L_2$ norm distance function is usually used as the loss
function for the reconstruction error. In this paper, we investigate using Sc
as the representation method within multi-instance learning framework, where a
sample is given as a bag of instances, and further represented as a histogram
of the quantized instances. We argue that for the data type of histogram, using
$L_2$ norm distance is not suitable, and propose to use the earth mover's
distance (EMD) instead of $L_2$ norm distance as a measure of the
reconstruction error. By minimizing the EMD between the histogram of a sample
and the its reconstruction from some basic histograms, a novel sparse coding
method is developed, which is refereed as SC-EMD. We evaluate its performances
as a histogram representation method in tow multi-instance learning problems
--- abnormal image detection in wireless capsule endoscopy videos, and protein
binding site retrieval. The encouraging results demonstrate the advantages of
the new method over the traditional method using $L_2$ norm distance.

We theoretically investigate the behavior of dark solitons in a
one-dimensional spin-orbit coupled atomic Fermi gas in harmonic traps, by
solving self-consistently the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. The dark soliton
- to be created by phase-imprinting in future experiments - is characterized by
a real order parameter, which changes sign at a point node and hosts localized
Andreev bound states near the node. By considering both cases of a single
soliton and of multiple solitons, we find that the energy of these bound states
decreases to zero, when the system is tuned to enter the topological superfluid
phase by increasing an external Zeeman field. As a result, two Majorana
fermions emerge in the vicinity of each soliton, in addition to the well-known
Majorana fermions at the trap edges associated with the nontrivial topology of
the superfluid. We propose that the soliton-induced Majorana fermions can be
directly observed by using spatially-resolved radio-frequency spectroscopy or
indirectly probed by measuring the density profile at the point node. For the
latter, the deep minimum in the density profile will disappear due to the
occupation of the soliton-induced zero-energy Majorana fermion modes. Our
prediction could be tested in a resonantly-interacting spin-orbit coupled
$^{40}$K Fermi gas confined in a two-dimensional optical lattice.

We examine a large collection of low resolution near-infrared spectra of
Kuiper belt objects and centaurs in an attempt to understand the presence of
water ice in the Kuiper belt. We find that water ice on the surface of these
objects occurs in three separate manners: (1) Haumea family members uniquely
show surfaces of nearly pure water ice, presumably a consequence of the
fragmentation of the icy mantle of a larger differentiated proto-Haumea; (2)
large objects with absolute magnitudes of $H<3$ (and a limited number to H=4.5)
have surface coverings of water ice - perhaps mixed with ammonia - that appears
to be related to possibly ancient cryovolcanism on these large objects; and (3)
smaller KBOs and centaurs which are neither Haumea family members nor
cold-classical KBOs appear to divide into two families (which we refer to as
"neutral" and "red"), each of which is a mixture of a common nearly-neutral
component and either a slightly red or very red component that also includes
water ice. A model suggesting that the difference between neutral and red
objects is due to formation in an early compact solar system either inside or
outside, respectively, of the ~20 AU methanol evaporation line is supported by
the observation that methanol is only detected on the reddest objects, which
are those which would be expected to have the most of the methanol containing
mixture.

The abstract focuses on the concept of "The Trouble with the Local Bubble," exploring its implications within urban economics and real estate markets. Historically, local bubbles have been characterized by rapid price increases followed by sharp declines, often leading to significant economic disruption. This research examines the multifaceted challenges posed by local bubbles, including their impact on housing affordability, financial stability, and long-term economic growth. Through a comparative analysis of various case studies, the study identifies key drivers of local bubble formation, such as speculative investment, regulatory gaps, and market misperceptions.  The methodology employed includes econometric analyses, historical data reviews, and qualitative assessments of policy responses across different regions. By integrating these diverse perspectives, the research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how local bubbles affect local economies. Key findings highlight the critical role of robust regulatory frameworks and effective communication between stakeholders in mitigating the adverse effects of local bubbles. The conclusion underscores the need for proactive measures to prevent future local bubbles, emphasizing the importance of sustained economic policies that balance short-term market dynamics with long-term sustainability.

The study investigates the temperature- and field-induced melting of charge order in (La,Pr,Ca)MnO₃ using Raman scattering spectroscopy. The research aims to elucidate the structural transitions that occur under varying conditions, providing insights into the complex interplay between magnetic and electronic phases. Employing high-resolution Raman spectroscopy, we analyzed the material's vibrational modes as a function of temperature and applied magnetic fields. Key findings include the identification of characteristic Raman peaks indicative of phase transitions and the observation of a shift in these peaks corresponding to changes in temperature and magnetic field strength. The results reveal distinct melting behaviors at different compositions and demonstrate the influence of Pr doping on the phase transition temperatures. This work contributes to our understanding of the magnetic and structural properties of (La,Pr,Ca)MnO₃, highlighting the potential of Raman spectroscopy as a powerful tool for studying charge order melting processes.

In this study, we investigate the feasibility of probing triple-Higgs production via the $4b2\gamma$ decay channel at a prospective 100 TeV hadron collider. The discovery of the Higgs boson and its role in the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the electroweak force underscores the importance of studying Higgs boson self-interactions. Triple-Higgs production processes provide a window into the Higgs potential, allowing us to probe beyond the Standard Model (SM) physics. We employ a comprehensive analysis, including the generation of signal and background events using Monte Carlo simulations, followed by an event selection criterion optimized for the $4b2\gamma$ final state. We implement advanced machine learning techniques to enhance the signal-to-background ratio, focusing on characteristics specific to the decay channel in question. Our findings suggest that a 100 TeV collider, with an integrated luminosity of 30 ab$^{-1}$, will be sensitive to triple-Higgs production with remarkable precision. We estimate an improvement in sensitivity of three orders of magnitude over current collider capabilities. This enhanced sensitivity significantly constrains the Higgs self-coupling, providing vital clues regarding new physics beyond the SM. Additionally, the study evaluates systematic uncertainties and potential experimental limitations, establishing the robustness of the results. These efforts contribute to a deeper understanding of electroweak symmetry breaking and the dynamics of the scalar sector, positioning future collider experiments at the forefront of particle physics research. Our methodology and results lay the groundwork for future theoretical and experimental explorations in Higgs physics.

Be stars have generally been characterized by the emission lines in their
spectra, and especially the time variability of those spectroscopic features.
They are known to also exhibit photometric variability at multiple timescales,
but have not been broadly compared and analyzed by that behavior. We have taken
advantage of the advent of wide-field, long-baseline, and high-cadence
photometric surveys that search for transiting exoplanets to perform a
comprehensive analysis of brightness variations among a large number of known
Be stars. The photometric data comes from the KELT transit survey, with a
typical cadence of 30 minutes, baseline of up to ten years, photometric
precision of about 1%, and coverage of about 60% of the sky. We analyze KELT
light curves of 610 known Be stars in both the Northern and Southern
hemispheres in an effort to study their variability. Consistent with other
studies of Be star variability, we find most of the stars to be photometrically
variable. We derive lower limits on the fraction of stars in our sample that
exhibit features consistent with non-radial pulsations (25%), outbursts (36%),
and long term trends in the circumstellar disk (37%), and show how these are
correlated with spectral sub-type. Other types of variability, such as those
owing to binarity, are also explored. Simultaneous spectroscopy for some of
these systems from the Be Star Spectral Database (BeSS) allow us to better
understand the physical causes for the observed variability, especially in
cases of outbursts and changes in the disk.

We conducted a comprehensive investigation of compact planetary nebulae within the Galactic disk to elucidate the characteristics and evolutionary status of their central stars. This study addresses the challenges inherent in accurately categorizing these central stars due to their often faint emission amidst nebular environments. We employed high-resolution spectral analysis, supplemented by photometric data, to discern the spectral types and derive key stellar parameters such as effective temperature, luminosity, and gravity. Our findings indicate a diverse range of stellar types, reflecting a broad spectrum of evolutionary phases from post-asymptotic giant branch stars to white dwarf transitions. Through comparative analysis, we identified correlations between nebular morphology and central star properties, suggesting that the central stars have a significant influence on shaping the nebulosity. Additionally, our results demonstrate a consistent pattern in which central stars of higher effective temperatures correspond to more symmetrical and less fragmented nebulae. This study contributes to the existing body of knowledge by enhancing our understanding of the role central stars play in the evolutionary pathways of planetary nebulae. Our methodology involved a blend of observational and theoretical approaches, combining observational data with stellar atmosphere and evolutionary models to validate our findings. This research underscores the importance of continued high-sensitivity and high-resolution observations in disentangling the complexities of central star characteristics and their impacts on the nebular envelope. The insights garnered will aid in refining models pertaining to stellar evolution and the lifecycle of planetary nebulae in the Galactic disk.

Coherence and phase synchronization between time series corresponding to
different spatial locations are usually interpreted as indicators of the
connectivity between locations. In neurophysiology, time series of electric
neuronal activity are essential for studying brain interconnectivity. Such
signals can either be invasively measured from depth electrodes, or computed
from very high time resolution, non-invasive, extracranial recordings of scalp
electric potential differences (EEG: electroencephalogram) and magnetic fields
(MEG: magnetoencephalogram) by means of a tomography such as sLORETA
(standardized low resolution brain electromagnetic tomography). There are two
problems in this case. First, in the usual situation of unknown cortical
geometry, the estimated signal at each brain location is a vector with three
components (i.e. a current density vector), which means that coherence and
phase synchronization must be generalized to pairs of multivariate time series.
Second, the inherent low spatial resolution of the EEG/MEG tomography
introduces artificially high zero-lag coherence and phase synchronization. In
this report, solutions to both problems are presented. Two additional
generalizations are briefly mentioned: (1) conditional coherence and phase
synchronization; and (2) non-stationary time-frequency analysis. Finally, a
non-parametric randomization method for connectivity significance testing is
outlined. The new connectivity measures proposed here can be applied to pairs
of univariate EEG/MEG signals, as is traditional in the published literature.
However, these calculations cannot be interpreted as connectivity, since it is
in general incorrect to associate an extracranial electrode or sensor to the
underlying cortex.

We investigate the presence of substellar companions around seven evolved intermediate-mass stars, aiming to enhance our understanding of stellar evolution and the mechanisms governing companion formation. Our study employs a combination of high-resolution spectroscopy and precise astrometric measurements, allowing us to detect and characterize potential planetary systems in proximity to these aging stars. Utilizing radial velocity techniques, we uncover evidence of short-period, low-mass companions, which offer insights into the migration processes and retention of substellar objects in the vicinity of more massive stars.   Our results indicate that several of the targeted stars possess companions with masses ranging from one to several Jupiter masses, suggesting a non-negligible occurrence rate of substellar bodies around evolved stellar environments. We highlight the evolutionary implications of these findings, particularly in terms of the potential host star's mass loss patterns and its impact on companion stability. Additionally, we explore the correlation between the mass and orbital characteristics of companions with their host stars' evolutionary stages, revealing interesting trends that may inform broader theories of stellar formation and interaction.  In summary, our work not only identifies and characterizes substellar companions to seven evolved intermediate-mass stars but also provides critical data that enhance ongoing discussions about the dynamical evolution of planetary systems as stellar characteristics shift over time. These findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge regarding companion formation and the long-term behavior of planetary systems around evolved stars.

This study introduces grim, a novel numerical scheme designed for solving relativistic fluid theories, aiming to balance computational efficiency with physical accuracy. The scheme is characterized by its flexibility in handling various fluid models and its conservative nature, ensuring energy and momentum conservation at each step of the simulation. Problematically, traditional methods often struggle with maintaining these properties while also accommodating complex fluid dynamics and high velocities typical in relativistic regimes. Our approach overcomes these challenges through a carefully crafted discretization strategy that minimizes numerical dissipation and dispersion errors. Key ideas include the use of a high-order Godunov method combined with a robust limiter to control oscillations and artificial viscosity tailored to the relativistic regime. Methodologically, grim employs a combination of finite volume and discontinuous Galerkin techniques, allowing for adaptive mesh refinement to focus computational resources where they are most needed. Results demonstrate significant improvements in both accuracy and stability compared to existing schemes, particularly in scenarios involving shock waves and relativistic jets. The efficacy of grim is validated through benchmark tests against known analytical solutions and direct comparison with other established codes.

In this study, we investigate generalized trapezoidal words, which are a generalization of classical trapezoidal words. We aim to characterize these words through their structure and identify properties that distinguish them from other types of words. Our research employs combinatorial methods to analyze sequences of symbols, focusing on patterns and symmetries within these sequences. We attempt to solve problems such as identifying minimal generating sets for generalized trapezoidal words and determining conditions under which two words can be transformed into each other by simple operations. Key methodologies include constructing and manipulating symbolic representations of words, applying automata theory, and employing computational algorithms to explore large sequences. The results obtained provide insights into the hierarchical structure of generalized trapezoidal words and offer new perspectives on their generation and classification.

Quantum calculations offer a powerful tool for understanding the behavior of biological ion channels. The voltage-sensing domain of the Kv1.2 channel plays a critical role in gating currents and ion permeation.   This research aims to employ quantum calculations to investigate the mechanism of proton transfer in the voltage-sensing domain of the Kv1.2 channel and its contribution to gating currents.   Quantum calculations were performed using density functional theory to explore the energetics and dynamics of proton transfer within the Kv1.2 channel voltage-sensing domain. Molecular dynamics simulations were also conducted to study the conformational changes associated with proton transfer.   Our results demonstrate that proton transfer within the Kv1.2 channel voltage-sensing domain is energetically favorable and contributes significantly to gating currents. The simulations reveal the key residues involved in proton transfer and shed light on the structural rearrangements accompanying this process.   Quantum calculations provide valuable insights into the role of proton transfer in gating currents of the Kv1.2 channel voltage-sensing domain. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying ion channel function is crucial for developing novel therapeutic strategies targeting channelopathies and neurological disorders.

We have investigated the molecular environment of the semicircular composite
supernova remnant (SNR) 3C396 and performed a Chandra spatially resolved
thermal X-ray spectroscopic study of this young SNR. With our CO millimeter
observations, we find that the molecular clouds (MCs) at V(LSR)~84km/s can
better explain the multiwavelength properties of the remnant than the
V(LSR)=67-72km/s MCs that are suggested by Lee et al. (2009). At around 84km/s,
the western boundary of the SNR is perfectly confined by the western molecular
wall. The CO emission fades out from west to east, indicating that the eastern
region is of low gas density. In particular, an intruding finger/pillar-like
MC, which may be shocked at the tip, can well explain the X-ray and radio
enhancement in the southwest and some infrared filaments there. The SNR-MC
interaction is also favored by the relatively elevated 12CO J=2-1/J=1-0 line
ratios in the southwestern "pillar tip" and the molecular patch on the
northwestern boundary. The redshifted 12CO (J=1-0 and J=2-1) wings (86-90km/s)
of an eastern 81km/s molecular patch may be the kinematic evidence for shock-MC
interaction. We suggest that the 69km/s MCs are in the foreground based on HI
self-absorption while the 84km/s MCs at a distance of 6.2 kpc (the tangent
point) are in physical contact with SNR 3C396. The X-ray spectral analysis
suggests an SNR age of ~3kyr. The metal enrichment of the X-ray emitting gas in
the north and south implies a 13-15Msun B1-B2 progenitor star.

We investigate the dynamical mass generation resulted from interaction terms
with four chiral superfields. The kind of interactions maybe considered a
supersymmetric generalization of the four-fermion interactions of the classic
Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model. A four-superfield interaction that contains a
four-fermion interaction as one of its component terms has been the standard
supersymmetrization of the NJL model for decades. Recently, we introduced a
holomorphic variant with a dimension five interaction term instead. The latter
is a main target of the present analysis. With the introduction of a new
perspective on the superfield gap equation, we derive it for each one of the
four-superfield interactions, using the supergraph technique. Through analyzing
solutions to the gap equations, we illustrate the dynamical generation of
superfield Dirac mass, including a supersymmetry breaking part. A dynamical
symmetry breaking generally goes along with the dynamical mass generation, for
which a bi-superfield condensate is responsible. The explicit illustration of
dynamical symmetry breaking from the holomorphic dimension five interaction is
reported for the first time. It has rich and novel features, which would be
easily missed without the superfield approach developed here. We also discuss
the nature of the bi-superfield condensate and its role of the effective Higgs
superfield picture for both cases, illustrating their difference. Note that
such a holomorphic quark superfield interaction term can successful account for
the electroweak symmetry breaking with Higgs superfields as composites.

In this work, we present the release note for VBFNLO version 2.7.0, a significant update to our numerical package dedicated to the simulation of Vector Boson Fusion processes in the context of particle collisions. Our primary objective was to enhance the computational efficiency and accuracy of the simulations while expanding the features available in the software. We incorporated new algorithms that optimize the evaluation of matrix elements, resulting in a substantial reduction in computational time. Moreover, we addressed several user-reported issues from the previous version, thereby improving the overall stability of the package.  Key features of VBFNLO 2.7.0 include the introduction of new processes with higher-order corrections, the implementation of a refined interface for parameter settings, and enhanced compatibility with external tools such as Pythia and HERWIG for parton shower simulations. We employed advanced techniques in Monte Carlo integration to ensure precise cross-section calculations and to facilitate the generation of realistic event samples.  We also conducted extensive benchmarking against existing theoretical predictions and experimental data, affirming the reliability of our results. By systematically documenting these enhancements and providing comprehensive user guidance, we aim to facilitate a broader utilization of VBFNLO in the research community. Ultimately, this update contributes to advancing the field of high-energy physics by providing researchers with more robust tools for studying vector boson interactions in collider experiments.

This study aims to verify the accuracy of real-time World Space Weather Advisory and Forecasting (WSA-ENLIL+Cone) simulations of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) arrival times at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) from 2010 to 2016. The WSA-ENLIL+Cone model is a widely used space weather forecasting tool that provides real-time predictions of CME arrival times and their associated effects on the Earth's magnetic field. However, the accuracy of these predictions is crucial for ensuring the reliability of space weather forecasts and warnings.  To verify the accuracy of the WSA-ENLIL+Cone model, this study analyzed the predicted CME arrival times from 2010 to 2016 and compared them with the actual arrival times recorded at the CCMC. The study utilized a dataset of 120 CME events, which were selected based on their impact on the Earth's magnetic field. The predicted and actual arrival times were compared using a statistical analysis, and the results were evaluated using a correlation coefficient and a Brier score.  The study found that the predicted CME arrival times from the WSA-ENLIL+Cone model were generally accurate, with a correlation coefficient of 0.85 and a Brier score of 0.65. However, the results also revealed some discrepancies between the predicted and actual arrival times, which were attributed to the limitations of the model and the complexity of the space weather phenomena involved. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the accuracy of the WSA-ENLIL+Cone model and highlight the need for continued improvements to the model to ensure its reliability in predicting CME arrival times and their associated effects on the Earth's magnetic field.

We analyze time-dependent transport through a quantum dot with
electron-electron interaction that is statically tunable to both repulsive and
attractive regimes, or even dynamically driven. Motivated by the recent
experimental realization [Hamo et. al, Nature 535, 395 (2016)] of such a system
in a static double quantum dot we compute the geometric pumping of charge in
the limit of weak tunneling, high temperature and slow driving. We analyze the
pumping responses for all pairs of driving parameters (gate voltage, bias
voltage, tunnel coupling, electron-electron interaction). We show that the
responses are analytically related when these different driving protocols are
governed by the same pumping mechanism, which is characterized by effective
driving parameters that differ from the experimental ones. For static
attractive interaction we find a characteristic pumping resonance despite the
'attractive Coulomb blockade' that hinders stationary transport. Moreover, we
identify a pumping mechanism that is unique to driving of the interaction.
Finally, although a single-dot model with orbital pseudo-spin describes most of
the physics of the mentioned experimental setup, it is crucial to account for
the additional (real-) spin degeneracies of the double dot and the associated
electron-hole symmetry breaking. This is necessary because the pumping response
is more sensitive than DC transport measurements and detects this difference
through pronounced qualitative effects.

We present a state-of-the-art calculation of the next-to-leading-order
electroweak corrections to ZZ production, including the leptonic decays of the
Z bosons into $\mu^+\mu^-\mathrm{e}^+\mathrm{e}^-$ or $\mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$
final states. We use complete leading-order and next-to-leading-order matrix
elements for four-lepton production, including contributions of virtual photons
and all off-shell effects of Z bosons, where the finite Z-boson width is taken
into account using the complex-mass scheme. The matrix elements are implemented
into Monte Carlo programs allowing for the evaluation of arbitrary differential
distributions. We present integrated and differential cross sections for the
LHC at 13 TeV both for an inclusive setup where only lepton identification cuts
are applied, and for a setup motivated by Higgs-boson analyses in the
four-lepton decay channel. The electroweak corrections are divided into
photonic and purely weak contributions. The former show the well-known
pronounced tails near kinematical thresholds and resonances; the latter are
generically at the level of $\sim-5\%$ and reach several $-10\%$ in the
high-energy tails of distributions. Comparing the results for
$\mu^+\mu^-\mathrm{e}^+\mathrm{e}^-$ and $\mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$ final states,
we find significant differences mainly in distributions that are sensitive to
the $\mu^+\mu^-$ pairing in the $\mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$ final state. Differences
between $\mu^+\mu^-\mathrm{e}^+\mathrm{e}^-$ and $\mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$
channels due to interferences of equal-flavour leptons in the final state can
reach up to $10\%$ in off-shell-sensitive regions. Contributions induced by
incoming photons, i.e. photon-photon and quark-photon channels, are included,
but turn out to be phenomenologically unimportant.

Type-II Weyl semimetals are a novel gapless topological phase of matter
discovered recently in 2015. Similar to normal (type-I) Weyl semimetals,
type-II Weyl semimetals consist of isolated band touching points. However,
unlike type-I Weyl semimetals which have a linear energy dispersion around the
band touching points forming a three dimensional (3D) Dirac cone, type-II Weyl
semimetals have a tilted cone-like structure around the band touching points.
This leads to various novel physical properties that are different from type-I
Weyl semimetals. In order to study further the properties of type-II Weyl
semimetals and perhaps realize them for future applications, generating
controllable type-II Weyl semimetals is desirable. In this paper, we propose a
way to generate a type-II Weyl semimetal via a generalized Harper model
interacting with a harmonic driving field. When the field is treated
classically, we find that only type-I Weyl points emerge. However, by treating
the field quantum mechanically, some of these type-I Weyl points may turn into
type-II Weyl points. Moreover, by tuning the coupling strength, it is possible
to control the tilt of the Weyl points and the energy difference between two
Weyl points, which makes it possible to generate a pair of mixed Weyl points of
type-I and type-II. We also discuss how to physically distinguish these two
types of Weyl points in the framework of our model via the Landau level
structures in the presence of an artificial magnetic field. The results are of
general interest to quantum optics as well as ongoing studies of Floquet
topological phases.

This study investigates the evolution of language usage in open source software (OSS) over time, focusing on changes in programming languages, documentation styles, and community communication methods. The objective was to analyze how these elements have shifted to reflect broader technological trends and cultural shifts within the OSS community. Methodologically, the study employed a longitudinal analysis of code repositories from major OSS platforms, alongside documentation and community forum data, spanning a decade. Key findings indicate a gradual shift towards more modern programming languages like JavaScript and Python, alongside a trend toward more verbose and detailed documentation. Community communication has also evolved, with increased use of collaborative platforms such as GitHub Discussions and Slack channels. These changes suggest that the OSS ecosystem adapts to technological advancements and community needs, influencing the future direction of software development practices.

This study investigates the security thresholds of multicarrier continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) systems. We aim to identify the conditions under which these systems can securely distribute keys against eavesdropping attacks. Through rigorous analysis and simulations, we explore the impact of various parameters such as signal-to-noise ratio, carrier frequencies, and number of carriers on the system's security. Our findings indicate that increasing the number of carriers enhances the security threshold significantly, provided that noise levels are adequately managed. Additionally, we propose a method to optimize the distribution of carrier frequencies to further enhance security. The methodology involves theoretical derivations combined with numerical simulations, providing a comprehensive understanding of the system’s robustness and practical feasibility. Our results contribute to the development of more secure and efficient multicarrier CV-QKD systems.

We address the problem where the X-ray emission lines are formed and
investigate orbital dynamics using Chandra HETG observations, photoionizing
calculations and numerical wind-particle simulations.The observed Si XIV (6.185
A) and S XVI (4.733 A) line profiles at four orbital phases were fitted with P
Cygni-type profiles consisting of an emission and a blue-shifted absorption
component. In the models, the emission originates in the photoionized wind of
the WR companion illuminated by a hybrid source: the X-ray radiation of the
compact star and the photospheric EUV-radiation from the WR star. The emission
component exhibits maximum blue-shift at phase 0.5 (when the compact star is in
front), while the velocity of the absorption component is constant (around -900
km/s). The simulated FeXXVI Ly alpha line (1.78 A) from the wind is weak
compared to the observed one. We suggest that it originates in the vicinity of
the compact star, with a maximum blue shift at phase 0.25 (compact star
approaching). By combining the mass function derived with that from the
infrared HeI absorption (arising from the WR companion), we constrain the
masses and inclination of the system. Both a neutron star at large inclination
(over 60 degrees) and a black hole at small inclination are possible solutions.

The ability of an Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) to find a global optimal
solution depends on its capacity to find a good rate between exploitation of
found so far elements and exploration of the search space. Inspired by natural
phenomena, researchers have developed many successful evolutionary algorithms
which, at original versions, define operators that mimic the way nature solves
complex problems, with no actual consideration of the exploration/exploitation
balance. In this paper, a novel nature-inspired algorithm called the States of
Matter Search (SMS) is introduced. The SMS algorithm is based on the simulation
of the states of matter phenomenon. In SMS, individuals emulate molecules which
interact to each other by using evolutionary operations which are based on the
physical principles of the thermal-energy motion mechanism. The algorithm is
devised by considering each state of matter at one different
exploration/exploitation ratio. The evolutionary process is divided into three
phases which emulate the three states of matter: gas, liquid and solid. In each
state, molecules (individuals) exhibit different movement capacities. Beginning
from the gas state (pure exploration), the algorithm modifies the intensities
of exploration and exploitation until the solid state (pure exploitation) is
reached. As a result, the approach can substantially improve the balance
between exploration/exploitation, yet preserving the good search capabilities
of an evolutionary approach.

In our study, we aimed to investigate the conditions under which one of the most massive stars in the Milky Way could have formed in isolation. Through detailed stellar evolution modeling and observational data analysis, we explored the potential environments that might allow such a star to form without significant interaction with other stars. Our results indicate that isolated formation is possible but requires specific initial conditions, including a low-density environment and minimal gas cloud fragmentation during the collapse phase. We identified several key parameters that contribute to this scenario, such as the initial mass function and the distribution of pre-collapse turbulence. The methodology involved sophisticated numerical simulations coupled with high-resolution observations of young stellar clusters and the use of hydrodynamical models to simulate star formation processes. These findings challenge the prevailing models that suggest massive stars typically form in dense clusters and highlight the importance of considering isolated formation pathways for understanding the diversity of stellar populations in galaxies.

We investigate the control of Rayleigh-like waves within thick plate Willis metamaterials, addressing the challenges associated with wave manipulation in anisotropic media. Our research aims to enhance the understanding and application of these metamaterials in various engineering and acoustic fields. We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that combines advanced analytical methods and numerical simulations to explore the influence of material properties and geometric configurations on wave propagation. Through our analysis, we derive explicit expressions for the dispersion relationships and investigate the role of coupling effects inherent to Willis materials. Our results demonstrate that by tuning the material parameters, such as shear and bulk moduli, we can effectively tailor wave characteristics, including phase velocities and attenuation rates. We observe distinct phenomena, such as waveguiding and energy localization, which are facilitated by the unique properties of the Willis metamaterials. Our findings reveal that specific configurations can support enhanced control over Rayleigh-like waves, leading to potential applications in noise reduction, vibration control, and structural health monitoring. Additionally, we corroborate our theoretical predictions with experimental data, validating the efficacy of our methodology. Through this work, we contribute to the burgeoning field of metamaterials, providing critical insights into the utilization of Willis-type materials for advanced wave manipulation and paving the way for future innovations in acoustic engineering.

Cyclic patterns of neuronal activity are ubiquitous in animal nervous
systems, and partially responsible for generating and controlling rhythmic
movements such as locomotion, respiration, swallowing and so on. Clarifying the
role of the network connectivities for generating cyclic patterns is
fundamental for understanding the generation of rhythmic movements. In this
paper, the storage of binary cycles in neural networks is investigated. We call
a cycle $\Sigma$ admissible if a connectivity matrix satisfying the cycle's
transition conditions exists, and construct it using the pseudoinverse learning
rule. Our main focus is on the structural features of admissible cycles and
corresponding network topology. We show that $\Sigma$ is admissible if and only
if its discrete Fourier transform contains exactly $r={rank}(\Sigma)$ nonzero
columns. Based on the decomposition of the rows of $\Sigma$ into loops, where a
loop is the set of all cyclic permutations of a row, cycles are classified as
simple cycles, separable or inseparable composite cycles. Simple cycles contain
rows from one loop only, and the network topology is a feedforward chain with
feedback to one neuron if the loop-vectors in $\Sigma$ are cyclic permutations
of each other. Composite cycles contain rows from at least two disjoint loops,
and the neurons corresponding to the rows in $\Sigma$ from the same loop are
identified with a cluster. Networks constructed from separable composite cycles
decompose into completely isolated clusters. For inseparable composite cycles
at least two clusters are connected, and the cluster-connectivity is related to
the intersections of the spaces spanned by the loop-vectors of the clusters.
Simulations showing successfully retrieved cycles in continuous-time
Hopfield-type networks and in networks of spiking neurons are presented.

Major components of ices on interstellar grains in molecular clouds - water
and carbon oxides - occur at various optical depths. This implies that
selective desorption mechanisms are at work. An astrochemical model of a
contracting low-mass molecular cloud core is presented. Ice was treated as
consisting of the surface and three subsurface layers (sublayers).
Photodesorption, reactive desorption, and indirect reactive desorption were
investigated. The latter manifests itself through desorption from H+H reaction
on grains. Desorption of shallow subsurface species was included. Modeling
results suggest the existence of a "photon-dominated ice" during the early
phases of core contraction. Subsurface ice is chemically processed by
interstellar photons, which produces complex organic molecules. Desorption from
the subsurface layer results in high COM gas-phase abundances at Av =
2.4...10mag. This may contribute towards an explanation for COM observations in
dark cores. It was found that photodesorption mostly governs the onset of ice
accumulation onto grains. Reaction-specific reactive desorption is efficient
for small molecules that form via highly exothermic atom-addition reactions.
Higher reactive desorption efficiency results in lower gas-phase abundances of
COMs. Indirect reactive desorption allows to closely reproduce the observed
H2O:CO:CO2 ratio towards a number of background stars. Presumably this can be
done by any mechanism whose efficiency fits with the sequence CO > CO2 >> H2O.
After the freeze-out has ended, the three sublayers represent chemically
distinct parts of the mantle. 8...10.5mag is the likely AV threshold for the
appearance of CO ice. The lower value is supported by observations.

We estimate the accretion rates onto the supermassive black holes that power
20 of the highest-redshift quasars, at z>5.8, including the quasar with the
highest redshift known to date -- ULAS J1120 at z=7.09. The analysis is based
on the observed (rest-frame) optical luminosities and reliable "virial"
estimates of the BH masses of the quasars, and utilizes scaling relations
derived from thin accretion disk theory. The mass accretion rates through the
postulated disks cover a wide range, dM_disk/dt~4-190 Msol/yr, with most of the
objects (80\%) having dM_disk/dt~10-65 Msol/yr, confirming the
Eddington-limited nature of the accretion flows. By combining our estimates of
dM_disk/dt with conservative, lower limits on the bolometric luminosities of
the quasars, we investigate which alternative values of \eta best account for
all the available data. We find that the vast majority of quasars (~85\%) can
be explained with radiative efficiencies in the range \eta~0.03-0.3, with a
median value close to the commonly assumed \eta=0.1. Within this range, we
obtain conservative estimates of \eta>0.14 for ULAS J1120 and SDSS J0100 (at
z=6.3), and of >0.19 for SDSS J1148 (at z=6.41; assuming their BH masses are
accurate). The implied accretion timescales are generally in the range t_acc =
M_BH / dM_BH/dt ~0.1-1 Gyr, suggesting that most quasars could have had ~1-10
mass e-foldings since BH seed formation. Our analysis therefore demonstrates
that the available luminosities and masses for the highest-redshift quasars can
be explained self-consistently within the thin, radiatively efficient accretion
disk paradigm. Episodes of radiatively inefficient, "super-critical" accretion
may have occurred at significantly earlier epochs (i.e., z~10 or above).

This study investigates the pH-dependent electrical potential and elastic modulus of a nanoscale DNA film and its impact on the bending signal generated by a microcantilever biosensor. Initially, we fabricated a DNA film on a silicon substrate and characterized its mechanical properties using atomic force microscopy (AFM). Subsequently, we varied the pH levels to observe changes in the DNA film's electrical potential and elastic modulus. These parameters were measured at different pH values and correlated with the resulting bending signals detected from a cantilever attached to the DNA film. Our results indicate that as pH levels shift, the electrical potential and elastic modulus of the DNA film change, leading to variations in the bending response of the cantilever. Key methodologies involved AFM for surface characterization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for electrical potential measurements, and optical lever detection for cantilever deflection analysis. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how pH influences biosensing performance, offering insights for improving the sensitivity and specificity of DNA-based biosensors.

We present a detailed analysis of 317 $2.0 \leq z \leq 2.7$ star-forming
galaxies from the Keck Baryonic Structure Survey (KBSS). Using complementary
spectroscopic observations with Keck/LRIS and Keck/MOSFIRE, as well as spectral
energy distribution (SED) fits to broadband photometry, we examine the joint
rest-UV and rest-optical properties of the same galaxies, including stellar and
nebular dust attenuation, metallicity, and star formation rate (SFR). The
inferred parameters of the stellar population (reddening, age, SFR, and stellar
mass) are strongly dependent on the details of the assumed stellar population
model and the shape of the attenuation curve. Nebular reddening is generally
larger than continuum reddening, but with large scatter. Compared to local
galaxies, high-redshift galaxies have lower gas-phase metallicities (and/or
higher nebular excitation) at fixed nebular reddening, and higher nebular
reddening at fixed stellar mass, consistent with gas fractions that increase
with redshift. We find that continuum reddening is correlated with
$12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H})_{\mathrm{O3N2}}$ at $3.0\sigma$ significance,
whereas nebular reddening is correlated with only $1.1\sigma$ significance.
This may reflect the dependence of both continuum reddening and O3N2 on the
shape of the ionizing radiation field produced by the massive stars. Finally,
we show that H$\alpha$-based and SED-based estimates of SFR exhibit significant
scatter relative to one another, and agree on average only for particular
combinations of spectral synthesis models and attenuation curves. We find that
the SMC extinction curve predicts consistent SFRs if we assume the sub-solar
($0.14Z_{\odot}$) binary star models that are favored for high-redshift
galaxies.

There are 134,459 distinct initial hands at the video poker game Jacks or
Better, taking suit exchangeability into account. A computer program can
determine the optimal strategy (i.e., which cards to hold) for each such hand,
but a complete list of these strategies would require a book-length manuscript.
Instead, a hand-rank table, which fits on a single page and reproduces the
optimal strategy perfectly, was found for Jacks or Better as early as the mid
1990s. Is there a systematic way to derive such a hand-rank table? We show that
there is indeed, and it involves finding the exact optimal conditional expected
return, given the initial hand. In the case of Jacks or Better (paying 800, 50,
25, 9, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0), this is a random variable with 1,153 distinct values,
of which 766 correspond to garbage hands for which it is optimal to draw five
new cards. We describe the hands corresponding to each of the remaining 387
values of the optimal conditional expected return (sorted from largest to
smallest) and show how this leads readily to an optimal strategy hand-rank
table for Jacks or Better. Of course, the method applies to other video poker
games as well.

The study of superintegrability in N-dimensional curved spaces has gained considerable attention in recent years due to its potential applications in various fields of physics, including quantum mechanics and string theory. Superintegrability refers to the existence of additional first integrals of motion in classical systems beyond the energy and angular momentum. In this work, we explore the concept of superintegrability in N-dimensional curved spaces by focusing on central potentials, centrifugal terms, and monopoles.  We begin with a review of the background and fundamental concepts of superintegrability in flat spaces and extend this understanding to N-dimensional curved spaces. Central potentials, which admit quadratic Hamiltonians, are analyzed using the quadratic superintegrable systems' technique. We then study the addition of centrifugal terms to these systems and demonstrate how they lead to new superintegrable potentials with specific forms.  Next, we delve into the connection between superintegrability and monopoles in curved spaces. We reveal that superintegrable systems on N-dimensional curved spaces can be obtained by lifting flat space superintegrable systems to the corresponding manifolds, and the monopole charges can be identified as new constants of motion. Furthermore, we illustrate the construction of new superintegrable systems by introducing specific forms of monopole potentials.  Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between superintegrability and monopoles in N-dimensional curved spaces and reveal potential applications in various areas of theoretical physics. The obtained results could be of significance for exploring and developing new models in quantum mechanics, string theory, and gravitational physics.

Observations of spiral galaxies show a strong linear correlation between the
ratio of molecular to atomic hydrogen surface density R_mol and midplane
pressure. To explain this, we simulate three-dimensional, magnetized
turbulence, including simplified treatments of non-equilibrium chemistry and
the propagation of dissociating radiation, to follow the formation of H_2 from
cold atomic gas. The formation time scale for H_2 is sufficiently long that
equilibrium is not reached within the 20-30 Myr lifetimes of molecular clouds.
The equilibrium balance between radiative dissociation and H_2 formation on
dust grains fails to predict the time-dependent molecular fractions we find. A
simple, time-dependent model of H_2 formation can reproduce the gross behavior,
although turbulent density perturbations increase molecular fractions by a
factor of few above it. In contradiction to equilibrium models, radiative
dissociation of molecules plays little role in our model for diffuse radiation
fields with strengths less than ten times that of the solar neighborhood,
because of the effective self-shielding of H_2. The observed correlation of
R_mol with pressure corresponds to a correlation with local gas density if the
effective temperature in the cold neutral medium of galactic disks is roughly
constant. We indeed find such a correlation of R_mol with density. If we
examine the value of R_mol in our local models after a free-fall time at their
average density, as expected for models of molecular cloud formation by
large-scale gravitational instability, our models reproduce the observed
correlation over more than an order of magnitude range in density.

The research paper investigates the approximate sum-capacity of K-user cognitive interference channels with cumulative message sharing. The study aims to determine the maximum rate at which information can be reliably transmitted over the channels when multiple users are involved. The methodology involves analyzing the channel's capacity under the cognitive radio paradigm, where secondary users opportunistically access the spectrum in the presence of primary users. By incorporating cumulative message sharing among users, the paper explores improved communication strategies to enhance overall system performance. Key findings indicate that leveraging cumulative message sharing can significantly boost the sum-capacity of the system compared to traditional approaches. Through analytical derivations and simulations, the research demonstrates the benefits of collaborative communication schemes in multi-user interference channels with cognitive radio capabilities. In conclusion, the study underscores the effectiveness of cumulative message sharing in enhancing the sum-capacity of K-user cognitive interference channels, offering valuable insights for the design of efficient communication systems with improved spectral efficiency and throughput.

This research paper introduces 6thSense, a novel context-aware sensor-based attack detector specifically designed to safeguard smart devices against a wide range of cyber threats. The increasing dependence on smart devices has led to a significant rise in cyber attacks, making it imperative to develop effective detection mechanisms. However, existing solutions often rely on static signature-based approaches, which are limited in their ability to detect novel and evolving threats.  The objective of this research is to develop a context-aware sensor-based attack detector that can effectively identify and mitigate cyber threats in smart devices. The proposed 6thSense system integrates machine learning, sensor fusion, and network analysis to create a comprehensive threat detection framework. By leveraging real-time sensor data, network traffic patterns, and device metadata, 6thSense can detect anomalies and predict potential attacks, enabling proactive defense measures.  The proposed system was evaluated using a combination of simulation-based testing and real-world experimentation, involving 1000 smart devices with various operating systems and applications. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of 6thSense in detecting a wide range of cyber threats, including malware, DoS attacks, and phishing attempts. Furthermore, the system's ability to adapt to changing network conditions and device configurations was shown to be robust and reliable. The findings of this research contribute to the development of more effective smart device security solutions, and the proposed 6thSense system is expected to play a crucial role in mitigating the growing threat landscape of smart devices.

Our work focuses on developing the R2-D2, a novel ColoR-inspired Convolutional NeuRal Network (CNN)-based AndroiD malware detection system. We address the crucial problem of efficiently detecting Android malware using deep learning techniques, specifically inspired by the unique design of the popular character R2-D2 from Star Wars. The key idea behind our approach is to leverage color features from Android application icons to enhance the malware detection capabilities of CNNs.   Through extensive experimentation on a diverse dataset of Android malware samples, we achieved promising results in terms of detection accuracy and efficiency. By combining traditional CNN features with color inspiration from R2-D2, our system demonstrated superior performance in distinguishing between benign and malicious Android applications compared to existing methods.   Our methodology involved preprocessing Android application icons to extract meaningful color features and training the CNN model on these representations. The trained model was then evaluated on a test set to assess its detection performance. The results indicate that our proposed R2-D2 system holds significant potential for enhancing Android malware detection capabilities, providing a valuable contribution to the field of cybersecurity.

In this study, we employed a data set of photospheric magnetic features extracted from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) onboard Solar Dynamics Observatory to examine the solar differential rotation and meridional circulation. By performing cross-correlation analyses on pairs of magnetically conjugated features, we quantified the radial and latitudinal displacements of solar magnetic elements, thereby measuring the solar differential rotation rates in various latitude bands. Our results revealed that the solar differential rotation is strongest near the equator and gradually decays towards the polar regions, with an average value of 15.07°/day at the equator and 7.44°/day at the pole. We further analyzed the meridional circulation by calculating the mean zonal and meridional flows in different latitude zones. Our findings indicated a net equatorward flow in the torsional mode region and a net poleward flow in the vicinity of the solar activity belt. These results provide important insights into the dynamics of solar interior and contribute to the understanding of the solar magnetic cycle. By utilizing the HMI data, we were able to make unprecedented measurements of solar differential rotation and meridional circulation based on the behavior of magnetic features in the solar photosphere. The technique employed in this study can be further applied to investigate the dynamics of other astrophysical objects with complex magnetized structures.

Aims: The interactions of velocity scales on the Sun's surface, from
granulation to supergranulation are still not understood, nor are their
interaction with magnetic fields. We thus aim at giving a better description of
dynamics in the mesoscale range which lies between the two scales mentioned
above. Method: We analyse a 48h high-resolution time sequence of the quiet Sun
photosphere at the disk center obtained with the Solar Optical Telescope
onboard Hinode. The observations, which have a field of view of 100
\arcsec$\times$ 100 \arcsec, typically contain four supergranules. We monitor
in detail the motion and evolution of granules as well as those of the radial
magnetic field. Results: This analysis allows us to better characterize Trees
of Fragmenting Granules issued from repeated fragmentation of granules,
especially their lifetime statistics. Using floating corks advected by measured
velocity fields, we show their crucial role in the advection of the magnetic
field and in the build up of the network. Finally, thanks to the long duration
of the time series, we estimate that the turbulent diffusion coefficient
induced by horizontal motion is approximately $430 \mathrm{km}^2
\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that the long living
families contribute to the formation of the magnetic network and suggest that
supergranulation could be an emergent length scale building up as small
magnetic elements are advected and concentrated by TFG flows. Our estimate for
the magnetic diffusion associated with this horizontal motion might provide a
useful input for mean-field dynamo models.

The carbon monolayer band structure calculated in the approximation of weakly
interacting {\pi} electrons corresponds to massless electron excitations known
as Dirac fermions not previously observed in any other material. However, if
strong Coulomb and exchange interactions between {\pi} electrons are taken into
account, another picture of the {\pi} electron state emerges. These
interactions result in {\pi} electron localization and electron crystal
formation. The atomically flat layer can be regarded as a simplest
quasi-two-dimensional mesoscopic quantum system consisting of a carbon ion
plane and two {\pi} electron crystals on opposite sides of the plane. Such a
system must have dielectric and pronounced diamagnetic properties and a high
sensitivity to external factors distorting its electron crystals. The
instability manifests itself in a tendency of the monolayer to be transformed
into a more stable carbon modification with a rolled-up or wrapped-up carbon
skeleton which is observed as a monolayer corrugation (or ripples). The
corrugated monolayer is characterized by the presence of excited {\pi}
electrons which are responsible for its physical and chemical properties. The
approach can prove useful for investigation of carbon nanotubes, fullerenes,
graphite, and also topological insulators and complicated quantum systems with
a layered structure. Calculations of the quasi-two-dimensional quantum system
faces a many-body problem and are beyond the band-structure description, which
forces us to confine ourselves to purely qualitative analysis

We present Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array observations of the CO J=1-0
transition in a sample of four $z\sim2$ main sequence galaxies. These galaxies
are in the blue sequence of star-forming galaxies at their redshift, and are
part of the IRAM Plateau de Bure HIgh-$z$ Blue Sequence Survey (PHIBSS) which
imaged them in CO J=3-2. Two galaxies are imaged here at high signal-to-noise,
allowing determinations of their disk sizes, line profiles, molecular surface
densities, and excitation. Using these and published measurements, we show that
the CO and optical disks have similar sizes in main-sequence galaxies, and in
the galaxy where we can compare CO J=1-0 and J=3-2 sizes we find these are also
very similar. Assuming a Galactic CO-to-H$_2$ conversion, we measure surface
densities of $\Sigma_{mol}\sim1200$ M$_\odot$pc$^{-2}$ in projection and
estimate $\Sigma_{mol}\sim500-900$ M$_\odot$pc$^{-2}$ deprojected. Finally, our
data yields velocity-integrated Rayleigh-Jeans brightness temperature line
ratios $r_{31}$ that are approximately unity. In addition to the similar disk
sizes, the very similar line profiles in J=1-0 and J=3-2 indicate that both
transitions sample the same kinematics, implying that their emission is
coextensive. We conclude that in these two main sequence galaxies there is no
evidence for significant excitation gradients or a large molecular reservoir
that is diffuse or cold and not involved in active star-formation. We suggest
that $r_{31}$ in very actively star-forming galaxies is likely an indicator of
how well mixed the star formation activity and the molecular reservoir are.

We study the near-threshold pion-induced production of $\phi$ mesons off
nuclei in the kinematical conditions of the HADES experiment, recently
performed at GSI. The calculations have been performed within a collision model
based on the nuclear spectral function. The model accounts for both the primary
$\pi^-$ meson--proton ${\pi^-}p \to {\phi}n$ and the secondary pion--nucleon
${\pi}N \to {\phi}N$ $\phi$ production processes as well as the effects of the
nuclear $\phi$ and nucleon mean-field potentials. We find that the primary
reaction channel ${\pi^-}p \to {\phi}n$ dominates in the $\phi$ production off
$^{12}$C and $^{184}$W target nuclei in the HADES acceptance window at incident
pion momentum of 1.7 GeV/c. We calculate the momentum dependence of the
absolute and relative (transparency ratio) $\phi$ meson yields from the above
direct channel. The calculations have been performed for this initial pion
momentum allowing for different options for the ${\phi}N$ absorption cross
section $\sigma_{{\phi}N}$ and different scenarios for the in-medium mass
shifts of the $\phi$ meson and secondary neutron, produced together with $\phi$
in this channel. We demonstrate that the transparency ratio for the $\phi$
mesons has, contrary to the absolute cross sections, an insignificant
sensitivity to the $\phi$ meson and secondary neutron in-medium mass shifts at
$\phi$ momenta studied in the HADES experiment. On the other hand, we show that
there are measurable changes in the transparency ratio due to the ${\phi}N$
absorption cross section, which means that such relative observable can be
useful to help determine this cross section from the data taken in the HADES
experiment.

We investigated the efficacy of cutting-and-shuffling as a novel approach to optimized mixing in various applications, including chemical reactions, food preparation, and pharmaceutical manufacturing. Our research aimed to develop a systematic framework for optimizing mixing processes through the strategic manipulation of cutting and shuffling operations.  Through a series of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that the cutting-and-shuffling technique can significantly improve mixing efficiency, uniformity, and product quality. By analyzing the effects of different cutting and shuffling patterns, we identified optimal configurations that yield enhanced mixing performance. These findings were validated through experiments involving a range of mixable fluids and solids, including Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, powders, and granular materials.  Our results show that the cutting-and-shuffling technique can outperform traditional mixing methods, such as stirring and blending, in terms of mixing time, energy efficiency, and product consistency. We also explored the potential applications of cutting-and-shuffling in various industries, including biotechnology, food processing, and pharmaceutical manufacturing. By optimizing mixing processes through cutting-and-shuffling, we can reduce production costs, improve product quality, and enhance overall process efficiency. Our research provides a foundation for the development of novel mixing technologies that can address the complex challenges faced in various industrial applications.

A distinct set of broad emission features at 3.3, 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.3, and
12.7 $\mu$m, is often detected in protoplanetary disks (PPDs). These features
are commonly attributed to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We model
these emission features in the infrared spectra of 69 PPDs around 14 T Tauri
and 55 Herbig Ae/Be stars in terms of astronomical-PAHs. For each PPD, we
derive the size distribution and the charge state of PAHs. We then examine the
correlations of the PAH properties (i.e., sizes and ionization fractions) with
the stellar properties (e.g., stellar effective temperature, luminosity, and
