mass). We find that the characteristic size of PAHs shows a tendency of
correlating with the stellar effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) and
interpret this as the preferential photodissociation of small PAHs in systems
with higher $T_{\rm eff}$ of which the stellar photons are more energetic. In
addition, the PAH size shows a moderate correlation with the red-ward
wavelength-shift of the 7.7 $\mu$m PAH feature that is commonly observed in
disks around cool stars. The ionization fraction of PAHs does not seem to
correlate with any stellar parameters. This is because the charging of PAHs
depends on not only the stellar properties (e.g., $T_{\rm eff}$, luminosity)
but also the spatial distribution of PAHs in the disks. The mere negative
correlation between the PAH size and the stellar age suggests that continuous
replenishment of PAHs via the outgassing of cometary bodies and/or the
collisional grinding of planetesimals and asteroids is required to maintain the
abundance of small PAHs against complete destruction by photodissociation.

In this study, we conduct a comprehensive comparison of various exoplanet mass detection techniques applied to a carefully selected sample of main-sequence intermediate-type stars. Our objective is to determine the most effective methodologies for mass detection limits in stellar environments characterized by these spectral types. We examine radial velocity, transit timing variations, and astrometric methods, evaluating their sensitivity, accuracy, and applicability to intermediate-type stars. By utilizing observational data from contemporary astronomical surveys, we calibrate our methodologies against known exoplanetary systems, ensuring methodical consistency and validation. We observe that while radial velocity methods offer precise mass estimations, their efficacy is often challenged by intrinsic stellar pulsations and rotation effects prevalent in intermediate-type stars. On the other hand, transit timing variations provide substantial sensitivity to potential exoplanets with longer periods but are limited by inclination constraints. Astrometric measurements, although generally underutilized, showcase promising mass detection potential through high-precision instrumentation advances. Our results indicate that a hybrid approach, employing astrometry for initial mass detection followed by radial velocity confirmation, consistently enhances detection limits. Furthermore, we provide evidence suggesting that the integration of these methods, tailored to individual stellar characteristics, significantly improves the sensitivity and reliability of exoplanet mass detection. This work highlights the necessity for adaptive methodologies in exoplanet discovery around intermediate-type stars and sets a foundation for future explorations enhancing both theoretical understanding and observational strategies in the field of exoplanetary science.

We present an analysis of 8 years of Fermi-LAT ( > 0.1 GeV) gamma-ray data
obtained for the radio galaxy NGC 1275. The gamma-ray flux from NGC 1275 is
highly variable on short (~ days to weeks) timescales, and has steadily
increased over this 8-year timespan. By examining the changes in its flux and
spectral shape in the LAT energy band over the entire dataset, we found that
its spectral behavior changed around 2011 February (~ MJD 55600). The gamma-ray
spectra at the early times evolve largely at high energies, while the photon
indices were unchanged in the latter times despite rather large flux
variations. To explain these observations, we suggest that the flux changes in
the early times were caused by injection of high-energy electrons into the jet,
while later, the gamma-ray flares were caused by a changing Doppler factor
owing to variations in the jet Lorentz factor and/or changes in the angle to
our line of sight. To demonstrate the viability of these scenarios, we fit the
broad-band spectral energy distribution data with a one-zone synchrotron
self-Compton (SSC) model for flaring and quiescent intervals before and after
2011 February. To explain the gamma-ray spectral behavior in the context of the
SSC model, the maximum electron Lorentz factor would have changed in the early
times, while a modest change in the Doppler factor adequately fits the
quiescent and flaring state gamma-ray spectra in the later times.

In the realm of stellar astrophysics, understanding the intricacies of thermonuclear bursts (TNs) in cataclysmic variables (CVs) is of paramount importance due to their crucial role in shaping the structure and evolution of these systems. In this study, we examine a comprehensive dataset of TN observations from various telescopes and present a comparative analysis of selected thermal evolution models. Our objective is to identify the best-fit model based on the available observational data. We employ a statistical approach to evaluate the goodness of fit for each model and quantify the uncertainties.  Our analysis includes observations of 23 TNs spanning a range of optical magnitudes and durations. We apply four state-of-the-art thermal evolution models, considering their physical assumptions, complexity, and compatibility with existing literature. The models under scrutiny are the Baldwin-Wickman model, the Mapplefield-Thompson model, the Schwarzschild-Schmidt model, and the Xiong-Dheng model. We present a detailed comparison of the key findings derived from these models and critically discuss their implications.  Our results reveal that the Xiong-Dheng model provides the best overall fit to our dataset, given its superior ability to capture the peak and decay characteristics of the TNs. The Baldwin-Wickman model and the Schwarzschild-Schmidt model, despite their historical significance, have notable shortcomings in reproducing the observed data. The Mapplefield-Thompson model offers a reasonable fit, but it lacks the complexity required to precisely model the intricate features of the TNs. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the latest theoretical advancements when modeling TNs in CVs.  Future work involves applying these models to a larger and more diverse dataset, as well as incorporating additional observables, such as UV and X-ray data, to improve the model accuracy and robustness.
